13306-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, volume fifty-five, number 339, January 1844, mixes politics, fiction, and criticism for a Tory readership. Contents run from state prosecutions and adventures in Texas to Clitophon and Leucippe. They add the new art of printing by a designing devil, the banking-house, Kieff from the Russian of Kozloff, and Marston, memoirs of a statesman. The number is a substantial monthly.

A review of a Greek romance notes its characters come from Grecian citizens in polished social life. Amid villa gardens, banquets, processions, and courts of law, with no talismanic rings or secret fortunes, interest turns on an elopement. Later, a dialogue has Mrs. Allcraft ask pardon for a great sinner, and Mr. Middleton answer that heaven regards not what we have been but what we are. The issue is a window on 1844 letters.
13633-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
The April 1844 number of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine mixes fiction, history, and politics in the style of a leading Tory monthly. The second part of The Pirates of Segna, a tale of Venice and the Adriatic, runs beside a study of the slave trade. A history of Muslim Spain under the Arabs of Cordova and a traveller's fragment from southern Mexico also appear.

A serial memoir of a statesman continues. A piece on the British fleet follows a chase in which a captain calmly counts enemy sail, from eight to twenty-seven ships of the line. The number shows Blackwood's range: adventure and scholarship side by side, aimed at readers who wanted both entertainment and argument. It is a good snapshot of Victorian magazine culture.
13719-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for July 1844 opens its second half-year volume. Contents include an essay on the causes of crime, a tour of Sicily, and poems and ballads of Goethe. A sketch of first love in New York and an ode on Martin Luther add variety. A serial, Portugal Marston, continues its memoirs of a statesman.

Blackwood's mixed politics, literature, and travel for a Tory readership. Short tales from Upper Lusatia and a piece on the week of an emperor round out the number. The magazine's sharp, confident voice comes through in reviews and essays. This issue captures Scottish periodical culture at mid-century. It rewards readers who enjoy Victorian magazines in full.
14778-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for March 1844 opens with Ethiopia, a review of Major Cornwallis Harris's Highlands of Ethiopia, and moves through a wide contents list. Lorgnon writes on operative classes, pirates of Segna tell a tale of Venice and the Adriatic, and Colonel Davidson travels in India.

Belfront Castle offers a retrospective review, Dumas rides in his curricle, Marston's memoirs of a statesman reach part nine, and an Olympic Jupiter and a Roman idyll supply classical colour. Goethe, a hermit's hymn, a luckless lover and a debate on free trade and the Corn Laws close the number. It is a rich sample of a Victorian monthly at full range.
15634-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for August 1844, number 346 of volume 56, came from William Blackwood and Sons in Edinburgh and London. The number opens with a long piece on Afghanistan. Etched thoughts by the Etching Club follow, with a love chase in prose. A study of the ancient canal between the Nile and the Red Sea completes the opening set. Scottish, literary, and foreign matter share the issue.

Later contents include an old Scottish cavalier, tales of Upper Lusatia, and remarks on Schiller's Maid of Orleans. A stolen child, a piece on M. Girardin, and a piece on Lord Eldon complete the table. The lead article recalls Kabul, Tezeen, and the loss of seventeen thousand lives with bitter anger. The number shows Blackwood's at mid-century: Tory, literary, and willing to argue over empire as well as art.
15970-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's weekly paper for boys and girls, number forty-four, dated September 9, 1897. Five cents bought news, science, and stories in words young readers could follow. One new subscription earned a bound volume of The Great Round World itself, neatly bound and sent post-paid. The paper rewarded loyalty with its own back numbers.

This number turns to the week's events abroad and at home, with nature notes and serial tales beside. Editors explain treaties and inventions in short, clear paragraphs. Picture items keep young eyes moving. Seen now, the issue captures early autumn 1897 for American children: a paper growing up with its readers, volume by volume.
19383-the-knickerbocker-or-new-york-mont:
This volume of the Knickerbocker, New York's monthly magazine, gathers its issues from the early months of eighteen forty-four. Poems, tales, travel notes, and essays sit beside letters to the editor. They include an ascent of Mount Etna by the painter Thomas Cole and a night on the prairie by a buffalo hunter.

The mix shows a young nation's magazine at work: humor, moral talk, and reports from far places, all aimed at a general reader. For students of American print culture, the volume is a rich sample of what city readers read, argued over, and laughed at.
19542-the-knickerbocker-or-new-york-mont:
This February number of the Knickerbocker, New York's monthly magazine, opens with Thomas Cole on Sicilian scenery and antiquities. The painter recalls a land of fertile fields and grand ruins, and notes that travel's pleasure comes best after the journey, told by one's own fireside.

Other pieces turn to home life: a small family at its board, a bride and groom in a cottage door at dusk, and the quiet content of simple fare. The number shows the magazine's range, from Old World art to New World domestic scenes. A sea sketch draws a long-bodied shipmate on very small legs, forever in hot water with passengers and crew.
23529-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number three hundred forty four for June eighteen forty four, gathers tales, poems, and essays in the strong Tory voice that made the journal famed. Traditions and tales of Upper Lusatia lead, with a fairies' sabbath opening a set of folk stories from a border land.

Poems on Columbus and on swallows at departure, a diligence leaf from a journal, and a debate over who wrote Gil Blas follow. A tale of Michael Kalliphournas and a piece on Africa, the slave trade, and tropical colonies also follow. A narration by Herbert Willis and a portrait of Beau Brummell close the contents shown. Readers of Victorian magazines will enjoy the mix of fancy, fact, and opinion, all in Blackwood's confident, combative style.
25047-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for May 1844, volume fifty five, number 343, opens with Imprisonment and Transportation on the increase of crime. Rhine and Rhinelanders, the Monster Misery of Literature, Marston's memoirs, Indian affairs at Gwalior, the Freethinker, Delta's Snow, Love in the Wilderness, and Ireland's landlord and tenant question follow. The crime essay calls the constant increase of crime extraordinary and alarming, and blames Liberals for shutting their eyes to the sad illustration of their favourite theories.

The selfish majority care nothing for neighbours murdered or robbed so long as they escape unscathed. Yet they roar if the smallest percentage is proposed to arrest the evils that industry brings. Indian affairs turn to the Indus, where a broad belt of impenetrable jungle impedes navigation and shelters ambush, and where the Ameers cling to their game preserves with desperate pertinacity. The number is periodical writing at its most opinionated.
30421-the-age-of-pope-1700-1744:
John Dennis writes The Age of Pope, 1700 to 1744, in the Handbooks of English Literature edited by Professor Hales, published in London by G. Bell and Sons in 1921, in an eleventh edition, first published in 1894 and reprinted in 1896, 1899, 1901, 1906, 1908, 1909, 1913, 1917, 1918, and 1921. Dennis, author of Studies in English Literature, gives the Pope age its place among companion volumes on Alfred, Chaucer, Milton, Dryden, Johnson, Wordsworth, and Tennyson.

The series lists the age of Alfred from 664 to 1154 and the age of Chaucer from 1346 to 1400, both by F. J. Snell, the age of Milton from 1632 to 1660 by J. H. B. Masterman, with an introduction by J. Bass Mullinger, and the age of Dryden from 1660 to 1700 by R. Garnett, in eighth editions. The age of Johnson from 1748 to 1798 by Thomas Seccombe stands in a seventh edition, revised. The age of Tennyson from 1830 to 1870 by Hugh Walker stands in a ninth edition.
adeptus-ineptus-oder-entdeckung-der-fals:
Adeptus Ineptus, printed in 1744 by Georg Wilhelm Wegener, announces itself in its German subtitle as the discovery, or exposure, of the falsely celebrated art called alchemy. Its title figure is the inept adept, the would-be master whose art cannot do what it promises. At nearly five hundred pages, the book is no squib but a full-scale unmasking.

Wegener writes from the skeptical side of the Enlightenment, when alchemy's credit was collapsing among the learned. The exposure sets out the art's claims and shows where they fail, for readers who wanted the case against the adepts made at length. It preserves the prosecution's brief in the long trial of alchemy, from the decade when chemistry was winning.
an-epitome-of-phrenology-1844: An Epitome of Phrenology, dated 1844 and credited to E H Sanford, distills phrenology to its essentials in thirty-six small pages. An epitome is a condensation, and this cover-titled pamphlet reduces the science of head reading to the part a beginner must carry: the faculties, their organs, and how they are judged. It guided newcomers who wanted the system without a large treatise, in the years when phrenology was a popular American movement.
artemidorus-oneirocritica-english-1644:
Artemidorus of Daldis wrote the Oneirocritica, antiquity's only complete surviving dream book. Robert Wood's English translation appeared in London in 1644, the first in the language. Artemidorus had traveled widely collecting dreams and their outcomes.

Across five books he catalogues what dream images signify for dreamers. Flying, losing teeth, snakes, and weddings all receive careful readings. He insists each dream be read against the dreamer's own station and life. Professional interpreters used manuals like his across the Roman world. The 1644 translation preserves early modern English in its rendering. Long before Freud, dream interpretation had this systematic ancient handbook.
arxiv-2412-00144:
Maruzzelli, Lewandowski, and Chen propose a way to shrink diffusion models in twenty twenty-four. Diffusion models make high quality images by a slow denoising process. Quantization, which stores numbers with fewer bits, can speed them up. Using one fixed bit width for all layers wastes room, the authors argue.

Layers differ in how much they depend on each other at each sampling step. The new scheme gives each layer its own bit width for weights and activations. A measure of network orthogonality stands in for layer importance. A uniform sampling trick keeps the cost of measuring it low. On two image data sets, image quality scores improved a lot over fixed precision methods. The work points to faster image generation with less loss.
arxiv-2412-00244:
Gordon Lim, Stefan Larson, and Kevin Leach wrote this machine learning paper, published in two thousand twenty-four, on testing models that must learn from mislabeled data. Real label errors come from people, and they cluster in ways that random synthetic flips do not capture.

The team first studied how models memorize a real noisy data set's quirks. From those insights they built Cluster-Based Noise, a generator that flips labels in feature-dependent patterns that mimic human slips. Standard noise-robust methods score worse under this harsher, more honest test. The authors then propose Soft Neighbor Label Sampling, which borrows labels softly from nearby examples. It beat existing methods on the cluster-based noise. The paper argues that the field's yardstick, not just its methods, needs to grow up.
arxiv-2412-00444:
Dhananjay Singh and Arvind Kumar compute how hot, dense quark matter flows and conducts in a 2024 paper. This matter, made of quarks and gluons in strong interaction, is created briefly in heavy-ion collisions. Its transport traits, such as how sticky it is and how well it carries heat and charge, shape what experiments see.

Their model blends a chiral quark picture with a Polyakov loop that tracks confinement. Into it they feed a generalized statistics that allows a nonextensive setting, tuned by a single parameter. They work out shear and bulk stickiness, electrical and thermal conduction, plus the speed of sound and heat capacity, all as functions of temperature. The nonextensive setting shifted every one of these traits in a clear way against the standard case. The study shows how sensitive flow measures are to the assumed statistics.
arxiv-2412-01044:
Jenifer, Ghosh, and Muruganandam study how groups sync up, in a 2024 preprint, when their links can both help and hinder and involve more than pairs. Real systems like brains and crowds interact in groups, not just pairs. Their links also adapt, sometimes cooperatively and sometimes competitively. Most models miss one or both traits. This model includes both, on structures called simplicial complexes that encode group ties. The authors ask how the mix changes the road to synchrony.

Under competitive adaptation, stronger group coupling softens the sync jump from abrupt to gradual. Sync can even arise with no pairwise links, if group coupling is strong enough. Pure competition gives clustered, gradual transitions. Mixing both adaptation types restores a sharp jump, with no fallback on the way back. The authors show the transition style can be tuned by coupling choices. That control matters where sudden sync is dangerous or desired.
arxiv-2412-01944:
Gatti and six colleagues compare neural networks for mapping crops from satellite images in twenty twenty-four. Crop maps from image time series support farm monitoring and land use planning. Convolutional networks are the usual tool for this task. Transformer models offer another way to capture patterns over space and time.

Six models were tested on Munich and Lombardia data sets. Three were convolutional and three were transformers. A transformer called TSViT gave the best overall results. It slightly beat the strongest convolutional baseline. Another transformer, VistaFormer, was the most efficient. Models that treated time as just another spatial axis did worse. The authors conclude explicit time modelling is critical for satellite series.
arxiv-2412-02644:
Gabriele Giudici and co-authors show that a robot arm can be steered by touch alone, without cameras. Remote manipulation usually leans on video, which fails when views are blocked or smoke and darkness ruin the image. Their system reads tactile sensors on the gripper, rebuilds the touched object as a 3D model inside a virtual reality scene, and feeds touch sensations back to the operator's hand. A blindfolded user completed precise pick-and-place tasks this way.

The authors present the result as a feasibility proof, not a finished product. Still, tasks that once depended on cameras were done by feel. That opens settings where cameras struggle, such as disaster sites or underwater work. The study also matters for training robot agents, where touch-based demonstrations could teach skills that vision alone cannot capture. Future work can add complexity beyond simple pick-and-place.
arxiv-2412-03144:
Stephane Vennes and Adela Kawka revisit a close pair of white dwarfs, the dense remnants of dead stars, and measure the pair's total mass. Their paper came out in 2024. One star is rich in hydrogen and the other is polluted with carbon, a rare combination that records the pair's shared past.

New high-resolution spectra confirm the orbital period and constrain the mass ratio. The carbon-polluted star turns out to be up to about six percent more massive than its companion. Using a precise distance from the Gaia mission, their atmosphere models give lower masses and temperatures than earlier estimates for both stars. The carbon star's atmosphere holds more carbon and nitrogen than previously thought. The two stars appear to be nearly the same age, consistent with formation in a single shared-envelope event.
arxiv-2412-03244:
Clustering logarithms are the subject of this physics paper by K. Khelifa-Kerfa, published in 2024. It computes a family of correction terms that appear when physicists group the spray of particles from high-energy collisions into jets.

These terms arise for certain delicate measurements that are sensitive to particles outside the jets. They follow a neat pattern that lets them be summed into a compact exponential form. Working from a recent formula for how one common jet algorithm clusters particles, the author pushed the calculation to six loops, far beyond a rough estimate. The paper then compares the summed result with full numerical calculations done by others. Such checks sharpen the predictions that collider experiments rely on when they test the theory of the strong force.
arxiv-2412-03944:
Hao Yang, Qinghua Zhao, and Lei Li looked inside chain-of-thought prompting in 2024, the technique where a language model reasons step by step before answering. It plainly works, and many studies tune its surface features, but its internal mechanics were murky. The authors probe three stages of the process: how tokens are decoded, how internal representations are projected, and which neurons activate, comparing chain-of-thought against plain prompting throughout.

Three findings stand out. The model imitates the format of the examples it was shown while genuinely integrating the question's content, rather than merely copying. During generation its token scores fluctuate more, yet the final distribution over next tokens ends up more concentrated, as if the reasoning commits it. And in the last layers, chain-of-thought switches on a broader set of neurons than standard prompts, consistent with wider knowledge being retrieved for the answer.
arxiv-2412-04144:
Muhammad Khalifa and eight co-authors show that discarded checkpoints from big model training can be merged into a model better than any single one. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Frontier training runs leave behind many near-miss models. Each trades skill in one area against another, like chat versus code.

The team gathers such checkpoints from varied runs and merges them with tuned weights. Their optimizer searches the blend for a model on the best tradeoff frontier. The result beat both the single checkpoints and standard merging baselines. Good blends drew on nearly every checkpoint, even the weak-looking ones. That finding recasts leftovers as assets rather than waste. The work matters as training costs soar and checkpoint pools grow. It suggests labs should keep, not trash, their suboptimal runs.
arxiv-2412-05844:
Deepak Patel and Praveen Srivastava calculate the rate of a rare double electron capture process in krypton-78 using large-scale shell-model computations. The process, two-neutrino double electron capture, probes nuclear structure and weak interactions. They use the GWBXG effective interaction for the calculations.

First they validate the interaction by reproducing measured energy spectra, moments of inertia, and transition probabilities for the parent and grand-daughter nuclei. They then analyze how the nuclear matrix element accumulates over intermediate states in bromine-78. The estimated half-life agrees well with the experimental value. Gamow-Teller transitions through the lowest intermediate state are discussed for both capture and decay channels.
arxiv-2412-07544:
Amin Abyaneh, Mahrokh Boroujeni, Hsiu-Chin Lin, and Giancarlo Ferrari-Trecate wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2024. It builds imitation learning policies, which copy an expert's behavior, in the form of contractive dynamical systems, so the copy recovers gracefully when it strays into situations the expert never showed.

Imitation policies often fail outside their training data. Systems guaranteed stable will at least return to the target, but may wander oddly on the way. Contractive systems pull all paths together, so any start converges and surprises wash out. The authors build such policies from special network blocks that keep the guarantee for any settings, leaving training unconstrained. They bound the worst and average copying loss. In robot arm and navigation tests, the policies handled out-of-sample starts far better than standard imitation.
arxiv-2412-07644:
Alan Chávez, Jolbyn Castañeda, Alexis Carranza, and Kamal Khalil characterize compact almost automorphic functions in many dimensions. Their paper from twenty twenty-four studies functions that near-repeat under shifts, valued in a Banach space. A finer family, tied to a chosen subset of shift vectors, frames the study. Two fresh descriptions of the compact class come out of that frame.

One description uses the integer lattice as the shift set. The other uses a dense subset of the space. The team also shows the function space stays closed under integral operators with near-automorphic kernels. Uses land on two classic equations: Poisson's and the heat equation. Their near-automorphic dynamics are traced through the new tools. The work serves analysts of almost periodic motion in higher dimensions.
arxiv-2412-08844:
Parthapratim Pradhan and John Moffat present a study from twenty twenty-four on what a spinning black hole in a changed gravity theory turns into as its mass drops to zero. Past work split on the plain case: some found flat space, others a wormhole. Their case adds a modified gravity twist to the Kerr form.

They show the zero mass limit gives a wormhole with a flat local shape. They also recast the hole in a Kerr-Schild form by shifts of the axes. The wormhole is then read in round coordinates with two patches. A charged cousin case is checked too. Its limit is not a wormhole unless both mass and charge are set to zero.
arxiv-2412-09144:
Mpoki Mwaisela and five colleagues wrote a 2024 report on speeding up a privacy tool called homomorphic encryption. This tool lets cloud computers work on locked data without ever unlocking it. The catch is that the math is slow and uses a lot of memory.

Most past fixes used graphics chips or custom boards to cut compute time. Far less work tackled the memory load. The team tested processing in memory, where data is worked on where it sits, to move less of it around. They share hands-on results on how well this path works in practice. Their findings may help make private cloud computing fast enough for daily use.
arxiv-2412-09344:
Kirtiman Ghosh, Katri Huitu, and Rameswar Sahu take a fresh look at a model where all known fields live in one small extra dim, while gravity roams in more, large ones. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

In this fat-brane form, the copies of known particles can decay through gravity. That gives rare end states: hard photons, jets, heavy bosons, and large lost energy from unseen gravity copies. The team reworks past collider searches to bound the model's space. They find that searches built for a kin theory may miss these marks. They give new search plans that use learning tools to tag boosted bosons and lift the signal.
arxiv-2412-13244:
Maximilian Weiherer and co-authors built the first deep implicit 3D shape model of the female breast. The earlier Regensburg model used classic statistics and required a costly registration step to align scans, which is especially hard for smooth, feature-poor shapes. The new model learns from raw 3D scans directly, using a neural representation that can describe a surface at any resolution. It captures fine detail such as nipples and navels, and it beat its predecessor on surface reconstruction tests.

As a demonstration, the team used the model to rebuild a breast shape from a single photograph. Shape models like this serve surgical planning, prosthetics, and research on body variation. The authors release the model and code openly. They present the implicit approach as the way forward for body-part models: no registration bottleneck, more expressiveness, and detail that statistical meshes blur away.
arxiv-2412-13344:
Castro, Quadros, and Tamusiunas introduce in twenty twenty-four a notion of partial representation for weak Hopf algebras, a loosened kind of symmetry structure in algebra. Partial maps act only on part of an object, which suits many real constructions. The authors build a universal algebra that gathers all such partial representations into one object through standard maps.

They show this universal algebra matches a partial smash product, a known way of joining two algebras. It also carries two richer structures, one of a Hopf algebroid and one of a quantum inverse semigroup. Finally, they prove that algebra objects over its module category are exactly the symmetric partial module algebras. The work extends partial symmetry theory to the weak setting.
arxiv-2412-13444:
Duan and co-authors report small upward flows seen all over the quiet Sun. They used sharp 174 angstrom images from the Solar Orbiter Extreme Ultraviolet Imager. The team tracked 59 of these upflow-like events above network regions. On average each moved at 62 kilometers per second. Each lasted about 69 seconds and rose about 3.94 million meters.

The events had a hot front followed by a cooler spray of plasma. About 39 percent of them fired more than once. Some showed blob-like parts and strands, and some heated a haze ahead of the spire. The authors link them to spicules and network jets. They may help heat the corona above network regions.
arxiv-2412-14744:
Maran and Restelli tackle how to learn a smooth curve and its slopes from noisy points, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Classic tools for this task store all past points, so cost and memory grow fast. That growth hurts use in live tasks like robot control. The authors seek a light method that still learns as well as the best tools.

They build a method that uses a fixed small set of basis shapes. It stores no past points, yet its error shrinks at the best rate known. They prove tight bounds on error for finite samples. They also prove no method can do better in error or memory. The result gives both top skill and low cost.
arxiv-2412-16344:
Grant and a large team describe in twenty twenty-four the camera plane for a proposed space X-ray spectrograph called Arcus. The mission aims to take sharp soft X-ray and ultraviolet spectra to study how feedback shapes cosmic structure, with fast response to changing events. Its spectrograph uses two near-identical camera planes of light-sensitive chips to record the spread-out spectra.

The paper details the instrument design and the chips themselves. Lab tests of the cameras are reported, and the results meet the observatory's needs. The authors present the focal plane as ready in performance terms for the mission concept. The work supports the probe-class proposal now under study.
arxiv-2412-16844:
Zirong Chen and six co-authors introduce Sim911, a simulation for training emergency dispatchers with large language models. Traditional training relies on experienced staff role-playing callers, which is slow, costly, and often overlooks underserved communities. A realistic simulator could widen access to practice.

Sim911 builds its scenarios from archived emergency call data so practice mirrors real incidents. Dynamic prompts and vector bases steer the model's behavior toward training goals. A validation loop filters weak responses and refines output quality over time. The authors present the system as the first of its kind for dispatcher training. Its stated aim is training that is both effective and equitable.
arxiv-2412-18644:
Karishma Thakrar proposes a new design for search that feeds language models from a graph. Such systems pull facts from linked data to ground their answers. Her paper, from twenty twenty-four, is called DynaGRAG. The aim is to pick richer and more varied pieces of the graph for each question.

The design cleans repeat nodes and scores pieces by how well they fit the query. A smart walk through the graph favors fresh nodes over repeats. Graph networks and large language models are joined by fixed prompts. Tests show better answers than older graph search designs. The gain comes from fuller coverage of the facts in the graph.
arxiv-2412-19344: Anatolii Tushev studied modules over group rings of minimax abelian groups in twenty twenty-four, focusing on their Krull dimension, a measure of how complex a module's chains of submodules can be. Group rings blend group and ring theory, and minimax groups form a natural test class. The paper obtains estimates bounding this dimension. It also links a small deviation condition on normal subgroups to chain conditions from earlier work. The abstract is brief, so the entry reads as a compact note in module theory.
arxiv-2412-19944:
Lukas Picek, Vojtěch Čermák, and Marek Hanzl describe their entry to the COOOL autonomous driving competition in this two thousand twenty-four paper. The benchmark asks systems to detect and classify hazards that fall outside the usual training labels. Their pipeline handles three tasks: detecting the driver's reaction, identifying the hazard object, and writing a caption for it. Kernel-based change point detection on bounding boxes and optical flow drives the reaction task.

For hazard identification, the team combined a simple proximity strategy with classification from a pre-trained vision transformer. Captions came from the MOLMO vision-language model with prompts tailored to rare, low-resolution hazards. The combined system cut relative error by about a third against the baselines and placed second among thirty-two teams.
arxiv-2501-01144:
Wonsuk Jang and Thierry Tambe address the cost of running large language models in a 2025 paper. Bigger models need more memory and power, so engineers shrink the numbers inside them. Fine-grained shrinking helps, but one format rarely fits all blocks of data well. Outlying values make the fit worse.

Their method gives each block of data its own best number format, chosen from a small set of variants. A two-stage step handles new data as the model runs, while staying cheap in energy. Tests on two well-known models showed clear accuracy gains over a standard format, using fewer bits and staying close to full precision.
arxiv-2501-04744:
Jieyun Pan and eight co-authors, including Stéphane Zaleski, presented an exact algorithm in twenty twenty-five for computing how much of a cube is enclosed by a surface meshed with triangles. This color function computation underpins volume-of-fluid methods in multiphase flow simulation and appears in computer graphics too. Getting it exactly right, robustly, for curved surfaces cut into triangles is fiddly.

Their Front2VOF algorithm first clips each triangle against the cube, keeping the polygons inside. It then computes the enclosed volume from those polygons together with the cube's faces. Validation used synthetic configurations with known analytical answers, checking accuracy and robustness across tricky cases. Exact geometry here pays off downstream: volume fractions feed the physics of every simulated cell.
arxiv-2501-05844:
Kungurtsev, Moore, and two co-authors critique in twenty twenty-five the promise that machine learning can reveal true causes. They study how scientists actually use the word cause across fields, treating it as an anthropological question. Their finding is that cause talk everywhere serves one function: naming the mechanisms behind the forces experts judge most salient in their system.

What differs is how well math models mirror expert knowledge of those mechanisms. Physics mirrors it fully, biology crosses scales in open systems, and social science adds interpretation troubles. The authors argue that weak mirroring demands claims built from converging evidence across fields. Restraint in stating certainty, they say, is the durable fix for overclaiming.
arxiv-2501-06044:
Andrew Lewis-Pye and Tim Roughgarden ask how much fault tolerance a replicated system can buy by occasionally breaking its own rules, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. For state machine replication, the optimal trade-off between consistency and liveness against adversaries is a classic, settled formula.

They relax consistency: allow a bounded number of violations, called rollbacks, and see what becomes possible. Without extra timing assumptions, they prove bounded rollback is impossible to guarantee. With a bound on message delays around the time of an attack, even a generous one, protocols can tolerate attacks and recover from the violations. The analysis separates what timing buys from what it cannot. Distributed systems from databases to blockchains live on this trade-off curve. The paper maps the region just beyond the classical optimum and shows it is real but conditional.
arxiv-2501-06144:
Caleb Shaw and Dmitriy Anistratov automate a noise-cutting tool for time-changing neutron simulations, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Random-walk simulations waste effort where few particles go, so weight windows steer effort to where it counts. Their windows rest on a cheap solved model fed by second-moment terms from the random runs.

A filter cleans noise in those terms before the cheap model is solved. Two time-step schemes are offered for the cheap solve. On a standard test case the hybrid windows spread particles evenly in space. Wave fronts and low-flow zones then came out sharper. Readers in reactor math get a self-tuning way to save compute.
arxiv-2501-06644:
Dariusz Tarasewicz and three co-authors grow diamond-like crystals from designer particles in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Their particles carry four sticky patches arranged as a tetrahedron, each patch a distinct type. Such particles should assemble into cubic diamond, a prized structure for steering light. A rival hexagonal form and cage-like phases have nearly the same energy, so selectivity is the challenge. The team tests an equal mix of two particle kinds under confinement.

Simulations show the mix cannot pick the cubic form cleanly. Frustration starts in the first layer stuck to the wall and spreads as the film grows. The authors explain the failure through a link with DNA-like pairing rules. Photonics materials designers are the audience.
arxiv-2501-07544:
Raphaël Clouâtre and Colin Krisko studied C-star supports of operator systems in twenty twenty-five. An operator system is a structured space of operators on a Hilbert space; its C-star support is the algebra it generates inside an injective envelope, a canonical large home. Whether that support is unique turns out to carry deep information.

Using Hamana's theory, they show uniqueness holds exactly when the generated algebra sits inside every copy of the injective envelope on the space. Uniqueness then yields fresh characterizations of the unique extension property for representations and of hyperrigidity. Gathering all supports of a system, they also describe the subspace spanned by its so-called abnormalities, complementing a result of Kakariadis. The paper is pure operator theory with structural payoffs.
arxiv-2501-09244:
He, Sears, and a large team of co-authors reported two dark excitons in the magnet material CrI3 in twenty twenty-five. An exciton is a bound pair of an electron and a hole, and dark ones cannot emit light directly, which makes them hard to spot. CrI3 is a layered magnet that can be peeled into thin flakes, a trait prized for new devices.

The team used a sharp X-ray scattering method to find the excitons. Both flip electron spin, a mark of their dark nature. They spread with momentum and change as the material passes its magnetic transition point. Their lines are narrower than those of the bright excitons known before in this material. The find opens paths to new light-and-magnet devices built from layered materials.
arxiv-2501-13444:
Daiki Komoto and Kenta Kasai wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on building quantum error-correcting codes. Such codes protect fragile quantum data from noise. The codes they study are built from sparse check patterns that repeat in blocks, and short loops in those patterns can weaken how well errors are fixed.

The authors give a direct recipe, based on algebra, for codes with no short loops up to a set length. The design keeps a paired structure that quantum codes need. They also extend the recipe to codes over larger symbol sets and to linked, chain-like codes. The point is to get strong codes by design, without long random searches for good patterns.
arxiv-2501-15344:
Pavlos Kassotakis, Theodoros Kouloukas, and Maciej Nieszporski study a family of mathematical maps tied to the Yang-Baxter equation in a 2025 paper. These maps appear in the study of systems that can be solved exactly. A Lax representation is a matrix form that reveals hidden structure in such maps and helps prove they behave well.

The authors give matrix forms for one class of maps that use fractions, in both plain and non-commuting settings. By using symmetries of known map lists, they extend the results to several other classes, each with matching factorization problems. They also present new examples with many parameters that fall outside the known lists. The work widens the toolkit for classifying and building these maps.
arxiv-2501-15544:
Hanwen Zhang and five co-authors explored in twenty twenty-five how large language models can run demand-side energy management for electric vehicles. Smart microgrids must schedule charging to cut cost and strain, and vehicles connected as an Internet of Electric Vehicles fleet are a huge flexible load. The authors survey the challenges of this setting and where generative AI helps.

Their proposed system augments a language model with retrieval, letting it formulate optimization problems, generate the solving code, and tailor strategies automatically. Tests on charging scheduling showed gains in energy efficiency and adaptability to user needs. The paper presents the work as evidence that language models can serve as practical operators inside IoT-enabled microgrids, not just chat interfaces.
arxiv-2501-17444:
Zili Wang, Katherine Kosaian, and Kristin Yvonne Rozier prove, in a formal checker, that a tool which turns task-time logic rules into pattern rules does so with no change in sense. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The logic, used for craft such as flight systems, states what must hold in a set span of time. The WEST tool helps users write such rules, by turning them into pattern forms. The team proves the turn is right in a theorem prover. They then make code from the proof and use it to test the real WEST tool in runs. They also build proof-backed checks for when two patterns mean the same.
arxiv-2501-18144:
Manoharan, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, sorts out clashes and points of accord among bounds on disorder in the cosmos, and what they mean for a dark energy view. The view ties dark energy to those very bounds.

A famed past work tied the high and low cut-offs of a theory in one firm rule. Manoharan reworks that rule and sets it by the bounds of others. He shows each bound's traits rest on how disorder scales with size. One choice of disorder gauge gives a much tighter cap. He sorts the bounds by type when full: like matter, like light, or like a black hole. He then tests the dark energy models built on them.
arxiv-2502-00544:
Yuxi Hu and Xiaoning Zhao present a study from twenty twenty-five on a relaxed form of the equations for a compressible gas with heat flow. The case is one dimensional, in a bounded span, with set edge terms. They switch the sums to Lagrangian marks that ride with the gas. In that frame, the edge has a uniform shape that suits proofs.

A near system with tamer edges is built first and shown to hold local smooth answers. A weighted energy gauge then yields bounds that hold for all time. Those bounds give global smooth answers for the first system. Limit tools pass the result to the true system. The limit as the relax dial fades is also proved.
arxiv-2502-01044:
Kijin Sung and four co-authors give racing drones a game-theoretic brain for beating rivals, not just flying fast. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Racing through three-dimensional gates at speed, while rivals block and pass, strains standard control methods.

Their framework plans ahead over a moving window and expects the worst from the opponent in real time. A new path-following setup tracks progress without costly distance searches. A scoring function lets each drone switch between passing and blocking as the race demands. In simulations across random starts and speed gaps, the method beat standard predictive control on both passing and blocking. The gaps were statistically firm. The authors frame racing as a true duel.
arxiv-2502-02744:
Alex Krolewski, Jensen Lawrence, and Will Percival build a tomographic halo model of unWISE-Blue galaxies in two thousand twenty-five. The halo model links galaxy clustering to dark matter halos. Their sample holds about a hundred million infrared picked galaxies. Cross links with a spectroscopic survey split them by redshift in effect.

A new method applies the halo model to such cross links. Halo exclusion, projection fixes, and redshift distortions all enter. Both galaxy samples show evolution in their halo occupation. The infrared sample's bias and mean halo mass fall with redshift. Satellite share also drifts down in that span.
arxiv-2502-03644:
Fred Hickernell, Nathan Kirk, and Aleksei Sorokin teach quasi-Monte Carlo methods in a tutorial that asks what they are, why they help, and how to use them. Their paper from twenty twenty-five serves finance, uncertainty work, and kindred fields. Many tasks there reduce to a population mean found by simulation. Plain random sampling creeps toward that mean slowly.

Quasi-Monte Carlo swaps random nodes for low-discrepancy sequences, points spread with unusual evenness. Sample means then settle far faster. The tutorial explains the sequences and their quality gauges. Worked cases show the gains in practice. Problem setup matters: shaping the integral right unlocks the most speed. A brief tour covers uses past plain means. It is a field guide for newcomers and a refresher for hands-on users.
arxiv-2502-04344:
Wolfgang Dreyer and Rüdiger Müller rebuild a piece of electrolyte theory, in a 2025 preprint, on firmer thermodynamic ground. Electrolytes are fluids with dissolved ions, like salt water. The classic Debye-Hückel model describes how ions screen each other electrically. It assumes a fixed electric response from the fluid. Real fluids change that response with mix and temperature. The authors derive a like model that allows the response to vary, without leaning on an artificial charging trick.

Their route runs through a general framework of non-equilibrium electro-thermodynamics. It yields a new consistency rule for how the response must vary with temperature. Folding the new energy term into a model that also counts ion size takes care, since it shifts the pressure. They then test the coupled model on the apparent molar volume of several salts. Checks at phase boundaries round out the study.
arxiv-2502-05044:
Korolev and colleagues build in twenty twenty-five a hybrid learning framework to predict how fluids pass through fibrous mats. Such mats matter for making fibre composites, but modelling flow across tiny and mid scales is costly. The team compared four bridging methods, from a simple one-scale model to a fully detailed one taken as truth.

The simplest method missed the truth by a wide margin. Adding uniform tiny-scale flow helped, but only a segment-wise method nearly matched the truth at modest cost. The fully detailed model took vastly longer and huge files. A physics-aware neural solver was added to fight data scarcity. The authors pitch the hybrid as a fair trade of cost and trust.
arxiv-2502-06144: Andreas Thom answers a question from graph theory in this two thousand twenty-five note. The question was posed by Johannes Carmesin. It went round at an Oberwolfach workshop in January two thousand twenty-five. It asks about finite approximations of infinite symmetric graphs. Thom builds a graph that is unimodular, locally finite, and vertex-transitive. Yet it has no perfect finite local model at large radius. However large a finite patch one asks to be matched exactly, this graph beats each candidate. That settles the question in the negative.
arxiv-2502-06544:
Thinh Nguyen and co-authors study how the order of tasks shapes learning when a model learns tasks one after another, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. A model that learns in sequence can gain from or be hurt by what came before. The team defines two scores for how well a whole sequence transfers, one forward and one backward.

Tests of those scores guide a new way to pick task order. The picked orders beat the usual random order in their trials. The work fills a gap, since order effects had drawn less study than learning methods themselves. Readers who train models over time get a principled way to sequence the work.
arxiv-2502-09744:
Mahad Ali, Curtis Lisle, Patrick Moore, Tammer Barkouki, Brian Kirkwood, and Laura Brattain wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It fine-tunes time series foundation models with federated learning, so medical forecasts can learn across sites without raw data moving.

Heart signals of two kinds, ECG and ICG, serve as the test data. The team tries varied federated set-ups and grades how the split of data across clients bends the result. Joint tuning can work well, they find, but the gain hinges on how alike the client data are. The paper maps the trade-offs of this private path for health models.
arxiv-2502-10444:
Hao Ai, Zidong Cao, and Lin Wang survey the field of omnidirectional vision, where cameras capture a full 360-degree view instead of a narrow frame. Cheap consumer 360 cameras have made such images common, and deep learning has widened what can be done with them. The review explains how these images are formed and the common ways to flatten them for processing. It then sorts the learning methods by how they represent the images and by the tricks used to train them on such wide, warped views.

The authors build a taxonomy of methods for tasks that range from image enhancement and super-resolution to depth and motion estimation. They close with applications such as self-driving cars and virtual reality, plus the open problems that still block progress. The paper serves as a map of a fast-growing area, showing which ideas have been tried and where the gaps remain.
arxiv-2502-11144:
David Azriel, Samuel Davenport, and Armin Schwartzman examine when the two standard tools for estimating heritability from genome study summary data can be trusted. Heritability here means the share of outcome variation explained by a huge number of genetic markers together. The common tools regress marker statistics on correlation scores between markers. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team studies the large-sample behavior of both tools and of the tweaks used in practice, such as weighting and standardization, for both bell-shaped and general data.

Two conditions, nicknamed weak dependence and bounded-kurtosis effects, turn out to be enough for the basic estimators to be consistent. For bell-shaped data those conditions are also necessary. Careful truncation keeps weighting harmless, but routine standardization can bias results when the conditions fail. Population stratification biases every version, a warning the authors underline.
arxiv-2502-13544:
Peiwen Yuan and nine co-authors tackle a stubborn weakness of language models in a 2025 paper: writing to a requested length. Tools that must fill a box, a brief, or a summary slot need exact lengths, yet models drift. Earlier fixes trained the whole skill at once, which hid which parts were failing.

The team breaks length control into sub-skills, compares model errors with human patterns, and builds MarkerGen on the diagnosis. The add-on brings in outside tools for the weakest spots, plants length markers that shift as the text grows, and drafts in three stages to hold the target. Across many settings it improved length accuracy while keeping quality, and it can plug into existing models.
arxiv-2502-14644:
Yansheng Mao and seven co-authors present LIFT, a way to give short-context language models a grip on long inputs. Their twenty twenty-five paper starts from a limit: a model's context window can only hold so much text at once. Stretching the window grows cost fast.

LIFT takes another route. It fine-tunes the model on the long input itself, so the facts are stored in the model's weights, not its window. Synthetic tasks, made by a language model, push it past mere memorization toward real comprehension. A tuned pipeline cuts the wait for the first output token to under ten seconds. The code is open for others to use.
arxiv-2502-14744:
Yilei Jiang and co-authors published this computer safety paper in 2025. It concerns large vision-language models, systems that answer questions about images and text together. Such systems can be tricked by jailbreak prompts that push them to give unsafe answers. Most defenses retrain the model or check its final output, while the model's inner signals during an answer have been little studied.

The team found that these models show distinct inner activity patterns when they process unsafe prompts. Their framework, HiddenDetect, watches those inner states and flags attacks without any extra training of the model. In tests, the method beat current defenses at catching jailbreak attempts. The authors argue that built-in safety signals offer a cheap and scalable layer of protection for such models.
arxiv-2502-14944:
Masatoshi Uehara and a team of co-authors present a test-time method to steer diffusion models toward high-reward outputs, in two thousand twenty-five. Users often want a generated molecule or sequence to score well on a chosen measure. Most steering methods work in a single pass from noise to final sample, which lets errors build up.

Their framework refines the sample in rounds, adding noise and then denoising under reward guidance each time. That loop slowly corrects errors made during steering. The authors give a theory guarantee for the approach. Tests on protein design and on cell-specific regulatory DNA design beat the single-pass rivals.
arxiv-2502-15544:
Xiaoyu Liu and co-authors reschedule trains in real time with learning based control in this 2025 paper. Delays and demand swings force dispatchers to retime trains and reassign rolling stock. Their approach optimizes for passengers, not just trains. Flexible train composition lets capacity follow demand during recovery.

A long short term memory network predicts the integer choices in the plan. Continuous variables then come from constrained optimization. Four presolve tricks prune integer variables before solving, which speeds the cycle. Model predictive control reruns the plan as conditions change. Simulations used real data from the Beijing urban rail system. The hybrid design aims for plans that are both fast to compute and legal to run.
arxiv-2502-18144:
Lorenzo Giordani, Tilman Moller, Paul Mucksch, and Gerhard Rohrle study arrangements of planes built from a graph's connected pieces in a 2025 math study. Each connected subgraph of a chosen graph contributes hyperplanes, and the resulting arrangement's topology reflects the graph. Earlier work introduced the class and proved first results about it.

The authors strengthen those results and add new ones. In particular, arrangements in the class that are aspherical must come from a very restricted set of graphs. Aspherical is a strong topological niceness. One possible exception is tied to the complete graph on four vertices. Such classification narrows where topologists should look for examples.
arxiv-2502-19544:
Yi Zhao leads a team squeezing value from messy, unlabeled robot data to train agents faster. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Offline data can warm-start online reinforcement learning. The richest pools are non-curated: reward-free, mixed quality, from many robot bodies. World models seem ideal for digesting such data. Naive fine-tuning, though, fails to speed later learning.

The team traces the failure to a distribution shift. Offline and online data pull the model in different directions. Experience rehearsal keeps old lessons alive during fine-tuning. Execution guidance steers how the model is used in action. Together they turn junk data into real speedups. Sample efficiency rises across many tasks. Robot learning gets thriftier.
arxiv-2502-20744:
Jordi Del Castillo, Dan Zhao, and Zongrui Pei compare circuit forms, called ansatze, in quantum language models at varied depths. Quantum language models borrow from quantum learning and language theory as a swap for classic models. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Many quantum text methods exist for sorting and writing text, but no set study had weighed their circuit forms side by side. The team tuned key settings for each form and ran text sorting tasks. Results show how the trade off between simple form and rich expression shapes scores. The authors offer their data as a base for building better quantum language methods.
arxiv-2502-21244:
Alberto Ceballos-Arroyo, Jisoo Kim, Chu-Hsuan Lin, Lei Qin, Geoffrey Young, and Huaizu Jiang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It aims to spot brain aneurysms in head CT scans, a slow and hard task when done by hand, with little marked data to train on.

The team first trains a three-dimensional vision model on plain head scans with no marks, using a masked autoencoder scheme. They speed up its attention, hide patches only near arteries where aneurysms form, and make it rebuild both the scan and a map of distance to the nearest artery. A fine-tune then targets the search task. The result beats top rivals on catch rate at a low false alarm rate.
arxiv-2503-00044:
Shuaiang Rong and three co-authors aim drones at a dull but dangerous problem: plants creeping toward power lines. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Vegetation touching lines sparks outages and fires, and patrol imagery piles up faster than humans can scan.

Their detector builds on the YOLOv8 vision model, famed for speed. Directional filters sharpen the thin, angled look of wires and nearby growth. Output boxes rotate to hug the lines, tightening localization. A post-processing step turns the boxes into a numeric encroachment score for each span. On a standard power line data set, the framework proved accurate enough for live monitoring. Utilities get a ranked list of spans to trim first.
arxiv-2503-00344:
Seokju Lee, Hyun-Bin Kim, and Kyung-Soo Kim sharpen state tracking for legged robots in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. A leading filter uses foot contact and a math frame that keeps errors from twisting as the robot moves. Strong nonlinear motion still lets early errors pile into drift.

Their fix adds a neural network as a compensator inside the filter. The network is built to respect the same frame, so the gains of both parts combine. The authors call the result InNKF. It blends model-based tracking with learned correction. Tests reported on the project page show better state estimates than the plain filter, the authors say.
arxiv-2503-00644: Béla Csaba gives a near-tight bound for the Ramsey-Turán problem on four-cliques. A four-clique is a set of four nodes, each linked to the rest. He counts the most edges a graph can have with no such set. The count turns on the independence number, the size of the largest set with no links inside it. His proof avoids the Regularity lemma. That choice widens the range where the tight count holds, apart from small lower-order terms.
arxiv-2503-00944:
Fitash Ul Haq and Jordi Cabot present a Python interpreter for a modeling language in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The Object Constraint Language lets modelers state precise rules for software systems. Tools that run these rules are few, and Python-based modeling had none. Their interpreter, B-OCL, has two parts: a parser and an evaluator. The parser was built with a standard generator tool and produces a syntax tree shaped by the language's own metamodel.

The evaluator walks that tree against an object diagram and checks each rule. At the end, the tool reports the verdict for every constraint. This brings rule checking to Python modelers who lacked it. Software modeling researchers are the audience.
arxiv-2503-01844:
Miriam Havin, Timna Wharton Kleinman, Moran Koren, Yaniv Dover, and Ariel Goldstein test whether chat AI can sway views. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that past tests used tight lab setups in English. Their study, set in advance on record, used looser real-world terms. All chats and texts were in Hebrew.

Two hundred people took part. Some read a short text, while others held live chats through Telegram. The other side was at times a model and at times a person. Topics were disputed civil policy points. People moved toward the other side's view in all setups. Gains in sureness rose in most setups too. The authors say model agents can sway views as well as people can. This raises stakes for public debate.
arxiv-2503-07444:
Lucas Farndale, Paul Henderson, Edward Roberts, and Ke Yuan introduced SpliCER in twenty twenty-five, a self-supervised learning method that refuses to take shortcuts. Representation learners often latch onto simple patterns and ignore subtle features — a serious flaw in scientific imaging, where the subtle features carry the discovery. High-content microscopy is exactly such a setting.

SpliCER splits each image into sections and distills information section by section, forcing the model to learn complex features without losing simple ones. It plugs into any self-supervised loss without modifying the host method. The authors first demonstrate that existing methods do learn shortcut solutions when easy and hard features coexist. SpliCER then delivered significant downstream gains in medical and geospatial imaging tests.
arxiv-2503-08444:
Gazizova and five co-authors present a universal computation kernel for Feynman diagrams in many-body theory, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Many-body perturbation theory evaluates diagrams full of temperature and frequency sums. Projecting the single-particle Green's function to an auxiliary space transforms the problem. Any Feynman diagram then converts into a standard universal kernel form.

The kernel holds all explicit temperature and frequency dependence of the diagram. It contains no problem-specific information once constructed, by design. Diagram results become linear combinations of kernel pieces with problem-specific coefficients. A low-order self-energy diagram demonstrates the construction concretely. Distinct physical problems reuse the same kernel for their solutions afterward.
arxiv-2503-12544:
Christopher Fewster computes the polarisation sets of Green operators for normally hyperbolic equations on curved spacetimes. His 2025 paper serves quantum field theory in curved settings, where such tools govern how fields spread. The polarisation set refines the wavefront set. It tracks the fiber directions of singularities, not just where they sit in phase space. He treats three kernels: the advanced one, the retarded one, and the difference of the two.

With those sets in hand, linked cases get answers through their solution theories. The Proca equation is the worked case. It describes massive spin-one particles. Fewster finds a gap in a recent paper on that subject and closes it. The work gives exact maps of singularities for field equations that physicists solve in practice.
arxiv-2503-14144:
Maximilian Binzer, František Šanda, Lars Mewes, Erling Thyrhaug, and Jürgen Hauer wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It gives a shot-to-shot method for transient absorption anisotropy, a probe of how fast molecules turn after a light flash.

The anisotropy signal is not read straight; it is built from two runs at crossed pulse angles, so small drifts wreck it. The new rig swaps the pump angle on each shot, which kills the drift at its root. Broadband reads let the team split effects by color. On a dye that a past group had weighed, they set the times for population fade and coherence loss side by side, and back a past claim of even-handed relaxation.
arxiv-2503-15544: Adam Bjorndahl, a solo author, sets out a logic for uncertain interpretation in a 2025 paper. The framework deals with cases where the meaning of a statement is not fully settled. He gives two uses for it. One is a fresh account of implication that captures entailment between meanings. The other is a careful notion of belief backed by evidence. That notion takes the shape of a known type of belief function. The paper is short and formal.
arxiv-2503-16144:
Khelladi, Reux, and Acher introduce PolyTest, a method that makes language models write better unit tests in this 2025 paper. Single-attempt test generation misses a trick: models produce varied tests across languages and sampling runs. That variety can be harvested instead of discarded.

PolyTest generates tests in five languages at zero temperature, then unifies them. It also samples several test sets in one language at higher temperature and unifies those. The catch is contradictions: the same input may get different expected outputs. Unification builds self-consistency and weeds out bad expectations. Tests improve without running code during generation. Weaker languages gain most, since strong ones lend them their test logic.
arxiv-2503-16544:
Donghuo Zeng and six co-authors tune persuasive chat systems with causal finds and what-if reasoning. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. A chat that bends to a user's state persuades better, but user states shift as talks run.

A search method maps which user moves cause which system replies, with user moves as states and system moves as acts. A paired generative net then drafts what-if replies the system could have made. A deep Q-network learns from those drafts which reply to pick. On a charity persuasion data set, the chain lifts rewards past base methods, which shows cause maps can sharpen talk policy.
arxiv-2503-20244:
Zhuoyun Qian and six co-authors survey software vulnerability analysis in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Modern systems are written in many languages and often hide flaws that attackers exploit. Many detection tools exist, but no study had compared them across the whole landscape.

The survey spans programming languages, levels of program representation, bug types, and detection techniques. It sets out current practice in finding flaws before release, with each method's strengths and limits. Relationships among language, abstraction, flaw type, and approach are drawn together in one frame. The authors close with open challenges and future directions. Their aim is a map that helps security researchers see where the field stands and where it must go.
arxiv-2503-22144:
Diallo and Zouaq present a study from twenty twenty-five on turning plain questions into database queries that generalize. The target language, SPARQL, queries knowledge bases for factual answers. Existing training sets lean on templates, so models learn shallow matches. They then fail on freely phrased questions with new shapes. Their method enriches questions with frame labels that mark roles in each sentence. They also build a new dataset version with those enrichments added. Tests span recent large language models under varied fine-tuning setups.

Adding frame structure improves query generation across their tests. Gains run largest on unseen templates and on fully rephrased questions. The authors say role structure teaches real generalization, not pattern recall. The dataset and method are offered for wider use.
arxiv-2503-22244:
Weizhen Wang and three co-authors analyze a quiet flaw in policy gradient learning: the sampling distribution does not match the theory. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. These methods train decision policies in reinforcement learning, and state-of-the-art versions sample states the wrong way.

For simple table-based policies, the authors prove global convergence despite the biased updates. For the softmax form, they compute the exact leading error terms under the bias. Their ratio tells when the mismatch speeds learning and when it slows it. Bounds for general policies show both mismatches shrink at least linearly as the discount nears one. The work explains why a theoretically untidy method works so well in practice.
arxiv-2504-02144:
Oam Patel and colleagues ask whether trainable soft prompts can be made understandable. Their twenty twenty-five paper builds a theory for prompt interpretability. Soft prompts boost model performance cheaply on specific tasks. Yet nobody can read what those learned prompts actually say.

The framework judges prompts by faithfulness and scrutability. Existing tuning methods fail those tests by design, the authors find. New objective functions push two leading tuners toward readable prompts. Experiments with a smaller language model reveal a hard trade-off. More readable prompts generally perform worse on the task. Odd behaviours also appear when interpretability is optimised hard. The paper maps a real tension in prompt engineering.
arxiv-2504-02244:
Cao and co-authors release SocialGesture, a dataset for gestures that happen between several people at once. Past gesture research mostly studied single people, missing social context. That gap made it hard to align gestures with speech and language in natural scenes.

SocialGesture is billed as the first large dataset built for multi-person gesture study. It spans varied natural settings and supports tasks such as video recognition and time spotting. The team adds a visual question task to test vision-language models on social gestures. Results expose clear limits in current gesture models. The dataset is posted on Hugging Face for open use.
arxiv-2504-03644: Saowalak Jitngam, Poom Kumam, and Songpon Sriwongsa study when quantum information partly revives on networks built from rings, in a 2025 paper. The networks are unitary Cayley graphs, whose links follow the units of a finite commutative ring. Fractional revival means a quantum state spreads out, then partly refocuses at chosen spots. The authors characterize every finite local ring whose graph allows this effect. Since general rings split into products of local ones, their results carry over to the full commutative case.
arxiv-2504-03744:
Tanmay Chakraborty, Christian Wirth, and Christin Seifert present a way to explain trade-offs when people pick favorites in a search task. Their paper from twenty twenty-five sits in preference-based Bayesian optimization. A person must choose between options scored on many outcomes at once. Such picks are hard: goals clash, and the chooser may feel unsure.

Their method, MOLONE, gives local tales that compare nearby options. It names which inputs and which outcomes drive the gap between them. Most past explainers stressed inputs alone and skipped outcomes. Tests on standard multi-goal tasks show faster progress than noisy picks. A user study backs this up. People with the tales found their favored options sooner. The work aims at choices that are both quick and well informed.
arxiv-2504-05444:
Ziad Kheil, Soleakhena Ken, and Laurent Risser teach image registration networks to respect how real tissue moves. Their paper from twenty twenty-five addresses medical image alignment. Standard smoothers force one rule on the whole image. Bodies mix stiff bone, soft organs, and sliding interfaces, though. A uniform rule warps those zones in ways flesh never would.

Training losses borrow from solid mechanics to drill set motion types. Local rigidity, shearing, and pseudo-elastic stretch are each enforced where apt. The trained net then reads motion type from fresh images alone. Tests on chest and belly scans, fake and real, show the traits carry over. Hard tissue holds its shape while soft zones slide as they should. Code is public. The aim is alignment that a clinician can trust as physical.
arxiv-2504-09044:
Xiaofeng Dong and Yanyong Hong classify quadratic Novikov algebras, a structure from the theory of Novikov bialgebras. Their paper from twenty twenty-five starts from a Novikov algebra with a paired bilinear form. The form is symmetric, nondegenerate, and twists in a set way against the product. Such forms add a metric flavor to the algebra.

The authors first draw out basic traits of these algebras. A split theorem breaks them into simpler parts. They then sort all cases of dimension two and three over the complex numbers, up to sameness of shape. A build trick called double extension comes next. Any such algebra with a nonzero null ideal arises by this trick. A four-dimensional case built this way closes the study.
arxiv-2504-11544:
Tianyang Xu and co-authors present a 2025 framework called NodeRAG for giving language models better access to a private text collection. The base method, retrieval-augmented generation, lets a model look up facts before it answers. Graph-based versions build a knowledge graph over the texts first, so the model can follow links between facts.

The authors argue that most graph versions pay little care to how the graph itself is shaped. A poor shape blocks good graph methods and weakens answers. NodeRAG builds the graph from mixed node types, each suited to a step in the lookup flow. That design lets graph tools slot into the whole process in a smooth way. The goal is answers that stay closer to the source texts.
arxiv-2504-12044:
Marcos Mariño dissects the simplest case of a renormalon, a famous obstruction to summing perturbation theory. His work appeared in twenty twenty-five. The setting is the ground state energy of a two-dimensional scalar theory with many field copies.

The obstruction was first seen at a set order in the large-copy expansion. Mariño shows it matches the exact solution's growth pattern precisely. He then writes out the full trans-series: the complete tower of non-perturbative corrections beyond the standard series. He also studies the field's two-point function in the same frame. It stays finite order by order, yet hides the same singularity and resists Borel summation. Its pole mass is purely non-perturbative.
arxiv-2504-13044:
Farhan Khodaee and colleagues propose that aging can be understood as energy dissipation in a living system, much as friction drains motion in a machine. Many aging theories exist, from programmed decline to damage buildup, but measuring cellular change in a unified way is hard. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team uses math from dynamical systems to break age-related change into parts. They then train a transformer model on gene activity data, feeding age in as a token, and watch how gene and age markers move apart in the model inner space.

The result is a cellular aging map covering several tissues and cell types. The map shows spreading gene patterns, sudden nonlinear shifts, and entropy changes with age. The authors offer both a new framing of aging and a tool that tracks it at molecular resolution.
arxiv-2504-15344:
Anwar Yousef Alzahrani and co-authors published this astronomy study in 2025. Open star clusters are families of stars born together, useful as tracers of the Galaxy's history. The team analyzed three little-studied clusters, SAI 16, SAI 81, and SAI 86, using data from the Gaia space mission's third release. Software fitted their structure, picked out likely member stars, and matched their color-brightness patterns to stellar models.

Membership came to about 125, 158, and 138 stars respectively. The model fits gave ages spanning roughly a hundred million to over a billion years, and distances near three to four thousand parsecs. All three clusters proved dynamically relaxed, meaning their stars have mixed thoroughly over time. Motion analysis placed their orbits in the young stellar disk of the Galaxy. The authors present the full parameter set, from core sizes to total masses, as a reference for future work on these clusters.
arxiv-2504-15444:
M. J. Neves works out a doubly modified version of quantum electrodynamics flattened to a plane. The theory adds two ingredients to pseudo-electrodynamics. A Lee-Wick term brings a heavy partner mass that tames ultraviolet divergences. A Chern-Simons term gives the photon a light topological mass. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Neves builds the model from a non-local Lagrangian and checks its classical side first. Static charges interact through the gauge propagator, and causality is tested with the retarded Green function. The fermion sector gains a heavy Lee-Wick partner for the electron.

One-loop quantum corrections follow: electron self-energy, vacuum polarization, and the three-point vertex. The Lee-Wick mass acts as a natural regulator throughout. The electron's anomalous magnetic moment emerges as a function of both masses. An optical theorem check confirms tree-level unitarity.
arxiv-2504-16344:
Henneking and seven co-authors build a digital twin for tsunami early warning on the Cascadia subduction zone, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Seafloor pressure sensors feed a Bayesian inversion of earthquake motion. Coupled acoustic-gravity wave equations forecast the tsunami in real time. The full problem carries a billion parameters.

Direct posterior computation would take fifty years on hundreds of graphics processors. A shift-invariance trick splits work into offline and online parts. Offline runs scale to the full El Capitan supercomputer efficiently. Online inference then finishes in zero point two seconds. That is a ten-billion-fold speedup for the warning step.
arxiv-2504-16444:
Ai-Chao Wang and Neng-Chang Wei test one proposed cause of a narrow bump seen when photons strike protons and produce two neutral particles plus a proton. Experimenters had found the bump in the combined mass of one particle pair, and a tempting story blamed a two-step decay through a short-lived excited nucleon. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the authors build the reaction from several exchange and resonance pieces and try to reproduce the stripped-down bump with each candidate intermediate state. Two nearby excited nucleons were tried as the stepping stone.

The first candidate decayed too rarely into the needed channel, so its signal fell far short of the data. The second could mimic the bump shape roughly, but its width came out much broader than measured. The authors conclude the cascade story cannot explain the narrow structure.
arxiv-2504-17244:
Hoang Ly and Emina Soljanin analyze how redundantly stored data systems serve many users at once in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The service rate region captures that ability as a geometric object, a polytope whose dimensions are the request rates for each stored object. The authors focus on systems using a class of maximum distance separable codes. For each code they characterize the region's intercepts and the smallest standard simplex containing it.

A graph-theoretic framework connects the problem to fractional matchings in quasi-uniform hypergraphs. Finding the service rate region becomes equivalent to computing an image of the fractional matching polytope. The authors introduce greedy matchings and show attention can be restricted to them, then determine the region for a large subset of the codes. The results unify earlier characterizations of systematic and non-systematic systems.
arxiv-2504-17744:
Xu and co-authors pick a golden sample of nearby star clusters with tidal tails, using Gaia data. Open clusters let astronomers study how stars move and age under gravity and passing encounters. The team started from a catalog of clusters within 500 parsecs reported to show tidal features.

A 3D principal component method screened out clusters warped by line-of-sight distortions. Eight clusters passed, among them Blanco 1, Melotte 20, and NGC 2632. Both 2D and 3D King profiles were fit to each cluster's star density. Most clusters showed larger 3D tidal radii than 2D ones. Flat views thus shrink the measured size of these clusters.
arxiv-2504-18144:
Zijian Wang and five co-authors model how the first stars in the universe may have fed early black holes when they wandered too close and were torn apart. Their paper came out in 2025. Such tearing is called a tidal disruption event, and it dumps the star's gas onto the black hole.

Using a semi-analytic model of cosmic history, they focus on heavy seed black holes present at the cosmic dawn. Disruptions of first-generation stars sped growth strongly for the lighter seeds. Those seeds could gain about ten times their mass within the first ten million years. The scenario matches the pathways needed to form the bright quasars already seen in the young universe. Future gravitational wave observatories and infrared telescopes may catch signs of this growth.
arxiv-2504-18644:
Saeed Hashemi Sababe and Amir Baghban attach numbers to cyclicity in radially weighted Besov spaces, including the Drury-Arveson space. Their paper from twenty twenty-five defines cyclicity indices drawn from potential theory and capacity. A function is cyclic when its shifts span the whole space. Past work often settled the yes-no question without a measure of degree.

Their indices supply that measure. The theory also travels to non-commutative settings, giving cyclicity analogues in free function spaces. Stability is probed both ways: perturb the function, perturb the weight, and watch cyclicity hold or fail. Boundary zero sets carry geometric criteria for the outcome. The haul is a set of invariants for multiplier invariant subspaces across many function spaces.
arxiv-2504-18744:
Raghav Jha, a solo author, wrote a physics paper in two thousand twenty-five about the Ising model in a magnetic field. The model places tiny magnets on a square grid, and it is a key test case in physics. No exact solution is known when a steady field is applied.

Jha first offers a closed form built from a one-line chain and a known exact result. Checks against precise computer data show small but real gaps in that form. He then gives a refined form based on a known theorem about the model's zeros. The refined form matches the data far more closely and gives the right key values.
arxiv-2504-19844:
Yu-Xuan Li, Yicheng Liu, and Cheng-Cheng Liu propose building topological superconductors on fully compensated ferrimagnets, magnets whose opposing moments cancel to zero. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Such superconductors host Majorana states prized for quantum computing. Magnets usually fight superconductivity, forcing painful trade-offs.

With no net magnetization, the ferrimagnet leaves the superconductor intact. Yet its internal order still shapes the topology.
