Symmetry analysis and microscopic models predict Majorana end modes in wires. Chiral edge modes appear in two-dimensional versions, and corner modes in higher-order phases. An electric field can flip the system between topological phases. Rotating the internal Néel vector moves the Majorana states around. Control without external magnets is the headline advantage. The platform spans one, two, and higher-order dimensions in one proposal.
arxiv-2504-21144:
Rob Behary and a team of co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on a light based gauge for electron beams. Beam checks that touch the beam can spoil it. Their gauge reads the beam from glow in a thin rubidium vapor. The beam's field shifts a high orbit state of the atoms, called a Rydberg state. That shift dims the glow in a narrow band.

Photos of the glow let them rebuild the beam's width, center, and current. They show the gauge on a beam at low current in a test rig. Stray fields in the rig pose the chief snag. The team sees strong promise for a gauge that leaves the beam near untouched.
arxiv-2504-21444:
Jihong Li leads a large team in framing how immersive traffic and legacy traffic can share one wireless network. The paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. Slicing the network apart for each kind can cut throughput and grow queues.

Their frame serves both kinds at once with quality in view. A drift theorem turns a long-run aim into a short-run one, weighted by queue length. A slicing scheme adapts against shifting channels, with a filter-based tracker for live change. Tests show a clear throughput gain, a big latency cut, and faster settling than past plans. Knobs let operators trade total flow against user feel.
arxiv-2505-00944: James Melbourne, Michael Roysdon, Colin Tang, and Tomasz Tkocz move from simplex slicing to sharp reverse Hölder inequalities in two thousand twenty-five. Simplex slicing caps the volume of central cuts of a regular simplex. The team lifts that sharp bound into a probability frame. Negative moments of centered log-concave variables get sharp bounds as well. A phase shift shows in which distribution attains the extreme. That shift marks the new reverse inequalities as curious in kind. The paper is a compact piece of convex geometry.
arxiv-2505-01244:
Leonidas Gkimisis and three co-authors set rules for learning dynamical systems from data safely. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. The method infers a sparse full-order model from snapshots of a system's motion. A least squares fit does the learning, with regularization to keep it tame. The authors probe when the learned model stays stable. Bad data spacing can make it blow up.

For linear advection they derive a sampling condition much like the classic CFL rule. It bounds the ratio of space and time steps in the training data. Simple one-dimensional diffusion and advection cases show the theory at work. Two harder nonlinear cases in two dimensions come next. The results guide how to gather data for model learning. Stability can be planned for, not just hoped for.
arxiv-2505-01344:
Garvan and Morrow proved new pattern rules in twenty twenty-five for a counting function invented by George Andrews, a leading figure in partition theory. The function counts ways to split a number into parts where every even part sits below every odd part, with one extra twist on the largest even part.

The authors show the counts obey repeating rules when divided by a large power of two, and the rules multiply together in a clean way. Similar rules hold for a wider family of related counting products. Their proofs borrow machinery from the theory of modular forms, including symmetry tricks and operators built for half-weight cases. The work follows a famous earlier result by Atkin on the ordinary partition function. Such hidden regularities hint at deep structure inside simple counting questions.
arxiv-2505-04844:
Alexander Shan, John Bauer, and Chris Manning published this machine learning paper in 2025. It introduces Osiris, a lightweight open-source system for catching hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation, where a language model answers from supplied source text. Even with sources in hand, models still produce claims the sources do not support. Checking for that today usually means slow human review or a costly closed model.

The team built a training set by taking multi-hop questions and deliberately planting hallucinations in the answers. They then fine-tuned a modest 7-billion-parameter model on that set. On the RAGTruth benchmark, the small model recalled more hallucinations than GPT-4o, with competitive precision and accuracy. The authors release the code, arguing that cheap, fast checking can make such systems safe enough for real deployment.
arxiv-2505-05444:
Giulia Gianfagna and a large team of co-authors report a soft X-ray transient called EP241021a in this 2025 paper. X-ray flashes are thought to be softer cousins of gamma ray bursts. The Einstein Probe satellite, with its soft X-ray view, is well placed to study them. Its wide field instrument caught the first flash of this event.

Follow up spanned radio, optical, and X-ray telescopes on the ground and in space. The afterglow showed several components over time. Models point to a structured jet seen off axis, plus a slower cocoon of material around it. A massive progenitor star fits the overall picture. Comparing jet and cocoon models against the light curves is the core of the analysis. The event shows how complex these explosions can be.
arxiv-2505-05844:
Rodriguez-Cardoso and a large team compare how simulation codes quench satellite galaxies in a Milky Way-mass halo, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Satellites lose gas and stop forming stars through several processes near their host. Local Group satellites quench with striking efficiency. Which mechanism dominates is still debated across codes and surveys.

All codes in the shared-halo suite match survey quenched fractions within scatter. Less massive satellites quench faster in every code, matching observations. Strangulation cuts fresh gas first, then ram pressure strips what remains. Stripping bites hardest below a set stellar mass. Efficiency still varies by code, driven by feedback recipes and hydro methods.
arxiv-2505-06144:
Nguyen Quang Bau and three colleagues wrote a 2025 physics paper on a one-atom-thick crystal called jacutingaite. This material, made of platinum, mercury, and selenium, acts as a quantum spin Hall insulator. That means its edges carry spin currents while its face blocks flow.

The team shines circularly polarized light on the sheet to reshape its states. Light-driven tuning can open spin- and valley-split states with no energy gap. They track two effects, the spin and orbital Edelstein effects, which turn charge flow into spin buildup. These effects act as probes of the light-driven phase changes. The work may feed future spin-based and valley-based devices.
arxiv-2505-07144:
Joe Baine, Tasman Fell, Anna Romanov, Alexander Sherman, and Geordie Williamson wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five. It introduces a new functor, a structured map between categories, acting on representations of reductive algebraic groups. Representations describe how groups act as symmetries, and the modular setting studies them over fields of prime size.

The authors stress that the functor has striking traits. It respects tensor products, the natural way to combine representations. It sends every standard and costandard object in the main block to a one-dimensional object. They link the functor to recent work by Gruber. They also conjecture that it matches a known construction under a major expected equivalence in the field.
arxiv-2505-08244:
Ethan Dickey examines why plagiarism checks often fail in competitive programming courses, in a research paper from 2025. In such courses, tasks tend to have one known best solution, so honest code can look alike. Dickey draws on seven terms of teaching a first course in the sequence at Purdue University.

The paper reviews past studies and surveys tools such as Moss and Kattis, plus human methods like code authorship interviews. Simple rewrites can fool automated similarity checks, and AI-written code can slip past them too. Interviews work well but cost much staff time. Dickey urges a mixed plan: better detectors, mastery-based learning, and assessments that make original work the natural path.
arxiv-2505-08444:
Wenyan Yang and six co-authors present Vis2Plan, a system that extracts visual plans for robots from unlabeled video. Visual planning gives a low-level controller a sequence of intermediate image goals for long manipulation tasks. Earlier methods generated those images with video models, which can hallucinate and run slowly.

Vis2Plan instead mines raw play data with vision foundation models to find a compact set of task symbols. Those symbols form a transition graph for planning across goals and stages. At test time the planner works at the symbolic level, then grounds the plan in real subgoal images. In robot trials it beat diffusion-based planners on success rate while planning far faster.
arxiv-2505-10244: Jason Li presents a simpler and faster algorithm for splitting directed graphs in this 2025 paper. A low diameter decomposition breaks a directed graph into clusters of small diameter. Such splits are a basic tool in graph algorithms. A 2025 result set the best known loss factor for the task, but with a slower method.
arxiv-2505-10344:
Alan Jeffares and Liyuan Liu wrote a tutorial in twenty twenty-five on discrete variational autoencoders. Standard autoencoders of this family squeeze data through a continuous Gaussian latent space. Discrete latent variables — categorical choices rather than smooth vectors — suit modalities like text and have grown popular, but the math behind them is often presented sketchily.

Assuming only a basic mathematical background, the authors derive every step from first principles: the model, the evidence lower bound objective, and how training works when the latent space is categorical. They finish with a concrete training recipe and a working example implementation shared openly. The tutorial aims to give practitioners and students a rigorous but usable on-ramp to a model class usually learned from fragments.
arxiv-2505-10944:
Three co-authors, Biedermann, Marin, and Barnouin, test whether a bright galaxy hides two giant black holes, in two thousand twenty-five. The galaxy is among the brightest of its kind in infrared light. Its core shows a sharp dip in near-ultraviolet light and a peak in polarized light at the same place.

The team fit a model with two black holes, each with its own disk of infalling matter. The heavier one's disk would make most of the visible light, while the lighter one's disk would shine in far ultraviolet light. The model matched both the light and its polarization well. It also predicts a second polarization peak that future checks could confirm or rule out.
arxiv-2505-12044:
Haixu Wu and co-authors speed up the attention step in neural networks when a bias term is added, in work from 2025. Attention is the core operation in modern models for vision, language, and protein folding. Adding prior knowledge as a bias matrix is common, but it breaks the fast memory pattern that makes standard attention quick on graphics hardware.

The team proves that the best possible speed for the fast attention method is set by the rank of the attention weight matrix. Building on that insight, their method compresses the bias by its low-rank structure. For many standard biases it computes the exact result fast, and for general biases it gives a fast close approximation. Protein and vision tests showed clear speedups with no accuracy loss. Code is public.
arxiv-2505-12244:
Haojin Wang, Zining Zhu, and Freda Shi study which next-word spreads a language model can be made to produce. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. At each step, such a model gives a spread of odds over words that may come next. They ask how close a tuned prompt can push that spread to any target spread a user sets.

Some targets are far harder to hit than others. Spreads with very low or very high spread of odds are easier than those in the middle. Targets with outlier words are easier at the same level. Targets made by a model itself are easier than random ones. The finds bear on the use of models as spread proposers.
arxiv-2505-13844:
Yin and a team including Zhang, Wen, and Li wrote a twenty twenty-five study on how well large language models match the human brain. People link new speech to past facts held in mind as they listen. The team asks if that same step can help a model track brain waves.

They first map model acts to brain acts for speech. They then add linked facts to the text fed to the model. The match grows in brain zones tied to this kind of recall. Fine-tuned large models match best, aided by a new set of one thousand tales built for the task.
arxiv-2505-13944:
Dao and five co-authors present a paper from twenty twenty-five on continual relation extraction without storing old examples. Systems must learn new relation types task after task. Storing past samples costs memory and raises privacy worries. Prompt methods avoid storage but misjudge tasks and forget. Their design gives each task its own prompt pool. That captures variation within and across tasks more safely. Label wordings add global context for telling relations apart.

A training-free trick sharpens task guessing at test time. A generative model folds old knowledge into shared weights. Tests beat both prompt and rehearsal rivals. Robust continual learning is the claimed payoff.
arxiv-2505-16044:
Gowtham Premananth, Philip Resnik, Sonia Bansal, Deanna Kelly, and Carol Espy-Wilson argue that schizophrenia assessment should gauge symptom severity. It should not just detect the disorder. Deep learning studies most often treat schizophrenia as a task of sorting, as present or absent. That makes a complex condition too simple. It also limits clinical use, since care rests on which symptoms are severe.

The study shifts focus to gauges of severity for each symptom, with a multimodal path. It joins speech, video, and text inputs. It builds models for each mode on its own and a frame that combines them. To catch a more detailed symptom profile can sharpen diagnostic precision. It can also support care that is tailored to the person. The team casts the path as a scalable, objective tool for mental health work.
arxiv-2505-19544:
Jialei Chen, Yuanbo Xu, and Yiheng Jiang wrote this computing paper in 2025 on sequential recommendation, the task of guessing what a user will want next. Diffusion models, which build data by undoing noise, have been tried for the task. The team found a flaw in past tries: the word codes inside the model collapse, losing the traits that set items apart.

Their fix, ADRec, noises each token on its own and spreads the process across the whole target sequence in training. An auto-regressive thread keeps the order of items in view. A three-stage training plan first sets the codes, then aligns them with the model, then fine-tunes all. At run time, only the last token is cleaned, so past tastes stay intact. Tests on six data sets showed gains in both accuracy and speed.
arxiv-2505-21544:
Semanto Mondal builds a phone-friendly assistant that names coffee leaf diseases and talks farmers through treatment, in a 2025 paper. The system weds a YOLOv8 vision model, which spots disease in a leaf photo, to a language model fed by retrieval. Retrieval grounds the advice in real documents, trimming the model's tendency to invent. The farmer submits a picture and gets a diagnosis plus remedies in plain words.

The design aims at less pesticide use, steadier livelihoods, and greener practice. Scalability and ease of use lead the requirements list. Mondal frames the project within precision farming's turn to joined-up AI: eyes, memory, and voice in one tool for the field.
arxiv-2505-21944:
Linli Zhou, Bokun Wang, My Thai, and Tianbao Yang made optimization algorithms in twenty twenty-five for two-way partial AUC. It is a classifier metric made for data that is not balanced. Plain accuracy hides how a model does in the ranges that count. Those are high true positive rates at low false positive rates. Partial AUC grades just those windows. But stochastic optimizers for it lagged. They leaned on approximations or had poor complexity.

Their two algorithms update primal and dual variables. They do so in stochastic block-coordinate style. One is for convex losses and one is for non-convex ones. Study of convergence shows better rates than past methods. On many benchmark data sets the new pair converged faster. They generalized better too. The work gives sharper tools for tasks such as screening and diagnosis. In such tasks, not all errors cost the same.
arxiv-2505-22044:
Kurchaninov and three co-authors described the design of timing electronics in twenty twenty-five for a particle detector built from glass plates. The detector, a multigap resistive plate chamber, records when particles pass with extreme precision. Its front-end electronics use constant fraction discrimination, a method that times a pulse at a fixed share of its height, which cancels timing drift from pulses of varied size.

The team designed and tuned the analog front end for chambers with ten and twelve gaps. Tests with cosmic rays and a muon beam at an accelerator in Protvino reached a total time resolution of forty picoseconds. That precision meets the needs of the SPD experiment at the NICA collider. The paper reports the design choices behind the result.
arxiv-2505-23944:
Thushara Manjari Naduvilakandy, Hyeju Jang, and Mohammad Al Hasan use large language models to mine cause links in two thousand twenty-five. Finding causes in text feeds tasks like fact extraction and knowledge graphs. Past rule based methods score poorly and need much hand work. Trained methods need big labeled sets that are scarce.

The team adds retrieval to the prompt given to the model. Fresh apt examples are pulled in for each new case, not fixed in advance. Tests span three data sets and five models. The dynamic prompts beat fixed prompts by a clear margin. The authors claim the best such scheme to date in this line of work.
arxiv-2505-24144:
Jiaheng Chen and Daniel Sanz-Alonso prove sharp bounds for random tensors in twenty twenty-five. Concentration inequalities say how tightly a random quantity huddles around its mean. For tensors, the asymmetric case holds a surprise. When a tensor has order three or more, a new effect can appear.

If the effective ranks of the component covariances fall on both sides of a critical line, an extra logarithmic factor shows up. That factor is absent in sharp bounds for symmetric tensors. To prove this, the authors extend empirical process theory to products of several function classes. They generalize generic chaining methods beyond the quadratic case. Readers in probability get a finer picture of how random tensors behave.
arxiv-2505-24244:
Nir Endy and five co-authors trace how facts move inside a newer kind of language model in a 2025 paper. Mamba models replace the attention mechanism of transformers with a state space design, and interpretability tools built for attention did not obviously transfer. The authors adapt the attention knockout method, which blocks information flow between tokens to see what matters, to both Mamba generations.

Knockouts revealed where subject information first appears and how it travels across layers. Some patterns matched transformers exactly, hinting they are universal to language models, while others were Mamba specific. Using Mamba's structured form, the team separated components that pass information between tokens from those that enrich single tokens.
arxiv-2505-24544:
Wei Zhong and four co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on a trick that speeds up large language models. The trick uses a small draft model to guess the next words. A big model then checks those guesses in one pass. Most draft models copy the big model's own attention style, which adds bulk and fuss.

Their draft model, called Beagle, uses cross attention instead, with no extra pooling layers. It matches the speed of a top rival draft model. A two stage training plan keeps its learning stable and fast. Tests on many models and data sets show like speed gains with better training yield. Memory use stays flat in training runs, which helps at scale.
arxiv-2506-00144:
Nóra Takács and ten co-authors report, in a 2025 preprint, three asteroids in the Hilda group that spin far faster than any found before. Hildas orbit in step with Jupiter, two of theirs for three of his, and their spins record the solar system's early violence. The space telescope TESS caught the trio's brightness flicker. Their periods run just over three hours. Ground surveys had never seen a mid-size Hilda below about five hours. Spinning that fast should tear a loose rubble pile apart.

To hold together, these bodies need real cohesion or a density well above the usual guess. Carbon-rich asteroids match that density, and a modest share of Hildas are of that type. The authors link the trio's frequency to that share. Outer-belt material, mixed inward during the giant planets' early shuffling, may explain them.
arxiv-2506-00244:
Pintu Kumar and Nandyala Hemachandra present a method that cleans noisy labels in graph data for node classification. Their 2025 paper notes that cheap data sets often carry wrong labels, graphs included. Their technique uses a small clean set plus an influence estimate: how much the model would change if one training node were removed.

Extending recent work, they estimate how removal changes validation loss, then relabel or flag suspect nodes with a theory-driven rule. Two variants find noisy nodes without knowing the noise pattern or its rate. For one variant they prove the flagged points genuinely raise risk. Experiments across data sets beat baseline denoisers on accuracy. Robust labels matter wherever graphs are labeled by crowds or weak rules.
arxiv-2506-00644:
Ana Rita Valente and co-authors present a dataset paper from 2025 on speech and stuttering. The team worked to improve a shared speech dataset called FluencyBank. They added a new way to label stuttering that follows rules used by trained clinicians in real practice.

Expert clinicians were hired to label the speech data by hand. Their labels cover sounds and video, and they mark stuttering moments, other behaviors, and scores for tension. The team also built a test set where experts agreed on the labels together. Tests with the new labels show how hard the task is. Good training and scoring of computer models need real clinical skill.
arxiv-2506-01944:
Ademi Adeniji and seven co-authors teach robots force-sensitive touch by recording how human hands press and grip. Their paper from twenty twenty-five tackles fine force control in manipulation. Robot-gathered data and simulation both fail to cover real contact variety. Human demos scale well but video alone hides the forces. Their FeelTheForce system closes that gap with a tactile glove.

The glove gauges contact force while a vision model tracks hand pose. A closed-loop policy learns to predict the forces a task needs as it unfolds. Shared sight and action codes port the policy to a Franka arm with tactile grippers. A PD controller then tracks the predicted forces by gripper squeeze. Across five force-sensitive tasks, success rates run high. Code and videos are public.
arxiv-2506-02844:
Ahmad Jafar Arifi, Ho-Meoyng Choi, and Chueng-Ryong Ji computed properties of the rho meson in twenty twenty-five within a light-front quark model. The rho, a short-lived particle made of a quark and antiquark, has decay constants for its lengthwise and crosswise polarizations. Distribution amplitudes describe how its momentum is shared between its parts, order by order in a twist expansion.

Using the Bakamjian-Thomas construction, they extract both decay constants self-consistently from local and nonlocal matrix elements, regardless of current component, polarization, or frame. Nonlocal elements mix the two constants, and the construction resolves that mixing cleanly. They present amplitudes up to twist four, with their moment expansions. The results firm up the model's account of vector meson structure.
arxiv-2506-02944:
Sergey Bondarenko, Dima Cheskis, and Raghvendra Singh model the inside of a black hole as a gas of scalar quasiparticles split into two zones. A dense core sits inside a crust round it. Quasiparticle kinetics control both zones. The model is thermodynamic and effective. It aims at an interior one can grasp, not at a full treatment in quantum gravity.

In the core, quasiparticles carry no classical kinetic energy. So an energy functional that rests just on their number is in charge. Its conjugate variable, a quantity like inverse temperature, takes the place of ordinary temperature. It can push core pressure and energy density to negative values. Crust particles keep finite temperature but cannot escape, which truncates the phase-space integrals. The frame ties that thermodynamics explicitly to gravity.
arxiv-2506-03444:
Yue Gong and Raul Castro Fernandez take on a choke point in work by screen: to judge which found links of traits earn care. Tools now bring up links in their thousands with scant guide on which are new. Their thought is to ask a language model what link it would look for in a pair of traits. That turns what it knows into a first spread.

Their Logit-based Calibrated Prior turns raw model scores into a smooth spread that is set right. On a test set of 2,096 real world trait pairs, it hit near seventy-nine per cent on sign truth. Its doubt bands were set right as well. It beat a tuned sort tool at rank of claims. It held for links not in its train past. That hints at thought that heeds the case, not rote recall.
arxiv-2506-04944:
Spyros Galanis wrote a 2025 economics theory paper on when trade should not happen at all. Classic no-trade results say that rational traders who share the same starting beliefs cannot both expect to gain from a bet on an unknown outcome. Past work loosened rules about shared beliefs or perfect reasoning to explain real trading.

Galanis adds a fresh angle: what if private facts can be checked, so a claim about the true value can be verified by others? That checkable quality changes when deals can form. He draws lessons for insider trading rules, for thin markets with little trade, and for trading on public blockchains that use outside data feeds.
arxiv-2506-06544:
Sophia Drossopoulou, Julian Mackay, Susan Eisenbach, and James Noble wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about proving software correct when it calls outside code. Modern programs mix trusted inner code with untrusted outer code. Even if the outer code is unknown, the inner code must still be shown to behave.

The authors propose new ways to state what outside calls may and may not do. Their approach rests on limiting access: inner code stays safe if it hands out only the powers that are truly needed. They build a logic for checking that a module keeps its promises despite outside calls. A running example with machine-checked proofs shows the method, and they prove the logic itself is sound.
arxiv-2506-06644:
Chong You and co-authors present the Spark Transformer, a neural network design that wakes up the sparsity sleeping inside large language models, in a 2025 paper. In trained networks of this kind, most inner units stay silent for any given word, a fact called the lazy neuron effect. Older designs gained speed from that silence, but newer ones dropped the switch that caused it, and past attempts to restore it hurt quality or slowed training.

Spark keeps only the top few units active in each layer and in the attention step that weighs context. A fast statistical shortcut picks those units without slow sorting, and spare parts of the network are reused as a cheap scout that predicts which units will fire. The result is a model with sparsity under direct control that keeps its quality, size, and normal training routine while doing less work per word.
arxiv-2506-07144:
Konstantin Bliokh, Zeyu Kuang, and Stefan Rotter split wave scattering shifts into two parts in two thousand twenty five. Since Berry's work, physics has split the phase of a wave into a path part and a pace part. That split has guided work in quantum, optical, and condensed matter fields for decades. They take the same split past phase and apply it to shifts seen in scattering.

Shifts in frequency, momentum, and position get this two part split, read from input to output state. A generalized Wigner-Smith operator sums up how scattering responds, in slopes of the scattering matrix. Slopes of its eigenvalues give the dynamic part, and slopes of its eigenvectors give the geometric part. The split stays gauge invariant, and cases run from waveplates and metasurfaces to beam shifts and Wigner time delays.
arxiv-2506-09044:
Javier Sanguino Bautiste and co-authors expose a risk in 2025 when AI models shape the data they later learn from. A bank's loan model, for instance, changes how people apply, which changes future data. Past theory assumed the model an institution uses is the same one the public sees and reacts to.

The authors model the split case, where the shown model differs from the hidden one in real use. They prove the institution can gain lower risk this way than under the honest setup. They even give a method that reliably finds such gains, and a measure for the deception users bear. Adding a self-set cost for that deception did not protect users, so the authors call for outside rules.
arxiv-2506-10444:
Yujie Lin writes a short geometry note from two thousand twenty-five on K3 surfaces, a well studied class of shapes. Earlier work showed that a twist map along the edge of a pierced K3 surface is not trivial in the smooth mapping class group. The new question is what happens after a step called abelianization, which simplifies that group.

Lin proves that the twist becomes trivial after that step. The proof rests on a block for families of a certain type, due to earlier authors, and on a classic global theorem about K3 surfaces. The note is brief and aimed at specialists in smooth topology.
arxiv-2506-10644:
Emmet Byrne and co-authors rewrite, in a 2025 particle physics paper, the scattering formulas for quarks and gluons in a minimal set of light-front variables. These formulas govern how particles fly apart in high-energy crashes. The new variables fold in all motion rules at once and split lengthwise from sideways motion in a natural way.

That split makes fake poles easy to drop and extreme speed gaps easy to take. The team pulls out all emission rules for two, three, and four partons in the high-speed limit, both central and edge types. They ship the results as a software library. Links between formulas become links between the rules, which supply strong self-checks.
arxiv-2506-10744:
Yan, Qiu, and Zhang proposed a defense in twenty twenty-five against bit-flip attacks on deep neural networks. In such attacks, flipping a handful of bits in a model's stored numbers can wreck its accuracy or bend its answers, and most defenses guard only one attack type or one platform.

Their method, ObfusBFA, sprinkles random dummy operations into the model's running steps. The noise scrambles the attacker's careful aim, turning precise sabotage into random damage the model can shrug off. New algorithms pick where to place the decoy operations for the most protection. Tests covered attacks on both the model's weights and its program code, including attackers who spent extra flips to adapt. Accuracy held up across datasets and model designs, and attack success fell sharply. The cost was small: little delay and little extra storage.
arxiv-2506-11844:
Qihai Zhang, Xinyue Sheng, Yuanfu Sun, and Qiaoyu Tan stress-test GraphLLMs, models that pair graph structure with language model reasoning. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that robustness work on these hybrids is scarce. That gap is risky for high-stakes use. TrustGLM attacks the models from three sides: node text, graph structure, and the task prompt.

Top attack methods from each angle were run on six benchmark sets. Small word swaps in node text fooled models with ease. Classic structure attacks cut scores hard as well. Even shuffling the label order in a prompt caused steep drops. The team then tried defenses tuned per angle, through data-augmented and adversarial training. Both showed promise. Their code library is open for fair, fast follow-up tests.
arxiv-2506-12444:
Duc Toan Nguyen, Trang Tran, and Lam Nguyen present an optimization algorithm called Adjusted Shuffling SARAH. Their twenty twenty-five paper works on training problems where data are shuffled each pass, a common and effective practice. SARAH is a variance-reduced method that reuses past gradients to cut noise.

Their version folds shuffling into SARAH with a dynamic weighting that shifts how much each gradient counts. Two modes are analyzed. The exact mode matches the best known guarantees for such methods, in both convex and non-convex cases. The inexact mode uses mini-batches, and its total cost does not grow with the data set size, a big win at scale.
arxiv-2506-13044:
Muhammad Reza Qorib, Junyi Li, and Hwee Tou Ng settle a live argument about whether parallel text still matters for training multilingual language models. Big models translate surprisingly well without direct parallel training data. Some credit scale; others credit bilingual scraps hiding in the training mix. Decoder models often skip parallel data fully. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team runs controlled experiments on what adding sentence-aligned parallel data does. Two skills are tested: translation itself, and multilingual common-sense reasoning.

The verdict is clear in their tests. Parallel data greatly improves multilingual skill on both fronts. The gains come from planned matching, not from stray bilingual traces. The paper pushes back on the fashion of skipping curated parallel corpora when building multilingual systems.
arxiv-2506-13544:
François Copie, Pierre Suret, and Stéphane Randoux wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It steers light solitons, self-held wave packets, around a fiber loop with shaped phase patterns set from outside.

Solitons hold their shape because spread and nonlinearity cancel. That steadiness serves photonics, yet live control in clean systems has stayed hard. The team runs a recirculating fiber loop where timed phase shifts act as made landscapes for the waves. They trap a soliton, shake it in a tuned way, and set two solitons to act on each other. The waves behave like classical particles, just as a Hamiltonian view predicts. The likeness to matter-wave solitons in cold gases hints at wide use for wave studies.
arxiv-2506-14944:
Majid Khabbazian speeds up fair data exchange in two thousand twenty-five. The Fair Data Exchange protocol swaps files for pay in an atomic way. Its chain footprint is fixed and small. But proof checks in past builds took hours for modest files.

His first build cuts client checks to a cost set by a security knob, not file size. Checks take about a second on a plain desktop. Proof making speeds up by a huge factor too. The second build swaps bulk cipher work for a hash mask. That shrinks transfers from ten fold bloat to a small overhead. A bridge to Bitcoin's Lightning cuts fees to near nil.
arxiv-2506-16344:
Hendrik Roch and the JETSCAPE collaboration study how late-stage particle collisions reshape jets in nuclear experiments, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Jets are sprays of particles born in high-energy crashes, and they carry clues about the hot matter they cross. Whether the final, cooler phase of a crash alters those sprays was an open question.

The team ran a full event simulator with an added afterburner stage that lets the final particles rescatter. Even in the smallest system they tried, electron-positron crashes, the rescattering changed jet and particle measures in visible ways. The result suggests the late phase cannot be ignored when reading jet data from any system size.
arxiv-2506-16844:
Victor Alejandre, Concha Bielza, and Pedro Larrañaga studied a key tuning choice in semiparametric Bayesian networks in twenty twenty-five. These networks blend fixed-form probability models with flexible kernel density estimates. The kernel's bandwidth sets how smooth the estimate is, trading bias against variance. The standard choice, a normal rule, assumes the data are bell-shaped.

Real data often break that assumption, and estimates suffer. The authors set up the theory for modern bandwidth selectors and test them inside these networks, extending an open software package to do so. Cross-validation and plug-in selectors both used added data better than the normal rule, which stalls as samples grow. Unbiased cross-validation won most clearly at large sample sizes. The results guide practice for flexible probabilistic models.
arxiv-2506-20444:
Xiang Lan, Tim Menzies, and Bowen Xu present Smart Cuts for finding flaws in code in two thousand twenty-five. Active learning picks the most telling samples to label by hand. Labels for flaws are dear and need expert eyes. Past pickers lean on model doubt alone.

Smart Cuts adds dataset maps that flag hard to learn samples. Those bad seeds are pruned from the pool up front. The picker then hunts among learnable, telling cases. Tests on a known code model and flaw set show big F1 gains. Gains top both random picks and standard active picks. The method also steadies scores across rounds.
arxiv-2506-23344:
Difeng Cai and Paulina Sepúlveda built a self-supervised method in twenty twenty-five for locating singularities hidden in data from partial differential equations. Singularities — spikes, jumps, thin layers — wreck numerical accuracy, and adaptive solvers need to know where they are. In the data-driven setting the input may be nothing but mesh vertices, with no labels at all.

Their framework learns from a filtering pretext task: two filters, one based on nearest neighbors and one on kernel density estimation, clean the raw points before learning. The authors show raw unfiltered data can produce pathological or wrong locations. Experiments covered interior circles, boundary layers, and concentric semicircles, and the method tolerated input noise and label corruption. Reliable singularity maps are the first step toward cheaper, adaptive simulation.
arxiv-2507-01344:
Priyanshu Pant, Surabhi Chakrabartty, and Ranveer Singh prove a matrix theorem built around the permanent in a 2025 mathematics study. The determinant decides matrix rank through the largest square block with a non-zero value. Swapping in the permanent, a close cousin without sign changes, defines permanental rank, while permanental nullity counts a root multiplicity in a related polynomial.

Permanents are notoriously hard to compute, which makes structural results valuable. For symmetric matrices with non-negative entries, the authors show rank and nullity in the permanental sense add up to the matrix size. That mirrors the classic rank-nullity theorem and extends its reach.
arxiv-2507-01644:
Miguel O'Malley presents a new way to write step charts for the rhythm game Dance Dance Revolution on its own. The paper appeared in twenty twenty-five. In the game, a song comes with a chart of arrow steps, and players hit a dance pad in time. A past method from twenty seventeen used a mixed net to write charts with fair success.

The new method, called DDCL, is built on a ConvLSTM net that reads space and time traits at once. O'Malley reports that it writes charts with much higher accuracy than the past method. Fans who make custom songs are the clear users. The gain comes with no change to how charts are played.
arxiv-2507-01744:
Benjamin Jin, Grant Mair, Joanna Wardlaw, and Maria Valdes Hernandez train vision transformers to outline calcium deposits in brain arteries on head CT scans. Their paper came out in 2025. These deposits are a sign linked to stroke and dementia, and measuring them at scale could improve risk checks.

The models first learn from unlabeled scans by hiding patches and predicting them, a method that needs no costly hand labels. Fine-tuned models then beat a strong standard medical network by a clear margin on overlap score. Small patch sizes proved crucial for these tiny deposits. The models also coped better with thicker scan slices. Risk group sorting in a clinical scenario improved substantially.
arxiv-2507-02044:
Aurora Ireland, Kuver Sinha, and Tao Xu propose a new probe of the early universe in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Tiny ripples in the young cosmos, at scales too small for standard maps, are hard to measure. Current limits there are weak or rest on model assumptions.

Large ripples at second order stir up gravitational waves, which leave a pattern in the polarization of the cosmic microwave background. The authors compute that B-mode signal for boosted small-scale ripples. It could rival the signal expected from inflation for the values next-generation experiments target. Their map of future sensitivity beats current limits at the scales of interest. The work motivates B-mode searches at finer angular detail.
arxiv-2507-02844:
Ziqi Miao, Yi Ding, Lijun Li, and Jing Shao study a new way to trick large models that take both images and text. Their paper from two thousand twenty-five calls the setup a vision-centric jailbreak. Here the image is not just a trigger; it is a key part of a fake but real-seeming scene.

Their attack, named VisCo, builds false chat context with four image-based tricks. It can make extra images as needed, then hides toxic cues and polishes the wording. On a safety test set, VisCo beat a baseline by a wide margin against a top closed model. The work shows why image input needs strong safety checks before open use.
arxiv-2507-07944:
Miguel Casanova and Francesco Ticozzi published this quantum control study in 2025. Quantum systems lose their delicate states through contact with the environment, a process called decoherence. One defense is to find protected corners of the system where quantum information can hide. The authors propose a different arrangement. They actively control only a small mediating part, dubbed the wall subsystem, which faces most of the environmental noise.

Held in the right state, that controlled part acts as a quantum wall shielding the untouched logic part behind it. Because the logic part is never driven directly, normal operations stay simple. The scheme also combines well with other protections such as dynamical decoupling, and it improved those methods in tests. Under suitable conditions the shield keeps the system's purity above a floor forever. The authors link that lasting protection to the spectrum of the system as control strength grows.
arxiv-2507-08344:
Jihao Gu, Fei Wang, Kun Li, Yanyan Wei, Zhiliang Wu, and Dan Guo win a micro-gesture recognition contest by fusing many views of the hand, in a 2025 paper. Micro-gestures are tiny, brief movements that standard cameras easily miss. Their system, MM-Gesture, blends six streams: joint positions, limb shapes, plain video, two motion-enhanced video forms, and depth video. Two proven network designs read the streams, and a weighted vote combines them.

Pretraining the video stream on a larger gesture dataset sharpened it further. On the standard iMiGUE benchmark the system hit 73.2 percent top-one accuracy, taking first place in its challenge track at a major AI conference. Tests removing one stream at a time confirmed each added value. The code is public.
arxiv-2507-09644:
Lopez-Garcia and Valencia study leaf form in lone webs from shut one-forms on orbi-folds. A shut one-form of Morse type drives the web in the work. Its leaves are the sheets that stack in the orbifold space. Marks say when all such leaves pack shut in the set. Marks say when leaves run open, and when both kinds mix. Those marks form the core of the work's top claims.

A famed claim by Calabi gets stretched to orbi-folds as a use. That claim gives a pure form mark for shut sound one-forms. It holds for Morse-type forms in the orbifold frame here. The stretch shows how leaf form ties to the drive form. Both shut and open leaves can sit in one web.
arxiv-2507-09844:
Nahid Binandeh Dehaghani, A. Pedro Aguiar, and Rafal Wisniewski applied optimal control theory in 2025 to a core quantum task: creating entanglement between two qubits reliably and quickly. Entanglement powers quantum methods, yet steering a quantum system into a highly entangled state within a fixed time, using only bounded control signals, is hard by the system's delicate motion.

Using Pontryagin's Minimum Rule, the authors derive needed conditions that shape time-based control fields aimed at the maximally entangled Bell states. Success is scored by concurrence, a standard entanglement measure, tested at the final time. Models of the governing quantum motion show that switching-style control plans reach robust entanglement in practice. The work offers guidance for implementing entanglement generation in future quantum networks.
arxiv-2507-10044:
Shaohan Shi and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on an interactive system that lets physicians correct bias in artificial intelligence tools that classify medical images. Images can carry many labels at once, in imbalanced shares. That imbalance bends the predictions of the tool. Physicians who spot the bias usually have to go through engineering staff to fix it, which is slow.

Their system, MEDebiaser, lets the physician work with the model directly. It pairs each prediction with a plain explanation of why it was made, and it scores loss in a way that pulls the attention of the model to the right areas. A ranking strategy keeps the system fast as labels pile up. In user studies, physicians reduced bias with no coding skill needed. The team reports that the feedback loop became faster and more reliable, and the system was easier to use.
arxiv-2507-10544:
Amanda de Araujo-Carvalho and four co-authors warn that distant galaxies can look deceptively well behaved. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Spin curves trace how fast stars and gas orbit at each radius, and flat curves prove dark matter rules a galaxy's outskirts.

Some young galaxies seemed to show falling curves, hinting at less dark matter long ago. The team took nineteen nearby stand-in galaxies and faked how they would look at a far greater distance. Dimming and blur made the faked curves smoother and smaller in their lopsidedness. Real distant galaxies are more disturbed than they appear. The authors urge caution: such curves may not trace the true gravity of young galaxies.
arxiv-2507-11644: Olivier Gasquet writes a short comment in two thousand twenty-five on a claimed result about quasi-dense modal logics. A recent work had claimed to settle whether these logics are decidable and gave a space bound for the task. Gasquet argues that the proof holds a major flaw that cannot be fixed. On his reading, the question of decidability for these logics is open once more.
arxiv-2507-12744:
Cheng Liu and four co-authors build a light vision system that spots cables and other bendy thin objects for moving robots. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Loose floor cables are a real hazard for robots that roam halls and homes. Most past spotting tools assume a fixed top-down camera on a robot arm.

Their network, ASCNet, uses strip-shaped filters stretched at several scales. That shape suits long, thin targets and keeps the cost low. A sliding window step then cleans up false hits caused by shifting views. The hard part is the view gap: training views come from arms, but the robot sees from the floor. On real mobile robot data the system scored well and ran at high speed. It stays small enough for the weak chips on such robots.
arxiv-2507-12844:
Nitu, Mühle, and Stöckl test how AI web agents handle online advertising in this 2025 study. Agents that browse and buy for users meet pages designed for human eyes. The team built a faithful clone of a news site and filled it with varied ads.

They ran 300 trials plus follow-ups across four agent systems and ten realistic tasks. The ads included banners, animations, carousels, videos, cookie dialogs, and paywalls. Agents barely scrolled and ignored purely visual calls to action, clicking only when text labels or button overlays gave meaning. Worryingly, two systems subscribed in every trial when a sweepstake required purchase. The authors distill five design principles that make ads readable to machines without hurting human experience.
arxiv-2507-14244:
Arpad Benyi and Branko Curgus study rounding functions in a mathematics paper from twenty twenty-five. The floor of a number is the greatest whole number at or below it, and the ceiling is the smallest whole number at or above it. Prompted by a question in earlier work, they look at families of functions built from the floor that depend on a parameter. They work out exactly which values those functions can take. Rational and irrational parameter values turn out to behave very differently.

Pinning down the ranges takes serious tools, including a classic approximation theorem for irrational numbers. The authors separate the behavior of rational parameters below one from those above one, and they support the split with extensive computer calculations. They close with several conjectures about irrational and larger rational cases that remain open for other mathematicians to settle.
arxiv-2507-14344:
Daniel Fein and Gabriela Aranguiz-Dias tested influence functions in twenty twenty-five for pruning noisy human preference data. Preference data sets steer language model fine-tuning but contain harmful examples mixed with good ones. Influence functions estimate how much each training example moves performance on a validation set, if approximated cheaply enough to use.

Adapting a summarization data set for reward model training, they filtered examples with conjugate-gradient influence estimates. Removing the worst ten percent and retraining lifted accuracy by about one and a half points. A surprise: plain gradient similarity found helpful examples better than influence functions did. The authors read this as evidence that local curvature matters for spotting harmful examples, less so for finding helpful ones.
arxiv-2507-14544:
Sujata Gaihre, Amir Thapa Magar, Prasuna Pokharel, and Laxmi Tiwari describe their entry to a medical vision challenge in a twenty twenty-five paper. The task is visual question answering for gastrointestinal endoscopy: given an image from inside the gut, answer clinical questions about it. It was Subtask 1 of the MEDVQA 2025 challenge.

The team built their pipeline on Florence, a large multimodal foundation model, pairing its image encoder with a text encoder. They added domain-specific image augmentations that vary the training data without harming medical traits. Fine-tuning Florence on the Kvasir data set gave accurate answers on the official metrics. Code is public.
arxiv-2507-18244:
Hantaek Bae, Milton Lopes Filho, Anna Mazzucato, and Helena Nussenzveig Lopes prove long-time existence of smooth solutions for two fluid equations, in a two thousand twenty-five mathematics paper. The equations are the two-dimensional ideal Boussinesq system and the density-dependent incompressible Euler equations.

The results cover initial data with small temperature or density perturbations layered on smooth background flows that need not be small. Both theorems were already known from earlier work by Danchin, Fanelli, and others. The contribution here is the proof technique, which the authors describe as elementary at the same time as broadly applicable. Readers get a simpler route to results that matter for understanding long-lived two-dimensional flows.
arxiv-2507-19644:
Angela Monti, Fasma Diele, and Dante Kalise make optimal control feasible for very large agent-based models. Such models capture emergent behavior like consensus formation, but thousands of agents with rich states overwhelm control algorithms. Their framework reduces the model twice: clustering similar agents and projecting states using proper orthogonal decomposition.

The reduced model sits inside a feedback loop where optimal control laws are designed and applied. Tests use opinion dynamics, where agents influence each other through state-dependent functions. The method improves control efficiency substantially, succeeding in cases where direct control fails from complexity alone. The authors also note environmental applications, like steering pro-environmental attitudes, where shaping consensus matters.
arxiv-2507-20744:
Kreckel and co-authors, a team of seventeen astronomers, chart the metal content of nearby spiral galaxies in 2025. Metals here mean elements heavier than helium, built up by stars over time. How their share changes from a galaxy's center to its edge tells how galaxies grow and mix their gas.

The team used a catalog of close to twenty-three thousand glowing gas clouds across nineteen galaxies. A faint temperature-sensitive line let them infer metal levels directly for hundreds of clouds. Stacking many faint clouds by position recovered the same smooth trends. Most galaxies showed well-mixed gas with little scatter. A handful of clouds were oddly poor in metals, and spiral arms showed no clear offset from the gaps between them.
arxiv-2507-22044:
Niharika Tamuli and Saumen Acharjee study spin flow in a graphene device in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Their device is a zigzag graphene nanoribbon with three terminals. Graphene ribbons can carry electron spin in ways that suit future low-power chips. The authors model how spin-polarized current moves through the ribbon when it travels without scattering. They use a tight binding model and a standard quantum transport method.

They vary the ribbon's width and length and add an out-of-plane magnetic field. Without magnetism, the flow depends strongly on ribbon size and edge states. With the field on, the device can pass one spin and block the other, acting like a spin filter. Narrow ribbons show this effect best. The results guide the design of graphene spin devices.
arxiv-2507-22144:
Miroslav Grmela, a solo author, compares three frameworks for modeling how complex fluids flow in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Rheology is the study of how materials such as polymer solutions flow and change shape. The first framework rests on the conservation of mass, momentum, and energy that comes from mechanics.

The second rests on how fluids left alone settle toward states of balance well described by thermodynamics. The third rests on a rule of least resistance to outside forces. Grmela works through the comparison with polymeric fluids held at one temperature that cannot be compressed. He weighs what each view takes for granted and what each can deliver. The result is a guide for researchers who must pick a base for flow models of complex fluids.
arxiv-2507-23344:
Tatsuya Mitomi and co-authors set dynamic prices for bike share systems with a fast agent based simulation, in work from twenty twenty-five. Bike share stations fill or empty as trips vary by place and hour. Moving bikes by truck costs money, so smart prices could steer riders instead.

Their simulation can be tuned by gradient methods, which speeds the search for good prices. In a test with twenty-five stations, the method cut loss by about three quarters and ran more than a hundred times faster than rivals. In a city scale test with near three hundred stations, prices balanced stock on their own. No truck moves were needed. Careful start settings kept discount costs low.
arxiv-2508-00544:
Joonas Tapaninaho and Mourad Oussalah propose a way to build language models faster by training small parallel paths first and merging them afterward. Even small modern language models can take days and several graphics cards to train. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the authors design a transformer variant in which several narrower paths run side by side and combine into one wider model. Each path can be trained on its own, even on different kinds of text, and the paths are then joined into the final network.

In their tests, the merged model reached better performance with fewer total parameters and less training time than a comparable single model trained in the usual way. The layout also invites customization, since a path could be tuned for a specific task before merging. The authors present the approach as a practical route to cheaper, more flexible model building.
arxiv-2508-00944:
Mahsa Shirmohammadi and James Worrell settle, in a 2025 math paper, a decision problem for a broadened family of number sequences. Nearly linear recurrences extend the classic linear kind and show up in control systems and program loops. The question is whether every sequence obeying the rule, from given starting values, stays non-negative at every term.

The pair give a working decision method for the second-order case. Its halting rests on a number theory result of wider interest. They prove that certain sums built from linear recurrence terms are transcendental, a fact that seals the method's soundness. The problem links program checking with deep facts about numbers.
arxiv-2508-01344:
Sruthiranjani Ravikularaman, Sarah Recchia, Vo Hong Minh Phan, and Stefano Gabici ask whether cosmic rays explain the unusually high ionization rates near the Galactic centre, in a two thousand twenty-five astrophysics paper. The Central Molecular Zone shows hydrogen ionization far above anywhere else in the Galaxy.

Dense gas there absorbs electromagnetic radiation, leaving low-energy cosmic rays as the only plausible ionizing agents. Yet no matching gamma-ray excess from high-energy cosmic rays is seen. The authors derive injection spectra from gamma-ray and radio data, add trial low-energy components, and propagate them numerically. In every scenario the energy needed to sustain the observed ionization is excessively high, so cosmic rays cannot be the whole story.
arxiv-2508-02744:
A team at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign wrote a survey in twenty twenty-five on agents built from large language models for data science work. The authors listed in the text are Ke Chen, Peiran Wang, Yaoning Yu, Xianyang Zhan, and Haohan Wang. The survey pulls together many recent studies in one place.

The team looks at the topic from two sides. From the agent side, they cover roles, how tasks are run, what the agent knows, and how it checks its own work. From the data side, they cover cleaning data, building models, testing them, and making charts. The goal is a clear map of a fast-growing field.
arxiv-2508-03544:
Anna Ashkinazi and co-authors trace how particle twist picks the handedness of liquid crystal phases. Bent rod molecules form a twist-bend phase where the alignment corkscrews through space. A twist built into each rod breaks the tie between left and right forms. Simulations and density theory follow the phase lineup as packing tightens.

The same-handed twist-bend phase wins fast as particle twist grows. Rods nestle along the helix lines and pack tighter that way. The cholesteric phase, by contrast, takes the opposite handedness. Weak particle twist explains that flip. A pinch of chiral rods in an achiral bath also steers the whole phase's hand.
arxiv-2508-03644:
Wenxuan Shen and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper that asks whether the benchmarks for document retrieval tools are fit for the job. Such tools fetch texts, then have a large model summarize them. Their benchmarks often measure one part of the chain, on synthetic data with thin ground truth. Real bottlenecks go unseen.

The team built a new benchmark set: over three thousand documents, in six languages and four document types, with over five thousand questions. The evidence pages for each question were scanned exhaustively and verified by hand. Runs of nine retrieval tools, four large models, and four full systems fill the study. Retrieval tools that read images close the gap on text ones. One flaw stood out: systems often answer with no evidence in hand, too confident in themselves.
arxiv-2508-03844:
Deepayan Banik, Kristen Menou, and Evan Anders wrote a 2025 paper on slow flows inside stars and planets. Meridional circulation is a vast loop that carries material from equator to pole and back. It moves angular momentum, which shapes how a body spins over time.

Inside layered bodies, gradients in molecular weight can resist this flow. The team extends a principle from atmospheric science, downward control, to cover this composition effect. Their math shows stable composition gradients slow how deep the flow sinks. Extra effects, like turbulence or magnetic fields, would be needed to stop it fully. The work sharpens models of how stars and planets evolve.
arxiv-2508-04344:
Charalampos Kleitsikas, Stefanos Leonardos, and Carmine Ventre give a mathematical form to performativity in market making in this 2025 paper. Performativity means a financial model shapes the market it claims only to describe. Prices drift toward what the dominant model predicts, a self fulfilling loop. Sociology discussed the idea, but markets lacked a formal model of it.

Their model embeds the financial model inside the price process itself, closing the feedback loop. Closed form solutions show how conformity grows over time. A performative market maker can infer the dominant strategies from prices. It can then arbitrage them while keeping quotes competitive and profits high. Machine learning checks support the theory. The paper bridges market microstructure and economic sociology.
arxiv-2508-04944:
Barnes and co-authors lay out Gen3, a free tool set for shared data banks. A data bank is a cloud home where a group holds, works, and shares data. Gen3 has built more than a dozen such banks to date. In sum they hold past 28 PB of data in store. Near 64 million fair-use data parts sit in those banks. To start a bank, a team first sets its data shape.

Gen3 then builds three parts on its own from that shape. One part lets users search and browse the bank holdings. One part lets users send new data in clean form. One part gives fair code paths for machine reads of data. A small set of stock parts sits under all banks. That base lets banks trade data with peer tools.
arxiv-2508-05844:
François Bachoc and three co-authors allocate budgets under uncertainty in twenty twenty-five. A learner must split a budget across many tasks each round. Each task succeeds with a probability that grows with its funding in an unknown way. Success brings a random reward, but the reward is visible only when the task succeeds.

That censored semi-bandit feedback models real settings. Splitting payments among crowdsourcing workers is one example. Distributing bids across simultaneous auctions is another. The authors design an optimism-based algorithm for the setting. In diminishing-returns regimes, its regret grows only polylogarithmically with time, without ad hoc tuning. General curves get their own analysis. Readers get a principled way to fund many uncertain tasks at once.
arxiv-2508-07544:
Bo Wang, Shaohang Luo, Zikuan Wang, and Wenjian Liu present, in twenty twenty-five, a fast algorithm to compute molecular Hessians, the matrices of second derivatives that give vibration frequencies. The standard seminumerical route needs energy gradients at a number of displaced shapes that grows with atom count. Their method, O1NumHess, needs only a constant number. The trick rests on a structural fact: Hessian blocks for distant atom groups have low rank, so the matrix has far fewer free entries than its size suggests.

A constant-size set of gradients then pins the Hessian down uniquely. Tests on alkanes, polyenes, metal reactions, and non-covalent complexes show errors only about twice those of the conventional method. The new method is always faster than the conventional one, often faster than analytic Hessians.
arxiv-2508-07644:
Yue Zhang, Xing Ji, and Kun Xu push a gas-kinetic flow solver toward the everyday jobs of aerodynamic engineering. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The method builds flows from a kinetic equation rather than the usual fluid equations. That gives it a unified grip on thin and thick flow effects, plus built-in control of numerical smearing.

Three upgrades carry the work. The solver now runs in rotating frames, so turbine and compressor flows can be tackled. An implicit stepping scheme, solved with an iterative method, removes the speed penalty of the explicit version. A standard turbulence model is coupled in for industrial flows. Tests cover a compressor rotor and flow over a full wing-body shape. The wing case settled in a few hundred steps on millions of cells.
arxiv-2508-07844:
Yadav and five co-authors modeled light nuclei production in this paper from twenty twenty-five. When lead nuclei collide at the LHC, loose protons and neutrons can stick into deuterons. Their model, called thermo-coalescence, treats the nucleons as born from a hot, expanding source. A coalescence rule then joins near neighbors into nuclei.

First the team fit proton momentum data with a blast-wave model of the expansion. The fitted heat and flow values fed the deuteron predictions, with two added joining parameters. A Bayesian fit pinned down the best values across the data. Total deuteron yields matched the ALICE measurements. The authors also recover the standard coalescence factor inside their framework for comparison.
arxiv-2508-08244:
Jingwen He and co-authors teach a video model the grammar of film editing in a 2025 paper. Anyone can generate a single pretty shot now; stringing shots into cinema is harder. Real editing follows patterns, like cutting between two speakers or slipping in a cutaway, and keeps strict continuity of place and motion. Current generators mostly chase surface consistency and miss that grammar.

Their framework, Cut2Next, defines the task as next shot generation and builds a diffusion transformer for it. A layered prompting scheme steers the model: broad prompts set the scene context and the editing relation between shots, while per-shot prompts fix content and camera choices. In-context tuning lets the model learn from the shot it must follow. The aim is generated film that an editor would recognize as editing.
arxiv-2508-10444:
Herun Wan and five co-authors present DiFaR, a frame that makes text reasons from large vision language models more varied, true, and on point, to aid fake news spotting. Such reasons now back trainable detectors, but they can be samey, false, or off topic. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

DiFaR uses five chain style prompts to draw varied thought traces from the models. A light filter then picks reason lines by their truth and fit scores at the sentence level. Tests on four known sets beat four rival groups of methods by clear margins and boosted live detectors as well. Human checks backed the gains in reason quality.
arxiv-2508-12244:
Fan Li and four co-authors present a benchmark for deep hypergraph learning in twenty twenty-five. Graphs link things in pairs, but many real systems join things in larger groups. Hypergraphs can model those group links, called higher-order interactions. Neural networks built for hypergraphs have grown fast in recent years.

Growth came without shared test rules, so results are hard to compare. Toolkits exist, but they cover few methods, data sets, and tasks, with thin results. DHG-Bench is offered as the first full benchmark for this field. It aims to give fair tests across many methods and tasks. Readers get a base for judging which hypergraph methods truly work best.
arxiv-2508-13144:
David Heineman and co-authors borrow a radio engineer's frame for judging language model tests, in a 2025 paper. Builders choose between models using small tests, yet many benchmarks wobble from run to run. The authors split a benchmark's worth into signal, its power to separate good models from bad, and noise, its jitter between training steps.

They show that tests with a better signal-to-noise balance give more reliable small-scale decisions and tighter forecasts of large-scale results. Three fixes follow: pick scoring metrics with cleaner signal, drop subtasks that mostly add jitter, and report uncertainty plainly. One example swaps raw accuracy for a smoother measure. The frame gives benchmark designers concrete dials to turn instead of gut feel.
arxiv-2508-13244:
Giordano, Bonazzi, Benini, and Magno presented an eye tracking system in twenty twenty-five that runs on a small, low-power microcontroller. Eye tracking follows where a person looks, but fast eye movements demand very quick sensing. Their system is built for devices such as smart glasses, where power and space are tight.

The system uses an event-based vision sensor that reacts to change in about two hundred microseconds. A compact neural network, tuned to the sensor and chip, predicts the pupil position. Its average error was about six pixels on a standard test set. The full process took under four hundred microseconds per step while using very little energy, showing real-time tracking can fit on tiny hardware.
arxiv-2508-13644:
Viktoria Koscinski, Mark Nelson, Ahmet Okutan, Robert Falso, and Mehdi Mirakhorli compare four systems that score software flaws in two thousand twenty-five. Scores guide which flaws to fix first, but the systems aim at distinct goals and often disagree. No large study had tied their scores to real outcomes.

The team built a set of six hundred real flaws from four months of Microsoft patch releases. They checked how the four scores relate, how each sorts flaws into triage tiers, and how well each tracks real exploit risk. The systems ranked the same flaws in far apart ways. The authors urge clearer, more consistent ways to grade severity and risk.
arxiv-2508-14144:
David Dickson brought in a model plan in 2025 for astrophysical flows that last too long to mimic. And applied it to Roche lobe overflow, where one star in a binary spills gas onto its partner. The new method, called TIME, alternates between short bursts of full 3D hydrodynamics and fast evolutionary modeling, adjusting its time resolution as it goes. And it works independently of the particular model code used inside the bursts.

Dickson made the first grid-based 3D time-domain model of the process, using the VH-1 code, and tested it on the massive X-ray binary M33 X-7. There, mass transfer stayed stable and non-conservative only below a key overflow level. Past it, transfer turned unstable yet fully conservative, beginning on thermal timescales and accelerating to completion within a century at higher overflow, a sharp shift with clear observational meaning.
arxiv-2508-14444: A large NVIDIA team described in twenty twenty-five a compact reasoning model that blends two net kinds, Mamba and Transformer, in one build. The re-port frames the model as both sharp in its answers and cheap to run. Hybrid builds aim to keep long-text grip while cut-ting the cost of the plain Transformer path.
arxiv-2508-15144:
Jiabo Ye and co-authors introduce a model that lets computers run phones and desktops by reading screens, in a 2025 paper. Their base model, GUI-Owl, looks at an interface, plans steps, and picks where to tap or type. The team also built Mobile-Agent-v3, a framework that uses the model to finish full tasks.

The model was trained with a self-improving loop in cloud copies of Android, Ubuntu, macOS, and Windows. It writes practice tasks, tries them, checks the results, and refines its own training data. On public tests the framework beat other open systems on both phone and desktop tasks. The authors release it as a base for building helpful screen agents.
arxiv-2508-15444:
Miha Ožbot and Igor Škrjanc propose a fast way to tell when data clusters overlap, in a research paper from 2025. The setting is online learning from data streams, where models must adapt as the data drift over time. Clustering on streams can spawn many groups that partly cover each other and should be merged.

Standard measures compare how unlike two distributions are, but they miss some cluster shapes and cost a lot to compute. The new measure aims straight at overlap for clusters shaped as multivariate Gaussians. It runs several times faster than the methods compared. Tests showed it catches truly overlapping clusters while sparing pairs that cross at right angles and should stay apart.
arxiv-2508-16444:
Benjamin Avanzi, Yanfeng Li, Greg Taylor, and Bernard Wong brought climate change into a key insurance tool. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with Dynamic Financial Analysis for general insurers. This tool gives a full view of money risks over time. But its classic form leaves out climate change, which will move both the physical and money worlds. The team stretched the steady form to hold climate risk.

Their frame tracks how climate shifts hit both what insurers own and what they owe. It spans the physical and economic sides across long spans. Readers who run or rule insurers get a base build for firm level climate checks. The work helps the trade face a slow but deep risk.
arxiv-2508-16944:
Li and Li present a paper from twenty twenty-five on how node centrality choice affects stability in energy flow networks. Such networks include power grids, transport systems, and finance webs. Picking critical nodes for intervention is key to control, yet high complexity hampers the choice. Many centrality scores exist, from Katz to PageRank variants. Their impact on stability outcomes was poorly understood. The team build a unified energy-flow dynamics model for tests. Simulations span small-world, scale-free, and random network families.

Stability outcomes vary widely with the centrality metric chosen. Even small ranking shifts sway results in their runs. The authors stress care in metric selection for real systems. Their findings aim at stronger control and robustness in practice.
arxiv-2508-17344:
Rajrupa Chattaraj and co-authors race two programming languages on green computing grounds in a 2025 study. Machine learning is everywhere in modern software, but training and running models burn real energy and emit real carbon. Accuracy and speed get studied endlessly; the power bill rarely does. The authors ask a pointed question for the two favorite languages of data work: R versus Python.

They measured energy use and run time for five machine learning algorithms across both languages, in training and in use. The exploratory study is less about crowning a winner than about making the cost visible. Language choice is usually made on libraries and habit, never on watts. Results of this kind give teams a new axis for decisions, and they nudge the field to report energy alongside accuracy.
arxiv-2508-18344:
TaeHun Kim, Philip Lu, and Volodymyr Takhistov set bounds on a zoo of dark stuff picks. The work came out in 2025. They watch how the picks would heat gas among the stars. The picks are spread-out dense goods: axion stars, Q-balls, and axion mini-clumps. It holds dark fermion stars and first black holes dressed in dark stuff rings.

As such a good plows through gas, its pull raises a wake at its back. If the good is dense enough, it draws in a flow of gas. Both acts dump heat into the gas. The frame beats old drag work in four ways. It adds finite size, in-side bulk marks, gas that passes through the good, and rules for when a disk of drawn gas forms. Sims of the heat are used on the Leo T dwarf star group.
arxiv-2508-20644:
Andronikos Paliathanasis and colleagues test whether a quantum correction to the uncertainty principle can replace or rival the standard model of the universe. If nature has a smallest measurable length, the equations of cosmic expansion change slightly, adding two adjustable numbers to the usual dark energy picture. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team builds that modified cosmology and checks that it returns to the standard model when the corrections vanish. They then fit it to cosmic chronometer data, the latest baryon acoustic oscillation results, and two supernova catalogs.

The modified model fit the combined data about as well as the standard model, and better on some subsets. The data pushed the main correction number negative, which acts like phantom dark energy that grows stronger over time. The authors present the framework as a live competitor worth sharper tests.
arxiv-2508-21544:
Del Castillo, Ferrón, and Fernández-Rossier show how a faint touch at one end of a spin chain can flip the state at the far end. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The chain is of the Haldane kind, whose ends hold split spin states. The team draws a four-level model that holds the chain's response to local prods. A small field at one edge drives a large swing in the pull at the far edge. With a slow sweep plan, that local knob can flip the far edge's pull in a set way. A spin-tuned scope tip could do the job in a lab. The work shows control at a distance in a quantum chain.
arxiv-2509-00044:
Mohammad Salehpour and five co-authors track Ostwald ripening of trapped gas in underground storage in 2025. Ripening is a drift where large bubbles grow at the cost of small ones, driven by surface curve. Stored gases, from carbon dioxide held for climate aims to hydrogen held for seasons, sit as trapped clusters in rock pores.

Fine microfluidic tests, which run fluids through tiny channels, watch trapped hydrogen evolve over weeks in realistic pore shapes. A fast first stage evens out nearby bubbles. A slow second stage then drains gas toward low-energy edges over long range. Clear stages over long spans help forecast where stored gas will drift and whether it stays put.
arxiv-2509-00144:
Reinaldo Francener, Victor P. Goncalves, and Diego R. Gratieri study nuclear effects in lepton-ion scattering at the Large Hadron Collider in 2025. Leptons are light particles such as muons and neutrinos. When they strike a heavy nucleus at high energy, the hit probes the nucleus's inner parts, a method called deep inelastic scattering.

Far-forward detectors at the collider can catch muon and neutrino hits on tungsten. The team estimates rates for broad hits and for hits that tag a charm quark in the debris. Varied models of nuclear parton distributions, which map how momentum is shared inside a nucleus, feed the rates. Muon and neutrino hits probe complementary ranges, so a joint study can test if distribution rules are universal.
arxiv-2509-00444:
Jin Cao, working with one co-author, Xiaoyu Su, studies a map linked to the Frobenius map, a tool that raises coordinates to a power in positive characteristic. Their subject is bundles, families of vector spaces tied to a curve, grouped in a moduli space, a space whose points stand for bundles of fixed rank and degree.

Cao and Su show that pulling back a typical semi-stable bundle, meaning a bundle that stays balanced under the test used here, by the Frobenius map keeps it semi-stable.
