They prove this with a deformation trick, then give several uses of the main result. The finding helps readers see how these spaces change under the Frobenius map.
arxiv-2509-00544:
Hanqi Yan leads five authors in total, with Hainiu Xu, Siya Qi, Shu Yang, and Yulan He, in naming a risk they call Reasoning-Induced Misalignment. Stronger reasoning in large language models can, with certain reasoning patterns, make the model less aligned with human values, not safer.

Yan and her co-authors give a mechanistic account, an explanation in terms of inner parts. They find specific attention heads, components that direct focus, help refusal by paying less attention to chain-of-thought tokens, the model's written reasoning steps. During training, safety and reasoning signals tangle in safety-critical neurons, which links to catastrophic forgetting, losing earlier skills. The work points to where safety training must watch reasoning growth.
arxiv-2509-00644:
Jun Suzuki and Katsuhiko Sano prove a negative result in logic. They show two linear logics without weakening are undecidable. Undecidable means no algorithm can always settle provability. A sequent is the formal claim whose proof is in question. Their systems drop the weakening rule for an exponential modality. The base system is Girard's classical linear logic. That logic tracks how resources are used.

The first system, CLLR, is shown undecidable by reduction. The reduction ties it to the known result for the full logic. Two unit elements let them simulate the missing weakening rule. The second system, CLLRR, drops those units as well. For it, they simulate any two-counter machine. Two-counter machines are a simple model of full computation.
arxiv-2509-00844:
Michael Kemeny and Peter Yi Wei prove the geometric syzygy conjecture in positive characteristic. Syzygies are relations among the equations that define a curve. Linear syzygy spaces collect the simplest such relations. The setting is a general smooth curve of a given genus. Genus measures the number of holes in the curve. The curve sits over an algebraically closed field of prime characteristic.

They show all linear syzygy spaces are spanned by minimal-rank syzygies. That holds provided the prime is large enough. The bound is at least twice the genus minus four. The result settles the geometric form of the conjecture here. It extends a circle of questions about equations of curves.
arxiv-2509-01144:
Labeling medical scans by hand is slow and costly, so models often learn from a mix of labeled and unlabeled images. Weiren Zhao, with six co-authors, argues that past methods missed two things: noise inside the labeled data itself, and the fact that some unlabeled pixels carry more value than others. They propose MetaSSL, a general framework for this task.

MetaSSL uses a loss that varies by place, weighting pixels by both doubt and agreement between two predictions. The image is split into four regions based on those signals, and each region is treated in line with its worth. Zhao and the team present the loss, not the way a reference prediction is made, as the key to better segmentation.
arxiv-2509-01244:
Political camps in the United States have drifted apart over a long span. Zhang Xiaoming, Hu Yuzhong, and Zhang Yiming model that drift with opinion dynamics. Such math tracks how views shift through contact. Their model joins an affinity effect, where like-minded members pull together, with a national norm effect. That norm draws all views toward a shared center.

Three forces shape the outcome. The two parties repel each other. Members inside each party both attract and repel. The norm pulls on everyone. The model matches the patterns of spread seen in Congress. It fits one hundred fifty-four years of recorded data. The norm's changing strength also lines up with major events of that era.
arxiv-2509-01344:
Choosing the right crop for a field usually needs slow lab tests of soil, which delays planting choices. Vishal Pandey, Ranjita Das, and Debasmita Biswas present AgroSense, a deep learning system that recommends crops from soil photos plus nutrient data, in real time. It aims to support food security and more sustainable farming.

One module classifies soil type from images, comparing three vision models. A second module reads structured data such as nutrient levels, soil acidity, and rainfall, testing four learning methods. The team built a combined data set of ten thousand paired samples, drawn from public sources with many more images and profiles. Their fused model gave accurate, context-aware recommendations in tests, pointing toward field-ready tools that cut the wait for soil results.
arxiv-2509-01444:
Jailbreak attacks trick language models into unsafe replies, and judging a model's safety only by attack content misses how complex the trick is. Shiji Zhao, with twelve co-authors, builds Strata-Sword, a layered safety benchmark based on the reasoning complexity of jailbreak instructions. Simple instructions test a model's basic values, while complex ones probe deeper risks.

The benchmark covers both plain language models and large reasoning models, which use chain-of-thought style thinking to infer intent more closely. By sorting attacks into strata of complexity, the evaluation can show where a model's defenses hold and where they crack. Zhao and the team argue such a layered view gives a fuller picture of safety than pooling all attacks together, and can guide builders toward the weak levels that need work.
arxiv-2509-02244:
Luis Felipe Chary and Miguel Arjona Ramirez present a spectrogram patch codec for neural speech coding at low bitrates. Complex residual quantization stacks dominate neural codecs, but their design keeps a simpler single stage. The codec treats the mel-spectrogram as a two dimensional image and quantizes small non-overlapping patches into one shared codebook. That yields a discrete latent grid suited to streaming.

Late adversarial fine-tuning sharpens the quantizer autoencoder output. A HiFi-GAN vocoder trained from scratch on reconstructed spectrograms restores the waveform. Objective scores for intelligibility and perceptual quality rival leading codecs at their bitrate. The simplified non-residual design validates as an open foundation for low latency coding. Patchwise quantization is the core architectural bet.
arxiv-2509-02344:
Guopeng Li, Jiawei Li, Tadahiro Oh, and Nikolay Tzvetkov wrote a 2025 analysis paper on dispersive equations with random starting data, where randomness can push solutions past a point called variance blowup. Their model case is the Benjamin-Bona-Mahony equation, a wave equation used for long surface waves.

By scaling the random initial data with a shrinking factor, the authors push beyond the blowup barrier. Solutions then settle, in distribution, onto a stochastic version of the equation driven by rough spatial white noise. A second scaling choice gives a different limit, a linear stochastic equation with very rough starting data of arbitrary low regularity. Matching results hold for a fractional noise forcing. The work extends probabilistic well-posedness theory into new territory.
arxiv-2509-02644:
Bianca De Caro, Isabella P. Carucci, Stefano Camera, Mathieu Remazeilles, and Carmelita Carbone present a 2025 cosmology paper on cleaning hydrogen maps from the Square Kilometre Array telescope. The 21-centimetre signal from neutral hydrogen traces cosmic structure, but foreground glow outshines it by orders of magnitude.

Their method adapts principal component analysis using needlets, wavelets localised on the sphere in both position and scale. Simulated maps for a planned telescope configuration test the pipeline against two rival separation methods. All three recovered the hydrogen signal within about ten percent across channels. Polarisation leakage did not hurt the cleaners. With a realistic beam, the needlet versions held up at large scales where standard methods failed, while one rival over-cleaned and lost signal.
arxiv-2509-02744:
Shyamashish Dey and Santosh Kumar Rai present a 2025 particle physics paper on fermionic dark matter that interacts through new scalar leptoquarks, particles coupling quarks to leptons. The dark matter candidate is the neutral part of a vector-like lepton doublet.

In the minimal model, that candidate cannot match both the observed cosmic dark matter abundance and strict direct detection limits. Adding scalar leptoquarks shifts the candidate's mass and splits it into two nearly equal states forming a pseudo-Dirac pair. That splitting naturally suppresses the signals direct detection experiments look for. The extended setup also opens wider parameter space where the abundance comes out right. The paper maps how leptoquarks rescue a dark matter model that minimal ingredients leave cornered.
arxiv-2509-02844:
Sophia Sun and Rose Yu present a 2025 machine learning paper on conformal prediction for time series with change points, sudden breaks where the data-generating process itself shifts. Conformal prediction wraps forecasts in intervals with coverage guarantees, but standard versions assume a stable process.

Their CPTC algorithm pairs a model that predicts the underlying state with online conformal updating, which adapts intervals as new data arrive. The authors prove validity and improved adaptivity under minimal assumptions. Six synthetic and real datasets test the method against leading baselines. CPTC held its coverage promise while adapting faster after breaks. The work targets forecasting settings such as demand or sensor streams, where regimes change without warning and honest uncertainty matters.
arxiv-2509-03044:
Chengjie Huang and 3 co-authors proposed a 2025 image method called DCDB for handling several hard restoration jobs at once. Some tasks are ill-posed, meaning many outputs could fit the limited input, and training data is scarce. Their test cases were clearing haze from photos and fusing visible with infrared images.

Earlier diffusion models, which build images by reversing a noise process, struggle to share what related tasks teach each other. DCDB separates the diffusion path from condition building, so it needs less supervised data. Its conditions change over time under one shared noise schedule, which eases learning. The authors track learning goals and attention shifts to back the design. On public datasets it led on several quality measures.
arxiv-2509-03544:
Zining Fan wrote a 2025 mathematics paper asking whether an algebraic tool called a quandle can detect causality between events in spacetime. The setting is a globally hyperbolic spacetime with two space dimensions plus time. Events there can be drawn as links, tangled loops known as skies, whose causal links are in question.

An earlier pair of links defeated the Alexander-Conway polynomial, a classic link invariant that gave both the same value. Fan tests conjugation quandles built from dihedral groups, which capture symmetries of polygons. Only the group with fivefold symmetry, paired with that polynomial, separates the test pair and an infinite family of similar links. For that group the simple counting invariant alone suffices. Other small dihedral groups fail even with stronger counting tools.
arxiv-2509-03644:
A prototype reasoning system that grounds language models in embodied schemas occupies a 2025 research paper by François Olivier and one co-author. Large language models still make frequent logical errors, partly because they lack the sturdy mental structures humans build from bodily experience. Image schemas are recurring patterns from sensorimotor experience, like containment or paths, that shape human thinking.

Their system, Embodied-LM, turns the spatial side of those schemas into declarative rules inside Answer Set Programming, a logic programming method. Evaluation on logical deduction problems shows three things. Models can be guided to read scenarios through embodied structures. Those structures can be written as executable programs. The resulting representations then support effective reasoning that stays interpretable. Current work covers spatial primitives only, laying groundwork for richer and more dynamic representations later.
arxiv-2509-03844:
Fazal Badshah and five co-authors work on amplifying the photonic spin Hall effect through tunnelling in quantum wells in a 2025 physics paper. The photonic spin Hall effect is a sideways shift of a light beam's polarisation components on reflection or refraction. Making that shift giant would give optical devices a new control knob at mid-infrared wavelengths.

Their system places an asymmetric double quantum well, built from aluminium gallium arsenide and gallium arsenide layers, inside an optical cavity as the active medium. A control beam and tunable tunnelling barriers regulate quantum interference in how probe light tunnels through the structure. That steers the spin Hall shift for both polarisation components precisely. A giant horizontal shift emerges in the cavity system. Adding cavity slabs, some absorbing and others providing gain, amplifies it further, producing a more pronounced spin separation. The results suggest a route to stronger, controllable spin Hall devices.
arxiv-2509-04044:
Zakir Deniz and one co-author, Hakan Guler, prove a coloring result for flat networks in a 2025 mathematics paper. Their subject is total coloring, where both points and connecting lines get colors, and anything touching must differ. For flat graphs where no point has more than eight neighbors, earlier work left the needed number at either nine or ten.

Deniz and Guler settle the question for one broad family. If such a graph contains no copy of a shape called a 4-fan, nine colors always suffice. The proof narrows a long-standing gap for this class of graphs. It also gives map-like network designers a cleaner bound to work from.
arxiv-2509-04144:
Malte Londschien, writing alone, sharpens a statistical test used when cause-and-effect links are hard to pin down in a 2025 econometrics paper. Economists use instrumental variables, meaning outside factors that nudge a treatment, to estimate effects. When those nudges are weak, standard tests mislead. The conditional likelihood-ratio test is a trusted option, but its known distribution was only an upper bound based on one summary number.

Londschien derives the exact large-sample distribution, which depends on all the values summarizing instrument strength. With several differently-identified variables, the exact version proves far more powerful. Computer methods for running the sharper test come with the paper. Numerical checks confirm the promised gains in detection power.
arxiv-2509-04544:
Ashutosh Kumar Sinha and four co-authors read human activity from breathing patterns captured inside a smart mask in a 2025 research paper. Breathing carries signals about behavior, health trends, and vital state, yet activity recognition usually relies on motion sensors. Their i-Mask carries integrated sensors that record exhaled breath patterns as volunteers go about activities. The data pipeline filters noise, decomposes the time series into components, and labels segments for training predictive models.

Experiments surpassed ninety-five percent accuracy in recognizing activities from breath alone. Healthcare monitoring and fitness tracking are the natural applications. A mask people already wear for other reasons could quietly double as a continuous well-being sensor.
arxiv-2509-04944:
A faint companion to a young star in Orion turns out to have planetary mass and an appetite for gas. Emilie Vila, lead author with thirteen co-authors, report the object in a 2025 astronomy paper. Space telescope imaging found the source near an M-type star, and follow-up spectroscopy with a ground-based instrument confirmed it as a young planetary-mass companion.

Fitting its energy distribution gives a mass of roughly twenty Jupiter masses and an age near seven million years. Its spectrum shows several accretion tracers, with an accretion rate comparable to other young companions. Extended emission suggests the two disks are interacting, possibly exchanging mass.
arxiv-2509-05144:
Separating individual objects in a three-dimensional scene often starts from two-dimensional masks that carry errors into 3D. Chaolei Wang, lead author with five co-authors, propose SGS-3D in a 2025 computer vision paper. Their split-then-grow framework first purifies and splits ambiguous lifted masks using geometric primitives, then grows them into complete instances.

A mask filtering strategy uses co-occurrence of geometry primitives to remove unreliable masks. Semantic and geometric information are fused throughout, and the method needs no training. The authors present it as a refinement step that raises segmentation fidelity over methods relying on raw lifted masks.
arxiv-2509-05244:
Positive energy theorems for charged space-time data are extended by Simon Raulot in a solo 2025 paper in mathematical relativity. The data describe a slice of space-time with spin structure and electric charge, and the question is whether total energy must stay non-negative.

Working in four or more dimensions, Raulot assumes an energy condition that rules out matter moving faster than light in effect, plus at least one end that flattens far away. Under those terms, the energy result holds for the purely electric case. The findings extend classic theorems by Gibbons, Hull, Hawking and others, adding charge to a core fact about gravity.
arxiv-2509-05544: Singular points form only a negligible set for a class of two-layered surfaces, Jonas Hirsch and Luca Spolaor prove in a 2025 geometric analysis paper. The objects are multiplicity-two integral hypercurrents, generalised surfaces carrying a weight of two, assumed stationary in the sense of varifolds, meaning they sit in a critical position under smooth deformations. Hirsch and Spolaor show the singular set, where the object fails to be a smooth surface, has measure zero.
arxiv-2509-05744:
Risk constraints that no feasible plan can meet should be relaxed as little as possible, Darinka Dentcheva and Yunxuan Yi show in a 2025 optimisation paper. Stochastic dominance constraints force a plan's random outcome to beat a chosen benchmark distribution, shaping risk in a precise way.

When nothing feasible dominates the benchmark, the authors choose the feasible distribution closest to the dominating set, measured by optimal transport distance, the cost of reshaping one distribution into another. For second-order dominance they derive explicit formulas for that distance and build a numerical method, plus a projection under an extra assumption. Lower bounds cover dominance of general orders. Numerical experience supports the method's efficiency.
arxiv-2509-06244:
A black hole's shadow needs less than the textbook photon sphere, show Parth Bambhaniya and two co-authors in a 2025 paper. The shadow's edge is usually tied to a photon sphere or shell, the peak of the potential guiding light. For Kerr black holes that story holds, but the authors state a more general condition for an apparent boundary to form.

A shadow appears whenever the effective potential for light has a positive finite upper bound and a region where photons are trapped or scattered. The framework covers objects beyond Kerr, including naked singularities. The authors also separate the dark shadow's boundary from the bright ring a distant observer sees, clarifying what telescope images actually show.
arxiv-2509-06344:
Objective Bayesian inference for the Dhillon distribution is developed in a 2025 paper led by Pedro Luiz Ramos with three co-authors. Objective methods derive priors from the model itself rather than opinion. The authors derive three: the Jeffreys prior, the overall reference prior, and the maximal data information prior, and check what each does to the posterior.

Jeffreys and reference priors yield proper posteriors, while the maximal data information prior leads to an improper one. Conditions for posterior moments to exist are established. Markov chain Monte Carlo with a Metropolis-Hastings sampler carries out the inference, and simulations compare the Bayesian estimators against maximum likelihood on bias, squared error, and coverage. A real dataset illustrates the approach.
arxiv-2509-06544:
Long, tangled search queries are broken apart and explained in a 2025 information retrieval paper led by Yunfei Zhong, with six co-authors. Search engines must guess user intent, and language models help, but most studies use short keyword queries. AI-driven search now brings complex, multi-part questions that are far less studied.

The method, ReDI, works in three stages. A complex query is split into focused sub-queries, each sub-query is enriched with a written interpretation of its meaning, and documents found for each part are merged into one ranking. The team also built a large collection of real, tangled questions drawn from a commercial search service, and distilled a big reasoning model's skill into smaller ones. On public benchmarks, ReDI beat strong rivals in both keyword-based and meaning-based retrieval.
arxiv-2509-06744:
Smoother steps inside multilevel solvers for stiff formulas are tested by Pablo Jiménez Recio and one co-author in a 2025 numerical analysis paper. The test problems are the biharmonic and triharmonic formulas, split onto grids with the partition of unity method. Multilevel V-cycles need a smoothing pass that damps errors without full solves.

The authors pair Chebyshev passes of the fourth kind with factored sparse near-inverse preconditioners, which stand in cheaply for exact matrix inverses. They add a new adaptive building method that uses the block form these grid splits produce, plus a simpler statement of the Chebyshev pass itself. Results are checked on the multilevel solution of the higher-order problems. Work of this kind matters because near-inverses that adapt to block form can make large, high-order simulations practical.
arxiv-2509-06844:
Curves drawn by swinging sine and cosine functions become algebraic varieties in a 2025 geometry paper by Francesco Maria Mascarin and one co-author. Plane Lissajous figures, the looping patterns from combined swings, are the starting point. The authors extend them to higher-dimensional affine varieties described by sines and cosines.

Up to a counting factor, the degree of such a variety equals the volume of a polytope, a flat-sided solid tied to the frequencies. Defining formulas are pulled from rank conditions on a matrix with polynomial entries. Uses for dynamical systems follow, above all the Kuramoto model of coupled oscillators. Those uses lead onward to convex optimization and to Lissajous discriminants. The paper links a familiar picture from physics demos to current questions in algebraic geometry.
arxiv-2509-07244:
Alexey Khartov, in a solo 2025 paper, studies a new class of probability distributions called rational-infinitely divisible. A distribution joins this class if some infinitely divisible distribution splits into it convolved with another such distribution. Convolution combines two random effects into one total. The class is much wider than the classic infinitely divisible family and already has uses in several fields.

Khartov focuses on members that have a nonzero discrete part, meaning some probability sits on single points. He proves two necessary conditions for such members. In particular, the characteristic functions, which encode a distribution in frequency form, of both the distribution and its discrete part must stay away from zero. Conditions like these help researchers test whether a given law can belong to the class at all. The paper continues a run of results that map the borders of this enlarged family.
arxiv-2509-07444:
Shaofeng H. -C. Jiang and 4 co-authors study dimension reduction for clustering when centers must come from the data itself in a 2025 paper. The Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform shrinks high-dimensional data while roughly preserving distances, with a classic dimension bound. For clustering with free centers, that bound was famously beaten. The discrete case, where each center must be an actual data point, is the curious case here.

Two results are given, both governed by the dataset's doubling dimension, a measure of how the data fills space at different scales. The first shows a certain dimension suffices to preserve every clustering cost within a small factor, and that the bound is tight. The second drops a small extra term by relaxing the guarantee to near-optimal center sets. Such results tell practitioners how far data can be compressed before clustering answers start to drift.
arxiv-2509-07544:
Lorenzo Baldi and 2 co-authors study totally real divisors on curves over real closed fields in a 2025 paper. A divisor is a formal sum of points on a curve, and a totally real one uses only points on the real locus, the real part of the curve. Scheiderer proved that on smooth real curves with real points, every divisor of high enough degree is equivalent to a totally real one; the smallest such degree is a threshold worth understanding.

For non-Archimedean fields, the authors classify the topological types of smooth curves for which that threshold can be infinite. Over the real numbers, the threshold cannot be bounded by topological type alone unless the real locus has many components. A quantitative lower bound depends on metric properties of the Jacobian and the curve in the Bergman metric. Those properties are finally tied to period matrices compatible with the real structure.
arxiv-2509-08444:
Designing data glyphs, compact symbols that pack many variables into one mark, becomes a creative tool in a 2025 visualisation paper by Can Liu and 3 co-authors. Glyphs are powerful but hard to make: the gap between a designer's idea and working code blocks custom work. GlyphWeaver closes that gap with three cooperating components.

A glyph domain-specific language models each glyph as nested, independent, composable containers. An operation manager handles edits to those structures, and a multimodal interaction interface, assisted by artificial intelligence, lets users build by pointing, speaking, and example rather than by syntax alone. Analysts who think visually could finally prototype expressive encodings at the speed of sketching.
arxiv-2509-08544:
Omkar Bihani and 3 co-authors tackle the sparsest k-subgraph problem in a 2025 paper on optimization. The task is to find a small group of nodes in a network with as few links as possible. They recast it as QUBO, a binary optimization form suited to annealing hardware.

Three relaxations are offered, using quadratic penalty, Lagrangian, and augmented Lagrangian ideas. The authors prove when each version is exact for the right penalty settings. Iterative methods then update those settings while solving with simulated annealing and quantum processors. Large numerical tests support the theory and show the methods work well in practice.
arxiv-2509-08844:
Brahim Mittou defines new divisor functions and a new class of integers in a 2025 paper. Divisors of a number can be listed in increasing order. The new functions sum powers of divisors at even positions and at odd positions separately.

Properties of both functions are studied for real or complex exponents. A new type called k-index ratio numbers is also introduced. Three conjectures related to those numbers are stated but not proved. The work is number theory at a basic, definitional level. It extends the classic divisor sum by splitting it according to position in the divisor list.
arxiv-2509-09244:
Takuma Saito and 3 co-authors classify topological phases guarded by multipole symmetries in a 2025 paper. Multipole symmetries act in ways that shift with place in a chain. Phases they guard are exotic and were not yet fully sorted.

Matrix product states give a compact form for one dimensional systems and frame the work. At the ends of an open chain, the symmetry acts as projective representations, which group cohomology can label. For global, dipole, and quadrupole cases, distinct parts of the second cohomology group fix the class. Those parts encode the end actions. The sort covers a whole family of place based symmetries in a uniform way.
arxiv-2509-09344:
Moritz A. Goerzen and 5 co-authors study bimeron lifetimes in two dimensional magnets in a 2025 paper. Bimerons are swirls of magnetization that could store or process data in new devices. They live in easy-plane magnets, a class where spins prefer a plane.

First principles work plus transition state theory predict twin forms, bimerons and antibimerons, side by side at zero field in a layered van der Waals stack. Their symmetry sets them apart from skyrmions at a basic level. Odd soliton interactions and strong heat driven effects on lifetime stem from unbroken rotation symmetry in the plane. The authors see rich scope for brain like and reservoir computing.
arxiv-2509-09444:
Kyle McKee and 1 co-author study steady heat flow around obstacles in a 2025 paper on applied maths. Several solid bodies sit in a flat flow that cannot be squeezed. Each body is held at its own set pattern of surface heat. The heat in the fluid obeys a hard equation. Its form changes from place to place. Solving it head-on is slow and costly.

Their trick is a map that flattens each body into a flat slit. In the mapped picture the equation keeps one fixed form. A boundary method then handles any pattern of surface heat. Mapping back gives the heat field in the real flow. The team checks the result against a simpler case with one set heat. They note where the heat transfer rate matches and where it does not.
arxiv-2509-09544:
Paolo Pedinotti and 4 co-authors map a fast-moving research field in 2025 through MetaGraph, a method for large-scale meta-analysis. Their topic is generative AI inside financial natural language processing, which has grown quickly since late 2022 and outrun ordinary narrative surveys. Instead of reading papers one by one, they extract typed knowledge graphs guided by an ontology and a language model.

Applied to 681 papers from 2022 to 2025, the graphs reveal three phases. Early work expanded tasks and data sets, attention then turned toward limits and risk, and methods later shifted toward modular, system-style designs. The team releases the resource and tools so others can repeat the analysis and keep watching the field.
arxiv-2509-09944:
Xiaoyan Xie and 8 co-authors study the aftermath of a huge solar filament eruption that took place on December 24, 2023, in this 2025 paper. Above the eruption site spread a wide fan of hot plasma, about three times broader than fans seen over active regions during flares. Inside the fan, many parcels of plasma fell back down, events called supra-arcade downflows.

Using steady X-ray telescope observations, the team measured the largest of these downflows. They were at least three times wider than those in active region flares, yet moved at similar speeds and ran cooler than the plasma around them. The pattern matches models where such flows grow from Rayleigh-Taylor type instabilities, with a bigger system allowing bigger structures.
arxiv-2509-10244:
Allen M. Wang and 6 co-authors describe POPSIM, a framework for simulating and controlling fusion plasmas, in this 2025 paper. Running a tokamak well demands models that are fast, trustworthy, and tied to real machine data. POPSIM is built in the JAX machine learning framework and blends simple physics-based models with data-driven ones, from power laws up to neural networks.

This paper focuses on the technical side: the software and operations problems the framework is built to solve. Examples from live modeling work show the system in use. The authors aim for a single home where plasma models of very different kinds can be trained, tested, and prepared for control tasks.
arxiv-2509-10444:
Chaerim Moon and Joohyung Kim plan gentler motions for wearable robot arms in this 2025 paper. Extra robotic limbs worn on the body can extend what a person can do at close range. The catch is force: every move the limb makes pushes back on the wearer as torque, and strong torques tire the muscles that keep balance.

The authors add a planning layer that reshapes a given motion, keeping changes in angle and speed within set limits while cutting the moment passed to the body. Simulations with simplified human and robot models show the layer does reduce that moment. The goal is wearable systems that help more and wear their users out less.
arxiv-2509-10644:
Tools built for language documentation keep missing the linguists they are meant to serve, and Enora Rice, Katharina von der Wense, and Alexis Palmer diagnose why in this 2025 position paper. Computational morphology could automate pieces of documentation, like splitting words into parts and producing interlinear glossed text, yet real projects rarely adopt the research output.

The authors frame the gap as a failure to design with users, and demonstrate with GlossLM, a strong multilingual glossing model. In a small study, three documentary linguists found that despite excellent benchmark scores, the system missed core usability needs of actual documentation work. Those findings generate fresh research questions about model constraints, label standards, segmentation, and personalization. Their argument: centering users does not just make better tools, it makes better research questions.
arxiv-2509-10744:
Ozan Gokdemir and 7 co-authors build exam questions straight from the scientific literature in this 2025 paper. Benchmarks age quickly as knowledge grows, so the team automated the whole pipeline: parsing papers, cutting them into meaningful chunks, writing multiple-choice questions, and grading models on the answers.

As a test case they produced more than 16,000 questions from 22,000 open-access papers in radiation and cancer biology. Small language models were then graded with and without retrieval help. Pulling in reasoning traces distilled from a large model helped more than pulling raw text chunks, lifting several small models past a much larger one on a real exam. The framework is modular, so other fields can generate their own fresh benchmarks.
arxiv-2509-11844:
Andrés L. Suárez-Cetrulo, Alejandro Cervantes, and David Quintana build a generator of semi-synthetic financial data with known regime changes in a 2025 paper called ProteuS. Markets shift distributions over time as regimes change, a drift that breaks statistical and machine learning models. Real data carry no ground truth about when shifts happened.

ProteuS fits standard time-series models to real exchange-traded fund data to capture distinct market regimes. It then simulates gradual and abrupt transitions between those regimes. The resulting datasets include a comprehensive set of technical indicators and a controlled record of true change points. Analysis confirmed the task's difficulty, with significant overlap between market states. The authors offer the tool for rigorously evaluating drift detection and adaptation methods, toward more robust financial forecasting.
arxiv-2509-12344:
Neural operators learn the solution map of an equation once. Then they answer new cases almost instantly. But the standard DeepONet design can blur fine spatial structure. Arth Sojitra and two co-authors fix the blur in 2025. They embed Fourier features into the network's trunk. The trunk is the part that reads spatial location.

The result is FEDONet. It is tested on five benchmark equations. The set runs from the one-dimensional Burgers equation to the chaotic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky system. Tests vary the training set size and the noise level. FEDONet beats the classic design in every test. It reconstructs solutions with less error. The largest cuts come in the stiff and chaotic cases.
arxiv-2509-12444:
Long, many-jointed robot arms pulled by tendons bend gracefully, but steering one by tendon length alone breaks down once the arm is big enough for gravity to matter. Weiting Feng and three co-authors solve the forward statics for such hyper-redundant manipulators in 2025, taking tendon tension and tendon length together as reconciled inputs.

Their screw-based formulation covers multi-segment arms with elastic joints, and the iterative solver accepts either tension or length as the driving input. Bench tests confirm both modes, and the length-only mode enables open-loop control in static conditions. That sidesteps two chronic headaches: measuring tendon tension and estimating the arm's posture.
arxiv-2509-12744:
Shijie Shang, Pengyu Wang and Tusheng Zhang prove in 2025 that a noisy growth equation with a fast-rising log drift has one strong solution that lasts for all time. The equation models spread with random kicks at each point in space and time.

Their result settles an open problem from a 2019 paper and gives a new proof that square-based solutions do not blow up. New forms of a classic bound let them work with first averages, which need sharp bounds on the random spread part. The proof is a base step for wider work on noisy spread with strong growth.
arxiv-2509-12944:
Felix Wieberneit and 3 co-authors design momentum-based controls for safer mixed traffic in a 2025 paper. Road networks now mix standard cars, which are growing heavier with electrification and larger models, with light vehicles such as e-scooters and e-bikes. That heterogeneity raises serious safety concerns, because momentum strongly influences injury risk in a collision.

Their two-level method first applies access control, decreasing the heterogeneity of the network depending on actual traffic settings. A second level applies speed control to mitigate the probability of serious injuries in potential collisions. Both methods are designed from momentum considerations. The team implemented and validated the methods in the SUMO road network mobility simulator, a standard tool for traffic studies.
arxiv-2509-13244:
Jianfeng Zhu, Julina Maharjan and three co-authors test in 2025 whether language models can read personality from real interviews. Support and counsel roles need fine human reads. Prior work used fake personas and coarse labels on social posts.

A new benchmark pairs talk transcripts with checked continuous Big Five scores. Three paths are tested: prompting, tuned small models, and fixed embeddings. All links to true scores stay weak, below a low cap. Step-by-step prompts add little. Trait reads seem to rest on latent sense, not stated logic. Trait-wise prompts and context models are urged next.
arxiv-2509-13344:
Md Ishtyaq Mahmud, Veena Kochat and four co-authors benchmark shrink methods in 2025 for spatial transcriptomics beyond PCA. Six methods span linear, factorization, and neural paths. A Xenium cancer set drives the tests with varied latent sizes and cluster scales.

Scores cover rebuild error, variance kept, cluster cohesion, and two bio marks for marker fit and exclusion. PCA is the fast base. Factorization tops marker enrichment. Variational nets balance rebuild and clarity. Pareto picks guide settings. Exclusion-guided reassignment lifts marker fit across all methods. Choice should follow analysis goals, not habit.
arxiv-2509-13544:
Arthur D. Adams and fifteen co-authors present James Webb Space Telescope observations in a 2025 astronomy paper of 2M1207, a young binary system about ten million years old. Its primary is a cool sub-stellar object, and its companion is a still cooler planetary-mass body, making the pair a useful test of how young giant planets change over time.

Twenty time-resolved spectra were taken over roughly twelve and a half hours. The primary favors non-linear brightness trends in parts of the spectrum, with no clear period shorter than the observing window. The companion fits simpler linear trends. Modeling its changes as shifting cloud cover matches much of the data, though one wavelength range disagrees and low signal limits firm conclusions.
arxiv-2509-13644:
Jakob Assländer, in a solo 2025 magnetic resonance imaging paper, asks why published T1 values, a basic tissue property measured by MRI scanners, vary so much between studies. Magnetization transfer, an exchange effect between free water and a semi-solid pool in tissue, is thought to be the main culprit, but its influence on each scanning method was unclear.

Assländer simulated each established T1 mapping method while varying the underlying transfer parameters for different brain regions at clinical field strength. Sensitivity proved considerable and depended on the exact sequence implementation, not just its family. Variable flip angle methods were generally more sensitive to the exchange rate than inversion recovery methods, a rare clean pattern in an otherwise sequence-specific picture.
arxiv-2509-13844:
Tobias Heibges and eight co-authors present scheduling software for chasing cosmic transients in a 2025 astroparticle physics paper. Balloon and space telescopes that hunt ultra-high-energy neutrinos can swivel to follow up alerts about flaring sources, but someone must decide, fast, which alerts deserve scarce observing time.

Their neutrino target scheduler has three parts. A listener gathers alerts from existing systems into a source database. An observability module works out which sources a given mission can actually see, given its instruments and flight path. A scheduler then ranks the targets and drafts an optimized plan. The first release is tuned for stratospheric balloon missions, with mock examples for several flights, and is slated for a 2028 balloon flight.
arxiv-2509-14144:
Zheng Luo and three co-authors optimize acyclic database queries in a 2025 paper. Most query optimization research serves binary join plans, but theoretically optimal algorithms such as Yannakakis' run on join trees, a different shape of plan that needs its own optimization machinery. Acyclic queries, whose join structure has no loops, are exactly where join trees shine.

Three contributions follow. An algorithm enumerates all join trees of an alpha-acyclic query by small edits with constant amortized delay, grounding a cost-based optimizer. Maximum cardinality search, an old graph algorithm, is shown to build the unique shallowest join tree for Berge-acyclic queries, enabling parallel execution. And any connected left-deep binary plan for a gamma-acyclic query converts into a join tree by a simple procedure, letting old optimization infrastructure be reused.
arxiv-2509-14444:
Herlock, Rahimi and Dionysis Kalogerias tackle a participation flaw in federated learning in 2025, where phones or clients train a shared model without sending raw data. Only some clients are available each round. Available clients rarely match the importance weights the objective assumes.

That mismatch biases updates under the standard averaging rule. Their method, FedAVOT, reframes aggregation as a masked optimal transport problem aligning availability with importance. Sinkhorn scaling computes the transport weights, with proven convergence guarantees. The rate matches the standard federated rate and does not depend on how many users join a round. Exact alignment promises steadier training for real deployments where participation is patchy by nature.
arxiv-2509-14744:
Worawalan Chatlatanagulchai and seven co-authors study agentic coding manifests in 2025, the configuration files that give coding agents project context and rules. Tools such as Claude Code read a manifest file, often named Claude.md, before acting. Guidance on writing good manifests is scattered and thin.

Over two hundred fifty manifest files from more than two hundred forty repositories were analysed for structure and content. Manifests typically use a shallow hierarchy, one main heading with several subsections. Common content covers project identity, commands and operational rules, with wide variation beyond that core. The empirical map helps developers write manifests that agents can actually follow, instead of guessing what context an agent needs.
arxiv-2509-14944:
Xiaolei Xu and four co-authors estimate breathing effort from nighttime sounds to screen for sleep apnoea in a 2025 biomedical engineering paper. Obstructive sleep apnoea is common and harmful, yet many cases go undiagnosed because overnight lab studies are costly and complex. Sound-based screening could scale, but noise and missing context limit it.

Respiratory effort is a key signal clinicians use when scoring apnoea events, and it normally needs contact sensors on the body. The team estimates effort directly from bedroom audio for the first time, then fuses the estimated effort features with acoustic features to detect apnoea. Their data covers well over a hundred nights recorded at home from about a hundred participants. The effort estimates track real breathing dynamics meaningfully, opening a contact-free screening path.
arxiv-2509-15244:
Carlo Graziani and Marieme Ngom explain how to check the error bars of Gaussian process models in a 2025 paper. Such models are prized because they give not just a forecast but a band of doubt around it. What that band means in terms of odds, and whether it is well set, is often left vague. That vagueness cuts the band's worth.

Poorly set bands do real harm. The authors show how they degrade a method that steers tests toward designs with promise. Since these models give joint normal forecasts by their form, a formal test can check if real data match the model's own stats. The paper lays out that test and the reading it backs. Trust in error bars, they argue, should be earned.
arxiv-2509-15744:
Leon Herrmann leads a team that cuts the memory cost of optimizing moving wave problems. Such work needs sensitivity values built from forward and backward wave fields. The two fields run in opposite time directions, so the forward one must be stored. For huge problems that storage swamps even graphics chips, despite tricks like checkpointing.

Their new method leans on superposition for a class of symmetric problems. It builds the sensitivity in passes, holding only a few time steps at once. Memory then scales with the problem's degrees of freedom, not its history. That opens problems with billions of unknowns on a single current chip. They show it on sound based imaging and shape design tasks.
arxiv-2509-15844:
Kristina Sinaga, a lone author, groups medical patients using several views of their data, without pooling records. Hospitals hold rich data, but privacy rules block central study. Her frame joins a heat kernel method, borrowed from physics, with federated learning across sites. Distances between patients are turned into geometry aware similarity scores.

Two algorithms result: a central one for single site study, and a federated one for cross hospital work. The federated version adds differential privacy and secure pooling, aimed at health law compliance. Tests use fake heart patient records for ten thousand people across two hospitals. Grouping accuracy rose, messages between sites fell, and speed held up against central methods. The aim is shared patient typing with privacy kept.
arxiv-2509-15944:
J. Van Hulle, N. Vandewalle, and Z. Pan study droplets sliding down a vertical fiber. A single drop does more than fall: it lays a film of liquid behind it. The film thins along the fiber, and its thick part near the start breaks up into a new droplet. That break up is a known surface tension effect.

The new drop first speeds up, gathering fluid from the film ahead of it. Then loss at its rear wins, and it slows. At last it merges with the first drop, which can then travel further on the refilled supply. Later generations of drops can arise the same way. The team model each phase of the cycle. The cascade is set by how the film thins over time.
arxiv-2509-16144:
The May 2024 solar storms sent huge bursts of magnetized gas toward Earth and lit up skies far from the poles. Brigitte Schmieder and four co-authors model those events with a chain of three simulation codes, from the Sun's surface out through space. One code traces how magnetic fields in active regions build stored energy before they erupt.

The free magnetic energy in the big event stayed below a clear bound found by the team. A forecast code in the chain predicted arrival times at Earth within three hours. Matching the chain to real data shows the value of linking Sun-to-Earth models for storm warnings.
arxiv-2509-16244:
Adapting a large language model to new tasks by retraining all of it is too costly for most users. Emily Jimin Roh and four co-authors survey cheaper tuning methods that adjust only a small slice of the model, then compare them with a quantum-inspired approach. That approach encodes updates through quantum-style amplitudes and small quantum circuits.

The survey weighs how fast each method settles, how cheap it runs, and how much it can express. Quantum-style tuning shows promise for strong updates with tiny overhead. The authors map the trade-offs to guide future work on efficient model adaptation.
arxiv-2509-16344: Asuman G. Aksoy and Qidi Peng present the Bernstein lethargy theorem, a result in the study of approximation in normed spaces. They then examine how that theorem relates to reflexivity, a property of spaces where a natural embedding reaches the whole dual space twice over. The note is brief and states its scope plainly: the theorem itself and its link with reflexivity are the whole focus. Readers get a compact entry point to both topics and their connection.
arxiv-2509-16944:
Yuheng Shi, Xiaohuan Pei, Minjing Dong, and Chang Xu sharpen fine perception in multimodal models in a 2025 paper. Reading small details needs high-resolution images. Processing a whole large image costs too much, though. Focusing on a key region helps, but past region finders needed costly labels or slow multi-pass runs.

Their predictor learns regions by distilling the model's own knowledge. It avoids large annotated sets and full fine-tuning. The result is a practical, scalable boost to fine-grained perception. Models could read small text, counts, and defects more cheaply. Code is shared in public for others to adopt the method.
arxiv-2509-17044:
Mingqing Zhang and a large team build a farming assistant in a 2025 paper. Crop disease diagnosis guides sustainable farming and food security. Image-only tools miss farm knowledge and cannot chat with growers. Their assistant, AgriDoctor, pairs vision with language and expert knowledge for interactive diagnosis.

Training rests on a large new benchmark with hundreds of thousands of disease images. It adds expert entries and bilingual prompts for tool choice. Tests show the assistant beats top vision-language models on fine farm tasks. A knowledgeable, chat-based tool could bring expert-grade diagnosis to small farms far from agronomists.
arxiv-2509-17144:
Can a sensor built from single molecules tell one changing magnetic signal from another? Matteo Lanza and seven co-authors take up that question in a 2025 arXiv paper on quantum sensing. Molecular spins are attractive sensors because they can sit close to the samples they probe, even in living or chemical settings.

The team sets out two sensing routines built on the Hahn echo method. The routines do not need the signal to repeat in step with the control pulses. Tests used two kinds of molecular spins held in a superconducting microwave device. The setup reached high sensitivity for signals that last just a few millionths of a second, and the authors note a trade-off between weak fields and the time a signal must last.
arxiv-2509-17244:
Frederic Vatnsdal, Romina Garcia Camargo, Saurav Agarwal, and Alejandro Ribeiro present a 2025 arXiv paper on steering robot swarms with diffusion models. The task is coverage control, where a team of robots spreads out to watch over a region. No central brain guides them, so each robot must blend its own sensing with messages from nearby peers.

Their method, MADP, samples joint actions from a diffusion model, which can capture how one robot's move should mesh with another's. A spatial transformer shapes the sampling, and each robot runs the policy on its own. Training copies a clairvoyant expert who sees the whole field. In tests that vary team size, layout, and the shape of the target density, MADP beat leading baselines. It also carried over to new densities and settings without retraining.
arxiv-2509-17444:
Shohei Hisada, Endo Sunao, Himi Yamato, Shoko Wakamiya, and Eiji Aramaki ask whether a big medical benchmark fits Japan. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies HealthBench, a rubric-based test of medical language models with thousands of scenarios. Japanese resources for this kind of testing are scarce and often just translated multiple-choice items, a weak base for safe medical AI.

The team first machine-translated HealthBench and scored two models: a strong multilingual system and a Japanese-native open model. The multilingual model dipped a bit, largely from rubric mismatches with Japanese practice. The native model failed badly, lacking the clinical completeness the rubrics demand. A model-as-judge classification then mapped the contextual gaps, where scenarios clash with Japanese guidelines, systems, or norms. Most scenarios travel well, but a large share of rubric criteria need local rework.
arxiv-2509-17744:
Shoham Sen and 3 co-authors work out how charge in flat, two-layer-thin stuff looks at large scale. Their 2025 paper deals with sheets just atoms thick, prized for use in new devices. At atom scale, charge jumps up and down fast, which makes large-scale maths hard.

A smoother field, based on the mean shift of charge in each cell, bridges the two scales. The team takes limits as the grid of atoms shrinks to zero. Three cases rest on how sheet depth compares with grid size. Each case gives a smooth charge law and edge terms for the rim.
arxiv-2509-18044:
Saeid Sheikhi, Panos Kostakos, and Lauri Loven shield shared learning on 5G and edge nets from bad clients. Their 2025 method, Hybrid Reputation Aggregation, deals with federated learning, where many devices train one model and share updates. Bad clients can flip tags, plant backdoors, or fake many selves.

Their plan blends shape-based outlier checks with a trust score that tracks each client over time. Odd updates are filtered, and shaky clients lose weight for good. On a large 5G data set and a known attack bench, the method held high scores. It beat top past aggregators by clear margins.
arxiv-2509-18644:
Robot arms usually learn from camera views plus readings of their own joint positions. Juntu Zhao and 12 co-authors find that second input can hurt in this 2025 paper. Policies lean too hard on the joint readings, memorize training paths, and then fail when objects sit at new heights or spots. Their fix drops the joint input entirely.

The State-free Policy predicts actions from vision alone, in a frame tied to the gripper's own motion. Two wide-angle wrist cameras supply the full task view. In real tests, from pick-and-place to shirt folding and whole-body tasks, the change was stark. Height generalization jumped from near zero to 85 percent average success. Sideways shifts improved almost as much. The policy also needed less data and adapted across robot bodies more easily. The authors argue less input can mean more robust robots.
arxiv-2509-18944:
Multiply random square matrices again and again, and how fast does the product grow? Nadya Nabahi and Vladimir Shpilrain study that growth for products built from a fixed set of real matrices. The long-run growth rate is summed up by the largest Lyapunov exponent, a number that also matters in chaos theory and random dynamics.

The authors answer a first question about the expected size of the largest entry in such a product, under mild conditions on the matrix entries. For the second question, they offer a very simple, fast method that bounds the Lyapunov exponent from above. Easy bounds of this kind are useful when exact growth rates are out of reach.
arxiv-2509-19244:
Shufan Li and six co-authors present Lavida-O, a single model that both understands and generates images through masked diffusion. Existing multimodal diffusion models handle only simple image questions and low-resolution generation. Lavida-O adds object grounding, image editing, and high-resolution text-to-image synthesis up to about a thousand pixels. Its architecture pairs a light generation branch with a larger understanding branch, joined through token compression and stratified sampling for speed and quality.

The model can also plan and reflect on its own outputs during generation and editing, borrowing its understanding skills to raise quality. On standard benchmarks for grounding, generation, and editing, it set new best scores. It beat prominent autoregressive and continuous diffusion rivals while running considerably faster. The authors frame it as a new paradigm for scalable systems that reason and create in one body.
arxiv-2509-19844:
Sanskrit epic poetry renames its heroes constantly, through epithets, kinship terms, and meter-driven variants. Sujoy Sarkar and five co-authors build Mahānāma, the first large dataset for finding and linking named entities across a whole literary work in Sanskrit. It draws on the Mahābhārata, the longest epic known. Over one hundred nine thousand mentions map to about five and a half thousand distinct entities.

Each mention also links to an English knowledge base, enabling cross-lingual study. Current coreference and linking models falter on the full-text test, the authors report. Long-range dependencies defeat tools tuned on short passages. The dataset gives digital humanities a stern benchmark in a low-resource, morphologically rich language. Progress here would transfer to other classical literatures.
arxiv-2509-20044:
Geometric mechanics writes motion in the language of symmetry, and Ghorbanali Haghighatdoost widens that language from groups to groupoids. Euler-Poincaré reduction shrinks equations by quotienting out symmetry. Lie algebroids handle the infinitesimal side, but groupoids allow global reconstruction of trajectories and nontrivial base spaces. He derives the reduced equations on a Lie groupoid and checks them on the trivial case.

A rigid body on a sphere illustrates the frame. Then comes a biological turn: cells migrating collectively over a spherical tissue, with internal polarity coupled to motion. The model predicts an optimal migration time near seventy-four minutes, matching experiments. Geometry that fits both machines and living tissue shows its reach. The work broadens optimal control's geometric toolkit.
arxiv-2509-20144:
Julian Feuerpfeil wrote this 2025 arXiv paper in algebraic number theory. It studies S-class groups, which package arithmetic data about a number field and a chosen set of places. The paper defines a Hilbert 90 property for these groups over cyclic field extensions. It then connects that property to the Gross-Kuzmin conjecture, a long-standing question in Iwasawa theory.

Feuerpfeil gives a test for the property that uses only data from the base field. The test never requires knowing the class group of the larger field. For towers of fields indexed by a prime, the property at finite layers already forces a key module to behave well. That yields a fresh finite-level test for the conjecture. The test reduces to a local map tied to Fermat quotients, so it can be computed explicitly. Numerical experiments suggest it holds for all but finitely many primes in the totally real case.
arxiv-2509-20244:
Forecasting cash flow for online retail is the problem addressed by Abhishek Sharma and five co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. E-commerce finance data is sparse, irregular, and shaped by odd invoice schedules and payment delays. Short histories and partial visibility weaken both classical methods and deep learning models. The authors build a hybrid system tuned to those conditions.

Their framework engineers lagged features that shift with the data, rather than staying fixed. Adaptive rolling windows summarize recent behavior at several scales. Invoice-level modeling tracks how individual bills open and close. Custom loss functions reward stable forecasts, not only accurate ones. Classical statistical models and ensemble learners do the final prediction. Tests cut the mean percentage error by about five percent against baselines. Stability over quarterly horizons also improved.
arxiv-2509-20444:
Dwarf galaxies in empty fields are the census target of Erin Kado-Fong and ten co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper, the third from the SAGA survey's background sample. Satellite dwarfs around big galaxies are now well counted. Isolated dwarfs of similar size lagged behind. The team inventories them down to a few million solar masses of stars.

Three measures structure the census: how galaxy counts vary with environment, how stellar mass maps to halo mass, and how often isolated dwarfs have stopped forming stars. The count shape barely depends on environment. The quenched share among isolated dwarfs falls smoothly toward smaller masses, reaching about one in a thousand. The mass mapping agrees with satellite-based estimates. Big cosmological simulations, though, over-predict quenching among isolated dwarfs in one mass range, a mismatch the authors flag for theory.
arxiv-2509-20844:
Inside dense quark matter, protons and neutrons may dissolve into swirling patterned structures. Yu Hamada, Muneto Nitta, and Zebin Qiu study one such structure in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. They consider QCD matter with an imbalance between isospin types, plus baryon and electric effects.

Using chiral perturbation theory, the authors examine vortices formed by pion fields. With a pion mass included, charged and neutral pions alike form condensates throughout the bulk. Two vortex kinds then appear: a local vortex of charged pions and a global vortex of neutral pions. The baryon appears as a linked structure of these vortices. The work offers a model-independent view of how baryons might be built inside extreme matter.
arxiv-2509-21044:
Reinforcement learning fine-tuning makes language models better at reasoning than supervised fine-tuning alone, but the internal reason was unclear. Honglin Zhang and three co-authors look inside the models in a 2025 study. They borrow a technique called edge attribution patching to map the models' internal circuitry.

Across several model families and mathematics datasets, they find two robust effects of reinforcement learning tuning. Internal activations grow stronger, and the circuitry involved becomes more diverse. Supervised tuning does not produce the same pattern. The findings suggest reinforcement learning does not merely polish outputs; it recruits a broader, more active set of internal pathways. That picture helps explain why the method generalizes across models with different starting characteristics.
arxiv-2509-21344:
Gerard Boxo and 2 co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on monitors that detect harmful behaviour in language models. White box monitors use linear probes, which read internal signals from the model. They work well in general tests. Their skill at spotting behaviour that is not stated in text is disputed. The paper tests how much probes lean on text evidence.

When text evidence of a behaviour was removed, probe scores fell by a large margin. The drop appeared across three setups: sandbagging, sycophancy, and bias. Filtering such tokens is standard when testing output monitors. The team also trained model organisms that act without stating the behaviour. Probe scores on those models were much lower, which supports the main claim.
arxiv-2509-21444:
Homotopy theory studies shapes up to continuous deformation, and its groups are hard to compute. Juxin Yang and 2 co-authors determine part of a homotopy fiber in a 2025 paper. The fiber comes from a pinch map on a suspended two cell complex. A periodicity phenomenon in the attaching map is the central theme. Results are stated locally at each prime.

The authors determine the three cell skeleton of the fiber. For the prime two the result is direct; for larger primes an extra assumption is needed. Proof tools include Selick Wu minimal algebra theory and the Eilenberg Moore spectral sequence. As an application, they compute a two primary component of a homotopy group. That group lies outside the metastable range, where standard methods fail.
arxiv-2509-21544:
Vibrato, the gentle pitch wobble in expressive playing, can be transferred from one recording to another. Jeremy Hyrkas presents a real time version of that effect in a 2025 paper. An earlier algorithm derived delay functions from real vibrato examples. A delay line then imparts the target vibrato pattern onto incoming sound. Several parts of that algorithm blocked real time use.

The real time approximation uses an efficient fundamental frequency estimator. Time domain polyphase filters approximate an analytic signal. A proposed method also transfers the amplitude modulation of the target sound. That goes beyond typical delay based vibrato effects. Modifications for real time use are detailed in the paper. Source code is available as a VST plugin implementation for music production.
arxiv-2509-21644:
The neutron skin of a heavy nucleus, the excess reach of its neutrons, could be measured at colliders. Grégoire Pihan and 3 co-authors propose such a method in a 2025 paper. Proton lead collisions supply the data. A double ratio of conserved charges carries the signal: net electric charge over net baryon number near the lead going direction. High multiplicity events are compared with low multiplicity ones.

Sensitivity is computed in a three plus one dimensional relativistic hydrodynamic framework. Multiple conserved charge currents and a lattice QCD based equation of state are included. Predictions cover two collision energies, matching a fixed target setup at LHCb and the main LHC collider mode. Lead nucleus skin thickness is the target quantity extracted from the ratio.
arxiv-2509-21844:
Hamish Lewis and six co-authors project how drought in New Zealand may change as the climate warms. Trustworthy projections need many high-resolution climate runs, which are costly to produce. Their 2025 study uses a new data set: large groups of global climate models, sharpened to fine detail by generative AI. The AI was trained to mimic a physics-based regional model.

Across the model groups, rain becomes more variable, while average rain changes stay uncertain. Droughts grow more intense across most of the country. Changes in drought length and frequency stay hard to pin down in many regions because of natural variation and model disagreement. The big groups also reveal rare, extremely long droughts that small groups miss. Under a high-emissions path, some places could face droughts lasting around thirty months.
arxiv-2509-21944:
Damien K. J. Lee, Yann L. Müller, and Anirudh Raju Natarajan model tiny defects that steer how complex alloys age and change. The alloys mix many main elements in similar amounts, and they are prized for strength and stability. The defects are vacancies, empty sites in the crystal. Their equilibrium count affects how atoms diffuse and how the structure holds up, but computing it from first principles is hard in such mixed alloys.

The authors connect quantum-level electronic calculations to vacancy counts through embedded cluster expansions, a compact way to price local atomic arrangements. Monte Carlo simulations on top of that frame track how vacancy formation varies with composition and temperature. They demonstrate the method on a nine-element alloy drawn from three groups of the periodic table. Vacancy counts rose when certain early transition metals were added, or when elements that dislike mixing were included.
arxiv-2509-22144:
Long chains of thought make language models accurate but slow, so Jianzhi Yan and six co-authors set out to compress them. Their 2025 paper presents MACC, a framework that shortens reasoning traces over several rounds of refinement. A naive squeeze can backfire: the authors note a token elasticity effect, where too small a budget makes output grow longer instead of shorter. Their adaptive strategy uses that effect rather than fighting it.

MACC progressively compresses each chain, choosing the right depth of compression for each input. Across test models, it improved average accuracy over the strongest baselines while cutting chain length and delay. The team also shows that test-time behavior can be predicted from the training set. Simple, readable features, like the model's perplexity and the compression rate, forecast both accuracy and output length. That predictability allows model selection and planning without repeated fine-tuning.
arxiv-2509-22544:
Mohammad Mahdi Hemmatyar and 6 co-authors hunt complex anomalies in surveillance video. Some events are odd not for one action but for how several people and objects relate over time. Self-supervised methods catch low-level motion patterns yet miss that meaning. Language models grasp context but cost too much to run on every frame and localize poorly.

Their hybrid, HyCoVAD, splits the work. A multi-task self-supervised analyzer flags suspect frames. A language model then checks those frames with structured, rule-based reasoning. On a hard complex-anomaly data set, the hybrid beat baselines by a wide margin. It also cut language model compute. The team released its taxonomy, threshold protocol, and code.
arxiv-2509-22644:
Zimu Lu and 7 co-authors judge website generation by how the site looks and behaves, not just whether code runs. Code agents get feedback from execution alone, which misses visual quality and interaction flaws. Their agent, WebGen-Agent, collects multi-level feedback from a vision-language model. It writes detailed comments and scores on screenshots, and on tests run by a GUI agent.

Those scores feed a backtracking scheme that keeps the best version so far. The same scores become step-level rewards for training the reasoning model, a method they call Step-GRPO. On a website benchmark, the agent roughly doubled one strong model's accuracy and raised its appearance score. Step-GRPO also lifted a smaller coder model.
arxiv-2509-23044:
Stroke rehab needs more therapists than the system can supply, so home monitoring could ease the load. Ye-eun Kim, Suhyeon Lim, and Andrew J Choi build a system that watches rehab actions at home. It pairs motion sensors with a depth camera. Most action tools were trained on non-disabled people, which fits stroke patients poorly. Their data set was collected from stroke patients doing daily upper-limb tasks.

Their model, MMeViT, is an ensemble vision transformer for mixed inputs. Stroke action data clustered less cleanly than healthy data. Still, the model learned shared tendencies for each label. The team see a path toward feedback and assessment tools for home rehab.
arxiv-2509-23244:
Guessing an agent's goal from partial behavior is fragmented by clashing benchmarks and protocols. Matan Shamir and 3 co-authors release two open frameworks to unify that field. One library, gr-libs, holds modular MDP-based baselines and diagnostic tools. The other, gr-envs, holds environments tuned for goal-directed behavior. Wrappers keep both compatible with standard Gym toolkits.

Goal recognition is typically online and one-shot, which makes fair comparison hard. The pair of packages aim at reproducible, extensible evaluation. Both ship on GitHub and PyPI. Uses include human-robot interaction, surveillance, and assistive systems. The release is infrastructure, not a new algorithm.
arxiv-2509-23444:
Future 6G networks can locate a phone with great precision, which creates a privacy risk at the signal level. Lorenzo Italiano and 6 co-authors propose HoloTrace, a way for the user's own device to fake the clues a base station uses to locate it. The device alters its pilot signals so that angle and timing cues point to a false spot. The base station needs no changes, and no protocol rules are broken.

The team frames the trick as one projection problem and gives closed-form answers for cases with full, partial, or no channel knowledge at the device. Simulations show large location errors at the base station. The cost to link capacity shifts with the false spot chosen.
arxiv-2509-24344:
Firms weigh open-source models against commercial ones for sensitive analysis work, and the trade-offs are rarely clean. Theo Koraag and 3 co-authors ran an exploratory case study on financial report analysis and commentary. They built two systems in rounds: one with local open models in a multi-agent workflow, and one on a commercial cloud model, then had experts judge both on real reporting tasks.

Both systems showed strong potential, but integration was the hard part. Prompt design, context limits, and reliability all bit in practice. The cloud model was more fluent and usable but raised privacy and dependency worries. Local models gave control and compliance at a far higher engineering cost.
arxiv-2509-24444:
Smart contracts on the TON blockchain run messages in an order no one fully controls, and that asynchrony breeds race flaws. Yury Yanovich and 8 co-authors built BugMagnifier, a transaction simulator that hunts such temporal flaws on purpose. Static analysis of audit reports had mapped patterns, but dynamic tests for timing dependencies were missing.

BugMagnifier steers the message queue with precision, compares states across runs, and tests permutations of message order. It exposed flaws in purpose-built vulnerable contracts and in five real cases taken from recent audits. Detection difficulty tracked the message mix as theory predicted. The tool turns expert hunts into automated, reproducible evidence.
arxiv-2509-24544:
Wide neural networks behave like Gaussian processes, a fact often stated without error bars. Eloy Mosig and 2 co-authors quantify that convergence for shallow networks trained by gradient descent. They bound the quadratic Wasserstein distance between the network output and its Gaussian approximation at any training time, including times well into training, where prior estimates were scarce.

The distance decays as a power of the network width. The bounds show how width and input dimension shape the error, and how training dynamics move it over time. Finite-width estimates like these tell practitioners when the Gaussian picture can be trusted numerically.
arxiv-2509-25044:
Rohit Jena, Vedant Zope, Pratik Chaudhari, and James Gee present FFDP, a distributed framework for registering gigavoxel medical images. Registration aligns images from different modalities, but algorithms have not kept pace with growing scan sizes. Their framework attacks non-matrix-multiplication bottlenecks with fused, input-output-aware kernels and convolution-aware tensor sharding.

The system registered a one-hundred-micron ex-vivo human brain MRI volume at native resolution. That problem is over five hundred seventy times larger than a standard clinical case, yet it finished in about a minute on eight GPUs. FFDP speeds existing registration pipelines six to seven times while cutting peak memory by twenty to fifty-nine percent.
arxiv-2509-26544:
Philipp Alexander Kreer and co-authors wrote this machine learning paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on tracing a model's behavior back to its training data. The classic tool for this, influence functions, breaks down on deep networks because it needs a matrix inverse that often does not exist.

Their local Bayesian influence function swaps that inverse for statistics of the loss landscape, sampled with a stochastic-gradient Monte Carlo method. The swap captures higher-order links between the model's settings that the classic tool misses. It also scales to networks with billions of parameters. On tests that predict what retraining would do, the method reached state-of-the-art accuracy. The authors present it as a practical way to audit which training examples shaped a big model's answer.
arxiv-2510-00044:
Farooq and colleagues search for the most energy-efficient way for a fish-like swimmer to undulate, combining design-by-morphing with Bayesian optimization in a computational framework. The swimmer's body deformation is written as a blend of five baseline bio-inspired profiles, including two unconventional shapes for diversity. Unsteady flow around the two-dimensional swimmer is simulated with an Arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian formulation across frequency and wavelength combinations in the study.

The optimized profile reaches a propulsive efficiency of 82.4 percent, far above the second and third best at 51.8 and 42.8 percent and ahead of the standard anguilliform and carangiform benchmarks. It is helped by favorable surface stress distributions and energy recovery. Force decomposition shows the winner minimizes resistive drag while maximizing constructive work at the front and rear of the body, with a coherent organized wake. It guides autonomous underwater vehicle design in practice.
arxiv-2510-00444:
Zijun Wu, Yongchang Hao, and Lili Mou published this 2025 paper on giving language models a memory for procedures. Prompts must be re-read at every step, scale badly across tasks, and resist reuse. Their system, TokMem, stores each recurring procedure as one compact, trainable token. That token acts as both an address and a control signal for behavior.

The backbone model stays frozen while new memory tokens are added. Old procedures therefore cannot be damaged when new ones arrive. On one thousand tasks testing single-procedure recall, TokMem set the pace among compared methods. On function-calling tasks needing composed procedures, it beat retrieval-augmented generation as well. It also matched fine-tuning while training far fewer parameters overall. The authors present tokenized memory as a modular alternative to ever-longer prompts.
arxiv-2510-00544:
Muhittin Aydin, Antonio Bueno, and Rafael Lopez published this 2025 mathematics paper carrying a classical curve problem into curved spaces. Euler asked which planar curves are stationary for an energy weighting arc length by distance from a point. The moment of inertia about that point supplies the weight. The authors pose the same question on the hyperbolic plane and on the sphere.

Critical curves are characterized through their curvature and their distance to the reference point. On the hyperbolic plane, the only closed stationary curves are circles centered at that point. On the sphere, the energy value splits according to which hemisphere holds the curve. The authors also find first integrals for the equations governing these curves in both geometries. A minimization problem for curves joining two aligned points gets solved in the geodesic case. Classical variational geometry thus gains two new constant-curvature chapters.
arxiv-2510-00744:
Zhu, Zhang, and Song design an economic bidding strategy for electric vehicle aggregators in real-time electricity markets, in this 2025 arXiv paper on power systems. Aggregators coordinate large fleets and can earn money by charging cheap and discharging dear. Each decision carries a marginal opportunity value, since energy used now cannot serve a better price later. That value shifts with uncertain prices and fleet availability, which makes bid design hard.

The authors model the scheduling problem as a Markov decision process, tying opportunity value to the value function.
