They derive probability distributions for marginal values across energy states under stochastic prices. Closed-form expressions then give marginal charging values and discharging costs for both risk-neutral and risk-averse aggregators. Those expressions convert directly into stepwise price-quantity bids, with no redundant computation. Case studies on real charging data and market prices showed the strategy adapts well.
arxiv-2510-01144:
Lee and Panagou study resilient leader-follower consensus when a network cannot meet the usual safety conditions, in this 2025 arXiv paper on multi-agent control. In leader-follower consensus, ordinary agents track a reference signal from a leader while adversaries inject false values. Standard algorithms guarantee success only when the whole communication graph is robust enough, and what happens below that bar was unexplored. The authors define partial consensus, where a subset of honest followers still tracks the leader correctly.

Their BP-MSR algorithm blends bootstrap percolation with the classic mean-subsequence-reduced update, letting each follower decide locally when to trust and share values. They prove sufficient conditions for individual followers to succeed on arbitrary time-varying graphs. Simulations showed guaranteed followers reaching consensus in cases where standard resilient algorithms fail outright. The result gives designers a per-agent answer instead of a single network-wide verdict.
arxiv-2510-01544:
Xie and co-authors tackle a training mismatch in diffusion language models, which draft and refine whole passages at once. Standard reinforcement rewards only the final answer, so lucky guesses can reinforce sloppy reasoning. The team first recasts hard problems as a ladder of smaller local choices.

Their method, Step-Aware Policy Optimization, scores the refinement steps themselves rather than only the outcome. Theory work shows when the hidden ladder structure can be recovered from data at all. A named failure mode, unstructured refinement, captures steps that churn without helping the solution. Rewarding real progress step by step should make diffusion models reason more honestly. Diffusion models revise in parallel, so their steps look nothing like a chain of thought. Step scoring gives credit where the draft actually improves. Coincidentally right answers stop paying off. Better reasoning hygiene matters most on long problems.
arxiv-2510-01744:
Demelius and four co-authors revisit a hopeful claim about private machine learning in this 2025 paper. Differentially private training, called DPSGD, protects people in the training data by adding noise. Many studies found that this noise hurts some groups more than others. A recent claim held that tuning the model's settings on the private model itself could erase that unfairness.

The authors tested the claim across several fairness measures and many settings on five datasets. Harm on one measure did not reliably signal harm on another measure. Tuning on the private model also failed to remove the uneven impact in a dependable way. It still beat reusing settings copied from a non-private model on balance. The authors warn that tuning itself leaks some privacy, and that a fairness-focused variant of the method proved fragile as well.
arxiv-2510-01844:
Vesco revisits a classic card trick with fresh math in this 2025 paper. In the traditional game, a performer guesses a secret number from the cards where it appears. The familiar version rests on binary representation, where each card marks one bit. Vesco asks what happens when the cards encode digits in any integer base instead.

For each base, he derives formulas in both directions of the design problem. One formula counts the cards needed to pin down a given number. The other gives the largest number reachable with a fixed stack of cards. Analysis and graphs agree on a clean verdict. Base two wins on both counts, needing the fewest cards and covering the widest range. Full proofs sit in the appendix, and street performer Giuseppe Polone's act inspired the study.
arxiv-2510-01944:
Valsecchi Oliva, Akyildiz, and Duncan put a classic training algorithm on continuous-time footing in this 2025 paper. Persistent contrastive divergence trains energy-based models by swapping parameter updates with sampling from the current model. Its discrete steps resist clean error analysis over long runs. The authors recast the whole procedure as coupled stochastic equations across two timescales.

In that form, sampling and optimization evolve at once rather than in turns. Moment bounds between the multiscale system and its averaged limit hold uniformly in time. Those bounds yield estimates of the gap between the algorithm's iterates and the true maximum likelihood solution. The team also supplies a discrete scheme based on stochastic orthogonal Runge-Kutta Chebyshev integrators, with long-time error estimates. The upshot is a training method for energy-based models with error guarantees that hold over long horizons.
arxiv-2510-02144:
Ferreira and four co-authors measure the universe's standard ruler in projection with DESI data in this 2025 cosmology paper. Baryon acoustic oscillations freeze a set scale into galaxy clustering. Measuring it angularly, on the sky, avoids some modeling assumptions of the three-dimensional approach. The team computed the angular two-point correlation function for DESI's first data release.

Completeness tests left only the Bright Galaxy Survey sample usable, at two effective redshifts. Mock catalogs built with first-order Lagrangian theory modeled the nonlinearities at those low redshifts. A purely statistical correction handled projection effects. The measured angular BAO scale came out near eleven point eight degrees for both subsamples, with errors near one degree. Those values agree reasonably with what the collaboration's own cosmological parameters predict. The exercise validates angular BAO as an independent check on the standard analysis. It also road-tests methods for future DESI releases.
arxiv-2510-02244:
Nyergesy, Márián, Trombettoni, and Nándori let the cooling universe flip its own cosmological constant in this 2025 cosmology paper. String theory tends to predict a negative constant, while observations demand a positive one driving today's expansion. Existing fixes risk unstable worlds or insert the sign flip by hand. Their proposal uses a modified thermal flow.

Temperature enters through the inverse radius of a compact time dimension, as in spacetime foliation work. A fixed temperature ratio is held as the flow runs to low energies. At high temperatures, the safe quantum gravity model yields a negative constant, matching string expectations. Flowing to low temperatures turns the same quantity positive, matching observation. The sign switch emerges from the physics rather than a manual edit. Early and late cosmology reconcile inside one framework.
arxiv-2510-02344:
Sadeghzadeh introduces a new projective invariant and wider metric classes in Finsler geometry. Her 2025 mathematics paper studies spaces where distance depends on direction. Finsler metrics generalize the familiar Riemannian ruler. Projective changes keep straightest paths fixed while bending other features. Invariants are quantities that survive such changes. She defines a weakly generalized Douglas-Weyl equation. That equation widens the known GDW metric family. The new W-GDW class contains every older GDW metric. Two further subclasses sit inside it.

One subclass softens the Weyl curvature demand. The other softens the Douglas curvature demand. The paper maps the properties of each class. Detailed examples show the classes are genuinely larger. Worked cases include metrics outside the older families. Classification results like this organize a crowded field. Geometers gain names and tests for structures they meet. Later curvature studies can build on the frame.
arxiv-2510-02544:
Chaudhari and co-authors close a loop between quantum calculations and lab tests to fight qubit defects. Their 2025 materials paper targets niobium superconducting devices. Surface oxides on niobium host two-level systems that sap performance. A metal cap can block oxide growth if chosen well. The team computes oxygen defect energies from first principles. Those energies become descriptors for a simple learned model. Logistic regression trains on a small set of lab outcomes. It predicts which caps will suppress oxide formation. Zirconium, hafnium, and tantalum emerged as effective barriers.

Lab checks confirmed those three candidates afterward. One descriptor, oxide formation energy per oxygen, worked nearly alone. Lattice mismatch added a second screen for clean interfaces. Zirconium and tantalum combined low oxide risk with small mismatch. Scandium appeared as a fresh candidate from the screen. Rational defect management generalizes beyond this one device family.
arxiv-2510-02944:
Tan and Vasudevan strengthen a bridge between two tasks in cryptography. Random local functions compute each output bit from a few input bits. Goldreich proposed them as cheap one-way functions. A distinguisher merely tells their output from random noise. An inverter recovers the input from the output. A search-to-decision reduction turns the first skill into the second.

Older reductions demanded special traits from the rule used. This one works for any rule of fixed size. Given a distinguisher with a small edge, it builds an inverter. The inverter needs more outputs but wins with fair odds. One result follows at once for builders. If such functions are one-way, shorter versions act as pseudorandom generators. The proof leans on mixing traits of graph transforms. It also stretches to noisy rules and slowly growing rule sizes.
arxiv-2510-03144:
Garner and co-authors map a giant star-forming cloud in the galaxy M33 at fine scales. The cloud, NGC 604, is the brightest of its kind there. Starlight from hot young clusters ionizes its gas. The SIGNALS survey recorded it with the SITELLE instrument. Line ratio maps trace how excitation changes across the cloud. A bright, high-excitation core hugs the central cluster. A dimmer, low-excitation halo wraps around that core.

The team shows the swings are not chemistry changes. Shifts in ionization drive the pattern instead. Gas motion maps tie the glow's shape to real flows. Two small sources hid inside the bright cloud. One is a known supernova remnant in the field. The other is a planetary nebula never cataloged before. Only fine spatial maps could have exposed them. The cloud forms stars slowly and holds a vast ionized mass.
arxiv-2510-03244:
Wang and co-authors forecast many time series at once by turning the data into pictures for a vision model. Large forecasting models usually treat each channel independently. That habit blinds them to links between variables. Rendering the series as an image exposes those links visually. A pretrained large vision model then reads the picture. Its features capture cross-channel patterns invisible to numeric models. A fusion stage aligns visual and temporal representations.

The vision model stays frozen during the whole training. Only a small slice of total parameters ever updates. That frugality keeps compute and memory demands low. Benchmarks across standard datasets showed competitive accuracy. Weather, power, transport, and finance series all fit the scheme. The visual route found stable spatiotemporal features in the data. Foundation model builders often hardwire channel handling early. VIFO suggests pictures can retrofit that missing structure later.
arxiv-2510-03444:
Cotăescu presents a 2025 arXiv paper that derives charged black hole solutions inside expanding universe models. The background is a flat FLRW space time, the frame for cosmology, filled with a perfect fluid. Earlier dynamical particle models carried no electric charge. The new metric tensors satisfy the Einstein Maxwell equations with spherical symmetry and time dependent mass. A Coulomb field from the black hole's changing charge adds stress and energy to the fluid source.

Two free parameters shape each solution. One mimics the effect of a cosmological constant. The other ties the charge to the cube root of the mass function, a link the author calls surprising. Worked examples show how such charged holes behave in a matter dominated universe. The models extend the study of black holes that live and evolve inside cosmology, rather than sitting in empty space. Horizons and physical frames receive close attention throughout.
arxiv-2510-03844:
Lotspeich and colleagues wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on filling gaps in electronic health records without costly chart review. Patient records often miss key values, such as lab results that were never entered. Clinicians once fixed such gaps by reading charts and using related diagnoses as clues, a slow process covering few patients. The authors test whether an algorithm guided by the same logic can do the job at scale.

Their algorithm follows a roadmap of linked diagnoses, expanded with help from a large language model and checked by clinicians. On records from a large health system, it recovered as much missing data as expert reviewers did. Results from the recovered data also matched the earlier chart-review study more closely than a naive analysis. The team suggests extending the method to check data plausibility as well. Such scalable recovery could make record research cheaper and more complete.
arxiv-2510-04044:
Yang and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on shrinking neural networks for small devices without losing accuracy. Quantization stores network weights in fewer bits, but choosing the right value range for each layer is delicate. A poor range wastes precision and degrades the compressed model, especially at very low bit widths. The authors treat range choice as an optimization problem in its own right.

They show the problem of minimizing quantization error layer by layer is locally convex, so an efficient search can find its best solution. Applying the same search in a transformed weight space improves results further,. On ResNet models and Inception-v3, their method beat prior state-of-the-art results on image classification accuracy. Eight-bit and six-bit models lost almost no accuracy at all. Better range estimation makes post-training quantization more practical for phones and edge devices.
arxiv-2510-04344:
Vogl and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv perspective on atomic defects in hexagonal boron nitride as building blocks for quantum technologies. Point defects in wide-bandgap solids can emit single photons and host spins at room temperature, but only a few host materials had qualified. Hexagonal boron nitride, an atomically thin two-dimensional insulator, has recently joined that short list. Its defects combine single-photon emission with electronic and nuclear spin access under ambient conditions.

The authors review rapid progress in understanding these defects' photophysics. They map the opportunities for quantum communication networks, computers, and sensors built from atomically thin devices. Open challenges include identifying exact defect structures and achieving reliable creation and control. Integration with photonic structures is natural for a layered material that can be stacked and transferred. The perspective argues hBN defects deserve a central place in the solid-state quantum roadmap.
arxiv-2510-05044:
Lawrence Hollom and Gregory B. Sorkin revisit a classic probability puzzle in this 2025 arXiv paper. Take a set of unit vectors and flip a fair coin for each one's sign. The signed sum lands somewhere near the origin. Littlewood and Offord first studied such sums in 1943, and the field still asks how likely a near-zero landing is.

The authors study the reverse question: how small can that probability be forced to become? They show the answer depends sharply on parity, on whether the count of vectors matches the dimension mod two. When the parity mismatches, some choice of signs always lands close to the origin. When it matches, the probability can be exactly zero. In two dimensions with an odd count, they build examples where it decays exponentially.
arxiv-2510-05144:
Muskaan Chopra, Lorenz Sparrenberg, and Rafet Sifa build a fresh test set for catching dangerous translation errors in this 2025 arXiv paper. Critical error detection asks whether a machine translation is safe to use. The older WMT21 English-German benchmark is small, unbalanced, and aging. Its narrow domains also limit what it can reveal.

Their dataset, SynCED-EnDe, holds 1,000 gold-labeled and 8,000 silver-labeled sentence pairs. Error and non-error cases are balanced evenly. Sentences come from recent StackExchange and GOV.UK sources. New annotations flag error subclasses, severity, and how hard each error is to localize. Benchmark tests with XLM-R and related encoders showed substantial gains over WMT21. The resource is hosted publicly for the research community.
arxiv-2510-05244:
Rishika Bhagwatkar and seven co-authors test a humble defense against prompt injection attacks in this 2025 arXiv paper. AI agents read untrusted web pages and tool outputs. Attackers hide malicious instructions inside that content. The authors place two firewalls at the agent-tool boundary, borrowing the classic network security idea.

A minimizer firewall filters what enters each tool, and a sanitizer cleans what comes back. Across four public benchmarks, this simple setup reached the lowest possible attack success rates. Task success stayed high at the same time. Yet the authors warn the benchmarks themselves are weak. They found flawed metrics, implementation bugs, and feeble attacks throughout. They even bypassed their own firewall in one travel scenario. Stronger adaptive attacks are needed before defenses can be trusted.
arxiv-2510-05444:
Dou and colleagues test whether fake users can judge AI assistants fairly. Human studies remain the gold standard for rating chat assistants over long conversations. Such studies are costly, slow, and hard to repeat with the same pool of people. Many teams now let language models play the user, with little proof that the trick works.

Their benchmark, SimulatorArena, holds 909 real conversations between people and assistants. The chats cover two tasks, math tutoring and document creation. Simulators are graded on how human their messages sound and how well their ratings match human ratings. Simulators given a user profile, with traits and writing style, matched human judgment closely. The team then used the best simulators to rank eighteen current assistants. The approach costs a small fraction of a full human study and can be repeated on demand.
arxiv-2510-05644:
Issaka and a large team confront the neglect of African languages in language technology. Africa holds nearly a third of the world's languages, yet most lack digital tools. About eighty-eight percent are severely underrepresented or ignored in computational linguistics. Their 2025 African Languages Lab pairs data collection with local capacity building.

The lab built a validated dataset spanning forty languages. It holds nineteen billion tokens of text and over twelve thousand hours of aligned speech. The pipeline enforces quality control before any data joins the corpus. Fine-tuned models gained about fifteen BLEU points on average across thirty-one languages. Scores on two other translation measures also rose sharply. Against Google Translate, the lab's models proved competitive in several languages. Abstracts were even translated into ten African languages using the lab's models. The program has also mentored fifteen early-career researchers on the continent.
arxiv-2510-05744:
Fretel and colleagues unify the names of observing facilities across catalog lists. The same telescope or spacecraft appears under rival names in rival sources. That split blocks data finding across the Virtual Observatory. Their 2025 method builds one mapping with a single label per site.

Names come from eight sources, including Wikidata and field resources. Every field feeds the matching, from labels to bands and launch dates. Bag-of-words, stepwise, and surface methods produce flexible matching scores. A large language model then accepts or rejects each pair with reasons. Repeated rounds enrich the matching as new name variants surface. A labeling effort now marks pairs as same or distinct by hand. That data set will benchmark both the scores and rival checking models. FAIR data rules drive the whole push for one naming scheme. Checked sets will feed a Name Resolver API and IVOA word lists.
arxiv-2510-05944:
Assif and Baryshnikov prove that minimal unimodal decomposition is NP-hard on graphs. A function is unimodal when all its super-level sets are contractible. Decomposing a density into fewest unimodal summands is fundamental in topological statistics. Their 2025 paper settles the complexity for edge-linear functions on graphs.

Hardness holds for decompositions into any fixed number k of components, at least two. Restricting to planar graphs does not restore tractability. A reduction from vertex cover also limits approximation quality. No algorithm beats a factor of two unless P equals NP. Extensions push the hardness to higher-dimensional complexes as well. Unimodality generalizes mode-counting beyond Gaussian mixtures and convexity assumptions. The Lusternik-Schnirelmann category is the topological cousin of the problem. Fixed-parameter tractability remains an open direction after this hardness. Greedy methods from trees can still produce non-minimal decompositions in practice.
arxiv-2510-06244:
Ahmed, Wu, and Botev evaluate word embedding frameworks for scientific text in a 2025 language technology study. The same word means different things across domains, so representation choice matters for scientific language processing. Transformers give strong contextual embeddings, but pretraining one from scratch costs heavy compute.

The study pursues two goals. First, it seeks the best pairing of representation algorithm and tokenization for scientific tasks. Second, it builds an evaluation suite that can judge future algorithms as they appear. The suite bundles several downstream tasks with relevant scientific datasets. The authors run various representation and tokenization algorithms through the suite head to head. A shared yardstick prevents each new method from reporting only its favorite tasks. For practitioners, the work narrows the search for representations respecting scientific vocabulary.
arxiv-2510-06444:
Pfeffer and six co-authors add performance forecasting to decentralized learning networks in a 2025 machine learning paper. Such networks combine many participants' predictions into one inference. Standard schemes weight models by historical performance. That makes them reactive and slow when conditions change.

The authors forecast how well each model will perform this epoch. A forecasting worker then weights models predicted accurate right now. This context-aware scheme improved inference accuracy in their tests. What the forecaster predicts matters greatly. Models forecasting regret, performance relative to the network inference, improved results most. Loss-forecasting models often failed to beat the naive historically weighted average. Performance proved sensitive to features and training length, so tuning is domain-specific. The experimental design follows the architecture of the Allora network. The idea generalizes: anywhere weighting should be predictive, not reactive, forecasting beats hindsight.
arxiv-2510-06644:
Leshu Li leads a team building real-time 3D mapping for small devices. Their 2025 paper, presented at the MICRO conference in Seoul, uses 3D Gaussian Splatting for SLAM. SLAM lets a device map its surroundings while tracking its own position. The splatting method renders scenes fast and accurately, but edge devices still run it too slowly.

The team found wasted work at several levels of the mapping pipeline. Their system, RTGS, removes that redundancy through joint algorithm and hardware design. It does so without spending its gains on the cost of finding the waste. In tests, RTGS ran up to 48.8 times faster than an edge graphics processor. Energy efficiency improved by up to 82.5 times in the same comparison. The system sustains over thirty frames per second, which counts as real time. The same co-design ideas may help other rendering systems too.
arxiv-2510-06744:
Mauri Valtonen leads a large international team studying a famous blazar called OJ 287. Their 2025 paper builds on 136 years of optical observations of the object. A binary black hole model explains its recurring flares. The smaller black hole orbits the larger one every twelve years and smacks through its disk, causing outbursts.

The team asks where the smaller black hole's own jet points on the sky. RadioAstron, a space radio telescope, imaged the system at extremely fine resolution in 2014. A huge one-day flare in late 2021 pointed to emission from the secondary's jet. The authors track the jet from the disk outward, correcting for relativity effects on its apparent direction. Aberration bends the jet's projected path in a specific way they calculate. Identifying the secondary jet in the radio map would confirm a long-standing model prediction. Few systems let astronomers watch two giant black holes interact this directly.
arxiv-2510-06844:
Nicole Hoess, Carlos Paradis, Rick Kazman, and Wolfgang Mauerer ask whether software mining tools can be trusted to agree. Their 2025 paper studies mining of software repositories, which tracks how projects evolve. Researchers use such tools to judge project health and derive best practices. Small design choices inside the tools may quietly change the answers.

The team replicated three published studies using four independently chosen mining tools. The original studies covered collaboration, maintenance, and software quality. They compared the extracted data, the analysis results, and the final conclusions for each question. Tiny technical details piled up along the tool pipelines. Those details caused substantial differences in the baseline data and its derivatives. Some individual results differed significantly between tools, so tools are not freely interchangeable. The study gives a clearer picture of uncertainty in mining pipelines. It also derives good practices to make future evolutionary analyses more trustworthy.
arxiv-2510-06944:
Flank Bezerra and Luís Salge prove that a family of sound-propagation equations has well-behaved solutions, at least for short times. Their 2025 paper studies semilinear Moore-Gibson-Thompson equations, a higher-order sound model. The equations involve elliptic operators with boundary conditions on a bounded region. The nonlinearity is kept below a growth threshold.

Well-posedness means a solution exists, is unique, and depends on the starting data. The linear part of their operator is sectorial, which unlocks a toolbox. Fractional power spaces let them measure solution smoothness in gradations. The framework clarifies how extrapolation spaces handle operator traits. In particular, the operator lacks two comforts analysts enjoy. Despite that, the semilinear Cauchy problem is locally well-posed under their conditions. Guarantees are the foundation for any study of these sound models. Without them, computer models rest on sand.
arxiv-2510-07044:
Hendrik Zarucha, Peter Jung, and Giuseppe Caire prove that a family of estimators handles noisy input well. Their 2025 paper studies estimators built from a shaping function and a set of candidate matrices. Real readings are always a bit off. An estimator is robust if small disturbances cause only small errors.

The first part proves robustness for the family under conditions. It picks the candidate matrix with the lowest cost built from eigenvalues. As the perturbation shrinks, the error can be made small. The second part applies the theory to spotting users in random access networks. There, many devices share antennas, and some transmit at once. Recovering their fading strengths becomes an estimation task. Both a maximum likelihood method and a least squares version fit the frame. Sharper results demand more antennas, a trade-off the authors measure. The guarantees matter for wireless systems that must spot which devices are active.
arxiv-2510-07244:
Mucka and Romanowska complete a two-part study of dyadic polygons. Their 2025 paper treats such a polygon as an algebra built on averaging pairs of points. The first part classified dyadic triangles and singled out standard forms called representative hats. This second part asks when two such triangles are really the same under isomorphism. 

The authors give a full list of isomorphism types for dyadic triangles. Each type is captured by a representative hat with a small triple of integers. Worked examples show how one hat transforms into its isomorphic partners across six cases. The result is a tidy catalog: any dyadic triangle falls into exactly one listed family. Such completeness matters in universal algebra, where these averaging structures serve as test cases.
arxiv-2510-07544:
Demir and Keskin model inflation as a thermodynamic field and ask why some economies settle while others spiral. Their 2025 paper builds a framework they call developmental symmetry. Inflation becomes a scalar field evolving under continuity equations, in deliberate analogy with an equation from gravitational dynamics. The system is run in two modes. Adiabatic economies, sealed from exchanges, never reach equilibrium in the model. Non-adiabatic ones can evolve toward stable states over time. The framework reproduces the observed spectrum of regimes, from hyperinflation down to stable low inflation, with characteristic transitions taking about a decade.

Two levers govern stability in the model: continuity of production and controlled monetary flow. Balance between purchasing power and asset values across the whole economic field suppresses the inflationary dynamic. The authors present the work as computational theory, with no new data attached.
arxiv-2510-07844:
Li and four coauthors wrote this 2025 theoretical physics paper on detecting Planck-scale effects with tabletop optics. Quantum gravity is expected to bend the rules of quantum mechanics near the Planck length. One sign is a deformed uncertainty principle, which shifts the behavior of oscillators. The authors model a nanogram-mass mechanical resonator whose motion departs a little from standard predictions. They ask how light can measure that departure.

Two quantum probe fields watch the resonator as its oscillation decays. One field reads amplitude linearly, while the other amplifies frequency shifts through high-order sidebands of its nonlinear response. Simulations with parameters from three systems set the reach of the scheme. The resolution reaches a precision fifteen orders of magnitude below the electroweak scale. The setup could test the deformation parameter far beyond earlier limits. Nonlinear optics may thus give quantum gravity a measurable low-energy footprint.
arxiv-2510-08044:
Yin and seven coauthors wrote this 2025 robotics paper on knowing when a language model's robot plan should not be trusted. Language models turn instructions into high-level plans, but hallucinations produce confident, unsafe plans. Their framework, CURE, separates epistemic uncertainty, what the model does not know, from intrinsic uncertainty in the task. Epistemic uncertainty splits further into task clarity and task familiarity.

Random network distillation and small regression heads fed by model features produce the estimates. Tests ran in kitchen manipulation and tabletop rearrangement. CURE's estimates aligned more closely with actual execution outcomes than existing methods managed. A flagged plan can be rechecked, clarified, or handed to a safer fallback. Separating why a model is unsure, rather than reporting one lump score, is the central lesson. That distinction makes uncertainty actionable for robots acting in the physical world.
arxiv-2510-08644:
Diyi Liu, Shuchen Zhu, Lin Lin, Guang Hao Low, and Chao Yang cut the cost of encoding many-body Hamiltonians for quantum computers in a 2025 arXiv paper. Block encoding embeds a Hamiltonian inside a larger unitary, a prerequisite for many quantum simulation algorithms. Early fault-tolerant machines need encodings with far fewer gates and helper qubits. Their constructions target second-quantized Hamiltonians, the standard language of quantum chemistry.

A SWAP-based data lookup strategy handles the sparsity oracle, while direct sampling with SELECT-SWAP handles amplitudes. The T gate count grows only with the square root of the number of interaction terms, up to log factors. Clifford gate counts improve by a constant factor as well. A second encoding targets fixed-particle subspaces directly, shrinking the subnormalization factor by the same square-root scaling. Extensions cover electronic Hamiltonians with translation invariance or decaying coefficient structure.
arxiv-2510-08744:
Liu and co-authors introduce DemoDiff in this 2025 arXiv paper, a system that designs new molecules with help from a few examples. Chemists often know the trait they want, such as how strongly a molecule binds, but have only a handful of scored examples. DemoDiff takes those examples as its guide instead of a written prompt. A diffusion model, which builds objects by slowly removing noise, then shapes new molecules to match the target trait.

A new encoding scheme represents each molecule at the level of small recurring parts, which cuts the graph size sharply. The team trained a model with well under a billion parameters on millions of example tasks drawn from drug and materials data. Across thirty-three design tasks, DemoDiff matched or beat language models hundreds of times larger. It also ranked ahead of methods built for single tasks.
arxiv-2510-08944:
Gharwi and Shu give a forecasting network a memory of its own recent mistakes, in this 2025 arXiv paper on time series prediction. Real data streams refuse to sit still: patterns shift, regimes change, and the noise itself grows and shrinks over time. Standard regression models, trained once, keep applying yesterday's calibration to today's drift. Their errors then carry information that the models simply throw away.

The new architecture, VARNN, stores recent prediction errors in a learned memory state that updates over a short window. That memory acts as a live signal of current variability and drift. Before each new prediction, the model recalibrates itself using the memory. Tests spanned appliance energy use, healthcare, and environmental monitoring. The model posted lower errors than static, dynamic, and recurrent rivals, with only slight added cost. The authors highlight its steadiness in drifting, volatile conditions as the main selling point.
arxiv-2510-09344:
Hui Wang and four co-authors introduce WildElder in a 2025 arXiv paper, a speech dataset of older Chinese speakers gathered from real online videos. Ageing changes speech through slower delivery and shaky voices, which makes automatic recognition harder. Most existing Chinese datasets were recorded in controlled rooms, so they miss the noise and variety of daily life.

WildElder pairs its recordings with careful human labels for the transcript, speaker age, gender, and accent strength. The team intends the corpus to support both speech recognition and speaker profiling, meaning the guessing of traits like age from voice. Their experiments show how hard elderly speech still is for recognisers. They also show that the dataset works as a tough new benchmark, and they release the data and code for other researchers.
arxiv-2510-09444:
Cana Elgvin and six co-authors review a microscopy technique for layered materials in a 2025 arXiv paper. The method is momentum-resolved electron energy-loss spectroscopy, or EELS, which fires fast electrons at a sample and records how much energy and momentum they lose. Layered stacks promise gains in many fields, but proving what happens inside them needs such probes.

Because the method records energy and momentum together at each beam position, it can resolve excited states that light cannot reach. These include phonons, which are vibrations, plasmons, which are electron oscillations, and excitons, which are bound electron-hole pairs, even beyond the first Brillouin zone. It keeps nanometre-level spatial detail while doing so. The review explains why that combination matters for studying how these states couple inside 2D materials and their stacked layers.
arxiv-2510-09544:
Qiguang Chen and nine co-authors examine a tension inside diffusion language models in a 2025 arXiv paper. Diffusion models generate text by refining many tokens in parallel, which gives high throughput. Yet rigorous reasoning often needs a strict step-by-step order, and the authors name this clash the Parallel-Sequential Contradiction.

Testing simple and complex reasoning tasks, they find the models act truly parallel only when the output can be decided directly. As difficulty grows, the models fall back on step-by-step behaviour much like ordinary step-by-step models. Prompting them in the sequential style nearly doubled the decoding steps without raising quality. The clash also limits self-checks, depth of thought, and breadth of search. The authors chart three scaling paths, parallel, diffusion, and sequential, and find only the first improves reliably. They propose fixes, including parallel-oriented prompting and early stopping of the diffusion.
arxiv-2510-09844:
Digvijay Redekar, Ronald Askin, and Feng Ju review how maritime ports keep supply chains running through disruptions in a 2025 arXiv paper. Maritime transport moves essential goods worldwide, and breaks in it ripple into border security and welfare. Threats range from natural disasters and accidents to chained failures, and now to cyberattack and terrorism against port sites.

The review builds a structured framework from research papers and government documents. It focuses on two aspects of resilience in maritime transportation supply chains: running operations well and system technology. Findings are classified to expose where ports are vulnerable and where past work is thin. The authors argue that resilience planning must now be inclusive of the full modern threat spectrum, not only storms and strikes. They highlight the vulnerable areas most in need of future research, aiming to guide both port operators and scholars toward stronger, more complete preparedness.
arxiv-2510-10044:
Rahul Vanukuri and co-authors make radio spectrograms with diffusion models in this 2025 arXiv paper on spectrum use. Shared bands such as CBRS need strong radar detection to shield military traffic from commercial 5G signals. Detectors in turn need large, varied, well-labeled sets of spectrograms, which are maps of radio energy over time and frequency.

Such labeled data is hard to gather in the field. The authors use diffusion models to make new spectrograms with no label needed for each sample. Fake data of this kind can then boost the training sets of radar detectors. The work ties image-making models to a real bottleneck: a detector is only as good as the data it learned from.
arxiv-2510-10344:
Iason Saganas, Grant Mayberry, and Barbara Ercolano revise the lifetime of submoons in this 2025 arXiv paper in planetary science. A submoon orbits a moon, which itself orbits a planet. Such nested worlds are exotic, and they have been suggested as possible homes for life.

Earlier studies estimated how long a submoon can survive before tides pull it apart or fling it away. The authors extend that work with the Euler-Lagrange equation, tracking tidal migration from the planet, the moon, and the submoon's own tides together. Their revised maximum lifetime sets where searches for submoons are worthwhile. A shorter lifetime would explain why none has been confirmed yet.
arxiv-2510-10444:
Jingyi Chen and five co-authors ask a pointed question in this 2025 arXiv paper: do large audio language models truly hear emotion, or do they mostly read the words? Understanding speech emotion needs both the words spoken, called lexical cues, and sound cues like pitch and tone, called acoustic cues. The team built a benchmark to pull these two channels apart.

They tested six leading audio language models on their new benchmark, named LISTEN. The models leaned hard on the words. When the words were neutral or missing, the models answered neutral. When word and sound cues agreed, scores rose only a little. When the cues clashed, the models failed to pick out clear emotions. On tasks that used sound alone, their accuracy fell close to pure chance. The authors conclude that today's models mostly transcribe speech instead of listening to it.
arxiv-2510-10544:
Abdelkrim Zitouni and five co-authors derive a guarantee for when reinforcement learning policies will generalize, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such guarantees are hard because training data arrives as a sequence, breaking the independence that classical bounds assume. Their PAC-Bayesian bound handles this through the chain's mixing time, which measures how fast the sequence forgets its past.

The bound gives non-vacuous certificates for modern off-policy algorithms such as Soft Actor-Critic, which learn from stored past experience. The team also builds PB-SAC, an algorithm that optimizes the bound itself during training to guide exploration. Across continuous control tasks, the approach gave meaningful confidence certificates while keeping performance competitive. The work matters because deployed agents need trustworthy estimates of how a policy trained in one setting will behave in new conditions.
arxiv-2510-10644:
Yi Zhang and five co-authors let a language model steer the optimization behind ride hailing dispatch, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Online platforms must balance supply and demand that shift across time and neighborhoods. Reinforcement learning methods are data hungry and struggle with real world constraints. Decomposition based optimization avoids that, but its high level objectives are designed by hand and ignore low level routing dynamics. The team's hybrid framework needs no training data.

A large language model acts as a meta optimizer, generating high level objectives as semantic heuristics. A low level optimizer enforces constraints and executes real time decisions. The heuristics evolve in a closed loop driven by harmony search, which adapts the model's prompts using feasibility and performance feedback. In experiments on New York and Chicago taxi scenarios, the approach improved on state of the art baselines by an average of 16 percent.
arxiv-2510-10744:
Mario Morawski, Anais Despres, and Rémi Rehm ask how much of a sequence can ever be learned, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Autoregressive models, used from finance to language, depend on patterns in the data. Misreading those patterns leads to misspecified models and worse predictions. The team builds on a recent metric of evolving patterns and defines predictive information: the mutual information between past and future.

This quantity yields an information theoretic learning curve, measuring how much predictive information grows with the observation window. The authors show that temporal patterns set a hard limit on learnability: even an optimal predictor cannot beat the intrinsic information limit of the data. Experiments on synthetic data validate the framework. It can judge whether a model class is adequate and quantify how complex a dataset inherently is. The message is that some prediction failures are properties of the data, not of the model.
arxiv-2510-10844:
Ryan E G Bushling proves a stronger form of a classical theorem about slicing fractal sets, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Marstrand's slicing theorem says that for almost every direction, slicing a set of dimension s by parallel planes leaves slices of the expected dimension. Bushling works in the Peres-Schlag framework of generalized projections, which covers nonlinear families of maps satisfying transversality and regularity conditions. He quantifies exactly how exceptional the bad parameters can be.

He shows the set of parameters where slices come out too small has Hausdorff dimension at most a clean bound built from the parameter count and the two dimensions involved. When the set has finite measure, one exceptional collection works universally for all its positive measure subsets at once. For families that are only slightly regular, a similar conclusion holds up to a small error term.
arxiv-2510-11044:
Yang Lu and five co-authors ask how to arrange movable antennas to keep wireless links private, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Pinching antennas slide along dielectric waveguides, letting a system reshape the wireless channel on demand. The team uses them for physical layer security: widen the channel quality gap between legitimate users and an eavesdropper. Their system has two waveguides, each carrying several antennas serving multiple users. The design question is geometric: should the waveguides run parallel or cross?

They model two levels of realism for signal travel inside the waveguides, then maximize the secure sum rate and the secrecy energy efficiency. A two stage optimizer first searches antenna positions with a feasibility aware swarm algorithm, then jointly tunes beamforming and artificial noise. Simulations confirm that adjusting antenna positions yields substantial gains in both security metrics. Orthogonal placement brought extra benefits for physical layer security in their results.
arxiv-2510-11144:
A planning agent that gets stuck could simply ask a teacher how to do the task, but answers range from full action lists to vague sub-goals. Gautier Dagan, Frank Keller, and Alex Lascarides study how agents can learn from such how-to questions in this 2025 arXiv paper. They introduce a memory agent framework that lets an agent ask questions, store the answers, and reuse them on later tasks.

The team evaluates the framework in Plancraft, a Minecraft crafting environment where agents assemble items by moving inventory objects. Teacher models answer at different levels of abstraction, from executable action sequences to high-level descriptions of sub-goals. The lifelong learning agents benefited most from answers that were abstracted and decoupled from the current game state, since those entries generalize for reuse. The framework offers language-model agents a way to build planning skill over time by asking questions.
arxiv-2510-11444:
Named entity recognition systems must keep learning new entity types as the world invents them, without forgetting the types they know. Yawen Yang and co-authors propose a generative approach to that continual learning problem in this 2025 arXiv natural language processing paper. Instead of classifying tokens or spans, their framework GenCNER converts the task into generating sequences of entity triplets with a pre-trained sequence-to-sequence model.

Two additions protect old knowledge during updates. A type-specific, confidence-based pseudo-labeling strategy supplies rehearsal examples, and knowledge distillation at the triplet level anchors the model to its earlier behavior and reduces the impact of label noise. The design also sidesteps the semantic shift problem of the non-entity label in other approaches. Experiments on benchmark datasets show GenCNER outperforming previous state-of-the-art methods across continual settings, with the smallest gap to models trained without that constraint.
arxiv-2510-11644:
When a top quark and antiquark are produced alongside dark matter particles at a collider, the dark matter escapes unseen, and reconstructing what happened requires inferring the invisible momenta event by event. E. Abasov and co-authors apply normalizing flows, generative models that learn full probability densities, to that reconstruction in this 2025 arXiv particle physics paper. Spin correlations between the top quarks are the prize.

The unified framework feeds the networks low-level four-momenta and missing transverse energy together with high-level kinematic and angular variables. The authors compare a baseline multilayer perceptron regressor, an autoregressive flow, and the conditional nu-Flows model, which learns the full conditional density. In the top-pair-plus-dark-matter final state all three models performed well, with high reconstruction quality in independent validation regions split by the pair's invariant mass. The approach should extend to three- and four-top final states.
arxiv-2510-11744:
Laura Sáez Ortuño, Santiago Forgas Coll, and Massimiliano Ferrara test whether quantum computing can help classify consumers. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds a hybrid pipeline around a quantum kernel support vector machine. Kernel methods judge how similar two customers are; a quantum circuit computes that similarity in ways classical circuits cannot copy cheaply. A second quantum module extracts features before classification.

The team benchmarked the pipeline in simulation and in short runs on real quantum hardware, which today is noisy and small. With fixed settings, their model reached about seventy-eight percent accuracy on the consumer task. It caught about eighty-six percent of the positive cases, a higher recall than the classical support vector machine, while precision stayed competitive. The authors stress that this is a starting point, not a final verdict. Their design favors shallow but expressive quantum circuits that stay robust under hardware noise.
arxiv-2510-11944:
Yupei Li, Philipp Borchert, and Gerasimos Lampouras teach math models using an unlikely textbook: ordinary software code. Language models struggle with autoformalisation, translating informal mathematics into machine-checkable statements for proof assistants like Lean. Training pairs of informal and formal math are scarce. Code, by contrast, is abundant, but its structure differs from formal math. Their 2025 arXiv paper proposes TopoAlign to close that structural gap.

TopoAlign takes code apart into docstrings, main functions, and dependency functions. It then reassembles those pieces into arrangements that mirror the shape of formal statements. Math models trained on this aligned code need no new human annotation. The gains were large for DeepSeek-Math, which improved by about eighteen percent on one benchmark measure and about sixty-nine percent on type checking. The already-specialized Herald model gained only slightly. Still, the result shows structural alignment, not new knowledge, is what transfers.
arxiv-2510-12144:
Ali Parsaee, Bei Jiang, Zachary Friggstad, and Russell Greiner spend a labeling budget on patients whose stories are unfinished. Survival data is censored: for many patients we know only that the event, death or relapse, had not happened by last contact. A budgeted learner can pay for follow-ups that de-censor chosen records, sometimes fully, sometimes buying just one more year of certainty. Their 2025 arXiv paper adapts active learning to that purchase.

The authors extend leading budgeted learning algorithms to survival data and analyze where they strain. Their approach carries performance bounds and time complexity asymptotically matching BatchBALD, the standard active learning benchmark. Empirically, across several survival tasks, their model beats alternative approaches on multiple benchmarks. The setting mirrors real cohort studies, where follow-up is expensive and partial: a patient traced for another year may still leave the record censored.
arxiv-2510-12244:
Scott develops a geometric framework that frees several core results of convex analysis from their usual side conditions, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Convex analysis studies curved sets and functions that bend upward, and its theorems often require the relative interiors of two domains to overlap. When they do not, standard rules for combining functions can fail.

Scott defines a joint facial subspace from the face of the difference set that contains the origin. Cutting each set by a shifted copy of this subspace yields faces of each set, a two sided reduction echoing facial reduction in conic programming. After this reduction the relative interiors always meet, so classical theorems apply without extra assumptions. The results cover subdifferential additivity, normal cones of intersections, a chain rule, and an exact Fenchel Rockafellar dual. An iterative process computes the subspace in at most as many steps as the dimension.
arxiv-2510-12444:
Zhou and colleagues survey the young field of generating radiology reports that compare a chest X-ray with the patient's earlier scans, in a 2025 arXiv review. Chest X-ray reporting is a heavy workload for radiologists, and vision language models increasingly automate it. Standard systems read a single image, so they cannot write the comparison statements that faithful reports need.

Longitudinal report generation adds historical studies, mirroring how radiologists work. The authors call theirs the first full review of this setting. They examine how data sets are built, which architectures are used and which parts are tailored to longitudinal data, and how performance is evaluated. Summarizing published results and ablation studies, they show that longitudinal information and design choices both matter greatly. Five major limitations of current research are identified, with future directions proposed. The survey aims to give newcomers a clear framework for designing models in this emerging area.
arxiv-2510-12544:
Tatakis gives a purely graph theoretic test for when the toric ideal of a graph is unimodular, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Toric ideals encode the algebraic relations among a graph's edges and appear in algebraic statistics and optimization. Unimodularity is a strong regularity property of the underlying matrix that, among other things, guarantees well behaved integer solutions.

He proves a necessary and sufficient characterization in terms of the graph's cycles. As a direct consequence, he describes the structure of unimodular graphs completely: the incidence matrix of a graph is unimodular exactly when any two odd cycles of the graph intersect. Odd cycles are loops of odd length, and the condition says such cycles can never sit disjointly in the graph. The result turns an algebraic question about ideals into a simple combinatorial check on cycle overlap.
arxiv-2510-12644:
Von Eckardstein presents GEFF, a Python package that models gauge field production during cosmic inflation, in a 2025 arXiv software paper. Inflation, the early universe's rapid expansion, can generate gauge fields efficiently. Their backreaction on inflation is strongly nonlinear and costly to simulate on lattices. The gradient expansion method offers a faster route. It recasts the dynamics as an endless tower of coupled ordinary differential equations, cut at some order.

The package solves them with a built in error checker and a self correction routine. It detects when the cutoff breaks down, cross checking against a momentum space approach. Ready to use model files cover two axion scenarios. One has a pure Abelian gauge sector. The other couples the inflaton to the Standard Model hypercharge field, producing fermions through the Schwinger effect. Users can add custom models, and tools for studying primordial gravitational waves from the gauge fields come with it.
arxiv-2510-13044:
Cho and colleagues teach motion generation models about their surroundings in this 2025 arXiv paper. Text-to-motion models produce rich, varied human movement. Scene-aware models keep motion physically consistent with a room or terrain. But training data rarely offers both text coverage and precise scene interaction at once. Building such combined datasets is extremely hard.

Their framework, SceneAdapt, bridges two disjoint datasets through motion inbetweening, filling movement between keyframes, which can be learned without text. A first stage adds keyframing layers that modulate internal motion features while preserving the model's latent structure. A second stage adds a scene-conditioning layer that queries local scene geometry through cross-attention. Experiments showed scene awareness was injected into text-to-motion models, and the authors analyze how that awareness emerges inside the network.
arxiv-2510-13344:
Liu and co-authors present UniMoE-Audio, a single model that generates both speech and music. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles a split in audio research, where speech and music systems are usually built apart. That split causes task conflicts and uneven training data, which hold back a truly unified model.

The team uses a mixture-of-experts design, where different expert networks handle different parts of each task. A routing rule called Top-P varies how many experts each input uses. Routed experts hold domain-specific skill, shared experts hold common features, and null experts let the model skip work. Training runs in three stages, from separate specialists to a joint final phase on balanced data. Tests show top results on speech and music benchmarks, with gains rather than the losses that naive joint training causes. The authors argue this design suits universal audio generation well.
arxiv-2510-13444:
Pelleriti and co-authors use a Transformer to speed up certifying that polynomials never go negative. Their 2025 arXiv paper addresses sum-of-squares certification, a sufficient test for such nonnegativity. Checking this property is NP-hard and matters for optimization, control, and robotics. Standard certification solves a semidefinite program whose size grows with the polynomial. A polynomial is a sum of squares when it splits into squared pieces added together.

Their Transformer predicts a near-minimal set of monomials to use for a given polynomial. A smaller monomial basis shrinks the semidefinite program drastically. The team generated over one hundred million example polynomials to train the model. A fallback mechanism guarantees the procedure still ends correctly when predictions fall short. On more than two hundred benchmark sets, the method ran over one hundred times faster than top solvers. It also solved instances where rival approaches failed outright.
arxiv-2510-13544:
Zhu, Bierman, Lu, and Li add state-specific orbital optimization to excited-state calculations on quantum computers. Their 2025 arXiv paper improves how electronic excited states are computed on near-term quantum hardware. Orbital choice strongly affects accuracy when only few orbitals fit on a device. Averaging one orbital set across all states limits what each state can achieve.

Their scheme optimizes orbitals separately for each state of interest. They derive the gradient of the overlap between states built from different orbitals. Gradient methods then rotate the orbitals to sharpen each state's description. The scheme can pair with any excited-state quantum eigensolver built on overlaps. Implemented with the variational quantum deflation algorithm, it beat the state-averaged scheme on test molecules. The gains held across several molecules, including H4 and lithium hydride.
arxiv-2510-13744:
Pandit and co-authors build Hard2Verify, a benchmark that grades how well AI verifiers catch single wrong steps in hard math proofs. Their 2025 arXiv paper responds to language models now winning gold-level scores at olympiad math. Training such reasoners needs verifiers that flag the exact step where a proof breaks. Easier benchmarks no longer separate strong verifiers from weak ones.

Human annotators spent over five hundred hours marking errors step by step. The questions are recent, open-ended, and answered by frontier models, making the errors subtle. Verifiers must annotate each step or name the first mistake in a response. The team tested twenty-nine generative critics and process reward models on the task. A few standouts aside, open-source verifiers trail closed ones by a wide margin. Analyses probe why verification fails, how extra compute helps, and whether models can check themselves.
arxiv-2510-14044:
Younghoon Kim, Zachary F. Fisher, and Vladas Pipiras improve a model that maps how brain or behavior variables influence each other across people, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The multi-subject vector autoregression model splits each person's network of lagged effects into paths shared by everyone and paths unique to that individual, revealing common structure in psychology and neuroscience data.

The existing model identifies shared effects with a weighted median. The authors show this is statistically inefficient. Accuracy for everyone is dragged down by the least sparse subject and the smallest sample. They propose an identifiability condition built on a communication-efficient data integration framework. It achieves convergence rates tailored to each subject's sparsity and sample size. They develop hypothesis tests, based on debiased estimators, for whether paths are zero or equal across subjects, plus a test for the shared paths. Simulations and a data application support the method.
arxiv-2510-14244:
Arnaud Judge and co-authors use reinforcement learning to adapt heart-ultrasound segmentation models to new hospitals and scanners without any expert labels, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Segmentation of echocardiography videos is critical, but models trained at one site degrade at another, and noise, artifacts, and consistency across heartbeats make the domain shift severe.

Their framework, RL4Seg3D, treats segmentation as a reinforcement learning problem with novel reward functions and a fusion scheme that sharpens key anatomical landmarks while processing full-sized videos. The design improves accuracy, anatomical validity, and temporal consistency together. As a side benefit, it yields a robust uncertainty estimator. That can further improve results at test time by flagging doubtful frames. Evaluated on more than thirty thousand echocardiographic videos, the framework outperformed domain adaptation techniques without a single target-domain label, addressing a bottleneck that blocks deployment of medical imaging AI.
arxiv-2510-14444:
Moritz Wagner and co-authors revisit how to repair a large language model after pruning, and find a 'free lunch' hiding in local reconstruction, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Pruning cuts inference costs but degrades quality unless the surviving weights adapt; global retraining is prohibitively expensive, so research chased cleverer pruning criteria that avoid adaptation.

Their local reconstruction adapts one subset of parameters at a time on a calibration set, training each piece to reproduce the model's activations. Across families and scales up to seventy-two billion parameters, local reconstruction matched post-pruning retraining while using over ten times less data and compute. They also find a free-lunch regime. Provided the reconstructed window contains at least one nonlinear submodule, quality barely depends on window size. Practitioners can choose granularity from memory constraints alone. The results reframe adaptation after pruning as cheap and forgiving rather than a last resort.
arxiv-2510-14544:
Borchiellini, Maurin, and Vecchi revisit, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a subtle decay process that affects cosmic rays traveling through the Galaxy. Some atomic nuclei can capture one of their own electrons and decay. How many have done so reveals the time between the nuclei being forged and being accelerated. Modelers have long used a shortcut that treats each nucleus as either bare or holding one electron.

The authors instead solve the transport equations with any number of attached electrons, in two standard models of cosmic ray travel. The decayed fractions look similar in shape between the models, though the absolute fluxes differ a lot. They confirm the old two-level shortcut is good enough in most situations. They also find the decay's effect on current data is negligible, except possibly for a few species involving chromium, iron, and cobalt. The conclusions hold despite large uncertainties in the underlying rates.
arxiv-2510-14844:
Melamed, Yehudai, and Vardi give, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a theoretical account of the simplest machine unlearning trick: gradient ascent. Unlearning means deleting one training point's influence from a trained model without retraining from scratch. Practitioners often just run training in reverse on the point to forget. Whether that actually works, and how well, lacked proof.

The authors lean on a known bias of gradient descent: it drifts toward solutions satisfying the optimality conditions of a margin maximization problem. They judge an unlearned model by how well it satisfies those same conditions on the data that remain. Formalizing this as a precise success criterion, they prove that a properly scaled gradient-ascent step meets it, for linear models and for two-layer ReLU networks on high-dimensional data. The resulting model closely approximates the retrained one. A synthetic test with Gaussian mixture data shows generalization survives the procedure.
arxiv-2510-15044:
Khan, Innan, Khalique, and Shafique build, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a quantum machine learning model for credit scoring that can explain itself. Lenders' decisions govern people's access to credit and face strict official scrutiny, so a black-box model is a liability. Quantum models are doubly opaque. The authors' framework, IQNN-CS, targets multiclass credit risk classification with transparency designed in rather than bolted on.

The architecture pairs a variational quantum neural network with explanation techniques for structured financial data. The paper's novelty is a metric, Inter-Class Attribution Alignment, which measures how the model's importance attributions diverge across predicted classes, exposing how it tells one risk category from another. Evaluated on two credit datasets, the system showed stable training dynamics and competitive performance, with markedly clearer explanations than is usual for quantum models. The authors offer it as a path to accountable quantum learning in finance.
arxiv-2510-15144:
Chance Jiajie Li and a large team at MIT and partner groups test whether language models can mimic how one specific person reasons. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that today's models tend to echo the average view of a crowd, flattening the quirks of individual thought. Their benchmark, HugAgent, instead asks a model to predict how a named person would reason and revise beliefs in a fresh scenario, given samples of that person's past views.

HugAgent runs on two tracks: a synthetic track that allows large, controlled stress tests, and a human track built from people thinking aloud. The score that matters is fidelity to the individual, capturing not just what someone believes but how their views shift. Trials with leading models exposed a persistent adaptation gap, meaning models kept sliding back toward consensus answers. The team released the benchmark openly to push research on more personal machine reasoning.
arxiv-2510-15244:
Lina Berrayana and five colleagues pair two different kinds of language model so one plans and the other writes the final answer. Their 2025 arXiv paper contrasts two model types. Autoregressive models generate text one token at a time and can be slow. Discrete diffusion models draft many tokens in parallel within fixed steps and show strength in planning. The question is whether teamwork beats either model alone.

First the pair communicated in plain text, the planner handing written steps to the executor. Then the team let them communicate in latent space, through a learned projector that feeds the planner's internal states straight into the executor, skipping words entirely. That switch sharply raised accuracy, doubling one hard reasoning score from 27 to 54 percent, with the gains stated at the level the authors report. The latent pipeline also reached strong scores using far fewer tokens than a leading single model.
arxiv-2510-15344:
Xavier Tan, Xiaoli Tang, and Han Yu design fairer pay deals for organizations that lend their data to shared AI training, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In federated learning, data owners train a joint model without handing over raw data, but buyers cannot see the data, so judging effort and quality is hard. Contracts set the incentives, yet standard contracts freeze terms until the job ends.

Freezing is the flaw the team targets: illness, budget cuts, or shifting priorities can leave an owner unable to deliver, wasting the buyer's budget. Their mechanism, RC-TIM, allows contracts to be renegotiated as behavior and budgets change, keeping incentives flexible and current. In experiments on three benchmark datasets it beat four leading rival mechanisms, raising buyer utility by up to about forty-six percent on average, as the authors report the figure. They present renegotiation as the missing piece for open federated learning markets.
arxiv-2510-15444:
Zhi Zhou and six colleagues give the first theory for a popular trick that makes language models reason better at test time. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies sampling-based scaling, where a model drafts many reasoning paths and the answers are combined. Two combination rules dominate, namely self-consistency, which votes among final answers, and perplexity, which trusts the model's own confidence scores.

Their framework, built on confidence estimation, exposes a flaw in each rule. Self-consistency carries high estimation error, while perplexity carries substantial modeling error that can even stop improving with more samples. Their hybrid method, Rpc, joins the two through perplexity consistency, which speeds error convergence from linear to exponential. A pruning step drops low-probability paths before they can drag quality down. Across seven benchmarks Rpc matched self-consistency's reasoning performance while halving sampling costs. It also produced confidence estimates the authors judge more reliable.
arxiv-2510-15744:
Haocong Luo and colleagues at ETH Zürich publish, in a 2025 paper, a rebuttal of an award-winning computer architecture study that claimed existing memory system simulators poorly match real hardware. The rebuttal argues that the earlier team misconfigured and misused the Ramulator 2.0 simulator, producing the wrong results on which its headline claims rested.

Re-running the experiments with correct settings, Luo's team shows that Ramulator 2.0's simulated memory performance actually matches real system behaviour well, which undercuts a central claimed contribution of the earlier benchmark paper. They also report that the earlier results could not be reproduced as published, despite the paper carrying a reproducibility badge, and they frame the episode as a caution about artifact evaluation.
arxiv-2510-15844:
Shahriyar Jafarzade and Richard Lebed refine a particle model in a 2025 paper. The model covers tetraquarks. These are exotic particles built from four quarks. The focus is hidden-strangeness versions. They contain a strange quark pair. Their dynamical diquark model treats the particle as two bound quark pairs. This work upgrades an earlier, simpler form. That form ignored nearby particle-pair thresholds.

The upgraded model tabulates all relevant thresholds. It computes how much of each predicted state is made of ordinary particle pairs. No hidden-strangeness candidate is dominated by such pair structure. This contrasts with the charm sector. Several known states remain strong tetraquark candidates. They sit above two giga-electronvolts. Their decay behaviour is distinctive.
arxiv-2510-15944:
Tianyu Bell Pan, Mengdi Zhu, Alexa Jordyn Cole, Ronald Wilson, and Damon L. Woodard build a controller that keeps multimodal learning steady when the data drift. Concept drift, a shift in the data distribution over time, degrades models trained on yesterday's patterns. Drift can hit one modality alone, and most systems lack a stable way to keep adapting.

Their framework, LS-OGD, adjusts the learning rate and the fusion weights between modalities online, in response to detected drift and changing prediction error. Pan and his four co-authors prove that under bounded drift the prediction error stays uniformly bounded in the long run, and it falls to zero if the drift stops. The adaptive fusion also isolates a badly drifting modality, which protects the rest of the system and supports fault tolerance in deployed multimodal tools.
arxiv-2510-16344:
Chenrui Tie and eleven co-authors teach robots to assemble things the way people do: by reading the manual. Most assembly planners sequence the parts and poses but treat the connectors, the screws, snaps, and slots that physically decide success, as an afterthought.

Manual2Skill++ makes connections first-class citizens, encoding each connector's type, specification, and location for every step in a hierarchical graph of parts and sub-assemblies. A large vision-language model reads the diagrams and annotations in real instruction manuals to build those graphs automatically. The team curates over twenty assembly tasks with varied connectors and tests the full pipeline, from manual understanding to simulated execution, on four complex scenarios spanning furniture, toys, and manufacturing parts.
arxiv-2510-16744:
Srinivas Vivek, writing alone, breaks a privacy-preserving ride-hailing design that was presented at NSS 2022 by Xie and co-authors. Ride-hailing services match riders with drivers. Privacy-preserving versions try to hide the locations of both sides from the service provider while still making matches.

Vivek shows a passive attack against that design. By only watching normal protocol traffic, the provider can fully recover the location of the rider and of the responding drivers in every request. The attack is cheap to run, and its cost does not grow with the security parameter. The result is a warning that the earlier scheme's privacy promise does not hold.
arxiv-2510-17344:
Some graph problems start from a broken layout that must be repaired by sliding tokens along edges, step by step, within a small budget of moves. Nicolas Bousquet and four co-authors ask when such repair tasks, called solution discovery, can be solved efficiently for whole families of problems stated in formal logic. Their focus is on which structural measures of a graph make the task tractable.

Bousquet and his co-authors prove positive results for two logic families under measures such as treewidth and neighbourhood diversity. They also prove hardness results for other measures, showing that efficient methods are unlikely there. Together, the findings nearly complete the map of which settings admit fast algorithms and which do not.
arxiv-2510-17444:
Memory can be built into matter itself when a particle future motion depends on where it has already been. Vaishnavi Gajendragad and Suropriya Saha explore that idea for active particles, whose speed includes a push set by their own past path, weighted by a memory rule. Because that memory is separate from random thermal noise, the system breaks the usual balance of microscopic physics from the start.

Gajendragad and Saha show that the crowding pattern of such particles follows a well known equation for phase separation, adjusted for this non-equilibrium push. They map the new features that appear and use delayed interactions as a worked example. Theory and simulations together show pattern forming behaviour that passive matter does not display.
arxiv-2510-17744:
Noah Kravitz and James Leng take on a covering puzzle called the Pyjama Problem. A pyjama stripe holds points whose real part lies near a whole number. The question asks whether finitely many rotated stripes can cover the whole plane. An earlier proof said yes but gave no count of rotations.

Kravitz and Leng supply the first explicit bound on that count. Their bound is a triple exponential in the stripe width parameter. The proof uses entropy tools built for a related doubling-and-tripling problem. Those tools came from Bourgain, Lindenstrauss, Michel, and Venkatesh. The result turns a pure existence claim into a measured one.
arxiv-2510-17944:
Sridhar Mahadevan, as sole author, extends Pearl's causal calculus into a setting where truth is local rather than global. The frame is a topos of sheaves, where interventions are treated as subobjects of a causal model. A modal operator then defines which claims hold on which patches of the setting.

The new rules replace global truth with local truth in the model's internal logic. Claims about independence and about interventions must stay stable across those patches. Three rule sets are given for sound reasoning in this frame. Readers in logic and causal theory get a formal path for reasoning where context changes the facts.
arxiv-2510-18244:
Ajinkya Khoche, with Gergő László Nagy and three co-authors, presents BlendCLIP in a 2025 paper on three-dimensional vision. The task is zero-shot classification, meaning naming objects the model never saw labeled examples of during training. Models trained on clean computer-made objects often fail on messy real LiDAR scans from cars.

BlendCLIP trains on both computer-made objects and real driving data together. The team built triples of point cloud, image, and text from real road scenes. A staged mixing plan starts with rich synthetic data, then slowly adds real scans. Adding even a tiny share of real samples sharply raised accuracy on road benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-18344:
Vipul Rathore, with Malik Hammad Faisal and two co-authors, presents HYDRE in a 2025 paper on relation extraction. Relation extraction finds stated links between entities in text, like who founded a company. Distant supervision labels data automatically from a knowledge base, which leaves noisy bag-level labels.

HYDRE first lets a trained specialist model shortlist candidate relations for each sentence. It then retrieves reliable sentence-level examples and places them in a language model prompt. That in-context learning, meaning learning from examples inside the prompt, produces the final answer. Tests report large score gains in English and across four low-resource Indic languages.
arxiv-2510-18544:
Will Chow, writing alone, presents a scheduler called SLICE. It runs large language models on edge devices. Such devices include robots and smart vehicles. Each app sets its own service goals. One goal is how fast the first token must appear. Another is how steady later tokens must flow. Old schedulers chase raw output speed alone. Deadline-style goals then get missed a lot. Real-time edge tasks suffer most from those misses.

SLICE pairs two tools. One schedules requests to raise a utility score. The other is a control loop. It adjusts output rates as conditions change. Tests pitted SLICE against Orca and FastServe. SLICE beat both by wide margins on goal attainment. In some tests it reached thirty-five times their score. It also finished tasks several times faster. Chow argues edge inference should serve stated goals. Raw throughput alone is the wrong target.
arxiv-2510-18844:
Selina Zhou and her eight co-authors generate an extremely broad spectrum of light in a chip-scale device, using a mechanism the field has largely skipped. Supercontinuum sources spread laser light across many colors for imaging, sensing, and frequency comb work.
