Most rely on cubic nonlinearities, but quadratic nonlinearities are usually stronger and can convert light both up and down in frequency through three-wave mixing.

With a new dispersion engineering principle in lithium niobate nano-waveguides, the team demonstrated purely quadratic supercontinuum generation that far surpassed earlier integrated demonstrations in coverage and efficiency. One device produced a robust multi-octave spectrum from mere femtojoules of pump energy, using a near-zero dispersion profile and a single patterning period. A second device, with a flatter dispersion profile, pushed coverage further into the mid-infrared, opening a more efficient route to broadband on-chip light.
arxiv-2510-19144:
Cheng Huang and twenty-one co-authors survey Tibetan language technology, covering its data resources, methods, and open challenges. Tibetan is a major low-resource language of Asia with distinctive linguistic and cultural traits, yet it has drawn little attention because accessible data, standard benchmarks, and dedicated tools are scarce.

The survey organizes existing datasets and tools, reviews work on language tasks, machine translation, and speech recognition, and compares performance where reports allow. It also tracks recent progress with large language models and names persistent gaps. For builders of language technology, it maps what exists and what Tibetan still needs.
arxiv-2510-19344:
Gwyn Bellamy traces the theory of Weyl algebras and their modules. The story starts with a landmark paper by Stafford. It appeared in nineteen seventy-eight. Weyl algebras are built from position and momentum style operators. They are basic in algebra and mathematical physics. Their modules proved far richer than expected.

Bellamy starts with classic theorems of Serre and Bass. He then explains how Stafford built simple modules that are not holonomic. A geometric construction of whole families comes next. Newer work links ideals in the first Weyl algebra to Calogero-Moser spaces. The survey ties fifty years into one story.
arxiv-2510-19644:
Daria Cherniuk and six co-authors present CoRoVA, a way to keep the benefits of retrieved context in code completion without paying its speed cost. Retrieval-augmented completion pulls in related code from the repository, but the long prompts slow the time to the first generated token, which hurts inside an editor. CoRoVA compresses the retrieved context into a few small vectors instead.

Only a small projector module needs training, and the compressed vectors stay meaningful to the code model. Prediction quality improved while the prompt grew by just a handful of tokens. On completion tasks the time to first token dropped by twenty to thirty-eight percent compared with uncompressed retrieval, a practical gain for interactive coding tools.
arxiv-2510-19744:
Damian Sobota and Tomasz Żuchowski study two traits of Boolean algebras built from ideals: the Nikodym trait and the Grothendieck trait. For an ideal in a complete Boolean algebra, they show one direction cleanly. If the algebra generated by the ideal lacks the Nikodym trait, it lacks the Grothendieck trait too. The converse fails. The paper builds large families of algebras that have the first trait but not the second.

For analytic P-ideals, four conditions turn out to be equivalent. They link boundedness traits with combinatorial features of the quotient algebra. The authors also confirm a conjecture of Drewnowski, Florencio, and Paúl. They exhibit analytic P-ideals with the Nikodym trait but without a local-to-global boundedness trait. A question of Stuart is answered too, using ideals induced by Kneser hypergraphs.
arxiv-2510-19844:
Isaac Wu and Michael Maslowski propose CourtGuard, a prompt injection detector that stages a miniature courtroom among language models. One model argues the incoming prompt is benign, another argues it is an attack, and a judge model rules. The whole system runs locally, which matters for sensitive applications where prompts cannot leave the building.

Compared with a direct judge-style detector, CourtGuard produced fewer false alarms on harmless prompts. It was, however, generally worse at catching actual injections. The authors argue the trade-off still teaches something important: a fair classifier must weigh the benign case seriously, and multiagent debate is a viable defensive pattern. Implementations for three open models are published.
arxiv-2510-19944:
Jiashi Feng and twenty-seven co-authors present Seed3D 1.0, a foundation model that turns a single image into a three-dimensional asset ready to drop into a physics simulator. Embodied AI needs training worlds that are both varied and physically accurate; video generators give variety without interactive physics, while physics engines need costly hand-built assets. Seed3D targets the gap.

Its assets carry accurate geometry, well-aligned textures, and realistic physically based materials, and they enter physics engines with minimal setup for robotics manipulation and simulation training. The system also assembles individual objects into coherent full scenes. The authors frame the release as infrastructure for scalable, physics-based world simulators.
arxiv-2510-20044:
Anna Hellers, Mathias Reichle, and Sven Klinkel present a polygonal plate element for the Reissner-Mindlin plate model based on the scaled boundary finite element method. Unlike the original semi-analytical version, their formulation uses linear shape functions for both the scaling and radial directions. The fully discretized result allows polygonal elements with any number of edges, even shapes that are not star-convex, which simplifies meshing.

To prevent transverse shear locking in the thin-plate limit, they derive an assumed natural strain treatment for these elements. A two-field variational form also lets three-dimensional material laws be used while enforcing plane stress conditions in the weak form. Several numerical examples demonstrate that the element performs as intended.
arxiv-2510-20244:
Minseok Kang and four co-authors propose DualGround for video temporal grounding, the task of finding the moments in a long untrimmed video that match a language query. The job combines moment retrieval and highlight detection, and strong vision-language models have advanced both. The authors show through controlled experiments that current models lean on the global meaning carried by one special token and underuse word-level signals.

DualGround splits the work into two branches: a sentence-level path handles global meaning, while word tokens are clustered into phrase-level units for local grounding. Token-role-aware interaction aligns video features with each kind of semantics in a separated way. The joint design improves both coarse alignment and fine-grained timing of the located segments.
arxiv-2510-20344:
Wei Cao and Shanshan Wang fit expectile nets to data where some reads are cut off, a case called censoring. Such nets catch spread and bent shapes in data well. But most past work needs full reads with no cuts. Their way, called DAERNN, fills the gaps with a data growth step and stays free of firm claims about the data form.

Fake data tests and real data runs show DAERNN ahead of past cut-data expectile nets. Its scores match nets trained on full data, a strong mark given the lost facts. One frame serves many cut types with no set form for the law of the data. That breadth suits real cut-data work, the team argues.
arxiv-2510-20544:
Diego Cifelli and Adolfo Anta test firm rules for grid-forming converters in new power grids with a high share of such gear. As converter stock grows, firm checks must scale with no full-grid sim runs. Small gain and small-phase rules were put forth for that aim. With grid-forming units, the sector claim at their heart tends to fail at low tones, which caps their use.

The pair grow mixed gain-phase rules with loop shape steps. Those steps restate unit and grid forms in new frames. The fix clears the low-tone flaw and cuts slack. Marks are shown first on an endless bus case, then on the IEEE 14-bus grid, to show scale and real use.
arxiv-2510-20844:
Jiawei Zhou, Ruicheng Zhu, Mengshi Chen, Jianwei Wang, and Kai Wang present TrustResearcher, a multi agent demo system that drafts research ideas from literature while keeping its reasoning open to inspection. Automated idea tools often act as black boxes, leaving scholars little control or trust in how a suggestion arose.

Four stages structure the work, curated knowledge building, varied idea drafting, multi stage idea selection, and expert panel review with synthesis. Logs, middle reasoning states, and adjustable agents stay visible throughout, and ideas come with evidence and critiques attached. A graph mining case on the k-truss breaking problem shows distinct plausible candidates, and the same pipeline can be set up for any field, with code and a live demo shared.
arxiv-2510-20944:
Max M Kurzner leads twenty one co-authors on morphological classification of Virgo cluster galaxies in the Next Generation Virgo Cluster Survey, paper forty in the series. Deep imaging in four bands covers nearly thirty seven hundred member galaxies across more than six orders of magnitude in stellar mass.

A new two component visual scheme records global structure and star formation activity separately, with sub codes for arms, bars, disks, shells, and streams. The scheme captures diversity from giant ellipticals down to faint dwarfs in one consistent system. Such a census anchors studies of how environment reshapes galaxies inside a rich cluster.
arxiv-2510-21144:
Hanyu Zhu leads four co-authors on NeuroGenPoisoning, a neuron guided attack that poisons lookup expanded generation systems through by evolution tuned outside knowledge. Retrieval lets models use fresh sources, but adversaries can plant poisoned documents that override internal memory.

Existing attacks edit lookup content or prompts while ignoring internal neuron dynamics and the conflict between planted knowledge and strong stored knowledge. Their method targets neuron level sensitivities to craft more effective poison. Studying the mechanism in depth strengthens defenses for lookup systems that enterprises now trust with live documents every day.
arxiv-2510-21444:
Julian Schulz and four co-authors bring three-dimensional micro-printing to photonic quantum gases. These are clouds of light particles held in tiny dye-filled cavities. Such gases let physicists probe open quantum systems under room conditions. Open systems constantly gain and lose energy. Shaping the landscape the light moves through had been crude until now.

Printed landscapes beat earlier ones by at least tenfold on several measures. They win on size, sharpness, depth, and grip on the light. They also allow far more coupled sites. As demonstrations, the team prints box-shaped traps with crisp walls. They print stretched harmonic traps and paired double wells as small as a wavelength of light. They also print lattices whose shape carries topological features. The control opens experiments on open quantum systems arranged in lattices.
arxiv-2510-21644:
Zheng Liu constructs families of theta lifts for orthogonal and unitary groups that stay definite. Theta lifts move automorphic forms from smaller groups to bigger ones. Hida families let a single construction vary in an arithmetic family. Their behavior at places above a fixed prime p is delicate to control.

The key ingredient is the choice of test Schwartz functions at those p-adic places. Those local inputs seed the lift. Liu selects a special type carrying an equivariance property. It concerns the action of the U_p operators, the local averaging operators that organize Hida theory. With that choice in hand, the families of lifts can be assembled. The work adds a working local ingredient to the broader program of p-adic variation of automorphic forms.
arxiv-2510-22044:
Kijung Jeon, Michael Muehlebach, and Molei Tao tackle sampling under constraints. The task is to draw fair samples from a distribution fenced in by equations and inequalities. Such fences make the allowed region nonconvex. Most samplers pay for costly projection steps to stay legal. Each older method handles only one kind of fence. Firm convergence guarantees are often missing too.

Their framework, OLLA, reshapes the random walk itself. Trajectories are corrected along the direction normal to the boundary. This landing move keeps samples feasible without projections. Both equalities and inequalities fit in one method. Cases that once needed separate tools are covered together. The authors aim for speed plus firm guarantees. Bayesian statistics, chemistry, and physics all need such sampling.
arxiv-2510-22144:
Tao Wu and Yan Li model the pulsations of Blue Large Amplitude Pulsators. These variable stars throb with large swings. Their periods run from a few minutes to just over an hour. The stars are hot and compact. Some wear helium-rich surfaces, and others hydrogen-rich ones. The identity of their pulsation modes remains unsettled. So does the road that formed them.

The pair runs non-adiabatic pulsation calculations across a grid of models. Such calculations track whether a vibration grows or dies. Low-order radial and dipole modes are examined. The radial fundamental mode matches many observed properties well. The analysis extends to how fast periods change. It also covers how modes relate in period. Element diffusion and radiative levitation are left out on purpose. Those processes make predicted surface compositions clash with observations.
arxiv-2510-22244:
Shijie Bao, Qi'an Guan, Zhitong Mi, and Zheng Yuan settle when a valuation, a way of measuring how strongly a function vanishes at a point, can be interpolated between given data. Working on rings of germs of holomorphic functions and of real analytic functions at the origin, they deploy Zhou valuations, Tian functions. A convergence theorem for relative types to obtain conditions that are both necessary and sufficient.

For polynomial rings over the complex and real numbers, separate necessary and sufficient conditions appear. The two meet when the common zero set of the given polynomials is exactly the origin. Further results characterize when a valuation has the form of a relative type against a tame maximal weight, extend a theorem of Boucksom, Favre. Jonsson to the Zhou setting, and relate Zhou valuations to the points where Tian functions can be differentiated.
arxiv-2510-22844:
Group talk weaves several topic threads at once. Tracing those threads in live speech is hard. Prerna Ravi leads a team with seven co-authors. In 2025 they test language models on this task. Their setting is collaborative learning in small groups.

The team wrote a guidebook for finding threads. It covers synchronous multi party transcripts. They benchmark prompts for automated threading. Then they test downstream coding of talk moves. Moves include agreeing, building, and eliciting. Clear thread data improved model coding scores. The work links discourse structure to learning analysis. Overlapping turns and implicit cues remain core challenges.
arxiv-2510-23144:
Ziyu Wang, Wenhao Li, and Ji Wu present DQ3D, a depth-guided method for finding objects in three dimensions from several camera views in traffic scenes. Many detectors seed object queries from three-dimensional reference points. Points that start far from any real object can trigger false detections and waste effort.

DQ3D uses depth information and two-dimensional detections to place reference points on or inside likely objects. Queries then begin where objects plausibly are. More accurate seeding should cut false positives on busy roads, helping self-driving systems tell real hazards from empty space.
arxiv-2510-23544:
Tingyu Song and four co-authors show that search reranking does not need huge amounts of training data. Reranking means taking a first list of search results and reordering it so the best matches rise to the top. Standard practice fine-tunes large language models on massive example sets, which costs a lot of computing time and money.

The authors built an open-source pipeline, LimRank-Synthesizer, that creates varied and hard training examples on its own. Fine-tuning on that synthetic data produced their model, LimRank, trained on under five percent of the data earlier work used. Even so, it scored competitively on two tough benchmarks, one for reasoning-heavy retrieval and one for following search instructions. Extra tests showed it also helps with science literature search and question answering that draws on retrieved text.
arxiv-2510-23644:
Yu. M. Poluektov proposes a method for describing charged relativistic Fermi fields, the quantum fields behind particles like electrons that obey Fermi statistics. A long-standing awkwardness in this theory is the place of negative-energy states, which complicate the picture of particles and antiparticles. Poluektov's approach treats particles of opposite charges on an equal footing from the start.

The method introduces a charge quantum number, a label that sorts states by their charge. Fields for particles and antiparticles with different charge quantum numbers are tied to wave functions that keep the Born interpretation, meaning their squared size still reads as a probability. Negative-energy states are excluded from the description altogether. The result is a cleaner relativistic framework in which charge is a built-in property rather than an add-on.
arxiv-2510-23744:
Eline M. Bovy and four co-authors extend a standard planning model for agents that act under partial observability. A POMDP captures decision-making when the true state is hidden, but real problems also carry model uncertainty: several experts may disagree on how the world responds. Multi-environment POMDPs bundle a set of such models, sharing states, actions, and observations while differing in dynamics and rewards.

The goal is one policy that does well against the worst model in the set. The authors generalize the setup to sets of starting beliefs, calling the result adversarial-belief POMDPs. They then show any such problem can be reshaped so uncertainty lives only in transitions and rewards, or only in observations and rewards, without changing the best policies. Exact and point-based approximate algorithms follow. Tests on POMDP benchmarks, widened to many environments, show the methods compute robust policies in practice.
arxiv-2510-23844:
Cameron M. Pike and three co-authors sharpen a method for predicting the nonlinear distortion that power amplifiers inflict on multi-carrier signals. Distortion matters because system designers must trade output power against network throughput, and guessing wrong is costly. Their approach uses the series form of the characteristic function method, which computes signal and distortion components separately and efficiently.

On the theory side, they model the signal as a bandpass Gaussian process that gets hard limited. In that case their method reproduces exactly what the classical Price theorem gives, a clean validation. On the practice side, they feed a fragmented-spectrum OFDM signal into an amplifier driven into compression, where the classical theorem is hard to apply. The predicted output spectrum matches laboratory measurements well. The method also yields signal-to-distortion ratios across settings like overdrive level, and it exploits the fast Fourier transform for speed.
arxiv-2510-24044:
Hui Sun and three co-authors study how a model trained in one setting can fail when used in a new setting with no labels. This failure is called negative transfer, where the move makes results worse instead of better. They trace the problem to features that are not true causes but shift with the environment.

When a model leans too much on those shifting features, its choices clash across settings and hurt transfer. Their method, RED, splits causal features from environmental ones and cuts that clash. Tests support the idea and show better results when the gap between source and target settings is large.
arxiv-2510-24144:
Lei Sun and four co-authors calculate the excited states of a charged nitrogen vacancy center in diamond, a defect used to prepare pure spin states with light. They use a hybrid density functional called HSE06 and optimize the orbitals directly for each state. The work covers the excited triplet and the two lowest singlet states above the ground triplet.

They also estimate how the atoms relax around the defect, using analytic forces. The drop in energy for the triplet and the resulting zero phonon line match lab estimates within a tenth of an electron volt. For the lower singlet, the relaxation is smaller, about six hundredths of an electron volt, found with spin purified forces.
arxiv-2510-24344:
Mostafa Raeisi Sarkandiz reviews why people choose to vote, using behavioral economics and an economic model of participation, working alone. He divides the factors behind turnout into two groups. The first covers broad conditions in a voter's life, including economic status, culture, and psychological traits, with inflation and unemployment as the key economic factors under consumer behavior theory.

The second group concerns the act of voting itself, with emphasis on how the sitting government performs. Incumbent governments and their supporters interact like players in a game, shaping turnout incentives. The review weighs these structural parameters to explain both how many people vote and how they decide.
arxiv-2510-24844:
Atsushi Tanimoto and seven co-authors model winds that blow off the disk of gas round a black hole in our own galaxy. Such winds show as blue shifted dips in X ray light, a sign of hot gas that flows out. Their model treats the wind as a hot stream driven by magnet fields that thread the disk.

With a Monte Carlo code, they track how light moves through the wind and sets its charge state in three dimensions. For the soft bright state of such a system, they built fake light curves to match the real dips. Slanted views gave strong multi ion dips with lopsided shapes, plus glow like that seen in real data.
arxiv-2510-25444:
E McKinnon-Gray led six co-authors on equatorial waves. D Shipley, J Methven, and T H A Frame helped. C Sanchez, A McCabe, and N M Roberts joined. Their 2025 paper studies convectively coupled equatorial waves. They bring episodes of widespread heavy precipitation. Models represent convection in varied ways.

Two Met Office Unified Model runs are compared. Both use identical kilometer-scale resolution. One parametrizes convection with a scheme called GAL9. The other permits explicit convection, called RAL3 here. Parametrized schemes remove instability without resolved plume circulation. The authors diagnose interscale energy transfer quantitatively. Upscale transfer moves energy from convection to large waves. Explicit convection raised average upscale transfer largely. Waves were more coherent in explicit runs. Energy transfer within waves was also greater there. Kelvin and Rossby waves showed upscale transfer patterns. Explicit convection likely matters for faithful wave run.
arxiv-2510-25844:
Cassandra Lochhaas leads thirteen co-authors in a simulation study of glowing gas around galaxies. The gas region, called the circumgalactic medium, holds flows moving in and out that control galaxy growth, but its thin, mixed gas is hard to observe. They focus on light from oxygen ions, known as O VI emission, that a planned small satellite called Aspera could map in nearby galaxies.

Using the FOGGIE simulations, Lochhaas and the team find the glow is brightest near small clumps close to the galaxy. Most of it comes from warm gas flowing inward, yet outflows matter too, because feedback enriches the inflow so it can glow. Heavier, more active galaxies glow brighter and wider.
arxiv-2510-26544:
Daiki Miura, Masaru Hongo, Hidetoshi Taya, and Tetsuo Hatsuda ask how a strong magnetic field changes the force between two nucleons. The force piece they study is the one-pion exchange potential, the pull carried by the lightest meson. Their tool is chiral perturbation theory, a step-by-step method for the strong force at low energy, with nucleons treated as heavy and slow.

Miura and his three co-authors derive the potential for fields up to about the pion mass scale, not just weak ones. The field alters how charged pions move, which shortens the force's range both along and across the field as it grows. The shift in the deuteron's binding energy can reach about one mega-electronvolt at the top of that range. That is on the scale of the binding energy itself.
arxiv-2510-26644:
Dominique Maldague, Hong Wang, and Dmitrii Zakharov attack Heilbronn's triangle problem in three dimensions. The problem asks how small a triangle must exist among points placed in a box: with many points, some three should form a tiny triangle. In the flat, two-dimensional version, bounds have been known for decades, but the spatial version had no nontrivial upper bound.

Maldague and her two co-authors prove a new bound for points in the unit cube. Among any n points, some triangle has area at most a stated power of n, slightly better than the plain guess. The proof rests on a new result about point-line pairs in space, which limits how many points and lines can keep a set distance apart. The planar cousin of that result was proved earlier by Cohen, Pohoata, and Zakharov.
arxiv-2510-27044:
Md Tanvirul Alam and Nidhi Rastogi probe whether a popular training method truly teaches language models to reason. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards rewards answers that can be checked as right or wrong. It lifts scores on math tasks, but whether models gain real reasoning or just sharper shortcuts has stayed unclear.

The pair test the method on two combinatorial problems with fully checkable answers and unique best solutions, activity scheduling and longest increasing subsequence. Across several reward designs, scores improve, yet models mostly reinforce surface heuristics rather than new strategies. The findings stress benchmarks that separate genuine reasoning from shortcut use. Code is released so others can repeat and extend the tests.
arxiv-2510-27144:
Yang Liu, Jonathan P. Williams, and Jan Hannig wrote this 2025 paper on a weak point in a widely used kind of statistics. Bayesian methods start with a prior, an early guess about unknown values, then update it with data. Many users pick the prior just to make the math run, not from real belief. The three authors ask when the results can still be trusted.

They show a real risk: if the prior clashes with how the values truly arise, the answers can mislead. Their fix is to tune the method's ranges, called credible regions, so they hold up under repeat sampling. A step-by-step tuning method does the job in practice. Tests and a real data case show the tuned version stays sound where the plain one does not.
arxiv-2510-27244:
Ora Nova Fandina leads eight co-authors in SparseAlign, a framework for validating language models used as judges when human labels are scarce. Modernizing legacy code in languages like COBOL needs scalable review, and model judges offer it, but unvalidated judges risk a circular loop where unreliable scores guide release decisions. Human alignment checks are principled yet starved of labeled data in real domains.

SparseAlign pairs a pairwise-confidence concept with a score-sensitive alignment metric that jointly capture ranking consistency and score closeness. This enables reliable evaluator selection where classic statistics fail on tiny samples. Applied internally to COBOL code explanation, the top-aligned judges entered assessment workflows and guided model release decisions. A four-judge case study demonstrates practical utility.
arxiv-2510-27544:
Nikolaus Holzer, William Fishell, Baishakhi Ray, and Mark Santolucito built TempoBench in 2025 as a test of cause and effect in large language models, which are programs that work with text. The test asks a model to track steps over time and judge which inputs truly caused an output. It uses made-up machines whose rules are known, so each answer can be checked.

Top models score well when they run a system forward step by step. They score far worse when asked which inputs were truly needed for a result. The team calls this drop the SIM/MIN gap. Training on the test data helps models on cause tasks, and the skill seems distinct from general skill with text, math, or code.
arxiv-2511-00344:
Xihang Qiu and six co-authors tackle emotion recognition in conversations when some signal channels go missing. Systems that fuse text, voice, and face cues work well until a modality drops out, which happens often in real settings. Older recovery methods train on complete data and can distort meaning when a channel is always absent. Their framework, FedDISC, brings federated learning into the repair task.

Separate diffusion models for each modality are trained across clients and shared with clients that lack that channel. A dialogue graph and a semantic network keep recovered content consistent in context, speaker, and meaning. A training scheme that freezes modules in turns steadies joint learning. On three standard conversation datasets, FedDISC beat earlier methods across many missing-channel patterns.
arxiv-2511-00444:
Benjamin Clavié and six co-authors announce LIR, the first workshop on late interaction and multi-vector retrieval, set for the ECIR 2026 conference. Late interaction methods, pioneered by ColBERT, score matches at the token level instead of compressing each text into one vector. They generalize well, especially outside their training domain, and suit newer uses such as reasoning-based and cross-modal search.

Growth has outpaced coordination: work is scattered across communities, practitioners are often left out, and efficiency, usability, and system integration questions lag. The workshop aims to gather researchers and builders in one highly interactive room. Early explorations, real-world outcomes, and even negative or puzzling results are explicitly welcome, with the goal of sparking collaboration across the field.
arxiv-2511-00944:
Qiang Liu, Zhi Liu, Guangren Yang, and Wang Zhou build methods for two elusive values in financial markets. One is the leverage effect, the link between returns and later volatility. The other is the volatility of volatility itself. Their data are high frequency price records, where sudden jumps can spoil standard estimates.

The construction starts with a spot volatility gauge based on the sample characteristic function of high frequency increments. It is designed to resist jumps, even very rough ones. Leverage and volatility of volatility estimators follow, with a fix for the bias introduced by estimating spot volatility first. Consistency and central limit results hold under weaker limits on jump activity than earlier work allowed, and matching variance tools make real inference feasible. Tests and a market application support the method.
arxiv-2511-01244:
Wajid Ali, Ayaz Akram, and Deepak Shankar simulate chiplet based processors, designs that assemble several small silicon dies into one package instead of building a single large chip. Chiplets promise flexibility and lower cost as monolithic chips get harder to manufacture, but their performance depends on how the pieces communicate.

Using the VisualSim tool, they built a detailed model of a multi die system with multicore ARM processor clusters joined by an ARM network on chip. The simulation measures inter chiplet communication latency, memory access efficiency, workload distribution, and the power performance trade off under varied workloads. The authors use the results to identify the factors that most influence chiplet system performance and to guide later designs.
arxiv-2511-01644:
Dinesh Kumar Keshari, Suryanarayan Nayak, Avijit Pal, and Bhaskar Paul study tuples of operators called contractions. The tuples are named after two structured domains and the tetrablock. They arise in multivariable operator theory and interpolation problems. For such tuples, a handful of fundamental operators govern almost everything, and the authors set out to characterize them.

They pin down the fundamental operators for both domain classes. They also show relations between the two families. For pure contractions they build functional models. These are concrete representations on function spaces. They also give a complete set of unitary invariants. That data decides when two tuples are the same up to a change of basis. Models are also described for certain completely non-unitary tuples satisfying stated commutation conditions, and for a class of tetrablock contractions.
arxiv-2511-01744:
Yi Han proves a circular law for a family of random matrices that are almost, but not quite, banded. The matrices are block tridiagonal and non-Hermitian, built from n blocks of growing size along the diagonal, with independent entries of mean zero and a fixed variance profile. The circular law says their eigenvalues, suitably normalized, fill a disk uniformly.

The sticking point is the bandwidth: earlier results needed it large compared with the matrix dimension, the delocalized regime. Han's theorem needs only that the block size grows without bound, at most polynomially, and that the entries have a bounded density and all moments finite. That growth condition is optimal, confirming the folklore conjecture that the circular law holds whenever the bandwidth increases with dimension, almost surely.
arxiv-2511-01944:
Dušan Oberta studies when fractional differential equations in Banach spaces have solutions at all. Fractional equations use derivatives of non whole number order, so a system's rate of change depends on its past, not just its present state. Banach spaces are complete spaces with a notion of length, and they make existence proofs harder because compactness tools are scarce there.

Oberta works with measures of non-compactness, tools that gauge how far a set sits from being compact, together with a Kamke function of fractional order. With them he gives sufficient conditions that guarantee a local solution exists. He then applies the main theorem to countable systems of such equations. Those systems arise when fractional partial differential equations with a p-Laplacian are semi-discretized, turning one hard equation into a large coupled system.
arxiv-2511-02044:
Vivswan Shah, Randy Cogill, Hanwei Yue, Gopinath Chennupati, and Rinat Khaziev test a simple idea for training language models to classify text: attach a short explanation to each training label. They rate conversational replies for naturalness, completeness, and staying on topic, using data generated by an ensemble of models to fine-tune a model with seven billion parameters.

Across six datasets and eighteen settings, training with explanations beat label-only training. Surprisingly, even nonsense explanations, made by shuffling the real ones, kept much of the benefit. The authors argue the extra tokens act as a regularizer, forcing richer internal computation before a decision, a claim supported by measurements of the model's internal activity.
arxiv-2511-02144:
Zhicheng Wang and Junbiao Pang measure the width of cracks in road surfaces from photographs, a number that drives decisions about road maintenance. Cracks have ragged, uneven edges, so simple measuring tools fail, and inspectors may need a width at any chosen pixel quickly. Their method chains two statistical techniques, principal component analysis and its robust variant, in a three-stage cascade.

First an established detection algorithm segments the crack into a binary image. Then principal component analysis finds the main orientation for cracks that run roughly parallel, while the robust version extracts a propagation axis for irregular shapes. Tested on three public datasets, the framework beat existing state-of-the-art methods on both speed and measurement accuracy, according to the authors.
arxiv-2511-02444:
Vered Karp, Aseel Omar, and Alejandro Cohen design a sampler that turns analogue signals into timing information while spending as few bits as possible. The starting point is the integrate-and-fire time encoding machine, a power-efficient device that records when a signal's integral crosses thresholds. Two earlier variants each saved something: an adaptive version lowered the sampling rate by tracking the signal. A compressed version cut bit usage by compressing before quantisation.

Their combined machine merges both ideas so each strengthens the other. They also propose a clockless time-to-digital converter architecture that folds the compression stage inside the converter itself. An evaluation on real audio signals showed lower reconstruction error with fewer bits than either parent design. Savings reached at least three bits out of nine against the adaptive version, and about sixty percent compression against the original machine, at the same recovery quality.
arxiv-2511-02744:
Visagan Ravindran and four colleagues test how well common methods in density functional theory match near-exact results. Chemists use these methods to predict electron behavior, but each one builds a different effective potential. Their 2025 study turns the problem around: starting from quantum Monte Carlo densities, they invert the Kohn-Sham equations to recover benchmark potentials.

The benchmarks cover a range of insulators and semiconductors. Different methods gave similar electron densities despite clearly different potentials, with most gaps coming from the exchange and correlation part. The gap from the Monte Carlo density was usually larger than the methods' gaps, Hartree-Fock excepted. The authors also warn that including semicore states shifts the gap, so care is needed when comparing with experiment.
arxiv-2511-02844:
Umar Farooq and Krishna Upadhyay report on a quantum computing course at Louisiana State University that pairs every lecture with a hands-on lab. Students must unlearn classical habits about fixed states and step-by-step debugging, and learn to reason with probability, measurement, and interference instead. Their 2025 paper describes the design for a mixed undergraduate and graduate class.

The course opens with Quantum Without Linear Algebra, using dictionary-style pictures for superposition and entanglement. It then moves to IBM Qiskit for circuit design, noise simulation, and full algorithms. Weekly labs let students test ideas and confront wrong intuitions directly. Student work showed better confidence and clarity, though debugging and measurement stayed hard. The authors argue the lab-integrated model makes the subject reachable.
arxiv-2511-03344:
Elif Arslan and colleagues present SORTeD, a method that lists many near-best sparse decision trees instead of only the single best one. Small trees are prized where stakes are high because people can read them. Yet several trees can score alike while stressing different variables, and that set, called a Rashomon set, helps judge importance and fairness.

Finding even one best tree is hard, so listing the set in score order is harder still. SORTeD improves scaling and can be stopped at any point with the best trees found so far already listed. Tests show faster enumeration than earlier routes. Users can then pick a simpler or fairer tree from the set without baking those wishes into the search itself.
arxiv-2511-03444:
Vesna Poprcova, Iulia Lefter, Martijn Warnier, and Frances Brazier ask what values should guide a robot built to ease social anxiety. Social anxiety is common and support for it often falls short, while social robots offer a possible new aid. Before building, the team ran a participatory workshop with mental health researchers.

Creative and reflective tasks let participants picture scenes where such a robot helps or harms. Values surfaced through that envisioning cover what users would find meaningful, acceptable, and truly helpful. Naming values early steers later design choices about tone, privacy, and control. The study treats value elicitation as the first engineering step, not a polish added once the robot exists.
arxiv-2511-03644:
Jeremy Coulson, Alberto Padoan, and Cyrus Mostajeran solve least squares fitting under geometric limits with a worst-case guard. Many models must respect shape constraints while data carry bounded uncertainty, so a plain best fit can prove fragile. They pose the task as a minimax problem on a product manifold, with one variable trapped in an uncertainty ball.

An exact penalty handles that trap, and a gradient descent-ascent method climbs toward the guarded optimum. Convergence traits are shown through a worked example. Signal processing and data-driven control both breed such geometry-bound fits, from antenna arrays to robot poses. A robust solver lets engineers fit boldly without fearing the worst plausible data shift.
arxiv-2511-03744:
Navid Mojahed, Mahdis Rabbani, and Shima Nazari build predictive compensation for two-player control games where one side's actions get corrupted by lingering noise. The setting is a finite-horizon linear quadratic game, where each player pursues a cost goal against the other. Deviations from equilibrium play follow a Gauss-Markov pattern with memory from step to step.

The clean player, seeing past deviations as they happen, feeds forward a prediction of their future effect. Closed-form recursions track mean and spread under that compensated loop, with boundedness and sensitivity results to match. Cost savings from optimal prediction are characterized and confirmed in simulations. Robotic and vehicle contests with sloppy actuators fit the frame well.
arxiv-2511-04144:
Boxuan Ma is the lead author among nine authors studying how generative AI tools shape metacognition, students' awareness of their own thinking, in university programming courses. Instant, personal help from chat tools promises much, yet most prior work checked correctness and ease of use rather than whether students still plan, monitor, and reflect.

More than ten thousand chat logs gathered over three years were analysed alongside surveys of students and educators. Prompts and responses were mapped to metacognitive phases and strategies. From the combined findings, the team distill design points for coding assistants that support metacognitive work instead of bypassing it. Help then strengthens learning processes rather than replacing the thinking that produces skill.
arxiv-2511-04244:
Irene Ferfoglia, Simone Silvetti, Gaia Saveri, Laura Nenzi, and Luca Bortolussi present STELLE, a neuro-symbolic method that classifies time series while explaining each call in temporal logic. Time series often feed safety-critical calls, yet black-box deep models hide their reasons, so a method whose explanations are built in, not bolted on, is a draw.

A signal temporal logic inspired kernel maps each series by its match with preset logic formulae. Predictions then come with the key concepts attached, as readable conditions for single cases and as class-defining formulae in general. Experiments on varied real benchmarks kept accuracy strong while reasons stayed logically faithful, a pairing black-box models cannot offer.
arxiv-2511-04344:
Muhammad Annas Shaikh, Hamza Zaman, and Arbaz Asif compare nine convolutional neural network architectures on a deliberately narrow task: telling horses from motorcycles in the VOC 2008 dataset. Class imbalance is handled head-on with minority-class augmentation, and both modern and classic designs are scored across several metrics.

ConvNeXt-Tiny led the field, reaching average precision in the mid-ninety percent range for horses and just under ninety percent for motorcycles in the reported figures. Substantial variation separated architectures overall. Augmentation significantly improved minority class detection and helped deeper networks most. The study offers practical guidance for architecture choice on imbalanced binary problems, beyond its two test classes.
arxiv-2511-04444:
Jia-Qi Wang leads fifteen authors shrinking an optical spectrometer onto a single chip. Spectrometers split light by wavelength for sensing, astronomy, and quantum work. Chip versions so far traded away sharpness or needed large, complex layouts.

Their chip uses stimulated Brillouin scattering, where sound waves shape a moving reflection grating in a hybrid chip. The grating reflects up to half the light and switches in microseconds. A straight waveguide just one millimeter long reaches resolution near half a nanometer. It covers a band of about one hundred ten nanometers, close to the basic physical limit for its size.
arxiv-2511-04744:
Gian Marcello Andolina leads six authors revisiting why the integer quantum Hall effect breaks down inside a cavity. A two-dimensional electron gas sits in a metallic split-ring resonator in the experiments. Vacuum effects were first blamed for the changed Hall conductance.

Within the same single-particle picture, the team tests an electrostatic alternative. Boundary effects alone can open non-chiral edge channels that spoil quantization. For realistic parameters, that effect beats vacuum-induced changes by many orders of magnitude. Its transport signatures and energy scales also match the observations, shifting the explanation from exotic cavity physics to plain electrostatics.
arxiv-2511-04844:
Matthew S. Zhang leads six authors showing diffusion samplers can run in far fewer steps than once thought. Denoising diffusion models make strong samples for many tasks. Older proofs tied their cost to the size of the data, at best.

Their method adds a randomized midpoint step to the sampling path. A new proof tool, the shifted composition rule, drives the error bounds. With mild smoothness in place, the error shrinks much faster than with the classic scheme. Fewer steps for high-dimensional data would cut the cost of image and data synthesis in practice.
arxiv-2511-04944:
Zixiang Ren and co-authors survey how to build a channel knowledge map, a map that stores what a radio channel is like at each place. Such maps help wireless nets plan ahead and tune links for place-aware service and sensing.

The survey first looks at classic gap-filling methods and their limits in real use. It then turns to image tools and generative AI, and to new wireless radiance field methods that build sharp maps from sparse tests. The close lists open needs, such as fast updates, use across domains, and low-cost rollout.
arxiv-2511-05244:
Giovanna Souza Rodrigues Costa and co-authors test whether glitches in the LIGO gravity-wave detectors arrive as a Poisson process, where events land at random with a steady rate. They sort glitches by shape, using labels from the Gravity Spy project.

The team built a stats method that grades how well real glitch counts fit an ideal Poisson model, with a fit score as the main gauge. They run it on real O3 data from both LIGO sites and on fake data sets. Gaps from the model can flag times when a detector's noise is not random.
arxiv-2511-05544:
Massimiliano Puglisi devotes his thesis to the Stolz sequence, a tool in geometry tied to spaces whose curvature is positive in a scalar sense. He adapts the sequence to two hard settings. One covers spaces with group actions whose symmetry groups fall in a fixed family. The other covers spaces with non-isolated singular points.

In both settings he shows the key groups depend only on a low part of the space's structure. He then builds a universal space that captures those groups for a whole class at once. Later chapters link the sequence to surgery theory for singular spaces, using an index theorem and the theory of special operator algebras.
arxiv-2511-05644:
Vida Saeedzadeh leads a FOGGIE collaboration paper on seeing the gas around galaxies glow. That gas, the circumgalactic medium, controls how galaxies grow, but it is faint and hard to map. Emission lines from ionized gas can trace its shape and motion directly.

Using detailed simulations of six Milky Way-mass halos, the team made mock emission maps in several lines. Each line traces a different gas phase, so many lines together give the fullest picture. Sensitivity, more than sharpness, limited what could be seen. They also found that telling apart gas phases, and inflows from outflows, needs fine spectral resolution out to large distances from the galaxy center.
arxiv-2511-05744:
Kexin Liang, Simeon Calvert, and Hans van Lint study how much time drivers need when a conditionally automated car hands control back. The car handles driving until it nears its limits, then the human must take over fast. Smooth handovers matter for safety in mixed traffic, where behavior varies widely.

The team focuses on the takeover buffer, the spare time after a driver resumes control to finish an evasive move. In simulator trials they varied buffer length and measured near-collision margins, braking, steering, and driver ratings. Buffers of about five to six seconds gave the best safety and comfort, and drivers liked steady buffers across traffic levels. Their framework sets the time budget by predicting takeover time plus that buffer.
arxiv-2511-05844:
Seyed Alireza Javid, Amirhossein Bagheri, and Nuria González-Prelcic fix a flaw in guided image making: early in cleanup, the guide is too sure of itself and its signal fades. Guided diffusion steers pictures toward a named class using a sorting model's slopes. When that model is too sure too early, the steering fades out.

Two fixes are offered. A light fine-tune based on a smooth scoring error makes the model's confidence honest, which lifted image quality scores. New sampling tricks then work with stock models and no retraining: tilted sampling, a spread-keeping rule, and a scheme based on gaps between spreads. On a standard image set their best guidance beat prior methods with no retraining of the base model.
arxiv-2511-05944:
Shiyu Gao and Hao Jiang generate high-definition road maps for self-driving cars by treating road elements as filled polygons. Such maps are a core input to driving perception. Popular online map builders detect vector shapes directly, but that style generalizes poorly, which hurts automated labeling pipelines.

Their framework, Polymap, first segments a raster image into instance masks with a transformer. A tracing step then converts those masks into clean vector map elements. The design is deliberately concise: segment, then vectorize. On the nuScenes data set the method showed strong accuracy and, above all, strong generalization. The authors pitch polygon-first mapping as the more reliable route for building labeling systems that must work in new places.
arxiv-2511-06244:
Shamika Likhite, Santiago López-Tapia, and Aggelos Katsaggelos improve motion deblurring by teaching the network some physics. Motion blur smears images along the direction of movement, and ordinary networks struggle to link distant parts of a smear. Their training framework weaves partial differential equation dynamics into existing restoration designs.

Advection-diffusion equations guide how features evolve inside the network, mirroring the directional flow of real blur. The added physics layer costs only about one percent more computation at run time. Across four well-known restoration designs and standard benchmarks, image quality scores rose consistently, which supports physics-guided design as a practical route for image restoration.
arxiv-2511-06844:
Mu Yang and six co-authors report an experiment that images how the energy spectrum of an open system deforms in complex momentum space. Non-Bloch band theory predicts this behavior for non-Hermitian systems, but its central link between complex momenta and energy bands had never been observed. The team built a non-Hermitian lattice with long-range couplings using photon modes inside a degenerate cavity.

By encoding complex momenta in the phase and amplitude of orbital-angular-momentum light modes. Designing a matching detection scheme, they reconstructed the spectrum as it morphs through distinct shapes on the complex plane. From those maps they extracted exceptional points, open-boundary spectra, and the generalized Brillouin zone, giving experimenters a versatile platform for non-Hermitian physics.
arxiv-2511-07044:
Mihael Arcan and David-Paul Niland evaluate how well automated systems detect anxiety, depression, and stress from text. More than a fifth of adults worldwide experience mental health disorders, yet symptom language is subtle and varied, making detection hard. The study compares large language models such as Llama and GPT against classic machine learning and transformer models including BERT, XLNet, and Distil-RoBERTa, using the DAIC-WOZ clinical interview dataset.

Models were fine-tuned for each condition, and synthetic data creation was used to fight class imbalance. Distil-RoBERTa scored highest on the anxiety scale, while XLNet led on the depression questionnaire tasks. A zero-shot synthetic approach performed best for stress. The authors conclude transformers plus augmentation improve recall and generalization, though calibration is needed to protect precision, a useful guide for automated mental health screening tools.
arxiv-2511-07544:
Lamis Ghodsi and colleagues map hot and cold molecular gas around a giant galaxy at a cluster heart. The brightest galaxy in MACS 1931-26, seen at redshift zero point three five, holds a huge hydrogen molecule reservoir, hosts a loud radio black hole, and is forming stars in a burst.

Webb observations trace warm gas above one hundred kelvin, while ALMA traces colder gas through carbon monoxide. Warm gas sits with cold gas in a tail stretching thirty kiloparsecs into surrounding space. Mid-infrared hydrogen lines reveal the energy state of the flow. The picture links black hole feedback, cooling gas, and star birth.
arxiv-2511-07644:
James Leung and the PanRadio collaboration introduce a radio survey that follows every southern gamma-ray burst for years. Bursts fade fast, and most never get patient radio follow-up. The Australia Telescope Compact Array program tracks afterglows from under an hour to years after each burst.

First results cover four hundred days of GRB 230815A, a long burst from a collapsing star. Heavy dust dimmed it and no distance is known, so normal programs would have skipped it. Steady radio watching still recovered its evolution. Systematic patience reveals burst physics that snapshot observing misses, especially for obscured events.
arxiv-2511-07744:
Daniel Cher, Brian Wei, and Srikumar Sastry generate satellite images from map polygons rather than loose captions. Analysts often need imagery that matches exact geographic outlines with labeled attributes. Text or rough layout conditioning cannot honor fine borders and land-use meaning together.

VectorSynth learns dense links between imagery and vector geometry through a vision-language alignment module. Pixel-level embeddings from polygon semantics steer a diffusion generator to respect both extent and labels. Users can mix language prompts with geometry edits interactively. Synthetic yet faithful overhead imagery could augment training data for mapping models starved of labeled examples.
arxiv-2511-07844:
Sebastian, Islam, Kolay, and collaborators probe a frustrated magnet that refuses to order. The compound KBaFe2(PO4)3 arranges iron ions on a double trillium lattice, a three-dimensional web that frustrates magnetic alignment. Strong coupling suggests order, yet none appears down to near absolute zero.

Magnetization, heat capacity, nuclear magnetic resonance, and muon experiments, backed by calculations, reveal a mixed dynamic state instead. Below a few kelvin, resonance lines settle into field-independent widths while spins keep fluctuating. Frustrated lattices that stay liquid-like are prized as hosts for exotic quantum phases and possible spin-liquid physics.
arxiv-2511-08144:
Paula Gomez-Alvarez, Miguel Torrejon, Jesus Algaba, and Felipe Blas simulate the three phase coexistence line of ethane hydrate. Hydrates trap gas molecules inside water cages and matter for energy and flow problems. Their direct coexistence setup places solid hydrate, water, and pure ethane together in one simulation box and watches which phase grows.

From energy changes over time, the equilibrium temperature is read off at pressures from one thousand to four thousand bar. Established water and ethane models run inside GROMACS under constant pressure and temperature. The predicted coexistence line matches experimental measurements closely across the full range, validating the method for this little studied system.
arxiv-2511-08544:
Randall Balestriero and Yann LeCun present a full theory for joint-embedding predictive architectures, a family of self-supervised methods that learn by predicting hidden representations. Their system, LeJEPA, aims to replace the ad hoc tricks that earlier versions relied on with one grounded training objective.

The theory singles out the isotropic Gaussian as the ideal shape for learned embeddings. A new regularizer, SIGReg, pushes embeddings toward that shape, and the combined loss needs only one trade-off setting. Training stays linear in time and memory, needs no teacher network or stop-gradient rules, and runs in about fifty lines of code. Tests across many datasets and architectures include a strong ImageNet result with a large vision transformer.
arxiv-2511-08644:
Punit Kumar, Asif Imran, and Tevfik Kosar measure what dataframe libraries cost inside full deep learning pipelines, not just in isolated benchmarks. They compare Pandas, Polars, and Dask, the three big Python tools for tabular data, while models train and run inference on real workloads.

The measurements cover runtime, memory use, disk use, and energy drawn by both CPU and GPU during loading, preprocessing, and batch feeding. These stages are easy to overlook, yet they sit on the critical path of every training run and can starve expensive graphics hardware. By embedding the libraries in complete pipelines across several models and datasets, the study shows where each tool helps or hurts total efficiency.
arxiv-2511-08744:
Amandine Aftalion and Rémy Rodiac study how vortices arrange themselves in a thin ring, guided by recent experiments on fermionic rings. The model is the Ginzburg-Landau energy, the standard description of superconductors and superfluids, minimized over an annulus with boundary data that winds a set number of times.

A critical winding degree, growing like the logarithm of the small Ginzburg-Landau parameter, decides the pattern. Below it, the ground state holds a single giant vortex in the middle. Above it, minimizers mix that giant vortex with smaller ones that drift toward the outer boundary as the parameter shrinks. The proof builds matching upper and lower energy bounds, extends the domain slightly, and minimizes a mean-field energy using the ring's symmetry.
arxiv-2511-08944:
Kazuki Iwahana and four co-authors scrub backdoors out of trained neural networks. A backdoored model behaves normally until a trigger pattern appears, then it misclassifies on cue. Defenses usually hunt the responsible neurons by measuring trigger-activated changes, the activation gap between clean and poisoned inputs.

Those gap estimates are imprecise, so the wrong neurons get cut. The new method reconstructs the gap in latent space by solving for the smallest perturbation that forces clean data into a chosen class, an optimization with a clean convex form. The poisoned class reveals itself through suspiciously small perturbation norms. Fine-tuning with that class's perturbation then removes the backdoor. On CIFAR-10, GTSRB, and TinyImageNet the method suppresses backdoors across attack types and architectures while keeping clean accuracy high, beating existing defenses.
arxiv-2511-09144:
Junyi Liu and Stanley Kok tackle a weakness in Gaussian process regression, a Bayesian method prized for giving uncertainty estimates alongside predictions. Older uncertainty bounds often need the actual input features, or lean on tuned settings and summary estimates. Their paper builds bounds that describe the model's global behavior without seeing specific inputs.

The authors use a chaining framework to bound the expected extreme values over unseen data, from above and below. They sharpen the bounds for widely used kernels such as RBF and Matérn, and gain extra tightness by avoiding loose analytical shortcuts. A second method gives local uncertainty at chosen inputs, using partition sizes to adapt to nearby structure. Tests on synthetic and real data beat earlier approaches.
arxiv-2511-09444:
Leone V. Luzzatto, Mathias Casiulis, Stefano Martiniani, and István A. Kovács propose reading phase transitions in active matter through the clusters that form near them. Studies of transitions usually lean on two-point correlation functions, which can miss higher-order structure. Cluster tomography instead slices clusters with one-dimensional cross-sections and studies their geometry and timing.

Using motility-induced phase separation as the test case, spatial cluster tomography recovers critical exponents without any system-specific order parameter. The temporal version extends burstiness analysis from complex networks to characterize how clusters evolve. Both tools are easy to implement, the authors argue. They present cluster tomography as a general addition to the statistical physics toolbox for non-equilibrium and living systems.
arxiv-2511-09544:
Shiming Gu and three co-authors test whether a cleaner weak-lensing analysis survives realistic galaxy alignment effects. Weak lensing measures how galaxy shapes are sheared by intervening matter, but nonlinear physics muddies the signal. The Bernardeau-Nishimichi-Taruya transform recombines shear data to localize it in scale and distance, and their earlier work showed it beats traditional analyses.

Galaxies also align intrinsically with their surroundings, a contaminant the earlier study omitted. With Euclid-like mock data and a strict scale cut, the transform still pins down the clustering parameter S8 precisely. Precision stays better than two percent when the alignment model is nearly right. When the model is fundamentally wrong, the transform exposes inconsistencies above five sigma, serving as a diagnostic.
arxiv-2511-09644:
Elizaveta Sazonova and eighteen co-authors measure how image quality distorts the measured shapes of galaxies, ahead of the Rubin Observatory's LSST survey. Morphology metrics track galaxy evolution, but resolution and depth changes bias them across a survey. The team tests every metric from the statmorph package plus single-component Sérsic fitting.

Geometric measurements like ellipticity and effective radius stay robust within ten percent at most depths, they find. Light concentration measures fall steadily as resolution worsens, making distant bulges masquerade as disks. The Sérsic index is unbiased but uncertain by twenty to forty percent. They supply empirical correction formulas, two new bias-resistant measurements, and a public package, and show JWST trends can be pure bias from observing.
arxiv-2511-09744:
Daniel Hwang, Juliet Whidden, and Josephine Yu work on a counting problem in geometry tied to polytopes, the flat-sided shapes defined by linear inequalities. When such a shape is stretched while its face directions stay fixed, weighted counts tied to the shape change in a structured way. Their paper asks how those counts, called weighted Ehrhart polynomials, behave across the whole family of deformations.

The authors prove the coefficients vary as piecewise polynomial functions of the numbers defining the shape. They also give an algorithm, with a working version in the SageMath software, for smooth polytopes such as type A alcoved polytopes. The computation rests on a weighted Euler-Maclaurin type formula, and they close by raising open questions about the signs of certain coefficients.
arxiv-2511-09844:
Frédéric Berdoz, Peer Rheinboldt, and Roger Wattenhofer improve speculative decoding, a trick that lets a small drafter model propose tokens that a big model verifies in parallel. Speed depends on the drafter guessing what the verifier would say, and misalignment wastes the effort. Pretrained drafters accept more tokens than tiny trained heads but align only offline in earlier work.

Their fix computes a steering vector from the verifier's hidden states and injects it into the pretrained drafter during generation, aligning it on the fly. Accepted tokens rose by up to thirty-five percent under standard sampling and twenty-two percent under greedy sampling, with negligible added cost. The method retrofits onto existing models, so adoption does not require retraining a system from scratch.
arxiv-2511-09944:
Zhiyuan Xu, Nan Min, Yuhang Guo, and Tong Wei improve 3D Gaussian Splatting for scenes with semi-transparent surfaces such as glass. The standard method assumes one depth per pixel, which breaks when several surfaces show through each other. Their method, TSPE-GS, samples transmittance uniformly to build a distribution over opacity and depth at each pixel instead of a single peak.

By progressively fusing truncated signed distance functions, the system reconstructs outer and inner surfaces separately inside one framework. The approach also plugs into other Gaussian-based pipelines without extra training cost. On public and self-collected datasets, both transparent and opaque, it improved semi-transparent geometry substantially while holding performance on ordinary opaque scenes.
arxiv-2511-10144:
Olaf Parczyk, Silas Rathke, and Tibor Szabó settle a problem posed by Santos about how large the diameter of a simplicial complex can be. A simplicial complex is a higher-dimensional cousin of a graph, and its diameter measures how many steps connect its farthest pieces. For complexes of dimension two on a given number of vertices, the maximum possible diameter was unknown.

For dimension two, the authors determine the exact maximum for every number of vertices, using an explicit construction that achieves it. Along the way they meet an appealing open problem about packing squares of Hamilton cycles in the complete graph. For that problem they obtain an infinite sequence of tight explicit constructions, so the paper closes one question completely while sharpening another.
arxiv-2511-10644:
Ezra Msolla and Ayngaran Thavanesan derive ready-to-use formulas for the primordial tensor power spectrum in curved inflation models of the early universe. Earlier work with formulas covered scalar modes in such curved models; this paper extends the treatment to tensor modes, the ripples that become gravitational waves, without assuming any chosen inflaton potential.

Their background history pairs an initial phase driven by motion with an ultra-slow-roll regime, which isolates the shared marks of curvature. The templates predict large-scale features, including low-multipole cut-offs and wavy patterns, matching computer results. Curvature acts as a steady shift in the key wavevectors. The features carry into the large-angle B-mode polarization of the cosmic microwave background, offering a possible test of curvature in coming surveys.
arxiv-2511-10744:
Ferdinand, W. V. Jacobson-Galán, M. M. Kasliwal, and Erez A. Zimmerman introduce XSNAP, an open-source software pipeline for analyzing X-ray observations of supernovae, and show it on the Type II supernova 2024ggi. X-ray data probe the shock physics of the explosion and the wind the progenitor star shed before dying.

The team gathered observations from Swift, Chandra, and XMM-Newton covering the first 344 days after first light from the supernova, which sits about 7 million parsecs away. XSNAP unifies instrument-specific reduction and spectral extraction behind one command-line tool, with Markov chain Monte Carlo fitting built in. Modeling the spectra as absorbed thermal bremsstrahlung gave a steady progenitor mass-loss rate, with the detected emission tracing the final 117 years before the explosion.
arxiv-2511-11044:
P. Zhang, Z. Zeng, and their colleagues report fresh background readings for the second phase of the China Jinping Underground Laboratory, called CJPL-II. The lab sits deep under rock and hosts searches for rare events that need an ultra-quiet setting. Its first phase filled up, so a larger second phase was built and finished in recent years.

The team measured the main background sources in place: cosmic-ray muons, radon gas, gamma rays, and neutrons. Readings show that the deep rock cover and careful background control keep levels very low. The data give experiment teams in the new halls a firm base for modeling the noise their detectors must handle.
arxiv-2511-11144:
Julian Alfredo Mendez and Timotheus Kampik present a metamodel for fairness, a formal frame for stating, studying, and comparing what fairness means in a given setting. Fairness debates often stall because terms like equity and equality are used loosely. A shared abstract frame can give each notion a precise form that software can then apply and test.

The authors fill the frame with examples, with a focus on how equity and equality differ. Their Tiles framework supplies modular parts that can be linked to encode varied fairness definitions, and an open-source tool supports modeling and evaluation. The aim is a sturdy route from definition to real use.
arxiv-2511-11344:
Pavel Rojtberg and Julius Kühn introduce YCB-Ev SD, a synthetic data set of event-camera recordings for estimating the full 3D pose of objects. Event cameras report pixel changes as they happen and suit fast motion, but the field lacks the large synthetic resources that frame-based vision enjoys. The set holds fifty thousand short event sequences rendered from physically based scenes of standard test objects.

Generation used simulated linear camera motion for full scene coverage, including background activity. A systematic study of event encodings for neural inference found that time surfaces with linear decay and two-channel polarity coding beat exponential decay and single-channel forms by wide margins. Polarity carried the largest share of the gains.
arxiv-2511-11744:
Carlos E. Cadenas R offers teaching notes on conformable differential equations. These form a family of fractional-order equations. The order ranges between zero and one. The solution strategy mirrors a standard undergraduate course. Nothing more than classical methods is used.

Separation of variables is adapted first. Homogeneous, linear, Bernoulli, and exact equations follow. Each case gets worked examples that show the method in action. New definitions and notation get special stress. They are where students tend to stumble. For teachers and self-learners, the notes lower the entry cost. A topic often taught through heavy machinery becomes approachable.
arxiv-2511-12144:
Atreyee Bhattacharya and Sayoojya Prakash study quasi-Einstein manifolds, a broad family that includes Einstein manifolds and gradient Ricci solitons. Such spaces link closely to warped product Einstein spaces. A central question is when a quasi-Einstein metric is rigid, meaning it in fact reduces to an Einstein metric.

Einstein metrics can be seen as fixed points of the Ricci flow, a process that evolves a metric by its curvature. Less is known about how quasi-Einstein metrics evolve under that flow. Using an identity tied to how curvature evolves, the authors prove rigidity for certain closed quasi-Einstein manifolds, narrowing when the broader class collapses to the classic one.
arxiv-2511-12544:
Mukul Lokhande and three co-authors present FERMI-ML, a memory chip design that computes inside the memory array to speed up tiny machine learning on small connected devices. Moving data between memory and processor wastes power, so in-situ computing is attractive for low-power inference. Their macro is built around a new bit cell that stores data and performs an XNOR operation in place.

A compressor-tree accumulator then carries out multiply-accumulate work across a wide range of precisions with low delay and power. The small macro doubles as content-addressable memory for lookups. Post-layout results at a standard process node show high throughput and energy efficiency while keeping output quality high on two image networks, in the authors' tests.
arxiv-2511-12644:
Sascha Lange, Roland Hafner, and Martin Riedmiller revisit a twenty-year-old method for teaching computers to control physical systems. Their subject is neural fitted Q-iteration, an early deep reinforcement learning method first tested on the CartPole task, where a pole must stay balanced on a moving cart. They propose an updated version, NFQ2.0, built and tested on real hardware made from standard industrial parts.

Working through ablation studies, where parts of the method are changed one at a time, the authors find which design choices and settings make learning stable and repeatable. The original method worked well but needed heavy tuning and was hard to reproduce. NFQ2.0 aims to fix that, and the paper closes with guidance for people who want to apply deep reinforcement learning in industrial settings.
arxiv-2511-13044:
Rosario Napoli and four co-authors squeeze more signal out of knowledge graphs whose nodes arrive with poor descriptions. Graph machine learning exploits relationships, but knowledge graphs hide much of their information in semantics that plain node features miss, and data is often too limited to train well. Bi-View builds richer embeddings without synthetic data by fusing two views: Node2Vec embeddings. Capture the graph's structure through random walks, enriched with centrality measures, feed a GraphSAGE model that aggregates neighborhoods in a supervised way, and a fusion layer merges the structural and semantic representations.

The dual-perspective embeddings carry both topological and semantic information, surfacing informative features that were in the data but not explicit. Downstream node classification improved, with the largest gains where initial features were poorest. For practitioners with small, sparse knowledge graphs, the method offers better embeddings from the graph itself.
arxiv-2511-13144:
Jiacheng Cheng and five co-authors compress federated learning traffic down to single bits. Federated learning trains models across many devices without centralizing their data, but shipping model updates both ways is expensive, and each client's data differs, so one global model fits nobody well. Their framework, pFed1BS, pursues personalization and compression together: clients send one-bit random sketches of their updates, the server broadcasts back a one-bit global consensus. A sign-based regularizer keeps each local model aligned with that consensus while respecting its own data.

Random sketching is made cheap with the Fast Hadamard Transform. The authors prove convergence to a stationary neighborhood of the global potential function, and simulations show communication costs dropping substantially while accuracy stays competitive with advanced communication-efficient methods. One-bit messages are near the floor of what communication can cost.
arxiv-2511-13244:
Nadav Bojan Sellam and 3 co-authors offer a way to guide protein structure generators with lab data that cannot be used in standard gradient methods. Correct protein shapes are key to grasping how proteins work, yet most predictors of lab signals block gradient-based sampling. Nuclear magnetic resonance data, rich in detail, face this problem most sharply.

Their framework pairs a diffusion-based generator with a genetic search driven by any black-box score. Tests cover distance limits, nuclear Overhauser effect restraints, and, for the first time, chemical shifts. Results show shift-guided generation can work, expose weak points in current predictors, and give a general path for data-guided protein modeling.
arxiv-2511-13544:
Arianna Salazar-Miranda asks whether the harms tied to American suburbs come from distance itself or from how neighborhoods are designed. Garden City Design, a leading suburban pattern since the early twentieth century, is her test case. She builds a composite measure of that design from street layouts and block shapes to score its spread nationwide.

Joining the score with mobility and emissions data, she applies least squares, matching, and an instrumental variables approach that uses historical adoption patterns. Garden City Design led to higher greenhouse gas emissions, greater social isolation, and more sedentary behavior. Its spread explains roughly a quarter to over a third of suburbanization's adverse effects.
arxiv-2511-13644:
Shrenik Patel and Daivik Patel present CacheFlow, a training-free pipeline that lets vision-language models answer questions over very long videos. Attention and key-value caches swell with runtime, forcing costly inference or short sliding windows that forget the past. CacheFlow instead prunes and compresses the stream as it plays.

A dynamic step drops patch tokens that barely change between frames, while surviving tokens are packed into fixed blocks. Each block's keys are summarized into a retrieval index and its full data stored aside, then only the most relevant blocks return at answer time. Tests on offline and streaming benchmarks beat strong baselines while processing far fewer tokens, with no fine-tuning needed.
arxiv-2511-13744:
Zhijie Qiao, Zhong Cao, and Henry X. Liu release nuCarla, a bird's-eye view perception dataset for self-driving built inside the CARLA simulator. Closed-loop driving models need interactive data where perception, planning, and control train together, but real datasets are recorded passively and cannot react. That gap leaves closed-loop models behind even simple rule-based drivers.

nuCarla mirrors the popular nuScenes format at comparable scale, so real-world perception models transfer directly, and its class balance is more even. Because it lives in simulation, the data plug straight into closed-loop deployment and testing. Strong perception backbones supplied with the release reach top detection results, giving the field an open benchmark for interactive driving research.
arxiv-2511-14144:
Naoki Shimoda and Akihiro Yamamoto answer multiple-choice questions by checking facts as graphs, keeping every step traceable. Transformer-based relation extraction can now build knowledge graphs straight from text, but a graph built from a false sentence encodes false facts. Their fill-in-the-blank method turns each candidate sentence into a relational graph and verifies it against trusted knowledge graphs.

Under a closed-world assumption, sentences whose graphs match known facts are treated as true. The method answered up to about seventy percent of questions correctly while exposing its reasoning path. The authors present the trade plainly: some accuracy is given up so that each answer can be audited step by step.
arxiv-2511-14544:
Jaume Ros, Alessio Arleo, and Fernando Paulovich introduce the Warping Index for judging dimension reduction plots. Such plots squeeze high dimensional data onto a flat page. Distortion is hard to spot and can mislead readers. Most quality scores check whether global or local structure survives, but ignore visual artifacts and empty space.

The new index rests on the idea that gaps between points must be preserved faithfully. Empty regions carry real information about clusters and outliers.
