Hiten Prakash Kothari and R. Michael Buehrer propose a U-Net autoencoder system to remove interference from communication signals. Signals can be mixed with noise plus interferers such as sinusoidal tones, LFM chirps, QPSK signals at varied sampling rates, and QAM interference. A single flexible cleaner is the goal.

The U-Net design uses multiscale feature extraction and skip connections to keep fine time structure while suppressing interference parts. Judged by bit error rate, the method consistently beat conventional cancellation in low and mid signal-to-interference regimes. It stayed competitive at high ratios. Extra tests covered model mismatch cases such as carrier offset and colored noise. The authors present multiscale neural models as a flexible platform for this task.
arxiv-2512-14344:
Eymen Ipek and Mario Hirz present a modular framework for electric vehicle powertrain modeling in a 2025 paper. Car electrification and growing powertrain complexity demand faster, cheaper development, and virtual validation can help if system level simulations are easy to build.

Data driven models are often built for single parts, but they rarely fit together into one whole vehicle simulation. The authors define standardized interfaces for the battery, inverter, and electric motor. Models of each part, whether data driven, physics based, or empirical, can then be plugged in and swapped. The modular setup supports scalable system level modeling. The aim is shorter development timelines that match the agile pace of the modern car industry.
arxiv-2512-14644:
Xinyue Sheng, Tuan Dung Pham, Zichi Zhang, Matt Nicholl, and Thai Son Mai present an attention based preprocessing framework for rare transient classification in a 2025 paper. Sky surveys find huge numbers of transients, and machine learning helps pick events for follow up, but rare types are hard to find.

Training sets suffer extreme class imbalance, and host galaxy images often contain bright foreground sources that confuse feature extraction. Their pipeline uses a Similarity Index to remove image artefacts and a masking step that drops unrelated sources while keeping the transient and its host. It also fits light curves with a two dimensional Gaussian process and builds synthetic training samples. For high confidence calls, purity reaches 75 percent for superluminous supernovae and 43 percent for tidal disruption events.
arxiv-2512-14744:
Adewale Akinfaderin and Shreyas Subramanian present VERAFI, a 2025 system meant to make AI answers about finance accurate enough for regulated work. Search tools can fetch the right documents, yet language models still make math errors and break rules while reasoning. VERAFI adds checks directly into the reasoning process.

The system combines dense retrieval with reranking, agents that can use financial tools, and written policies covering GAAP accounting rules, SEC requirements, and math validation. On FinanceBench it reached 94.7% factual correctness, up from 52.4% for retrieval with reranking alone. The policy layer by itself added 4.3 percentage points over agent processing alone, a gain aimed at the math and logic errors that persist after good retrieval.
arxiv-2512-14844:
Eleonora Parlanti and eight coauthors present a way to squeeze more from the James Webb Space Telescope when weighing distant black holes. Many black holes in the early universe look too heavy for their galaxies, but their masses rest on quick local formulas. Those single epoch formulas were tuned nearby and may mislead at high redshift.

Their data method doubles the wavelength span that the NIRSpec instrument can use at once, catching light lines that were out of reach. They test it on five quasars near redshift 2 whose masses are known from slower echo based measures. One line, H beta, matches those masses best, while H alpha based estimates scatter more. For the smallest and fastest feeding hole, all quick formulas overshot the mass tenfold, a warning sign for early universe studies.
arxiv-2512-15244:
Aditya Ghosh and Stefan Wager tackle causal inference in a 2025 paper on settings where treatment starts when a changing measure crosses a set line. A patient, for instance, may get preventive care once blood sugar passes a threshold. Past care can then shift later readings, which breaks standard cutoff methods.

The authors show that such dynamic designs identify a marginal policy effect, a quantity that contains the classic cutoff effect as a special case. They build a local linear estimator for it and prove it is consistent. A test case uses data from a Food and Drug Administration approved glucose simulator.
arxiv-2512-15444:
Zheng Liang and co authors describe a muon scattering tomography system in a 2025 paper. The method images dense, high atomic number materials by tracking how cosmic ray muons bend as they pass through matter. It needs no artificial radiation source, which suits border security checks and long term watching of nuclear material.

The team built a plastic scintillator detector with fine position sense, reaching a resolution of 0.09 times the strip pitch. Four layers, each 53 by 53 centimeters, form a full scale imaging system. The paper covers the simulated design, the build and testing of the detectors, and how well the finished system images test objects.
arxiv-2512-15544:
Parisa Parand and Mahmoud Samadpour test whether principal component analysis helps machine learning on hyperspectral images in a 2025 paper. Hyperspectral imaging records 150 spectral bands per point, giving rich detail about materials and moisture. That richness creates highly correlated features, which can overwhelm models when labeled data are scarce.

Using soil moisture as the target, the authors find that just two principal components keep more than 99 percent of the total variance. The reduced data show clearer separation of target values and simpler structure. A random forest trained on those two components predicts soil moisture with an R squared of 94.7 percent. The study supports PCA as an efficient first step in such workflows.
arxiv-2512-15644:
Qirui Li and co authors present InpaintDPO for foreground conditioned image inpainting in a 2025 paper. The task is to generate a background that fits a given foreground subject and a text prompt. Current methods often place that subject at a wrong scale, position, or viewpoint relative to the new background, a flaw the authors call spatial relationship hallucination.

Because spatial sense is subjective, standard reward training fits poorly. InpaintDPO instead uses direct preference optimization in three new ways. MaskDPO limits preference training to the background, a cropping based variant sharpens boundary coherence, and a shared commonality variant learns what good winning samples have in common. Together they promote plausible spatial relations.
arxiv-2512-15744:
Feng Liu and co authors ask how low and high frequency graph signals affect recommendation in a 2025 paper, dated December 10. Spectral graph neural networks work well for recommendation, and their success is often credited to low pass filtering. Recent studies, though, stress high frequency signals, leaving the true roles of each band unclear.

The authors prove the two bands have equivalent effects in recommendation, since both smooth similarities between user item pairs. They build a frequency signal scaler module that tunes that smoothing and plugs into any graph model. They also show graph embedding methods cannot fully capture graph signal traits, and add a space flip method to restore that power. Either band alone can suffice.
arxiv-2512-15844:
Frances Rigby and co authors report a JWST transmission spectrum of the temperate sub-Neptune TOI-732 c in a 2025 paper. Sub-Neptunes orbiting cool M dwarfs are a new frontier for atmosphere studies, and JWST has begun detecting carbon bearing molecules in them. TOI-732 c was observed across 0.9 to 12 microns with three JWST instruments.

The spectrum gives evidence for methane at about 1 percent by volume in a hydrogen rich atmosphere, with no detection of ammonia or hydrogen cyanide. A survey of 250 chemical species finds moderate to strong evidence for extra absorption from complex molecules, possibly higher hydrocarbons or sulfur bearing species. Those signals are strongly degenerate with methane, so more observations are needed.
arxiv-2512-16144:
Prime Intellect Team, with Mika Senghaas and many co-authors, reports a large open AI model in a technical report shared on arXiv in 2025. INTELLECT-3 has 106 billion parameters in a mixture-of-experts design, with only 12 billion active at once. It was trained with large-scale reinforcement learning on the team's own end-to-end infrastructure.

The model reaches state-of-the-art results for its size on math, code, science, and reasoning tests, beating many larger frontier models. The team open-sourced the model plus the full training stack, including their prime-rl framework, which scales from one machine to thousands of graphics cards. Training combined supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on the GLM-4.5-Air-Base model, running on up to 512 H200 chips. The release aims to make big reinforcement learning reproducible outside major labs.
arxiv-2512-16244:
Xueqi Ma and four co-authors extend anomaly detection on networks in a 2025 paper on arXiv, accepted to AAAI 2026. Graph neural networks sort nodes into known classes in tasks like fraud detection and medical diagnosis. Standard open-set methods lump every strange node into one reject pile, giving no hint what those outliers actually are.

Their framework, CFC, works coarse to fine. A language model first flags outliers and guesses their labels from meaning, then a graph network trains with those flagged samples to sharpen both detection and normal classification. A final language model pass refines the outlier labels. The method uses genuinely out-of-distribution examples rather than synthetic ones. It improved outlier detection by ten percent over leading methods and reached up to seventy percent accuracy at naming the outlier classes.
arxiv-2512-16544:
Michael M. Kay addresses a classic pricing task in finance. The task is to build a chance model for several assets at once. The model must match the market prices of plain European claims. Such claims pay once at a set date, based on asset values.

For one asset, the Dupire method gives a standard answer. For two or more, no natural unique build was known. Kay offers one based on martingale entropic optimal transport. That method moves chance mass at least cost while keeping fair-game rules. As a side gain, the build gives a hands-on proof of a classic result by Strassen. Kay also shows why a class of local link models can fail to match basket option prices.
arxiv-2512-16644:
Wisnu Uriawan and five coauthors built a Sharia-compliant chatbot that answers questions about Islam. The system joins Q-learning, a trial-and-reward learning method, with sentence transformers that map text by meaning, so replies stay on topic and grounded.

The team trained it on a curated set of 25,000 question and answer pairs drawn from the Qur'an, Hadith, and scholar rulings, stored in JSON form. A Flask back end and a Flutter phone app serve the bot. In tests it reached 87 percent accuracy on meaning across topics such as law, belief, worship, and daily dealings. The authors note limits from fixed learning and data reliance, and point to live updates as next steps.
arxiv-2512-16844:
Nianyi Chen and a large team link dual active galactic nuclei, pairs of feeding black holes in merging galaxies, to future gravitational wave finds. Using the ASTRID cosmic simulation, they build dual catalogs matched to current and planned searches.

With realistic selection rules, ASTRID copies the seen dual shares, gaps, and host traits across cosmic time. A large hidden pool of close pairs under 5 kiloparsecs should exist, missed by current surveys. Tracking pairs forward, 30 to 70 percent merge within a billion years, and many of those mergers should be heard by LISA. Duals that AXIS and Roman can see seed about 10 percent of low-redshift LISA events.
arxiv-2512-17244:
Lei Chen and Cheryl E Praeger classify a family of highly symmetric directed graphs. In these digraphs, arrows run one way between points, and the symmetry group can carry any chain of s arrows onto any other. For large s, such rich symmetry is rare and hard to pin down. The authors widen an older quotient tool to squeeze a big graph into a smaller one that keeps the key structure.

With that tool, they show every such graph with s at least 6 reduces either to a simple directed ring or to a smaller graph ruled by a near-simple group. They also give a fresh construction that doubles the symmetry chains, yielding examples for any s. The outcome focuses future work on the near-simple cases.
arxiv-2512-17344:
Haomin Qi and three co-authors tune large language models for many languages at once, including ones with little training text. Their method mixes two cheap tuning styles layer by layer and locks some layers to rotations that keep training stable. Alongside, simple data housekeeping — spotting each text's language, dropping near-duplicates, and filtering junk — guards the training set.

On the XNLI and FLORES test sets, the hybrid beat strong low-cost tuning baselines. It also kept answers balanced across languages and made the model's confidence scores more honest. Training cost stayed modest. One caution for readers: the arXiv record carries an admin note flagging substantial text overlap with an earlier paper, arXiv:2507.18076.
arxiv-2512-17444:
Javier Gonzalez-Ruiz and four co-authors simulate decades of power market choices with learning software agents. Each agent plays a power company that builds plants to chase profit, reacting to rivals, demand, and policy signals such as auctions and support schemes. The setup lets policy makers rehearse market rules before betting a country's grid on them.

The team tuned the agents until their free-for-all matched real competitive behavior, then ran the model on a simplified Italy. Outcomes swung hard with market design: some rule sets cut carbon smoothly, while others sparked price spikes along the way. Because many policies act at once in real life, a rehearsal stage where they collide first is the paper's main offer.
arxiv-2512-17544:
Elizaveta Iarovikova and three co-authors crack a forbidden-pattern problem about strings of symbols. Take all strings of length n over an alphabet. How large a family can you pick if no two strings are allowed to agree in exactly t minus 1 positions? Agreements in any other number of spots are fine; only that one count is banned. The puzzle descends from a famous Erdős-Sós question.

The team finds the exact maximum family size whenever the alphabet and the length both grow at least polynomially in t. That range reaches far past a recent result by Keevash and co-authors. The proof mixes two modern weapons of extremal combinatorics, spread approximation and hypercontractivity. Such sharp bounds matter wherever near-matching codes must be kept apart.
arxiv-2512-17644:
Nicholas Schweder-Souza and a large team test how well colors alone can pick globular clusters out of a crowded sky survey. These ancient star swarms trace how their host galaxies formed, but in survey photos they look like dots, easily confused with foreground stars and tiny background galaxies. The coming LSST survey will photograph millions of such dots.

Working with a labeled Fornax Cluster catalog in LSST style, the team fed all 15 color combinations to machine classifiers. The best color-only lists still held about 30 percent impostors, and simple color-color plots doubled that share. Compressing colors to four main components kept the same purity at no cost to completeness. Auto-encoders added nothing. The verdict: colors help, but clean lists need shape and infrared data too.
arxiv-2512-17844:
Rajni Dabas, Samir Khuller, and Emilie Rivkin study covering problems, where a small set of points must guard a large set of groups. In their main problem, each group of hyperedges needs a set share covered, and each chosen vertex has a cap on how much it can cover. The problem blends several classic covering tasks into one.

The authors give fast methods that come close to the best possible answer. One method handles the case where a vertex may be reused, and another handles the stricter single use case. They also solve a weighted edge cover variant exactly, with a cleaner and faster method than earlier work on the unweighted version.
arxiv-2512-17944:
Vitaliy Voytik revisits a classic rule of motion, Jacobi's principle, which picks the true path of a system by making a quantity called the full action stand still. The rule is well known for systems that keep their energy. Voytik asks whether it can also cover systems that lose energy, such as those with friction.

His approach varies not only the path's shape but also time itself, each on its own terms. From the widened rule he derives the matching equations of motion. The article runs 23 pages and is written in Russian. It aims to give the Jacobi view a wider reach in basic mechanics.
arxiv-2512-18044:
Tyler Gorda, Oleg Komoltsev, Aleksi Kurkela, and Eirik Sunde offer a safer way to guess the inner recipe of neutron stars. No lab can test matter that dense, so teams blend low and high density theory with telescope data. Many blends bend basic rules of heat and pressure along the way, which can taint the result.

Their method builds flexible random curves, called Gaussian process bridges, that obey those rules by construction. Any set of guide points can be added without breaking the rules, and the curve's wiggle can be tuned from strict to bold. Both low density and high density theory limits fit inside one frame, with no trial and error search needed.
arxiv-2512-18644:
Alexei D. Chepelianskii and Dima L. Shepelyansky study a kicked superconducting qubit in this 2025 physics paper. A fluxonium is driven by repeated short pulses while losing energy to its surroundings. In the classical limit its motion settles onto a strange chaotic attractor. The pair asks whether that fractal pattern survives in the quantum regime, working with the density matrix under Lindblad evolution.

They find that the steady state does converge to a quantum strange attractor much like the classical one. At strong or moderate dissipation the attractor's eigenstates stay localized. At weak dissipation the states spread out, an effect tied to the Ehrenfest explosion of the wave packet and to the Lyapunov exponent. The paper closes with possible experimental realizations using fluxonium circuits.
arxiv-2512-18744:
Jonah Baerman, Giovanni Ravazzini, and Joerg Teschner connect two deep structures in mathematical physics: Mathieu opers and the quantum Toda chain. Opers are special differential-equation connections; the authors study their Riemann-Hilbert problem on a twice-punctured sphere with mild irregular singularities, for connections of any rank. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, builds the solutions from one nonlinear integral equation.

From that construction, the generating function of the oper submanifold turns out to equal the Yang-Yang function of the quantum Toda chain, proving a conjecture of Nekrasov, Rosly, and Shatashvili. The Toda chain's quantization conditions can then be rewritten through the connection problem, which the authors also solve. They read the whole result as a variant of the Analytic Langlands Correspondence for the real Hitchin system tied to the Toda chain.
arxiv-2512-19644:
Gabrielle O'Brien, Alexis Parker, Nasir Eisty, and Jeffrey Carver surveyed 868 scientists who write code, asking how generative AI has entered their working lives. Programming is essential to modern research, yet most scientists feel undertrained for it, and earlier studies warn that AI coding help invites over-reliance, especially among beginners. The survey maps adoption, favorite tools, and what tracks with feeling more productive.

Adoption runs highest among students and less experienced programmers, and general chatbots like ChatGPT beat developer-specific tools by a wide margin. Feeling productive correlates with inexperience and with skipping practices like testing and code review, though the two interact. The strongest single predictor is how many generated lines a respondent typically accepts at once, suggesting productivity is being judged by code produced, not code checked.
arxiv-2512-19844:
Tomás Bortolin and three co-authors study a chain of magnetic impurities in a sea of electrons. The stage is one-dimensional. There, bosonization turns the electron band into a Luttinger liquid. Each impurity spin couples to the electrons by magnetic exchange. That coupling opens two rival stories. In one, each impurity is screened on its own, the Kondo way. In the other, impurities link through the electron sea, the RKKY way.

At two special values of the couplings, the model can be rewritten in exact form. It becomes free electrons mixed with a neat array of resonant levels. Those solvable cases expose the traits of each regime. One shows long-range algebraic order. The other shows local screening. A clear picture emerges. The sign of the electron-electron force picks which story wins.
arxiv-2512-20544:
Vahid Asadi, Akram Hasani Zonoozi, and Hosein Haghi race two ways of weighing a galaxy. The traditional route fits a spectral energy distribution with a code such as LePhare. Their challenger is Parametric t-SNE, a machine learning method trained on noise-injected stellar population models. Simulated COSMOS-like galaxies with known true masses provide the scoreboard.

The learning method wins decisively. Its root-mean-square error is barely half the fitting code's, and its bias is roughly ten times smaller. For low-mass galaxies the error drops by about half. Even using only six optical bands, it beats LePhare using all twenty-six. It also processes large data sets thousands of times faster. Survey astronomers take note.
arxiv-2512-20644: Matthew Mark Romano, JungHyun Bae, and Paul Cantonwine work on muon tomography, a way of imaging with muons. Their task is subpixel resolution: pinning down where a particle crossed a detector more finely than the detector's own blocks allow. They find that machine learning methods reconstruct particle positions in scintillation-based detectors more accurately than standard approaches. Finer positions mean finer images of what muons pass through.
arxiv-2512-21444:
Alan Haynes and Christopher Lutsko revisit the Gauss circle problem on an unusual set of points: the vertices of a Penrose tiling. The classic problem asks how many points of a grid fall inside a large circle, and how big the counting error is. A Penrose tiling covers the plane with rhombuses in a pattern that never repeats, so its vertices are far less regular than a grid.

The authors count the vertices of any unit-length rhombic Penrose tiling that fall inside a disk of a given radius. They prove the count grows like the disk's area times a constant of about one point two three. The error term grows more slowly than the radius raised to the two-thirds power, times a logarithmic factor. The result carries a classical counting technique into aperiodic order, the mathematics behind quasicrystals.
arxiv-2512-22044:
Gravitational waves circularize binary black holes long before detection, erasing the eccentricity that records their birth. Vishal Baibhav recovers that lost parameter through spin-orbit tilt. In isolated binary evolution, the second supernova's natal kick both tilts the plane and injects eccentricity, forging a link.

Measuring the spin tilt from gravitational waves therefore constrains the kick and reconstructs the formation eccentricity. Applied to GW190412 and GW241011 under the isolated-channel assumption, the method already bounds their birth eccentricity. Coming detectors and multiband observations with LISA promise tighter tilts, and with them the birth separation and redshift. All of this comes from the tilt alone.
arxiv-2512-22544:
Promit Ghosal and Guilherme Silva study fluctuations in the stochastic six vertex model, a member of the KPZ universality class of random growth processes. Typical fluctuations and extreme large deviations in such models are well understood, but the middle ground, moderate deviations, is not. Closing that gap needs fine control of the integrable structure underneath, here discrete orthogonal polynomial ensembles.

The authors analyze multiplicative statistics of these ensembles across scaling regimes, concentrating on a critical window where a full region meets a band. The asymptotics there cross over among Airy, Painlevé II, and Bessel behaviors. Their proofs use the Riemann-Hilbert problem method, including a new local parametrix that needs its own asymptotic analysis. A known identity links the height function to a Meixner point process. Combined with it, the results give moderate deviation estimates for both tails of the height distribution, with sharp exponents and constants.
arxiv-2512-22944:
Vincent Herrmann, Eric Alcaide, Michael Wand, and Jürgen Schmidhuber propose a simple gauge for how hard a language model is working. Standard loss scores say how surprised the model is by the next token, not how much reasoning a task demands. Earlier effort measures based on compressing hidden states are invasive and unstable. Their measure, Multiple Token Divergence, compares the model's full output distribution with the one from a shallow auxiliary prediction head.

The gap between the two distributions, a KL divergence, can be read off pretrained models that already carry several prediction heads, with no extra training. The team also turns the measure into a control knob called Divergence Steering, which steers generation toward higher or lower computational character. On benchmarks, the measure separated complex tasks from simple ones better than prior methods, rose with problem difficulty on math reasoning, and ran lower on runs that reasoned accurately.
arxiv-2512-23244:
Xingwei Ma, Shiyang Feng, Bo Zhang, and Bin Wang present ViLaCD-R1, a framework for spotting meaningful change between satellite images taken at different times. Change detection sounds simple, but pixel-based tools and encoder-decoder networks miss high-level semantics and react to differences in lighting or season. Vision-language models add semantic understanding, yet they localize changes poorly, draw sloppy boundaries, and are hard to interpret.

The design splits the job. A Multi-Image Reasoner, a vision-language model trained by supervised fine-tuning plus reinforcement learning on block-level two-date tasks, outputs a coarse change mask from paired image patches. A Mask-Guided Decoder then fuses features from both images with that coarse mask to produce a precise binary change map. Evaluations on benchmarks show better recognition of semantic change, stronger suppression of non-semantic variation, and state-of-the-art accuracy in complex scenes.
arxiv-2512-23344:
Raven Beutner and Bernd Finkbeiner tackle the verification of asynchronous hyperproperties, rules that compare system executions without forcing them to march in lockstep. Hyperproperties express security policies like observational determinism and non-inference, where what matters is how traces relate across different timings. The logic A-HLTL can state such properties by quantifying over traces and over stutterings, re-timings of traces. Model checking it was previously possible only for narrow fragments or terminating systems.

Their approach turns verification into a game. A verifier and a refuter take turns guiding pieces of the traces and their stutterings, challenging each other. A winning verifier strategy then amounts to concrete witnesses for the quantified traces and alignments. The authors pin down fragments where the game reading is complete, giving a finite-state decision procedure. The work extends automatic checking to security properties of reactive systems that synchronous logics cannot even express.
arxiv-2512-23444:
Zina-Sabrina Duma and co-authors give classical regression models something they normally lack: honest error bars. Partial least squares and principal component regression, are workhorses for turning spectra into values, but they output point estimates with no measure of confidence. The authors adapt ideas from conformal inference to attach prediction intervals to these models and to calibrate them.

Tests span synthetic data, lab near-infrared measurements, and airborne hyperspectral models of plant traits. On synthetic data the method found the uncertain regions and matched its size. In the real cases the calibrated intervals were neither overconfident nor timid: at the ninety-five percent level, about ninety-five percent of true values fell inside the predicted intervals on test data. That discipline is what users need before trusting a regression's numbers.
arxiv-2512-23544:
Alan Dow and István Juhász work in set-theoretic topology, asking how large a topological space can be if it contains no uncountable discrete subset, a property called countable spread. Whether such spaces can exceed the size of the continuum in a Hausdorff setting depends on the axioms assumed beyond standard set theory.

Assuming a weakly compact cardinal, they prove the consistency of a strong partition property for colorings of pairs from the continuum, together with a cardinal arithmetic equality. From those assumptions they derive that every Hausdorff space of countable spread has size at most the continuum. For infinite regular spaces, the number of open sets is exactly the continuum. The paper is an example of how consistency results can settle questions that standard axioms leave open.
arxiv-2512-23744:
Junhui Cao and six co-authors show that a cloud of exciton-polaritons, hybrid particles of light and matter in a semiconductor, can grow its own acoustic black hole. In earlier analogue-gravity experiments, the flow that traps sound had to be sculpted with external potentials or carefully designed pumping. Here the condensate's own nonlinear hydrodynamics does the job.

Starting from sharp, Riemann-type initial conditions in a Gross-Pitaevskii model, nonlinear dispersive shock waves form naturally. Inside the shocked region the fluid flows faster than its own speed of sound, so a transonic interface appears: an acoustic horizon that sound cannot cross from inside. Using Whitham modulation theory and simulations, the authors describe the subsonic-to-supersonic transition and work out the horizon's surface gravity and Hawking temperature. That opens a route to analogue Hawking emission in quantum fluids of light.
arxiv-2512-24044:
Yuan Xin and colleagues test whether jailbreak attacks on language models are as dangerous as earlier studies claimed. Jailbreaks are crafted prompts meant to slip past a model's safety training, and past work measured success against the model alone. Real deployments, though, also screen incoming prompts and outgoing replies with content filters.

Evaluating attacks against the full pipeline, filters included, changes the verdict. Almost every jailbreak technique tried could be caught by at least one filter, which suggests earlier reports overstated how often these attacks would succeed in practice. The filters are not perfect: the authors note room to improve the balance between catching harmful content and blocking harmless text. Their study reframes the safety contest as a property of whole systems, and points to sharper detection as the next step for both protection and user experience.
arxiv-2512-24344:
Anthony Brady collects six lectures on Gaussian bosonic systems and analogue gravity. The lectures were delivered at the Analogue Gravity meeting in Benasque in 2023. A unified phase-space framework describes linear bosonic quantum systems. It is the standard tool of quantum optics. It also underpins continuous-variable quantum information. Its appeal is simplicity and independence from any one platform.

The first three parts develop the formalism. Harmonic dynamics and Gaussian transformations come first. State description follows through moments, Wigner functions, and entanglement measures. The fourth part turns to semi-classical black holes. Hawking radiation is treated in this language. Quantum superradiance in rotating black holes joins it. Laboratory analogues in light-matter systems appear through toy models. The notes serve readers entering analogue gravity with a quantum optics toolkit.
arxiv-2512-24444:
Ralf Spatzier surveys the work of Zhiren Wang on rigidity in dynamics. The occasion is Wang receiving the Brin Prize. Rigidity results say that weak assumptions force a dynamical system into a short list of rigid models. Wang's work concerns higher rank abelian group actions. Lattices in higher rank semisimple groups are the second theme.

Spatzier reports on the main ideas and breakthroughs. Higher rank is the engine throughout. With several commuting directions, flexibility collapses and classification becomes possible. Wang's results are described as exciting and deep. The survey places them inside the broader rigidity program. It also marks what the prize honors. Readers in dynamics get a guided account of a major modern research line, written for the occasion rather than as a textbook.
arxiv-2512-24544:
M J Gerard and four colleagues characterize the shapes of plasma confinement surfaces. Tokamaks describe their flux surfaces with modes like elongation and triangularity. Stellarators add a twist, literally. In a non-axisymmetric device, each shaping mode rotates about the magnetic axis. Modern designs chase high magnetic quasi-symmetry through such shaping.

Fourier methods define the shaping modes for equilibrium cross-sections. The authors test several characterizations on quasi-symmetric configurations. The QUASR database supplies equilibria of varying symmetry quality. One method stands out. It picks cross-sections by shortest distance from the axis across symmetry contours. Shapes then need far fewer active modes to describe. Quasi-symmetry quality also tracks shape structure. Better symmetry means a tightly constrained, linear spread of modes. Shape complexity grows in step with rotation about the axis.
arxiv-2512-24744:
Debankan Sannamoth, Kristine Boone, and Arnaud Carignan-Dugas show a flaw in a standard way of estimating quantum gate errors, and a fix using easier random gates. Interleaved random testing compares series with and without a target gate, random with the multi-qubit Clifford group. Under coherent errors, that method can give highly inaccurate or even invalid error estimates.

Numerical and lab results support the critique. Simpler random choices give more accurate fidelity estimates in their tests. Quantum hardware readers get a useful testing lesson: the randomizer itself can bias the answer, and lighter randomization can make gate error numbers more trustworthy.
arxiv-2601-00044:
Tak-Pong Woo, writing alone, proposes an origin story for the Little Red Dots, compact red objects found by the James Webb Space Telescope in the early universe. Their 2026 traits are odd: broad hydrogen emission yet faint X-rays, pointing to heavy obscuring gas. Woo suggests these sources mark a short, hidden phase of rapid gas inflow inside the dense soliton cores of fuzzy dark matter halos, an ultralight dark matter model.

Matching observed sizes and the column density needed for such obscuration points to a narrow particle mass range and large soliton masses. A mass-budget check then suggests a static hot atmosphere cannot survive, since cooling outruns the dynamical time, favoring fast inflow or radiation-driven change. Simulations of merging solitons show compact dense cores can form. Woo frames the idea as a proposal with testable implications, needing fuller radiation-hydrodynamic modeling to predict counts and spectra.
arxiv-2601-00344:
Bruce Mugizi works with Sudi Murindanyi, Olivia Nakacwa, and Andrew Katumba on a traffic camera system built for Uganda roads. Speeding drives many road deaths in developing countries. Safety infrastructure there is often thin or missing. Their system watches traffic in real time. It detects vehicles, reads plates, and estimates speed. All three jobs run from camera feeds.

Training data came from a speed gun and two cameras. A detection model finds plates with high precision. A transformer reads plate characters with fewer errors than a CNN. Speed comes from tracking across two road regions. Error stays within a modest road margin. A database links plates to owner information. Tickets can then go out by text message automatically. The authors aim the design at resource tight settings. Automated enforcement could cut crashes where officers are few.
arxiv-2601-00544:
Shunya Adachi and Kazuki Hiroe wrote a 2026 math paper on a tool for studying flat sheets in space. The sheets are planes and their higher kin, cut out of a larger space. What sits on the space left around them can be summed up by rules for loops. A known method, due to Katz, mixes such rules to make new ones. The authors extend that method to their sheet setups.

Their aim is a test called Aomoto realizability. It asks whether a loop rule can be built from a flat link with fixed matrices at each sheet. The authors first widen the setup so the sheets project in a clean way. On the widened setup, their mixing method keeps the test true. They match it with an older algebraic form of the method, with no extra limits. The work widens a key tool of modern geometry.
arxiv-2601-00844:
Matthieu Destrade and four co-authors work, in 2026, on AI world models that can plan their own moves. Their base models learn by predicting: given a state, they guess the coded form of the next state. They learn good codes, yet plan poorly with them. The team reshape the code space to fix that flaw. They tie the gap between two state codes to the cost of reaching a goal.

Under that tie, a simple distance in code space mirrors the true value of a move. The team enforce the tie while training, with a workable trick. On simple control tasks, planning then works far better than with standard models. The agent can pick moves by reading plain distances, not by costly search. This gives JEPA models a clear path from prediction to action. It also hints at cheaper planning for robots and game agents.
arxiv-2601-01044:
Weighing dairy cows often means stress for the animals and work for the farm. Jin Wang and nine co-authors test whether cameras can do the job instead, using depth images and three-dimensional point clouds taken from above the cow. Their focus is small farms, which rarely have enough data to train a good model on their own.

The team gathered data from more than a thousand cows at a large farm, plus smaller groups at two other farms. They trained four deep learning models and asked whether skills learned at the big farm transfer to the small one. Transfer helped every model, matching or beating training on pooled data. Depth images and point clouds performed about the same. Since only trained model weights need to move between farms, the approach respects privacy and logistics limits.
arxiv-2601-01244:
Csibi and 8 co-authors describe Racka, a language model adapted for Hungarian on modest university hardware. Hungarian has far less training support than English or German, yet large models are costly to retrain. The team instead continued training a smaller open model using a low-cost tuning method.

They also rebuilt the word splitter so Hungarian text uses fewer pieces, while English and German skill is mostly kept. Training used a large mix of Hungarian, English, German, and code text, chosen to limit forgetting. Early results look modest but steady. The work, which won a conference award, shows a path for mid-size languages.
arxiv-2601-01444:
Four authors led by Haoxuan Xie present RadixGraph, a data structure for storing graphs that change constantly, such as social networks and transaction webs. As graphs grow, fast updates and compact storage fight each other. RadixGraph indexes vertices with a radix tree tuned to the best balance between lookup speed and space among its design family.

Edges live in a hybrid store that pairs snapshots with a log of changes, giving updates a constant average cost. The system handles millions of updates per second while staying competitive at analytics queries. In experiments, it ingested updates up to about sixteen times faster than the best baseline and used about forty percent less memory on average. The code is open source. For engineers whose graphs never sit still, the design shows that a careful index plus a log can beat general-purpose stores at their own game.
arxiv-2601-01644:
Dani Castellanos and Petr Jizba revisit a famous shortcut in nonequilibrium physics and push it further. The Jarzynski equality links the free energy gap between two states to averaged work done in fast, out-of-balance processes. A weaker result, Jarzynski's inequality, follows from it by a standard averaging step and is the focus here.

The pair identify extensions that do not come straight from the equality. They cover chemical systems near and far from the gentle linear regime, then use functional integral tools to carry the inequality to many-body quantum field systems. Links to the maximum work theorem and a classic fluctuation theory are also discussed.
arxiv-2601-01744:
Monica Garcia and Léa Lavoué work in representation theory, where algebras are studied through the modules built from them. Their short paper concerns skew-gentle algebras. This family extends the gentle algebras of surface geometry and cluster theory. The paper asks when such an algebra has only finitely many bricks. Bricks are its simplest building blocks, ones that cannot be split further.

The authors prove that a skew-gentle algebra is brick-finite exactly when it is representation-finite, meaning it has only finitely many indecomposable modules overall. The theorem extends Plamondon's earlier result for gentle algebras to the skew-gentle setting. Finiteness criteria like this matter because they tell researchers which algebras can, in principle, be fully classified, and which are too wild for complete description.
arxiv-2601-01844:
Clinical notes hold rich knowledge about cancer care, but turning free text into a structured knowledge graph that doctors can query demands accuracy that language models alone rarely guarantee. Udiptaman Das, Krishnasai Atmakuri, Duy Ho, Chi Lee, and Yugyung Lee build an end-to-end framework using several language models with retrieval support.

The pipeline works in stages. Prompting extracts entities and relations. Entropy scores the pipeline's own uncertainty. Output is aligned to an ontology in standard RDF and OWL form. Multiple models then cross-check each other to catch hallucinations. The method was applied to pancreatic and breast cancer cohorts. It produced graphs that can be read and queried. No gold-standard labels were used. It beat baselines on precision, relevance, and ontology compliance.
arxiv-2601-01944:
Open source software runs the world. AI libraries are spreading through it fast. Yet their effect on projects and communities is poorly measured. Matteo Esposito, Andrea Janes, Valentina Lenarduzzi, and Davide Taibi lay out a large-scale study. It compares Python and Java projects that adopt AI libraries with those that do not.

The plan covers up to about one hundred fifty-eight thousand candidate projects. It uses project and code metrics. Three fronts are compared: development activity, community engagement, and code complexity. The paper is a registered report, so it states expectations in advance. It expects clear differences on all three fronts. The eventual results should help maintainers judge what AI adoption actually changes in daily software work.
arxiv-2601-02044:
Studying how people read web pages usually means recording gaze coordinates, drawing regions of interest by hand, and computing metrics days later. Daniel Hienert, Heiko Schmidt, Thomas Krämer, and Dagmar Kern present EyeLiveMetrics, a browser plugin that maps raw gaze points onto the actual words and paragraphs of a page in real time.

Fixation, saccade, and reading measures are calculated, stored, and available instantly, so experiments and live applications can react while the reading is happening. A comparative evaluation accompanies the tool. By removing the manual mapping step, the plugin makes fine-grained reading research on real web content practical outside specialized laboratories.
arxiv-2601-02144:
Mixture-of-experts language models route each token to a few specialist subnetworks through a router trained once and then frozen, which makes routing brittle when the input distribution shifts. Boxuan Lyu, Soichiro Murakami, Hidetaka Kamigaito, and Peinan Zhang augment the router with memory: a nearest-neighbor store of past cases whose expert assignments were directly optimized offline.

At run time, retrieved neighbors vote on routing, weighted by their average similarity, which doubles as a confidence score: when nothing similar is found, the system falls back to the frozen router. Experiments show the method beats the zero-shot baseline and rivals expensive supervised fine-tuning. Routing by analogy turns the router from a fixed gate into a case-based reasoner.
arxiv-2601-02244:
Control engineer Luca Furieri asks a precise question about keeping a nonlinear system steady near a balance point. He looks at systems where control enters in a simple additive way and works in continuous time. The goal is fast, exponential return to the balance point after a small push, not just slow settling.

Furieri proves that every controller that does this job can be split in two parts. One part is plain linear feedback based on the system linearized at the balance point. The other part is extra stable internal dynamics whose output is added on top. He also shows the split can be learned with stable recurrent neural networks trained as neural differential equations, giving a safe starting form for learning better control.
arxiv-2601-02544:
Vibhuti Bhushan Jha and two co authors study how a family of two dimensional flows settles toward statistical balance when no friction acts. The flows are generalized by a parameter that sets how strongly the vorticity, the local spinning, couples to the streamfunction, which controls the strength of nonlinear interaction. Equilibrium solutions show a neat symmetry when that parameter flips sign, swapping the roles of generalized energy and enstrophy.

For starting conditions that form large condensates, simulations instead find long lived states that sit far from the thermal balance states predicted by ensemble theory, so the flow only partially thermalizes. As the parameter approaches zero and nonlinearity vanishes, the time needed for even partial settling grows in inverse proportion, meaning relaxation slows without limit. A reduced model from multiple scale analysis captures the same slowdown.
arxiv-2601-02744:
Hanqi Jiang and a team of co authors give language model agents a memory that works more like human memory. Standard retrieval augmentation fetches stored items by static similarity, which leaves long term agent memory disconnected, items that belong together are never linked. Their system, Synapse, models memory as a dynamic graph where relevance emerges from spreading activation, the cognitive process by which one memory wakes its neighbors.

Lateral inhibition sharpens the active set while temporal decay lets stale items fade, so relevant subgraphs light up and interference is filtered. Retrieval fuses three routes, geometric embeddings, activation based graph traversal, and the structure they share. On the LoCoMo benchmark of long conversations, Synapse significantly beats leading methods on complex temporal and multi hop reasoning questions, attacking what the authors call the contextual tunneling problem.
arxiv-2601-02844:
A. Abdollahi and six co-authors study how a scrambled ordering can be rebuilt from several noisy copies, where each copy may hold a few errors. Their focus is permutations, or rearrangements of n letters, measured with the Hamming metric, which counts positions where two orderings differ. The key quantity is the largest overlap between two error balls of a given radius.

Earlier work settled that overlap for radii up to four and gave rough bounds for larger radii. The authors derive exact formulas for radii five, six, and seven using group action methods. They also give a formula based on the characters of the symmetric group, plus an algorithm that computes values for much larger cases.
arxiv-2601-03144:
Andrew Shin reports that a language model equipped with self-verification can pass the Japanese bar examination under its real rules. The exam is a demanding benchmark: it needs advanced legal reasoning and strict obedience to a complex answer format in which several propositions are judged jointly. Earlier studies simplified questions into separate true-or-false judgments, leaving open whether models could handle the genuine exam.

Shin trains a self-verification model on a new dataset that faithfully replicates the exam's authentic format and scoring scale. The model scores above the official passing threshold on the actual exam scale, which the author presents as the first such demonstration without altering the questions or scoring. Comparisons with multi-agent setups and decomposition strategies round out the evaluation.
arxiv-2601-03344:
Uddipan Banik and Amitava Bhattacharjee connect two long-standing puzzles of plasma physics: why particle energies so often follow power-law distributions, and why the Sun's corona is far hotter than its surface. They develop a self-consistent quasilinear theory for electromagnetically driven, unmagnetized kinetic plasmas, written as a multi-species Fokker-Planck equation. The equation blends direct acceleration by waves, indirect acceleration by excited modes, and collisional diffusion and drag at small scales.

For turbulent electric fields with a steep enough spectrum, electrons and ions of every species relax toward one universal distribution, a high-energy tail equivalent to a kappa value of one point five. The universality comes from Debye screening: large-scale fields accelerate fast, unscreened particles but leave slow, screened ones alone. Shallower spectra give different, non-universal outcomes, which the theory also characterizes.
arxiv-2601-03444:
Weiyue Li and fourteen co-authors test whether the grading scale itself changes how well language model judges agree with human raters. Models are now used to score other models, but their scores can shift when prompts change. The team collected human and model ratings on three scales across six benchmarks with objective, subjective, and mixed tasks.

Using a standard agreement measure, they found model scores were not fully stable across scales on subjective tasks. The zero to five scale gave the strongest agreement between humans and models overall. Pooling results also hid big differences between benchmarks and between gender groups. The authors argue scale choice and subgroup checks belong in every judge protocol.
arxiv-2601-03544:
Ethan Ross wrote a doctoral thesis extending geometric quantization, a set of methods that turn classical phase spaces into quantum state spaces. The field began in the 1960s with work by Kirillov, Kostant, and Souriau. Ross targets singular spaces called symplectic stratified spaces, introduced in the 1990s, where the smooth tools of the classical theory break down.

To handle them, Ross builds a theory of stratified pseudobundles, which stand in for two aids the standard method needs: prequantum line bundles and polarizations. With that machinery he proves quantization commutes with reduction results for singular quotients of toric manifolds and cotangent bundles. He also works an example that earlier singular approaches could not reach. The thesis widens quantum methods to rougher, more realistic spaces.
arxiv-2601-03844:
Agostino Dovier and three co-authors built XAI-LAW, a tool that models parts of the Italian Criminal Code in answer set programming and learns legal rules from past verdicts. The aim is to support legal experts during the criminal trial phase with reasoning support and possible outcomes for new cases. Articles covering crimes against the person and property offenses were analyzed and encoded as logic rules.

The model is validated against previous verdicts and refined where it disagrees. Contradictions that surface during encoding are handled by the system, which can also generate possible decisions for new cases. Explanations come from the supportedness structure of stable models, letting users see why an outcome follows. A further component semi-automatically learns rules from example decisions, keeping human jurists in charge of the final encoding.
arxiv-2601-04144:
Jibril Ben Achour, Etera Livine, and Vincent Vennin revisit the symmetries behind long-wavelength ripples in the early universe. Such ripples are tied to large gauge transformations, coordinate changes that do alter the patch geometry. Those transformations act as true symmetries of perturbation theory, with uses from correlation rules to conservation laws.

The three authors prove two new points. First, known global symmetries extend to local ones with free time functions, generating soft low-multipole modes that change the mean curvature energy and angular momentum of the patch. They read those modes as a frame choice that must be fixed before observables are computed. Second, ripples made this way keep all background Killing symmetries in deformed form, which may let their effects be computed exactly.
arxiv-2601-04244:
Zihan Li and Son T. Nguyen test lattice methods on one-dimensional fermions that attract each other. Few-body systems in one dimension are ideal test beds because exact answers exist for comparison. Their two-component fermions interact by contact forces: an even wave channel between opposite spins and an odd wave channel between like spins.

Using exact diagonalisation on the lattice, Li and Nguyen fix all couplings from two-body data alone. They then compute ground states for three and four particles when both channels act together. Measured against the two-body threshold, both systems depend on just one dimensionless parameter. The pair conclude that two-body couplings fully determine the few-body physics in this setting, a clean benchmark for judging lattice systematics in stronger problems.
arxiv-2601-04344:
Sho Ebihara and six co-authors test an exotic explanation for a chemical oddity in one of the most distant galaxies known, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The James Webb Space Telescope found GN-z11, seen as it was when the universe was young, holding far more nitrogen relative to oxygen than ordinary star formation explains. One suspect is pollution from supermassive stars, whose winds should be nitrogen-rich.

Using a cosmological zoom-in simulation of galaxy formation — with rotating massive stars, supernovae, and aging giant stars evolving the chemistry — the team adds ejecta from a hypothetical supermassive star afterward. With polluted material making up a tenth to three tenths of the gas, the simulated pattern matches GN-z11's nitrogen, carbon, and oxygen ratios together. They check other nitrogen-rich young galaxies too, and find some fit the same story.
arxiv-2601-04444:
Sabee Grewal and four co-authors give a recipe for reading an unknown quantum state as fast as theory allows, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Pure state tomography means reconstructing a many-qubit state from measurements, and doing it with only simple single-qubit Pauli measurements, chosen in advance, is the practical dream. The cost is usually counted in copies of the state and in computing time, and earlier methods were wasteful in one or the other.

Their algorithm uses a number of copies and a running time both within a whisker of the information-theoretic minimum. still recovers the state with fidelity as high as requested, with high probability. It is, the authors state, the first tomography algorithm with near-optimal running time under such plain measurements. For laboratories characterizing ever larger quantum devices, that closes a long-standing efficiency gap.
arxiv-2601-04544:
Jiuzhou Zhao and eight co-authors route questions to the right artificial intelligence agent by making the router think first, in a 2026 arXiv paper. In enterprise multi-agent systems, the router that assigns each query to a specialist agent decides the system's accuracy, but conventional routers make one static label call. That design cannot absorb new agents as business domains grow, and it stumbles when agents' abilities overlap.

Their TCAndon-Router reasons before it routes: it writes out a natural-language reasoning chain, then proposes a set of candidate agents rather than a single pick. The chosen agents answer independently, and a dedicated refining agent merges their responses into one polished reply. On public datasets and real enterprise data, the authors report higher routing accuracy, fewer routing conflicts, and steadier behaviour on ambiguous queries. The router is released publicly for further research.
arxiv-2601-04644:
Nayana Mukherjee and Chitradipa Chakraborty model three decades of chickenpox across India in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their tool is a Bayesian SIRD model — tracking susceptible, infected, recovered, and deceased groups — split by age into juvenile, adult, and elderly groups, fitted to data from 1990 to 2021. Spread is modelled with a Holling-type incidence that saturates at high prevalence, and regions are clustered by their spread behaviour.

The clustering finds three distinct epidemiological regimes within India, differing in outbreak risk and age patterns. Across them, juveniles emerge as the primary drivers of spread, while the elderly carry a disproportionate share of deaths. Bayesian estimation keeps the uncertainty in spread, recovery, and mortality rates visible. The authors argue for age-focused interventions and a region-by-region strategy rather than a single national template, and check the model with a simulation study.
arxiv-2601-05044:
Assuming P differs from NP, every algorithm for an NP-complete problem must sometimes run for a super-polynomial time. Jesper Nederlof's 2026 survey asks the sharper question: what is the fastest worst-case run time actually achievable? For many problems, plain brute force is still the quickest method known, raising the provocative possibility that brute force is already optimal for them.

The survey invites readers into fine-grained complexity, the field that studies those exact run-time limits for NP-complete problems. It covers selected classic results and newer findings alike. The area matters because precise lower bounds tell algorithm designers when to stop hunting for speedups that provably cannot exist, and where cleverer methods might still hide.
arxiv-2601-05144:
Watermarking the output of reasoning models is tricky, because random token tweaks can wreck the logic mid-chain. Shuliang Liu and 8 co-authors present ReasonMark in a 2026 paper, a watermarking framework built specifically for reasoning-heavy language models. Token-based watermarking applies pseudo-random biases that corrupt reasoning flow, while semantic-aware alternatives add heavy latency or need auxiliary models, both painful in deployed systems.

ReasonMark splits output into two phases: thinking left untouched, and an answer that carries the watermark. It distills the thought first and watermarks only the final answer. The design follows a principle of semantic guidance to keep quality high. Provenance marking for AI text matters for accountability, and reasoning models need a version that does not sabotage their main selling point.
arxiv-2601-05444:
Dohyeong Ki and Adityanand Guntuboyina ask a basic question in their 2026 paper: what functions does XGBoost actually learn? XGBoost is a widely used machine learning method that combines many small decision trees. Its practical success has run ahead of theory explaining which function class it targets.

The authors define an infinite-dimensional class extending bounded-depth tree ensembles, plus a complexity measure matching the method's penalty term. Every optimizer of the XGBoost objective also solves an equivalent penalized regression over that class. They connect the class to Hardy-Krause variation, a classical smoothness notion, and prove a near-optimal convergence rate. One open problem remains: whether the algorithm itself reaches that optimum.
arxiv-2601-05644:
Immanuel Bomze and 3 co-authors formulate, in a 2026 paper, the maximum clique problem under adversarial uncertainty. A clique is a set of graph vertices all connected to each other, and finding the largest one is a classic hard problem. Here an adversary strategically perturbs the graph's edges, so a useful clique should survive those changes.

The model becomes a zero-sum game for two players, one seeking a clique and one working against it. A penalized continuous reformulation leads to a nonconvex, nonsmooth optimization problem. The authors define stable global solutions and prove they match the largest cliques common to all perturbed graphs. Their projection-free algorithm carries global convergence rates, and benchmark tests detected large common cliques efficiently.
arxiv-2601-05744:
Carlo Alberto Cremonini and 2 co-authors construct, in a 2026 paper, an interacting Yang-Mills theory that keeps duality invariance manifest. Duality swaps electric and magnetic descriptions of a field theory, and building an interacting deformation of Maxwell theory that preserves it openly has been a long-standing challenge.

Their building uses mutually local but interacting one-form and three-form fields. Unusually, the theory is written as a BRST-quantized gauge theory, a formalism used to handle gauge redundancy in quantum calculations. The underlying gauge-invariant Lagrangian before gauge fixing stays hidden. The gauge invariance itself rests on an associative symmetry rather than a standard Lie symmetry, marking a structurally new route to duality-invariant interactions. The result is a new kind of gauge theory, built to keep a key swap in plain sight.
arxiv-2601-05844:
Yutong Liang and 5 co-authors build DexterCap in 2026, an affordable optical system for capturing dexterous hand-object manipulation in fine detail. Fingers close together hide each other from cameras, and in-hand motions are subtle. Professional motion capture solves this with expensive rigs and heavy manual cleanup, while cheap vision methods lose accuracy under occlusion.

DexterCap uses dense, character-coded marker patches that stay trackable even under severe self-occlusion. An automated reconstruction pipeline needs minimal manual effort. With the system, the team created DexterHand, a dataset spanning simple shapes to articulated objects such as a Rubik's Cube. Both dataset and code are released to support research on dexterous hand-object interaction.
arxiv-2601-06444:
Design hunts in huge spaces break most tools. Each test run costs a lot, slopes are hard to trust, and good spots hide in a sea of poor ones. Suvo Banik and 6 co-authors bring a game-style hunt to this task in a 2026 paper. Their tree search thinks in moves, like a board game AI.

Group-level trees steer the hunt, with a stand-in model to point the way. Prize marks shape the walk, and the hunt swaps pace: wide search at one time, tight dig at the next. On stock test forms, it matched or beat the best past tools. Three real jobs showed its range: build a gem's bulk form from bits, fit the rules for how atoms pull, and solve a boxed design task. Each job kept its hard bounds and still hit the mark.
arxiv-2601-06544:
Quantum entanglement, usually a computing concept, can also reveal how atomic nuclei are put together. Rohit M. Shinde and 1 co-author apply entanglement measures to nuclei near the neutron number 20 island of inversion in a 2026 paper. In that region, nuclei deform unexpectedly because neutrons invade orbitals they would normally avoid.

Calculations used an ab initio valence-space method, solving nuclear structure from underlying interactions. Proton-neutron entanglement entropy highlighted how the island of inversion forms. Mutual information measured correlation strengths between single-particle states: proton-neutron correlations were weak in ground states but rivaled like-particle correlations in excited states. Relative entropy measures compared the lowest spin states across neon, magnesium, and silicon isotopes and the N=20 isotones, completing a quantum-information portrait of the region.
arxiv-2601-06644:
Yan Meng, Wafaa Mohammed, and Christof Monz test cross-language reasoning in 2026. Real-world information sources are inherently multilingual, they point out. That raises whether language models can synthesize information across languages.

They introduce a simple two-hop question answering setting for the test. Answering requires inferences over two multilingual documents together, they explain. One hop alone, in one language, cannot reach the answer. The setup isolates exactly the skill named in their title. Models may reason well within English yet fail across languages. Their benchmark shows where that gap opens in current systems. Multilingual AI readers get a clean, small test with large implications.
arxiv-2601-07144:
Research by Linus Bleistein linus.bleistein and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with optimal transport under group fairness constraints. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Ensuring fairness in matching algorithms is a key challenge in allocating scarce resources and positions.

Focusing on Optimal Transport (OT), the authors introduce a new notion of group fairness requiring that. The probability of matching two individuals from any two given groups in the OT plan satisfies a predefined target. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07444:
Zhipeng Chen, Haolun Tang, and Jingyi Zhan formalize a classic number theory topic inside a proof assistant. Their 2026 preprint presents the theory of amicable numbers in Lean 4. Two positive integers form an amicable pair when each equals the sum of the other's proper divisors. The famous pair 220 and 284 has been known since ancient times.

Formalization means turning definitions and proofs into code a computer can check line by line. Every step must be exact, with no gaps left to human judgment. Building this theory in Lean tests both the software library and the clarity of the math itself. Readers interested in verified mathematics get a concrete example of an old idea made machine-checkable.
arxiv-2601-07844:
A 2026 preprint in Entropy builds the math of epidemics on networks from single agents upward. Agent based SIR dynamics track at risk, sick, and healed people as a discrete state Markov process. The process captures the random spread of infection along network contacts. With indicator functions and their marginal chances, the authors derive a hierarchy of change equations. The hierarchy resembles the classical BBGKY hierarchy of statistical mechanics.

Such stacks are of use but hard to wield, since each level rests on the next. Closures in this stack cut them off at a set level with a close guess. The paper moves from agent based Markov dynamics to such closures on networks. Good closures keep the accuracy of agent simulations at a fraction of the cost. Those who model outbreaks are the readers. The work aims at rigorous shortcuts for large network outbreaks. The point is speed with care.
arxiv-2601-07944:
Roy Shivam Ram Shreshtth, Arnab Hazra, and Gourab Mukherjee test amortized Bayesian inference when conditions change. Approximate Bayesian inference has grown by absorbing new computational techniques for larger problems. Deep networks and foundation models now enable amortized inference, where a learned predictor performs inference quickly for many data sets. Their 2026 preprint assesses this approach statistically. Two stress factors are signal-to-noise variation and distribution shift.

Amortized methods are trained once and reused, so shifts can silently break them. A careful assessment shows when the speed is worth the risk. Signal-to-noise changes are routine in real instruments and surveys. Distribution shift is the norm when models meet new populations. The paper serves statisticians and machine learning scholars who deploy learned inference. It supplies evidence about failure modes rather than another success story.
arxiv-2601-08044:
Oleksandr Kuznetsov compiles neural networks into lookup tables to catch denial-of-service attacks on small devices. DoS attacks threaten Internet of Things ecosystems. Effective intrusion detection is hard to deploy on resource-constrained edge devices. Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks offer a compact alternative to standard multilayer perceptrons. They place learnable spline functions on edges rather than fixed activations on nodes, reaching competitive accuracy with fewer parameters. Kuznetsov's 2026 preprint compiles them into lookup tables.

A lookup table replaces computation with fast memory reads. Edge chips can then run detection at low power. Compiling after training keeps the model's accuracy while changing its form. The work targets the gap between security research and deployable devices. The paper serves IoT security engineers and edge AI scholars. It shows a path from a compact model class to running protection on site.
arxiv-2601-08344:
Gabrielle Taylor, Stefan Wagner, Alicja Wierzcholska, and Michael Zacharias review twenty years of blazar watching. Their 2026 arXiv paper covers Mrk 421 and Mrk 501 across many wavelengths. Both blazars vary on every observed timescale and are well studied at high energies on short scales.

The team instead characterizes long-term behavior at synchrotron energies: optical, ultraviolet, and X-ray bands. Long records test current models of how these objects produce their light. Blazars are jets pointed near our line of sight, so their slow trends reveal jet physics. The two-decade baseline offers modelers a rare check against short, campaign-style snapshots.
arxiv-2601-08444: Yuxiang Wang and co-authors present attributed table graphs for reasoning over tables. Their 2026 arXiv paper addresses table reasoning, answering questions from data stored in tabular form. Tables hold a large share of stored knowledge, so the task matters widely. Recent solutions lean on large language models for semantic understanding and reasoning. Attributed graphs offer a structured way to expose rows, columns, and their relations to the model. Better table structure could cut errors on questions that mix lookup, comparison, and arithmetic.
arxiv-2601-08744:
Nitin Kenjale and Anuradha Garge work on codes that fix errors in sent data. A code here is a set of words made of bits, used to spot and fix flaws. Old tools count how many ones sit in each word. The pair says that count misses where the ones sit, and place can matter a lot.

They set up two new tools. One tracks how ones spread across the spots in a word. The next builds a full list from that spread, like a sum over all words. These tools give a finer view of a code than the old count. A reader who works on safe data links gets a sharper way to judge and build codes.
arxiv-2601-08844:
Anandita Garg Harish and Uma Gaba Harish weigh small chat models next to large ones on cost to the earth. Large models need much power to train and to run. Each ask burns power, and asks come by the billions. The pair ask if a small model, tuned for one fixed task, can do that task with far less smoke and heat.

They test small tuned models on set tasks and track power use and task score side by side. The aim is not to crown small models for all work. It is to find tasks where they are good enough. A reader who runs AI at scale gets a trade map. It can guide which jobs to move off large models first.
arxiv-2601-08944:
Niklas Affolter and three co-authors set up a new frame for maps built from triple cross diagrams. Such diagrams code sets of points and lines in a plane view. Like maps show up in more than one branch of shape work. Each branch built its own tools for them, with its own terms and tricks.

The team gives one shared frame for all of them. In that frame, a rich set of group forms, called cluster algebras, can be built on each map. Those forms link counts and moves in a strict way. A reader in shape work gets a joint tongue for split fields. Work in one field may now aid work in a next with ease.
arxiv-2601-09044:
Fei Tan and four co-authors grow health scans past their edge while they keep growths in place. Scan sets oft lack rich cases of ill tissue. A model trained on thin sets learns ill marks poor. To grow a scan, a tool paints new zones round the old scan. A poor tool may wash out the very growth a doctor must see.

Their tool is called POWDR. It uses a wave based spread model, tuned to hold ill traits safe. New zones look real, yet the core growth stays as it was. A reader who trains health tools gets more train cases with out loss of the key trait. Rare cases can be grown, not just sought.
arxiv-2601-09444:
Lauri Suomela and four co-authors ask how much training data a navigating robot really needs. Their 2026 arXiv paper reports a large-scale study of data quantity and diversity for visual navigation. The policies learn by imitation and must work in places they never saw in training, without maps.

Generalization to new settings is the weak point of such end-to-end policies. The authors vary how much data, and how varied it is, then test in the real world. Their study is the first of its scale for map-free navigation. The findings give builders a sense of what data collection buys in robustness.
arxiv-2601-09544:
David Barnes and Niall Taggart use span categories to study diagrams built from profinite groups. Their 2026 arXiv paper is a case study in the homotopy theory of infinity-categories. A strength of that theory is its robust way of taking limits and colimits of whole categories.

The catch is that several rival versions of the category of categories exist. Picking the wrong one changes what the limits even mean. The authors show, in one concrete setting, how the choices behave. A worked example like this helps other mathematicians know which variant their own arguments need.
arxiv-2601-09644:
Yuta Kageura and seven co-authors find a new way to measure how opaque the early universe was. Their 2026 arXiv paper constrains the optical depth of reionization without leaning on the cosmic microwave background's large-scale polarization. That polarization signal may be biased by foreground dust and instrument effects.

A mild mismatch has appeared between baryon acoustic oscillation data and microwave background results. A higher optical depth could explain it. An independent route to the same number tests whether the mismatch is real physics. The authors build that route from the reionization history itself.
arxiv-2601-09844:
Nils Hüsken, Eric S. Swanson, and Adam Szczepaniak compare two flavors of a workhorse scattering model. Their 2026 arXiv paper contrasts dispersive and nondispersive K-matrix formalisms. Coupled-channel effects matter more as precise data pours in for hadron scattering processes.

The K-matrix is a powerful yet simple way to model scattering amplitudes with channels coupled. Which flavor a team picks changes how the amplitudes behave away from the data. The authors weigh the two formalisms against each other. A clear comparison helps phenomenologists read modern hadron spectra with far fewer artifacts of method.
arxiv-2601-10044:
Farshad Amani, Faezeh Ardali, and Amin Kargarian build a tool to fix power grids after storms. Storms and floods break grid gear in many places at once. Crews must be sent to fix sites in a good order. New harm news can force a fresh plan mid job.

The tool learns by trial and reward. It takes in new facts as they come. It then sends crews to tasks in real time. The aim is to bring power back fast. It also aims to cut waits that stem from a stale plan. Such a tool could help grid teams in the hard days after a storm.
arxiv-2601-10644:
Eugene Yang, Andrew Yates, Dawn Lawrie, James Mayfield, and Trevor Adriaanse present RoutIR, a tool for serving retrieval pipelines at speed. Retrieval sits at the heart of retrieval-augmented generation, where a system searches for documents, reads them, and then writes a reply. Real systems are dynamic. They may search several times before they answer.

Many strong retrieval methods live in academic platforms built for offline batch tests. All queries are known up front in those tests, unlike live service. RoutIR aims to run such pipelines fast in real time. It helps teams move research-grade search into products that must answer users now, not later.
arxiv-2601-10844:
C. A. Downing and M. S. Ukhtary revisit how a quantum battery gets charged. Their model has two qubits: one acts as the charger, the other as a single-cell battery. The Bloch sphere, the standard map of a qubit's states, frames the analysis. They rework the energetics and thermodynamics of the charging process.

Quantum batteries promise storage that exploits quantum effects for fast charging. A two-qubit model is the smallest lab for such ideas. Careful bookkeeping of work, heat, and coherence shows what charging can and cannot do. The paper speaks to the small but growing field of quantum thermodynamics, where energy rules meet quantum rules head on.
arxiv-2601-11144:
Yuejie Li and co-authors present Deep GraphRAG, a balanced approach to graph-based retrieval-augmented generation. GraphRAG systems answer questions by walking a knowledge graph. They face a trade-off: global search is thorough but slow, local search is fast but narrow. Large hierarchical graphs make paths hard to optimize, and exploration can crowd out exploitation.

Deep GraphRAG adds adaptive integration and robust multi-stage re-ranking. The aim is answers grounded in the right subgraph without scanning everything. Enterprises hold much of their knowledge in linked records, not flat text. A system that balances depth and speed could make graph question answering practical at real scale.
arxiv-2601-11344:
Parker Seegmiller and six coauthors ask how much doctors would edit AI drafts. Their 2026 preprint deals with replies to patient portal messages. Language models can draft such replies with real promise. Clinics still weigh whether drafts save time in real work.

A draft that needs heavy edits may save no time at all. Worse, it could add risk if flaws slip past a busy doctor. The team measures alignment with each clinician in depth. They check edits draft by draft, doctor by doctor. That edit load is a plain, honest test of value. It shows where drafts help and where they hinder. The study speaks to safe rollout of AI in clinics.
arxiv-2601-11444:
