Yuanze Luo and sixteen co-authors test the idea across post-starburst, star-forming, and quiet galaxies in the nearby universe, combining X-ray, mid-infrared, and radio data and stacking undetected galaxies to recover average behavior. Post-starburst galaxies' radio and X-ray light proves consistent with star formation alone.

Their mid-infrared black hole incidence runs about twice that of star-forming galaxies, but the inferred luminosities are small next to literature examples, and overall emission shows no strong enhancement over matched comparisons. Obscured, faint black holes fed by leftover starburst gas cannot be ruled out, but they look unlikely to drive quenching. The authors conclude feedback at low redshift is more preventive than ejective, restraining gas rather than blasting it away.
arxiv-2602-11944:
Two models can score nearly the same overall yet disagree sharply on individual cases. Karolin Frohnapfel and four co-authors call that phenomenon predictive multiplicity, and argue it clashes with the EU AI Act. That law asks providers of high-risk systems to report performance not just for datasets but for specific people. For a person caught between disagreeing models, another equally good model might have decided their case differently.

The paper puts that phenomenon in the context of the AI Act's accuracy provisions and derives practical tools. Case conflict ratios and delta-ambiguity quantify disagreement case by case and flag people subject to conflicting predictions. It also offers easy-to-implement rules for builders to evaluate it, and argues that deployers should receive that information so they can judge whether outputs for given people are reliable enough to use.
arxiv-2602-12144:
AI coding agents now write code for phone apps, but little hard data shows how well that code fares. Muhammad Ahmad Khan led this study with four co-authors, tracing 2,901 agent-written pull requests across 193 checked Android and iOS projects on GitHub. It is the first study of its kind at the level of task type.

Android projects took in twice as many agent requests as iOS projects, and accepted 71 percent against 63 percent for iOS. Routine jobs such as new features, fixes, and screen work did best, while rebuilds and large refactors took longer and failed more often. Android wait times improved through mid-2025, then worsened again. The numbers give a first baseline for judging agent help on phones.
arxiv-2602-12244:
Household robots must turn vague spoken wishes into long, workable action plans, a step where language models often invent plans that cannot run. Zhihong Liu led this work with five co-authors, recasting planning as learning to write checkable subgoals in a formal planning language. That bridge joins language sense to symbolic planners that can prove a plan is feasible.

Their training method, TGPO, uses verifier-based rewards, outside fixes to middle reasoning traces, and constrained updates that fold fixed traces back into training. On large household tasks with long horizons and vague instructions, TGPO beats prompting and reinforcement baselines, with the largest gains on abstract tasks. It also plugs into planners and executors for robust, general long-horizon behaviour.
arxiv-2602-12344:
Hadrons found inside jets offer a clean window on how partons turn into hadrons, a process described by fragmentation functions. Leonardo Bonino led this work with five co-authors, computing hadron-in-jet cross sections for electron-positron annihilation into two jets and into three jets, to next-to-next-to-leading order in perturbative QCD. Electron-positron collisions give a tidy setting, free of the mess of hadron collisions.

Comparing the new predictions with ALEPH experiment data shows what precision theory adds to phenomenology. The results sharpen how fragmentation functions can be extracted and tested, and they set a higher bar for future measurements of hadrons inside jets. Readers get a state-of-the-art calculation for a classic, well-measured process.
arxiv-2602-12444:
Reinforcement learning can optimise control, but it often lacks provable safety guarantees for safety-critical systems. Alexander W. Goodall led this work with one co-author, Francesco Belardinelli, presenting a recovery-based shielding framework for safe RL in unknown, non-linear continuous systems. A backup policy, or shield, joins the learning agent, using Gaussian process uncertainty estimates to predict safety violations.

When danger looms, the shield recovers the system to safe paths, intervening only when necessary. Experience from the shielded agent builds those models, and policy tuning uses internal model-based sampling, allowing free exploration and sample-efficient learning without compromising safety. Tests on continuous control settings show strong performance with strict safety compliance, giving learning agents a provable safety lower bound.
arxiv-2602-12644:
Line congruences are the source of key examples of maps of projective surfaces, such as the Laplace transform. Matthew Ryan led this work with one co-author, Michael T. Schultz, surveying results on that old subject, then deriving new formulae for the Laplace transform of the entire rank-4 linear system linked to an immersed projective surface.

Results are applied to the shape of surfaces defined by Appell's hypergeometric functions of rank-4, namely F2 and F4. The sequence of Laplace invariants for each is set respectively by the Euler-Poisson-Darboux equation for F2, and Darboux's Harmonic equation for F4. Further results show the natural line congruences made by these surfaces carry rich shape structure, linking old surface theory with special functions.
arxiv-2602-12744:
Deep models for classifying time series are accurate but heavy, which blocks their use on small devices. Javidan Abdullayev and five co-authors propose dynamic structured pruning, a method that trims whole filters automatically instead of relying on a hand-set pruning ratio. During training, a sparsity loss pushes channels toward zero, and a later check of activations picks out the filters that can safely go.

Tested on 128 UCR datasets with two leading architectures, the method cut model size by 58% for LITETime and 75% for InceptionTime while holding accuracy steady. Checks of the trimmed models confirm they keep compact, informative features rather than hollow shells. The result is a practical path to running strong time series classifiers where memory and compute are tight.
arxiv-2602-13044:
Heavy-ion crashes create quark-gluon plasma that spins and sits in strong magnet fields, and photons from that plasma carry clues to its conduct. Matteo Buzzegoli and four co-authors work out photon output from spinning synchro rays, dubbed RoSyRa, for a rigidly spinning plasma in thermal balance under an outside magnet field. They work out the non-prompt photon spectrum and oval flow at mid-speed, including finite-volume effects.

At low sideways push, magnet force induces large oval flow, while spin boosts synchro rays from minus-charged quarks. Those signs make RoSyRa a viable pick for cracking the direct photon puzzle, the long-standing mismatch between forecast and seen photon yields. The paper thus ties plasma spin and magnet force to a visible photon signal.
arxiv-2602-13344:
Editing an image from a written instruction demands a model that keeps identity, follows wording, and handles text inside pictures. FireRed-Image-Edit is a diffusion transformer built for that job, trained through data curation, multi-stage training, and careful benchmark design. Its corpus began at 1.6 billion samples, then cleaning and two-stage filtering kept over 100 million high-quality pairs balanced between generation and editing.

Training moves from pretraining through fine-tuning to reinforcement learning, with new tricks for batching, prompt alignment, gradient stability, and text-aware rewards. A new benchmark spanning 15 editing types shows competitive or leading results against open and proprietary rivals, and code, models, and benchmarks are public. The report comes from the Super Intelligence Team, with 18 named researchers behind it.
arxiv-2602-13444:
Vision-language-action models can sketch plausible robot motions yet fail at long, contact-rich tasks, because hand-object interaction structure is left implicit. FlowHOI makes that structure explicit with a two-stage flow-matching framework. It generates hand poses, object poses, and contact states over time, conditioned on an egocentric view, a language instruction, and a 3D Gaussian splatting scene reconstruction.

Grasping geometry and manipulation semantics are decoupled, with the latter grounded by compact scene tokens and a motion-text alignment loss. A reconstruction pipeline mines aligned hand-object trajectories from large-scale egocentric video to supply training signal. On GRAB and HOT3D, FlowHOI led on action recognition and physics success, with a 40-fold inference speedup, and it ran on real robots. Huajian Zeng leads the work with six co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13544:
Classical Merton theory prescribes fixed, state-based portfolio rules, yet lab and field evidence shows people often prefer random choices, producing noisy decisions. Additive perturbed utility explains that preference in a static setting but turns ill-posed or hard to solve dynamically. This paper introduces recursive perturbed utility, a random utility over time that folds an entropy-based taste for randomness into a recursive total.

The total weighs the value of random choice against bequest, with a time discount tied to past random choices, avoiding excess random choice and keeping the problem solvable. In a general market with CRRA tastes, the best portfolio rule is bell-shaped in closed form, independent of wealth, with its mean drifting from Merton at first order. Min Dai leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13644:
Turbulence inside solar-storm clouds shapes space weather, governing energy cascade, plasma heating, magnetic reconnection, and coupling between solar wind and magnetosphere. Yet turbulence had never been measured at multiple side-spread stations at a single vantage point. This paper presents the first multipoint analysis of plasma turbulence across storm-cloud regions, using four spacecraft at the Sun-Earth L1 point spread by 80 Earth radii along the dawn-dusk direction.

High-resolution magnetic data from Aditya L1, Wind, ACE, and DSCOVR cover the October 10, 2024 solar storm, the second strongest magnetic storm of solar cycle 25. Turbulence age varied markedly across small gaps, sheath turbulence was reshaped by shock-driven energy injection, and squashable turbulence at the flux rope meeting region points to internal reconnection shaping cloud evolution. Shibotosh Biswas leads the work with six co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13844:
Giorgio Chiesa and seven co-authors present a 2026 arXiv paper on making fake yet true-to-life video for robot surgery training. The work deals with the Da Vinci robot arms and the hard task of marking each tool in each frame. Real surgery video is scarce, so the team built a way to make more of it.

They rebuilt the arms in 3D, set them in motion, and varied light, motion, and fake blood to match real operating rooms. Each clip kept exact masks that show where each tool sits. Tests found a mix of real and fake clips trained models better than real clips alone, while too much fake data hurt results. The shared code and data give other teams a low-cost way to train surgery vision tools.
arxiv-2602-14244:
Ala Emrani and two co-authors present a 2026 arXiv framework for personalized federated learning. Federated learning protects privacy by training across clients, but clients differ statistically, so one shared model fits all poorly. Splitting networks into a shared extractor and client-specific heads creates a tradeoff: deep shared parts hinder personalization, while large local heads overfit scarce local data.

Their boosting-inspired framework builds an ensemble of T models per client, progressively deepening the personalized part across boosting rounds. Low-rank factorization or width shrinkage controls effective complexity at each step. That smooth control, the authors argue, navigates the personalization tradeoff in a principled way, where rigid shallow heads fail.
arxiv-2602-14444:
Ian Su and seven co-authors study a 2026 arXiv cost of incomplete reasoning in language models. Reasoning-specialized models devote heavy inference compute to chain-of-thought traces, yet reasoning tokens cost dearly. The paper constrains models to reason only through code, comments, both, or neither, then ablates token budgets to 10, 30, 50, and 70% of optimal.

Four frontier models were tested on math benchmarks including AIME, GSM8K, and HMMT. Truncated reasoning can hurt: DeepSeek-V3.2 scored 53% with no reasoning but only 17% with truncated chain-of-thought at half budget. Code degraded gracefully, with Gemini comments collapsing to 0% while code held 43 to 47%. Hybrid reasoning underperformed single modalities, and robustness varied by model, with Grok holding 80 to 90% at 30% budget where others fell to 7 to 27%.
arxiv-2602-14644:
Neutrino mass may arise not at tree level but through quantum loops. Monal Kashav studies loop-extended seesaw models, where ordinary symmetries fail to block the simpler tree-level terms. The paper asks what rule can force the loop term to dominate.

Non-invertible selection rules do that job, the author shows, while also stabilizing a dark matter candidate. One topology, called T4-2-i, gives a type-II one-loop seesaw in this frame. Kashav realizes it concretely from a Z7 Tambara-Yamagami fusion algebra. The result unites neutrino mass and dark-sector stability in one structure.
arxiv-2602-15444:
Kukusta and colleagues probe the layout of Ba4Ir3O10 in density-functional model using the broad slope guess with links. They use the wholly Einstein spin-aligned Dirac muffin-tin tool. Ba4Ir3O10 has a quasi-2D layout of bent layers making Ir3O12 trios of face-sharing cages.

Ir bits sit at two mismatched spots: center and two tips. The center-to-tip gap is tiny, about two and a half angstroms. This gives clear bonding and antibonding levels at the center spot. The big split steadies the dyz-leading antibonding t2g state and opens a wide gap at the Fermi tier. The gap starts only with Coulomb links at the tip spot. So, the blocking state is powered by pairing at the center and Mott blocking acts at the tip. They also probe echoing lossy bounce at the Ir L3 rim, fitting lab readings well.
arxiv-2602-15844:
Kang and colleagues ask whether already-deployed large language models can sort ordered data in web-native tables, skipping focused models or extensive retraining. The web holds rich ordered data in tables, from product catalogs and knowledge bases to scientific data sets. Their light method, Table Representation with Language Model, or TaRL, supports few-shot table sorting directly using meaning vectors of individual table rows.

Naive use of those vectors underperforms focused table models. But their potential unlocks with two key techniques: removing the common component from all vectors and tuning the softmax temperature. A simple learner, trained on hand-made features, learns to predict a right temperature. That approach achieves performance matching top models in low-data cases, with k at most 32, on tables rich in meaning. The findings show the worth of reusing existing language model setup for fast meaning-driven web table understanding.
arxiv-2602-15944:
Beem and Kulkarni test which graded unitary W3 vertex algebras can arise from four dimensional physics through the link between superconformal theories and vertex algebras. Their tool is graded unitarity, a formal version of four dimensional unitarity developed in recent work by the first author.

Assuming the R filtration counts weight with respect to the usual strong generators, they rule out every central charge except those of a specific family of minimal models. Those surviving algebras are exactly the ones obtained by principal Drinfeld Sokolov reduction from boundary admissible affine current algebras of sl3 type, which a similar analysis had already singled out. The same algebras are known to belong to a family of Argyres Douglas theories, tying the classification to concrete physical models.
arxiv-2602-16044:
Dominic Mashak leads a team of three chemists hunting for molecules with stronger nonlinear optical properties, prized for photonic, telecom, and laser uses. Searching chemical space is hard because the goals compete. They target the ratio of first to second hyperpolarizability. They also aim the HOMO-LUMO gap and linear polarizability at chosen ranges, and they seek low energy per atom. Molecules are encoded as SMILES strings and scored with quantum-chemical calculations.

The team compares five search methods, including NSGA-II, MAP-Elites, MOME, a single-objective evolutionary algorithm, and simulated annealing. NSGA-II scores high on every objective, while MOME ranges more widely and earns higher global hypervolume and quality-diversity scores. Quality-diversity methods keep archives across atom and bond counts, preserving structural variety. Each method yields promising candidates, with distinct strengths.
arxiv-2602-16144:
Rong Fu leads a team of seven authors building a way to delete one data channel from a sentiment system on request. Such systems now handle much private personal data. Users and regulators may ask that a specific channel be revoked. Privacy rules and own choice both support that demand. Their framework, Missing-by-Design, pairs structured learning of codes with a checkable chain for changing settings.

The system learns trait-aware codes. It uses generator-based reconstruction to recover missing channels while keeping task-relevant signals. When deletion is requested, weight-based choice plus a tuned Gaussian update produce a machine-proven deletion proof. Tests on benchmark data sets show strong forecast scores under partial inputs. They also show a real privacy-utility trade-off, placing precise forgetting as a cheap other path versus full retrain.
arxiv-2602-16244:
Shan Shan and coauthors propose a pinching antennas framework for integrated sensing and multicast communication. Comms performance is measured by group rate under max-min fairness, while sensing score is quantified by the Bayesian Cramer-Rao bound. Antenna placement is optimized under communications-centric, sensing-centric, and Pareto-optimal criteria, in single- and multi-antenna scenarios.

For the single-antenna case, a closed-form solution gives the communications-centric transmit spot. The sensing-centric design yields transmit and receive spots symmetric about the target. Enforcing that symmetry reduces the joint placement problem to transmit spot alone. For the multi-antenna case, an element-wise alternating optimization method sequentially optimizes all spots. Numerical results show the design substantially beating fixed-antenna baselines in both multicast rate and sensing accuracy.
arxiv-2602-16344:
Himanshu Miriyala, Rishabh Pal, and Arijit Sharma model an ultrastable cavity for transportable atomic clocks. Such clocks are the next generation of precision timekeeping, for positioning, navigation, and timing. Their performance depends on ultra-stable lasers held steady by a compact portable cavity. The cubic spacer design suits transport, since its symmetric shape and sturdy mounting limit vibration.

Longer cavities lower the thermal noise floor, but size must be balanced against transportability. The seven and a half centimetre dual-axis cavity beats smaller counterparts on that floor with a reasonable size, weight, and power budget. Its dual-axis design allows multi-wavelength laser stabilization. With the finite element method, the authors test mechanical and thermal stability against geometry, mounting forces, machining flaws, conduction, radiation, and mirror heating in a shielded vacuum chamber. The findings guide robust cavity design for positioning, geodesy, very long baseline interferometry, and deep space missions.
arxiv-2602-16444:
Yixue Zhang leads fourteen coauthors introducing RoboGene, an agentic framework generating diverse, physically plausible robot tasks. General-purpose robots are held back by scarce interaction data. Unlike web data for vision or language, robot data collection is an active process with prohibitive real costs, so automated task curation is a critical challenge. Manual methods do not scale and favor common tasks, while off-the-shelf foundation models often hallucinate infeasible instructions.

It automates task generation across single-arm, dual-arm, and mobile robots. Diversity-driven sampling gives broad coverage, self-reflection enforces real constraints, and human refinement gives continuous improvement. Large-scale experiments collect eighteen thousand trajectories and introduce new metrics for task quality and feasibility. It outperforms state-of-the-art foundation models such as GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Pro. Real-world tests show vision-language-action models pre-trained with RoboGene reach higher success rates and generalize better.
arxiv-2602-16944:
Philip Sosnin and co-authors bring in a verification frame giving sound and complete guarantees for data-poisoning attacks during neural network training. Data manipulation, model training, and test-time evaluation are formulated in a single mixed-integer quadratic programming problem. Finding the global optimum provably yields worst-case poisoning attacks. It also bounds the effectiveness of all possible attacks on the given training pipeline.

The frame encodes both gradient-based training dynamics and model evaluation at test time. That enables the first exact certification of training-time robustness. Tests on small models confirm the approach delivers a complete characterization of robustness against data poisoning. Security researchers get a rigorous tool for proving, not merely probing, how much poisoning a pipeline can withstand.
arxiv-2602-17044:
Temesgen Muruts Weldengus led a seven-author team on a tool that retouches photos in a user's own style, with no per-user fine-tuning at test time. Current personal retouching tools often demand that tuning step, or they fail to carry a style to new images well. The paper introduces RefRetouch, a general framework that reads a style from paired reference examples and applies it at once.

An asymmetric auto-encoder turns the reference pairs into a style code stripped of image content, so the style can move cleanly to a new photo. A retrieval step, called retrieval-augmented retouching, then pulls style codes from the references closest in content to the photo at hand. Tests cover single-reference, multi-reference, and mixed-style cases, plus photorealistic style transfer, where the tool also held up.
arxiv-2602-17144:
Shuqi Liu led a five-author team showing that adding experts can make learning to defer worse, not better. In learning to defer, a classifier may abstain and hand a case to an expert. The single-expert version is well studied, but the multi-expert version, the authors prove, suffers inherent underfitting that badly degrades predictions, while single-expert underfitting appears only under special conditions.

The root cause is expert identifiability: learning which expert in a diverse pool to trust is itself hard, and that difficulty breaks existing fixes. The team answers with PiCCE, a surrogate method that adaptively picks a confident and correct expert from empirical evidence, reducing the multi-expert problem to a single-expert-like one. They prove its consistency and its recovery of class probabilities and expert accuracies, and experiments across varied settings confirm the gains.
arxiv-2602-17244:
Oleksii Furman led a six-author team building better counterfactual explanations for model predictions. These name minimal input changes that would flip a verdict, but current methods struggle to produce many high-quality options that touch few inputs, handle mixed tabular data, and respect user constraints. The paper offers CounterFlowNet, an approach that treats building them as stepwise feature editing with conditional Generative Flow Networks.

The system samples them matching a user-set reward carrying validity, sparsity, proximity, and plausibility. That yields highly sparse edits across continuous and categorical features alike. Use rules like fixed features and rising-only rules are applied at run time through action masking, with no new training. Tests on eight data sets under two setups showed better trade-offs among those four plus range, with all constraints met.
arxiv-2602-17344:
Peter Elbau led a two-author paper on what raster scan diffraction tomography can actually recover. This imaging reads an object's scatter profile from recorded wave fields. In the classic setup, plane waves from many angles strike the object, and the Fourier theorem links transforms of profile and data straight. Real systems, however, use focused beams swept across the object to bring regions into focus.

The analysis rests on a newly derived Fourier link tying data to Fourier numbers of the scatter profile. That link yields no direct rebuild formula, only a linear system for those numbers. The authors prove that in dimensions above two, all numbers in the links are usually uniquely fixed. In 2D, only a select subset of Fourier range is uniquely fixed, while distinct numbers outside it may produce matching data.
arxiv-2602-18244:
Deepak Sehrawat and one co-author determine coloring numbers for two families of signed graphs. Their 2026 paper treats graphs where each edge carries a plus or minus sign, and colorings assign colors to vertex-edge incidences under a sign-flip rule at each edge. The chromatic index is the smallest number of colors that allows such a coloring.

The authors settle that index for signed generalized book graphs, a family built by gluing pages along a shared spine. They also settle it for signed complete graphs up to order six, where every pair of vertices is joined. The results give exact answers where only bounds or partial cases stood before, and they sharpen the toolkit for coloring signed structures.
arxiv-2602-18644:
Mohamed Benchat and eleven co-authors recover robot designs from code. Their 2026 paper notes Model-Driven Engineering relies on clear models to record systems. For ROS 2, subsystem structure is usually encoded implicitly in spread files, most notably launch files. Existing ROS 2 approaches cover node entities and wiring but do not make decomposition a first-class view.

The team contributes a UML-based idea for designs. A blueprint-guided pipeline rebuilds models from code and files by combining extraction with language-model agents. The blueprint of nodes, topics, interfaces, and wiring is encoded as contracts for synthesis and checks. Evaluation on three repositories, including an industrial subset, shows high precision, while subsystem recall drops with complexity due to implicit semantics.
arxiv-2602-18944:
Covering maps are a classical tool in topology, but the fundamental group itself can carry different group shapes. Naghme Shahami, with one co-author, generalises covering maps in 2026 with respect to a topology on the fundamental group of a space. The work starts from classical covering theory.

The new notion is a covering map defined relative to a group shape on the fundamental group. Famous notions turn out to be special cases of it. Covering, semicovering, generalised covering, and fibration maps all fit inside the new notion. The authors present traits of the new notion and compare its versions across several famous group shapes on the fundamental group. That comparison clarifies how the choice of group shape affects what counts as a covering map. One notion, many cases. That unity is the point.
arxiv-2602-19044:
Do early galaxies bunch up at regular spacings in cosmic time? Takeshi Fukuyama, writing alone in 2026, tests that idea with early James Webb Space Telescope data. He uses a public catalog of over three hundred compact sources at high redshift. A smooth baseline is removed first. Then an unbinned frequency scan hunts for periodic structure in log redshift.

A clear peak emerges at a logarithmic spacing near one third. That means a multiplicative spacing near 1.4 in one plus redshift. Chance alone would rarely produce such a peak. Holdout tests and field checks support its robustness. The result does not depend on what the sources physically are. If larger samples confirm it, a preferred multiplicative scale shapes the early source distribution. Recurrent condensate dynamics offer one possible reading, but the statistics stand alone.
arxiv-2602-19544:
Pavel Guerzhoy studies congruences for traces of singular moduli and Hurwitz-Kronecker class numbers. Traces of singular moduli, introduced by Zagier in 1998, are simultaneously values of a modular function (the j-invariant), and also Fourier coefficients of modular forms. That pairing is known as Zagier's duality. Much research since has explored their properties, congruences in particular.

The paper offers a new viewpoint: these congruences become congruences between certain modular forms of weight 3/2 under repeated U-operator action. That yields a general result covering several known results as special cases. The approach works best for small prime moduli, explaining numerical observations, quantifying qualitative results, and giving, as an application, results modulo 11.
arxiv-2602-19744:
A piecewise fractional linear map is built from a few simple fractional pieces, each acting on its own interval. A 2026 arXiv paper by Fritz Schweiger, working alone, studies such maps with three branches and asks a precise question about their invariant measures.

Given a map, a related map is formed by replacing some branches with flipped versions, branches taken from one minus the original map. The paper's main question is whether the original and the related map share a common invariant measure, a distribution the dynamics leaves unchanged. A brief closing section offers measures of a new kind. The work is brief and technical, aimed at readers of ergodic theory and dynamical systems.
arxiv-2602-19844:
Language-model apps now reason through complex tasks, but their hard-to-predict, hard-to-verify behaviour widens the attack surface in new ways. A 2026 arXiv paper by Yedi Zhang and four co-authors argues, as a position paper, that system-level threat monitoring is a prerequisite for trustworthy use.

The authors contend that safety risks in such apps should be treated as expected working conditions, not rare exceptions, and that the main barrier is no longer model power alone. What is missing, they say, is oversight that detects security-relevant events after deployment and puts them in context, an area underexplored beyond testing and guardrails. Steady watching, in their view, grounds both sound operation and ready response plans.
arxiv-2602-19944:
Camouflaged animals and objects blend into their surroundings, so finding them in an image and outlining them precisely are two different hard problems. A 2026 arXiv paper by Yilong Yang and three co-authors proposes a three-step mechanism, Discover-Segment-Select, for zero-shot camouflaged object segmentation.

Current pipelines usually ask a multimodal model to find the object, then hand the result to a segmentation model. The first step often misplaces objects, invents extras, or misses some entirely. The new method first generates diverse object proposals from visual features. It then refines each through segmentation. Finally a multimodal model judges the candidate masks and picks the best. With no training or supervision, it leads prior methods on several benchmarks, above all in scenes with multiple instances.
arxiv-2602-20044:
Soon after launch, an AI-native social platform can already show extreme clumping of attention and clear role split. A 2026 arXiv paper by H. C. W. Price and four co-authors analyzes the first twelve days of Moltbook, an agent-facing social platform, from public traces.

Building co-participation and directed-comment graphs, the authors report reciprocity, community structure, and content themes. Interaction proves strongly lopsided, with reciprocity near one percent, and centrality splits cleanly into hub and authority roles, matching broadcast-style attention more than mutual exchange. Attention concentrates far more than production, early accounts gather far more upvotes before adjusting for exposure, and taking part is brief and bursty, with most posts in a few peak hours. Topic modelling finds technical talk about memory and identity. It also finds onboarding messages and formulaic token-minting content. The paper offers an early structural baseline for agent-agent social life.
arxiv-2602-20444:
The Fischer-Lynch-Paterson impossibility result says no set method can promise agreement in an async system with even one faulty process. Paul Borrill argues in this essay that the result is a theorem about one system model, not a law of physics. Open Atomic Ethernet sidesteps it, he says, by rejecting the async model at its root. For forty years, he notes, the field has designed around it with random protocols, failure watchers, and weaker consistency models.

Borrill coins the term bisynchronous for the key trait of Open Atomic Ethernet: bounded-time two-way outcome. Both sides reach common knowledge of the outcome at every round edge, a stronger promise than sync alone. A bisynchronous, swap-based protocol at Layer 2 thus achieves deterministic atomic teamwork, in his argument, without breaking any such limit.
arxiv-2602-20544:
Learners in mixed fields must make sense of scattered facts, and e-lessons shape how they search. Hannah Kim and seven co-authors compare plain and AI-run e-lessons using the three search modes of orienteering. In a between-subject study, learners used either a plain lesson or an AI lesson over the same base facts. Plain users kept a greater sense of place and focus across the fact space.

AI users, by contrast, acted more on their own and by roaming, with lower mental load from query-led use. The contrast suggests mixed lesson designs serve mixed search needs. Set guidance helps keep bearings, while AI querying helps roaming. The findings give guidance for building e-learning lessons that match use style to learning goals.
arxiv-2602-20844:
Networks appear in biology, society, and technology, and researchers often need to test whether a model fits an observed network. Subhro Ghosh, Rathindra Nath Karmakar, and Samriddha Lahiry build such tests from the principle of maximum entropy in this 2026 arXiv paper. They set up a constrained entropy-maximization problem over networks and derive test statistics from its Lagrange multipliers.

The authors prove consistency when the vertex count is fixed, then extend the theory to growing graphs in both dense and sparse regimes. Dense cases cover exponential random graph models, while sparse cases cover Erdos-Renyi graphs, using recent nonlinear large-deviation theory. The framework also connects to classical score tests for constrained likelihood. Readers get one entropy-based toolkit for network testing across growth regimes.
arxiv-2602-21144:
State-space models handle long contexts well, but single-GPU memory, bandwidth, and latency cap their inference. Anurag Dutt, Nimit Shah, Hazem Masarani, and Anshul Gandhi scale them across GPUs in this 2026 arXiv paper via a communication-efficient tensor-parallel design for selective state-space inference. Three engineering challenges anchor the design: a state cache across prefill and decode, local recurrent updates through careful parameter partitioning, and cheaper aggregation via quantized AllReduce.

Tests on three representative models across two GPU clusters show throughput rising about one and a half to two times on two GPUs. Gains reach about two and a half to four times on four GPUs, with the largest gains at long contexts. Quantized aggregation adds a further ten to eighteen percent. Readers get a practical recipe for multi-GPU state-space serving.
arxiv-2602-21244:
Direct Simulation Monte Carlo is the gold standard for thin gas motion, but its cost blows up near smooth-flow zones and for true-to-life force fields. Ehsan Roohi, Ahmad Shoja-Sani, and Stefan Stefanov speed it up in this 2026 arXiv paper with a unified physics-bound neural-tool setup that keeps kept traits and randomness for long-time kinetic runs. A local neural crash kernel swaps the rule-of-thumb variable hard sphere model.

A random layer with latent-noise feed-in brings back heat jitters, while cell-wise moment matching holds push and energy keeping. Zero-shot carry-over takes a model trained only on 1D Couette flow to a hard 2D cavity flow. A second tool for quantum bounce, checked on a Mach ten argon flow, cuts cost by about one fifth against direct adding up.
arxiv-2602-21744:
Boxuan Xie and five co-authors study a dual-hop system that pairs visible light communication with backscatter communication under finite blocklength limits, aimed at energy-neutral ambient Internet of Things deployments. Indoor LED access points provide light and send data over light to a backscatter device, which harvests optical energy and reflects the messages to user devices with radio front ends. Forwarding from light to radio needs no carrier synthesizers or power amplifiers at the IoT node.

Modeling the end-to-end link with short-packet IoT traffic and realistic interference between neighboring light coverage areas, the team analyzes outage performance and achievable data rate. Simulations show that backscatter device placement and orientation, plus the chosen code rate, shape reliability and data rate. The insights point toward ambient-powered IoT solutions and future hybrid light-radio network designs.
arxiv-2602-22244:
Europe's GDPR gives groups just three days to notify authorities of a personal data breach, but responders must hand-translate forensic traces into legally framed reports. Aurora Arrus and three co-authors propose a hybrid malware-analysis pipeline that automates that translation, focusing on data-stealing Linux and ARM malware spreading with IoT devices. Static analysis flags potential data thieves; dynamic analysis rebuilds their behavior.

By bridging low-level evidence and rule-book language, the pipeline aims to cut delays, incomplete notices, and analyst overload. It targets the exact bottleneck that makes the deadline so punishing: turning malware traces, logs, and captures into structured breach facts. Incident teams gain a faster path from detection to a compliant report.
arxiv-2602-22444:
Doubly Special Relativity adds a second fixed scale tied to the Planck regime, alongside the speed of light. Boumali and Jafari measure its effects in a solvable test case: the three-dimensional Klein-Gordon oscillator, held by a non-minimal momentum coupling that keeps rotational symmetry. They study two standard DSR versions plus a broad framework expanding in the Planck length.

After steady-state reduction and split in spherical coordinates, the eigenfunctions keep the generalized-Laguerre and spherical-harmonic shape known from the plain problem. The analysis covers two named DSR versions and a broad first-order framework. Physicists gain a measured picture of how a second fixed scale reshapes a textbook oscillator.
arxiv-2602-22544:
Khuram Naveed and one co-author present HARU-Net, a denoising network for cone-beam CT, the 3D dental and facial imaging that suffers heavy noise at low dose. Low-dose scans blur soft tissue and fine anatomy, and classic filters tend to wipe out edges along with noise. Deep learning helps, but scarce high-resolution training data has limited its use for this scanner type.

Trained on cadaver jaw scans from a high-resolution 3D Accuitomo 170 system, HARU-Net mixes three design parts. Hybrid attention transformer blocks sit in its skip connections. A residual attention group at its bottleneck strengthens long-range modelling. Residual convolutional blocks support stable deep feature learning. It beat leading methods including SwinIR and Uformer, reaching nearly 38 decibels peak signal quality, about 96 percent structural similarity, and the lowest gradient error, at clearly lower compute cost.
arxiv-2602-22644:
Siqi Lu and five co-authors harden multi-input models against missing inputs. When one input drops out, scores often crash. The team traces the weakness to lopsided learning: the model leans on favoured inputs and starves the rest. Their insight is that this skew can be read in wave patterns.

A ratio score first gauges input preference from wave-domain traits. Guided by that score, a weight-sharing module then re-balances each branch's share during training, pushing learning toward a fuller picture. The module plugs into varied bases, from convolutional nets to vision transformers. It gave steady gains across tasks and input mixes, even lifting leading methods built for the missing-input problem.
arxiv-2602-22844:
Michael Ruzhansky and two co-authors pin down when Walsh multiplier operators are compact. Working in Lebesgue spaces over the unit interval, they build on known boundedness criteria to prove an exact compactness test. In maps from Lp to itself for all finite p above one, and from Lp to L2 for p above two, compactness holds exactly when the multiplier symbol tends to zero.

The team also maps the point spectrum in detail with strict spectral inclusions. In the Hilbert-space case, p equals two, the spectrum gets a complete description. For other p values, they stress the limits of carrying diagonal arguments across, shaping results to block false generalizations.
arxiv-2602-23444:
Zimeng Wang and one co-author build a single framework for stochastic gradient descent with momentum, a workhorse tool for training machine learning models. Existing theory covers only single momentum schemes or leans on narrow assumptions, leaving the broad family of methods without shared guarantees.

Their generalized framework unifies many momentum methods, including SGD with Polyak momentum and SGD with Nesterov momentum. For convex problems, they prove broad ergodic convergence with fixed settings and faster iterate rates with time-varying settings. For nonconvex problems, they prove sublinear convergence to stationary points and linear convergence near the optimum under the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition. Flexible parameter choices let many existing methods inherit guarantees as special cases.
arxiv-2602-24244:
Alyssa M. Guzman and Norman A. Grogin examine the long-term behavior of superbias calibration frames for the Hubble Space Telescope's Advanced Camera for Surveys Wide Field Channel. The 2026 paper asks whether superbias frames could be produced less often without harming calibration. Frames are currently generated after each anneal and delivered monthly; detector-level bias structure is what they remove from science images.

Analyzing frames from 2007 through 2024 with visual inspection, pixel-level comparison, and principal component analysis, the team finds that superbias structure has stayed fairly stable since Servicing Mission 4. No significant global trends or systematic shifts appear over a fifteen-year span. That stability might suggest a sparser cadence, like the annual schedule used for another Hubble camera. However, unstable hot columns and rising readout dark current mean more frequent updates likely still benefit this camera, so the authors stop short of recommending the annual cadence.
arxiv-2603-00044: Che's team builds a property-driven test method for graph neural networks, whose power on basic graph traits stays open. Using the Alloy spec language, they build two dataset groups. GraphRandom holds graphs that meet or break chosen traits. GraphPerturb adds set shape changes. Together they total hundreds of sets, each with at least ten thousand tagged graphs, across sixteen traits. Their pooling study finds attention-based pooling best for breadth and robustness, second-order pooling best for sensitivity, and no single approach best across all traits.
arxiv-2603-00144: Geng and colleagues present DHVAE, a latent-diffusion system for making realistic 3D human-human interaction that users can steer. It splits the big-picture interaction setting from single motion patterns into two linked latent parts via a CoTransformer module. Contrastive learning rules sharpen the latent interaction space toward sharp, true-to-life contacts, curbing penetration and missed contact. A DDIM-based diffusion pass with a skip-connected AdaLN-Transformer denoiser then builds high-fidelity interaction, beating rivals on motion fidelity, text match and physical plausibility with less compute.
arxiv-2603-00444: Lawlor-Forsyth and five colleagues use the TNG50 simulation to find observable traits that separate quenching galaxies, still forming stars slowly, from fully star forming ones. Shape metrics track how concentrated star formation is, how large the star forming disk runs, and where star formation cuts off sharply. The metrics split quenching galaxies into inside out and outside in groups, tied to central field galaxies and dense environment satellites with different quenching times. Later stage quenchers separate most cleanly, and progress through quenching can be read for both groups.
arxiv-2603-00544: Gupte and five colleagues ask for best possible one time programs, letting a user run a program once while learning nothing else. Classical versions need hardware, and quantum measurement offers a physical basis, yet deterministic functions stay impossible under gentle measurement attacks. Recent work covers randomised high entropy functions, but the strongest achievable security stays unclear. The team proves no generic best possible compiler exists for classical randomised functions under a standard complexity assumption, then develops testable compilers and a simplified simulation security notion for quantum channels.
arxiv-2603-00744: Pathak, Ahuja, and de Sturler improve genomic prediction by turning genotype sequences into images and then tensors. Feeding genotypes as character strings to one dimensional convolutions misses interactions, while a two dimensional image form captures them but forces every layer to do the work. Their ResGene-T converts the two dimensional image into a three dimensional tensor for a ResNet-18 backbone, lifting training efficiency. Across three crop species, ten traits, and seven rival models spanning statistics, machine learning, and deep learning, ResGene-T performs best.
arxiv-2603-00844: Danhoni, Mullins, and Noronha generalize the jet transport coefficient into a frame-independent diffusion tensor for jets crossing matter far from equilibrium. The tensor form captures energy spread and cross-links between energy and momentum exchange that a single scalar misses. In a simple massless scalar theory they solve the medium's evolution and find that non-equilibrium effects can either strengthen or weaken jet broadening, depending on the starting distribution.
arxiv-2603-01044: Labini and Straccamore map the velocity field of the irregular galaxy ESO 358-60 from hydrogen measurements. They use the Velocity Ring Model, which assumes a flat disk. Tangential motion rules the inner regions while radial motion grows toward the edges. This contradicts the Tilted Ring Model's picture of a strong warp. A toy model suggests that warp is an artifact of the tilted-ring assumptions. A dark-matter disk model gives a total mass about three times lower with a slightly better rotation-curve fit.
arxiv-2603-01244: Klocker and Fink prove the stacking puzzle Hexasort is NP-hard, meaning no fast general solution is expected, even for single-color stacks and tightly constrained graph classes. In Hexasort, colored stacks sit on graph vertices, and adjacent same-color stacks merge and vanish by fixed rules. Their proof reaches strong NP-hardness on trees of bounded height or degree. They also find settings where the problem becomes polynomial-time solvable and give dynamic programming algorithms for those cases.
arxiv-2603-01344: Risk, Tung, and Wang develop a robust plan for Constant Function Market Makers, moving from token reserves to price and built-in flow coords. They give a standard mapping of the bonding curve keeping unit match across trading functions like Uniswap's and Balancer's, showing stocks and values depend in line on built-in flow. That structure eases arb-free pricing, delta hedging, and risk control. Using the Carr-Madan spanning formula, they cast Impermanent Loss as a weighted strip of vanilla options, giving a fine-grained implied swings structure.
arxiv-2603-02444:
Marta Loletti, Alejandro Molina-Sánchez, Juan Sebastián Reparaz, and colleagues compute heat flow in a magnetic monolayer in this 2026 paper. CrSBr is a layered magnetic material that can be peeled to one sheet thick. Heat flow in such sheets guides device design and cooling. The team calculates its thermal conductivity from first principles.

Heat flows notably better along one crystal axis than the other. The ratio between the two directions sits near two to one. Both phonon speeds and phonon lifetimes shape that directional gap. Shrinking the flake suppresses long-traveling phonons and tunes the gap further. Size control thus offers a knob for directional heat management. Magnetic two-dimensional materials could exploit that knob in future devices.
arxiv-2603-02544:
Wengxi Li, Jingze Tian, and Can Liu turn spoken thoughts into an editable canvas in this 2026 paper. People talk aloud to clarify and organize their thinking. Raw transcripts, though, are full of stumbles, repeats, and drift. Their system, Orality, extracts key content from speech and analyzes its meaning.

Extracted ideas become nodes in a linked diagram on an interactive canvas. Users rearrange clusters by hand or by spoken instruction. The system can re-extract and reorganize content on request. It also poses inspirational questions and flags logical conflicts between ideas. Twelve participants compared Orality with voice chat using a leading chatbot. Orality better supported clarifying and developing thoughts, the study found. Both graphical and conversational tools showed distinct strengths for thinking.
arxiv-2603-02644:
Péter Udvarhelyi asks what the atoms inside a set of glowing defects in silicon actually look like. His 2026 paper studies color centers, tiny flaws that can hold spin and emit light. Such centers could serve as qubits, the basic units of quantum computers, if their structure is known.

Using first-principles calculations, which simulate matter from basic physics laws, Udvarhelyi tests candidate structures for the observed N-line series. He proposes that the first center pairs a carbon atom with a nitrogen atom sitting between lattice sites. Larger defects with oxygen also fit the later lines, giving a family of possible qubits that emit near telecom wavelengths.
arxiv-2603-02744:
Gyeongmin Ha, Kazuki Hirota, Takahiro Kashiwazaki, and colleagues produce record squeezed light with a waveguide amplifier. Their 2026 paper reports squeezing past twelve decibels from a lithium niobate waveguide device. Squeezed light quiets noise in one property of light, and single-pass amplifiers offer it across huge bandwidths.

Loss from a shape mismatch between the squeezed beam and the reference beam had capped earlier results near ten decibels. The team placed a spatial light modulator, tuned by machine learning, in the reference path to fix the shapes. A double-reflection layout added control, and the measured squeezing level itself guided the tuning. Better mode matching, not a stronger amplifier, unlocked the gain.
arxiv-2603-03044:
Tong-Gang Yue, Zhen Zhang, and Lie-Wen Chen hunt for a clean probe of an elusive nuclear force. The spin-orbit force inside nuclei is well established, but how it differs for protons and neutrons, its isovector part, has resisted direct measurement. Their 2026 paper builds on a recent finding about calcium-48.

In that nucleus, the gap between charge and weak form factors reacts strongly to the isovector strength, and boosting it resolves a standing puzzle from electron scattering experiments. Extending the test, zirconium-90 shows the same sensitivity, thanks to its unpaired neutrons, while lead-208 and nickel-62 barely respond. The split suggests a two-pronged plan: measure the sensitive nuclei to pin the force, and the quiet ones to constrain the symmetry energy instead.
arxiv-2603-03144:
Michael Blank, Gregor Schubert, and Miao Ben Zhang measure what generative AI does to evenings at home. Their 2026 paper uses detailed browsing records from many United States home devices between 2021 and 2024. Households that browsed in AI-friendly ways before ChatGPT launched serve as the lever for identifying adoption effects afterward.

Adopting generative AI sharply raised leisure browsing at home, while time on productive digital tasks stayed flat. Reading the activity around ChatGPT use shows households mainly aim it at productive non-market chores, like drafting, planning, and information work. The pattern suggests AI speeds those chores and hands the saved time back as leisure. A standard time-allocation model turns that reading into large implied productivity gains.
arxiv-2603-03444:
Xu Han and Gordan Krnjaic chart exact targets for detectors hunting light dark matter. Experiments watching for electron recoils are now reaching the predicted signals of thermal-relic dark matter below a billion electron volts in mass. Such light thermal candidates need light mediator particles to annihilate efficiently in the early universe, a constraint set by the classic Lee-Weinberg bound. Their 2026 paper computes the milestones for vector mediators.

The mediators covered are new gauge bosons from the minimal consistent extensions of the Standard Model: the dark photon and bosons tied to baryon and lepton number combinations. Because the same interaction sets both cosmic production and scattering in detectors, each target is firmly predictive: experiments can truly confirm or kill these models. Together the results complete the list for this whole class.
arxiv-2603-03644:
Daijin Yang, Erica Kleinman, and Casper Harteveld give teachers a shared language for designing games with artificial intelligence. Educational games build thinking skills and motivation, but instructors struggle to design games that hit specific learning goals. Existing tools hide the hard parts behind opaque machine suggestions. Their 2026 paper presents a web tool where language itself is the interface for co-creation.

Inside, a teacher and a language model assistant jointly develop a structured language mapping pedagogy onto gameplay through four linked components. Every pedagogical intention stays explicit and editable on screen. The authors argue this lowers design barriers for non-experts and keeps human agency over the critical decisions. It also lets designers check alignment between teaching goals and game mechanics during and after creation, instead of discovering mismatches in the classroom.
arxiv-2603-03744:
Tuan Duc Ngo and six others split three-dimensional reconstruction into a fast stream and a sharp stream. Estimating consistent shape and camera poses from uncalibrated video is hardest exactly where it matters: high resolution and long sequences. Their 2026 transformer, DAGE, disentangles global coherence from fine detail so each can be computed at its natural cost.

A low-resolution stream reads heavily downsampled frames with alternating attention to build a view-consistent representation and estimate cameras cheaply. A detailed stream processes the original frames one by one, preserving crisp boundaries and small structures. A light adapter fuses the streams by cross-attention, injecting global context without disturbing the pretrained single-frame pathway. Resolution and clip length scale independently, inputs reach two-thousand-pixel class sizes, and the results set new state-of-the-art marks for video shape and multi-view reconstruction.
arxiv-2603-04144: Lee and others propose HBRB-BoW, a retrained bag-of-words vocabulary for ORB-SLAM. ORB-SLAM's binary vocabulary suffers sharpness loss, and binary clustering cannot represent subtle spreads, degrading visual words as errors accumulate. Their hierarchical binary-to-real-and-back training integrates a global real-valued flow, keeping descriptor information until final binarization.
arxiv-2603-04244: Pourasad and colleagues present FeedAIde, guiding app users to submit rich feedback reports by asking context-aware follow-up questions. User feedback is essential for mobile app success, yet user reports and developer needs often differ. They built an iOS framework of FeedAIde and tested it with users of a gym's app. Against the app's basic feedback form, participants rated FeedAIde easier and more helpful for reporting feedback.
arxiv-2603-04644: Karamanlis and Kravaris study embeddings of cubes into dense subsets of cubes. The question is how large N must be so every delta-dense subset contains an embedding of the k-cube. For a bi-Lipschitz map with distortion, N is about epsilon to the minus 2, log of 1 over delta, and k cubed. For isometric maps with rescaling, N grows like log of 1 over delta times an exponential in k. With bounded rescaling, N grows doubly exponentially. Path results prove the density analog of a Rödl-Sales coloring theorem.
arxiv-2603-04744: McGarry and colleagues show tunable quantum modeling of odd motion in a trapped-ion system. CV-DV boxes suit bosonic motion, yet coding any motion stays an open challenge. Odd motion, common across physics and chem, resists modeling on highly even springs. The team builds time-step tools with a bosonic-quantum-signal-work routine, tuning wells between tests via plain knobs. They watch packets tunnel through barriers in varied double wells with clean motion. Adding tilt by code kills this leak effect.
arxiv-2603-05344: Nghi D. Q. Bui presents OPENDEV, an open-source Rust terminal agent. AI coding help shifts from IDE plugins to agents managing source control and builds. Autonomous help needs safety controls and context handling against bloat and decay. OPENDEV meets these needs with model routing, a dual-agent split, lazy tool discovery, and context compaction reducing older observations. Automated memory accumulates project knowledge and counters instruction fade-out with reminders. Explicit reasoning phases make OPENDEV a secure command-line-first base.
arxiv-2603-05544: Vieira gives a simple algebra rework of the Yates covariance decomposition for the Brier score, splitting it into three terms never below zero on their own. They are a calibration-in-the-large term, a correlation deficit term, and a variance mismatch term. The rework makes perfect forecast rules clear: the optimal forecast must match the spread of results, link up perfectly the same way with results, and equal the results' mean. Gaps from these rules add an extra amount to the Brier score.
arxiv-2603-05744: Suri and team present CodeScout, turning vague requests into usable problem statements via lightweight pre-look of the target codebase. Current code help tools struggle with poorly-defined statements lacking context and needs spec. Failures on vague requests go with longer paths involving extra looking. It performs context scoping and multi-view study, then makes statements with repro steps, expected actions, and study hints. This pre-look reduces non-closing paths. On SWE-bench-Verified, it improves fix rates by 20%, with up to 27 more issues resolved.
arxiv-2603-06044: Guarini extracts cubic interactions from Chiral Higher Spin Gravity's covariant equations of motion and computes the corresponding amplitudes. These amplitudes agree with earlier light-cone gauge results. The author also classifies all cubic amplitudes constructible from chiral fields arising in twistor theory. Propagators for arbitrary spin in Feynman and Lorenz gauges are derived. These propagators solve Berends-Giele recursions for a truncated Chiral Higher Spin Gravity, an extension of self-dual Yang-Mills to higher spin. The author confirms that all tree-level amplitudes vanish.
arxiv-2603-06144: Grimes and his team show that an electric field can switch phonon angular momentum in ferroelectric barium titanate, toward sure control of chiral phonons. They probe it with circularly dichroic resonant inelastic X-ray scattering at the oxygen K edge, and set the dichroism they measure next to first principles results. The match is good, with a dichroism contrast that shifts with momentum and a reversible gyroelectric effect that holds for 15 hours or more. This points to non volatile control of chiral phonons for information and energy uses.
arxiv-2603-06544: Zhou and team focus on redundancy as a missed data quality issue in vehicle datasets, where it varies across sources and kinds from conditions and limits. Using two sets, they model and measure it in camera data and image-LiDAR data, and test how removing labels affects YOLOv8 detection. Cutting redundant image labels from cameras with fields of view improves scores, while shared pairs stay at baseline under pruning. In Argoverse 2, cutting a share of labels leaves scores near baseline, and it emerges as a seen quality factor.
arxiv-2603-06744: Greff and colleagues study how architected thin films shape failure at the interface of two-layer composites. Graded structures can prescribe where failure occurs at the interface, yet they add little fracture toughness. Hierarchically patterned layers do both: they localize failure at the interface and raise its toughness, by forcing a buffer zone where elastic energy dissipates as diffuse damage. A new network formalism, joining discrete differential geometry with spectral graph theory, analyzes the load patterns.
arxiv-2603-06944: Darvishi and colleagues propose Two-Stage Normalizing Flows for estimating complex densities. Many target distributions lack a closed form and cannot be sampled directly. Instead they split into parts, some known only through simulator samples or outside datasets, others given by tractable rules or statistical assumptions about variable links. Joining such mixed sources coherently remains an open challenge. Their method first learns densities for sample-only parts, then joins those outputs with analytic terms in a second stage to rebuild the target. It allows point-wise scoring and sample generation.
arxiv-2603-07044: Yu and colleagues explore user needs for sensor-powered smart car cabins built by retrofit. Retrofit can add to and extend built-in smart cabin sensors from car makers. To learn how retrofit fixes should be built, they ran a two-phase study. First, guided talks with 18 people studied snags with built-in sensors and found gaps where retrofit could help. Second, probe-based hands-on design sessions with 15 people found user needs and hopes for good retrofit fixes, yielding design tips for future work.
arxiv-2603-07144: Jin and colleagues build CanoVerse, a standard 3D data set of 320K objects across 1,156 categories, an order of magnitude larger than prior work. Raw 3D assets arrive with random whole spin, which blocks pose-steady making and stable way meaning. Their lining up system cuts lining up from minutes to seconds per object through compact guess making and light human checks. At this scale, way meaning becomes learnable, lifting making safety, cross-modal finding, and zero-shot aim guessing.
arxiv-2603-07444: Zhu and Wang build a human-in-the-loop pipeline for empirical economics research with specialized agents. Fully autonomous discovery risks questions the data cannot answer, so their HLER system grounds question generation in dataset structure, variable availability and diagnostics. Agents audit and profile data, pose questions, run econometric analysis, draft manuscripts and review them, with human gates at key stages. Dataset-aware questions prove feasible far more often than unconstrained ones.
arxiv-2603-07544: Franzreb and colleagues weigh privacy against Parkinson's detection in anonymized speech. Masking voices protects speakers but may erase the disease cues the task needs. They compare two anonymizer tools on Spanish data sets: one speech-to-text-to-speech route gives better privacy but severely degrades scores by wiping prosody. A voice-conversion route preserves macro-prosody such as duration and pitch contours, losing only a few percent of score, proving private detection viable.
arxiv-2603-07844: Georgiev and colleagues link two close fields, optimal planning and reinforcement learning, both rooted in step-by-step choice math. Planning tends to use fixed models, set goals and least cost, while learning tends to use chance models, endless horizons and most reward. They strip chance from learning and compare it with value iteration and Dijkstra's method. They pin down when least cost matches most reward, when one-shot goals match endless learning, and when discounting blocks a goal. They urge teams to define true cost plainly.
arxiv-2603-08044: Kumar and colleagues introduce the Weighted Planar Stochastic Porous Lattice, a disordered substrate built by splitting a unit square step by step. Each step picks a block with probability tied to its area, divides it into four parts, and keeps or drops one part with odds tied to q. It shows multifractality, and snapshots at different times look statistically self-similar. Its dual forms a network with a power-law degree distribution. On this lattice they study bond percolation, finding a threshold and critical exponents that shift with q.
arxiv-2603-08144: Ding and colleagues probe the CP property of axion-like particle photon interactions at future lepton colliders. They study a CP-odd axion-like particle with both CP-conserving and CP-violating photon couplings, made in electron-positron collisions yielding two electrons plus two photons. The CP structure can be read from the azimuthal angle difference between the final-state electrons. Projected sensitivity reaches about a thousandth of an inverse TeV, beating current limits from the electron electric dipole moment and collider searches.
arxiv-2603-08244: Wu and colleagues analyze security for non-orthogonal multiple access systems where fluid antennas meet smart surfaces under hardware flaws. The convergence of fluid systems and reconfigurable surfaces offers secure radio links. But the real effects of hardware flaws on this pairing remain largely unexplored. The authors build a math framework tracing antenna fluidity, surface reconfiguration, and hardware distortion. They use it to assess secrecy performance under real hardware limits.
arxiv-2603-08344: Lehner explains that two examples of invariance under duality for a localizing invariant hold purely formally when it is K-theory. But the general statement for arbitrary ones does not reduce to a formal statement. In this short remark, he records a counterexample to the claim that the universal one is invariant under taking opposite categories, due to Tabuada. The gap matters: formal proofs that work for K-theory need not extend to the general setting, so duality there requires separate proof.
arxiv-2603-09044: George Edwards and Mahdi Eslamimehr detect zero-day AI malware with concolic runs plus LLM guidance. AI malware evades signature and rule defenses with shifting, morphing, and context-aware tricks. Their hybrid framework pairs concolic runs with LLM path ranking and deep-learning flaw sorting, proving soundness and relative fullness given classifier truth. It scores 98.7 percent on old malware and high on AI threats.
arxiv-2603-09244: Christoph Englert and colleagues ask how robust collider limits on the type-II seesaw stay when the model is extended. Triplet Higgs extensions are well motivated by lepton flavour data and are squeezed by both low-energy measurements and searches for doubly charged Higgs bosons. The authors survey motivated extensions and map how they change the expected production and decay patterns of exotic Higgs particles. Those shifts show where standard sensitivity projections for the seesaw could mislead.
arxiv-2603-09444: Yassine Bouzeraib and colleagues study vector-like dark matter inside an alternative left-right symmetric model with an extra non-abelian SU(2) gauge symmetry. One generation of vector-like leptons joins the particle content, and the neutral member of its multiplet serves as a stable dark matter candidate. A discrete parity forbids mixing with standard model leptons, so the dark sector talks to ours only through vector and lepton portal processes. They map the parameter space surviving relic abundance and collider bounds.
arxiv-2603-09544: Jia Hu and colleagues investigate whether large language model based program repair can secure cross-compartment interfaces in compartmentalized software. Compartmentalization confines an attacker who takes one compartment, yet most real systems leak at the interfaces between compartments, which are notoriously hard to secure by hand. The authors find existing repair tools and general code models unfit as-is for this task. They design and build a dedicated repair framework and report its early results as a work in progress.
arxiv-2603-09844: Boschetti and Campiglia give a new proof of the old log soft graviton law, in the frame set out by Compère, Gralla and Wei. They use only Einstein's laws near far past, far future and far space, plus rules that link those zones. Their proof works the same if time runs back, and it lets soft waves come in too. If no soft memory comes in, the old factor comes back, its past future gap traced to a jump of the field at far space.
arxiv-2603-10044: David Gringras measures how much the wrapping around a model, and the test format itself, change measured safety. Six leading models face four safety benchmarks through a direct interface and three scaffolds, in tens of thousands of scored runs. Switching an item between multiple choice and open ended form shifts measured safety far more than scaffold choice does. Map reduce scaffolds do lower pooled safety, while benchmark choice explains far more variance.
arxiv-2603-10144: Osborne, Monteiro and Bradlyn resolve a clash between Kubo response counts and old elasticity theory. Response counts for anisotropic systems seemed to yield odd elastic moduli, which would break energy conservation in Hamiltonian systems. Their frame shows the geometry of strain space adds factors that restore agreement with the old theory. A magnetised two dimensional electron gas makes the point clear, with sum rules showing how contact terms show up in tests.
arxiv-2603-10244: Christian Coester settles a fifty year old conjecture by Rivest about the transposition rule for the list update problem. In that problem, each request costs the requested item's position in a list, and requests arrive independently from a fixed unknown distribution. Simply swapping each requested item with its predecessor, Coester proves, costs at most one more than the optimal static order in stationarity. The proof rests on a sign eliminating combinatorial injection.
arxiv-2603-10344: Xiang-Qian Meng and co-authors use machine learning to spot the arrow of time in solid-state spins, on a ten-qubit processor built around a nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond. Unitary evolution keeps time symmetry, so projective measurements were inserted to produce entropy, and their outcomes form each trajectory. An unsupervised clustering method split trajectories into two groups with no prior knowledge. A neural network then read the time direction of single trajectories with high accuracy, and a diffusion model reproduced signs of energy flow.
arxiv-2603-10444: Hengjie Cao and co-authors trace a cause of trouble in FP4 training of large language models: a rank-one mean bias in the activations. Outliers that wreck blockwise quantization are not random sparse events, they argue, but largely follow this mean part, which grows in training and is reshaped by attention and feed-forward layers. Their fix, Averis, splits the mean off before quantization using only reductions and subtractions. It kept loss close to BF16 in tests, with tiny overhead, and combined well with Hadamard smoothing.
arxiv-2603-10644: Jelena Katić, Darko Milinković, and Milan Perić use the complexity function of an invariant subset, taken from a two-sided shift space, to compute polynomial entropy. The dynamics are induced maps acting on the hyperspace of continua, in some one-dimensional systems. Complexity counts how distinguishable patterns grow, and entropy turns that growth into one number for the induced motion on sets. They also give a simple criterion on the map which forces infinite topological entropy.
arxiv-2603-10744: Wenhao Sun and Zhaoqiang Liu introduce Just-in-Time, a training-free framework that speeds up diffusion transformers in the spatial domain. Sampling is costly, and older methods focus on time steps, missing spatial redundancy, where global structure forms long before fine detail. JiT drives the full latent state from computations on a sparse, dynamically chosen set of anchor tokens. A deterministic micro-flow keeps transitions seamless as new tokens join. On FLUX.1-dev it reached up to sevenfold speedup with nearly lossless quality.
arxiv-2603-11244: Andrea Rubbi and coauthors present GGE, an open-source tool for judging generative models of single-cell gene expression data under one shared standard. Current practice is a patchwork. Metrics are built inconsistently, and hyperparameters are chosen with no shared rule. Few are grounded in biology. GGE supplies distributional metrics with stated computation-space choices. It supplies tests from biology on differentially expressed genes and perturbation effects. Their survey of past work shows metric values swing widely with implementation choices, showing the need for one standard.
arxiv-2603-11344: Don Yin and coauthors fuse two fixes for slow brain imaging statistics into one hybrid. It keeps exact cluster sizes and analytical p-values, skipping permutation testing altogether. Threshold-free cluster enhancement gains power by integrating cluster extent across thresholds. Exact versions permute, and probabilistic versions discretize the threshold grid. Their union-find structure builds the cluster hierarchy in one pass. This enables exact size queries at any threshold. Gaussian random field theory then converts sizes to analytical p-values. Validation shows controlled error rates on phantoms and cohorts.
arxiv-2603-11444: Mohne and co-authors built EducaSim, a practice space where new teachers rehearse with simulated students. Role play trains teachers well, yet it needs trained partners and so rarely scales. The need is sharp in huge online courses with hundreds of novice teachers. EducaSim fills a small-group section with generative agents that carry set personas and real course material. It ran in a six-week CS1 course serving 20,000 students. Teachers who tried it mostly rated the practice as a good experience.
arxiv-2603-11844: Vairat and co-authors study germanium halide perovskites CsGeX3 with mixed halogens at the X site. Using first-principles methods, they find the mixed crystals settle into a polar monoclinic phase at room temperature. Energy checks on soft-mode shifts back the phase. Polarization runs along [101] and grows by 10 to 15% over the pure materials. Spin splitting spans 25 to 250 meV in the valence band, with Rashba and persistent spin textures. The team flags these crystals as candidates for Datta-Das spin transistors.
arxiv-2603-12244: Batley, Sarker, Mostakim, Klichine, and Saha propose separable neural architectures as a shared base unit for AI. Many systems hide structure that splits into factors, which monolithic networks never state outright. Their class unifies additive, quadratic, and tensor-decomposed models under one form. Limits on interaction order and tensor rank split big maps into low-arity parts. Separability often appears only after a change of coordinates, a point their frame makes central. Tests span navigation, microstructure design, turbulent flow, and language modeling.
arxiv-2603-12344: Le and co-authors teach language models molecular property prediction from decision trees. LLMs promise generalist skill here, yet their raw scores fall short of practical use. TreeKD trains a specialist decision tree per property on functional group features. The tree's rule is then turned into words and placed into prompts for LLM training. A random forest variant adds rule-consistency scaling at test time across prompts. On 22 TDC tasks with two LLMs, the method lifts accuracy by a wide margin.
arxiv-2603-12444: Paul and Paban compute, for a scalar field on a product spacetime, the stress-energy tensor when one compact dimension can shrink or grow in time. The background pairs an FLRW universe with a circle whose size can change in time. A modified adiabatic regularization yields analytic forms for both three and four dimensions. In the massless, conformally coupled limit, the lead terms match known static Casimir results. Higher-order time terms also match known FLRW results when the two scale factors coincide in that limit.
arxiv-2603-12644: Zonghao Ying and co-authors map security threats in OpenClaw, a framework that gives AI agents system-level powers. Tool-calling agents can run complex workflows, so old content filters no longer suffice. The report names flaws like prompt injection leading to remote code execution, chained tool attacks, context amnesia, and supply chain contamination. A three-layer risk taxonomy sorts flaws across cognition, execution, and information systems. Their defense blueprint, FASA, rests on zero-trust execution and intent checks.
arxiv-2603-12744: Alexander Taylor and co-authors test whether theorem prover language models generalize beyond MathLib. Most prover benchmarks use MathLib definitions, which biases training and scores. Their TaoBench comes from Tao's Analysis I, where core concepts are built from scratch. Each problem also gets an equivalent MathLib version for direct comparison. Top provers did well in MathLib form but dropped by roughly 26% on the Tao form. The bottleneck is thus framework shift, not task difficulty.
arxiv-2603-12944: Gerard Misiołek and co-authors study how smooth the solution maps of generalized surface quasi-geostrophic equations are. The family includes both 2D Euler flow and the standard surface model. In Lagrangian form, the maps act as Riemannian exponential maps on a diffeomorphism group. Those maps prove to be real analytic, so local well-posedness follows. In Eulerian form, the same maps are nowhere locally uniformly continuous in Sobolev terms. The split between the two views is thus sharp and striking.
arxiv-2603-13144: Romain Dalidet and co-authors map the trade-offs that set real performance in N00N-state interferometry. Ideal scalings ignore loss, state imbalance, and photon number, which all interact in practice. In a folded Franson setup with partly entangled states, they derive exact fringe visibility and Fisher information. Loss asymmetry can always be offset by input imbalance to restore full contrast.
