Scaling temperature spreads diversity at the token level, not the sequence level, leaving thin search, weak answers, and repeat actions. DORA makes trial actions, rates them with sequence-level scores, and samples one via a tunable knob. In Multi-Armed Bandit tests, DORA clearly beats temperature-based sampling. On TALES, DORA gives gains, lifting Qwen-2.5 7B in TextWorld from about 31 percent with ReAct to about 46 percent. DORA also prevents loops.
arxiv-2604-17644: Bertacchi reports measurements of rare electroweak penguin B decays and B decays to final states with missing energy, from Belle and Belle II data. The experiments collected a 1.3 inverse attobarn sample of electron-positron collisions to B-antib meson pairs at the Upsilon(4S) energy. Results cover b to s lepton-pair transitions for electrons and muons, b to s tau pairs, and b to s neutrino pairs, presented on these datasets.
arxiv-2604-17744: Wu studies input variance suppression for continuous-control reinforcement learning under non-normal transient amplification. Continuous-control RL shows large closed-loop variance, fast jitter, and response to disturbances, usually blamed on action noise, exploration noise, or policy roughness. Wu takes an amplifier-side view: in stable closed loops that are non-normal, small input perturbations can grow transiently into far larger covariance. An input variance suppression layer between policy and plant cuts input variance and jitter. Two interventions test it, varying eigenvector geometry and input stats.
arxiv-2604-18344: Guan and seven colleagues present DiffTSP, a diffusion model that predicts missing fact sets in knowledge graphs without preset queries. Older methods score triples one by one, sometimes filtering out valid facts through entity-pair preselection. DiffTSP instead generates the missing relational structure directly as a conditional subgraph, learning masked relation states at varied corruption levels. A structure-aware denoising network combines local relational patterns with broader graph attention, and tests on three data sets beat strong baselines with fewer conflicts.
arxiv-2604-18744: Zhang and three colleagues present Match-Any-Events, the first event-camera matching model to achieve wide-baseline correspondence across data sets with no target-domain fine-tuning. A motion-robust attention backbone learns multi-timescale features from event streams, with sparsity-aware token selection keeping large-scale training feasible. A motion-synthesis framework supplies the wide-baseline supervision the model needs. Across benchmarks, the system improves on the previous best event matching methods by about 38 percent.
arxiv-2604-18844: Chen and three colleagues analyze pulsar selection rules for autonomous X-ray pulsar navigation, using NICER data for realistic noise estimates. Pulsed flux, pulsar visibility, geometric configuration, and long term timing stability guide selection, and an extended Kalman filter tracks spacecraft state on board. The system is tested for a Low Earth Orbit satellite at 600 km and an Earth to Jupiter transfer. Including the Crab pulsar gives position errors below 7 km in orbit and 20 km on transfer, but its limited timing causes filter divergence after 20 days without timing model updates.
arxiv-2604-18944: Jiang and four colleagues study why named entity recognition collapses on noisy user generated content. Surface symptoms share one root cause: low information density, shown by controlled resampling tests. The authors introduce Attention Spectrum Analysis to measure how sparse input blunts attention. They then propose the Window-Aware Optimization Module, which finds sparse regions and uses back translation to raise semantic density. On standard social media sets, the module gains up to 4.5 percent absolute F1 over mainstream models.
arxiv-2604-19044: Gao and Luo study optimal taxation in monopoly screening with a redistribution-minded regulator. When it moves first, any nondecreasing allocation can be the monopolist's optimum under a tax schedule. Despite this flexibility, the regulator never gains strictly from randomization or nonlinear taxes. Under strong regularity, the frontier needs only a per-unit excise tax plus a lump-sum rebate, with every rate from the surplus maximizing rate to the Laffer peak appearing. Subsidies are never used, and every frontier policy rations more than the unregulated monopolist.
arxiv-2604-19344: Ziegltrum and colleagues test sparse-gated mixture-of-experts designs, which use only a subset of weights at run time, for vision-based quadruped parkour. Robotic parkour over steps and gaps is a hard movement benchmark, but recent policies usually rely on dense perceptron nets. The authors compare expert and standard policies with matched active weights at inference. The test shows whether sparse expert routing itself lifts agile movement, rather than merely adding size.
arxiv-2604-19444: Zollo, Wang, and Zemel introduce Binary Agreement for Self-consistency Calibration, a method for calibrating confidence in reasoning language models without correctness labels. Such models often lack steady scores for reliable use, notably with small sampling budgets. The key insight is that agreement between an anchor response and one independent probe is a Bernoulli observation whose mean is the anchor's latent self-consistency. Pooling these cases across unlabeled queries supports both fixing current scores and learning sharper scores first, using as few as two responses per query.
arxiv-2604-19744: Qu and 53 colleagues report the sharpest readings yet of the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect around luminous red galaxies. The signal appears at 18 sigma in both harmonic and configuration space. They cross-correlate 2.4 million spectroscopic red galaxies from the DESI DR2 sample with ACT data release 6. A new harmonic-space method with momentum-weighted maps turns galaxy gas profiles into halo gas profiles, with help from halo occupation models.
arxiv-2604-19844: Chang and five colleagues study trust boundary confusion in vision-language agentic systems, where agents must heed real environmental cues while resisting misleading ones. Traffic lights are key in-band signals that should shape agent behavior, yet similar signals can be crafted as visual injections that override user intent and create security risks. The team builds a dual-intent dataset and evaluation framework to test this tension.
arxiv-2604-19944: Kuraptsev and Sokolov study collective light effects in atomic ensembles inside a waveguide, where evanescent modes of the electromagnetic field play a special role. These modes shape cooperative spontaneous decay and radiation transfer through the ensemble. Under some conditions their influence beats that of ordinary radiation modes. The mechanism is a shift in dipole-dipole interaction between atoms, the force by which atoms exchange photons.
arxiv-2604-20144: Zhang and four colleagues present Metadata Reasoner, an agentic approach that picks a small sufficient set of data sources for tasks. A table-search engine retrieves candidates, and the agent consults metadata to judge fit. Evaluated on KramaBench, it averages an F1 score of 88.63 percent, beating the strongest baseline by about 11 percentage points. On a synthetic BIRD-based benchmark it holds over 93 percent F1 and never picks low-quality tables. Interleaving selection with partial-query execution adds about five points to selection F1 and task accuracy alike.
arxiv-2604-20244: Zhu and three colleagues reframe knowledge distillation for language models as a reweighted token-level likelihood goal, tying past methods together. Their Hybrid Policy Distillation blends forward and reverse KL, balancing broad mode cover with sharp mode seeking, and mixes off-policy data with light near on-policy sampling. Tests on long math reasoning plus short dialogue and code tasks show steadier optimization, lower compute cost, and stronger final scores across model families and sizes.
arxiv-2604-20544: Jia and three colleagues build Evian, a framework for auditing visual instruction-tuning data. Filters rely on coarse scores that miss subtle flaws like logical fallacies and factual errors. Evian splits each response into visual description, subjective inference, and factual claim, then scores them for image-text consistency, logical coherence, and factual accuracy. The team builds a sample benchmark by injecting subtle defects. A model tuned on a small subset chosen by Evian beats models trained on far larger datasets, with logical coherence the key quality factor.
arxiv-2604-20844: Hou, Yuan, Zhou, Chen, Liang, Wang, Liu, and Huang propose the Atom-Entity Graph for knowledge representation and indexing. GraphRAG work has brought graph structures into text indexing and retrieval, linking text chunks through knowledge graph triples. Yet taking a text chunk as the smallest unit lumps several atomic facts into a rigid bundle. Their design stores knowledge as knowledge atoms, each one a self-contained fact, instead of coarse-grained text chunks. Accurate links between entities are kept by pairing personalized PageRank with relevance-based filtering.
arxiv-2604-21144: Biswesh Mohapatra and three colleagues give dialogue agents a visual memory for shared context, countering a flaw they call representational blur, where similar entities melt into one description. Their scaffolding turns dialogue state step by step into a lasting visual record retrieved when answering. On the IndiRef test, incremental externalization alone helps, visual scaffolding adds more, and mixing visual with textual records works best overall.
arxiv-2604-21244: Thi-Hau Nguyen, Minh-Tien Tran, and Van-Nham Phan map how mass imbalance and Coulomb attraction shape polaritonic condensates in semiconductor and semimetal microcavities. A Hartree-Fock two-band model tracks spectral functions and luminescence. In semiconducting samples, a positive band gap stabilizes tightly bound excitons and yields BEC-like condensates at low density, crossing toward BCS-like pairing as density rises and imbalance falls. Semimetallic samples instead favor BCS-like pairing throughout, with BEC coherence only at strong interaction and large imbalance.
arxiv-2604-21344: Azher Ahmed Efat, Seok Hwan Song, and Wallapak Tavanapong introduce PolyChartQA, a benchmark for answering questions over multiple charts at once, a common real-world reading task. It holds 534 multi-chart images with 2,297 sub-charts from computer-science papers and 2,694 question-answer pairs. Nine state-of-the-art multimodal models show a 27.4 percent accuracy drop on human-authored questions versus model-generated ones, while the authors' prompting method gains about 5 percent. The gap shows multi-chart reasoning remains hard even for strong models.
arxiv-2604-21544: Sakshi Dang and three colleagues view locally recoverable codes with maximal recoverability and maximum distance profile convolutional codes through matrix completion. They present techniques general enough to construct both code types. A shared feature of their constructions is sparse generator matrices, many of whose entries lie in a small subfield of a larger extension field.
arxiv-2604-21644: Mohammad Almuhaihi and Dennis Bernstein design an adaptive Kalman filter for state estimation when the process noise is colored, meaning its errors follow patterns over time. The coloring pattern itself is unknown. Their whitening filter embeds an unknown coloring filter in a larger state model. It tunes itself by driving the measurement innovations toward whiteness, the sign of a correct noise model. The result gives back near-optimal results without knowing the noise pattern in advance.
arxiv-2604-21744: Palmblad, Ragland, and Neely propose GROUNDING.md, a community-run, field-specific grounding file for agentic AI coding, illustrated with mass spectrometry proteomics. The file would state hard constraints, the non-negotiable validity rules of a field, plus convention parameters, the agreed default settings. Those rules would override other prompts, letting non-experts generate code with best practice built in, while keeping domain experts in the loop.
arxiv-2604-22144: Miyoshi and ten colleagues track short-timescale 340 GHz flux changes in Sagittarius A* with ALMA data. Careful self-calibration allows 10 s snapshots with very high signal-to-noise, enabling fast monitoring. They measure Sagittarius A* against steady sources in-field. They correct apparent variability from u-v coverage and PSF changes with static-model simulations. Searching timescales from 20 s to one-third of observing time, they find no dominant narrow periodicity. Instead, a flat, white-noise-like regime below about 2 to 6.3 minutes gives way to red-noise-like behavior.
arxiv-2604-22344: Šťovíček and Pelantová study square matrices with cyclically monotone rows, where each row runs down in a cycle from a maximal diagonal entry. They prove such a matrix is regular when every diagonal entry exceeds all other entries in its row. That property solves an open problem from Cantor numeration systems, systems for writing numbers in non-standard bases. The problem concerns a one-to-one link between alternate Cantor real bases and lists of p non-negative integer sequences meeting the Parry condition.
arxiv-2604-22744: Possenti, Girelli, Tieri, and Petti treat mental-health signs as a linked web, not as side effects of a hidden illness, using multiplex hypergraphs that catch group links beyond pairs. Their theory-based model splits synergy, where joint signs add fresh clues, from redundancy, where clues just overlap. Synergy shows a firm core shared across illness types plus mixes that fit each type alone.
arxiv-2604-23044: Corbin and Kramer present a scalable method for nonlinear balanced truncation model reduction, an approach keeping stability, controllability, and observability. Their approach uses polynomial fits with Kronecker product form, building on recent numerical linear algebra gains. They derive polynomial fits for the balancing map and the balanced form of the full-order model. Cutting extra state parts yields true nonlinear reduced-order models, tested on cases showing gains and limits unseen in past work.
arxiv-2604-23744: Auerbach, Gelman, and Wolkovich show that the classic thermal-sum model of spring timing needs no extra mechanisms. It explains two puzzling trends: slowing advancement and growing variability of spring events under warming. As spring events move toward the winter solstice and away from the equinox, the same model predicts they scatter and desynchronise. By 2100, they predict, much of the American South will face such a scattered spring under high warming, with flowering gaps widening by weeks.
arxiv-2604-23844: Dahan and colleagues compare prompting strategies for cross-lingual text simplification between English and French, where translation and simplification must happen together. They test direct prompts, translate-then-simplify and simplify-then-translate in one prompt, and the same splits across two prompts, across five corpora and seven leading models. Direct prompting wins on meaning fidelity, while translate-then-simplify wins on simplicity, the study finds.
arxiv-2604-24144: Sarkar and seven colleagues analyze Murchison Widefield Array drift scans to bound the 21-cm signal from the Epoch of Reionization. A broad peak traces the bright source Fornax A in the main beam, with a smaller peak from its first sidelobe, while one angular range follows point-source Poisson behavior. One quiet pointing range proves relatively foreground-free, and combining 23 pointings yields the tightest MWA upper limit at redshift 8.2, about three times lower than earlier MWA limits but still well above theory.
arxiv-2604-24444: Baumler and five colleagues study whether users can reshape language-model drafts to match own style. In a pre-registered online study with 81 people, post-editing increases likeness to people's solo writing. It reduces likeness to model-generated output. Yet post-edited text stays closer to model text than to solo control text, with reduced stylistic diversity versus solo human text. Perceived authenticity and model-measured likeness diverge: post-edited text often feels representative of own style despite detectable model stylistic traces.
arxiv-2604-24544: Sordo, Du and three colleagues build STELLAR-E, a fully automated tool that creates synthetic test sets for language-model programs without needing existing data or much human input. It adapts a self-instruction engine to control size and topic, then checks each set with statistical and model-based scores. In tests its sets scored 5.7 percent above existing language benchmarks on judge ratings, showing comparable quality while cutting manual work.
arxiv-2604-24644: Weinberg asks whether pooling evidence across cyber campaigns improves attribution of actors. Current methods often work one case at a time. His ARCANE system builds lasting actor profiles from passive beacon data. The profiles combine deeds, tools and timing features. A Bayesian network updates them as new evidence arrives. On test threat profiles, same-actor likeness exceeds cross-actor likeness. Yet distinct actors stay hard to separate, because skilled foes share practices. Pooling alone does not resolve attribution doubt.
arxiv-2604-24844: Taylor and Zhu study three-gluon scattering amplitudes in global de Sitter spacetime, using the angular-momentum basis of SO(1,4) representations. At tree level, intertwiner integrals of harmonic one-forms over the three-sphere fix the amplitudes. The authors derive a general formula covering every helicity setup of incoming and outgoing gluons, writing the amplitudes with Wigner 3j symbols. The paper thus gives a compact representation-theoretic account of three-gluon scattering in de Sitter space.
arxiv-2604-25044: Benko, Gfrerer, Ye, Zhang and Zhou derive second-order optimality conditions for problems with generalized equation constraints. This frame covers hard cases such as variational-inequality-constrained programs and bilevel programs. The conditions are new even for those special cases, and the authors work out the variational-inequality case in full. Their main tool is first- and second-order variational analysis of the constraint system, which captures how the feasible set curves locally.
arxiv-2604-25544: Wang introduces medoid alignment for cross-plant unknown attack detection. Deploying a detector from one plant to another is hard: site-bound traffic, scarce labels, unseen attacks. Instead of matching all samples head-on, the method compresses traffic, then extracts medoid prototypes. A tuned objective aligns target with source prototypes, preserving discrimination and confident predictions. This cuts noisy matching and adds stability. Tests on gas and water systems show the best scores, reaching 0.843 accuracy, with F1 nearly as high. Analysis shows transfer asymmetry, and medoid guidance helps most in reverse.
arxiv-2604-25644: Berti and Ghisoni improve quantum state preparation on Bucket Brigade QRAM. Building on a Bucket Brigade QRAM segment-tree frame for amplitude encoding, they offer two improvements. First, they remove a subroutine by precomputing rotation angles from the segment tree and storing them directly in QRAM cells. Second, they extend the build to complex-valued matrices by storing a leaf phase beside each precomputed rotation angle and using a two-step magnitude-then-phase method. At unchanged query complexity, the quantum process reduces to QRAM retrievals and controlled-rotation cascades.
arxiv-2604-25844: Avilés and Diez build an analytical black hole in a theory combining Einstein-Maxwell-Yang-Mills fields with a conformally coupled scalar. It extends the charged Martínez-Troncoso-Zanelli black hole with non-Abelian gauge fields. The gauge group follows horizon curvature: SU(N) when positive, SU(N-1,1) when negative. As a conformal seed, it yields new meronic spacetimes with all renormalizable scalar terms, extending the Anabalón-Cisterna solution. A non-Noetherian extension still gives a second-order conformally invariant scalar equation and charged static solutions.
arxiv-2604-25944: Uehlein and five colleagues offer a workflow for reproducible, FAIR-aligned simulation research in numerical physics. Simulation data comes from software developed actively for years. Reproducibility therefore needs explicit links between code versions, inputs, outputs, analysis steps, and figures. Their workflow joins version control, code review, testing automation, structured logs, rich metadata output, and standard post-processing. The ideas are shown on one simulation framework but apply broadly across computational physics and data-heavy science.
arxiv-2604-26044: Gamal' proves that a non-stable pure subnormal contraction must possess a nontrivial hyperinvariant subspace. Here non-stable means the operator's powers do not shrink to zero in the strong sense. The argument finds a singular inner function whose range under the operator fails to be dense. That failure forces such a subspace to exist, building on results of Esterle and Kérchy. The paper also gives examples of stable subnormal contractions where every nonzero analytic function's range stays dense, marking the boundary of the result.
arxiv-2604-26544: Kim and Lee tested how far integrability survives for root-Kerr probe dynamics around a Kerr-Newman black hole. A scalar particle stays integrable via the Carter charge, and spin adds the Rüdiger charge at low spin orders. In the simpler root-Kerr model, leading-order integrability holds to all spin orders when probe vertices follow the Newman-Janis shift. At second order in probe charge, integrability reaches spin-squared order but fails at spin-cubic order, and no action deformation can restore it.
arxiv-2604-26844: El-Naggar, Kuribayashi and Briscoe ask which languages are easy for language models to learn when training follows a curriculum, starting from simple sentences rather than random order. Languages range from very common feature combinations to rare or impossible ones, and earlier work tested whether model biases alone reproduce those typological patterns. Adding a simple curriculum variant to existing experiments, they find the training order substantially shifts the models' apparent biases. The learning scenario, not just the model's built-in tendencies, thus shapes which language patterns emerge.
arxiv-2604-27044: The CMS team presents Higgs pair production in the four-bottom-quark final state from 13.6 TeV proton-proton collisions, with 62 inverse femtobarns. Higgs decays are rebuilt as small-radius jet pairs (resolved) and single large-radius jets (merged). Combining both analyses with new trigger and selection methods gives an observed upper limit near four and a half at 95 percent confidence. Adding 13 TeV data gives about five observed against about three expected, the most stringent 4b constraints to date.
arxiv-2604-27144: Dang and four colleagues find strong signs that forces from chiral effective field theory favor Wigner supermultiplet symmetry. They do not assume a large-color limit or pick special nuclei. Using the ab initio Symmetry Adapted Model, they trace the pattern in nuclear structure. They note suppressed spin-isospin polarizability. Most of the helium-4, lithium-6, and helium-6 wave functions sit in a few U(4) representations. That points to a way to shrink many-body bases while keeping key configurations.
arxiv-2604-27244: Tian, Ganguly, and Macdonald propose RAQG-QPP, query quality guessing using retrieved query variants and query generation from retrieved queries. Guessing retrieval quality without human ratings helps query-specific choices, but label-free methods lag for neural rankers. Query variants, queries with similar information needs, can boost accuracy. Yet term-added variants often turn incoherent, made-up, or off-topic. Retrieved variants and generation from retrieved queries aim to supply variants that stay faithful to the original need.
arxiv-2604-27444: Oshiro, Matsuyama, and Nakamura study current-density disturbances caused by radiative collapse, a driver of tokamak plasma disruptions, using a reaction-diffusion model. In their model, the reaction term, which depends on radial derivatives of the resistivity profile, creates a disturbance in a layer at the cold front. Current density rises where the electron temperature gradient is steep, and falls behind the front where the temperature profile curves downward. The tokamak code INDEX simulates the electrothermal dynamics, shaped by the contest of Ohmic heating against impurity radiation.
arxiv-2604-27844: Lin and four colleagues introduce ZipCCL, a lossless library for LLM training. Training data, including activations, gradients, and parameters, often follows a near-Gaussian curve. ZipCCL uses exponent coding using the Gaussian curve of LLM tensors. It uses GPU-tuned compression kernels with traffic-aware data layout, and adaptive strategies switching operations by workload. On a 64-GPU cluster with mixture-of-experts and dense models, ZipCCL cuts traffic time by up to 1.35 times. It speeds end-to-end training by about 18 percent with no impact on quality.
arxiv-2604-28144: Wolf, Fatkhullin and He propose Policy Gradient Penalty, a single-loop method for limited maximum-entropy exploration in reinforcement learning. Entropy maximisation lacks add-up structure, blocking Bellman methods, and policy tuning adds bends to goal and constraints. Their squared-penalty method imposes convex occupancy constraints through pseudo-rewards, and hidden convexity plus strong duality yield global last-iterate settling to near-optimal, nearly feasible policies, tested on grid-world and continuous-control tasks.
arxiv-2605-00244:
Yajvan Ravan and 10 co-authors introduce Lucid-XR, a data engine that creates training material for robots inside extended reality. At its core sits vuer, a physics simulation that runs in a web browser on the headset itself. That setup lets people anywhere supply natural hand and body demonstrations without special laboratory gear.

Demonstrations are retargeted from human poses to robot poses, then amplified by a physics-guided video generator that a user can steer with plain language. Robot vision policies trained only on this synthetic data worked in real rooms they had never seen, including cluttered and badly lit ones. Example tasks involve soft materials, loose particles, and firm objects in contact.
arxiv-2605-00344:
Chow-Choong Ngeow and Anupam Bhardwaj test how well the new Vera C. Rubin Observatory measures RR Lyrae stars, the pulsating old stars astronomers use as distance markers. They work with the observatory's first data preview, cross-matching its fields against two public variable star catalogs. About six hundred RR Lyrae stars had light curves sampled well enough to study.

Most of the stars sit in the 47 Tucanae cluster field and the Fornax dwarf galaxy field. From the color data the authors estimate metal content, finding good agreement with published values where sampling is dense enough for template fitting. Distance estimates from one theoretical relation matched the literature closely, while another ran systematically high, which they trace to calibration limits in evolved star models. They expect later data releases to sharpen all of these measures greatly.
arxiv-2605-00444:
Kerui Chen and 5 co-authors scale up video understanding by letting several small agents collaborate in a shared latent space. Video-capable language models cannot watch a long video at once, since each pass has a bounded context budget. Older multi-agent fixes preprocess by rules, losing information, costing much, and funneling everything through text. Their framework, MACF, splits the problem differently.

The video is cut into segments, each watched by an agent with its own small budget. Agents encode what they see into compact tokens in a shared embedding space, and a central coordinator reasons over those tokens, keeping the visual evidence intact. A staged training curriculum first aligns meanings, then teaches summarization of evidence, then coordination across agents. On varied video benchmarks, MACF beat leading single models and multi-agent systems under the same budget limits.
arxiv-2605-00644:
Jiali Cui, Zhiqiang Lao, and Heather Yu teach energy-based models to generate coherent multimodal data, such as matched images and text, by enlisting a variational auto-encoder as a partner. Energy-based models are flexible but hard to train: learning needs sampling by Markov chains in the joint data space, and chains started from noise mix poorly and miss the links between modalities. Multimodal auto-encoders capture those links through a shared latent generator, yet their simple Gaussian shapes limit realism.

The framework interweaves likelihood training of all three models with Markov chain refinements in data and latent spaces. The generator produces coherent samples that seed the energy model's chains, while the inference model supplies smart latent starting points for the generator's sampling. Each model thus rescues the other's sampling. Experiments show better synthesis quality and cross-modal coherence than various baselines.
arxiv-2605-00844:
Theodor Spiro tests whether large language models used as forecasters share the same errors, which would undermine collective intelligence. Three conditions for an epistemic monoculture are examined. In the first study, GPT-4o, Claude, and Gemini show highly correlated errors across hundreds of resolved binary prediction questions, despite being built by different organizations.

A second study tracks human crowd forecasts around the ChatGPT launch and finds shifts toward model-like answers are fully explained by rational updating toward the truth. A third finds human bias patterns already resembled the model pattern before ChatGPT, and the resemblance later weakened. Spiro concludes the shared failure mode is built, but not yet activated in human forecasts.
arxiv-2605-00944:
Xu Zheng, Feiyu Wu, Linhong Wu, Zhuocheng Wang, and Hui Li study stable ranking of training examples in language datasets full of redundancy. Rankings guide filtering, debugging, and curation, yet most pipelines score items one by one as if separate. Duplicates, near-duplicates, and paraphrases make relative order unstable across random seeds, because similar examples can swap places by chance.

Their SCARV framework layers robust multi-seed combining and a structure-aware step over redundancy clusters on top of an existing scoring method. Across synthetic and naturally mined redundancy, several tasks, and fine-tuning tests, SCARV improves stability and makes ranking-based decisions more reproducible. Multi-seed combining is the main stabilizer, while the structure-aware part helps most at low budgets or with informative clusters.
arxiv-2605-01044:
Katharina T. Huber and Katherine St. John give an efficient way to reconstruct arboreal networks, a class of multi-rooted phylogenetic networks whose underlying graph is a tree. Such networks model evolutionary histories that do not fit a single rooted tree. The authors encode stack-free arboreal networks using triplets, which record relations among three taxa, together with a new concept they call a duet.

That encoding yields a polynomial-time algorithm that constructs the networks from complete triplet and duet systems. Classification results establish correctness of the construction. The encoding also leads naturally to a metric on these multi-rooted networks, giving a principled way to measure distance between competing evolutionary histories in this class.
arxiv-2605-01144:
Suryakant Singh and three co-authors present SCOUT, a concept-grounded multimodal transformer for generating pathology reports from whole-slide images. Report generation must integrate local tissue patterns, global slide context, and diagnostic concepts, yet existing approaches rely on fixed pretrained visual features and can miss key concepts. SCOUT maintains an evolving visual representation alongside recursively updated slide-level and concept-conditioned views.

Visual and contextual information co-evolve across encoder depth, and separate attention pathways feed an adaptive fusion module for each token. On more than twenty thousand slide-report pairs across several cancer types, SCOUT beats leading methods on standard text scores and on a clinical report quality score. Ablations confirm both iterative refinement and the fusion step contribute.
arxiv-2605-01344:
Jun Zheng and Guchuan Zhu wrote a tutorial on a method for proving that systems described by partial differential equations stay stable when outside inputs push on them. The property at stake is input-to-state stability: bounded pushes should cause only bounded drift, even when the push acts at the boundary.

Classic Lyapunov methods, which track an energy-like score, strain under complex boundary pushes. The generalized method lets the score depend on the input itself, which adds freedom and speed. Step by step, the tutorial builds such scores for three cases: a nonlinear heat-type equation with mixed boundary pushes, a first-order flow equation, and a wave equation with boundary damping and pushes. Each case ends with explicit stability bounds in a range of norms. Open problems and control uses close the tour.
arxiv-2605-01744:
Teppei Kitahara promotes a rare kaon decay into a clean probe of CP violation, the matter-antimatter asymmetry written into particle law. The decays of the two neutral kaon states into a muon pair have long looked hopeless for short-distance physics, swamped by long-distance effects through two-photon exchange.

The new lever is interference between the long-lived and short-lived kaon states. That cross term answers directly to direct CP violation in the underlying quark transition, turning a muddy channel into a sharp one. Kitahara, writing a conference contribution, lays out the mechanism and a flavor-tagging plan suited to an LHCb-style detector. He gives projected reach. A key CKM parameter combination could be pinned to about a third of its standard model value. A long-standing sign ambiguity in a related decay could be resolved past three sigma by the high-luminosity LHC's end.
arxiv-2605-01844:
Lang Gao and nine co-authors give model steering a new geometry. Steering, nudging a language model's activations toward a concept, works erratically, and the reigning linear picture, which assumes concepts can be made fully orthogonal, predicts a tidiness that practice refuses to show.

Relax the orthogonality demand and a cylinder appears. Each concept gets a central axis, the direction between its absence and presence, which drives generation of the concept. Around it lies a normal plane that sets steering sensitivity: only certain sectors of that plane ease the axis into action, while others suppress or delay it. The plane can be located reliably from difference vectors, but the sensitive sector cannot, and that blind spot, the authors argue, is the principled source of steering's mood swings. Experiments confirm the cylindrical structure in real models and show the reading predicts steering behavior usefully.
arxiv-2605-02744:
Jenny Lynn Almerol and three co-authors test how a gravitational N-body simulation, the kind used to model star clusters, can run across several RISC-V-based accelerators. The chips, Tenstorrent Wormhole cards, were designed for AI work, but interest in them for high-performance science computing is growing. Porting a code that tracks every body's pull on every other is a useful stress test.

Three strategies for spreading the simulation across multiple cards are presented and compared. The authors measure both run time and energy use on a representative run. From those measures they pick the setup with the best balance of speed and efficiency. The study is an early data point on whether AI-born hardware can serve traditional simulation workloads well.
arxiv-2605-03144:
Amirreza Mahbod, Ramona Woitek, and Jeanne Shen argue that how nuclear segmentation is scored in pathology images needs fixing before models can be compared fairly. Separating single cell nuclei is a core task with many clinical uses, and deep models for it are judged by evaluation pipelines that have known flaws.

Their NucEval framework handles vague regions, score normalization, overlapping nuclei, and border uncertainty in one pipeline. Tests on the NuInsSeg dataset plus two outside sets, with three modern models, show how each fix changes the scores. Code, guidance, and worked examples are public for reuse.
arxiv-2605-03244:
Mingzhe Lu, Yanbing Liu, Qihao Wang, Jiarui Zhang, Jiayue Wu, Yue Hu, Yunpeng Li, and Yangyan Xu present a movie script summarizer built on story theory, not surface salience. Scripts jump across time and plot lines, so methods that pick striking lines often lose the core story.

Their S-squared-tory framework follows character growth paths to find plot nuclei, the events that drive the story, and filters out side events that only add mood. A narrative expert agent's reasoning trains a small model to spot nuclei, which then guide the summary. On MovieSum it set a new mark for semantic fidelity, and it transferred well to book summaries.
arxiv-2605-03444:
Subha Dey and fifteen co-authors show that coupled phase transitions survive even in oxides with extreme chemical disorder. High-entropy oxides usually lock into symmetric cubic forms, so symmetry-lowering transitions tied to magnetism and orbitals were thought rare in such messy lattices.

In a spinel with five A-site metals including two Jahn-Teller active ions, cooling triggers an orbital-driven transition and then a magnetism-driven one at lower temperature. Swapping A-site metals shows nickel and copper are both essential, with opposing local distortions around each while other sites stay quiet. Order emerges, the authors argue, through competition among local distortions.
arxiv-2605-03544:
Carlijn Lems and fifty-five co-authors introduce DALPHIN, an open benchmark that tests artificial intelligence copilots for digital pathology against human pathologists. The dataset holds 1,236 images from 300 cases, covering 130 diagnoses from rare to common, drawn from six countries and fourteen subspecialties. Thirty-one pathologists from ten countries set the human comparison scores.

The team tests two general-purpose systems, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro, plus the pathology-specific PathChat+, on sequential and independent question answering. The pathology copilot matched expert-level results on four of six tasks, ahead of the general systems. DALPHIN is released publicly, with its ground truth kept sequestered to keep the benchmark durable.
arxiv-2605-04144:
G. Quadri and eleven co-authors investigate the dark matter halo of the Big Wheel, a giant disc galaxy found by JWST in a massive node of the Cosmic Web at redshift about three. The galaxy is almost three times larger than expected for typical discs of similar stellar mass at that epoch, and explaining it requires halo properties that JWST observations alone cannot supply. The team combines a physically motivated dynamical model with deep ALMA kinematical data.

Using priors from JWST photometry and carbon monoxide kinematics, they infer a halo mass and stellar mass whose ratio is significantly higher than state-of-the-art empirical relations predict. The implication is that the Big Wheel assembled its stellar content much more efficiently than the general galaxy population at that redshift, an unusual formation history for such an early, orderly disc.
arxiv-2605-04344:
Zetai Cen and three co-authors develop a statistical theory for when language models can predict text unlike anything in their training data. Their idea is simple: before predicting the next token, first nudge the given prefix to a nearby text with similar meaning, then predict from that altered version.

This perturbation defines a layered noise model, within which they prove five properties covering adaptation, stability, and reliable prediction beyond the training support. Tests on synthetic and real language data show the method consistently improves out-of-support prediction while staying competitive on ordinary text. The work reframes extrapolation as something a small, principled perturbation can buy.
arxiv-2605-04544:
Tuomas Hakoniemi, Nutan Limaye, and Iddo Tzameret prove lower bounds for a powerful algebraic proof system. Their test cases are formulas in conjunctive normal form, the standard format of basic logic. The Ideal Proof System verifies that a set of polynomial equations has no solution. Researchers had bounded its size for many algebraic formulas, but not for logical ones.

That gap was a central open problem. It separated the algebra side from the logical statements that proof complexity ultimately cares about. For a restricted but important version of the system, based on read-once branching programs, the authors resolve it. They use a rank-based interpolation argument. It shows certain hard logical formulas genuinely require large refutations.
arxiv-2605-04844:
Xinze Li and six co-authors speed up 3D Gaussian Splatting, a method that renders new views of a scene from many soft three-dimensional blobs. A costly step is finding exactly which screen tiles each projected blob touches. Loose bounds make the renderer check many tiles that do not matter.

Their method, QuadBox, wraps each projection in four aligned boxes shaped by the blob's geometry, largely excluding needless tiles. A single-pass routine called QPass then checks tiles with simple interval tests. On public datasets the approach made rendering about one point eight five times faster, and the authors release their code for others to use.
arxiv-2605-05044:
Qi Cheng and six co-authors speed up database query optimisation by letting rewrite decisions depend on estimated cost without paying for repeated full optimisation. A database optimiser first rewrites a query, then searches for a cheap execution plan. Some rewrites help only sometimes, but checking each one with a fresh cost search is too slow.

Their framework caches intermediate cost results at several levels to avoid redundant work and uses upper cost bounds to prune the search space. Methods for reusing partial plans inside a bottom-up optimiser are also contributed. Implemented in the GaussDB optimiser, the framework significantly cut overall optimisation time in experiments.
arxiv-2605-05244:
Florian Geissler and three co-authors make retrieval-augmented generation safer by judging how factual its retrieved context and final answers really are. Retrieval can mislead the model with irrelevant passages, so users need a useful trust signal. Their two-stage approach first uses conformal prediction to keep only retrieved chunks likely to come from the correct source.

That filtering alone improved answer quality on some datasets, but its formal guarantees depend on the retriever setup, so the authors add checks for whether the setup fits. A second, attention-based scorer then rates whether the final answer is in line with the retrieved context. It caught mismatched answers with solid success in their tests.
arxiv-2605-05444:
The LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA collaborations searched their fourth observing run for mergers involving a body lighter than the Sun. Such sub-solar objects cannot form from normal stars, so a find would point to exotic origins like primordial black holes. The search covered masses from a fifth to one solar mass in LIGO data from 2023 into early 2024.

No convincing candidates turned up in the data. The teams therefore set upper limits on merger rates and on how much dark matter such objects could make up. They also reported, for the first time, sensitivity to binaries with sub-solar neutron stars.
arxiv-2605-05944:
Zimeng Wang and Alp Yurtsever propose a universal adaptive method for proximal gradient optimization. The problems covered pair a simple convex term with a second term that may be nonconvex smooth, convex nonsmooth, or convex smooth. Most methods need problem parameters in advance or work for only one of those classes.

Their method sets its step size by accumulating past gradient mapping norms in a denominator. With no tuning and no knowledge of parameters, it converges across all three classes, in both deterministic and stochastic settings. Rates match the standard proximal gradient method up to logarithmic factors. An accelerated variant improves the smooth convex rate further, and new noise control techniques support the analysis throughout.
arxiv-2605-06044:
Rui Min and Yi-Xiang Wang study magnetotransport in nodal-line semimetals, motivated by recent experiments on the material EuGa4. Passing a magnetic field through such a material can reveal its band structure, Berry phase, Fermi surface, and carrier density. The authors focus on quantum oscillations and on resistance that keeps growing with field strength instead of leveling off.

They find two distinct oscillation frequencies, traced to the torus shaped Fermi surface that marks this class of material. That pair serves as an experimental signature of nodal-line semimetals, they argue. Their resistance calculation is nonsaturating in the low energy region, matching the observed trend. Its size, though, comes out much smaller than the ratio reported in the experiment, a gap they note openly.
arxiv-2605-06144:
Michael Wagner and nine co-authors study how miscible liquids mix in a stirred tank when their densities differ. Blending liquids to a uniform product is basic industrial work, yet the flow physics is complex and product quality hangs on it. Their simulations use an even fifty fifty split of two liquids in the tank.

The team varied the Reynolds and Richardson numbers, which capture flow speed and buoyancy effects, in a systematic sweep. Mixing time rose with the Richardson number, in line with earlier reports, while the Reynolds effect was less clear. Combining power, Froude, and Richardson numbers, they derived an exponential scaling law for dimensionless mixing time. That single law collapsed all of their simulation data onto one master curve.
arxiv-2605-06244:
Jiayi Gu and three co-authors compute large deviation functions for open quantum systems with strong symmetries. The global rate function in such systems is typically non convex, so the standard Gartner-Ellis route from the generating function fails directly. That blocks a clean description of rare fluctuation events, which matter for nanoscale devices and quantum transport alike.

Their framework applies the theorem locally inside each symmetry sector instead. Local rate functions are computed sector by sector, and the global function is rebuilt as the lowest envelope of those local pieces. An exactly solvable model illustrates the method. On an open Heisenberg chain with continuous non Abelian symmetries, the approach reveals fluctuations ranging from Poissonian to super Poissonian by sector, together with emergent intermittency in the dynamics.
arxiv-2605-06544:
Eric Ding and ten co-authors present CCL-Bench, a trace-based benchmark for language model infrastructure. Claims about which hardware and software run a workload fastest depend on many interacting settings. Existing benchmarks publish a few end numbers that cannot explain why one setup beats another, so tuning stays guesswork.

Each CCL-Bench data point packages an execution trace, a workload card, and launch scripts, with a toolkit computing compute, memory, and communication metrics. Findings include cases where more compute-communication overlap still slows training, and where doubling interconnect bandwidth helps TPU setups far more than GPU ones on smaller workloads. Framework choice alone can triple step time.
arxiv-2605-06744:
Ágatha de Freitas, Marcos A. Simplicio, Bruno C. Albertini, and Renan C. A. Alves build a firmware system that stops malicious USB and PCIe peripherals from connecting. A rogue device can attack a computer before the operating system even loads, and users cannot easily verify hardware authenticity. Their design uses the SPDM security protocol inside UEFI firmware to authenticate devices as they connect.

An open-source proof of concept, tested in emulation with kernel virtualization, restricts connections to an allowed list. Boot measurements show instruction counts rising about thirteen percent and processor cycles about eight percent during firmware execution, overhead the authors call acceptable for the added protection. High-security institutions could tailor the system to their needs.
arxiv-2605-06844:
Morris Brooks, Jakob Oldenburg, and Diane Saint Aubin review how to construct trial states for the dilute Bose gas that capture its ground state correlations. The dilute Bose gas is a cornerstone model of interacting bosons, and proving its ground state energy in the thermodynamic limit needs clever trial wavefunctions. A local particle number cutoff is the key device organizing the construction surveyed here.

The note explains how that cutoff builds states carrying the substantial correlation structure of the true ground state. As a payoff, the authors give a simplified derivation of the Lee-Huang-Yang correction, the famous next-order term, as an upper bound on the ground state energy. The short note serves readers entering rigorous Bose gas theory.
arxiv-2605-06944:
Brian Henn and twenty co-authors launch AIMIP, a comparison project that tests AI weather and climate models under one common protocol. Borrowed from climate science tradition, the project fixes the experiment, output format, and training rules. Models train on historical reanalysis. They must simulate the atmosphere given prescribed historical sea surface temperatures from 1979 to 2024. Shared rules expose which framework and architecture choices actually change behavior.

Models are scored on biases, trends, response to El Niño patterns, temporal variability, and out-of-sample generalization. The AI models simulate past climate and forcing responses about as well as a conventional physics-based model. Some, however, underestimate past warming trends, and predictions diverge on the generalization tests. The phase one dataset is public for further evaluation.
arxiv-2605-07144:
Yang Wei Koh and Youjin Deng model quantum annealing with a simple particle-in-a-box setup. Annealing searches for low-energy states by slowly changing a system, but rough landscapes trap it in local minima. The authors solve the Schrödinger equation directly for three landscape shapes, each with many local minima under different envelopes.

They study both the energy spectrum and how much energy remains after annealing at different speeds. Surprisingly, residual energy depended little on landscape roughness or annealing depth, and jumps between states were common. A feature they call flat gaps helps explain how the wave function gets trapped during those jumps.
arxiv-2605-07244:
Xiaoze Liu and five co-authors let several different language models train together and share experience without merging. Their Mutual Reinforcement Learning framework keeps each model's settings, goals, and tokenizer separate, while a shared exchange passes typed records between them. A special layer re-splits text so traces align across mismatched word lists.

Three sharing styles are tested: sharing rollouts, sharing advantage values, and passing on verified successes. A bandit-style analysis places each on a trade-off between balance and support. In the regime evaluated, sharing outcomes occupied the best point of that trade-off, suggesting peer successes are the safest currency for mutual learning.
arxiv-2605-07444:
Mahdi Naderibeni, Liang Wu, and David M. J. Tax study how much training data physics-guided flow predictors really need inside factory stirred tanks. Running flow models is costly, so learned stand-ins promise far faster field forecasts. The team made steady flows across impeller speeds and liquid heights with standard turbulence runs, then trained neural field models.

Error fell as data grew, but with clear fading returns past mid-size datasets. Physics-based constraints helped most when data were scarce, lifting scores and steadier tracer transport. Reasonable interpolation across speeds and heights was possible, though constraint benefits faded as datasets grew large.
arxiv-2605-07544:
Vo offers a textbook that bridges pixels and language for readers who want real multimodal understanding. The book, From Pixels to Prompts, covers vision language models, systems that read images and handle language about them. It is a guided tour, not a replacement for original papers, and it warns that the fast moving field will outrun any fixed text.

Early chapters explain visual encoders, prompting, instruction following, and how big language models gain the ability to handle images. Later chapters cover training, existing architectures, datasets, benchmarks, and practical evaluation and deployment guidance. Readers are urged to work actively, sketching architectures and comparing claims with models they meet in papers and code. Vo also stresses the risks, since these systems caption personal photos, read charts, and generate text easily mistaken for human writing. Understanding their strengths, blind spots and data biases is presented as a responsibility, not just an academic exercise.
arxiv-2605-07644:
Shiri Chechik and two co-authors improve deterministic graph coloring in the semi-streaming model, where a huge graph's edges arrive as a stream and memory is barely more than the vertex count. Randomness helps a lot here: randomized algorithms color in one pass with few colors, while deterministic ones provably need either many colors or many passes.

Their new deterministic algorithm colors with a number of colors linear in the maximum degree while using only about the square root of the logarithm of the degree many passes. That beats the best earlier trade-offs, which needed logarithmically many passes for a similar palette. It is the first deterministic streaming algorithm to pair a linear-size palette with sub-logarithmic pass complexity.
arxiv-2605-07744:
Yu Kumagai and Keisuke Okumura study target assignment and pathfinding together: a planner must give each agent a distinct target and a collision-free route to it. Until now the only approach was conflict-based search, which fuses assignment and routing into one expensive procedure that does not scale to large fleets.

Their framework decouples the two jobs and iterates. A fast modern pathfinding solver routes the current assignment, feedback identifies the bottleneck agents, and the assignment is refined for the next round, all within a fixed time budget. Experiments show this feedback loop scales well beyond the reach of the conflict-based state of the art while keeping solution quality decent, a step toward practical large-scale use.
arxiv-2605-08044:
Julie Kallini and colleagues speed up byte-level language models. Such models match token-based models without a fixed subword vocabulary, but they generate text one byte at a time, which makes them slow. The work targets the Byte Latent Transformer and attacks the bottleneck on two fronts.

First, a diffusion variant trains with a block-wise objective beside the normal next-byte loss, so decoding can emit several bytes in parallel. Second, two speculative methods let the local decoder draft bytes past its usual patch edges and verify them in one full pass. Together the variants trade a little quality for large gains in generation speed.
arxiv-2605-08144:
Haokai Zhao and colleagues ask a neglected question about diffusion model training: does the exact random noise drawn for a sample matter? Training randomness has two parts, the timestep and the noise itself. Timesteps are heavily studied through schedules and weights, while noise draws are usually treated as interchangeable.

Their NoiseRater network scores each noise instance for a given sample and timestep. It is learned by bilevel optimization: its scores reweight the training loss, and it is updated to lower validation loss. Top-scored noise improved training over random draws, while bottom-scored noise hurt, showing that noise quality varies and can be selected for gain.
arxiv-2605-08244:
V. J. Valadão, M. Cencini, F. De Lillo, S. Musacchio, and coauthors examine the butterfly effect in a spatially extended flow. In surface quasi-geostrophic turbulence, a simple model of mesoscale geophysical motion, a tiny localized error does not simply grow at one steady rate, because the flow holds many scales at once.

The team tracks infinitesimal localized perturbations and finds highly variable behavior. Many perturbations first lose energy in a transient stage while their spectrum shifts from the injection scale toward the most unstable pattern of the system. That transient can last a few or many small-scale times depending on where the perturbation starts, complicating error forecasts for geophysical models.
arxiv-2605-08344:
Alec Helbling, Sebastian Gutierrez Hernandez, Benjamin Hoover, Duen Horng Chau, and coauthors explain a small mystery in flow matching: models trained without being told the interpolation time still work. Time normally disambiguates the velocity a model should predict, so a time-blind model looks underinformed.

Decomposing the time-blind loss separates two error sources, coupling variance from ambiguous pairings and a true time-blindness gap, which proves the blind task is strictly harder. The resolution is geometric: when data concentrate near a low-dimensional subspace, the time can be read back from the statistical shape of a noisy sample itself. High-dimensional data geometry quietly hands the model the clock it was denied.
arxiv-2605-08544:
Yamato Ureshino, Hajime Kawahara, Hibiki Yama, and Kento Masuda map the surface of a spinning brown dwarf with a fully probability based method. Doppler imaging reads shifting spectral lines to infer bright and dark patches, but surface maps and spin geometry are usually fit apart. Their approach infers both at once, treating the map with a smooth prior and sampling the geometry directly.

Synthetic tests recover patch longitudes and pin down spin speed and tilt under the stated assumptions. Applied to telescope spectra of Luhman 16B, the method finds a large dark region at middle latitudes with honest uncertainty ranges. Exoplanet and brown dwarf mapping gains a more complete accounting of what the data can and cannot show.
arxiv-2605-08644:
Barron Han, Hikmet Yildiz, and Babak Hassibi study error correcting codes whose parity checks may only touch allowed sets of symbols. Such support limits arise in low density codes, locally repairable storage, hardware constrained systems, and quantum codes where sparse checks cut measurement noise. The team derives the best minimum distance any code can reach under a given support mask.

Large enough fields achieve that optimum, yet a counterexample built from a complete bipartite graph shows parity check codes cannot always ride inside generalized Reed-Solomon codes, unlike the generator side. Structured mask families get numeric design guidance. Coding theory gains sharp limits and a warning about which construction shortcuts fail.
arxiv-2605-08744:
Yang and eight colleagues fix an all or nothing flaw in mesh generation. Autoregressive models produce high quality meshes, but when one region disappoints, the entire mesh must be regenerated, wasting compute and destroying good structure. Their framework, MeshFIM, regenerates only a chosen region of a low poly mesh, given the surrounding context.

It tackles three challenges: exact attachment along the exposed boundary, topological order in the context, and overflow beyond the region. Five choices carry the work: markers on boundary vertices, positional embeddings for context, wider context, context augmentation, and a geometry encoder. A gated subtraction mechanism in the encoder focuses generation on the missing region, using the difference between reference and existing mesh. Two applications are shown: brush editing by hand and automatic defect repair on low poly meshes. Experiments show MeshFIM beats baselines in refinement, repair, whole mesh generation, and a stitch back scheme.
arxiv-2605-08844:
Thomas Cass and three coauthors build rough path math for laws driven by two traits at once. Two kernel laws spur the work. One is the signature kernel law. One is the Schwinger-Dyson kernel law. Both live on box or tri form fields. They need sums over two way slices at low smooth rank, past past work. Their frame of jointly held rough paths gives those sums.

In that frame, the signature law is well set and firm. The Schwinger-Dyson law grows from smooth drivers to rough ones. It has a sole fit in the right spaces. Smooth cases tie back to part laws and sum laws. A scheme with worked out cost runs well in tests.
arxiv-2605-09044:
Jiuqi Wang and five co-authors ask a practical question about networks that keep learning new tasks: can we predict whether a trained network can still learn more? Networks often lose this flexibility, called plasticity, after earlier training, and several gauges claim to measure the loss.

The authors show, with counterexamples, that two popular gauges can fail to predict future learning gains in both number and class prediction tasks. They propose a new gauge that mixes how strong a network's learning signal is with how reliable it stays. It carries a proof that it bounds the gain from one training step. In tests it ranked checkpoints by readiness to learn more dependably than the older gauges.
arxiv-2605-09844:
Oliveira built the Metacognitive Probe, an exploratory diagnostic that splits a language model's confidence behavior into five distinct dimensions. Standard composite benchmarks ask whether a model answers correctly, but stay silent on whether it knows when it is wrong. The Probe covers confidence calibration, epistemic vigilance, knowledge boundary, calibration range, and reasoning-chain validation across five tasks and 15 slots.

It ran on a panel of 8 frontier models and 69 human calibrators, motivated by classic work from Flavell and from Nelson and Narens. The author stresses it is a behavioral probe of knowing when you are wrong, not a validated metacognition scale. Its pre-specified human developmental hypothesis was falsified, a result the paper reports openly rather than burying. Knowing when you are wrong, the Probe suggests, deserves its own measurement.
arxiv-2605-10344:
George Wu and nine colleagues scale test-time compute by letting specialized agents team up. Test-time scaling improves language-model reasoning by spending more compute during inference. Yet current methods coordinate parallel paths weakly, or reuse noisy past data with no choice of what to keep. Their 2026 paper proposes TMAS, a framework for multi-agent synergy.

TMAS runs inference as teamwork among specialized agents, with set flows across agents, paths, and rounds. Layered memories aid teamwork: an experience bank reuses sound mid-step conclusions and local feedback, while a guideline bank logs explored high-level plans to steer later runs away from repeat reasoning. Hybrid-reward training keeps basic reasoning, improves experience use, and spurs exploration. On IMO-AnswerBench, TMAS lifted a 30-billion-parameter Qwen3 model from about 65 to about 77 on first-try pass rate, and TMAS with Hybrid-RL lifted a 4-billion-parameter model from about 54 to about 74.
arxiv-2605-10444:
Y. Ricardo Espinosa and two colleagues investigate how urea, a classic denaturant, perturbs bovine serum albumin, a well-studied transport protein, in its acid-expanded F form at pH 3.7. Using dynamics simulations across urea levels from zero to a fully urea-solvated system, their 2026 paper traces how the protein's water shell dries and rewets as urea levels change.

At low urea levels, protein-water hydrogen bonds fall markedly, by 40 percent, while protein-urea links rise, consistent with competitive solvation. At higher levels, urea-urea clumping grows significant, limiting direct protein-urea contact and promoting partial rewetting of the protein surface. Despite these solvent rearrangements, secondary structure stays largely preserved. Local and higher-order features, particularly in Domain III, show increased solvent exposure and flexibility. The findings point to a dynamic balancing mechanism in which urea partly takes water's place in the solvation shell without fully breaking up the bonding network.
arxiv-2605-10544:
Jinchang Zhu and six colleagues reframe long-context tuning as a training problem. Long-context tuning is commonly treated as window scaling: raise training sequence length, keep pretraining, and expect better long-context behavior. That view misses a token-level training mismatch. Longer windows allow longer possible contexts, while causal modeling delivers training one target token at a time. Their 2026 paper introduces EXACT.

EXACT, or Effective-context Allocation for Context Training, measures the exposure spread across real left contexts. It assigns a fixed extra training weight to long real-context targets, distributed by inverse frequency within the long-context tail. Across seven Qwen and LLaMA training setups, EXACT improves all twenty-eight trained and unseen NoLiMa and RULER comparisons. On Qwen2.5-0.5B, it improves NoLiMa by 10.09 points in trained lengths and 5.34 in unseen lengths. Standard QA and reasoning hold steady, with a 0.24 macro change across six benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-10944:
Gabriel Roberto Silva de Lima, Carla Silva Oliveira, and João Domingos Gomes da Silva Junior study the eigenvalues of L-alpha matrices, a family that blends adjacency and degree matrices into one spectrum. The blend offers a single framework for reading adjacency, degree, and Laplacian spectra together.

The team tracks how the spectrum behaves under graph operations and within special graph families, mapping the unified view onto concrete cases. The unified view also clarifies how the three spectra relate as the blend parameter moves. Spectral graph theorists get results that connect three classical matrix pictures through one parameter, simplifying comparisons across graph types.
arxiv-2605-11244: Alexander Pigazzini studies the critical spherical catenoid, a minimal annulus in hyperbolic space whose index Medvedev showed to be at least four. Pigazzini proves its Robin nullity and index in angular mode one both equal two, with kernel spanned by rotation fields. This refines Medvedev's bound. He also gives the boundary radius as the parameter grows large, and the degenerate limit as it approaches one half.
arxiv-2605-11344: Bryan Min and three colleagues build a design space for abstraction in interactive systems, a principle that guides design yet lacks a framework for how it shapes interaction. They survey 457 papers and sort abstraction techniques along six dimensions. They then reframe the gulfs of execution and evaluation through abstraction, spelling out how users and systems cross the abstraction gap. The model ties existing views together and points to new design chances.
arxiv-2605-11444: Eunho Lee, Rei Kawakami and Youngbae Hwang propose a language-model-guided framework for all-in-one image restoration, recovering clean images from diverse unknown degradations. Treating degradations as fixed categories misses the continuous structure of composite damage. Their method injects language-model features into an encoder-decoder through a guided fusion block. It adds a mixture-of-frequency-experts module with a guided router and relational alignment loss. It sets a new best result on the CDD11 dataset, beating prior methods by up to 1 point 35 decibels.
arxiv-2605-11644: Takayuki Kuriyama studies finite watch in good-data learning of context-free tongues. Good data can show two tuples share a context without proving swap. Using finite built-up watches via monoid maps, he defines a watch-guarded tuple swap rule. He gives a set-driven learner getting every language in the full meaning slice for fixed fan-out. Under a fixed branching cap, building is quick. A fixed bound on unknown watch size folds into all-purpose tuning giving back ID, while the endless union stays un-ID-able.
arxiv-2605-11944: Antoine Debouchage and three colleagues address entropic optimal transport when the ground cost function is latent and unseen. Rather than fixing a shape cost, they reveal a shared cost only through samples from a sample optimal coupling. Their transfer system finds couplings for new inputs through a step-by-step path-wise tilting method, moving the coupling jointly with a transport path. Joined with conditional flow matching, it yields a usable paired-data sampler with a global error rate of order delta.
arxiv-2605-12344: Chi and four colleagues ran a preregistered experiment with 470 people to see what happens when AI writes your goals. Machine-written goals scored far higher on SMART quality measures, yet their owners felt less ownership, commitment and importance than people who wrote their own. Two weeks later, far fewer AI-goal owners had acted on two or more goals. Ownership, not goal quality, explained the later outcomes, and the drop hit low-confidence people hardest.
arxiv-2605-12644: Ramler and eighteen colleagues measure fundamental parameters for eighteen hot stars among Ariel mission candidates. Ariel, launching in 2029, will probe many exoplanet atmospheres, so it needs precise host star data beforehand. Uniform values will set the final target list and ground reliable reading of planetary formation and evolution. Cool host stars have been done in full, but hot stars had not. The team applies an iterative spectro-trigonometric method tuned for high-temperature stars.
arxiv-2605-12744: Martínez Alberga and Roitzheim fully describe model category structures for the nonmodular lattice N5. They explain how these structures relate to each other via Bousfield localisation. The work relies heavily on combinatorial objects from equivariant homotopy theory known as transfer systems, yielding a wealth of interactions between combinatorial and homotopical methods. The description covers all model structures on this small but nonmodular lattice, showing how localisation moves between them and how transfer systems encode the relevant data.
arxiv-2605-12944: Wu, Zhang, Hu and Zhang recast fine-tuning data selection as recipe search rather than simple ranking. Instead of scoring examples and keeping a top-k set, their AutoSelection solver hunts for an ordered recipe of filtering, mixing and deduplication steps from a fixed pool. It uses cheap probes and cached signals before any costly full evaluation. On a 90,000-example pool it beats full-data training and simpler selectors across three base models.
arxiv-2605-13444: Hamza Nasir and seven colleagues isolate the monoclinic phase of alpha-RuCl3 in tiny single crystals. Most work applies magnetic fields to suppress antiferromagnetic order and seek a quantum spin liquid. Their magnetic readings map that order's boundary across heat, field and angle. The monoclinic diagram resembles the rhombohedral one, shifted to higher heat and fields. The authors argue that reported spin-liquid anomalies instead come from boundaries between mixed monoclinic and rhombohedral domains. Their results offer a thermal reference for judging spin-liquid claims.
arxiv-2605-13644: Ashok Krishnan, Helene Le Cadre and Ana Busic study games where utility sums a social term and an individual cost or reward term. Agents misread their individual cost or reward. The multi-outcome game is smoothed, and its strictly concave potential function picks a unique equilibrium. That picked equilibrium is an epsilon-equilibrium of the first game, with epsilon set by the smoothing function. A minorisation-maximisation learning scheme moves to the potential-best point faster than gradient and best-reply methods.
arxiv-2605-13844: M. Archita and Karim Johannes Becher study fields where torsion forms split. Over a real field extending a fully square-sum base field by one transcendental step, every torsion square form splits into a right-angle sum of 2-sized torsion forms. The result comes from a broader look at weakly isotropic forms on henselian valued fields and over function fields in a single variable.
arxiv-2605-14344: Wu and three co-authors propose CrystalReasoner, an end-to-end LLM framework for crystals from language instructions through reasoning. CrysReas introduces priors as thinking tokens: symmetry, coordination, and predicted traits, before atomic coordinates. CrysReas then uses reinforcement learning with a dense reward to align generation with validity and stability. Against baselines without thinking traces or RL, CrysReas performs better on diverse metrics, triples S.U.N. ratio, and achieves better results.
arxiv-2605-14644: Morgillo and team build a new way to make positive non-decomposable maps. Such maps are a key tool for spotting bound entangled states, states that stay entangled yet pass a common test. The method uses differentiable semidefinite programming, a form of optimisation with matrix constraints. Certificates of positivity and non-decomposability join gradient search over maps of varied input and output size, under flexible limits on Choi matrices. The search yields new number examples, a parametrised family from masked Choi matrices, and real non-decomposable maps.
arxiv-2605-14844: Witt introduces XFP, a dynamic weight quantizer for language-model inference that flips the usual workflow. The operator sets quality floors on per-channel cosine similarity, and XFP picks codebook size, outlier budget, plus packing per layer, with no Hessian, calibration data, or manual bit-width. Each weight matrix splits into a sparse outlier residual and a dense index tensor into a per-group codebook. On a Qwen model, XFP decodes at one hundred and thirty-eight tokens per second at about ninety-four percent on GSM8K.
arxiv-2605-15044: KiHyun Nam and four others present SpeakerLLM, an audio language model built for speaker understanding. It unifies four jobs in one natural-language interface: profiling a single utterance, reading recording conditions, comparing utterance pairs, and checking claims with evidence in order. A decision policy keeps profile-level evidence apart from the final same-or-different call, laying out conditions, evidence, and call as a structured trace. A layered speaker tokenizer captures speaker evidence at several levels of detail.
arxiv-2605-15544: Dongjin Oh and ten colleagues map the orbital angular momentum texture of a one-dimensional chiral crystal, (TaSe4)2I. They use photoemission with circular dichroism. They find a p-wave orbital texture with dipole shapes. It is tied to the crystal's handedness and can be steered by it. Spin-check tests and first-principles sums show orbital pull swamps spin pull at low energies. The find proves a new kind of orbital texture in crystals. It points to spin-free orbitronics.
arxiv-2605-15744: Haruna Aida and Taro Kimura pin down the multicritical scaling limit of the shifted Schur measure. Under apt scaling and set limits they name the limit shape of strict partitions drawn from the measure. With a multicritical rule in place, they show the edge limit of the correlation function tends to a determinant of the higher-order Airy kernel. This proves in full rigor a shift from a Pfaffian point process to a determinantal law in the scaling limit.
arxiv-2605-16044: Slim and four colleagues present the Quantum Feature Amplification Network, a quantum generative model that reuses one small circuit block by block. Qubit counts then track block size, not data size. With only four qubits it generated full-resolution calorimeter showers of 368 voxels in simulation. A three-qubit version produced small images on IBM hardware, bringing high-dimensional scientific data closer to near-term quantum devices.
arxiv-2605-16144: Quadri and Li propose MAxLM, a multi-agent framework that uses a small pretrained language model to schedule users and allocate resources in MU-MIMO-OFDMA wireless networks. Joint multi-user transmission can lift throughput sharply, but scheduling many stations at once is hard. Their WiSER platform supports autonomous scheduling and resource allocation for uplink scheduled access. Tests with varying station counts and antenna settings show higher uplink throughput than benchmark methods.
arxiv-2605-16344: Zhou and eleven others propose PRL-PUTS, a live RL tool for per-user utility tuning in Pinterest feeds. Utility weights that combine forecast results into one score are usually tuned by hand for all users, slow to track shifting priorities. Their one-step value-based agent selects a utility-weight vector per request context to boost session rewards. At run time, Pareto frontier sweeping via a scalar knob yields a family of policies and a seen frontier for control. Online tests on Pinterest Homefeed raised successful sessions by 0.13 percent.
arxiv-2605-16544: Mousavi and Wang propose TARIPlay in their 2026 study, a testing framework for augmented-reality apps. It finds usable interaction zones inside recorded playback videos. AR interfaces come from the surrounding world rather than fixed screens, so the tool tracks candidate areas over time. It keeps only stable, visible areas for an automated tester to tap. Tested on four open-source apps and nine videos, it reached 55.8% branch coverage on AR code against 41.98% for the Monkey tool in the same experiment.
arxiv-2605-16644: Nonlinear Bayesian filtering struggles to represent belief distributions, and moment filters with polynomial moments need maximum-entropy closure whose partition function cost grows fast with dimension. Iwasaki's team avoids that function outright, using score matching and Stein's identity to reduce the density fit to one linear solve. Their Score Kalman Filter reportedly recovers the classical information-form Kalman filter as one special case. On coupled-oscillator networks up to size 20, it reportedly beats extended, unscented, ensemble, and particle baselines on error.
arxiv-2605-16944: Karni, Cohen and Pick present a quantum adiabatic algorithm for maximum independent set problems on Rydberg atoms, engineered from graph degrees. It extends an earlier method that excites atoms under global controls while the Rydberg blockade blocks neighbouring excitations. Local light shifts favour low-degree nodes, and the final Hamiltonian is constrained so energy scales inversely with excitation count, steering away from non-independent-set states. On one thousand test instances, their degree-dependent method widens the minimal spectral gap and scales better than the standard global protocol.
arxiv-2605-17144: Miao and colleagues steer robot vision-language-action models toward success without retraining them. Their COAST method builds conceptors, linear operators that capture the subspaces linked to successful runs, from a few examples of wins and failures. At run time it nudges the model's hidden states into those subspaces. Tests on three robot policies lift real-robot success by over 40 percent and simulation success by over 20 percent.
arxiv-2605-17244: Chenrui Ma and colleagues propose Drift Flow Matching, a framework joining one-step drift models with iterative flow-based generation.
