It keeps the speed of direct transport maps while letting generation improve across extra inference steps when wanted. That bridge lets sampling compute adapt to quality-versus-efficiency needs, and tests across tasks and datasets show the approach works broadly.
arxiv-2605-17844: Zhiqiang Dai and Yifeng Zhang classify molecules and cells in Gelfand S_n-graphs. W-graphs encode the multiplication action of the standard basis on the canonical basis in the Iwahori-Hecke algebra. Marberg generalized them to Gelfand W-graphs for Hecke algebra modules. The pair introduce a recursive structure for S_n and study its action on molecules. Using it, they prove the distinguished nonnesting molecule is a cell.
arxiv-2605-18144: Christiaan G. A. Viviers's 2026 paper presents pArticleMap, a system that maps the nanomedicine literature and drafts evidence-backed research ideas. Rather than forecast which concepts will co-occur, it hunts thin bridge zones between article clusters and builds citation-grounded hypotheses from retrieved evidence packs. On a retrospective test with a historical cut-off, pooled gold recovery reached 10.8 percent, while about 61 percent of retained ideas landed in the right forward neighbourhood. Human readers agreed only modestly with the internal scores, so the tool supports rather than replaces expert judgement.
arxiv-2605-18244: Shaukat Khan's 2026 paper reports a double-slit experiment in time using light from a single electron. In two back-to-back undulators split by a magnetic detour, one electron emits two time-split pulses whose spectrum carries fringes, just as two spatial slits fringe an angular pattern. Runs at DELTA in Germany and at UVSOR-III in Japan show one electron's spectrum matches a beam spectrum. The result shows coherent photon emission spread over several metres, opening spectral ranges beyond laser-based quantum optics.
arxiv-2605-18344: Barabash and 16 colleagues report in 2026 the first detection of single beta decay in zirconium-96, measured with a low-background detector at the Baksan Neutrino Observatory. The team used enriched zirconium samples and tracked the gamma-ray cascade from the daughter nucleus as it settled to its ground state. Their measured half-life is about 2.27 times ten to the twentieth power years.
arxiv-2605-18944: Arturo de Giorgi, Daniel Naredo-Tuero and Xavier Ponce Díaz map the viable window where majoron dark matter and thermal leptogenesis coexist. The majoron, the Nambu-Goldstone boson of B-L symmetry, touches three puzzles: neutrino mass, the matter-antimatter imbalance and dark matter. Successful leptogenesis makes the scenario predictive by pinning the right-handed neutrino mass scale, fixing the freeze-in abundance and decay couplings. Against warm dark matter limits and indirect searches, part of the surviving window stays open to X-ray and gamma-ray telescopes.
arxiv-2605-19044: Aleksander Cieślak studies the splitting ideal, a combinatorial ideal on the natural numbers, computing its cardinal invariants and its place in the Katětov order. He examines antichain numbers for power-set quotient algebras modulo Borel ideals. For a class including F-sigma and analytic P-ideals, he proves a lower bound for the antichain number from two cardinal invariants. He shows the bounding number bounds the convergent and boring ideals from below, while the reverse inequality is consistent for the Van der Waerden and linear-growth ideals.
arxiv-2605-19144: The CMS Collaboration searches for Higgs boson decays into two neutral scalars of unequal mass, ending with b quarks and tau leptons. The heavier scalar can cascade into two lighter ones when masses allow, with one lighter scalar decaying to two tau leptons. The search uses proton-proton collisions at 13 teraelectronvolts from the CMS detector, totalling 138 inverse femtobarns. No significant excess over Standard Model expectations appears. Upper limits on the decay products range from 0.9 to 36.8 picobarns at 95 percent confidence, varying with mass hypothesis and decay scenario.
arxiv-2605-19344: Yi-Fan Yeh and colleagues study linguistic calibration: the trust words language models use, 'I believe' and 'probably.' Plain scores hide how readers take such hedges, and mixed cues add to the puzzle. They treat trust talk as a spread of likely odds for a claim, and add faithfulness, scored by a new gap measure, as a second test. Their rewrite pipeline, fed by retrieved examples, puts tuned cues back into plain words, lifting faithfulness by up to 66 percent and tuning by up to 58 percent on quiz sets.
arxiv-2605-19444: Lin and team argue that test-time reinforcement gains on math benchmarks are misread. Most gains sharpen already-solvable problems, while problems flipped from right to wrong outnumber truly learned ones, and damage sticks once majority vote locks onto a wrong answer. Tracking single problems shows correct signals in weak problems flash briefly, then vanish, a pattern they call the correct-answer extinction window. Their TTRL-Guard adds flip-aware reward scaling, minority-preserving sampling and sparse risk updates, lifting AIME 2025 results by 54 percent over plain TTRL.
arxiv-2605-19544: Fajfer and Saad revisit weak-triplet models that promise to separate neutrino magnetic moments from masses. Experimental limits on these moments still sit far above Standard Model predictions, so any detection would prove new physics. In Dirac-neutrino models, mechanisms boosting the moment usually inflate mass too, but mixing with weak-triplet fermions was argued to decouple the two. The authors show the minimal version can decouple them only with delicate tuning, and in extended versions decoupling fails: boosting the moment drags mass up with it.
arxiv-2605-20044: Guiyu Liu and four co-workers give 3D Gaussian splatting primitives a clear object identity with a system called OP2GS. Each primitive gains an instance identity plus a second opacity for object-mask rendering, while the original opacity still handles visual reconstruction. That dual-opacity split lets mislabelled Gaussians stay visible in images yet turn transparent in the object-mask branch. Object-level semantic descriptors, gathered by multi-view aggregation, then avoid storing features per Gaussian, and tests show strong open-vocabulary performance at much lower overhead.
arxiv-2605-20244: Jialin Lu and six co-workers present Lean Refactor, a plug-in framework for multi-objective refactoring of Lean proofs. LLM-made proofs are often right but wordy and brittle across library versions. Lean Refactor tackles challenges: proofs balance length, cost, and version fit. It guides a frozen agentic LLM using retrievals from strategies, tagged with versions and compile-cost cuts. Tests show over seventy percent compression on benchmarks, over twenty percent on repos, and up to sixty percent compile-time cuts. Filtered retrieval lifts compression on the target version.
arxiv-2605-20344: V. Vasilyev and nine co-workers study spectral-line sensitivity to granulation, from the Sun to K-type stars. Their line-by-line test from 3D magneto-convection simulations tracks Doppler shift and strength against convective velocity and thermodynamic swings. They test it via MPS-ATLAS spectra from MURaM runs of the Sun, late-G dwarfs, and K dwarfs. With falling temperature, FeI lines show less velocity sensitivity and strength swing; FeII lines react more. Sun-tuned picks do not travel well to cooler stars.
arxiv-2605-20544: Doguhan Yeke and five colleagues study when robot agents should refuse to act, a problem they call the yes-man syndrome. Vision-language planners often press on with vague, impossible, or false instructions instead of abstaining. The authors build a taxonomy of refusal cases and a framework, RoboAbstention, that generates test instructions from images in five robotics datasets. It uses visual grounding, constraint derivation, and controlled generation in three phases.
arxiv-2605-20744: Amit Roth and four colleagues introduce hack-verifiable testbeds for measuring reward hacking at scale. Reward hacking lets agents look successful under a scoring signal while violating the intended goal, yet reliable large-scale measurement was lacking. Earlier studies mostly inspected agent paths after the fact. Their approach instead plants detectable hacking chances directly into testbeds, making cheating checkable by design, and they release Hack-Verifiable TextArena as a first testbed.
arxiv-2605-21044: Cristian Gebhardt, Kundan Kumar, and Florin Radu give a rigorous design for the data-driven stress problem under only normal homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions. Data-driven continuum mechanics enhances classical theory by using finite sets of experimental material data directly, skipping constitutive models. Despite recent progress, its analytical base remains at an early stage. Their problem seeks a stress field meeting balance of linear and angular momenta plus the boundary rules, set within that design.
arxiv-2605-22044: Mengxiao Wang and co-authors propose a physiology and anatomy aware method for spotting myocardial infarction, or heart attack damage, for a cardiac digital twin. Accurate infarct location guides risk stratification, yet late gadolinium enhancement MRI, the gold standard, is costly. Their framework combines cine MRI with multi-lead ECG data to spot infarct areas across varied locations, sizes, extents, and depths, while respecting realistic scar shape and cardiac repolarization. It beats existing inverse inference methods, scoring Dice 0.7391 for scar and 0.5503 for border zone segmentation.
arxiv-2605-22244: Kumari and Kumar study two commuting transcendental entire functions, one of a special polynomial-like form, and prove their escaping sets, filled Julia sets and bungee sets all coincide. The Julia sets therefore match as well, extending a 1998 result by Poon and Yang. They also prove the same coincidence more generally for permutable functions linked through a polynomial relation.
arxiv-2605-22344: The Bernini Team and colleagues unify video generation and editing through a split of labour. A multimodal language model plans meaning, while a diffusion model renders pixels from that plan. The planner predicts a semantic code in embedding space, and the renderer builds pixels from the plan plus text features. Meaning is the interface, so the two parts train mostly apart. A new position embedding handles multiple visual inputs. Bernini leads on a wide range of video generation and editing benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-22444: Hermansson-Truedsson and Kanwar develop normalizing-flow transformations for all-orders quantum electrodynamics corrections in lattice field theory. The method yields all-order corrections without extra Monte Carlo sampling, bypassing complex Wick-contraction diagrams at fixed order. Applied to lattice scalar QED in two, three and four spacetime dimensions, both analytical and machine-learned flows give estimates with far lower variance than standard methods. Flows trained on small lattices still work well on much larger lattices. A fermion generalisation is envisaged, pointing toward lattice quantum chromodynamics applications.
arxiv-2605-22544: Kostiuk and Enevoldsen study prompt effects in task vector models, each tested with a single prompt. Single-point testing misses task phrasing effects. Across 6 models and 11 datasets, shown scores skew score spreads over likely prompts. The default prompt can lowball or hype scores. Rankings are not robust to prompt picks: coders can lift rank by cherry-picking prompts, and under rigged picks any model can reach first place. Single-prompt testing is too thin; benchmarks should use many prompts or report effects with point scores.
arxiv-2605-22944: Mukovnikov and Sousa derive formulas for the ultra-high-frequency second peak of the gravitational wave background from cosmic strings. The peak comes from loops born when friction ruled the early universe. Their formulas fit that share well across the key frequencies and a wide range of string settings, enabling fast and exact characterization. They also map the full range where the peak stands out, wider than earlier reports suggested.
arxiv-2605-23244: Feng and Pilanci propose COALA, a light plan for aligning language models on one GPU. Fine-tuning drove systems like Gemini, but RLHF stays costly. Direct Preference Optimization is simpler but suffers inconsistent ranking accuracy. COALA uses convex tuning, drops the reference model, and cuts training time and VRAM use. Tests across four datasets and six models show good scores using about 17.6 percent of DPO total TFLOPs. COALA shows rising rewards and reaches peak margins faster than DPO. This is the first use of convex tuning.
arxiv-2605-23444: Anzhi Sheng and colleagues build a math framework for random processes on hypergraphs, networks where ties link whole groups rather than pairs. Each person joins several groups of a fixed size. For evolving games, the framework extends the classic rule for when cooperation spreads and gives tipping ratios for multiplayer public goods games that pairs alone cannot capture. For contagions that pass inside groups, it yields a formula for the chance a rare trait takes over.
arxiv-2605-23544: Liu, Tao, and Xin construct polytopes whose Ehrhart polynomials realize any given sign pattern, solving a problem posed by Hibi, Higashitani, Tsuchiya, and Yoshida. The question asks whether a d-dimensional polytope can have negative coefficients at chosen spots and positive ones outside. They first build simplices whose Ehrhart polynomial has leading coefficient m and all other coefficients positive constants. Then, using the product of those simplices with the Reeve tetrahedron, they obtain the first complete solution, plus a fast algorithm for h-star polynomials of a simplex class.
arxiv-2605-23644: Nagy and Weiner study intersection sizes in finite geometries and vector spaces. For a projective plane of order q, the worst-case line count grows like q to the power three halves. The argument extends to balanced block designs and uniform block systems, with upper bounds under weak dependence or bounded pairwise intersections. This yields results for subspaces over finite fields. An elliptic curve construction in prime-order affine planes nearly reaches the optimal order. Every n-uniform linear hypergraph with n edges admits a legitimate 2-coloring.
arxiv-2605-23844: Marko Mićić reports a rare catch: a minor merger, mass ratio near 35 to 1, at redshift 1.824, where the smaller galaxy hosts a bright active nucleus. Webb imaging shows tidal wreckage from an ongoing collision. Chandra counts plus optical spectra pin a luminous output near several times ten to the 45 ergs per second. Standard scaling would demand extreme super Eddington feeding for a small black hole. So Mićić concludes the secondary nucleus hides an overmassive, fast feeding black hole. That gives direct backing for minor merger driven growth.
arxiv-2605-23944: Dong, Jhunjhunwala, and Kanoria model a user telling an AI recommender their preferences through a costly, noisy message. The assistant, acting as a Bayesian agent, forms a posterior belief about preferences and chooses how many recommendations to show, weighing expected choice benefit against search cost. Two user costs are modelled with mutual-information functions: message precision cost and recommendation-set size cost. For large preference spaces, they show posterior sampling demands joint tuning of message bits and set size, while tilted sampling uses only the cheaper of communication and search.
arxiv-2605-24144: Duan and ten co-authors present EVA, a design that speeds large-language-model decoding, the stage where small matrix-vector steps underuse accelerators. Weight-only vector quantization shrinks weights into a shared codebook, but lookups still waste compute and hit memory-bank clashes. EVA instead dots input vectors against the codebook, turning decoding into matrix-matrix work, then reads results through lookups that dodge bank conflicts. Tests report about eleven times the speed and about seven times the energy efficiency of the best lookup design, with precision kept.
arxiv-2605-24244: Chang, Zikry, and Allen present MEDAL, turning static manifold embeddings into models for held-out validation. Methods like t-SNE and UMAP for nonlinear dimension reduction are often picked for looks. Yet their embeddings offer no out-of-sample map and no inverse, blocking held-out checks. MEDAL distills a fitted embedding into a constrained autoencoder whose bottleneck matches the teacher embedding. That yields out-of-sample maps, an approximate inverse, and a distortion measure. Across benchmarks and cases, MEDAL picks embeddings and tunings and spots distribution shift.
arxiv-2605-24444: Kassabov studies time-like surfaces in 3D Minkowski space that admit real limit lines. A Bonnet-type key rule is found: a surface in this class is fixed, up to a motion, by four fixed functions meeting some plain partial slope rules. Standard settings are then defined. In those settings, a surface is fixed, up to a motion, by only two fixed functions. Those functions can be the Gauss and mean curves, meeting a partial slope rule matching the Gauss rule.
arxiv-2605-24544: Maximilian Pierzyna presents JAX-SCM version 1.0, an open-source single-column atmospheric model for boundary-layer research built with the JAX library in Python. It tracks horizontal wind, potential temperature, and specific humidity, with turbulence handled by the MYNN-2.5 closure scheme. Tests on three benchmarks for neutral, stable, and convective cases show close agreement with reference results. Built on JAX, the model gains fast compilation and built-in GPU support, though it is not yet fully differentiable.
arxiv-2605-24644: Long Nguyen-Chi and others study quadratically regularized optimal transport, an alternative to entropic regularization with sparse couplings. One open question was how fast optimizer support concentrates around the Monge coupling. They prove concentration cannot beat a stated power-law rate in directed Hausdorff distance. That rate matches the conjectured best exponent. The value gap also controls mean-squared deviation at a related rate. In the affine Brenier case, a sharp pointwise tube bound follows by reduction to self-transport. A synthetic high-dimensional experiment backs the theory.
arxiv-2605-24744: Ehsan Roohi builds a validation framework for neural scattering kernels used in direct simulation Monte Carlo. A small pointwise deflection-angle error alone cannot prove a learned map is kinetically reliable. Viscosity, collision rates, angular redistribution, mixture relaxation, and diffusion all derive from one measure. The checks combine angular regression, transport cross sections, cumulative measures, spectral content, robustness checks, loss ablations, and mixture tests. On argon-argon and helium-argon data, the surrogate preserves transport numbers within roughly two percent. Mixture tests reproduce mass flow and shear behavior.
arxiv-2605-24844: Chenyou Guo and co-authors introduce Geo-Expert, geological language models tuned with Low-Rank Adaptation. General models often hallucinate about subsurface structures and deep time, while Earth-science AI targets surface sensing and GIS. Geo-Expert fine-tunes three base models on a curated instruction set built with a synthesis pipeline. On Geo-Eval, a domain-aligned 8B model beats large open generalists and GPT-4o on specialized geological reasoning. A 32B variant approaches frontier models, and the tuned 8B model offers competitive cost-performance.
arxiv-2605-25244: Yu Wang and colleagues track how a language model's confidence moves as it reasons, and find a telling split. Correct solution paths tend to gain confidence step by step, while wrong ones flatten or fade. Their confidence-dynamic voting method weighs whole answers by that trajectory rather than by final confidence alone. Across four open model families and several contest benchmarks, the method beats standard repeated-sampling baselines, offering a sturdy signal for picking among candidate answers.
arxiv-2605-25644: Vigliano, Longo and Bošnjak revisit claimed links between high-energy detection in gamma-ray bursts and the shapes of their X-ray afterglows. Earlier claims rested on small or mixed samples. They analyze the full Swift-XRT catalog of more than 1400 events with one uniform, model-free pipeline. They find that both afterglow complexity and plateaus track the observation start time. Once that timing is accounted for, the apparent links to high-energy emission vanish, showing early X-ray shape does not predict high-energy detection.
arxiv-2605-25744: Casagrande, Manacorda and Fodor model how beating oval particles change shape together in dense groups, inspired by the uneven stretching of heart muscle cells. They introduce two deformation types where each particle's stretch follows a regular drive. They map the mix of nematic order and synced shape change across a phase diagram. A fluid description from coarse-graining captures the main collective states of the small-scale dynamics. The model shows how active anisotropic shape change creates waves that self-organize into varied changing patterns.
arxiv-2605-26144: Guo and colleagues introduce VISTA, a benchmark for coding agents turning visual designs into working apps. A pretty screen is not a working app, yet current benchmarks score looks without a backend, or test behaviour from text alone. VISTA hands agents multi-page Figma handoffs and demands runnable full-stack apps. It provides 8,487 human-annotated interactive components. Those span 18 applications. 126 web pages and 576 Android screens are covered. An executable evaluator finds each component in the running app and probes it, giving scores traceable to single requirements.
arxiv-2605-26244: The 2026 benchmark from Tengfei Liu and nineteen colleagues, LongAV-Compass, judges minute-long audio-video generation across text, image, and video prompts. Its 284 curated cases span text-to-audio-video, image-to-audio-video, and video-to-audio-video tasks. They are scored on more than twenty dimensions from segment quality and cross-segment consistency to story coherence and sound-picture sync. Trials on eleven representative models, checked against human judgment, expose losses of identity, narrative, and alignment over longer horizons.
arxiv-2605-26344: García-Cuadrillero, Capitán, and Revuelta introduce Strong Trajectorial Ontological Differentiation, a tool that finds phase-space structures by comparing paths. Unlike older tools, it skips the tangent flow, canceling path parts against each other as in ontological differentiation for word networks. A reversed-time version, FinSTOD, is applied to five model systems of growing complexity, both steady and time-varying kinds. It finds phase-space structures well, adding a useful new tool for chaotic motion.
arxiv-2605-26844: Wang and eight colleagues ask which teacher signals in on-policy distillation actually teach the student. Raw disagreement between teacher and student mixes learnable gaps, where the teacher backs the student's own top candidates, with incompatible gaps, where teacher mass sits outside student support. Their token teachability score separates the two and predicts gains better than raw divergence. A teachability-aware method then beats full-token training while keeping only 5 percent of tokens.
arxiv-2605-26944: In their 2026 study, Karke and five colleagues ask whether object pose and shape estimation is mature enough to beat end-to-end grasp synthesis for robot grippers. Testing parallel-jaw grasps from single-view RGB-D images, they compare one end-to-end method against three modular methods that first estimate pose and shape, then sample antipodal grasps. The modular methods win in every test, even for small objects where the end-to-end method fails, though clutter degrades them. Pose and shape accuracy, they conclude, is the deciding factor.
arxiv-2605-27044: Tan and five co-authors present BatteryMFormer, a multi-level Transformer for predicting full-life battery health paths from early data. An aging-aware decoder injects aging priors, and a meta pattern memory retrieves path prototypes for long-horizon forecasts. A dual-view encoder captures time-based dynamics and state-of-charge-local voltage-current shifts. Tests on four battery domains show it always beats state-of-the-art baselines.
arxiv-2605-27344: Nicholas Boyer and Sharon Hammes-Schiffer present a constrained traveling proton basis for real-time nuclear-electronic orbital theory. The method pins each proton basis center to its proton position expectation value as dynamics unfold. It conserves energy exactly and proves accurate for vibrational frequencies and single and double proton transfer cases.
arxiv-2605-27444: Ruben Belo, Marta Guimaraes, and Claudia Soares test retrieval-augmented generation setups for space operations. They compare search methods, embedding models, and model answers for right answers, good fit, and trust on real domain texts. The setups greatly improve knowledge access, cut doubt, and support hard choices in complex space operations.
arxiv-2605-27644: Marcus Muller and colleagues unify class-specific semantic segmentation with class-agnostic terrain segmentation for outdoor robots. Their Trinity network segments terrain from visual appearance alone, without preset labels or robot-dependent movement scores, learning shared visual terrain priors. Training extends the OAISYS simulator with a synthetic RUGDSynth dataset, plus a real-world EXTerra dataset carrying both label types.
arxiv-2605-27744: Rui Zhang, Chaeeun Kim, and Liting Hu insert a policy-driven runtime layer between agent frameworks and serving engines for multi-agent language models. The layer exposes observe, score, predict, and act primitives sharing agent identity as the common coordinate, hosting nine concrete policies. Validated on KV caching across sessions as CacheScout, it lifts cache hit rate by 13 to 37 points and cuts time to first token by 12 to 29 percent.
arxiv-2605-28344: Tackney and colleagues test digital health scores drawn from full curves, not just hand-picked summary numbers. Layered curve scores track how each person strays from main variation trends at each time scale. In watch-ECG trials and Parkinson's motion data, curve scores held steady, told groups apart, and beat single numbers against gold standards.
arxiv-2605-28444: Jungyong Son and three colleagues tackle reuse of fine-tuning expertise when a new base model version appears. Task vectors, the parameter gap between fine-tuned and base models, cannot transfer directly across different parameterizations. They show such vectors arise as accumulated bilinear interactions between input activations and output gradients. Their BiCo framework aligns both spaces with orthogonal mappings from one forward-backward pass on a small calibration sample, beating existing transfer methods across vision and language benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-28644: Antoine Rocher rechecks the Poisson guess for satellite galaxies in halo occupation models. Standard models assume their counts follow a Poisson distribution at fixed halo mass. He introduces the Conway-Maxwell-Poisson form, adding one knob to explore sub- and super-Poisson ways, with hand estimates and a number scheme true to about five percent. Varying count variance shifts small-scale clumping by up to about ten percent and counts-in-tubes stats by up to about thirty percent, while the tree-level bispectrum barely moves.
arxiv-2605-28844: Yifu Zhao and eleven colleagues propose WASHH, a whale-guided tunable hyper-method for smooth black-box tuning. WASHH uses whale optimization as its hunt core, treating swarm memory, grey-wolf mixing, differential-evolution changes, local search, and anchor refinement as moves. A reward boss hands out tests by gains, while anchor tuning exploits cheap standard setups like box centers. On ten benchmark functions WASHH ranks best or tied on all ten. On breast cancer tests it attains the lowest mean check log loss among rivals.
arxiv-2605-28944: Marco Cusinato, Martin Obergaulinger, and Miguel Ángel Aloy simulate a rapidly spinning 35-solar-mass star collapse with five equations of state. They track how dense-matter physics shapes the low-T-over-W instability in the proto-neutron star and its gravitational-wave and neutrino signals. The instability appears in every model, but its onset time, lifetime, and frequencies vary with structure and spin profile. Its wave frequency rises with compactness and stiffness, so the signal may diagnose the dense-matter equation of state.
arxiv-2605-29044: J. Chamoun-Contreras and colleagues study spectral changes of the B giant star HD75149 between 2004 and 2025. From 25 nightly spectra, they measure speeds and line strengths of 17 lines. H-alpha emission, absorption, and P-Cygni profiles are fit with the ISOSCELES grid. H-alpha varies within days, while metal lines show small speed swings matching pulsation. The largest mass-loss jump is a factor of 1.8 within four days, while terminal velocity hardly shifts, pointing to slow-wind mass-loss bursts and no close partner.
arxiv-2605-29244: Rachel Wang studies energy loss in magnetic structures during turbulent reconnection in Earth's magnetotail. Using data from the Magnetospheric Multiscale mission, she traces how magnetic energy becomes particle energy near reconnecting regions. She finds that electrons moving across the field dominate the loss. Unlike the standard picture of one-way transfer in flat cases, energy flow here tends to run both ways, with only a small net gain for particles. Several electron heating routes are measured, including electric fields along the field and curvature drift.
arxiv-2605-29444: Alvin Hong Yao Yan studies ranking with hidden group bonuses. Determining a linear utility function that correlates with rankings is foundational, and these models assume visibility into the feature sets. But scenarios involve attributes that are hidden or partly observed, yet influence outcomes through bonuses. They study a variant where features are unobserved but may influence rankings through boosts. They develop a framework that infers the parameters and group bonuses matching rankings. Determining it is NP-hard, but with constant feature dimension and group count, a fast solution exists.
arxiv-2605-29544: Duong Thi Huong and Pham Hung Quy prove a sharp bound for the Frobenius test exponent of parameter ideals in generalized Cohen-Macaulay local rings of prime characteristic. The bound combines a logarithmic term in the power where the maximal ideal kills lower local cohomology with a standard invariant of the ring. Sharpness means no smaller general bound of this shape can hold, tightening control over how many Frobenius iterations testing an ideal requires.
arxiv-2605-29744: Yanan Wang and five colleagues ask whether specialist medical models still matter now that generalist chat models shine in clinics. Their answer is a team of generalists, specialists, and clinicians working together. Their frame, HetMedAgent, fuses evidence with an eye to conflicts, calls a clinician when doubt runs high, and tunes decision thresholds on the fly. On three real clinical decision tasks, the mixed team beat either model type alone, with specialists proving hard to replace for modality-specific reads. The paper argues for orchestration over one giant model.
arxiv-2605-29944: Alexis de Colnet and five colleagues simulate quantum circuits by summing Feynman paths over Boolean path variables forming a graph. For a quadratic sum with even modulus and width-k rank decomposition, their program computes an amplitude in a modest exponential in k times polynomial steps. Clifford-plus-T circuits sit at modulus eight, with rank-width never topping linear rank-width. A stabilizer-rank tweak using Gauss-sum tables keeps cost at the same bound, yet turns polynomial on mixed families where pure guarantees blow up.
arxiv-2605-30044: Evgueni Dinvay and Henrik Kalisch introduce a regularized version of the shallow-water equations, the standard model for long waves in shallow water. In the classic system, steep gradients can sharpen into shocks in finite time, breaking the long-wave assumptions behind the model. Their variant softens the nonlinear terms with a bounded operator, removing the usual shock-forming mechanism while staying true to the long-wave regime. They prove local and small-data global well-posedness in Sobolev spaces that rule out singularities, and simulations suggest solitary waves survive.
arxiv-2605-30144: Yulei Ye and 25 colleagues introduce AgentSchool, a multi-agent simulator modelling classroom learning as state transition, not prompted role-play. Simpler simulators collapse learning into persona play. AgentSchool pairs growing student agents with adaptive teacher agents in a multi-scale simulator. Students carry knowledge graphs, thinking workflows and misconceptions. Teachers reflect, scaffold, and plan along the zone of proximal development. Structured students show more mastery and misconception traces than a baseline, and the system shows social patterns such as clique formation.
arxiv-2605-30344: Xiaona Zhou and four co-authors construct VisAnomBench, a benchmark from time-series sets with notes from large VLMs using chosen rewards. Public anomaly benchmarks provide interval labels but not reasons, making VLM fine-tuning for grounded, clear calls hard. Fine-tuning on this benchmark yields VisAnomReasoner, a compact VLM for finding anomalies. On VisAnomBench, VisAnomReasoner spots anomalies better and beats all rivals, raising scores by at least 21 and 23 points. On another benchmark, it transfers strongly, raising scores by about 10 and 13 points.
arxiv-2605-30744: Zhu and colleagues present BijectiveRemesh, keeping a smooth, bijective mapping across remeshing steps on triangle surfaces and tetrahedral meshes. Unlike interpolation or projection methods, it builds a composite map from input to output mesh by chaining local atlases. A Shared Scaffold structure for triangle meshes keeps global bijectivity through local orientation preservation, now covering splits, swaps, and smoothing beyond folds. For tetrahedral meshes, local atlas building extends using Steinitz's Theorem and Maxwell-Cremona lifting. The method enables exact tracking of points, curves, and surfaces across remeshing.
arxiv-2605-30844: Cheng, Tian, and Xu ask whether fine-tuning dulls language models, once output length is held in view. They offer Canopy Entropy, a tree view of generation that counts all possible rollouts, joining length and token choice in one total. From it they draw a plain gauge: whether longer outputs carry more or less news per token. Tuned models show a stronger link between length and news per token, even as total spread falls. Fine-tuning, they argue, does not just shrink doubt but reshapes it into more telling output.
arxiv-2605-31044: Lademann and colleagues study deploying reinforcement learning in an industrial energy system, a thermal heating network. Most prior studies stay in simulation, while real use brings distinct difficulties. They formulate the task as a Markov decision process and analyze challenges along its formal structure, including partial observability, action space design, reward design, and the simulation-to-reality gap. The challenges are grounded in an existing site, where it runs steadily but shows a large performance gap versus simulation.
arxiv-2605-31144: Kimari, Djurabekova and Sarakinos simulate thin films atom by atom with a kinetic Monte Carlo method that teaches itself as it runs. A machine-learning model estimates jump rates from local atomic surroundings, calling in costly exact calculations only where its uncertainty runs high. As confidence grows, fast estimates take over, and a silver-on-silver test reproduces island shapes and densities matching theory and experiment.
arxiv-2605-31244: Nikolaou and colleagues explain neural scaling laws through a new measure called spectral position. It tracks which eigenvalues of the neural tangent kernel drive loss reduction at each point in training. Learning moves from dominant modes into the spectral tail as training proceeds, they find, and bigger models push deeper into the tail than small ones. That extra reach, dubbed spectral reach, may explain why larger models end with lower loss. Feature learning enables the reach by amplifying gradients as training advances.
arxiv-2605-31444: Bankosegger, Eiter and Oetsch try Answer-Set Programming for CARCASS abstractions. Agents learn moves from trial, but huge state spaces make learning hard. Relational learning reasons about things and links, and CARCASS shows how logic-based models map Markov Decision Processes in first-order worlds. First built in Prolog, CARCASS uses domain knowledge for abstractions. The team builds CARCASS abstractions in Answer-Set Programming, a fully declarative language, unlike Prolog. Tests in Blocks World and Minigrid show CARCASS with ASP gives strong abstractions where domain knowledge is at hand.
arxiv-2606-00044:
Aiersilan argues that clinical AI functions as medical regulation, whether lawmakers admit it or not, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Using Lawrence Lessig's idea that code is law, the author contends that system architecture sets the effective standard of care and shifts liability. A tension drives the analysis: algorithms reason by odds, while expert physicians rely on intuition built over years of practice. Existing law assumed human judgment alone, leaving a regulatory vacuum as foundation models enter diagnosis.

The paper likens AI hallucination to human errors such as confirmation bias and premature closure, settling on a diagnosis too early. Because both failure modes mirror each other, they demand one governance response rather than separate regimes. The proposal is a paired standard of care treating the AI-physician pair as a single diagnostic entity. That standard would mandate combining algorithmic precision with human judgment under strong data governance and privacy protection.
arxiv-2606-00144:
He and co-authors speed up text tools that must run on tight hardware. Their method, BudgetDraft, pairs a small drafter with a big checker. The drafter hints at next words, and the checker tests them in bulk. A sparse cache keeps memory low, but match rates fall as text grows long.

BudgetDraft trains the drafter on many cache sizes at once. Each sparse view learns to match one shared full-cache goal. A loss tied to match rates sharpens the full branch. Tests use three long-text sets. The authors report speed gains of up to 6.55 times at 4K length. Gains hold at 4.46 times for 8K and 2.10 times for 16K. Memory stays lean through the run.
arxiv-2606-00244:
Anjapuli, Yadav, and Yanikomeroglu add a high sky relay to help users at a cell's edge. Edge users in towns face weak links from loss, shade, and clash with next cells. A high-altitude platform can catch their data and pass it on. Clear sight lines from that height make the hop strong.

Ground posts send edge data up to the sky post for relay. The team frames a beam-shape task that lifts energy thrift at both posts. The task is bent in shape, so they build a graph net to solve it live. The net reads the web's form as part of its math. Sims show clear gains for edge users. The worst-off fifth of users gain most in thrift terms.
arxiv-2606-00344:
Massion, Makhlouf, and Massart ask how the code used for class tags shapes a late quirk of nets. Trained past clean scores, a net's last traits fall into neat forms. This quirk is called neural collapse in the field. Tag codes had not been put at the core of that tale.

The team use a free-trait model with square-miss training. With one-hot tags and fair data, class means form a tied star at first. As the last-layer fine grows, that star turns to a square frame. The shift mirrors the square shape of one-hot tags. For free tag codes, the last bias works to center the tags. It makes up for the gap twixt tag mean and core.
arxiv-2606-00444:
Ramlal and Zelek test if fixed web forms can join dream-splat views for live physics runs. Physics runs need a fixed mesh web to spot hits fast. Top build tools vary that web to hone shape truth. The team ask if a swap step can bridge the two wants.

Their frame pairs a fixed-web mesh for physics with splat views for show. Run-time point feeds keep the pair in step at speed. Two swap routes are tried: path-tracked links and cast-based casts. Both are set next to a born-fixed tool on a shared set. Each swap route drops shape truth by vast shares. The born-fixed tool wins in spite of the rival's head start. Shape truth and physics form are split aims, they end.
arxiv-2606-00544:
Amin and co-authors show that more than one good reply per prompt can lift model training. Stock fine-tune pairs each prompt with just one reply. Many prompts hold more than one sound end, though. That cut turns a rich spread to a one-draw view, a mode lottery in their words.

Their multi-reply training keeps more than one reply per prompt in the set. Prompts and replies act as split pools of proof in their math. More prompts cut doubt on what comes in. More replies cut doubt on what should go out. That trade calls when extra replies pay and when they fade. Pick rules for replies are weighed with care as well. Gains peak when replies are rich and prompts do not repeat.
arxiv-2606-00644:
Tian and co-authors present ForeSci, a 2026 test of how well AI agents judge future research paths. The test asks which bottleneck to attack or which line of work to back, before proof exists. It holds 500 tasks from four fast-moving AI fields and four kinds of choice.

Each task ships with a knowledge base cut off at a fixed date. Later papers stay hidden and serve only to check the answers. The team tests plain language models, a hybrid search setup, and three research agents. Agents give clearer traces of their proof than search does. But their picks beat plain models only by a small, uneven margin. The authors find a key flaw: agents cite the right proof yet pick the wrong target. Checks that tie each choice back to its proof cut this drift.
arxiv-2606-00744:
Singh and Das design a chip-level way to find edges in images in this 2026 paper. Edge detection is a base step in computer vision. Classic methods like Canny work well but burn much energy and run slow on standard CMOS chips. That hurts small devices where power and speed are tight.

Their method uses magnetic tunnel junction devices, in a spin-based design called SOT-MTJ. The team gives a device-level study of the full system. They set out its write, read, and reset cycles step by step. They then test the design against the standard Canny method. On measures of energy use and delay, they report, the spin-based design looks strong. They present it as a path to low-power, high-speed image work. The study stays at the level of device analysis and measured metrics.
arxiv-2606-00944:
Wang and Zhang add privacy to a popular fine-tuning method in this 2026 paper. LoRA adapts a big model by training a small low-rank update, written as a product of two factor matrices. Many factor pairs give the same update, a freedom called gauge choice. That freedom breaks naive private training.

Standard DP-SGD noise, added to the factors, lands on the update in a gauge-dependent way. The pair show this can blow noise up without bound. Their method, PRISM, adds noise in the tangent space of the update itself. It is gauge-invariant by design and skips the bilinear blow-up. A fast low-dimensional sampler draws the noise. A closed form describes the true noise on the update, so privacy and utility can be traded with care. They prove standard epsilon-delta privacy for PRISM.
arxiv-2606-01344:
Abdussami and co-authors rank old coal sites for future fusion plants. Fusion nears commercial use, and siting needs a system. Good sites must meet technical and economic needs. They must also win public acceptance. Fission history shows the cost of poor siting choices. Their framework is a first of its kind for fusion. It is applied to 85 retired US coal sites. Those plants closed between 2020 and 2025.

The frame scores 21 sub-criteria under four attributes. Policy, risk, and connectivity factors all enter. Five fusion experts weight the sub-criteria via a fuzzy method. Federal incentives and transport rank as top factors. Landslide hazards sway rank stability the most. Sites from three fusion firms get compared too.
arxiv-2606-01544:
Park prunes large language models after training, with a faster search. Deploying such models costs much memory and compute. Post-training pruning cuts weights with no extra training. RIA scores weights by relative importance, normalized by row and column sums. It leads on accuracy among such methods. But RIA uses only 1D cross-shaped directional data. It also weights row and column shares equally. CRePE adds 2D local neighborhood context to the score.

Adaptive coefficients tune the row-column balance in CRePE. It beats existing pruning methods across models and sparsities. Finding those coefficients by perplexity search took about 11 hours. PHO, a proxy-based search, cuts that to about 20 minutes. The found settings transfer well to other models.
arxiv-2606-01644:
Tingay and co-authors describe the Phase III upgrade of the Murchison Widefield Array. This radio telescope sits in Western Australia. The paper is the fourth in a series on its evolution. A new fleet of digital receivers was designed, built, and deployed. They optimize the array for Epoch of Reionisation observations. The array can now correlate all 256 antenna tiles at once. Before, only 128 tiles could correlate at any time. Maximum sensitivity doubles as a direct result.

The count of interferometric baselines roughly quadruples as well. The MWAX correlator fundamentally enables the upgrade. Other subsystem improvements add operational benefits and flexibility. The paper also covers the coming transition toward SKA-Low. Joint MWA and SKA-Low science opportunities get a comment.
arxiv-2606-02144:
Pal studies when averages on a sphere can go wrong in a specific way called smeariness. The work concerns probability measures on a sphere that are absolutely continuous, and it asks how much support they need before smeariness is ruled out. Smeariness comes from degeneracy of the Hessian of the Fréchet function, and that degeneracy can break the classical central limit theorem for Fréchet means. Wald type inference built on that theorem then fails as well.

For densities with rotational symmetry, Pal shows that full smeariness and directional smeariness are in fact the same thing. Two explicit radii that depend on the geometry govern the Hessian and the fourth order terms. In dimensions two and three, such smeariness cannot occur at all for these densities. In higher dimensions, support inside a ball of the larger radius rules smeariness out.
arxiv-2606-02244:
Khawaja and Siksek study a unit equation inside cubic number fields. The equation adds two units of the field to an integer. That integer n excludes minus two, zero, and two. Units epsilon and delta are the unknowns. Cubic fields supply the setting for the equation.

The pair show the equation has no solutions in most fields. For 100 percent of cubic fields, no solutions exist. Fields are ordered by discriminant for that claim. The result matches a recent conjecture by the authors. Number theorists gain a density result on unit equations. Almost all cubic fields are ruled out at once. The remaining exceptional fields are the rare cases left. The proof sharpens what was known about such sums.
arxiv-2606-02444:
Pucci and co-authors study how chatbots respond to people with eating disorders. Such users often seek advice and comfort from language models. The models feel expert, neutral, and easy to reach. Yet they are not built to give clinical advice. The team asks where the interaction turns unsafe.

With clinical eating disorder experts, the team tests prompt patterns. Certain word cues in a prompt raise the odds of an unsafe reply. The team varies the risk level in the prompt step by step. Models adapt to the user without pushback. That adaptation can aid requests that are unsafe or self-harming. The paper maps how far that adaptation goes. It shows the danger in models that simply agree with the user. The findings point to a need for safer guardrails in these chats.
arxiv-2606-02544:
Cui and co-authors bring speculative decoding to diffusion language models. Such models generate text in parallel blocks. They are a fast alternative to autoregressive models. Standard speculative decoding does not fit them. Causal masks give valid token contexts in autoregressive models. Diffusion models use mask tokens and bidirectional attention instead. Context shifts across denoising steps, blocking direct verification.

Their method, SimSD, adds a plug-and-play masking strategy. Reference tokens come from a draft model's predictions. A designed attention mask governs how they interact with current-step tokens. The model then scores drafted tokens in a single forward pass. The method is training-free. It stacks with KV cache and blockwise decoding. Tests on SDAR-family models across four benchmarks show up to 7.46 times higher throughput. Generation quality holds or improves.
arxiv-2606-02644:
Jones and co-authors set out when AI agents should refuse cybersecurity tasks. Agent scaffolds have boosted performance on long, complex tasks. Offensive security gains both benefits and risks. Current benchmarks measure proficiency at attack tasks. They skip the refusal question. This work presents the first framework for refusal boundaries in offensive security.

Three parts define the framework. Principled criteria say when tasks should be refused. Categories list which tasks warrant refusal. An evaluation method measures robustness under benign and adversarial conditions. The framework is applied to web-based offensive security scenarios. Six of eight frontier models show near-zero refusal rates. Only GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.1 Codex refuse in any meaningful way. The gap between skill and restraint is stark. The framework gives the field a way to measure both at once.
arxiv-2606-02844:
Lira and Peralta address a known flaw in density functional theory, or DFT. The flaw arises when chemists compute magnetic exchange couplings for open-shell systems. Broken-symmetry solutions can suffer from spin contamination. That error tends to inflate the coupling values.

The pair try a different route. They add a constraint to the DFT energy that forces a target value for the spin-squared expectation. A Lagrange multiplier enforces the target during the calculation. They derive the formulas needed to use the constraint in a generalized Kohn-Sham scheme. They then test the method on three systems, from a small helium pair to a copper complex. The constrained results are lower and more consistent across functionals than three rival schemes. The authors present the method as a general tool for magnetic studies.
arxiv-2606-03444:
Tang and co-authors merge many vision foundation models into one lean model. Each such model has its own strengths in reading images. A single distilled model often suffers negative transfer, where skills clash and weaken. Their framework, PRISM, avoids that clash by design. It uses a dual-stream mixture of experts.

The build runs in two stages. First, a router that knows the teacher guides experts to split into distinct skill areas. That split cuts the interference between them. Next, the router learns to recombine experts for each new task. It assembles custom paths through the expert pool as needed. Tests on PASCAL-Context and NYUD-v2 set new best scores. The gains support sparse, self-organized specialization as a path that scales. Readers see how rival model strengths can add up instead of canceling out.
arxiv-2606-03744:
Wang, Balwada, and Xie split ocean kinetic energy into wave and mean-flow parts across scales. Separating waves from mean flows is a basic problem in ocean dynamics. Passive-tracer time series in the Lagrangian frame split cleanly by time scale. The team applies that filtering to surface drifter data. A generalized Lagrangian mean frame assigns filtered velocities to mean positions, not particle paths.

Gulf of Mexico drifters supply the observations. Second-order structure functions are computed for each component across spatial scales. Helmholtz splits of unfiltered data alone, the authors warn, are not a true wave-mean split. Mean-flow energy is rotation-dominated above about one kilometer. Below that scale, divergent and rotational parts share energy evenly in both seasons. Winter mean flows are more active than summer ones. Wave energy sits at smaller scales in winter than summer. Oceanographers get sharper scale budgets for surface motion.
arxiv-2606-04644:
Buffa, Miehling, Picasso, and Renoldner establish the mathematical foundations for simulating shear Alfvén waves in plasma, in a 2026 arXiv paper. It is a simplified sub-model of the drift-reduced Braginskii equations used for fusion plasmas. They add a Poincaré-type inequality along the field's integral curves. It is valid under a geometric directedness condition on the field.

They show the geometric condition holds in tokamak and stellarator configurations, the two leading fusion device shapes. It conserves a discrete energy exactly in the homogeneous case. It comes with error estimates in the natural energy norm. Numerical experiments in two and three dimensions confirm the theory.
arxiv-2606-04744:
She and coauthors work on writing whole numbers as sums of three squares in this 2026 arXiv paper. An almost prime number has only a bounded count of prime factors, counted with repeats, in this study. Their target numbers are large, leave remainder three on division by twenty four, and avoid factor five.

They prove each such number is a sum of three squares whose product has at most sixty seven prime factors. Each number being squared can also be chosen with at most twenty seven prime factors. Both bounds beat the earlier best bound of seventy two prime factors for the product case. Their proof mixes higher dimensional sieve methods, which filter numbers by prime factors, with a weighted sieve method. A side result cuts a related bound from one hundred eighteen prime factors down to just eighteen.
arxiv-2606-04844:
Vo, Zaheer, and Park rescue automatic sound classification from background noise using only text, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Contrastive audio-language models like CLAP classify sounds zero-shot by matching audio embeddings to text prompts, with no labeled audio. Under acoustic noise this matching breaks down: accuracy and mean average precision fall by twelve to thirty percentage points at zero-decibel signal-to-noise ratio. Their Drift-Augmented Scoring adds a small per-class bonus to the cosine score.

The bonus rewards a class when the noisy audio embedding drifts in the direction that the class's noise-conditioned text prompts predict. It is derived from text alone and costs one inner product per class at inference. On a LAION CLAP backbone, the method improved every test condition, gaining up to 5.75 accuracy points on UrbanSound8K and up to 1.74 mean average precision points on FSD50K.
arxiv-2606-04944:
Ou and colleagues show that a plain perceptron, properly taught, beats architectures at predicting clicks, in a 2026 arXiv recommender systems paper. Click-through rate prediction drives online advertising revenue, and research has chased complex dual-stream designs. Those designs suffer heavy computation, overfitting risk, and imbalance. Their DS-MLP instead distills explicit knowledge into a main perceptron while a parallel perceptron captures implicit interactions.

Two alignment strategies keep the twin streams compatible during training, so neither swamps the other. The final model is just the vanilla perceptron structure, yet it achieves state-of-the-art performance across three widely used benchmarks. The result is a useful corrective for the field: the gains attributed to complexity may largely be available from careful training of a simple model.
arxiv-2606-05144:
Yimeng Tang and colleagues measure new distances to galaxies in the NGC 1052 field in this 2026 arXiv paper, testing the bullet-dwarf origin proposed for a trail of dwarf galaxies. Two ultra-diffuse galaxies, DF2 and DF4, appear to lack dark matter. A third, DF9, was added to a trail said to have formed when two gas-rich dwarfs collided head-on at high speed. The trail might instead be a projection artifact overlapping a foreground group near 13 megaparsecs.

Using Hubble imaging, the team derived surface brightness fluctuation distances for eight trail dwarfs plus the galaxies NGC 1052 and NGC 1035. All the dwarfs sit near 20 megaparsecs, not with the foreground group. For DF2, their distance of 17.7 megaparsecs disagrees with the red-giant-branch value of 21.7 megaparsecs, while new James Webb observations give 17.6 megaparsecs, matching the fluctuation result. The authors call for uniform Webb imaging of the remaining trail dwarfs.
arxiv-2606-05344:
Cassidy Walker and Darryl Seligman compute how fast interstellar objects move across the sky and what that means for discovering them, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Three macroscopic interstellar objects have been found passing through the Solar System in the past decade, implying a much larger unseen galactic population.

The authors derive an analytic solution for the apparent sky motion of an object on an arbitrary orbit observed from an arbitrary location. It is faster and leaner than the usual numerical approach. They generate three populations of one hundred thousand objects inside heliocentric spheres of different radii and compute sky motions as the objects brighten past various detection thresholds. The three known objects move at speeds broadly typical of populations with similar brightness. The distribution tails extend beyond the discovery speed of the first known object, suggesting dim, fast interstellar visitors traverse the Solar System undetected.
arxiv-2606-05544:
Chuyang Chen and colleagues test what sound models actually learn about space in a 2026 arXiv paper. Modern audio models turn recordings into compact codes for later tasks. Some are trained on spatial audio, which carries clues about where sounds come from. How much of that spatial detail survives in the codes was unclear. The team built a controlled test set, called SARL, to probe the codes directly.

SARL checks source traits such as direction, height, distance, and sound type. It also checks room traits such as echo time, size, and shape. Across many models, source traits proved far easier to read from the codes than room traits. How a model takes in sound, and how it was trained, shaped what it kept. Small controlled changes to the sound drew uneven responses. The authors release SARL freely so others can repeat the test.
arxiv-2606-05744:
Minxin Chen and colleagues test vision-language models on the maps planners actually draw in a 2026 arXiv paper. Planning maps encode land rules, strategy, and law in dense visual form. Reading them demands fine perception, spatial reasoning, and professional judgment at once. General image benchmarks miss that mix. PlanBench-V is the first benchmark built for planning map reading.

Its database holds two hundred twenty-three expert-annotated maps and over sixteen hundred question pairs. Planners from many regions and styles supplied the material. Scoring climbs four steps: perception, reasoning, association, and implementation. Those steps mirror how a human planner works through a map. Two generations of vision-language models took the test. Scores show a clear line of progress between generations. Hard problems persist, above all where policy knowledge must guide the eyes. The benchmark gives the planning field a shared yardstick for AI readiness.
arxiv-2606-05844:
Hassan Jalil Hadi, Yasmin, and Shoker benchmark language models as writers of intrusion defense rules in a 2026 arXiv paper. Rule-based detection systems block known attacks, but hand-written rules lag new threats. Public datasets teach traffic labeling, not rule writing. The GenTI dataset gathers one hundred fifty thousand detection rules from Snort, Suricata, and threat feeds. Fifty thousand YARA rules join them, annotated with behavior and response data.

A model pipeline turns analyst prompts and sample payloads into deployable rules. A verification loop checks each rule's syntax, meaning, and safety before release. The system earned a composite quality score near eighty-nine percent. Its rules covered about ninety-five percent of the linked threat intelligence. Detection of unseen attacks jumped from forty-five percent to about eighty-seven percent. False positives fell as well. Generated rules, the authors argue, can keep pace with zero-day threats.
arxiv-2606-06244:
Xi Yang and co-authors expose a way to steer chatbot opinions with fake evidence in this 2026 arXiv paper on language model safety. Their attack, Ghostwriter, starts with a misleading claim and dresses it in fabricated rationales that carry markers of credibility, such as formal structure and confident sourcing. The target model is then prompted to fold those viewpoints into its answers. The worry is that models trust supplied context far too easily.

Tests on the BBQ and ToxiGen benchmarks and a specialized dataset showed commercial models without external safety classifiers were highly vulnerable. Even frontier models guarded by classifiers, including GPT 5.4 class systems, reduced the attack but did not stop it. The team also tried defenses. A tailored safety policy let the gpt oss safeguard model catch eighty one percent of the attacks, the best result they found, though a real gap remains.
arxiv-2606-06744:
Dating apps, job markets, and residency matches all pair two sides that learn about each other slowly. Zong, Liang, Zhou, and Jaques argue that standard matching models miss that slow reveal in this 2026 arXiv paper. They build a framework where feedback stretches over time: interviews cost effort, meetings give noisy clues, and partners can stay or split as hidden traits emerge.

Their testbed, Learn2Match, lets software agents decide whom to interview, whom to match with, and when to walk away. It scores policies on regret, total welfare, and a friction loss that measures the welfare lost because true preferences stay partly hidden. A reinforcement learning method beat a bandit style baseline on welfare and regret, yet it still lost more to hidden information than structured matching methods do. The authors offer the benchmark as a proving ground for the next generation of matching algorithms.
arxiv-2606-07144:
After a fireball fades, a surviving meteorite drifts with the wind for its last thirty kilometers. Devillepoix and Cupák model that dark flight in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their Freo Doctor system runs weather models at one kilometer resolution over the fall zone. Different model start times give different winds, and the spread becomes an uncertainty estimate.

The shifts matter more than hunters assumed. A one kilogram meteorite lands a median of one hundred forty three meters from the no wind prediction. A ten gram rock doubles that offset. Both figures vary by over tenfold between events, worst during extreme weather. The wind uncertainty beats the error in the fireball's measured trajectory. Higher resolution models outperformed coarser ones. The team has guided searches to twelve recovered meteorites with these forecasts. They release over a thousand model runs covering falls and spacecraft re-entries worldwide.
arxiv-2606-07344:
Nelli studies how a few restless agents can rewire how a whole system connects in this 2026 arXiv paper on agent-based models. Agents wander a landscape with several attractor regions, natural resting zones. Most agents stay local, while a small fraction move far more and explore. The question is when those explorers knit a fragmented landscape into one connected transition network, and what does the knitting.

Testing random-walk exploration, interface-sensitive movement, novelty-seeking, and a flat-landscape control revealed a clear pattern. Switching between regions happened overwhelmingly near the boundaries between attractors, making interfaces the critical gateways. As the explorer fraction rose, the system shifted from split to more connected, and local boundary crossings accumulated into global structure. The effect survived even with plain random walks, so no intelligence or tuning is required. Removing the landscape structure destroyed the mechanism entirely, showing structure and mobility differences must interact.
arxiv-2606-07544:
Etchie and Taiwo propose embedding AI tutoring inside the school learning platform itself, in this 2026 arXiv paper. They also propose following students for years to measure what changes. Middle schoolers who fall behind often get help too late, after misconceptions harden, while learning management systems shuffle assignments and grades. Their design adds policy-gated AI assistance to coursework: formative feedback and hints, review recommendations, adaptive practice driven by mastery estimates, and teacher dashboards flagging misconception patterns and struggle.

Because the users are minors, the design is privacy-first, with data minimization, role-based access, age-appropriate response constraints, and auditable interaction logs. The accompanying longitudinal study would track learning traces, attempts, revisions, help-seeking, and pacing, and link them to outcomes through high school and beyond where institutions allow. That horizon is the paper's distinguishing bet: separating tool adoption from changes in learning trajectories requires following students across school transitions.
arxiv-2606-07644:
Jacobs and Frank build a spectral theory for scale-invariant operators and show two exponents that physics treats as one are independent, in this 2026 arXiv physics paper. Their setting is operators on the multiplicative half-line, where rescaling inputs rescales the kernel by a power law. They prove such kernels must factor into a power-law envelope times a shape function of the ratio. The Mellin transform, a transform adapted to scaling, diagonalizes them into power-law eigenfunctions. Eigenvalues come from the transform of the shape.

The geometric exponent governs how matrices scale under dilation, while the other, read from how eigenvalues decay in approximations, depends on the shape function. For an exponential-in-logarithm kernel, the eigenvalue profile is a Lorentzian bump rather than a power law, so the two exponents differ. Equality marks a critical fixed point of the renormalization group; inequality is their characterization of multicriticality.
arxiv-2606-08044:
Enyi Jiang and co-authors show that a language model can pass every behavioural safety test while staying easy to corrupt, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Safety is usually judged by outputs: does the model refuse harmful requests? The authors name the blind spot the audit gap, the difference between safe behaviour and robustness when someone intervenes inside the model, through fine-tuning or direct perturbation of its internal activations.

To measure the gap they build dissociated models: systems trained to behave safely on the surface while staying vulnerable inside. Their Latent Vulnerability Score measures how easily bounded internal perturbations elicit harmful behaviour. Intermediate layers proved most sensitive. Across aligned models, behavioural metrics failed to predict the score: dissociated models scored substantially higher despite refusal behaviour matching robust models. Output-level audits alone, they conclude, certify less than the field assumes.
arxiv-2606-08344:
César–Adair Rodríguez–Castro and co-authors bring game-theoretic control to a delayed temperature system, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The design extends the Nash equilibrium algorithm from game theory, where each controller's strategy is a best response to the others. It targets systems whose state depends on past values, a delay common in thermal processes. The performance index is of linear-quadratic type, balancing state deviation against control effort, with cross terms coupling the players' costs.

The derivation proposes the strategies' form, closes the loop, and fixes the strategy parameters using the Bellman equation as a constraint. The closed loop is shown to be stable, so the rival controllers cannot upset the plant. The algorithm was implemented on a thermal prototype run by an ESP32 microcontroller. It was compared against tuned proportional-integral controls in two commercial units.
arxiv-2606-08444:
Jieming Zheng, Guan, and Liu study language models inventing software libraries that do not exist, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Package hallucination, where a model confidently suggests a non-existent dependency, is an emerging security risk. Attackers can register the invented name and poison future installs. Earlier studies covered popular languages such as Python and JavaScript. This paper presents the first large-scale study of crate hallucination in generated Rust code, where libraries are called crates.

The authors built a multi-source dataset combining coding tasks from question sites and code repositories. They evaluated commercial and open-source models under various decoding settings. Rust behaved differently from the earlier languages. Different models showed surprisingly consistent hallucination rates. The analysis characterizes when invented crates appear and evaluates mitigation strategies. The upshot for Rust teams is plain: check each crate a model names before you trust it in a build.
arxiv-2606-08644:
Soyoung Oh and Demberg identify the circuit a language model uses to keep track of who has what, in this 2026 arXiv paper. To interpret context correctly, a model must bind entities to their attributes and update those bindings as state changes. If two characters swap objects, later pronouns depend on the new bindings. Using causal interventions, patching internal activations to test their effect, the authors analyze this binding process in dynamic state tracking tasks across two model families.

They identify a retrieval-conditioned rebinding mechanism: a compact circuit of attention heads that encodes swap-relevant binding information and reinstates it at readout, when the answer is produced. The circuit supports rebinding in both families, but its signature differs. In one family it is expressed in the query and key subspaces of the relevant heads. In the other it rides primarily in the key vectors.
arxiv-2606-08844:
Liu, Wang, and Shen fuse fisheye cameras with LiDAR so cheap vehicles can still detect objects in 3D, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Cost-sensitive platforms pair two wide fisheye cameras with one roof LiDAR instead of a robotaxi's dense sensor suite. The catch is geometry: fisheye images are distorted, the cameras barely overlap, and standard fusion forces both sensors into one flat grid early, mangling fisheye features. GA-HF respects each sensor's geometry.

Fisheye features are lifted into a polar grid preserving their angular density, while LiDAR stays in Cartesian space for box fitting. A dual-attention module then cleans the warped camera features, suppressing junk at the distorted edges. On the KITTI-360 benchmark the method improved the score by 4.2 percent over Cartesian baselines. On Dur360BEV it beat LiDAR-only sensing and BEVFusion, with much lower orientation error, and on Fisheye3DOD it scored highest among fusion methods.
arxiv-2606-08944:
Ye and colleagues use cooperating language-model agents to optimize hardware designs too long for one model to read, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Real RTL code, the register-transfer-level description from which chips are built, runs to thousands of entangled lines with few module boundaries. That defeats LLM optimizers built for short snippets. Their framework, LongRTL, splits the work among three agents guided by graph similarity. A Partition Agent cuts the design into syntax-tree subtrees, matched against reusable templates.

An Optimization Agent then rewrites each submodule, guided by retrieval over both syntax trees and RTL examples. A Reconstruction Agent reassembles the pieces in logic-aware order, checking the whole still computes the same function. The authors report that the synthesized results keep full functional equivalence while improving power, performance, and area by about 25 percent on average over the original designs. That showing surpassed all baselines tested.
arxiv-2606-09044:
Tonioni and colleagues build a surrogate forecasting near-wall turbulence from sensors, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Turbulent flow near a wall cycles through active and quiet phases, but simulation is expensive. The team studied the minimal flow unit, the smallest channel that sustains turbulence, at a friction Reynolds number of 200. Their framework compresses flow fields into a four-dimensional latent space with a beta-VAE-GAN. A sensor-conditioned Transformer then forecasts the latent variables.

Compression recovered 87 percent of turbulent kinetic energy in four latent dimensions, beating the baseline by more than 10 percent. The latent coordinates proved meaningful, capturing the near-wall regeneration cycle's rhythm. From a window of only 128 time units, the Transformer stayed accurate over 17,288 time units. End-to-end, reconstruction retained 82 percent of the energy. The weakness is rare, extreme-amplitude events, which the bottleneck smooths away because the encoder favors common states.
arxiv-2606-09144:
Researchers present a packaged version of a brain-imaging data organizer, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The text carries no byline; BIDSme was developed at the GIGA-CRC Human Imaging research unit. BIDS, the Brain Imaging Data Structure, is the standard for organizing neuroimaging datasets for sharing. Converting raw scans into BIDS format is complex and often manual, because protocols vary widely.

BIDSme is a semi-automated tool for that conversion, handling renaming, restructuring, and metadata enrichment more flexibly than rigid converters. Its weakness was distribution: local installation kept it from non-technical users. The paper containerizes BIDSme with Docker and Docker Compose, so the environment travels with the tool. The authors detail design choices and validation, aiming at a lightweight application integrating with platforms like Neurodesk. Containerization turns a lab utility into something any imaging group can run identically, a real reproducibility win.
arxiv-2606-09344:
Lin-Qing Chen and Flaminia Giacomini ask how to describe gravity in relative terms when the reference frames themselves are quantum in this 2026 arXiv paper. General relativity has no external stage: positions and times must be defined against physical parts inside the theory. Once gravity is quantum, those reference systems are quantum objects too, and their back-reaction cannot be ignored.

Working within weak-field quantum gravity, the authors introduce quantum reference fields. These are four dynamical scalar fields whose stress-energy enters the gravitational constraints, serving as local reference systems throughout spacetime. Generalising the perspective-neutral approach to quantum reference frames, they show that gauge-invariant relational observables have reduced descriptions from each field's perspective. They derive the unitary transformations connecting those perspectives, which act like coordinate changes with a quantum field in place of the classical gauge parameter.
arxiv-2606-09644:
Yimu Wang and his co-authors build a test that checks not just what a vision-language model answers, but where it looked in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such models score well on image questions. Yet a right answer can rest on the wrong view. In driving scenes, six cameras ring the car, and a hazard may show in only one of them.

Their benchmark draws on the NuScenes driving set. It holds one hundred twenty-two conflict-centred questions from seventy-three scenes. The themes span cause, what-if twists, and intent. For each, the model must name the view that holds the proof. The team tests view choice alone, answers given the true view, and both tasks in one pass. An automatic miner proposed the view labels, and humans checked them. By splitting source choice from answer skill, the test exposes grounding faults that plain scores hide.
arxiv-2606-09844:
Faouzi El Yagoubi, Godwin Badu-Marfo, and Ranwa Al Mallah show that chatbots guard private data less tightly when the asker is a machine in this 2026 arXiv paper. Safety tuning was built for human users. In live systems, models now talk to other agents through set protocols. The team call the gap the Interlocutor Effect: the model's care drops as the recipient sounds more technical.

They tested two hundred twenty-two touchy scenes across three thousand four hundred sixty-four chats. Framing the recipient as an AI agent raised leaks of personal data by up to twenty-three points. A factorial design pinned part of the blame on the technical framing itself. Inside one model, a pilot probe backed a sharper claim. Safety-linked attention heads seem to go quiet in agent chats. Killing one such head in a test model sparked leaks, while waking it restored the guard.
arxiv-2606-09944:
Kandasamy proposes a new way to track whether national prosperity is truly shared, in a 2026 arXiv paper on economic measurement. Headline GDP per capita, the average output per person, ignores both income inequality and price differences. Existing adjusted measures exist, but none works as a simple yearly trigger that regulators can compute from public data. His index aims to fill that operational gap.

The index, called GAGI, rescales GDP per capita by one minus the Gini coefficient, a standard inequality score, and by price level, against a 2010 baseline. Applied to the G7 economies from 2010 to 2026, GAGI shows welfare-adjusted prosperity pulling away from headline growth, with the gap widening sharply after 2022. The United States shows automation without absorption, while Italy and Japan show stagnation without automation, patterns that look identical in plain GDP terms. Nordic comparators Denmark and Sweden instead show automation paired with absorption.
arxiv-2606-10144:
Nathan Sitaraman and his team grow a sharper guard layer for superconducting quantum devices, in a 2026 arXiv paper on materials science. Superconductor-dielectric interfaces strongly affect coherence times, the brief windows during which quantum devices hold information. The damage is blamed on two-level system defects in disordered surface oxides, which couple to device fields and cause dissipation.

The team explains zirconium oxide's special behavior through the chemistry of the niobium-zirconium-oxygen system: it forms a crystalline layer, keeps a sharp boundary with metallic niobium, and prevents oxide regrowth. They show a new growth method making air-stable zirconium oxide with higher crystallinity and a sharper interface than shown before.
