Microscopic analysis, including X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and electron ptychography, gives the first full picture of these capping layers. The advances target lower-loss interfaces and longer coherence in superconducting quantum circuits.
arxiv-2606-10244:
Ohkawa and colleagues present a handheld interface for collecting bimanual robot manipulation data at scale, in a 2026 arXiv paper on robotics. Robotic foundation models improve with the volume and diversity of training demonstrations, but collecting them with real robots is slow and costly. Handheld gripper systems in the UMI tradition let operators demonstrate tasks without a robot, recording wrist-camera views and trajectories. Existing designs use pistol grips that offset the operator's fingers from the gripper's pinch point, adding bulk that limits dexterity, and some tracking setups require heavy headsets.

Their interface, YUBI, is a lightweight finger-aligned gripper that mirrors human finger kinematics, so the operator's digits drive the gripper directly. By making demonstration collection cheaper and more natural, YUBI facilitates curating a large-scale, high-quality bimanual dataset to advance robotic foundation models and vision-language-action policies.
arxiv-2606-10344:
Morris and colleagues prove that a class of nonlinear control systems can be rewritten exactly as bilinear systems in a lifted space, in a 2026 arXiv paper on control theory. Focusing on discrete-time systems, they show that under smoothness and regularity conditions, nonlinear dynamics become exactly bilinear when states and inputs are separately lifted into reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces.

Their function space is defined by a linear-radial product kernel chosen to respect knowledge of an equilibrium at the origin. Its functions are spanned by products of component and radial basis functions. The stabilization problem, finding a feedback law certified by a Lyapunov function, is then addressed in the lifted bilinear form, where more control machinery applies. Numerical experiments with publicly released code illustrate the approach. The exactness of the representation, rather than an approximation, is the paper's central theoretical claim.
arxiv-2606-10644:
Yang and Sergey revisit a solver experiment in this 2026 arXiv extended abstract on programming tools. The setting is e-graphs, data structures storing many equivalent versions of a program expression, used by equality saturation optimisers. Extracting the cheapest expression is NP-hard, and a 2023 attempt by Philip Zucker to use answer set programming gave unconvincing results. The authors pinpoint what makes the answer set approach work in practice.

With those fixes, the naive encoding runs comparably to the well-optimised integer programming extractor in the extraction-gym benchmark. It even finds several extra optimal extractions on complex instances. The piece closes as part experience report, part research agenda on answer set programming as a more powerful Datalog partner for e-graphs.
arxiv-2606-10744:
Bhargava and colleagues make two noisy quantum channels cancel each other in this 2026 arXiv paper on quantum information. Quantum channels, the processes a quantum system undergoes, usually degrade coherence and entanglement. This work superposes two channels, using one control qubit to combine their Stinespring dilations, the embeddings of noisy processes, on a shared ancilla. The authors derive rules for such a combination to be a valid channel, then apply it to dephasing and depolarising channels.

Two dephasing channels can cancel destructively, restoring the coherence each alone would destroy, and two zero-capacity depolarising channels can transmit quantum data: superactivation of capacity. Both effects are shown on NMR hardware: dephasing cancellation on a three-qubit register, depolarising cancellation on a five-qubit register. It is a new form of noise control, built from interference rather than correction, with possible uses in quantum communication.
arxiv-2606-10944:
Gong and colleagues make attention approximation usable inside language models in this 2026 arXiv paper. Attention costs grow with the square of sequence length, and the best approximations ignore the causal mask, the rule that each token may only see earlier ones. Their tool, Express, converts a non-causal approximation into a causal one with matching guarantees.

Paired with the Thinformer approximation, Express beats the best known causal guarantees, at memory linear in a tunable budget and modest compression overhead. An I/O-aware Triton implementation runs substantially faster than FlashAttention 2. The authors aim it at four bottlenecks: long-context prefill, cache compression, and long-form decoding under tight memory or compute.
arxiv-2606-11044:
Jonkers and Ziegel extend a forecasting method in a 2026 arXiv paper on uncertainty quantification, putting honest error bands around predictions. Conformal predictive systems output calibrated bands of distribution functions, ranges containing the truth at stated rates, but classic versions assume exchangeability, that data arrive in no special order. Real data shifts: new cases differ systematically from old ones, breaking that assumption.

Their generalization encodes shift through observation-specific permutation weights, numbers saying how likely each past case is to stand in for the test case. The system stays valid whenever the test point is, in effect, a weighted draw from the observed sample. Because weights are usually estimated, they add weight-uncertainty boxes and build robust envelopes with finite-sample or asymptotic guarantees, plus efficient computation for three variants. Experiments under covariate shift and biomolecular design show bands widening as shifts grow stronger and tightening as sample size increases.
arxiv-2606-11244:
Liu and five co-authors present SPEAR in a 2026 arXiv paper, a system for serving large language models cheaply at low bit-widths. Quantization, storing weights in fewer bits, is the main lever for cutting serving cost. Even strong 4-bit quantizers leave a quality gap versus FP16, worst at smaller scales. The authors trace the gap to a mismatch: quantization error is strongly input-dependent, varying several-fold across tokens, while existing compensation is static.

SPEAR adds lightweight Error Compensators, small correction modules with per-token gates, at the most error-sensitive layers, which a Centered Kernel Alignment diagnostic identifies. Systems work keeps them cheap: adaptive kernel fusion, an epilogue-integrated peer-reduction kernel, and SLO-constrained scheduling. Across challenging per-channel settings, SPEAR closed 56 to 75 percent of the perplexity gap between 4-bit and FP16 models. It added under one percent extra memory at latency comparable to standard 4-bit serving.
arxiv-2606-11344:
Ziampras and Birnstiel simulate planet formation during accretion outbursts in a 2026 arXiv paper. Accretion outbursts occur in many young stellar objects, but models of them have mostly been axisymmetric, because full simulations are expensive. The authors ask whether outbursts are azimuthally stable, and what happens to planetesimal formation during them, at the inner edge of the disk's dead zone.

They ran high-resolution 2D multifluid radiation-hydrodynamical simulations of the inner ten astronomical units of protoplanetary disks, with growing dust and realistic dust opacity. Outbursts prove highly unstable to the Rossby-wave instability: the burst front diffuses into many small vortices that coalesce into one compact vortex. The vortices drive vigorous turbulent diffusion, strongly suppressing planetesimal formation. The authors conclude such asymmetries should be common and harmful to planet formation, though formation resumes post-burst, as vortices decay and a pressure bump remains near one AU.
arxiv-2606-11544:
Yu, Li, Pan, Wang, and Qiao report a neutron star whose nuclear burst shook its accretion disk in a 2026 arXiv paper. NICER and MAXI observed a long thermonuclear X-ray burst from the low-mass X-ray binary MAXI J0911-655, previously in a low, hard state at about one percent of the Eddington accretion limit. The cooling tail's decay time is near forty-three minutes, and the burst released around ten to the forty-two ergs in total.

About a day later, the source unexpectedly re-brightened into an outburst-like flare. The persistent power-law flux rose roughly fivefold over its pre-burst level, with significant spectral softening. It then decayed back to baseline. The authors argue burst irradiation amplified the disk's thermal-viscous process, driving an inside-out heating front that briefly raised the accretion rate. It is compelling evidence of a burst directly modulating the disk.
arxiv-2606-11744:
Sidney Tio, Arunesh Sinha and Pradeep Varakantham structure AI tutoring in this 2026 arXiv paper. People increasingly learn through open chat with language models, but a chat has no curriculum and no record of the student. The authors show that even frontier and education-tuned models tutor poorly over long sessions. Good tutoring needs three skills at once: sequencing material, holding a Socratic dialogue, and inferring what the student knows.

Their system splits the jobs. From a query it builds a prerequisite knowledge graph, where subtopics are nodes and dependencies are links. A lightweight policy trained with reinforcement learning decides which node to teach next and how many turns to spend there. The language model runs the Socratic exchange at that node and reports progress. Across held-out topics, the paired tutor beats baselines, frontier models and a specialised Socratic model on mastery rate and turns needed.
arxiv-2606-11944:
Corey McInerney mines examiner reports to find where physics students lose marks in this 2026 arXiv paper. Examiner reports, written by the markers of UK A-level exams, record recurring student errors. He gathered reports from six major exam boards published between twenty seventeen and twenty twenty-five, focusing on gravity questions. The thematic analysis covers one hundred thirty-seven gravity questions from past papers.

The source of difficulty depends on topic and question style. In calculation questions, mathematical errors, such as equation manipulation and unit conversion, account for most lost marks, especially in orbital mechanics. In questions on fields, energy and potential, the losses come mainly from weak grasp of the concepts and imprecise definitions. McInerney distils a taxonomy of difficult concepts and procedural traps. His advice splits accordingly: drill algebraic skills for orbit topics, and prioritise qualitative modelling plus precise definitions for field theory.
arxiv-2606-12044:
Jaden Yang Chen and Can Urgun rebuild a classic decision theory from preferences alone in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multi-armed bandit models usually start with arms, states and rewards already defined. The authors start instead with preferences over stopped local contingent schedules.

Each schedule is a possible unfolding of one project, running in its own local time, which a decision maker may advance or postpone. Behavioural axioms on single schedules yield a representation with current utility, local discounting and a general continuation aggregator. A common-tail compensation axiom then prices calendar time across different schedules. Imposing a tight constraint on elapsed calendar time generates a bandit problem, and index policies prove optimal. Many familiar models fall out as special cases, including expected utility, learning and Pandora's box problems. The analogy is consumer theory: demand comes from preferences plus a budget; the bandit comes from schedules plus a calendar.
arxiv-2606-12144:
Ruichen Qiu and co-authors prove that a core algebra task stays hard even when the answer is small, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The task is the greatest common divisor of two sparse polynomials, where sparse means only nonzero terms are stored. Coefficients live in a finite field, a system where arithmetic wraps around a fixed size. An output-sensitive method would run in time tied to input and output sizes.

No such randomized method exists under standard assumptions, the authors show, making the problem NP-hard. This settles Challenge Five of a 2009 problem list for the finite-field case. Roots-of-unity detection is also NP-hard: even deciding whether a sparse polynomial shares a factor with a simple reference polynomial resists fast methods. The proof rules out speed even when every size stays small.
arxiv-2606-12244:
The STIS instrument team at the Space Telescope Science Institute describes a new timing utility for the Hubble Space Telescope, in this 2026 arXiv instrument report. Timestamps from any telescope must be shifted to the solar system's center of mass, the barycenter, so events can be compared fairly. Light travel time makes this barycentric correction swing by about 8.3 minutes either way. Pulsar timing and similar work needs the correction right to about a millisecond.

The new Python tool, inside the stistools package, replaces a retired IRAF routine. It uses astropy for time conversions and fetches Hubble's position from JPL Horizons, ending separate orbit files. Millisecond accuracy is demanding: light covers about 300 kilometers in that time. A one-arcminute sky position error alone can shift timing by up to 0.28 seconds. The report details verification tests and the known absolute accuracy of STIS timestamps.
arxiv-2606-12444:
Boumali and Makhlouf rescue a deformed calculus from a flaw, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Borges dual-q derivative twists differentiation with a knob q. Used in the kinetic term, it yields a nonlinear Schrödinger equation, breaking the linear rules quantum mechanics needs. The fix is a change of variables: rewrite both the coordinate and the wave function, and a linear equation emerges in the new coordinate.

Back in physical space, the result is a Hamiltonian whose mass depends on position. The particle grows heavier or lighter from place to place, with q setting the profile and an effective geometry. Tests cover a free particle, an infinite well, a barrier, and a harmonic oscillator. For q below one, the well effectively shrinks: levels rise and barrier tunneling grows. For q above one, levels drop and tunneling fades. The structure matches a nonadditive-translation route, grounding the formalism geometrically.
arxiv-2606-12644:
Canevari and colleagues extend an analysis of structures in a 2-dimensional model of ferronematics, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Ferronematics are mixed materials made by spreading magnetic nanoparticles in a liquid crystal. The model couples 2 order parameters. One is a Landau-de Gennes Q-tensor describing the liquid crystal's alignment. The other is a magnetisation vector M for the nanoparticles, governed by a Ginzburg-Landau-type energy with a term favouring alignment between them.

The authors study critical points of the energy as a parameter tends to zero. Earlier in the work, the energy density of the Q-component was shown to gather on finitely many singular points. Here they prove the M-component's energy density concentrates along a 1-dimensional rectifiable set, a curve-like set. The curvature of that set, the first variation of the varifold, sits on finitely many points, the singular points of the Q-component.
arxiv-2606-12744:
Allabadi and colleagues present GRIP, a retriever that picks better demonstration examples for large multimodal models, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In-context learning adapts a model by placing a few examples in its prompt, with no retraining. For image-and-text models, those examples are usually chosen by similarity, on the assumption that look-alike examples help most. The authors show that assumption often fails: similar examples can still mislead.

GRIP instead learns from the model's own feedback. Each candidate example is labelled by whether adding it improves or harms the model's score, and a vision-only retriever is trained contrastively to rank helpful examples above harmful look-alikes. Across classification, captioning, and visual question answering, GRIP improves over similarity-based retrieval on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, strongest in classification on Idefics2-8B. Retrievers trained on one model's feedback transfer to other models, including GPT-4o and Gemini systems.
arxiv-2606-12844:
Lu and colleagues propose 3D-URAM, an active perception framework for building radio maps in new 3-dimensional air-ground environments, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A radio map records how wireless signal strength varies across space, and drone networks need such maps to plan drone connectivity.

The framework splits mapping into 2 offline-trained stages. In stage 1, a Bayesian UNet rebuilds radio maps from sparse measurements and partial geometry while giving calibrated predictive uncertainty, a measure of where the reconstruction is unreliable. In stage 2, a dynamic probabilistic roadmap and a transformer-based waypoint policy, trained with proximal policy optimisation, choose flight paths that cut long-horizon uncertainty most under travel budgets. Tests show 3D-URAM cuts reconstruction error by over 50 percent against typical baselines. Field tests in a 300 by 200 by 100 metre volume further confirm active radio map building in the real world.
arxiv-2606-13444:
Luna and Figueiredo propose a self-learning framework for clustering attributed networks in this 2026 arXiv paper. Graph clustering divides network nodes into groups that reflect structure, such as communities or roles. Nodes also carry attributes, information beyond the connections, and clusters should use both sources. The authors build on graph neural networks, models that learn node representations by passing messages along edges. Their framework works in rounds, without labels.

In each round, the network generates representations and a clustering is computed from them. That clustering reshapes the graph used in the next round, so the structure the model sees improves as groupings improve. This feedback loop is the self-learning mechanism. The authors argue it sharpens clusters beyond what one pass achieves. The setting is practical: social, citation, and commerce networks carry node attributes, and unsupervised methods matter because ground-truth groupings are unavailable.
arxiv-2606-13744:
Cassaigne and Kaboré study recurrence and complexity in infinite words in this 2026 arXiv paper. An infinite word is a sequence of symbols, and its complexity counts how many blocks of each length it contains. The authors introduce two kinds of modulo-recurrence, notions tracking how patterns return when positions are considered modulo an integer. They show that Sturmian words, the simplest aperiodic balanced sequences, and maximal complexity words are strongly modulo-recurrent. They then connect window complexity, a refinement counting factors through sliding windows, to the complexity of the Thue-Morse word.

The paper also constructs an aperiodic recurrent word whose window complexity stays bounded. It also builds a family whose window complexity grows like a fractional power of length, tightly from above and below infinitely often. The window complexity of any recurrent aperiodic word is proved unbounded. These results map a complexity measure's landscape, giving examples at every regime.
arxiv-2606-13844:
Luo and colleagues at ETH Zürich release Ramulator 2.1, a major overhaul of their simulator for computer memory chips. DRAM is the fast working memory in computers, and chip designers use simulators to test new memory standards before building them. Their 2026 arXiv paper adds recent standards, makes the tool easier to extend, and strengthens checks that its results can be trusted.

New coverage includes HBM3 and HBM4, LPDDR5 and LPDDR6, and GDDR7, plus features such as split two-phase row activation. A Python interface now hides the low-level C++ code. Two-way code generation turns plain Python descriptions of a standard into simulator code and back into Python controls. Validation spans single timing rules and whole-system speed curves. The resulting latency and throughput curves match those expected from real systems for eleven DRAM standards. The new version also needs far fewer code lines per standard than version 2.0.
arxiv-2606-14044:
Sato and colleagues hunt for the faintest class of exploding stars, electron-capture supernovae, hiding among Type II events. These occur when a low-mass star's oxygen-neon-magnesium core collapses under electron capture; theory predicts low energies. Only one convincing modern candidate, SN 2018zd, was known. Their 2026 arXiv paper applies a color diagnostic, blue colors mid-plateau, to past events and a Zwicky Transient Facility sample, selecting ten candidates.

Three candidates are gold, with spectra ruling out interaction effects that fake blue colors; seven are silver. Matching light curves to models gave explosion energies of zero point four to one point seven times ten to the fiftieth erg for the gold set, matching first-principles predictions. Inferred mass-loss rates ran higher than expected. The rate among Type II supernovae falls between three percent (gold) and fifteen point seven percent (with silver): lower and upper limits.
arxiv-2606-14144:
Peters connects two research threads in voting theory and shows each is secretly the other. Metric distortion measures how much welfare a voting rule loses by seeing only rankings, not true distances; no deterministic rule beats distortion three. Undominated committees are candidate sets few voters wholly reject for an outsider. His 2026 arXiv paper, a research note, proves the two notions necessary and sufficient for each other in the bi-criteria setting.

One direction: any sufficiently undominated committee, its fraction at most one half minus a constant gap, achieves distortion strictly below three. In particular, a committee of size five with distortion at most two point seven three eight four exists. Conversely, any committee beating three by a constant gap must be undominated with fraction near one. A corollary constrains randomized rules: the support of any lottery beating three minus epsilon is itself undominated.
arxiv-2606-14344:
Rimon and colleagues rebuild tactile imaging around one idea: touch is local, so the representation should be local too. Tactile imaging reconstructs the structure of soft objects from touch, for diagnosis and robots, but prior self-supervised methods compress a scene into one global vector, generalizing poorly. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes LESS, a Local Encoder for Spatial Sensing. The scene becomes a grid of recurrent encoders with local receptive fields. Their states fuse into images of what lies inside.

The compositional design pays off: models trained on single-inclusion phantoms imaged objects with multiple inclusions. The local structure also supports spatial uncertainty estimates, marking where the image is trustworthy. The team enabled hand-held imaging, via pose tracking and human-like palpation motions, and extended reconstruction to 3D. The forward pass takes 250 milliseconds, roughly four predictions per second; training data included 1,409 full scans from recorded motions such as pokes.
arxiv-2606-14644:
Ren and co-authors search theoretically for a bound state of two charmed mesons in a 2026 arXiv paper. The proposed state is called X(3700). It would be a D and anti-D meson bound together. It should leave fingerprints in decays of heavier particles. Those include B mesons and Lambda-b baryons producing D pairs plus a kaon or a Lambda.

The team models the production mechanisms with care. They stress the final-state interaction between the charmed mesons. That interaction also generates the related X(3930) state. They normalize distributions at a known resonance peak. The D-pair mass distribution then differs strongly just above threshold between reactions. The presence of X(3700) enhances the distribution by about an order of magnitude. That compares with calculations omitting it. They urge measurement of these distributions in upcoming LHCb upgrades.
arxiv-2606-14844:
Blackman and co-authors test whether a new spectrograph can resolve hydrogen light from forming planets in a 2026 arXiv paper. The instrument is RISTRETTO, being built for the Very Large Telescope. It pairs a coronagraph, which blocks starlight, with optics that correct atmospheric blur. Its resolving power is about one hundred forty thousand. Young planets glow in H-alpha light as gas falls onto them. That glow is hard to split from the star's own signal.

The team mixed synthetic and real observations to find detection limits. They covered separations from thirty-seven to six hundred milliarcseconds. Models of four known candidate protoplanets, including PDS70b and PDS70c, were used. Their H-alpha lines could be resolved in a one-hour exposure. Line shapes would also reveal the density and speed of the infalling gas. That pins down how fast the planet is growing.
arxiv-2606-15044:
Lee and coauthors compare fair tokenizers for multilingual language models on Southeast Asian languages in a 2026 study. Byte-pair encoding favors Latin scripts, so speakers of Burmese or Khmer pay more tokens per sentence. That gap raises inference costs and weakens long-context reasoning for underrepresented languages. The team tests equitable alternatives under matched conditions.

Four tokenizers face off across eleven languages: byte-level BPE, parity-aware BPE, morphology-driven encoding, and the Byte Latent Transformer. Beyond compression and parity measures, the authors train models to check downstream effects. Parity-aware BPE sits on the efficiency-equity frontier and is recommended as the default. Morphology-driven encoding gives the best semantic reasoning and translation, at higher compute cost. The byte latent approach lags, likely starved of low-resource data. The findings show fairness and efficiency need not conflict, guiding tokenizer choice for hundreds of millions of speakers.
arxiv-2606-15144:
Montalan and coauthors probe whether language models understand Filipino word structure with a diagnostic benchmark in a 2026 study. Filipino builds words with infixes that split roots and with syllable copying, stress marks that text usually omits. Subword tokenizers slice such words at boundaries that ignore morpheme structure. The benchmark, PACUTE, holds forty-six hundred tasks across six skill levels.

Levels run from basic character handling up through morpheme splitting and full word transformations. Open-weight models score near chance on morpheme decomposition at every size tested. Frontier commercial models recover single affixes far better under lenient scoring. They still fall well short of their own character-level ceilings on composition and syllabification tasks. Extra training with alternative tokenizers does not lift the morpheme floor. The authors blame missing morphological knowledge in pretraining data more than model capacity. The hierarchy offers a template for testing other morphologically rich, low-resource languages.
arxiv-2606-15344:
Wang and coauthors use room-temperature polariton condensates as a physical layer inside a generative model, in a 2026 photonics paper. Generative networks need random nonlinear changes, which digital hardware supplies at growing energy cost. Polaritons form when light couples strongly to excitons inside a tiny cavity. Their condensates evolve with rich dynamics and natural randomness. The team placed condensates from an organic dye cavity inside a GAN. The physical system transforms signals on the way to generating images.

The setup performed guided digit-to-image translation as its test task. It beat digital noise sampling on inception score and digit accuracy. It also beat a laser-based physical baseline on structure match. Correlated output variations steadied training and widened output range. The results cast polariton condensation as a genuine computing resource. Physics-enhanced hardware could ease AI's energy bottleneck.
arxiv-2606-15444:
McGinnis and coauthors prove a conservation law for physical learning in a 2026 paper. Equilibrium propagation and coupled learning train physical systems, such as resistor networks, by comparing two equilibrium states and updating each component from local information alone. Such local rules are attractive because a circuit evaluates itself almost for free, unlike a digital model. The authors ask what the training dynamics secretly preserve.

In the continuous-time, small-nudging limit, both methods conserve a mass-like quantity built from the trainable parameters; for linear circuits it is half the sum of squared conductances. Three independent proofs establish the law. Conservation then delivers guarantees: fast convergence on crossbar arrays, and convergence or edge death in single-input settings. Ignoring the conserved quantity lets parameter scale drift until training hits a boundary and fails. The result gives designers of analog learning hardware a check and a design rule at once.
arxiv-2606-15844:
Song and colleagues forecast how multi-band gravitational-wave observations sharpen dark-siren cosmology in 2026. Dark sirens are mergers without light counterparts: distances come from the waves, redshifts statistically from galaxy surveys. Combining space and ground detectors improves sky localisation by two to three orders of magnitude, directly lowering cross-correlation noise.

Their Fisher forecast cross-correlates mergers seen by the Einstein Telescope, Cosmic Explorer, and B-DECIGO with the CSST galaxy survey. In the standard model, the multi-band network pins the Hubble constant's error to about a third of a percent over ten years. That beats the ground-only network by over a third, and the space detector by much more. The striking gain is the clustering bias, measured per bin: at redshifts one to two, multi-band data reach three percent precision where rivals manage eight to sixty. Such measurements can discriminate how compact binaries form.
arxiv-2606-16144:
Bei and colleagues present EconCSLib in 2026, an early formal mathematics library for computational economics built in the Lean 4 prover. Formalization turns informal statements into machine-checked proofs a computer can verify line by line. The success of mathlib showed this approach can scale for pure mathematics. Economics has lacked an equivalent shared foundation.

EconCSLib aims to supply reusable definitions and theorems for game theory, mechanism design, social choice, and related areas. Beyond verified proofs of known results, it plans to host machine-checked open problems and formalizations of modern papers. The authors discuss design principles and lessons from building it with AI assistance. AI tools make large-scale formalization more practical, they argue, while reusable abstraction design still needs domain experts. The long-term goal is infrastructure for reliable formalization and AI-assisted discovery in economics.
arxiv-2606-16244:
Xu and co-authors argue in 2026 that language models write insecure code not from missing knowledge but from failing to activate it. Training corpora hold plenty of security material, they note. Without a brief cue, though, common coding patterns crowd out the safer ones. Their system, SPARK, is a training-free harness that runs at inference time and adds almost no cost per query.

One part of SPARK looks up the Common Weakness Enumeration entries tied to each coding task and appends a short structured cue to the prompt. A second part adds a precomputed token bias, drawn from a safe direction found with paired examples, to the output scores at every step. Across six open-source models and three coding languages, SPARK matches or beats the strongest fine-tuning, prompt, and retrieval baselines on every pairing. It also keeps scores on the HumanEval coding benchmark intact.
arxiv-2606-16444:
Mvondo-She gives in 2026 a geometric reading of the logarithmic graviton, a mode that appears at a special point of topologically massive gravity. At the chiral point, the massive graviton becomes degenerate with the left-moving graviton, yielding a logarithmic mode and a rank-two Jordan structure. This log graviton is the bulk counterpart, in the AdS3/LCFT2 duality, of a partner in the boundary theory. Its meaning has stayed algebraic.

Starting from the log graviton of Grumiller and Johansson, the author tracks its coefficient toward the AdS3 boundary. There it takes the form of a complex parameter combining radius and time. The same value appears in the power series of the Virasoro generator L0 acting on a rank-two Jordan cell. The logarithmic monodromy around the origin is exactly that Jordan flow after one circuit. The match recasts a puzzling mode as flow along a complexified Virasoro direction.
arxiv-2606-16544:
Guo, Luo and Wei present a 2026 mathematics study of a coupled wave system called the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger system. The system links several wave components, each one affecting all the others. Such systems model multi-component Bose-Einstein condensates, which are ultracold gases, and light pulses in nonlinear optics. Earlier work had settled the cases of two and three components only.

For any number of components, the authors classify every nontrivial standing solution completely. They also prove that the linearized operator at each solution is nondegenerate, meaning small perturbations reveal no hidden flat directions. A further result gives the exact mass of each component in terms of its parameter. Together these results settle conjectures raised by Frank, Gontier and Lewin and by the authors themselves. They also give a firm basis for studying stability and normalized solutions in coupled wave models.
arxiv-2606-16744:
Bläser, Dutta and Okyay settle complexity questions in a 2026 theoretical computer science paper on finitary diagrams. These diagrams model systems whose behavior can be compared through bisimilarity, a strong notion of two systems acting alike. Earlier work decided such questions using a logic fragment about invertible matrices over the real numbers, giving very high cost bounds.

The new results cut those bounds sharply. An efficient randomized algorithm for the matrix fragment lifts the whole analysis: bisimilarity for finitary diagrams now sits in a lower exponential class, and over finite fields lower still. Model checking for the diagrammatic path logic drops to a much smaller class, and the authors prove a matching hardness result, so that classification is exact. Their hardness proof routes through layered poset problems and quiver theory, tools of independent interest. A determinant-one variant turns out as hard as full real existential theory.
arxiv-2606-17244:
Islam and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on tuning magnetic behaviour in a family of double perovskite oxides by swapping some neodymium for strontium. The swap adds holes and disorder at once, letting the team steer exchange bias, a shift in magnetic response prized for device design. Neutron diffraction and X-ray spectroscopy track how the crystal structure and cobalt valence change across the series as the strontium share grows.

The structure moves from an ordered monoclinic phase to a disordered rhombohedral one, while cobalt shifts toward a higher valence and manganese stays put. Magnetism measurements show ferromagnetism weakening with doping, yet one mid-series composition shows cluster-glass behaviour and the largest exchange bias in the set. After correcting for minor-loop effects, that same composition shows robust inverse exchange bias, blamed on competing magnetic interfaces and frustration.
arxiv-2606-17344:
Liu and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on how some hot Jupiters may form through secular chaos in wide binary star systems. A distant companion can pump a planet's orbit to extreme eccentricity, after which tides shrink it into a close orbit. Most theory uses a tidy three-body setup, but real systems may hold an extra planet or brown dwarf whose influence changes the pathways to those extreme orbits dramatically.

The team studies hierarchical three-plus-one systems, a binary star hosting both a planet and an intermediate companion. Chaos switches on according to the ratio of the two Kozai-Lidov oscillation timescales in the system. Near equal timescales, most systems migrate even at modest mutual tilts, well below the classic critical angle for such oscillations. The model predicts hot Jupiters on near-polar orbits, testable as surveys uncover more such systems.
arxiv-2606-17444:
Liang and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper giving a multiwavelength case study of GRB 250424A, a long-duration gamma-ray burst tracked to late times. Spectra from the Keck ten-metre telescope join X-ray and optical light curves in the data set. The afterglow shows a clear shallow decay phase in both X-ray and optical bands at once. It then makes a colour-free switch to a standard decay, pointing to one shared emission source.

Broadband spectra fit a single power law, consistent with synchrotron radiation from a relativistic forward shock. The team reads the shallow phase as that shock being refreshed by steady energy injection from the engine. Their fit gives a large isotropic kinetic energy and an injection index near a third, in a constant-density setting. No clear supernova bump appears at late times, though a typical one is not ruled out.
arxiv-2606-18044:
Panarotto and colleagues sort city trips into shared patterns while honestly handling how fuzzy phone locations are, in a 2026 statistics paper. Their mobility data come from telephonic records around Padova, Italy, where a device's position is uncertain at every moment. Instead of pretending otherwise, each trip is encoded as a composition: at each time, the shares of road types that could match the observed position.

These share trajectories live on a simplex and evolve over time, so the team builds a state-space model that separates measurement error from the latent movement process. Clustering then mixes several such models, grouping trips whose hidden dynamics evolve alike. The Padova study recovers readable mobility patterns at the population level, each with its own character that planners can use. The framework suits any setting where tracked movement arrives with positional doubt.
arxiv-2606-18144:
Chen treats a robot's memory chip as a depleting bank account in a 2026 paper on embodied agents. Every saved memory spends one of a few thousand program and erase cycles in the robot's flash storage, and the stock never refills. Yet no fielded system prices which memories deserve an erase cycle. Chen prices the stock with a single endurance shadow price. Placement across RAM, onboard storage, and cloud becomes a threshold rule on a wear-augmented value index.

The rule's shape holds whatever the link between a memory's value and its write frequency. Only when that link is positive does the optimum do something startling, pushing the robot's most valuable memories off its own flash. Measuring the link on real robot logs, Chen finds its sign depends on the deployment. It is positive for recurrent long-horizon manipulation, absent or negative elsewhere. The budget binds mainly on cheap commodity storage.
arxiv-2606-18244:
Donnan and colleagues map glowing carbon molecules inside distant galaxies with the JWST telescope, in a 2026 astronomy paper. These molecules, called PAHs, shine at set infrared wavelengths, and their relative brightness reveals their size and charge. The PAHSPECS program used the MIRI instrument to make the first resolved maps of these features in normal star-forming galaxies at cosmic noon, when cosmic star formation peaked.

By modeling the data cubes, the team recovered clean profiles for four PAH bands and one argon line, then built ratio maps across each disk. The maps reverse the local pattern: PAHs grow larger and more neutral farther from the center. The trend instead matches nearby luminous infrared galaxies, and it follows the hardness of the local light field. The mix of these molecules in normal galaxies, the authors argue, was different at that era.
arxiv-2606-18544:
Turk and Polson turn the mathematics of path signatures onto chess, treating each game as an ordered stream of events rather than a bundle of averages, in a 2026 statistics paper. A game carries move-by-move engine evaluations, accuracy, position complexity, and clock readings, and the order in which those channels move together is exactly what summary statistics throw away.

Applying the signature transform from rough-path theory gives a graded feature set that records those interactions. Their main application is cheating detection, recast as an anytime-valid sequential test whose error stays controlled at every sample size. The telling signal lives in the signature's area terms, which capture whether a player's accuracy rises precisely when positions get hard, the fingerprint of engine help. In controlled studies the test kept exact error control and caught blatant assistance with high power.
arxiv-2606-19344:
Pelossi and colleagues present TreeTracer in 2026, a visual analytics tool for exposing hidden bias in language models. Model bias is hard to evaluate because text generation is stochastic. Standard audits inspect a single output or use static metrics. Those approaches hide the underlying probability distributions and miss biases sitting in lower-probability generation branches, exactly where subtle skews can live unseen by reviewers.

The tool runs a perturbation pipeline on each prompt. It swaps ontology-defined terms, then aggregates hundreds of random generations into a syntax-aligned tree structure. An auxiliary model merges nodes by class. The result is drawn as a custom Sankey diagram. Placing two ontology-driven trees side by side lets analysts compare semantic contexts directly. Contrastive inference also computes counterfactual token probabilities across contexts and displays them. The system supports systematic bias detection that single-sample audits cannot offer.
arxiv-2606-19444:
Wang and colleagues propose Rydberg atom simulators for probing emergent fermions in 2026, with one approach per mode. Rydberg platforms, analog and digital, draw interest for their versatile, reconfigurable geometry. Emergent fermions are notoriously hard to probe, since they are defined nonlocally inside a bosonic system. The team uses that freedom to make those fermionic states measurable.

In analog mode, atoms are assembled into a Möbius band shape that preserves local couplings. That geometry realizes antiperiodic boundary conditions, where fermionic states reside. Spectra in that sector then reveal universal energy ratios of bosonic and fermion states. In digital mode, the team runs a fermionic version of Kibble-Zurek ramping with a quantum circuit. It addresses the fermion scaling form. That freedom gives an exponential speed-up, with modest circuit-depth overhead. The work establishes Rydberg simulators as a strong platform for emergent fermions, excitations that usually hide from measurement.
arxiv-2606-19544:
Justin Norman, Michael Rivera, and D Alex Hughes audit language models used as judges in 2026. LLM-as-a-judge setups let one model grade another's output, and now dominate model evaluation. Most validation leans on exact-match agreement, which ignores chance and inflates apparent skill.

The audit covers 21 judges from nine providers on MT-Bench, JudgeBench, and RewardBench. Three protocols test agreement, consistency, and bias across 118 runs and about 541,000 judgments. Exact match overstates Cohen's kappa by 33 to 41 points on MT-Bench for every judge. Rankings swing by up to fourteen places between benchmarks. Two deployed judges pair test-retest reliability above 0.95 with strong position bias, a consistency-bias paradox. Verbosity bias stays small under a single pairwise rubric. The authors distil the findings into a Minimum Viable Validation Protocol for judge users.
arxiv-2606-19644:
Richard Sserunjogi, Daniel Ogenrwot, and John Businge link prompt quality to pull request outcomes in 2026. Developers increasingly draft code with chat assistants inside open-source projects. Whether prompt structure shapes merged results has stayed unclear.

The study hand-checks 265 developer and ChatGPT exchanges drawn from self-admitted use in pull requests. Prompt structure scores rest on three dimensions: Context, Specificity, and Verification. Model-assisted annotation matches human judges unevenly across those dimensions. Specificity agrees most stably, Context gets underscored by the model, and Verification resists steady scoring. A hybrid human and model workflow follows from that audit. Specificity and Context best predict actionable code generation. Verification best predicts code adoption, while Context best predicts integration depth. Prompt craft thus acts upstream, shaping generation, adoption, and reuse in distinct ways.
arxiv-2606-19744:
Pranav Bhandari and four colleagues study forgetting in sequential preference training in 2026. Aligning language models often stacks behavioural objectives one after another. Direct Preference Optimisation applies each objective in turn, but later stages may erode earlier ones.

Four preference settings cover distributional conflict, multi-attribute interaction, strong safety signal, and compatible quality goals. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA adapters trains stage by stage. Every objective is re-graded after each stage against a fixed reference. No single forgetting pattern emerges from the runs. Change ranges from partial loss to stability, pair-level reshuffling, or positive transfer. Aggregate scores mask that variety; quartile splits expose high-confidence pairs moving either way. Stage-two gradients sit near-orthogonal to earlier objectives, so direct gradient clash explains little. Pipelines should weigh objective compatibility and signal strength, not assume uniform erosion. Grading every goal after each stage makes that full map possible.
arxiv-2606-19844:
Tianxiang Ma and four colleagues show in 2026 that epithelial cell sheets form a mixed polar-nematic phase. Epithelia are the tissue sheets lining organs and skin. Their cells align like liquid crystals while also carrying head-tail polarity.

A shape-based order measure captures each cell's structural asymmetry. Bright-field imaging pairs with traction force microscopy to map that polarity. Shape polarity unifies signals from nematic directors, main stresses, and cell motion. The tissue hosts integer and half-integer topological defects side by side. Substrate stiffness and cell-cell adhesion tune defect density and domain wall length. A minimal continuum model of polar-nematic active matter reproduces the mixed phase. Active stresses fighting polar-nematic elasticity drive the pattern, the model shows. Living sheets thus count as nematopolar matter with coupled order.
arxiv-2606-20944:
John Gallagher and four colleagues prove equivalence results in 2026 between big-step and small-step derivations for Horn clauses, with applications to programming language semantics. Big-step semantics judge a whole computation at once. Small-step semantics advance one move at a time. Both styles are familiar from language theory. Horn clauses generalize the setting, since logic programs and interpreters can be written in that form.

Equivalence is proved between big-step derivations and two small-step versions. By specializing interpreters for these strategies, any clause set can be transformed into an equivalent one with the chosen behavior. A language whose big-step semantics is written as Horn clauses can thus gain a small-step version automatically. Experiments cover several programming languages. Equivalent semantics matter because some proofs and tools need step-by-step traces, while definitions are often far easier to write in big-step form.
arxiv-2606-21144:
Xingyu Chen and three colleagues propose AdaMem in 2026, a memory method that learns what a personalized agent should remember for each user. Long-term memory systems often try to remember everything. In production, inference cost and finite context make that untenable. Irrelevant trivia crowds out useful facts. Question-answering accuracy erodes as memory bloats. What is worth keeping, they argue, depends on the user's role.

AdaMem maintains a structured, role-specific memory policy. It refines that policy from weekly question feedback through a light self-reflection step with rollback on failure. A new benchmark simulates weeks of interaction with weekly questions. Tests span two extraction models and two feedback modes. Learning write control, what to store at all, may matter as much as retrieval for agents that live with users over months rather than single sessions.
arxiv-2606-21444:
Kevin van de Glind, Matthias Volk, and Tim Willemse extend formal verification in 2026 to Markov automata whose transition rates are not fully known. Markov automata model systems mixing nondeterministic choice with continuous timing, and they underlie reliability formalisms such as dynamic fault trees. Until now, checking them demanded every rate be pinned down, an unrealistic demand when the environment is uncertain.

Their parametric Markov automata carry symbolic parameters instead of fixed rates. Two questions are answered for time-bounded reachability: whether any parameter choice makes the model pass or fail, and how the whole parameter space splits into passing and failing regions. The route discretizes to a parametric Markov decision process and bounds the reachability probability, with error shrinkable at will. Experiments in the Storm checker show discretization is the main bottleneck.
arxiv-2606-21544:
Jonas Kirchhoff examines a modeling framework in 2026 that describes physical systems through energy balance and network structure, and shows it wears two different port-Hamiltonian faces. Such systems split a model into conservative, dissipative, and connecting parts linked by an energy-routing structure, which makes large systems composable. Altmann and Schulze recently proposed energy-based models as a widening of that class.

Kirchhoff demonstrates that their framework admits two distinct forms as port-Hamiltonian systems. The split turns on the role played by the algebraic variable, and it differs from the familiar coordinate ambiguity in classical port-Hamiltonian geometry. A simple extension then covers systems with feedthrough, where inputs pass straight to outputs. Pinning down which form is in play matters for later sampling and model reduction work.
arxiv-2606-21644:
Paul Obernolte and Manfred Salmhofer solve Polchinski's equation with unusual completeness in 2026. Polchinski's equation governs how a quantum field theory's effective action flows as fluctuations are averaged out scale by scale. They write its solution as an expansion over binary trees, each tree organizing how couplings branch through the flow.

The hard part is convergence, and they prove it for fermionic theories under stated decay assumptions on the covariance. New combinatorial estimates count the leaf trees hanging from each binary tree, taming the growth that usually limits such expansions to formal power series. The method applies to standard models of fermionic quantum field theory and quantum statistical mechanics. For mathematical physics, it turns a workhorse flow equation into a construction with proven convergence.
arxiv-2606-21744:
Sebastian Dorer, Clemens Trunner, and six colleagues report a measurement artifact at Vienna's TRIGA Mk II research reactor in 2026 that precision experiments ignore at their peril. During steady 250 kW operation, helium-3 neutron detectors show a statistically significant count-rate drop of 1.5 to 3 percent in the first two to two and a half hours after start-up. The dip tracks pool temperature: as the water warms, counts fall.

Simultaneous neutron and temperature measurements at several beam tubes map the effect's behavior across configurations. The count rate settles only once thermal equilibrium is reached. The team identifies plausible origins and proposes follow-up measurements to pin down the root cause. Until then, high-precision work at TRIGA reactors may need a thermal correction for this slow, temperature-driven drift in apparent neutron flux.
arxiv-2606-21844:
Hager and colleagues present Inverse Turing Bench in 2026, a test of whether language models can tell human conversation apart from human-machine conversation. The classic Turing test asks if a machine can pass as human; this benchmark reverses the roles and makes the model the judge. Each item pairs two multi-turn transcripts, one between two people and one between a person and an artificial intelligence.

The judge must pick which dialogue is human-only, a harder task than spotting single machine-written passages because turns are short, casual, and context-dependent. In the first evaluation, GPTZero scored highest at 89.41 percent accuracy, ahead of two large language models at about 78 and 76 percent of pairs judged correctly. The authors report that statistical detectors have semantic blind spots, while meaning-based judges can be fooled by persona prompting. They frame the task as a probe of machine theory of mind.
arxiv-2606-21944:
Yang and colleagues compute, in 2026, how fast molecules can be when a conveyor-belt magneto-optical trap captures them directly from a beam. These traps use polarization-gradient forces from blue-detuned light to cool, confine, and load molecules in one step. A recent experiment with barium fluoride showed direct loading can beat a conventional trap, and the authors ask whether the trick extends to other heavy molecules.

Using optical Bloch equation force calculations with classical trajectory simulations, their model reproduced the observed trend for the demonstrated molecule: capture velocity grows with laser intensity. They then tested two harder relatives in simulation. One has dense hyperfine structure that complicates conventional trapping, and the other has a narrower linewidth and longer wavelength that weaken the available force. In both cases the conveyor-belt trap kept a broad region of nonzero capture velocity, marking where direct loading should remain practical.
arxiv-2606-22144:
Oli and colleagues introduce SAGE in 2026, an expert-annotated endoscopy dataset from South Asia for multimodal learning and hallucination checks. Nearly all open gastrointestinal datasets come from European patients, so population bias in diagnostic models has been hard to measure. SAGE contains 1,300 endoscopy images with expert captions and hallucination tags.

The dataset also carries eighteen labels and 14,726 question-answer pairs. It supports image captioning, multi-label classification, and visual question answering. The authors benchmark task-specific models and contemporary large multimodal models on it. Task-specific classifiers suffer most from the population shift. Their performance drops by fifty-eight percent on average when evaluated on the South Asian data. The benchmarks give the region's first open testbed for diagnostic AI built for all populations.
arxiv-2606-22244:
Zhou and Gorshkov prove, in 2026, a case of Markel's S3-conjecture for finite groups whose prime divisors lie among two, three, and five. An ah-group is a finite group in which any two distinct conjugacy classes have distinct sizes. The symmetric group on three letters is the unique known nontrivial example, with class sizes one, two, and three.

Markel conjectured in 1973 that every nontrivial ah-group is isomorphic to that symmetric group. The conjecture is settled for solvable groups, but non-solvable cases remain open. Zhou and Gorshkov prove the case where all prime divisors of the group's order lie in the set two, three, five. Any such ah-group must be the symmetric group S3. The result extends the verified range of the conjecture toward the remaining non-solvable cases.
arxiv-2606-22644:
Shang-Shun Zhang introduces a neural method for excited states of quantum matter in this 2026 physics paper. Knowing a many-body ground state is not enough: dynamical properties depend on quasiparticle excitations, the particle-like ripples above that state. Learning a separate wave function for every excitation is costly and unstructured.

The neural polaron ansatz instead learns an operator that dresses the ground state into an excitation. A compact neural head sits on the feature map of a pretrained ground-state network and defines the dressing operator. It builds in translation symmetry, momentum resolution, and locality, while keeping ground-state correlations separate. Benchmarked on the square-lattice J1-J2 Heisenberg model, the method reproduced magnon dispersions and spectral weights well across a broad frustration range. It also captured the anomaly at momentum (pi, 0) and its gradual softening as frustration grows.
arxiv-2606-22844:
Wei Yang and four colleagues improve long-term memory for language model agents in this 2026 paper. Memory systems now store past experiences compactly and retrieve them well. But retrieval alone does not show a memory is valid evidence for the current query, since compressed fragments from different situations can look equally relevant when they share entities or user states.

The authors call that failure context collapse, and their framework, RaMem, turns retrieved fragments into checkable evidence. It anchors each memory in its original conditions, such as event time, mention time, session span, and participants. It then derives the evidence conditions implied by the query and retrieves memories fitting those conditions, keeping content-relevant ones as fallback. Synthesis preserves the chosen memories' context for the generator. On long-term memory benchmarks, RaMem beat strong baselines consistently, with average F1 gains of more than ten percent across several model backbones.
arxiv-2606-23044:
Hyunsang Hwang, Suhyun Bae, and Donghun Lee give neural networks a number code built from primes in a 2026 paper. Standard embeddings hide the algebraic structure of integers, so networks must rediscover modular arithmetic from scratch. Modular arithmetic is clock-style arithmetic, where numbers wrap around after a fixed modulus. The team's Prime Fourier Embeddings encode each integer as sine and cosine pairs, one channel per prime. With that code, a modular task reduces to picking the right prime channel.

Hwang and colleagues prove that any linear map respecting the code's symmetry must split into independent blocks, one per prime. The Chinese Remainder Theorem then predicts which channels a given modulus needs. Experiments confirm both predictions sharply. Channels the task needed responded hundreds of times more strongly than irrelevant ones. Test accuracy was perfect on every square-free composite modulus tried.
arxiv-2606-23244:
Flavio Ferrarotti and Klaus-Dieter Schewe give a formal theory of probabilistic algorithms in a 2026 paper. A probabilistic algorithm makes random choices as it runs, like a randomized sampling procedure. The authors ask what such algorithms are, in the abstract. They work in the spirit of earlier theories of ordinary algorithms. Their definition rests on four postulates. The postulates cover random branching time, abstract states, a background vocabulary, and random bounded exploration. Bounded exploration means each step inspects only a bounded part of the state.

Ferrarotti and Schewe then introduce probabilistic Abstract State Machines as a concrete specification language. They show these machines do specify such algorithms under the postulates. The main theorem runs the other way. Every algorithm meeting the postulates can be matched step by step by an equivalent machine with the same signature and background.
arxiv-2606-23344:
Cheng Cui and colleagues present RT-DocLayout, a real-time system for document layout analysis, in a 2026 paper. Layout analysis finds the blocks of a page, classifies them, and recovers their reading order. It remains a bottleneck for document parsing, thanks to mixed element types, warped or photographed pages, and tangled reading orders. Older systems chain separate stages, spreading errors, or use heavy generative transformers. RT-DocLayout handles classification, detection, and reading order, plus pixel-level segmentation, inside one modest thirty-three-million-parameter model, built on a real-time detection transformer.

Cui and colleagues unify the four tasks in a single query-based decoder. Each query classifies an element, draws its box, paints its mask, and links it into the reading order. Learning geometry and structure jointly improves both. The design targets wild documents rather than clean scans, serving as an efficient front end for parsing pipelines.
arxiv-2606-23444:
Pratyaksh Rao and colleagues build a world model for real-time quadrotor control in a 2026 robotics paper. Agile drones need accurate dynamics models to decide well under uncertainty. Neural dynamics models capture complex effects, but step-by-step rollout compounds errors over long horizons. Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures instead model dynamics in a latent space. Prior work used them mostly for slow kinematic planning, not high-frequency control. Their model, SkyJEPA, adds a physics-inspired prober that maps the frozen latent state back to interpretable physical state, grounding long-horizon prediction.

Rao and colleagues pair the learned model with sampling-based optimal control for real-time decisions on embedded hardware. An automated pipeline generates training data, cutting the need for risky real-world collection. In open-loop tests and outdoor closed-loop flights, the system predicted accurately. It also transferred from simulation to real quadrotors with no real-world training.
arxiv-2606-23544:
Dai, Hasselgren, and Kiumi cut the sampling cost of randomized quantum simulation without adding bias, in a 2026 paper on quantum computing. Hamiltonian simulation mimics how a quantum system evolves over time, a core task for future quantum machines. Randomized methods run many random circuits and average the results. Their average can be exactly right while each run still fluctuates, so the remaining error is statistical. Less fluctuation means fewer runs.

The team first builds an unbiased estimator called continuous TE PAI, which removes discretization error with finite depth random circuits. They then split estimator variance into a counting part and an ordering part, caused by terms that fail to commute, which dominates the cost. Classical variance reduction tricks aimed at each part cut error by about seventy percent on small systems. Tensor network tests on a thirty spin chain reach sampling cost cuts above ninety percent.
arxiv-2606-23844:
Costa builds a perfectly periodic motion whose statistics are nonetheless about as complicated as a flow can get, in a 2026 paper on dynamical systems. Emergence measures how many distinct statistical patterns are needed to describe the long run behavior of most orbits to a given precision. Periodic maps score low almost by definition, and one might expect flows to match. Costa shows they need not.

He builds a smooth periodic flow, one where every orbit closes and nothing blows up, whose score grows faster than any polynomial in the precision demanded. The construction reshapes a famous Epstein and Vogt counterexample to the Periodic Orbit Conjecture. Onto that base he grafts the high emergence mechanism of Berger and Bochi. The result splits flows from maps: in continuous time, perfect periodicity can coexist with extreme complexity.
arxiv-2606-24044:
Bouthat and Parisé study Hardy-type inequalities, bounds that control averages of a function by the function's overall size. Their setting generalises the classic result: a space is split into nested pieces, each piece contributes a weighted average, and extra weights act on the resulting sequence of averages. The 2026 paper asks exactly when such an averaging operator stays bounded, meaning outputs cannot blow up relative to inputs.

Boundedness turns out to hinge on a single testing quantity computed from the weights and the nesting. The best constant in the inequality sits between that quantity and at most twice its value, so the characterisation is never far off. A second route, modelled on Broadbent's proof of Hardy's original inequality, gives a local condition that often produces sharper constants. That route also recovers several known cases, including the classical weighted Hardy inequality, as special instances of the general framework.
arxiv-2606-24444:
Zhou and colleagues take a census of the Milky Way's molecular clouds, the cold gas factories where stars form. The MWISP survey mapped carbon monoxide emission in three isotopologues, variants of the molecule differing in atomic weight. Across swathes of the inner and outer Galaxy, a few thousand well resolved clouds, from tens of thousands found, support the 2026 statistical analysis.

Clouds turn out typically oblate, flattened like lentils. They tend to lie along the Galactic disk. A nearby subsample exposes strong distance dependent selection effects, contaminating some measured parameters, though the bias direction can itself flag distance influence. Specific environments stand out: clouds in a spiral shock region, clouds in interarm spurs, and the brightest in the rarest isotopologue. Clouds with velocity dispersion above the classic Larson relation are mostly small and likely young. Zhou's statistics give cloud evolution a population level baseline.
arxiv-2606-24644:
Han, Balepur, Boyd-Graber, and Carpuat measure what users think speech translation systems can and cannot do. Millions use machine translation daily. Their mental models of system limits are nearly unstudied, though. The team's 2026 framework uses cross lingual question answering as the probe. Users hear foreign language information through translation. They either accept the machine output, or pay for professional re translation before answering.

Behaviour and accuracy across varying translation qualities reveal how well users predict where the system errs, and how that model evolves. Users' mental models grow stronger with practice, especially when they know some of the source language. They rely primarily on surface level error cues. Providing speech transcriptions also measurably improves the models users build. Han's study validates cross lingual question answering as a downstream instrument for studying human AI collaboration, with a direct design implication: expose the cues users actually read.
arxiv-2606-25144:
Carbon enhanced metal poor stars carry the chemical fingerprints of ancient nuclear processes. Tatyana Sitnova and Lyudmila Mashonkina measure barium abundances and isotope mixes in three such stars, two of the s type and one of the rs type. The spectroscopy is corrected for departures from local thermodynamic equilibrium.

The odd isotope fraction of barium separates the classes cleanly. The rs star shows a fraction around 0.65, while both s stars sit near 0.23. The split backs the authors' earlier finding that the barium isotope ratio marks which process, slow neutron capture or the intermediate process, enriched the star. More element abundances will be needed to pin down the intermediate process itself. To help, the team publishes a tool that generates barium line lists for any chosen isotope fraction.
arxiv-2606-25544:
On the Fock space of entire functions, weighted composition operators mix a change of variable with a multiplication, and their symmetry properties are delicate. Aakriti Sharma studies in 2026 which such operators commute with a given complex symmetric one. Commuting pairs matter because they reveal the rigid structure behind symmetry: an operator built from a conjugation should admit only tightly constrained partners. Sharma characterises exactly which symbol pairs produce a commuting operator.

The analysis pins down the allowable forms of both the composition symbol and the weight function. Within that family, extra conditions separate the self adjoint members from the normal ones, two stronger symmetry classes. The results extend the known picture for plain composition operators into the weighted, complex symmetric setting, where the weight's phase interacts with the conjugation in ways earlier work had only partially mapped.
arxiv-2606-25644:
Colouring a graph drawn on a surface can hit forbidden values. A famous theorem says four sided faces on the projective plane never need exactly three colours. Reza Naserasr, Cyril Pujol, and Lujia Wang unify such gaps in 2026 through winding numbers. A winding number measures how a colouring wraps around cycles when extended to a continuous map. Their framework covers circular colourings, a finer colour measure. It also handles faces of one fixed odd length, settled before only for triangles.

Signed graphs, whose edges carry plus or minus marks, join the theory through a link with vertex switching. New forbidden bands follow. On the projective plane, positive faced signed graphs skip one band of values, and negative faced ones skip another. A construction with arbitrary negative girth shows the signed world is richer. In the unsigned case, the complete graph on six vertices stands alone.
arxiv-2606-25844:
Turning a data stream into a picture lets photo trained vision models read it, and pictures that look natural tend to score better. Faruk Alpay and Barış Başaran ask in 2026 whether that naturalness causes the success, or merely predicts it. They build WorldStream, two hundred ninety nine live series from weather, markets, quakes, and space weather, cut into thousands of windows for a nine way source recognition task. Across seven image encodings and six frozen backbones, distance from natural images predicted accuracy strongly. Then came controlled interventions.

An invertible encoder let them tune only the image's spectrum. Accuracy stayed flat and poor while naturalness peaked exactly where theory said it should. Scrambling phases instead, holding the spectrum fixed and wrecking local structure, dragged accuracy and naturalness down together. The correlation, they conclude, runs through local structure, not spectra. Full fine tuning never closed the gap either.
arxiv-2606-25944:
I. Karaaslan and K. DiPetrillo, joined by Fermilab colleagues David Neuffer, Dimitri Stratakis, and Katsuya Yonehara, work on beam optics for a future ten-tera-electronvolt muon collider. Muons decay quickly, so their beam must be cooled fast: ionization cooling shrinks the beam's spread before the particles vanish. The final cooling stage must squeeze the sideways spread hard, normally using forty-tesla solenoids that strain magnet technology.

A wedge-based scheme offers an alternative route to the same target, but only if stray dispersion, the sideways drift tied to momentum, is suppressed almost completely. Karaaslan's team designs and simulates a suppressor channel that brings dispersion in the target direction down to about a thousandth of a metre. Reaching that value keeps the wedge design viable without leaning on extreme-field magnets.
arxiv-2606-26344:
Akash Kothari, Shaowei Zhu, Daniel Kroening, and Chungha Sung present Axon, a compiler that synthesizes fast kernels for AI accelerators instead of relying on hand-written rewrite rules. Writing such kernels well demands rare expertise in tiling, layout, and fusion.

Axon generates target instructions from formal meaning specifications, then explores equivalent program variants and picks the fastest by measurement. An SMT solver over unbounded tensors guarantees each transformation preserves meaning. On Amazon's Trainium chip it beats the vendor compiler by up to 3.7 times on single operators and 19 times on multi-operator kernels, and even edges out hand-tuned kernels.
arxiv-2606-26444:
D.-H.-Minh Nguyen explores the quantum Hall effect in a fully three-dimensional lattice. In that effect, electrical conduction across a material becomes exactly quantized. Quantized means it locks onto fixed values. Two fields act together along one crystal axis. A magnetic field bends electron paths into circles. An electric field makes electrons oscillate in place through the lattice.

Alone, each field quantizes only part of the electron motion. No complete energy gaps form. Together, Nguyen finds, they confine electrons in all three dimensions. Their paths lie on the surface of a finite cylinder. The spectrum forms a three-dimensional cousin of the Hofstadter butterfly. That is a famous fractal energy pattern. When the Fermi level sits in a gap, sideways conduction is quantized. The Fermi level separates filled states from empty ones. The crystal edges also carry protected hinge currents. Topological numbers called Chern numbers guide those currents.
arxiv-2606-26944:
Hossein Movasati gathers evidence toward a possible counterexample to a conjecture of J. Harris about octic surfaces. Surfaces of degree eight in three-dimensional projective space carry curves whose classes generate deep arithmetic structure. The Noether-Lefschetz locus collects surfaces with extra curve classes. Harris conjectured limits on how special its components can be.

Movasati works on the Fermat octic surface. He takes a line plus a rational multiple of a complete intersection curve of type three-three, the two curves not meeting. For all but finitely many multiples, he assembles strong evidence that the attached loci are distinct surfaces of one codimension, meeting in one higher codimension. Since the maximum possible codimension is only slightly higher, the construction would contradict the conjecture if the evidence is confirmed. The author presents it as a possible counterexample.
arxiv-2606-27344:
Mao and colleagues let robot hands feel contact through vibration, then teach policies in simulation on that same signal. Piezoelectric microphones sense those events with high bandwidth, but raw vibration audio is nearly impossible to simulate faithfully. Their VibeAct framework bridges the gap with a shared physical format: per-finger contact and slip. Real recordings are replayed in a digital clone to label that format on its own.

A tactile estimator learns to read contact and slip from real microphone waveforms. Policies train virtually on the identical format computed from simulated contacts. Five contact-rich tasks, from regrasping to insertion, show consistent wins over a proprioception-and-point-cloud baseline in tests. The continuous slip channel proves most informative where reactive control matters. The learned policies carry over to a real dexterous hand-arm platform with improved success.
arxiv-2606-27444:
Mao leads a team localising drones by matching what they see against semantic three-dimensional city models, no satellite signals required. Aerial pose estimation usually leans on precise navigation signals or rich textured reconstructions, both hard to scale on board. SemCityLoc reframes the problem as surface registration: foundation-model visual priors supply labels and depth, and lightweight city models supply the map. Aligning semantic surfaces sharpens pose discrimination in repetitive, occluded streets in this robotics paper from 2026.

A companion benchmark pairs centimetre-accurate drone poses with city models at three detail levels and hard low-altitude imagery, the first of its kind. Recall improves by up to thirty-six percent over existing map-based approaches in the reported tests. Mean positional error falls from about nine point nine metres to about two point six metres in tight urban canyons. Structured meaning proves sufficient for high-precision flight.
arxiv-2606-27544:
Bautista leads a team working out how a gravitational wave scatters off a spinless point particle, carried to fourth order in Newton's constant. Waveform templates for coalescing binaries demand such work, done here in worldline quantum field theory, which treats the particle as a line through spacetime. A decomposition of the master integrals using Murua coefficients bypasses the cut subtraction needed to reach the Magnusian, the quantity mapping onto the scattering phase shift. Elliptic functions enter the momentum-space result for the first time at this order, in a gravitation paper published in 2026.

The result is matched against black hole perturbation theory. The match shows point-particle worldline theory describes Schwarzschild black holes accurately up to this fourth order. Effective descriptions of black holes gain another storey. Waveform models inherit the precision.
arxiv-2606-27844:
Preferential attachment graphs link new nodes to well-connected old ones. Their degree distributions can have infinite variance. Peter Mörters and Lucas Schätze study bond percolation on such graphs in 2026. Edges are kept with some probability, and the rest are deleted. With any fixed positive keeping probability, one giant component exists. The interesting regime shrinks that probability toward zero.

A moving critical window sits at a power of the graph size, set by the degree exponent. Above the window, the largest component is unique and macroscopic, with size following a stated power law. Below the window, the largest components are non-unique and star-shaped. Inside the window, the largest component, scaled by the square root of the size, converges to a positive random limit whose law comes from a subcritical Norros–Reittu graph. This differs markedly from other scale-free graph classes.
arxiv-2606-28144:
Rebuilding a relightable 3D avatar from one casual photo is an ill-posed problem. PBR training data are scarce, and telling lighting apart from materials is hard. Hong Li and twelve colleagues present a data-efficient framework in 2026. It builds on a unified pretrained diffusion backbone. Cascaded low-rank adaptations handle each sub-task in UV space.

An inpainting module completes textures hidden by occlusion. A light-homogenisation module and a cross-intrinsic attention mechanism remove baked-in lighting. They build pixel-aligned maps for albedo, normal, roughness, specular, and displacement. A UV-space loss on shading keeps the result honest to physics during decomposition. The generative process must satisfy the rendering equation directly. Training used fewer than one hundred real 3D scans. The system still produces complete 4K PBR assets. Realism beats state-of-the-art methods in the reported tests.
arxiv-2606-28344:
Yichuan Wang and seven colleagues argue that web retrieval should skip text altogether. Today's retrieval systems parse web pages into plain text, throwing away layout, formatting, and visual structure, even though the web was designed to be seen. Their PixelRAG system instead stores and reads pages as screenshots.

PixelRAG indexes tens of millions of Wikipedia screenshots with a visual retrieval model fine-tuned on screenshot pairs, then hands retrieved images straight to a vision-language model. It beat text-based and no-retrieval baselines across question answering benchmarks, even text-centered ones, with gains reaching roughly eighteen percent on some tasks. Lower-resolution screenshots cut token costs up to threefold while holding accuracy. Keeping pages in their native visual form, the results suggest, can improve both quality and efficiency.
