arxiv-2606-28444:
Yi-Shan Chu, writing alone, asks why neural network training starts from random weights when the data's own geometry could give a head start. Classical theorems guarantee that one-hidden-layer sigmoid networks can approximate anything, but say nothing about how initial weights should reflect the shape of a dataset.

Chu proposes S-GAI, which reads each class's spectral geometry, its mean, principal directions, and scales, using singular value decomposition. Every retained direction becomes two sigmoid gates in a shared hidden layer, initialized straight from the training images. On MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10, networks initialized this way began from a far more informative state than random initialization and reached comparable final accuracy. Even with the hidden layer frozen, they beat frozen random gates, evidence the geometry truly transfers.
arxiv-2606-28744:
Chaubet, Godfried and Tzou study how long a wandering process takes to first reach a tiny target on a special curved surface. The surfaces are Zoll surfaces, where all shortest closed paths share the same length. The wanderer follows a Levy flight, a random walk whose steps sometimes jump far, bent along the surface's geodesics, its straightest paths.

They measure the mean first capture time, the average wait until the process hits a shrinking geodesic ball. The leading behaviour turns out to be universal, the same for every such surface. The first correction term, though, carries real geometric information. It is set completely by the conjugate locus's local singularity type, the set of points where geodesics refocus, measured by a degree. Different values of the Levy exponent, which controls how wild the jumps are, produce a hierarchy of distinct asymptotic regimes.
arxiv-2606-28844:
Notaro settles a question in set theory and lattice theory that Ditor posed in 1984 about structures called n-ladders. A ladder is a lower finite lattice, an ordering where each element has finitely many elements below it. Each element has at most n lower covers, meaning neighbours directly beneath it. Ditor proved every n-ladder has size at most a certain infinite cardinal, and that the bound is reached for n equal to one and two.

Whether the bound is reached for n of three or more stayed open. A positive answer was known to be consistent with the standard axioms of set theory, called ZFC. Notaro proves the question is independent of those axioms, relative to the consistency strength of Mahlo cardinals, a very large infinite size. The non-existence of a 3-ladder of the critical size carries exactly the same consistency strength as such a cardinal.
arxiv-2606-28944:
Higaki and Sueur prove a precise approximation theorem for the linearised equations of resistive magnetohydrodynamics, the physics of electrically conducting fluids threaded by magnetic fields. Their context is magnetic relaxation, where a field settles toward equilibrium inside a bounded domain. Domain topology matters deeply here: in non-resistive regimes, complex field geometry can obstruct relaxation, while resistive flows relax stably toward a harmonic equilibrium.

Working in the resistive case, they take a control-theoretic viewpoint. The bounded-domain solution splits into a time-evolving part and a stationary part. They then approximate the whole settling path by a global solution on all of three-dimensional space, driven by a remote forcing applied far away. The forcing cost is given in full in terms of the error, so accuracy can be traded against effort. The theorem holds for bounded domains of arbitrary topology.
arxiv-2606-29144:
Mi, Huang and Zhang study quantum steering, a strong form of quantum correlation, in an expanding universe. Their system is a coupled three-mode squeezed vacuum, a three-part light state with special steerability. Expansion complicates matters: causal separation hides some modes behind an event horizon, so observers Alice, Bob and Charlie cannot access all the quantum information.

The authors analyse steering separately for physically accessible modes and inaccessible ones. Steering strength grows with the state's total mean photon number and momentum, and weakens as the expansion volume and expansion rate rise. For the inaccessible modes, steering shows a sudden death phenomenon: past a critical threshold value of a key parameter, it vanishes entirely rather than fading gradually. Accessible modes behave differently, keeping the contrast between the two regimes sharp. The results, the authors argue, give novel insight into how quantum correlations survive, or fail to survive, in curved spacetime.
arxiv-2606-29244:
Ahrazoglu and three colleagues work out a full link budget for very fast wireless links from space. Non-terrestrial networks use satellites and aerial platforms to give worldwide coverage. The sixth generation of mobile systems wants extremely high data rates there, and millimetre-wave and terahertz frequencies offer the bandwidth. But such signals suffer heavy losses from air, weather and pointing errors.

Their analysis counts far more than free-space loss: atmospheric absorption, weather effects, ionospheric disturbance, polarisation mismatch, feeder losses, antenna and circuit limits, fading, pointing error and non-white noise. They vary frequency, altitude and direction across every link type, from ground-satellite to inter-satellite. The layered structure of these networks, they find, cuts losses enough that high-gain directional antennas can sustain multi-gigabit links, making such systems feasible for 6G.
arxiv-2606-29344:
Lagos and Matsypura give an exact algorithm for a class of two-level optimisation problems under uncertainty. In these mixed-integer bilevel stochastic programs, a leader fixes a first-stage decision before uncertainty is revealed. A follower then solves its own mixed-integer problem for each revealed scenario. Discrete choices at both levels make such problems provably hard, and standard single-level rewrites are out of reach.

Their algorithm combines a deterministic value-function reformulation with a split by scenario. An extended single-level form and a matching relaxation make the split possible. A stochastic subgradient cutting-plane scheme then generates follower optimality cuts on the fly while updating Lagrange multipliers. Under boundedness assumptions, they prove the algorithm reaches a true global optimum in finite time. It also maintains valid upper and lower bounds on the answer throughout its run.
arxiv-2606-29744:
Ahmed and five colleagues present HTC-SGA Former, a network that segments blood vessels in coronary angiography images. Digital Subtraction Angiography, or DSA, images guide diagnosis and treatment planning for coronary artery disease. Thin, low-contrast vessels and severe class imbalance make weak branches hard to trace.

Their design is a lightweight hybrid of a convolutional encoder and a Transformer decoder. A multi-scale window attention block handles global-local modelling efficiently. A self-guided attention module strengthens weak-vessel responses. A new boundary-weighted adaptive loss emphasizes thin-vessel boundaries under imbalance. On private left and right coronary DSA subsets, the model outperforms fourteen state-of-the-art methods while using under a million parameters. The new loss also improves four other architectures.
arxiv-2606-29844:
Ma and fourteen colleagues tackle the cost of attention in large language models. Attention, the mechanism that lets a model weigh earlier words, grows quadratically with text length, which makes very long inputs expensive.

Cheaper sparse attention, which looks at only some positions, often fails at tasks needing exact recall of distant details. The team's framework, MATCH, pairs sparse attention with a fast retrieval system that pulls relevant in-context information back in as needed. In experiments on synthetic tests and real language tasks, MATCH significantly improves sparse-attention models while keeping their efficiency. The authors present it as a general way to give thinned-out attention a reliable memory of the full text.
arxiv-2606-30244:
Kun Li, Shengxi Gui, Francesco Nex, and Michael Yang segment objects in aerial images from written descriptions. A user names a target in natural language. The system must find and outline that region in remote sensing imagery. Full fine-tuning of foundation models is expensive for this task. It can also distort the broad knowledge those models carry.

Their framework adapts models by updating only a small parameter share. A dual-encoder adapter design drives the cross-modal interaction. The text adapter distills language proxies from word-level embeddings using learnable queries. The visual adapter refines multi-scale features with a dense extractor. A language-guided mechanism then selects the right scale and spatial regions. Only about two percent of backbone parameters change during tuning. The model still reaches state-of-the-art results on two benchmarks. Efficiency and precision both suit complex aerial scenes.
arxiv-2606-30544:
Heejeong Nam and four colleagues learn action-like signals from videos where many things move at once. Latent action models infer actions from changes between frames. In busy scenes, distractors and camera motion pollute those changes. The true source of any change becomes ambiguous. Their Observed Transition Factorization splits each transition into primitives. A sparse set of reusable motion pieces describes what changed.

Those primitives become the interface for learning latent actions. One model wraps them in the standard inverse–forward dynamics setup. A second variant predicts future states in a frozen feature space. It needs no pixel decoder. The primitives transfer zero-shot across controlled changes. Carrier and body-shape shifts both preserve their usefulness. Downstream policy learning matches or beats the baselines. That holds under complex transition ambiguity. Structuring change into reusable effects is the paper's core bet. It pays off where raw latent actions confuse sources.
arxiv-2606-30644:
James Rogers and Hilke Schlichting ask whether young sub-Neptune planets mix hydrogen into their rocky interiors. Sub-Neptunes are planets larger than Earth but smaller than Neptune. If hydrogen and silicate rock are miscible, meaning they blend into one fluid, a planet can hide most of its hydrogen inside, safe from being blown away by its star. That storage would change how the planet cools and shrinks.

The pair model miscibility together with stellar-driven atmospheric escape. For roughly the first hundred million years, planets keep most hydrogen in their interiors. As escape strips the envelope, fresh hydrogen seeps out of the interior, refilling it and slowing contraction. Their models still match young planet observations from the TESS telescope. They also design a population test using slower contraction, and estimate that seventy to one hundred observed young sub-Neptunes would settle how common mixing is.
arxiv-2606-31244:
Chen and four colleagues update the YBC database of stellar bolometric corrections, values that convert a star's total light output into what a given telescope filter would record. Telescope images of distant stars are often stretched by gravity and shifted by cosmic expansion. The new zYBC version builds corrections for such cosmologically redshifted stars.

The team redshifts spectra from public stellar libraries, dims them with dust curves for both the host galaxy and our own Milky Way, then folds them through filter curves. Added non-LTE model libraries, which drop a simplifying equilibrium assumption, cover hot massive O and B stars with winds. The database serves Hubble, James Webb, and the coming Chinese space station telescope, aiding work on magnified stars in the early universe.
arxiv-2606-31344:
Ciancia and four colleagues speed up spatial model checking of images by shrinking the model first. Spatial logics describe properties of regions, such as a pixel being reachable from another under conditions. The closure models behind them grow large, so checking every state directly is slow.

Their minimisation targets CoPa bisimilarity, an equivalence for quasi-discrete closure models with forward and backward reachability. By encoding closure models as labelled transition systems, branching bisimilarity algorithms can compute the CoPa classes. Their VoxMinX prototype keeps the link between each class and its pixels in the source image. The minimised model can then be checked in place of the full one, bringing spatial verification of image properties within practical reach.
arxiv-2606-31544:
Rudnick classifies the real quadratic fields that satisfy Hammarhjelm's condition. Such a field has unique factorization in its ring of integers, and the Minkowski lattice of that ring avoids a certain rectangle fixed by its fundamental unit. These fields recently surfaced in work on visible points within algebraic cut-and-project sets.

Exactly seven fields qualify, with discriminants 8, 5, 13, 29, 53, 173, and 293. The proof shows the fundamental unit must be small relative to the discriminant for the condition to hold. Genus theory then narrows the field, and Biró's classification of class number one fields in Yokoi's family finishes the list. A condition that looked open-ended turns out to admit a short, complete answer.
arxiv-2606-31644:
Shafiei, Li and Tsvetkov show that language models can look morally fair in tests while behaving less fairly in realistic disguise, a failure they name performative compliance. Standard fairness evaluations state demographic identity as an explicit label, exactly the format safety training teaches models to handle carefully. Real decisions in healthcare, law and hiring usually carry identity implicitly.

Their cue-variation method holds the moral dilemma and the person's identity fixed while changing only how that identity is conveyed, including hiding it inside a short logic puzzle. Removing the explicit label raises harmful decisions by 4.4 percentage points and reshuffles model safety rankings, even when models correctly infer the identity, ruling out simple misreading. A proposed Cue Visibility Gap metric lets any fairness benchmark separate genuine moral safety from surface compliance.
arxiv-2606-31844:
Wang and three others tackle a mismatch between how traffic simulators learn and where they run. Simulators train on ego-centric driving logs, where the recording car sees rich local detail but surrounding agents stay partly hidden. Deployed in fully observable closed-loop settings, the learned habits can produce abnormal stops, unsafe interactions and rule violations.

Their framework, CRAFT, rolls out what-if scenarios inside the simulator to expose such failures on purpose. A Contextual Preference Evaluator, trained on the grounded failures, then scores the actions put forward at inference time under full scene context. Decoding is reweighted toward behavior that is coherent as a whole, with no retraining of the base simulator. Collisions fall by 31.2 percent in their tests, and traffic violations drop by 33.2 percent.
arxiv-2608-00144:
Maricato studies per-document data leakage from language models, beyond aggregate membership inference. Membership scores are usually summed up by ROC-AUC. Such summaries can mislead, he argues. Blind baselines can split members from non-members on surface text alone. Sampling-based extraction gives a sharper probe of real harm.

On WikiMIA, a blind classifier reached AUC 0.97, and sampling added nothing. On a Pile split, aggregate sampling measures did not beat the blind baseline either. Yet sampling extracted identifiers verbatim for a tail of documents. In Pythia-6.9B, 16.6 percent of identifier-bearing documents leaked their identifier. Code leaked about three times more strongly than prose. He urges audits to report per-document extraction, not just aggregate scores.
arxiv-2608-00344:
Das and co-authors study a spinning Brownian particle in a viscoelastic fluid. Tests show spin boosts the particle's long-time diffusivity. It also makes cross-correlations between sideways shifts that flip sign in time. Those shifts sit in the plane normal to the spin axis. A minimal linear model explains both effects.

A tracer couples to a slow bath variable in the model. Spin enters via an advective link. Dropping the bath variable gives a generalized Langevin equation. Its memory kernel is non-reciprocal and spins in time as a log spiral. The kernel obeys Onsager-Casimir symmetry when spin is reversed. A geometric build links cross-correlations to transverse response. Tests and theory agree in broad terms, they report.
arxiv-2608-00444:
Wan and co-authors propose DMD, a mask-guided diffusion method for medical anomaly detection. Unsupervised detection learns normal anatomy from healthy images and flags deviations at test time. Reconstruction gaps are the usual evidence signal. That signal can mislead in both directions. Strong models may rebuild pathological structures, while benign variation and noise leave large gaps.

DMD adds reconstruction-shift discrimination to residual localization. It first learns a compact quantized latent code of normal images. Masks perturb chosen latent regions, and a diffusion model rebuilds them. Those rebuilds, paired with the originals, define a self-supervised classification task. At test time, the classifier scores whole images while residuals map pixels. On five data sets, DMD gave the best overall results among top baselines.
as-you-like-it-pg2244: Arden heals all in this edition: the exiled Duke, Rosalind in doublet and hose, and Jaques with his seven ages find refuge in the forest. Four couples marry as the greenwood works its magic. The sunniest of the comedies, dappled with philosophy.
berkeley-siris-1744:
Siris, from 1744, is George Berkeley's strangest and most wide-ranging late work. Its full title promises a chain of philosophical reflexions and inquiries. The subject at the chain's foot is tar water, a folk tonic of pine tar stirred in water. Berkeley praised it as a cure for fevers and ills, in verse and prose alike.

All 367 sections are here, and the chain climbs far from the tonic bottle. Berkeley rises through chemistry and the fine fluid called aether to Plato, the Trinity, and God himself. The book joins medicine, physics, and theology in one ascending argument. It is the old immaterialist's last word, and his boldest.
blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-volume-55:
January 1844 opens Blackwood's fifty-fifth volume with State Prosecutions, then rides to Texas for the third adventure, the Struggle. Clitophon and Leucippe revives the Greek romance; a Designing Devil explains the new art of printing; Kíeff comes from the Russian of Kozlóff; and Marston reaches part seven. A Letter from Lemuel Gulliver borrows Swift's traveller for modern satire, and the position and prospects of the government closes the politics.

The Banking-House ends its run here, and its rogue Planner enjoys the darkest hour of the sampled pages — nearer, in it, to deliverance and perfect peace than ever before. Planner was essentially a lucky dog: dropped from a house-top he would land on his feet. Led to the gallows, the noose would slip. While Michael is immersed in managing his loans, the machinery of the fraud grinds toward its comic deliverance.

Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for March 1844 is the monthly literary and political number CCCXLI, volume LV, from the Edinburgh house of William Blackwood. Like its companion issues it mixes fiction, travel writing, poetry, and Tory comment on public affairs. Many pieces ran without a byline, in the magazine's house style.

Fiction leads with part one of The Pirates of Segna, a tale of Venice and the Adriatic, and part nine of the serial Marston, about a statesman. Review essays take up Major Harris on Ethiopia and Colonel Davidson's travels in India. Poems include A Roman Idyl and Hymn of a Hermit. A long closing essay argues the case against free trade and for keeping the Corn Laws. Readers get a full cross-section of the magazine at its height.

April 1844 brings number CCCXLII of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, volume LV, the Edinburgh monthly that mixed serial fiction with sharp Tory reviewing. Contributors wrote without bylines, so the number speaks in one editorial voice. Its pages move between adventure tales, history, naval matters, and Irish politics.

Part two of The Pirates of Segna, a tale of Venice and the Adriatic, opens the number, and part ten of Marston carries the statesman serial forward. Essays treat the slave trade, Moslem histories of Spain and the Arabs of Cordova, and the state of the British fleet. A traveller's fragment gives two nights in southern Mexico. Verse and short pieces fill the gaps, and a closing article on Ireland argues the Unionist case at length for British readers of the day.
blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-volume-56:
Number CCCXLV of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine opens volume LVI in July 1844, printed in Edinburgh by Ballantyne and Hughes for William Blackwood and Sons. The monthly number gathers essays, serial fiction, travel sketches, and verse under one cover. Its writers stay unnamed, as the magazine preferred.

An opening essay counts the causes of a sharp rise in crime across Britain and Ireland. Other pieces give a month's tour in Sicily, the heart of the Bruce, and traditions and tales of Upper Lusatia. Goethe's poems and ballads appear in translation, and a sketch recalls a first love in New York. Part twelve of Marston continues the statesman serial. Portugal, Martin Luther in verse, and an emperor's week round out a varied number for general readers.

August 1844 in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine is number CCCXLVI, volume LVI, issued from George Street, Edinburgh, by William Blackwood and Sons. The monthly miscellany joins political essays to tales, poems, and literary notice. As usual, its contributors publish without names.

A fierce lead essay revisits the Afghan war and the Kabul disaster, demanding a clear verdict on blame. Tales follow: A Love Chase in prose, The Old Scottish Cavalier, and The Dwarf's Well from the traditions of Upper Lusatia. The Etching Club shows its etched thoughts, and an essay traces the ancient canal between the Nile and the Red Sea. Remarks on Schiller's Maid of Orleans, a stolen-child story, a piece on M Girardin, and a memoir of Lord Eldon complete the number.
chambers-vestiges-1844:
Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation appeared anonymously in 1844 and became a sensation. Its author, revealed only after his death, was Robert Chambers, an Edinburgh publisher. The book popularized evolution, human evolution included, fifteen years before Darwin's Origin of Species.

Chambers argues that all life, man included, rose by natural law from simple beginnings, as planets form and species unfold. The science is shaky in places, but the sweep carried thousands of readers into deep time. Clergy denounced it; drawing rooms devoured it; Darwin read the storm and took care to build his own case stronger. The book Darwin had to answer still repays reading.
cia-0000007544:
Volume 9, number 2 of Studies in Intelligence followed in spring 1965, carrying a miscellaneous collection of material. The journal served as the CIA's internal forum, where officers wrote up lessons from analysis and operations. A mixed issue gathers shorter pieces that fit no single theme.

Even miscellany has value: it shows the range of questions working officers raised in 1965. Readers today meet the agency thinking on paper about sources, secrecy, and judgment. Because the audience was internal, the tone stays practical rather than public-facing. Declassification turned staff reading into a public record of Cold War intelligence practice.
cia-0000008444:
Could South Vietnam hold a stable government? A CIA paper from August 1964 put that question at its center. Saigon had seen a revolving door of leaders since Diem's fall the year before. Generals competed for power while the Viet Cong pressed in the countryside.

The paper weighs the coups, factions, and weak institutions that made stability so hard. Its answer mattered because Washington was tying its own credibility to Saigon's survival. Readers now can compare the analysts' doubts with the escalation that followed. The file preserves a clear statement of the problem at the war's turning point.
cia-0000008844:
Germany's future sat at the center of a 1947 CIA review of Soviet, British, and French programs. Two years after the Second World War, the victors still shared occupation zones but not a plan. Each power pushed its own design for the defeated country.

The review compares those designs and what each implied for Europe's balance. Washington needed to know where allies agreed, where they clashed, and where Moscow gained. Papers like this one date from the CIA's first months of life. They show the young agency starting with the largest question on the map: Germany divided between East and West.
cia-0000009044:
Quang Binh province, in North Vietnam, appears in a May 1972 report of an American prisoner of war sighted there. The heading notes a cover item traveling with the report, though its text is cut off in the title. Quang Binh bordered the demilitarized zone and absorbed years of bombing.

Prisoner sightings from this corridor were common, because captives moved north through it. Each sighting had to be timed and placed to test whether it fit known movements. Most stayed unconfirmed, yet the file kept them all. This one preserves a mid-war glimpse of a captive passing through the border country.
cia-0000009444:
One American and five Vietnamese prisoners were sighted together in Ba Xuyen province, a September 1971 report states. Ba Xuyen sits in South Vietnam's Mekong Delta, where Viet Cong camps hid in swamps and canals. Mixed groups of prisoners were common in the southern system.

A sighting naming both nationalities shows how the southern prisons actually held people: together, not apart. For the American's file, the report fixed a time, a place, and company. For historians, it corrects a Hanoi-centered picture of captivity. The Delta's camps held thousands of Vietnamese beside a smaller number of Americans.
cia-0000012244:
Guided democracy was Sukarno's name for his rule over Indonesia, and in February 1962 a CIA paper weighed the country's prospects under it. Sukarno balanced the army against the growing communist party, the PKI, while ruling by decree and grand spectacle. Indonesia, newly free of Dutch rule, was poor, vast, and hard to hold together as one state.

The paper judges the strongman's grip and the forces straining at it day by day. It weighs the communists' rise, the army's patience, and the economy's steady decay. Read later, it senses a founding father's twilight years before the storm that ended his rule.
cia-0000012444:
Castro, Model 1966: a CIA profile from February 1966 assesses the Cuban leader seven years after his revolution. The title treats him like a yearly model of a car, updated for the season. By 1966 Fidel Castro was a fixture of the hemisphere. He ruled an island ninety miles from Florida, defiant, bearded, and bound to Moscow. Washington had failed at every attempt to dislodge him.

The profile tries to see past the beard to the regime beneath it. It weighs his health, his grip, and his likely moves for the year. For readers, it shows the analysts' yearly ritual of modeling a stubborn man.
cia-0000013244:
What happened to North Vietnamese prisoners after their own side took them back? A CIA paper from October 1967 studies the treatment of released prisoners on their return to North Vietnam. The returnees' reception was weighed from defectors' and agents' reports. The analysts found suspicion waiting for them, not parades. Men who had been in enemy hands were doubted, watched, and questioned by their own security services.

The paper is the files' mirror image of the captivity story. The enemy's freed faced their own hard homecoming across the lines. For readers, it shows the prisoner's fate as both sides' systems understood it.
cia-0000015244: Contact with Leon Davidson was person to person, in a CIA file dated November 5, 1957. Davidson was writing a piece, and the file follows his press contacts. He pushed the Air Force and the CIA hard on flying saucer claims. Files like this chart the odd dance between keen amateurs and tight lipped offices.
cia-0000015344: The flying saucers problem is the blunt title of a CIA file dated September 2, 1952. Problem was the right word that fall, with reports pouring in. Framing it so plainly shows officers saw a task, not a thrill. The file stands near the start of the agency's formal work on the question.
cia-0000036844:
A Hanoi correspondent's dispatch in English, sent for the Prensa service, fills a CIA record dated September 3, 1967. It carries an interview with John McCain, the captured American pilot. Prensa Latina was Cuba's news agency, and its copy reached papers across Latin America.

The dispatch lets readers trace how Hanoi's account of a prisoner spread abroad. Interviews given in captivity were checked word by word against other reports. The file shows enemy news, wire copy, and intelligence work meeting on a single page. English was the language chosen so the story could travel far beyond Cuba and Vietnam alike.
cia-0000044044:
Archbishop Rivera y Damas urged Cristiani to investigate the killings, in a CIA record dated October 1, 1989 in the catalog. The title ties his urging to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. The archbishop's moral standing made his pressure hard to shrug off.

Inside, the church's demand for a real inquiry is placed on record. A president could delay many critics, but not his archbishop for long. The plea joined grief to a concrete demand for action. The file preserves the church leaning on the state in public, a stance that shaped the case's course from its first days in the headlines.
cia-0000046944: Remains, dog tags, and a claimed live sighting in Laos fill a CIA item dated August 4, 1990. The three kinds of evidence sat at very different levels of proof, from the solid to the hoped-for. Together they show the missing-men search still running on fragments, fifteen years after the war ended.
cia-0000049144: A Newsweek article reported on December 2 is preserved in a CIA item from 1989, kept with the Truth Commission records. The capital had just come through the FMLN's November offensive and the Jesuit murders, and American magazines were the war's loudest witnesses. The clipping shows editors abroad framing events that the files recorded hour by hour.
cia-0000049244:
Progress and problems on human rights in El Salvador are weighed in a CIA paper from 1987, preserved in the Truth Commission file series. By then, American aid hung on regular judgments about whether the Salvadoran forces were abusing fewer people than before. The paper is one of those judgments, made mid-war.

Inside, gains are set against failures: units or practices that improved, and the killings and cover-ups that continued. The mixed verdict was the era's standard product, since a clean report would have been disbelieved and a wholly black one would have cut the aid. Read now, it shows the grading system under which the war was supplied.
cia-0000095044: Current status of UAR President Nasir's health is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000095044, dated June 1, 1967. The heading uses the period name for Egypt's president, spelled Nasir in the record. Readers find a short declassified health status item, a reminder that leaders' health was itself tracked as intelligence in the agency's files.
cia-0000096944: Proposed CIA response to requests for information received from an unnamed source, in the cut-short heading, is declassified CIA document 0000096944, dated February 3, 1973. The title ends mid-phrase in the catalog. Readers get a draft-response record sharing its date with the routing sheet nearby, the pair showing an answer and its paperwork together.
cia-0000098744: Cardoen spokesman discusses new helicopter is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000098744, dated April 1, 1990. The heading names the firm and a spokesman's topic. The brief file records remarks about a new helicopter as its subject. It is a short company-statement item. The agency preserved it among its technology and industry records from that spring.
cia-0000102944: Use of Forced Labor in BAM Railroad and Sakhalin Island is the first numbered topic of declassified CIA document 0000102944, dated August 5, 1983. A railroad and an island share the heading. The brief file closes the catalog run as a labor record joining two distant places, the last entry in this slice's long Soviet cluster.
cia-0000107344: Current Intelligence Staff Study - New Stage of the Sino-soviet Dispute Octob is the heading, cut off mid-month, on declassified CIA document 0000107344, dated January 1, 1962. The title marks a staff study on a new stage in the split between Moscow and Beijing. Its trailing month breaks off at Octob in the heading. The brief record is a staff study item from 1962.
cia-0000112344: Ufo Research Organization to Hold Conference in Beijing is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112344, dated March 4, 1992. The title reports a planned conference in Beijing by a UFO research organization. The organization is not named in the heading itself. The brief record is a conference item, filed in the spring of 1992 as released in the files.
cia-0000119744: A CIA report gives the Hungarian situation as of 1 a.m. Eastern time during the 1956 crisis. Overnight editions like this one kept Washington posted while Budapest slept, and the paper preserves that early morning picture of the revolt. Hour-stamped reports from that autumn survive as a minute-by-minute layer in the record of the uprising, each one fixing what was known when.
cia-0000132144: An August 1988 CIA Middle East Brief for August 18 carries a Pakistan situation report: a crash has killed the Pakistani president and the American ambassador. President Zia-ul-Haq died in that crash the day before. The brief covers the crisis as it broke. Zia's death left Pakistan's course suddenly open, and a same-week brief on the crash belongs to the first hours of a succession no one had scripted.
cia-0000132444:
A proposed Cuban conference of underdeveloped nations fills a CIA document dated January 4, 1960. Havana wanted to gather poor countries together and speak as their leader. The idea of a third world standing apart from both Cold War camps was still new at the time.

The document covers the proposal and the planning behind it. Cuba hoped the meeting would raise its standing far beyond the Caribbean. For readers, the entry shows the young revolution thinking globally from its first year. It also shows Washington watching that ambition closely and counting which governments might answer Havana's call.
cia-0000132644: Central American republics possibly acting together to break relations fill a CIA item dated May 1, 1960. The headline breaks off at the word relati, plainly meaning relations with Cuba. Joint action was the playbook regional bodies used on the Cuba problem. A shared break would isolate Havana across the isthmus at once. The short item reports the possible move and its backers.
cia-0000132744:
The running series Cuban Developments continued on November 4, 1960, four days before the American presidential election. By late 1960 the break between Washington and Castro was effectively complete. The United States was backing Cuban exiles against his government.

Against that backdrop, the series kept its steady watch: regular entries recording the revolution's course while policy hardened around it. The November paper stands between the summer's collapsing relations and the new year, when planning turned to invasion. Now open to the public, the declassified briefing preserves one entry in that unbroken watch. The watch itself continued without pause.
cia-0000134244: Dated 1961, this declassified CIA item is a letter addressed to the Special Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs, the president's top national security aide. The catalog title is cut off mid-word, and it gives neither a sender nor a subject. The record does not say what the letter concerns, so no subject is claimed. It is preserved as released through the CIA Reading Room, a piece of correspondence to the White House whose text must speak for itself.
cia-0000135744: Dated 4 March 1961, a Spanish text from the papers of Brigade 2506. The exile brigade was nearing the end of its training for the invasion of Cuba, which the CIA had organized in secret over the previous year. The catalog record names no subject for this document. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, one of a close run of brigade items from the first days of March 1961.
cia-0000136144: A declassified CIA cable dated 2 April 1954 turns to sending a Spanish text cable directed toward a reader the heading leaves cut off. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136344: Castillo needed twenty thousand quetzales urgently, according to the radio material from the night of 28 June 1954 summarized in this cable. Weather had improved, he had a patrol southwest of Zacapa, and another force was told to aid a maneuver by attacking Zacapa from the west. Other messages report railway bridges over the Tamaras and Uluazapa rivers that must be blown to stop night supply shipments. The war was ending, but the orders kept flowing.
cia-0000136744: Dated 4 February 1961, a Spanish text from the papers of Brigade 2506. The exile force was drilling through its final winter, weeks from embarkation. The catalog record gives this document no individual subject. It survives in the original Spanish in the declassified release, a dated unit in the brigade's February archive, and it is described here on the strength of the record alone.
cia-0000139044: Hans Berger reviews Walter Lippmann in this September 1944 OSS note. The heading calls it a German communist view of Germany. Berger held an important rank in the international communist movement. He praised Lippmann's earlier book on foreign policy. It stressed ending isolationism once and for all. The new book draws his fire. Lippmann offers an ersatz system of orbits, Berger argues. Germany would be made dependent on maritime commerce. It would sit inside an Atlantic Community. Berger calls it a Chamberlain thesis in new garb.
cia-03189344:
Central Intelligence Bulletin dated 25 June 1960, marked Top Secret, opens with the first Soviet press announcement of a demobilized army division. The bulletin notes that foreign observers were allowed, for the first time, to see troop cuts inside the Soviet Union under the current manpower reduction program. That item anchors the Communist Bloc section for the day.

Asia-Africa items report Algerian rebels planning a tough line in talks with France, and Turkey's president declining an invitation to Moscow. The brief also covers approval of Lumumba's cabinet in the Congo, separatist feeling there, Afghan criticism of the West, and Nationalist artillery fire around Chinmen. Western items cover Venezuela, Trujillo, Cuba, and Chancellor Raab's coming meeting with Khrushchev in Austria.
cia-06232644:
Central Intelligence Bulletin for 20 November 1958, marked Top Secret, leads with a strong Soviet line on Berlin. The bulletin reports Gromyko telling West Germany's ambassador that Moscow would hand its Berlin rights to East Germany without more talks. Ambassador Thompson's list of Khrushchev's likely aims in the move is also noted.

A second bloc item treats Chinese communes as a sore point between Moscow and Peiping. The bulletin reports that Chinese statements had lately stressed socialist construction and dropped claims that communes had brought China near to Communism. Asia-Africa items cover Sudan, Iran's chief of staff voicing disillusion with the Baghdad Pact, and Iraqi steps against United Arab Republic plotting. Thailand's Marshal Sarit and Venezuela's Larrazabal close the summary.
cia-06714444:
Role sheets for a collection game assign each player a part in the intelligence process. One sheet makes a player the political analyst, judging foreign governments' goals, motives, and decision making. Another makes a player the military analyst, weighing the capabilities and intentions of foreign security forces and non-state armed groups.

On a turn, a player may take two actions, such as moving between collectors or placing colored gems at a location. Dice are rolled against gems placed to gain reporting, which can fill a reports circle or reduce a crisis. A collaboration bonus rewards players who share a space with the political analyst. Later sheets list the collectors: State, Defense HUMINT, the Open Source Enterprise, and the CIA Directorate of Operations among them. Their one-line duties describe what each one gathers or passes on.
coke-institutes-part4-1644:
The Fourth Part of Coke's Institutes was printed in 1644, in the heat of the English Civil War. Its subject is the jurisdiction of courts: which court may hear which kind of case. Coke, who had presided over the system he describes, maps the whole machinery of English justice.

He surveys courts from Parliament and the great courts at Westminster down to local and special tribunals. For each, he gives its powers, its officers, and its limits. The survey doubles as a defense of the common law courts against rival royal courts of his own day. Read as a whole, the volume is the constitution of England in legal dress, an institutional map drawn by the man who knew the terrain best. It completes Coke's great design for the Institutes.
doe-osti-3010790-final-technical-report-:
Control of bright electron beams is covered by Jared Maxson of Cornell in a final report for DOE award DE-SC0020144, dated December 29, 2025, spanning September 2019 to August 2025. Ultrafast electron pulses, shorter than a trillionth of a second, film atoms in materials far from equilibrium.

The weak point is beam quality: photoemitted ultrafast pulses are dimmer and less coherent than standard beams. A reconstruction method built here brings back the full emitted phase space, space and momentum spread together, from 4D emittance measurements at several photocathode spots plus a symplectic condition from Hamiltonian mechanics. Space charge studies with apertures found best settings that give up some charge on purpose. The tools target DOE's ultrafast facilities.
doe-osti-3362717-final-report-sc0022244:
Eugene A. Olevsky and Wenwu Xu of San Diego State University report final results under grant SC0022244, for work from September 2021 to August 2024, prepared in October 2025. Their method, electro-nano-pulsing, fires capacitor discharges lasting nanoseconds to microseconds through a material. The pulses heat grain boundaries, the seams between crystals, almost instantly and only at the nanoscale, letting engineers reshape a material inner structure faster than normal furnace work allows.

Guided by computer models, the pulses cut nanoscale steps and serrations into grain boundaries of Nichrome-80. They also turned loose dislocations into jagged lines and ordered walls, at local densities near 10 to the 15th per square meter. A single 330 nanosecond pulse at set strength triggered controlled precipitation, hinting at property tuning by pulse alone.
dumas-corsican-brothers-1844:
Alexandre Dumas published The Corsican Brothers in 1844, here in Henry Frith's English translation. The eerie tale is the definitive literary treatment of the Corsican blood feud in fiction. Dumas had toured Corsica and filled the tale with its wild hills and stern codes.

Twin brothers, joined at birth and split by surgery, still share each other's pains across distance. One lives a Paris dandy, the other a mountain man bound to vendetta and honor in Corsica. A duel over a woman in Paris is felt, wound for wound, by the brother at home. The surviving twin takes up the feud, and the debt of blood is paid in full. Frith's version kept the tale a staple of English Gothic and sensation shelves.
dumas-count-of-monte-cristo-1844:
Alexandre Dumas published The Count of Monte Cristo in 1844, in serial form in Paris. The vast tale of betrayal and revenge became one of the world's most popular novels ever. Dumas drew its germ from a police file tale of a man falsely jailed for years.

Edmond Dantès, a young sailor, is jailed on his wedding day by rivals' false charges. In the Château d'If, Abbé Faria teaches him and tells of a vast treasure on Monte Cristo. Dantès escapes, finds the gold, and returns as the Count to ruin his three betrayers. Each revenge is patient, rich, and exact, yet mercy checks his hand at the brink. The book's grip on readers, from schoolboys to statesmen, has never loosened since 1844.
dumas-regents-daughter-1844:
Alexandre Dumas published The Regent's Daughter in 1844, opening his Regency cycle of historical romance. The tale retells the Cellamare conspiracy against the Regent, Philippe d'Orléans, in early 1700s France. It appeared the same year as The Three Musketeers, in Dumas's flood of serial triumphs then.

Gaston de Chanlay, a Breton noble, joins a Spanish-backed plot to kidnap the Regent in Paris. He loves Hélène, a convent girl who proves to be the Regent's own hidden daughter in secret. Duty to the plot and love for Hélène tear the young conspirator in two at Paris. The Regent's mercy and the block await the plotters in a close of mixed grace. Dumas finds pathos in a minor plot that most histories pass in a page.
dumas-three-musketeers-1844:
Alexandre Dumas published The Three Musketeers in 1844, in serial form in a Paris paper. The swashbuckling tale of d'Artagnan and his three friends became a byword for adventure in France. Its motto, all for one and one for all, is known far beyond the book.

Young d'Artagnan rides to Paris with a letter, a horse, and dreams of the King's Musketeers. He falls in with Athos, Porthos, and Aramis, and duels become brotherhood in a single day. Queen Anne's diamond studs, Richelieu's plots, and the spy Milady drive the swift intrigue along. The siege of La Rochelle gives the private vendettas a grand public stage of war. Dumas's pace, humor, and swordplay still set the bar for historical adventure tales.
emerson-essays-second-series-1844:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published Essays: Second Series in 1844, with The Poet and Experience inside. The set is the mature statement of transcendentalist aesthetics in Emerson's evolving and deepening public thought. Grief for his dead son darkens Experience, giving the later essays a chastened, autumnal tone throughout them.

The Poet calls for an American bard who will sing the facts of farms, trades, and rivers. Experience asks what life teaches when sorrow shows how little the soul can truly hold fast. Character, Manners, and Gifts weigh how spirit shows in conduct, breeding, and the things we give. Emerson's sentences here are denser, more oracular, and less sure than in the first bright series. Whitman and later poets took The Poet as a personal commission to write America.
europmc-pmc10029244:
Zhang and co-workers review the roles of tumor-linked macrophages in checkpoint immunotherapy for solid cancers, in a 2023 paper. Checkpoint drugs free T cells to attack tumors, yet only a small share of patients gains lasting benefit. The cells around the tumor, including macrophages, help decide who responds.

The review explains how these macrophages can block or aid the drugs' effects. It surveys ways to reprogram them, such as blocking their signals or clearing them out. The authors argue that pairing such steps with checkpoint drugs could widen the circle of patients who benefit.
europmc-pmc10172144:
Gordon and a large team report that a body-and-mind action network alternates with movement zones in the motor cortex, in a 2023 study. The motor cortex is the brain strip that controls movement. Textbooks drew it as a smooth map running from foot to face, yet hints of a more complex layout had built up for years.

Using precise brain imaging, the team found zones for whole-body action planning wedged between zones for single body parts. The finding rewrites a classic brain map. It may also help explain links between movement, thought, and body control.
europmc-pmc10543444:
Panwar and co-authors reviewed the mTOR signal path in 2023, a master switch for cell growth. mTOR is an enzyme that steers fuel use, growth, survival, and cell movement. It works in two teams, called mTORC1 and mTORC2. It also controls autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning process.

When the path sticks on, harm can follow across the body. Panwar links such faults to ageing, brain disease, and many cancers. The path also feeds cancer stem cells and drug resistance. Long non-coding RNAs, gene strips that build no protein, tune the path as well. The review weighs drugs that block mTOR for cancer care. It asks how to make them hit harder in clinics.
europmc-pmc10599644:
Wang, Wang, Yang, and Liu reviewed in 2023 how gut microbes may shape brain growth in children. Microbes in the gut talk to the brain through a two-way route, the microbiota-gut-brain axis. That talk steers body processes as the brain forms. Faults in the talk may feed disorders of brain growth.

Three paths carry the signals, Wang reports: immune, nerve, and hormone routes. The paths overlap and cross-talk as they run. Studies now link the axis to autism, ADHD, and Rett syndrome, a rare growth disorder. The review sums up what each link rests on. It also flags where proof is thin and what tests come next.
europmc-pmc11701544:
Paysan-Lafosse and a large team update the Pfam protein families database in this 2025 paper. Pfam groups proteins into families and domains, the reusable parts of proteins, to aid genome annotation and protein study. Since 2020 the old Pfam website was shut and the resource folded into InterPro, a larger hub.

Curation grew for families from metagenomes, meaning DNA read straight from the environment, and for microproteins and repeat-rich families. The scheme was harmonised with the ECOD structural classification. AlphaFold structure predictions now help refine domain boundaries and spot new domains. Large-scale scans of AlphaFold models found new families. A deep learning add-on, Pfam-N, widened coverage, lifting coverage of the UniProtKB protein archive by 8.8 percent. More frequent releases are planned.
europmc-pmc1240944:
Gurgueira and co-authors exposed rats to concentrated city air particles in 2002. Dish studies had hinted that reactive oxygen species drive particle harm. Whether breathing particles raises those species in living tissue was untested. Rats breathed concentrated particles or filtered air for up to five hours.

After five hours, oxidant signals rose sharply in lung and heart tissue. Lung readings hit 41 counts versus 24 in clean-air controls. Heart readings showed the same jump, while liver showed none. Toxic fly ash particles raised lung readings still higher. Inert carbon black caused no such rise.
europmc-pmc1298944:
Wendler and co-authors tested whether minorities refuse health research more often in 2006. The claim is widespread in the United States. Hard data behind it were scarce. A full literature search found every study reporting consent by race or ethnicity.

Twenty studies covered over 70,000 enrollment decisions. Research types ran from interviews to drug and surgical trials. Most studies were American, with two large multi-country exceptions. Consent patterns were compared across groups study by study. Wendler checks a repeated assumption against the actual record. Most of the twenty studies were single-site American studies.
europmc-pmc1343544:
Olssøn, Mykletun, and Dahl tested an anxiety and depression scale in general practice in 2005. Family doctors often miss generalized anxiety and major depression. Short questionnaires could sharpen their detection. The scale tested was the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Rating Scale.

Survey data covered 1,781 patients of 141 doctors across Norway. Patient-rated reference questionnaires defined true cases. For anxiety, the best cutoff was a score of 8 or more. At that cutoff, sensitivity was 0.89 and specificity 0.75. The scale was also compared against doctor severity ratings. Data were gathered over three days in September 2001.
europmc-pmc1397844:
Zwakhalen, Hamers, Abu-Saad, and Berger reviewed pain scales for severe dementia in 2006. Pain affects 40 to 80 percent of elderly nursing home residents. People with severe dementia cannot report pain directly. Behavior-based scales are the main assessment route.

The search covered four databases plus citations from 1988 to 2005. Twenty-nine publications on behavioral tools were selected. Twelve watch-based scales were evaluated for measurement quality and clinical use. Named scales include PAINAD, PACSLAC, and DOLOPLUS2. Quality criteria judged reliability and validity of each scale. Zwakhalen guides tool choice for dementia care. Scales were judged for use in daily care too. Pain checks are step one in good pain care for these old people. Good tools must be quick for staff to use at the bed side.
europmc-pmc1435944:
Linking a gene to a disease takes many kinds of proof. Yue, Melamud, and Moult built a web tool for that task in 2006, called SNPs3D. One part names genes that may drive a chosen disease. A second part shows how those genes relate to each other.

A third part judges how a single letter change, a SNP, may harm a protein. It uses protein shape and clues from how species keep the spot alike. Each gene page links to papers, activity data, and mouse studies. Yue shows the tool at work on swelling responses and high blood pressure, helping users form testable models fast.
europmc-pmc1698944:
A common cold-sore kin rewires a cell's chemistry to feed its own copying. Munger and co-authors measured that rewiring in 2006 during human cytomegalovirus infection of fibroblasts. They tracked 63 metabolites over time with mass spectrometry.

As infection advanced, metabolites in sugar burning, the citric acid cycle, and pyrimidine building climbed markedly. Gene activity for the matching enzymes rose in parallel. Peak levels far exceeded those in growing or resting uninfected cells. Munger concludes the virus imposes its own metabolic program, quite unlike normal cell states, to secure energy and building blocks.
europmc-pmc1866244:
Van Ert, Keim and co-authors charted the world family tree of the anthrax bacterium in 2007. Bacillus anthracis causes anthrax in animals and people, and its global spread was long known only from anecdotes. Typing its strains precisely also matters for tracing outbreaks and attacks.

The team sequenced seven diverse strains end to end to find rare single-letter DNA differences. Those markers, plus 15 repeat-length markers, were used to type 1,033 isolates from 42 countries. The collection split into three known major lineages, then 12 clonal sub-lineages, and finally 221 unique genotypes. Variation proved very rare, as expected for a recently emerged clone. The map documents how the bacterium evolved and diversified as it spread around the world with livestock trade.
europmc-pmc1885944:
Keays, Flint and colleagues traced in 2007 a mouse brain defect to a fault in a skeleton protein, then found the human counterpart. Building the brain requires neurons to migrate into neat layers, and failures cause lissencephaly, a smooth-brain disorder in children. A chemically mutagenized mouse strain showed scrambled layers in cortex and hippocampus.

The fault sat in the energy-binding pocket of alpha-1 tubulin, a building block of the cell's internal rails. It disturbed pairing of tubulin units, which neurons need to move. The match with known lissencephaly models prompted screening of patients with developmental brain anomalies. Two patients carried brand-new mutations in TUBA3, the human version of the mouse gene. The study shows mouse mutagenesis can crack open the basis of human brain disorders.
europmc-pmc1892244:
Schmierer, Miller and co-authors tested in 2007 whether an advanced MRI method truly reflects tissue damage in multiple sclerosis brain after death. Standard MRI predicts patients' disability poorly, likely because it is not specific to the damage that matters. Diffusion tensor imaging, which tracks water movement along nerve fibers, promised better specificity.

They scanned unfixed post mortem MS brain on a standard 1.5-tesla machine, then measured myelin, axon counts, and scarring under the microscope. Both diffusion measures came out lower after death than in living scans. Still, the known contrast held: lesions showed freer water movement and less directionality than normal-looking white matter. Myelin content correlated strongly with both measures, including a correlation of minus 0.79 for the directionality index, and with axon counts as well.
europmc-pmc2064944:
Warady and Chadha reviewed chronic kidney disease in children worldwide in 2007. Knowledge of care has grown through large studies, yet basic counts of how many children are affected remain limited and imprecise. Methods differ between data sources, making comparisons hard. Causes also vary by region, shaped by environment, ancestry, genetics and marriage within families.

Nearly half of childhood cases come from birth defects of the kidney and urinary tract. These include blocked urine flow and underdeveloped kidneys. Kidney transplant is the favoured final treatment for children. But scarce health resources and high death rates in poorer countries limit dialysis and transplant provision. That in turn skews global patient counts. The authors call for better worldwide tracking of the disease in children.
europmc-pmc2065844:
Al-Sakere and co-workers reported in 2007 the first successful use of irreversible electroporation to destroy tumours in mice. The method uses short, strong electric pulses to open permanent holes in cell membranes. Unlike heat or freezing methods, it kills without cooking tissue. Maths models of the electric and heat fields guided a protocol with minimal heating. Aggressive skin tumours were implanted in mice for the test.

Tissue studies confirmed tumours died directly from permanent membrane damage. Success depended on field strength, total pulse length and pulse timing. The best setting used plate electrodes giving 80 pulses of 100 microseconds at 2,500 volts per centimetre. That treatment fully cleared 12 of 13 tumours, a 92 percent success rate, with no tissue heating. The authors present it as a new non-thermal ablation option.
europmc-pmc2100144:
Baral, Sifakis, Cleghorn and Beyrer reviewed HIV risk in 2007 among men who have sex with men living in poorer countries. Reports from the former Soviet Union, Asia, Africa and Latin America showed high infection rates in this group. The team systematically reviewed studies from 2000 to 2006 across low- and middle-income countries. They pooled prevalence data and compared risk with general adult populations.

Risk was far higher for these men in nearly every setting. The pooled odds ratio reached 58.4 in very low-prevalence countries, and 14.4 in low-prevalence ones. It fell to 9.6 where HIV was common. That is still a nine-fold excess, and it remained after pooling across all of the regions studied in this review. By region, the Americas showed the highest ratio at 33.3, and Africa the lowest at 3.8, and the authors call this group understudied and underserved.
europmc-pmc2124944:
F. H. McCrudden and Helen L. Fales, at the Hospital of the Rockefeller Institute, published complete balance studies in 1912 on two cases of intestinal infantilism. Herter's name for the condition pointed to the gut. A normal child was studied the same way as a control.

The pattern is consistent. All five elements were poorly absorbed from the intestines, and urinary output of them ran low. Urinary calcium was so small as to be negligible, while calcium passed into the intestines in increased amounts. The balances give the sharpest result: the other elements were retained by the body, but calcium was lost. One case kept thirty-eight per cent of food nitrogen against the normal boy's seven and a half. Readers get exact bookkeeping on a childhood disorder of absorption.
europmc-pmc2125544:
Edwards A. Park removed the thymus from guinea pigs in 1917 and then, sectioning the necks serially, discovered why earlier thymus experiments, his own included, could not mean what they claimed. Accessory thymus lobes, budded from the third pharyngeal pouch and nestled against the matching parathyroids, turned up in eleven of fourteen animals, and probably in all fourteen but for a technical slip.

Complete thymectomy in the guinea pig is therefore rarely, if ever, accomplished, and the whole earlier literature must be reread as partial extirpation. Park's own removals produced no changes at all. As a by-product, his sections confirm Ruben on the fourth-pouch parathyroid: much smaller than the third, sometimes rudimentary, sometimes absent on one side. Readers get a gland's verdict delivered by anatomy: the experimental animal itself was unfit for the question.
europmc-pmc2125644:
Alwin M. Pappenheimer tested immune sera against lymphocytes and small thymus cells in 1917, and began by distrusting the literature. Leukotoxic sera were said to be easy to raise, but their specificity was doubtful, and the methods invited error. No washing frees an organ suspension of blood entirely, . Pearce had shown that traces of blood suffice to evoke hemolysins. A serum's lymph damage might be borrowed from its blood-directed powers.

His experiments pry the factors apart. The lymphotoxic and clumping powers are, to a considerable degree, distinct from the hemolytic and blood-clumping ones, since absorption can remove one set and leave the other. The work adds evidence that the thymus's small cells are in nature related to, if not identical with, lymph-gland lymphocytes. Readers get cell-specific immunity rescued from its artifacts, and two white cell populations declared kin.
europmc-pmc2131444:
Guzman Barron and John Bumstead studied early obstructive jaundice in a 1928 paper in The Journal of Experimental Medicine. Jaundice is the yellowing that follows when bile cannot flow out of the liver. They tied off the bile ducts of dogs and followed the blood pigment bilirubin and the liver tissue hour by hour, to learn how the pigment first reaches the blood.

Two phases stood out. First, the bilirubin already circling in the blood built up, giving one form of the Van den Bergh test reaction. Then bile bilirubin itself appeared, giving the other reaction. The second phase began before any bile channels had burst. Sections showed the tiny bile channels swollen into pouches against blood spaces, and the authors suggest bile seeps through those thin walls under rising pressure.
europmc-pmc2140444:
Selig Hecht, at Creighton University in Omaha, tested which wave lengths of light drive the clam Mya's light sense in a 1921 paper. First he describes a simple way to get strong beams of single-color light. Then he tried colors across the spectrum on Mya, the clam of his earlier dark adaptation work.

The most effective part of the spectrum for stimulating Mya lies near the green middle of the visible range. From the numbers he maps, tentatively, the absorption spectrum of the clam's photosensitive substance, the range of colors it drinks in. The reading is interpreted through the photochemical model of his earlier papers, in which a sensitive substance splits under light and rebuilds in darkness.
europmc-pmc2140544:
John Northrop and Paul De Kruif wrote part three of their bacterial suspension stability series in 1922, at The Rockefeller Institute. Bacteria floating in water clump together, agglutinate, under set conditions. This part adds proteins, normal serum, and immune serum to suspensions of typhoid bacilli and rabbit septicemia germs, across acidities.

Added protein or serum widened the acid clumping zone and shifted the germs' isoelectric point to that of the added substance. Far less serum was needed to clump the germs near their own acid clumping point. Immune serum stopped salt from weakening the stick between organisms, so clumping then turned only on the electric potential: below a set millivolt level, the suspension clumped.
europmc-pmc2265044:
Calafat, Ye, Wong, Reidy and Needham measured the antibacterial chemical triclosan in 2008 in urine from a national United States survey. Triclosan is used widely in soaps, toothpaste, textiles and kitchen plastics. The team analysed 2,517 urine samples from the 2003-2004 survey of people aged six and older, using automated extraction and mass spectrometry. They compared levels across age, income, race and sex groups.

Triclosan was detected in 74.6 percent of samples, spanning concentrations from 2.4 to 3,790 micrograms per litre. The geometric mean was 13.0 micrograms per litre, while the 95th percentile reached 459.0 on the same scale. A minority thus carry far higher body burdens than typical. Levels peaked in the third decade of life. People in high-income households had significantly higher levels than lower-income groups. Race and sex showed no differences.
europmc-pmc2395244:
Haas and colleagues introduced an automated gene-finding tool for complex genomes in 2008. Annotating a genome means marking where each gene starts, ends, and is spliced. For eukaryotes, organisms with a cell nucleus, doing this by hand is far too slow, and single computer programs often disagree.

Their tool, EVidenceModeler, weighs predictions from many sources and merges them into one best gene model for each region. A partner program, the Program to Assemble Spliced Alignments, feeds it evidence from aligned gene transcripts. Together they predict protein-coding regions, alternative splice forms, where one gene yields several message versions, and the untranslated regions at message ends. The authors offered the pair as a standard pipeline for new genome projects.
europmc-pmc2556744:
De Backer and fellow specialists reported in 2007 the consensus of a round table conference on how to judge the microcirculation, the body's smallest blood vessels. Faults there help drive organ failure in critical illness, especially sepsis, and new cameras let doctors watch these vessels directly. But laboratories scored the images in incompatible ways, so the group met in Amsterdam to agree on standards.

They fixed five rules for good imaging. Sample five sites per organ. Avoid pressing on the tissue. Clear away secretions. Keep focus and contrast right. Check recording quality. Scoring should report vessel density and the share of vessels carrying flow. It should also report a flow index and a heterogeneity index for how uneven flow is. Values should be given separately for vessels under 20 micrometres wide, the true capillaries.
europmc-pmc2633044:
Depienne and colleagues identified in 2009 a second gene behind a Dravet-like epileptic encephalopathy of infancy. Dravet syndrome, a severe seizure disorder with developmental regression, is usually caused by mutations in SCN1A, but 27 percent of the team's patients tested negative. Screening 41 such patients with dense gene chips uncovered a deletion removing the PCDH19 gene on the X chromosome in one boy.

Sequencing PCDH19 in 73 more negative patients found nine different mutations in 11 unrelated girls. The boy's skin cells proved mosaic: only some cells carried the deletion. That supports a cellular interference mechanism for this female-predominant disorder. Patients with PCDH19 mutations closely resembled Dravet cases. They had early fever-linked seizures in clusters and language delays. But their myoclonic jerks and atypical absences were rarer.
europmc-pmc2653744:
Wolin and colleagues combined results from 52 studies in 2009 to measure how much physical activity lowers the risk of colon cancer. The link between exercise and lower risk was well known, but no up-to-date pooled number existed. The team searched the literature through June 2008 and kept only studies that reported colon cancer on its own.

Across the studies, the most active people had about a 24 percent lower risk than the least active. The benefit looked much the same for men and for women. Studies that asked patients to recall past activity after diagnosis showed a stronger effect than studies that followed healthy people forward in time. The authors note plausible reasons: less inflammation, faster passage of food through the gut, and lower insulin levels in active people.
europmc-pmc2708144:
Evans reviewed in 2009 neurofibromatosis type 2, a rare inherited disorder that grows tumors on nerves and in the brain and spine. About one person in sixty thousand has it, and most first notice one-sided hearing loss or ringing in the ear. Tumors on both hearing nerves are its hallmark and often lead to deafness.

The review covers other tumors such as meningiomas, growths on the coverings of the brain, plus eye signs like cataracts and skin lumps. Faults in the NF2 gene on chromosome 22 cause it, and over half of cases are new faults, not inherited ones. Surgery stays the main treatment, with watchful scans for slow tumors.
europmc-pmc2756044:
Devaraj and co-authors showed in 2007 how the SARS coronavirus blocks the innate interferon defense in infected lung cells. SARS, a severe contagious respiratory disease, induces only a weak interferon response in culture, and its key transcription factor IRF-3 is not activated. Whether the virus hides from sensors or actively counteracts defenses was uncertain.

Searching viral proteins, they found the papain-like protease domain is a potent interferon antagonist, and its protease activity is not even required. The domain binds IRF-3 and blocks its phosphorylation and move into the nucleus, cutting off type I interferon production through two sensing pathways. That sabotage may help SARS-CoV establish infection before adaptive immunity can respond.
europmc-pmc2816644:
Buffa, Harris, West, and Miller built a shared gene signature in 2010 for low oxygen inside tumors, a state called hypoxia that drives growth and resists therapy. Signatures trained on one cancer often fail in others, so the team hunted for one that holds across cancers. They combined known oxygen-sensitive genes with activity patterns from eight cancer datasets, three for head and neck tumors and five for breast tumors.

Genes that rose and fell together with the known oxygen genes across all datasets formed the signature, and it predicted patient outcomes in combined analyses. A trimmed version using only the top few genes, including VEGFA, beat both the full signature and older published ones in fresh head, breast, and lung data.
europmc-pmc2846344:
Fernández-Riejos and colleagues reviewed in 2010 how leptin, the fullness hormone released by fat cells, switches on and shapes the immune system. Fat tissue acts as an active hormone organ, and leptin ties nutritional state to immune strength. Low leptin states come with higher infection risk, while too much leptin accompanies immune attacks on the body's own tissues.

The review gathers lab and clinical evidence that leptin touches nearly every immune branch: it rallies first-response cells, shapes T cell behavior, and fuels inflammation when oversupplied in obesity. The hormone thus sits at the crossing of feeding, energy balance, and defense, helping explain why both starvation and heavy obesity weaken or distort immune responses.
europmc-pmc2860244:
Pardo and co-authors built in 2010 a much larger map of proteins that bind Oct4, the master switch of embryo stem cells. Working in mouse embryo stem cells, they pulled down Oct4 with its attached partners and named them with sensitive protein tools. The study ran in parallel with related work and widened the known Oct4 circle greatly.

Half of the partner proteins are themselves controlled by Oct4 or by fellow stem cell switches, which weaves a tight feedback web. About a third change their levels sharply once cells start to specialize. Most partners tested so far kill early embryos when mutated in mice. Some human versions are already tied to birth defects or to cancer, which gives the map medical reach.
europmc-pmc2901944:
Perencevich and colleagues measured in 2003 what surgical site infections cost when they surface after the patient has gone home, which is when most appear. They followed over forty-five hundred operations and confirmed post-discharge infection in about two percent. Infected patients and matched controls reported their health and care use across the eight weeks after surgery.

Infection brought significantly more outpatient and emergency visits, imaging, readmissions, and home health aide hours. Total costs over the eight weeks averaged about five thousand one hundred dollars per infected patient against roughly one thousand eight hundred for controls, nearly triple. Mental health scores also fell only in the infected group. Hospitals that stop counting at discharge miss most of the true burden of these infections.
europmc-pmc2907344:
Smith and co-authors pooled in 2010 fifty-five randomized trials to pin down how much anthracycline chemotherapy drugs endanger the heart. These drugs are staples against breast and ovarian cancer, lymphoma, myeloma, and sarcoma, but they can damage heart muscle early or years later. Trials of alternative regimens let the team compare clinical heart failure and silent damage rates directly.

Regimens built on anthracyclines carried over five times the odds of clinical heart toxicity of non-anthracycline regimens. One older comparator drug was safer, and drug delivery mattered too: quick bolus dosing roughly quadrupled risk against slow infusion. Two gentler options stood out, the relative epirubicin and fat-wrapped liposomal doxorubicin, each cutting risk steeply. Dose and delivery choices let oncologists trade a measure of punch for heart safety.
europmc-pmc2913244:
Theveneau and colleagues worked out in 2010 how a cluster of embryonic cells migrates toward a chemical beacon without breaking apart. Neural crest cells, among the embryo's most mobile, travel in streams and their movement resembles cancer invasion. A chemokine called Sdf1 attracts the cluster, but single cells alone barely respond, which posed the puzzle.

Filming the cells showed Sdf1 does not create direction from scratch; it stabilizes the polarity that cell contact already sets up. Where two cells touch, the adhesion molecule N-cadherin damps the protrusion machinery, while the free outer edge stays active and extends. The beacon amplifies that front-back difference until the whole group crawls toward it. Contact inhibition of movement, once seen as a brake, turns out to steer collective travel.
europmc-pmc2939644:
Leung, Lam, and Chan checked three lengths of a standard stress questionnaire in Chinese heart patients who smoked, in a 2010 validation study. Stress can trigger smoking and relapse, so measuring it well matters for quit programmes.

Nearly two thousand patients from ten Hong Kong hospital clinics completed the survey. Analysis backed a two-part structure for all three versions, with positive and negative item groups pulling in opposite directions, and acceptable consistency within each part. Links with smoking habits and health measures also behaved as expected. Shorter versions held up well enough for busy clinic use.
europmc-pmc2954944:
Levac, Colquhoun, and O'Brien offered clearer guidance for scoping studies, a style of evidence review that maps a field rather than answering one narrow question, in a 2010 methods article. A widely used framework from 2005 left several steps vague.

From running three such studies themselves, they recommend tying each review's question tightly to its purpose and balancing breadth against what a team can finish. Study picking and data extraction should proceed in rounds with the whole team. Results need both counts and themes, plus thought about use, and asking stakeholders should be a required final step.
europmc-pmc2970544:
Ndimubanzi and colleagues systematically reviewed reports on neurocysticercosis, brain infection by pork tapeworm larvae, with special attention to people with epilepsy, in a 2010 study. Estimates of its frequency varied wildly worldwide.

Searching dozens of databases for studies from 1990 to mid-2008, they winnowed hundreds of papers down to a small set using brain imaging for diagnosis. Despite wide variation across groups, one figure held steady: roughly three in ten people with epilepsy in the pooled studies harboured the infection. Only one community survey measured its frequency in a whole village population.
europmc-pmc2993644:
Souza and the WHO survey group analysed caesarean births without medical indication in a 2010 study of the WHO Global Survey on Maternal and Perinatal Health. Sections chosen for non-medical reasons were under worldwide debate, and harms needed firmer numbers.

Records covered well over a quarter million deliveries in hundreds of facilities across twenty-four countries. About one percent of births were sections with no recorded indication. Compared with natural vaginal birth, every other delivery mode, including such sections, carried higher risk of death, intensive care admission, transfusion, or womb removal for the mother. The pattern strengthens caution about elective surgery.
europmc-pmc3019144:
Bozdagi and co-authors studied mice missing one copy of Shank3, a scaffolding gene at nerve junctions whose loss causes a deletion syndrome and autism in people, in a 2010 study. The gene recruits receptor and skeleton parts to the receiving side of synapses.

Heterozygous mice showed weaker miniature synaptic currents and altered plasticity in brain slices, plus sparser staining for one receptor type in a memory region. Behaviour tests found faults in social interaction and communication. Modelling the single-copy loss in mice ties the human syndrome's social features to measurable synaptic weakness, offering a test bed for treatments.
europmc-pmc3056144:
Labute presented in 2009 a computer method that fills in the hydrogen atoms missing from most macromolecule structures. Experiments usually locate only the heavy atoms of proteins and bound drugs, yet hydrogen positions decide how molecules bind and react. His program, Protonate3D, places hydrogens automatically while also trying flipped side chains, alternate shapes, and different charge states for each group.

Its scoring weighs crowding, electric forces, solvent effects, and the cost of each charge state at a given acidity. Tests on known structures suggest the placements are accurate. Getting hydrogens right matters for drug design, since a flipped group or a wrong charge can change a predicted binding completely. The tool was built to prepare structures for the modeling work that follows structure solving. It handles ligands and solvent molecules alongside the main chain.
europmc-pmc3069744:
