Vonrhein and colleagues described in 2011 the autoPROC toolbox, software that automates the messy first stage of X ray crystal work. Real diffraction data rarely match the textbook ideal. Crystals split, beam centers drift, several lattices overlap, and headers carry wrong values, any of which can quietly ruin a dataset.

The paper walks through these common failure modes and the checks the toolbox applies to catch them. It tests beam center conventions against the images themselves, hunts for extra lattices across many frames, and keeps indexing consistent across sweeps of data. Automation calls established processing programs under the hood and flags trouble for the user. The goal is to rescue borderline datasets that manual processing might discard, and to make routine datasets boringly reliable. Synchrotron users with heavy data flows are the main audience.
europmc-pmc3087144:
Backes, Markham, Moorehead, Cordero, Nankervis, and Giannone reviewed in 2011 how preeclampsia, a dangerous pregnancy disorder affecting many organs, affects newborn babies. The illness is progressive, and often the only way to protect the mother is to deliver early. That rescue trades one risk for another, since early birth itself harms babies, not only the extremely early ones.

Babies born just a few weeks early, the late preterm group, make up about two thirds of all preterm births and face real risks of illness and death. The review covers how the disorder is diagnosed, how pregnancies are managed, and what outcomes late preterm infants face. It then weighs strategies to time delivery and support the fetus for the best joint outcome. The authors stress how incomplete the evidence guiding these decisions remains.
europmc-pmc3156644:
Christopher Mann and colleagues reviewed how muscle repair goes wrong and turns to scarring in a 2011 paper in Skeletal Muscle. Healthy repair after injury is a choreographed act among immune cells, muscle stem cells, and support cells, guided by local and body-wide signals. In chronic diseases such as muscular dystrophy, the choreography breaks down.

Inflammation refuses to switch off, support cells stay activated, and the stem cells that should rebuild fibres tire out. The end state is fibrosis, stiff scar tissue replacing working muscle, shared by nearly all long-running muscle diseases. The review gathers new findings on signals among stem cells, immune cells, fibroblasts, and the surrounding matrix, arguing muscle offers a model for wound healing across the body.
europmc-pmc3164644:
Taisei Kikuchi and colleagues sequenced the genome of a pine-killing nematode worm in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. The worm causes a devastating pine wilt epidemic across Asia and Europe. It took up plant parasitism independently from other parasitic worms, while also feeding on fungi and hitching rides on insects. Its genome thus offers a fresh window on how parasitism evolves.

The worm carries the largest digestive enzyme set known in any nematode, plus expanded detox and transport families, suiting its varied foods and habitats. Its plant-wall softening proteins came not from worm ancestors but by gene transfer from fungi, and it lacks the weapon proteins of other plant parasites entirely. Gene-silencing machinery and stress systems are rich, while smell receptors are trimmed. The genome confirms a wholly separate route into plant parasitism.
europmc-pmc3169444:
Catrine Tudor-Locke and colleagues converted activity guidelines into step targets for older and less mobile adults in a 2011 paper. Step counters offer an easy way to track walking, but nobody had stated how many steps embody the official advice for these groups. The review pooled typical counts and intervention results.

Healthy older adults average a few thousand steps daily, and people with disability or chronic illness fewer still. Walking programmes added a modest daily rise in older adults and a larger one in special populations. Half an hour of brisk walking beyond daily routine lands near eight thousand steps on active days, within a broad whole-day band. Frailer groups may never reach brisk pace, the authors note, so targets must flex.
europmc-pmc3240744:
Cláudia Rosa-Ferreira and Sean Munro worked out how lysosomes hitch onto the motor that carries them outward in the cell, in this 2011 study in Developmental Cell. Lysosomes travel both ways along microtubule tracks, and a small switch protein called Arl8 was known to promote their movement. The team searched for what Arl8 grabs onto.

They found Arl8 binds a soluble protein called SKIP, previously known as a target of a Salmonella effector that hijacks the same motor for the bacterium's vacuole. In uninfected cells, both Arl8 and SKIP were required for lysosomes to spread away from the cell center. SKIP carries two docking motifs for the kinesin-1 motor's light chain; without them lysosomes fail to load the motor and stay put. A natural splice variant lacking one motif cannot drive movement, suggesting fine-tuning.
europmc-pmc3262844:
John Morris and colleagues built clusterMaker, a plugin that brings many clustering algorithms into the Cytoscape network platform, in this 2011 paper in BMC Bioinformatics. Biologists drowning in high-throughput data need to group similar items, genes, proteins, or samples, to see meaningful patterns, and to combine datasets from different experiments. Accessible tools for that were lacking.

The plugin implements a wide menu of algorithms, including hierarchical clustering, k-means, k-medoid, and several network-specific methods, some available to Cytoscape users nowhere else. Results appear as network views, dendrograms, and heat maps that stay linked: selecting items in one view highlights them everywhere. The authors demonstrate three uses, finding phenotype-specific mouse interaction networks, dissecting a yeast protein complex, and reannotating an enzyme family member. Session files for each scenario accompany the paper.
europmc-pmc3285644:
Michael Fehlings and colleagues reported the STASCIS trial, a multicenter study of surgical timing after cervical spinal cord injury, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Animal evidence strongly favors decompressing the cord early, but proof in patients was lacking. The prospective study enrolled adults with traumatic neck cord injuries at six North American centers and compared surgery within a day of injury against later surgery.

Of the patients with six-month follow-up, the early group fared better. About one in five had improved by at least two grades on the standard impairment scale. In the late group the share was roughly one in eleven. After adjusting for initial severity and steroid use, early surgery nearly tripled the odds of that improvement. Deaths were one in each group, and complication rates were similar, slightly favoring early surgery. The authors conclude early decompression is safe and improves recovery.
europmc-pmc3329544:
Ritchie and Romanuk combined trials to judge whether probiotics, foods and supplements carrying live helpful bacteria, really ease gut diseases, in a 2012 analysis. Separate reviews had praised probiotics for single conditions, but nobody had compared their value across diseases with very different causes. The team pooled randomized trials in people across eight gastrointestinal conditions.

Probiotics helped overall, cutting the risk of a poor outcome by roughly two fifths across the trials. Benefits were clear in six of the eight diseases, including pouchitis, infectious diarrhea, irritable bowel syndrome, and diarrhea caused by antibiotics. Traveler's diarrhea and a severe intestinal disease of premature babies showed no clear benefit. Most bacterial species helped, though three popular ones did not. The authors advise matching the disease and the bacterial strain carefully when choosing a probiotic.
europmc-pmc3400644:
Zhang and colleagues validated a shortened depression questionnaire in 2012 for people living with HIV in British Columbia, Canada. The standard scale runs twenty items; the short form keeps ten. Their test group was more than five hundred patients starting antiretroviral therapy in the provincial drug program.

Scores on the short form tracked the full scale almost perfectly. Its internal consistency was strong, and it classified patients with depressive symptoms nearly as accurately as the original, with high sensitivity and specificity. Analysis showed the short form kept the same two underlying themes, positive and negative feeling. The authors conclude the ten-item version is a sound, quicker stand-in for research with HIV-positive patients.
europmc-pmc3441244:
Marleau, Chen, Joyce, and Tullis proposed in 2012 that filtering cancer's messenger vesicles out of the blood could become a treatment in its own right. Tumors shed huge numbers of these exosomes, tiny sacs that carry growth proteins and immune-damping cargo to other cells. In HER2-driven breast cancer, vesicles bearing that growth protein even soak up the antibody drug meant to block it.

Drug strategies to block vesicle release or action carry toxicity and interaction risks. The authors instead describe a dialysis-like platform that traps vesicles on binding agents as blood circulates outside the body. A sibling device already cuts virus loads in hepatitis C patients, and viruses match exosomes in size and surface sugars. Removing the messengers, they argue, could restore immune attack.
europmc-pmc3503744:
Long studies leak participants, and Kristin Gustavson, Tilmann von Soest, Evalill Karevold, and Espen Roysamb measure how much damage that leakage does in 2012. They re-examine a Norwegian population study of 913 mothers enrolled in 1993, of whom 56 percent had dropped out fifteen years later, and they add a Monte Carlo simulation.

Dropouts had lower education at the start but matched stayers on mental health and relationship measures. Baseline links between variables were the same in both groups. Simulations show averages can bias badly even when dropout depends only weakly on study variables. Associations between variables prove hardier. Attrition, the study concludes, distorts levels more readily than relationships.
europmc-pmc3510444:
Cells eat invading bacteria by autophagy, and Natalia von Muhlinen and eight colleagues show one protein pairing is indispensable in 2012. Autophagy receptors grab cargo and dock onto ATG8 family proteins on the disposal membrane; mammals carry several ATG8 versions, and this study asks whether the choice among them matters.

The receptor NDP52 binds selectively to one version, LC3C, through an unusual docking motif missing its usual aromatic anchor. Cells lacking NDP52 or LC3C cannot protect their cytoplasm against Salmonella, and other ATG8 versions cannot substitute. Structural analysis shows how the odd motif fits LC3C's unique surface. Selective pairing, the study proves, is functional, not decorative.
europmc-pmc3574144:
Natacha Bodenhausen, Matthew Horton, and Joy Bergelson catalogued the bacteria living on a model plant in PLoS ONE in 2013. Arabidopsis thaliana is a workhorse of plant research, yet its own resident bacteria under natural conditions were barely known. The team collected wild plants at four sites and used high-throughput gene sequencing to name the bacteria on leaf and root surfaces and inside the tissues.

Three large bacterial groups dominated both organs. Two genera, Massilia and Flavobacterium, turned up everywhere. Which organ and which layer a sample came from shaped the community strongly: root surfaces held richer communities than root interiors, with the pattern flipped in leaves. Leaf and root interiors held similar counts of kinds but different members. The census gives plant scientists a baseline for testing how these tenants affect health and growth.
europmc-pmc3596344:
York Hunt Ng and colleagues hunted for tiny message packets in the womb in PLoS ONE in 2013. Before an embryo can implant, it and the uterus lining must exchange signals. Exosomes and microvesicles, membrane bubbles a hundred or so nanometers wide that cells shed with RNA cargo inside, were candidate couriers. The team tested whether the lining's surface cells release them into the uterine space and what RNA they carry.

Marker proteins of exosomes sat on the lining cells' outer surface in tissue samples, one of them rising and falling with the menstrual cycle. Bubbles pelleted from cultured lining cells and from uterine fluid proved to be the right size, mostly fifty to one hundred fifty nanometers, and carried the markers. Their microRNA cargo was sorted, not random: thirteen of 227 kinds appeared only in the bubbles. The findings open a new channel for embryo-womb conversation.
europmc-pmc3618244:
Anne Gabory and colleagues placed the placenta at the start of sex differences in disease in Biology of Sex Differences in 2013. Men and women differ in rates of diabetes, heart disease, mental illness, and cancer, and much of that gap may be programmed before birth. The placenta feeds and shields the fetus, senses the mother's diet, infections, and stress, and passes the consequences forward. As one of the few human tissues easy to collect, it is a natural window on early programming.

Male and female placentas answer the same stresses differently, the review shows. Some divergence is written before hormones enter the story: sex chromosomes differ from conception, and epigenetic marks, the chemical annotations on DNA, diverge early too. Lifelong hormone differences then layer over this early split. The paper maps how one temporary organ seeds lasting differences in health.
europmc-pmc3634444:
Vicent Arbona and colleagues reviewed metabolomics for plant stress research in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2013. A plant's metabolites, its sugars, acids, and defensive chemicals, sit closest to its actual condition, integrating gene activity and protein work into a chemical snapshot. Profiling them has become a favored way to find what separates plants that endure drought, salt, heat, cold, or flooding from those that fail.

Primary metabolites recur as central players: sugars and amino acids double as osmotic balancers that keep cells hydrated, and Krebs cycle intermediates flag failing photosynthesis. Secondary metabolites answer more narrowly, acting as antioxidants, radical scavengers, and sunscreens, and stress-induced ones can double as protection against pests, linking the two stress worlds. Combined with gene data, metabolite patterns become markers breeders can select for, the review's closing promise for tougher crops.
europmc-pmc3654944:
A waste product of hard-working tissue doubles as a bedside gauge in intensive care, Bakker, Nijsten and Jansen review in a 2013 Annals of Intensive Care article. The gauge is lactate, a chemical long tied to low oxygen in tissue. Two recent studies showed that watching lactate change during early revival care improves how treatment is steered.

The review clears up terms first: blood acidity tracks lactate only at high levels, so lactate-linked acidosis is the fairer name. It then walks through what raises lactate besides low oxygen, since many body processes feed into the level. That breadth is why one reading can mislead and a run of readings guides better. Their advice is plain: set lactate checks into revival plans as a fixed step.
europmc-pmc3665844:
Rare species carry the most unusual jobs in rich ecosystems, Mouillot and eleven colleagues show in a 2013 PLoS Biology study. Most species are rare, with few members and small ranges, and their loss was long assumed to matter little for how an ecosystem works. The team tested that view with trait and abundance data from three species-rich systems: 846 coral reef fishes, 2,979 alpine plants and 662 tropical trees.

The most distinct trait blends in each system sat mostly in rare species. Jobs held by such species are the least insured: no common stand-in does the same work. Vulnerable jobs proved rarer than chance alone would set, at both local and regional scales. The most distinct species all ranged over less than half their regions. Guarding rare species, the authors argue, guards the very jobs ecosystems can least afford to lose.
europmc-pmc3686844:
Bergman and colleagues combined the trials of vitamin D for preventing respiratory infections. Their meta-analysis covered eleven trials with 5,660 patients and found a protective effect overall: the odds of infection were lower in people given vitamin D.

The schedule mattered. Daily dosing protected more strongly than large intermittent doses, and effects varied a good deal between trials. The authors note signs that unpublished negative results could inflate the benefit, so they present the protection as real but uncertain in size. The analysis supports daily low-dose vitamin D as the regimen worth testing further, rather than occasional large doses. It also gives doctors a concrete, low-cost option to weigh for patients who face repeated chest infections each winter.
europmc-pmc3694844:
Rönn and colleagues tested whether six months of exercise changes the chemical tagging of DNA in human fat tissue. They profiled methylation across the genome in fat samples from twenty-three healthy, previously inactive men, before and after the training program. They also compared people with and without a family history of type 2 diabetes.

Exercise altered methylation at nearly eighteen thousand sites across more than seven thousand genes. About a third of those genes also changed their activity, and silencing two of them in cultured fat cells increased fat production. Diabetes and obesity candidate genes were among the responders. The authors conclude that training rewires fat tissue partly through methylation, with effects on fat cell metabolism.
europmc-pmc3714544:
Miguel Gueimonde, Borja Sánchez, Clara de los Reyes-Gavilán, and Abelardo Margolles wrote a review in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2013 on antibiotic resistance in probiotic bacteria. Probiotics are live microbes, mostly Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, that are added to foods and are meant to help health. The question is when their resistance to antibiotics is safe and when it is a risk.

Resistance built into a strain's own makeup, or caused by a simple mutation, is not by itself a safety worry, and it can even help restore gut microbes after antibiotic treatment. The risk comes from resistance genes carried on moving pieces of DNA, such as tetracycline resistance genes. Those genes can pass to microbes that cause disease, so the authors treat them as a real safety issue for food use.
europmc-pmc3736544:
Liang Ge, David Melville, Min Zhang, and Randy Schekman reported a cell study in eLife in 2013 on autophagy, the process by which cells break down their own material inside double-walled sacs. Where the membrane for those sacs comes from was unknown. The team built a test-tube assay based on a key step, the fat-tagging of a protein called LC3.

By sorting cell membranes in a systematic way, they found that a small compartment between the endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi, called the ERGIC, could trigger the tagging step on its own. Tests in living cells showed the ERGIC is also needed to build the sacs there. It works in part by drawing in an early marker protein, ATG14, a step needed to form the young sac membrane.
europmc-pmc3738444:
Cristina Barbosa, Isabel Peixeiro, and Luísa Romão wrote a review in PLoS Genetics in 2013 on upstream open reading frames, or uORFs. These are short coding stretches that sit before the main coding region of a gene's message. Nearly half of human messages carry them, and they can raise or lower how much protein the main gene makes.

A uORF can steer the protein-making machinery, trigger decay of the message, or change how a cell answers stress. When mutations disturb that control, disease can follow, including cancers, metabolic and brain disorders, and inherited syndromes. The review walks through the mechanisms, then uses case examples to link specific uORF changes to symptoms. The authors argue that finding more such cases will sharpen diagnosis and treatment.
europmc-pmc374244:
Michael Kobor and seven co-authors reported a yeast study in PLoS Biology in 2004 on how a histone variant reaches the right place in chromatin. Chromatin is the packed form of DNA, and swapping in the variant H2A.Z keeps active regions from being silenced. The swap mechanism was unknown.

Working in baker's yeast, the team found a protein complex of 13 parts tied to a free pool of H2A.Z. They named it SWR1-Com after its engine subunit, Swr1p. Cells lacking Swr1p failed badly at placing H2A.Z at the active regions flanking a silenced mating-type cassette and at 12 other sites tested. Gene activity faults in those cells mostly matched cells lacking H2A.Z itself. The authors propose that related enzymes in flies and humans do the same job.
europmc-pmc3760644:
Richard Simpson, Hina Kalra, and Suresh Mathivanan described a database called ExoCarta in the Journal of Extracellular Vesicles in 2012. Exosomes are small vesicles of internal origin that cells secrete; they carry proteins, RNA, and lipids that mirror the state of their source cell. Interest in them has produced a flood of data sets that are hard to use until they are gathered in one place.

ExoCarta is a hand-curated database of exosomal proteins, RNA, and lipids, built from published and unpublished studies. Since its launch in 2009 it had drawn more than 16,000 users. The authors explain how the resource can serve exosome research and urge researchers in the field to deposit their own data sets directly, so the collection keeps growing.
europmc-pmc3850944:
Martin H. Prins and a team of co-authors pool two drug trials in Thrombosis Journal in 2013. The trials test a pill, rivaroxaban, against standard care for blood clots in veins. Standard care pairs a heparin shot with a vitamin K blocker pill that needs blood checks.

Over eight thousand patients with leg or lung clots took part in the two trials. Clots came back at much the same low rate on the pill as on standard care, meeting the set bar for equal effect. Major bleeding ran a bit lower on the pill. The pooled result backs a single-drug path that skips shots and routine lab checks, which eases care for patients and clinics alike.
europmc-pmc3877844:
Graham K. Sheridan and Keith J. Murphy review a brain signal pair in Open Biology in 2013. Neurons and glia talk both ways to keep the brain working. One channel for that talk is fractalkine, a signal on neurons, and its receiver on microglia, the brain's immune cells.

The pair helps guide microglia into the young brain and shapes the pruning of synapses as the brain matures. In the adult hippocampus it supports learning and memory processes. It can hold microglia calm in quiet times yet rouse them during inflammation. That double face means the pair protects in some settings and harms in others. Many slow brain diseases show a broken version of this signal, which makes it a drug target of wide interest.
europmc-pmc3902944:
Alexander Henderson and a team of co-authors build a DNA probe tool in Nucleic Acids Research, with the record dated 2014. Guanine-rich DNA can fold into four-stranded knots called G-quadruplexes. Such knots are tied to gene control and other cell jobs, yet tools to see them inside living cells were scarce.

The team made mouse antibodies that grip distinct knot shapes. One antibody lit up cell nuclei in most human and mouse cells. Drugs that lock knots in place raised the glow. Cells missing a knot-unwinding enzyme glowed stronger still, as if knots piled up without it. The results back the claim that these knots truly form in mammalian cells, and give labs a tool to study them.
europmc-pmc3931944:
Diego Jarquín and colleagues present a statistical model for picking better crop lines when genes and weather interact, in Theoretical and Applied Genetics in 2014. A wheat line's yield depends on its genes and on the fields where it grows, and the best genes in one place may not win in another. Genotyping now yields thousands of markers, and weather records are just as dense, so modeling every gene-by-weather pairing directly is impossible.

Their reaction norm model handles the flood by working with similarity patterns among lines and among environments instead of single pairings. Tested on wheat, it predicted grain yield more accurately, both across different environments and within one environment, than models without the interaction terms. Breeders gain a workable way to use genomic and weather data together.
europmc-pmc3987044:
Kirsten M. M. Beyer and colleagues test whether greener neighborhoods come with better mental health across Wisconsin, in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health in 2014. Lab studies in environmental psychology link nature exposure to recovered attention and lower stress, but population evidence, especially outside cities, was thin. The team used the Survey of the Health of Wisconsin, a population database spanning city to countryside, and joined each respondent's mental health scores to the green space around their home.

More neighborhood green space went with significantly lower symptom levels for depression, anxiety, and stress, after accounting for many other factors. The analysis also adjusted for how long people had lived in their neighborhood, to blunt the worry that healthier people simply choose greener areas. The authors float greening as a population-level mental health strategy.
europmc-pmc3995444:
Ahmad Oryan, Soodeh Alidadi, Ali Moshiri, and Nicola Maffulli review ways to regrow bone, in the Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research in 2014. Bone can heal itself after many breaks, but large gaps and poor blood flow can stall repair. Surgeons then turn to grafts, material placed to spur new bone growth.

Grafts taken from the patient's own body remain the gold standard, since they bring living cells, growth signals, and a frame for new bone. Their limits are harm at the harvest site and small supply. Grafts from donors or animals add risks of disease spread and rejection. The review weighs each classic option, then turns to tissue engineering. That newer route mixes frames, growth factors, and gene therapy, and may soon add parts printed in three dimensions to fit a defect.
europmc-pmc4016844:
Yu Wang, Yanmin Zhou, and Dana T. Graves review a family of gene switches called FOXO, in BioMed Research International in 2014. These switches turn genes on or off and shape cell growth, death, self-cleaning, and stress defence. They are active in many cell types, from liver and bone to heart and skin.

Control of the switches is tight. Chemical edits can add or remove tags that move a switch out of the cell nucleus or mark it for disposal. Two major survival pathways do much of this editing. The review maps how the switches act across body processes such as metabolism, inflammation, immunity, and wound healing. Their roles touch cancer, diabetes and its side effects, heart disease, and host defence. Since they can help in some settings and harm in others, drugs that raise or lower their action may each find a use.
europmc-pmc4053844:
Daehwan Kim and five colleagues release TopHat2, an upgraded aligner for RNA sequencing reads, in Genome Biology in 2013. RNA reads must be mapped to the genome across the gaps where introns were spliced out. The original TopHat became a standard tool, but newer data exposed its limits.

The new version handles reads of varied lengths from current machines. It allows insertions and deletions of flexible size against the reference. It can also map reads that straddle fusion breaks, where two genes have been joined by a chromosome swap, a common cancer event. Known transcripts and fresh splice discovery are combined in one pass. The design copes with repeat-rich genomes and with pseudogenes, the gene copies that often trap reads into wrong placements. Tests show gains in sensitivity and accuracy over the first version.
europmc-pmc4097944:
Stephen M. Fleming and Hakwan C. Lau reviewed how to measure metacognition, a person's ability to judge their own thinking. Their paper appeared in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience in 2014. One common approach compares trial-by-trial accuracy with confidence: people with good insight are right more often when they feel confident.

Many studies simply correlate accuracy and confidence, but such measures are distorted by response bias. The authors present bias-free alternatives built on signal detection theory and receiver operating curves. They also separate metacognitive bias, feeling more or less confident at the same performance, from sensitivity, telling one's own right answers from wrong ones. The measures link to calibration tools from probability forecasting. They urge wider use of the bias-free options.
europmc-pmc4117444:
Elaine T. Lim, Daniel G. MacArthur, Aarno Palotie, and a large team mapped gene-breaking variants in Finland's founder population. Their study appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2014. Isolated populations with past bottlenecks carry harmful rare variants at higher rates and fewer neutral ones, easing the hunt for disease links.

Comparing exome data from three thousand Finns with the same number of other Europeans, the team found Finns carry more low-frequency loss-of-function variants and complete gene knockouts despite fewer variable sites overall. They then tested eighty-three enriched variants against sixty traits in more than thirty-six thousand Finns, finding five associations. The work shows how a founder population can expose the medical impact of broken genes.
europmc-pmc4154644:
Claire S. Leblond, Thomas Bourgeron, and a large team screened for faults in the SHANK genes in people with autism and pooled all past data on the point. Their study came out in PLoS Genetics in 2014. SHANK proteins build the frame on the side of a synapse that takes in signals, and help grow the spines where signals land. How often they lie at the root of autism was not clear.

Gene count data held more than five thousand sick people and nineteen thousand well peers, with code reads from smaller sets. Faults that break a SHANK gene showed up in about one in a hundred sick people. Which gene was hit set the form. One gene's faults were rare and came with plain IQ in males. A second's came with mild loss of wits. The worst sat in a third.
europmc-pmc4160344:
Tatsuo Fukagawa and William C. Earnshaw reviewed the centromere, the part of a chromosome that builds the gear for cell division. Their review came out in Developmental Cell in 2014. Since the find of its own histone, CENP-A, the centromere has been seen as the patch of chromatin where the kinetochore, the grip for the spindle, is built.

In most forms of life, what makes a centromere is passed on by marks, not by a set DNA code. The team covers old and new work, most of it in backboned animals. They weigh the role of the repeat DNA found there. They set out the parts and marks that place CENP-A and switch it on. Tests with made chromosomes show how the site works. The review frames this patch as the base for true splits of chromosomes.
europmc-pmc4320144:
Emad Yousif and Raghad Haddad review how sunlight degrades plastics, with a focus on polystyrene. Their review appeared in SpringerPlus in 2013. Ultraviolet light drives photo-oxidation that snaps polymer chains, spawns free radicals, and shrinks the long molecules that give plastics their strength, until parts turn yellow, brittle, and useless.

Polystyrene, cheap and widely used, yellows fast and embrittles in sun and air. The review explains the radical chemistry inside solid films, where mobile hydrogen radicals wander and recombine, and surveys stabilizers that absorb light or quench radicals to slow the damage. It serves materials engineers who need outdoor plastics to last and recyclers judging weathered stock.
europmc-pmc4344544:
Rachael C Dellar, Sarah Dlamini, and Quarraisha Abdool Karim argue that adolescent girls and young women are the key population for bringing HIV under control in southern Africa. Their article appeared in the Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2015. Girls and women aged fifteen to twenty four account for a disproportionate share of new infections there and catch the virus years earlier than male peers.

Their risk, up to eight times that of young men, is compounded by older partners, transactional sex, lost schooling, food insecurity, gender based violence, and biological factors. Proven prevention options aimed at this group remain scarce, and excluding adolescents from trials is a major barrier. The authors set out what epidemic control demands for this group.
europmc-pmc4345344:
Yong-Chan Kwon and Michael C Jewett present simpler ways to prepare the cell extracts used in cell free protein synthesis. Their paper appeared in Scientific Reports in 2015. In this technology, the protein making machinery of lysed cells works in a tube, allowing fast protein production and testing of genetic parts without growing engineered cells.

Good extracts normally demand costly gear and fussy lysis steps, and results vary between labs. The authors' high throughput method uses cheap, widely available equipment and yields extracts whose performance holds up across batches. Standardizing this base step lowers the entry barrier for new labs and for large programs that screen many genetic designs at once.
europmc-pmc4356144:
Yangrong Cao and co-authors rethought how the plant Arabidopsis senses fungi, in a 2014 eLife study. Plants detect chitin, a part of fungal cell walls, with receptor proteins on their cells. One receptor, CERK1, was thought to be the main sensor, yet it binds chitin only weakly. The team tested a related receptor called LYK5 and asked whether it does the main sensing work, alone or with its relatives.

Plants with faults in LYK5 responded much less to chitin, and plants missing both LYK4 and LYK5 lost the response almost fully. LYK5 bound chitin far more tightly than CERK1 did. When chitin was present, LYK5 joined CERK1 in a complex, and that binding was needed for CERK1 to switch on. The results cast LYK5 as the primary chitin sensor that starts plant defense.
europmc-pmc4366544:
Alan Liu, Raymond Chang, Ronald Pearce, and Steve Gentleman revisited a small brain region tied to memory loss, in Acta Neuropathologica in 2015. The nucleus basalis of Meynert sends chemical signals across the cortex, and its nerve cells die in Alzheimer's disease in step with mental decline. Friedrich Lewy first saw his named inclusion bodies there in Parkinson's disease, where cell loss can be just as heavy. Confusion over the region's name and exact borders has lasted for decades.

The review traces the term's history and urges a standard way to sample the region in brain studies. Reports suggest a front-to-back pattern of cell loss in Alzheimer's disease, while Parkinson's findings stay unclear for lack of studies. The authors predict a different loss pattern in Lewy body diseases, matching their distinct symptoms.
europmc-pmc4377644:
Xiaotu Ma and a large team traced how childhood leukemia clones change between diagnosis and relapse, in Nature Communications in 2015. B-acute lymphoblastic leukemia is the classic case where treatment fails through evolution: a minor clone survives therapy and returns. The team used deep gene sequencing on samples from 20 children, taken at diagnosis and again at relapse, to rebuild each cancer's family tree of subclones.

Diversity was about as high at relapse as at diagnosis, and survival of a clone did not depend on how many mutations it carried. Six pathways were hit often, and several genes, including NT5C2 and TP53, were enriched at relapse. Half the cases held several subclonal hits in one pathway at diagnosis, yet usually one minor clone survived, gained more changes, and founded the relapse. Spotting such clones early could warn of failure.
europmc-pmc4381044:
Melanie Schirmer, Umer Ijaz, Rosalinda D'Amore, Neil Hall, William Sloan, and Christopher Quince mapped the errors of a popular DNA sequencing machine, in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. The Illumina MiSeq reads DNA fast and cheaply, and small labs now use it for gene surveys and microbe studies. Yet its error patterns were poorly known, which risks false claims about real genetic variation. The team ran a large test using gene-marker sequencing data from microbial samples.

How the sample library was prepared, and which primers were chosen, proved the biggest sources of bias, each leaving distinct error patterns. The team also tested cleanup strategies head to head. Trimming low-quality ends, correcting errors, then overlapping paired reads cut substitution errors by 93 percent on average. Their recipe gives labs a firmer base for telling real variation from machine noise.
europmc-pmc4384744:
Ci-Xiu Li and co-authors sequenced viruses from joint-legged animals and found an unsuspected deep family tree, in eLife in 2015. Arthropods carry many viruses and spread some to people, yet their viral diversity and role in virus evolution were murky. The team read RNA from 70 arthropod species and discovered 112 new viruses. Many appear ancestral to much of the known diversity of negative-sense RNA viruses, the group that includes influenza and rabies viruses.

Arthropod viruses fell at the base of major groups that infect vertebrates, including the families behind hemorrhagic fevers. Some viral genomes also persisted as copies inside host genomes. Genome shapes varied remarkably, including a possible circular form. The findings cast arthropods as a central reservoir in virus evolution, not just as carriers that move viruses between hosts.
europmc-pmc4386144:
Gillian Potter, Francesca Chappell, Zoe Morris, and Joanna Wardlaw built a rating scale for spaces around brain blood vessels, in Cerebrovascular Diseases in 2015. Perivascular spaces show on MRI scans and form part of small vessel disease, which drives stroke and dementia. They are hard to count consistently, and experts had called for a robust, easy scale. The team reviewed older scales, kept their best features, and wrote a fuller one covering three brain regions.

Two specialist radiologists tested the scale on scans of 60 patients from stroke and aging studies, chosen to span the full range of spaces and related damage. Counts in two regions use a five-step scale from none to more than forty; the midbrain is scored simply visible or not. Agreement statistics checked consistency within and between raters, and the team examined why raters disagreed, to harden the rules.
europmc-pmc4416444:
James Stegen, Xueju Lin, Jim Fredrickson, and Allan Konopka extended a framework for mapping how microbial communities assemble, in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2015. Communities form through selection by the environment, through dispersal between sites, and through random drift in numbers. Selection can be uniform or vary by place, and dispersal can be too weak to connect sites or so strong that it evens them out. Their method estimates the share of each process for a given community.

They checked the method's accuracy in simulations, then applied it to subsurface microbes across two geologic formations. The shares varied substantially even within a single formation. By linking process shares to environmental and spatial features, the team could draw maps of which process dominates in each place. Such maps show not just which microbes live somewhere, but why those and not others.
europmc-pmc4443744:
Nicolas Merle, Remi Noe, Lise Halbwachs-Mecarelli, Veronique Fremeaux-Bacchi, and Lubka Roumenina reviewed the complement system and immunity in Frontiers in Immunology in 2015, in the second part of a two-part review. Complement is a set of blood proteins once seen as a simple chain that punches holes in bacteria. It is now known as a broad watch system of innate immunity.

In health, complement quietly clears dead cells and helps living cells survive. In defense, it coats microbes so other cells can eat them, triggers inflammation through small fragments, and can kill directly with a membrane attack complex. It also helps launch antibody and T cell responses. But microbes can hijack its controls for shelter, and faulty activation itself causes disease. The review balances these friend and foe roles with recent findings.
europmc-pmc4534844:
David Secco leads a ten-author team tracking DNA marks in starved rice, in eLife in 2015. Methylation, a chemical tag on DNA, can quiet genes and jumping elements. How the tag answers environmental stress was little known. The team grew rice without phosphate, a key nutrient, then fed it again, reading methylation across the whole genome over time.

Stress switched on many genes, and methylation rose soon after in jumping elements sitting near those genes, as if to hush the neighbors. The changes followed, not led, the gene switching, largely skipped one known small-RNA path, and passed partly to daughter cells but not to seeds. In Arabidopsis the same stress barely moved the marks, so the response seems species-specific.
europmc-pmc4625044:
Deepti Singh and Ashverya Laxmi published a 2015 review of how plants switch genes on and off during drought. Drought cuts crop yields worldwide and is set to worsen. The plant hormone abscisic acid, or ABA, drives much of the drought response by changing gene activity. The review appeared in Frontiers in Plant Science.

The authors describe a tangled network of transcription factors, proteins that control other genes. One family reads ABA signals directly, while other families act without it. Further groups, including MYB, WRKY, and NF-Y factors, join in, and the families cross-talk with each other. Mapping this web matters because breeders hope to tune whole response programs, not single genes, to build crops that keep yielding with less water.
europmc-pmc4650444:
Working with colleagues, Cynthia Lebeaupin published a 2015 study on how stress inside liver cells triggers inflammation and cell death in fatty liver disease. Fat build-up in the liver is common in obesity, and a quarter of those patients develop steatohepatitis, which can advance to cancer. The endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's protein workshop, is stressed in obesity. The work appeared in Cell Death and Differentiation.

In obese mouse livers, bacterial toxin or a stress drug switched on two stress sensors, raising a protein called CHOP. CHOP then activated the NLRP3 inflammasome and death programs in liver cells. A drug that relieves the stress blocked the whole chain and rescued cells. Silencing CHOP in isolated liver cells confirmed its central role in the damage.
europmc-pmc4712844:
James Briscoe and Stephen Small distilled the design rules of morphogen patterning in Development in 2015. Morphogens are signals that spread from one edge of an embryo tissue and tell cells where they are, so different cell types arise in the right places. Two classic tissues anchor the review: the early fly embryo and the vertebrate neural tube. Both are patterned by gradients flowing from opposite poles, and both, despite deep differences, run strikingly similar logic.

Three shared principles emerge. Gradients set starting conditions, but no fixed concentration maps neatly onto each boundary. Gene networks then mix broad activators with local repressors to draft the pattern. And timing matters: where boundaries land depends on how those networks move in space and time. The authors argue these are general engineering rules for building patterned tissue, likely reused wherever embryos draw with gradients.
europmc-pmc4730344:
Patrick Maier, Linda Hartmann, Frederik Wenz, and Carsten Herskind reviewed how cells respond to ionizing radiation, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2016. Radiotherapy cures many tumors but is limited twice over: some tumor cells resist it, and normal tissue in the beam gets hurt. Widening that gap needs drugs that sensitize tumors or shield healthy cells, and both need targets. The review maps the pathways a cell runs after irradiation.

DNA double-strand breaks trigger repair programs, cell-cycle halts, and death routes including apoptosis, mitotic catastrophe, and senescence. Key proteins in each route are flagged as drug targets. The authors stress that no sensitizer can be designed without this pathway map, since the same machinery decides survival in tumor and normal cells alike. Their synthesis gives drug hunters a short list of leverage points for making radiotherapy both stronger and gentler.
europmc-pmc4783344:
Rute Martins, Gordon J. Lithgow, and Wolfgang Link review the FOXO proteins in Aging Cell in 2016. FOXO switches sit at the end of the insulin signal path and steer stress defense, fuel use, cell-cycle pauses, and cell death. Across worms, flies, and mammals, tuning them shifts lifespan, which makes them prime suspects in the genetics of long life.

The review follows the family from simple animals with one FOXO gene to mammals with four. It sets out how the switches are turned on and off and what each setting does inside cells. Human studies tie one member, FOXO3, to extreme old age again and again. Gaps remain in how the four split their work, and the authors map the open questions for the field.
europmc-pmc4819444:
Simon Hanslmayr, Bernhard P. Staresina, and Howard Bowman tackle a puzzle about brain rhythms and memory in Trends in Neurosciences in 2016. Studies of episodic memory, the recall of lived events, point two ways at once. Some show brain waves syncing up when memory forms; others show them loosening. Both cannot be the whole story, and the authors set out to reconcile them.

Their frame splits the work between two systems. The hippocampus, a fast binder of events, works through synchronized rhythms that tie cell groups together. The outer cortex, which holds the content, works through loosened rhythms that free up capacity to encode detail. The rhythms are not rivals but partners, coupled across frequencies. The paper lays out the scheme and the evidence that would test it.
europmc-pmc4822044:
Xinyong Tao leads a twelve-author team in Nature Communications in 2016 on a design rule for lithium-sulfur batteries. Such batteries promise about six times the energy of standard lithium-ion cells, but sulfur's intermediates dissolve and wander, draining the cell. Metal oxide particles set into the cathode can catch the wanderers; which oxide works best, and why, was unclear.

The team grew several nonconductive oxides on carbon flakes by a biological templating route and tested the cells. Oxides of magnesium, cerium, and lanthanum gave the strongest cycling. Bench tests and theory showed the catch works through a single surface layer of chemical bonds. Yet capture alone is not enough: the caught species must also glide across the surface to deposit well. The best oxide balances grip against glide.
europmc-pmc4847344:
Amy J. Hobbs and co-authors studied how caesarean birth affects breastfeeding in the first four months after birth, in work from 2016 in Calgary, Canada. The caesarean rate in Canada stood at 27.1 percent, well above the range the World Health Organization suggested in 2009. The All Our Babies cohort tracked women through pregnancy and asked about feeding start, length, and trouble at four months.

Caesarean birth, planned or emergency, went with more feeding trouble, more use of support services, and shorter feeding length than vaginal birth. Planned surgery paired with no intent to breastfeed fared worst. The findings support extra feeding help for surgical births, offered early and without pressure on mothers.
europmc-pmc4897744:
Henrik Lilljebjörn and co-authors mapped fusion genes in 195 childhood B-cell leukemia cases in Nature Communications in 2016. Fusion genes, formed when two genes join, drive many cancers. RNA sequencing found frame-keeping fusions in 127 cases, 65 percent, including 27 never reported before. Two fresh subtypes stood out from the scan.

One subtype, making up 4 percent of cases, joins DUX4 to partner genes and floods cells with DUX4 protein, often beside deletions inside ERG. The other mimics the known ETV6-RUNX1 subtype in gene activity without carrying its fusion. Sorting leukemias by these marks guides risk calls and treatment intensity for children, where cure odds hinge on the subtype.
europmc-pmc4975844:
Josephine Ocloo and Rachel Matthews argue that patient and public involvement in healthcare must move from tokenism to real power. Their essay appeared in BMJ Quality and Safety in 2016. Policy calls to center patients have grown louder after serious care failings in the United Kingdom and abroad. Yet involvement stays patchy and shallow, often limited to a narrow circle of the usual voices. The authors drew on a selective literature search across health, social care, policy, and research.

Patients can join at most stages of care and improvement, with real benefits. But methods for doing it well, judging its impact, and reaching diverse people stay unsettled. That gap leaves involvement open to charges of exclusivity. The authors call for a critical rethink of methods and a genuine debate about power, so partnership means influence over decisions, not a seat at the table.
europmc-pmc5022044:
Davide Francioli and five co-authors report a century-long fertilizer trial's soil microbes, in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2016. Farms feed crops with mineral fertilizer, manure, or both, but how soil microbes answer over the very long term was poorly known. The team sampled plots kept under each regime for more than a hundred years and profiled the bacterial and fungal communities, their bulk, and their enzyme work.

Both feeds raised soil carbon and microbial bulk, manure most of all. Manure also widened bacterial diversity and favored groups that thrive on rich food and break down complex matter. Unmanured soils held leaner communities fitted to scarce food. Enzyme activity rose under both feeds, though two key enzymes peaked under mineral feed alone. The feeds also shifted helpful and harmful crop microbes in opposite ways, which may feed back on yield and stability.
europmc-pmc5063044:
M. H. Wright and S. A. Sieber review chemical proteomics for natural product targets in Natural Product Reports in 2016. Natural products inspired many drugs, but when one changes a living cell, finding which proteins it actually touches is hard. Chemical proteomics answers with tailor-made probes: a product is fitted with a handle that lets researchers fish out its protein partners from living cells and name them.

The review surveys the last five years of probe designs, from light-activated traps to two-step tagging done after the probe has found its mark inside the cell. Working in living cells at natural protein levels is the field's strength, and dose and competition tests can even measure binding strength in place. The authors then face the weaknesses head-on: probes that stick to many proteins, background noise, and handles that change how the product behaves, with practical fixes for each.
europmc-pmc5085744:
Caterina Catalanotto, Carlo Cogoni, and Giuseppe Zardo review the nuclear life of microRNAs in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2016. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA strands famous for throttling gene output in the cell's cytoplasm, by degrading messages or blocking their translation. A growing body of work shows the same molecules also act inside the nucleus, where genes are first read.

There they may steady or destabilize messages in the nucleolus, influence how messages are spliced, and, most debated, switch genes on or off at the promoter itself. The favored model has a microRNA pairing with a non-coding RNA that overlaps the promoter, guided by the short seed region of the microRNA. Direct contact with single-stranded promoter DNA has also been proposed. The authors close on the versatility of these small regulators: one molecule class, working in two compartments, by several distinct mechanisms.
europmc-pmc5121944:
Allison Clark and Núria Mach reviewed exercise stress, gut microbes, and diet in athletes for the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition in 2016. Hard training often brings fatigue, low mood, poor performance, and gut trouble, and the review links these through the gut-microbiota-brain axis.

Intense exercise fires stress systems that release hormones and inflammatory signals, while gut microbes shape metabolism, immunity, and even brain chemistry. Mouse work shows exercise stress shifts gut microbe mixes, including mucus-eating species. The authors note that elite diets are often low in plant fiber, which starves microbe diversity, and they discuss early probiotic and prebiotic results. They argue athlete diets should feed the gut community, not just muscles.
europmc-pmc5125044:
Rocio Acuna-Hidalgo, Joris A. Veltman, and Alexander Hoischen reviewed brand-new gene mutations in Genome Biology in 2016. Acuna-Hidalgo leads with her first surname, as Spanish naming prints two. Beyond the DNA inherited from parents, each child is born with a small set of mutations that arose in egg, sperm, or the early embryo.

Sequencing studies of parents and children have now counted and mapped these de novo mutations. They are a major cause of severe early disorders such as intellectual disability and autism, which persist in the population because each generation creates them afresh. Most come from the father, and their number climbs with the father's age. The review covers how the mutations are found, how they arise, and their weight in health and disease.
europmc-pmc522844:
Gian Paolo Castelli, Claudio Pognani, Michael Meisner, Antonio Stuani, Daniela Bellomi, and Laura Sgarbi compared two sepsis markers in intensive care patients in Critical Care in 2004. Procalcitonin and C-reactive protein both rise in blood during severe infection, but how tightly each tracks illness severity, rather than infection itself, was disputed.

The team followed 150 adult intensive care patients for ten days, grouping them by systemic inflammatory response, sepsis at several severity levels, organ failure, and trauma without infection. Both markers ran higher in infected patients than in non-infected patients at the same level of organ dysfunction, though each tracked the organ failure score only weakly. C-reactive protein neared its peak early, while procalcitonin peaked at higher severity and reacted faster to change. The differing patterns suggest the two tests serve different clinical uses.
europmc-pmc5288344:
Petr Kralik and Matteo Ricchi wrote a basic guide to real-time PCR for microbial diagnostics in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2017. Real-time PCR, also called quantitative PCR or qPCR, copies a chosen stretch of DNA over and over while watching the growth by fluorescence. It is now a standard way to detect, count, and type microbes in clinical and veterinary testing and in food safety. The concept is simple, the guide warns, but practice is full of traps.

The guide walks through correct terms and definitions, how the reaction works, and how to read and present results. It sets out the method's limits in different settings and the measures a test should report. One caution stands out. Results are counted on a logarithmic scale, so a modest-looking gap in cycle numbers can mean a near hundred-thousand-fold gap in real microbe counts. Statistics must respect that.
europmc-pmc5295344:
Ayansina Segun Ayangbenro and Olubukola Oluranti Babalola reviewed microbial biosorbents for cleaning heavy metal pollution in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health in 2017. Metals such as cadmium, chromium, and lead are toxic at low levels, cannot be broken down, and build up through food webs. Standard physical and chemical cleanup is costly and produces large volumes of chemical waste.

Biosorption offers an alternative: living or dead microbial biomass, and parts of it, can soak up and hold metals from polluted water and soil, cheaply and with little secondary waste. Microbes bind metals by several mechanisms and often have large uptake capacities. The review surveys where the toxic metals come from and which microorganism groups show the most promise as sorbents. Its caution is practical: most reported studies are small lab batch tests, so picking the right organism and conditions for real industrial effluent still needs work.
europmc-pmc5296644:
Hyunwoo Yuk, Shaoting Lin, Chu Ma, Mahdi Takaffoli, Nicolas X. Fang, and Xuanhe Zhao built water-driven hydrogel robots that hide in plain sight, in Nature Communications in 2017. Young eels are nearly invisible because their bodies are active transparent gels, and the team wanted machines with the same trick. Existing gel actuators, driven by swelling, are slow and weak, and camouflage had not been attempted.

Pumping water hydraulically through shaped hydrogel structures changed the trade-off: the actuators move fast, push hard, and stay tough over repeated cycles because the gel resists fatigue. Being mostly water, the robots are optically transparent and acoustically quiet in water, matching their surroundings on both channels. The demonstrations are playful and pointed: the devices swim, kick a rubber ball, and, most strikingly, catch a live fish, all while hard for prey or observer to detect.
europmc-pmc5343844:
Rick Kamps and co-authors reviewed fast gene reading in cancer care in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2017. New machines read millions of DNA chunks at once, with far better speed, cost, and trust than older methods. That leap has brought gene reading into daily clinic work. The review sorts its uses in oncology, field by field.

Panel and whole-code reading can find the flaws behind inherited cancer risk in a family. RNA reading spots bad splicing of gene messages. The same tools scan a tumor's own flaws, guess how a patient will handle a drug, and test blood for loose tumor DNA. Uses reach even to embryo checks before pregnancy. The authors close with the limits: reading the data well, training doctors, and the ethics of what tests turn up by chance.
europmc-pmc5353544:
Jana Sperschneider and co-authors built a tool to predict where proteins go in plant cells, in Scientific Reports in 2017. Germs that infect plants shoot helper proteins, called effectors, into plant cells. Some slip into set rooms of the cell by copying the plant's own address tags. Old forecast tools read plant proteins well but fail on these foreign helpers, which limits the hunt for key infection tricks.

Their tool, LOCALIZER, forecasts trips to three rooms: the green food sacs, the powerhouses, and the cell core. On hundreds of plant proteins it beat past tools for the first two rooms. On a set of more than a hundred effectors it also came top. It found a hidden green-sac tag on a known toxin, and lab tests showed the toxin does enter tobacco green sacs. Wide scans hint that rust fungi aim many helpers at green sacs and cores.
europmc-pmc5380844:
S. J. Anthony led a large team that found a MERS kin virus in a Ugandan bat, in mBio in 2017. MERS is a grave lung disease that first showed in the Middle East. Its deep roots are unknown, but bats are the prime suspect as the first host. The team caught a bat of a small insect eating kind in Uganda. It read the full genome of a virus the bat carried.

Across most of its genome, the bat virus sits as a close kin of the MERS virus, which backs a shared grandparent. Its spike, the part that grips host cells, told a split tale: less than half of its building blocks match. Key grip spots bore changes that should block it from the human door the MERS virus uses. A test clone with the bat spike grew in lab cells but could not spread to fresh ones.
europmc-pmc5382944:
Gerd Tinkhauser and six co-authors report a 2017 study in Brain on adaptive deep brain stimulation for Parkinson's disease. Standard treatment sends a steady stream of pulses to the brain. The adaptive form reads brain signals and adjusts. The team focused on beta waves in one deep brain area, which rise and fall in bursts tied to movement problems.

Long beta bursts carried larger signals and matched worse movement when stimulation was off. Adaptive stimulation cut the long bursts short, leaving shorter, weaker ones. Standard stimulation lowered beta signals overall but did not change burst length in the same way. The authors say this selective effect may explain why the adaptive form could work better.
europmc-pmc5438344:
Liu and co-authors compare short viral peptides that let one vector express several genes at once. Their research article appeared in Scientific Reports. The peptides are called 2A sequences. They make the ribosome skip a bond during protein building. Two separate proteins then emerge from one chain. The trick is small and efficient. Labs use it for reprogramming, gene therapy, and imaging. No head-to-head guide covered the main variants.

The team built vectors with two, three, and four genes in a row. They mixed four 2A types in varied orders. Protein output fell as a gene moved toward the end. Position thus shapes the final ratio. They tested the vectors in direct heart cell reprogramming. A fluorescent tag worked best in the second slot. A four-gene build with one peptide order beat the rest. The results can guide vector design for research and clinics.
europmc-pmc5486644:
Paillusson and co-authors report a cell study in Acta Neuropathologica on alpha-synuclein, a protein tied to Parkinson's disease. How this protein harms neurons is still not fully clear. Many damaged neuron tasks involve signaling between two organelles, the ER and mitochondria. A tether protein pair, VAPB and PTPIP51, holds those organelles close.

Alpha-synuclein binds VAPB and breaks the tether, they report. Extra synuclein, normal or mutant, loosened the organelle contacts. Neurons grown from Parkinson's patients' stem cells showed the same break. Calcium exchange between the organelles then faltered. Energy output from mitochondria fell with it.
europmc-pmc5518144:
Berens, Jensen, and Nelson present a review in BMC Medicine on the biology of childhood adversity. Abuse, neglect, and household violence in childhood track with disease decades later. Diabetes, heart disease, cancer, and mental illness all rise. The review explains how brief early exposures leave lasting marks. It pulls evidence from across body systems into one frame.

Stress systems, brain networks, and immune tone all shift under early adversity, they report. Chronic low-grade inflammation links many of the changes. More harm follows from more kinds of adversity. The authors urge routine screening in clinics. They also call for wider use of proven family supports.
europmc-pmc5539844:
Dekkers and co-authors present a research article in Frontiers in Immunology. Their subject is the sugar coating on human IgG antibodies. That coating, called a glycan, sits on the antibody tail. Its exact form affects how well the antibody triggers immune defenses.

The team built all 20 major forms of the IgG1 glycan. They used six engineering methods to do so. Tests then measured binding to Fc receptors and to the complement protein C1q. Low fucose raised some receptor binding sharply, and more galactose boosted complement action. Bisection had no clear effect. Readers learn which glycan traits matter most for antibody therapy design.
europmc-pmc5548844:
Wichniak and co-authors review how antidepressants affect sleep in Current Psychiatry Reports. Broken sleep is part of depression itself. Waking in the middle of the night is its most common leftover symptom. A good drug should restore sleep, not wreck it.

Effects split by drug type. Activating drugs like fluoxetine and venlafaxine can disrupt sleep at first. Sedating ones like doxepin, mirtazapine, and trazodone improve it fast. Long-term sedation can then become a problem of its own. Dose and timing matter as much as the drug choice. A tiny dose, taken early in the evening, often works best. Some drugs can also trigger restless legs, teeth grinding, or nightmares. Readers get a practical guide to matching drug and patient.
europmc-pmc5563544:
Yoon and co-authors introduce EzBioCloud, a united database for bacteria and archaea, in the International Journal of Systematic and Evolutionary Microbiology. Naming microbes now rests on genome data. Public genome stores are huge but messy. Names attached to them often need heavy cleaning.

EzBioCloud merges the full taxonomic tree with checked sequences. It holds quality-controlled 16S rRNA gene records. Whole-genome assemblies were screened for poor quality. Survivors passed through an identification pipeline using gene searches and average nucleotide identity. The result covers 61,700 species and phylotypes. Over 62,000 assemblies got firm labels at genus, species, or subspecies level. Genome size and G+C content come with each entry. Readers gain a trusted base for genome-based naming.
europmc-pmc5565844:
Calhoun and co-authors compare brain-scan alignment methods in Human Brain Mapping. Group fMRI studies need every brain warped into one standard space. The functional scans, called EPI, suffer distortion and signal loss. Two template routes dominate the field.

One route warps the EPI scan straight to an EPI template. The other routes through the sharper T1 anatomy scan. Distortion correction can fix the mismatch, but many labs skip it. Across four large datasets, the direct EPI route won. It showed less spread between subjects. Alignment distances between brains came out smaller. A task dataset produced higher test values too. The gain equaled boosting sample size by 12 to 25 percent. Readers get a clear default: use the EPI route when no distortion correction is applied.
europmc-pmc5700944:
Schmid and co-authors aim cancer drugs at T cells instead of tumors. Their study uses antibody-coated nanoparticles that bind CD8+ T cells in mice. Those immune cells travel on their own into tumors. Direct attempts to target tumors have shown limited benefit. The team used cells already in blood, lymph tissue, and tumors.

The particles reached PD-1 positive T cells in blood and in tumors. Loaded with a drug that blocks TGF-beta signaling, they extended survival in tumor-bearing mice. Free drug at the same dose had no effect. The platform also sent a second immune drug to the tumor site. That raised tumor CD8+ T cell counts and made later anti-PD-1 treatment work better.
europmc-pmc5705244:
Novakova and co-authors test a blood marker for disease activity in multiple sclerosis. Their study measures neurofilament light protein, or NFL, in serum. NFL leaks from injured axons, the long fibers of nerve cells. It has long been tracked in spinal fluid, which needs a lumbar puncture.

The team measured 521 paired serum and spinal fluid samples. The group held 286 patients with multiple sclerosis plus controls. Serum and fluid levels tracked each other closely. Patients with active disease or new MRI lesions had higher serum levels. Disease-modifying treatment lowered serum NFL over time. The authors say blood tests could replace spinal taps for this marker.
europmc-pmc5793244:
Lin and co-authors review how zinc shapes wound healing. Wound care is a major health cost, from burns to diabetic foot ulcers. Healing runs through set steps, from clotting to new tissue and matrix remodeling. Zinc, a trace nutrient, supports many enzymes behind those steps.

Lack of zinc brings skin lesions, slow growth, weak immunity, and poor healing. The review traces zinc's roles at the cell and molecular level. It covers membrane repair, cell growth, and immune function. The authors aim to turn this knowledge into better clinical care for hard wounds.
europmc-pmc5796144:
Riaz and co-authors review ways to aim liposomes at solid tumors. Liposomes are tiny fat bubbles that carry cancer drugs. Loaded drugs cause fewer side effects than free ones. Yet body barriers and tumor conditions block delivery. Surface engineering tries to beat those blocks.

The review sorts targets on cancer cells, inside them, and in the tumor's vessels and surroundings. Ligands and surface methods for each target are described. Some liposomes release their cargo when they sense heat, acid, or other cues. Fresh delivery approaches and open challenges close the account. Smart designs are the future, they argue.
europmc-pmc5799244:
Hahn-Holbrook and co-authors pool studies on postpartum depression across nations. Depression after childbirth harms mothers and children. Rates seemed to vary widely by country. The team asks how common it is and why nations differ.

Their meta-analysis covers 291 studies and 296,284 women in 56 nations. They report a pooled rate of 17.7 percent. Rates ranged from 3 percent in Singapore to 38 percent in Chile. Income inequality and mother and child deaths explained much of the gap. Readers get firm global figures and social clues. Every study used the same Edinburgh screening scale for symptoms.
europmc-pmc5823944:
Clark and co-authors unveil scNMT-seq, a triple-readout method for single cells. One cell holds three story layers: gene activity, DNA methylation, and chromatin access. Reading all three at once can reveal how they sway each other.

A tagging enzyme marks open chromatin before sequencing runs. The team tests the method on mouse stem cells as they differentiate. Links appear among all three layers across that change. Couplings shift in step with cell identity. Readers get a tool for probing how gene control layers move together inside a single living cell.
europmc-pmc5889544:
Gopinathan and Noh review recent trends in bioinks for 3D printing. Their article appeared in Biomaterials Research. Demand for organ replacement and tissue repair keeps rising. Bioprinting builds tissues layer by layer from living material. The bioink is the key ingredient in that process. It must carry cells and hold shape after printing. The review covers polymer-based bioinks in current use.

Basic needs for a good bioink are set out first. Cell friendliness, printability, and strength all matter. The authors detail materials that tune each property. Blends of cells, polymers, and signals are discussed. Newer inks can be adjusted more finely than before. Such inks promise more complex printed organs ahead.
europmc-pmc5898944:
Miotto and co-authors set a standard way to link tuberculosis mutations to drug resistance. Their article appeared in the European Respiratory Journal. Fast gene tests need a clear map from mutation to resistance. The team drew raw data from a broad systematic review. They covered ten drugs, from rifampicin to pyrazinamide. Each mutation got a confidence grade.

They graded 286 mutations tied to resistance, they report. For rifampicin, gene calls matched lab tests well on both sensitivity and specificity. Second-line drugs varied more in how well calls performed. The grades can guide reading of rapid tests and sequencing. Clinicians get firmer ground for tailored treatment choices.
europmc-pmc5905044:
Macpherson gave an address on what he called the problem of the feeble-minded. It was delivered to the Glasgow Eugenics Education Society in February 1912. The text appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal. Macpherson was a Commissioner in Lunacy for Scotland. He framed the topic as scientific, social, and political at once. He said none of those sides had been solved.

The address first seeks a clearer sense of the term itself. It discusses how body and mind relate, in his view. Instinct and intelligence are compared across animal life. Human minds, he argues, show high intelligence but less instinct. The piece is a period record of early eugenics thought. Modern readers meet views now widely rejected.
europmc-pmc5917244:
Hallion and co-authors test a scale for difficulties in emotion regulation. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Psychology. They studied 427 adults seeking treatment for emotional disorders. The scale and three short forms were all examined. Such disorders include anxiety, mood, and trauma conditions. The scale is widely used but poorly checked in this group.

The full scale held together well, they report. One subscale, Awareness, was the weak exception. A general dysregulation factor best explained the pattern. That factor predicted both severity and therapy outcome. Short forms kept most of that value with less burden. Clinicians get guidance on which version to use.
europmc-pmc5932344:
Gubbels Bupp and Jorgensen review how androgens suppress immune activity. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Sex hormones shape far more than body sex traits. They also tune immune cells and tissue risk. Autoimmune diseases strike women more often than men. Cancer shows the reverse pattern across sexes.

The review traces androgen action on many immune cell types. Working androgen receptors are required for those effects. Dampened responses may raise some risks while lowering others. Disease onset and course in lupus and arthritis are covered. Multiple sclerosis and cancer also feature. Readers get a hormone-level view of sex gaps in disease.
europmc-pmc6042544:
Lennon and co-authors set out a framework for trajectory modelling. Their article appeared in BMJ Open. The method sorts people into groups by life-course patterns. Body weight over time is a typical example. Many model choices can change the groups found.

The framework runs through eight ordered steps. It starts with a scoping model. It then refines class count and model structure. Adequacy checks and clear graphics come next. Extra tools judge how well classes separate. Clinical sense and sensitivity tests close the process. The team illustrated it with a large cohort. Data covered 288,993 people and weight history. Five classes emerged for each gender. Readers get a shared recipe for building such models.
europmc-pmc6060544:
Pan and co-authors compare forms of exercise for type 2 diabetes. Their network meta-analysis pooled 37 trials with 2,208 patients. It appeared in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity. Aerobic, resistance, and mixed training were ranked head to head. Supervised and home-based forms counted as separate arms.

Mixed training improved blood sugar control the most. Guided aerobic work cut HbA1c by 0.30 percent versus no exercise. It also improved fasting glucose and several blood fats. Guided strength work lowered blood pressure and cholesterol. Plans with staff present beat plans done alone for sugar control and weight. Readers get a ranked guide for prescribing exercise in diabetes care.
europmc-pmc6082844:
Jing and co-authors present PEGASOS, a clearing method for hard and soft tissues alike. Their research article appeared in Cell Research. Clearing turns opaque tissue transparent for 3-D imaging. Old methods left blind spots behind. Bones and teeth resisted nearly every protocol.

The new solvent system handled nearly all tissue types. It preserved the glow of fluorescent proteins. Whole adult mice turned transparent. A full mouse head imaged with no blind areas. Bones, teeth, brain, and muscle appeared together. Individual neurons traced over long distances. The team also mapped nerves inside bone marrow. Readers get a general tool for whole-organ imaging.
europmc-pmc6089144:
Zhou and co-authors show how iron overload pushes macrophages toward inflammation. Their research article appeared in Cancer Medicine. Macrophages come in calm and inflammatory types. Tumor-linked ones usually sit in the calm mode. Iron builds up inside macrophages and flips the switch.

In mouse macrophages, iron raised reactive oxygen species. That boost increased acetylation of the protein p53. Acetylated p53 then drove the inflammatory program. A scavenger that cut reactive oxygen blocked the flip. A drug blocking the acetyl writer did the same. In mice, iron injections shifted tumor macrophages too. Readers get a mechanism that may serve tumor immunotherapy.
europmc-pmc6141544:
Klestil and co-authors offer a systematic review and meta-analysis in Scientific Reports on surgery timing for hip fractures in older patients. Hip fractures in old age can end mobility for good. Whether faster surgery saves lives has been much debated. The team pooled studies of patients aged 60 years and up.

They kept 28 studies with 31,242 patients. Surgery within 48 hours cut the risk of death within a year by about 20 percent. Early surgery also meant fewer complications around the operation. One study found more pressure ulcers as delays grew. A 24-hour cutoff showed no clear extra gain. The authors back prompt surgery within two days.
europmc-pmc6185944:
Gallego and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications on how motor cortex populations support many movements. The primary motor cortex drives a rich set of skilled behaviors. Single neurons change their activity from task to task. The team asked whether the wider population keeps a stable structure.

They recorded cortical activity in monkeys doing wrist and reach-to-grasp tasks. Muscle and single-cell patterns differed by task. Yet the dominant neural modes, the main patterns of joint activity, were largely preserved. Two sets of modes stayed task-independent, capturing general timing features. The findings suggest the cortex reuses one neural manifold, a stable activity space, across very different movements.
europmc-pmc6222344:
Pantsar and Poso wrote an opinion paper on docking and binding strength. Docking places a small molecule inside a target protein. It predicts the binding pose fast. Many users also expect a binding strength estimate. The paper appeared in Molecules.

The authors say docking is the wrong tool for that estimate. Past broad analyses reached the same verdict. Scoring accuracy is barely better than decades ago. They examine why progress has stalled. Water around the binding site is poorly handled. Hydrogen bonding is also described poorly. The true motion of the system is mostly ignored. The authors discuss fixes for each flaw. They aim to guide more honest use of docking.
europmc-pmc6244944:
Zhang and co-authors review resistance to a cancer drug called 5-fluorouracil. The drug has treated colon cancer since 1957. It is also used for breast and head and neck cancers. It mimics a building block of DNA and RNA. The review appeared in Molecules.

Inserted into DNA and RNA, the drug kills cancer cells. Yet resistance limits its use in the clinic. Response rates for advanced colon cancer stay low with the drug alone. The review first explains how the drug acts. It then covers studies of resistance mechanisms. A third part covers gene-finding with microarray tools. The authors detail how resistance starts and how it might be reversed. That knowledge could restore the drug's value.
europmc-pmc6245444:
Li and co-authors review fucoidan, a sugar chain compound found in brown seaweed. Their review appeared in Molecules. Fucoidan is rich in the sugar fucose and carries sulfate groups. It was first isolated from brown algae in 1913. Interest has grown because early tests suggest many biological effects. Drug hunters have also begun to study it closely.

Work so far links fucoidan to effects on blood clotting, viruses, and tumours. Immune calming and cholesterol lowering effects have also been reported.
