The review gathers what is known about its structure from many seaweed species. It then asks how structure shapes each effect. That structure to effect map matters for future drug and food uses. The authors note that sources are cheap and widely available.
europmc-pmc6273244:
Domingo, Ríos-Gutiérrez, and Pérez review indices that predict how organic molecules react. Their review appeared in Molecules. The indices come from conceptual density functional theory. They turn electron density maths into simple numbers. Global indices rate a whole molecule's hunger for electrons. Local indices rate single atoms within it. Together they guide which bonds will form.

The review explains the main global and local measures. Chemical potential, electrophilicity, and nucleophilicity lead the global set. Parr functions lead the local set. Worked examples show how each index is used. The theory rests on the Hohenberg and Kohn theorems from the 1960s. It offers a middle path between rough rules and full simulation. Chemists can screen reactions before running them. The authors present the indices as a practical design tool.
europmc-pmc6321244:
Tarafdar and Pula review NADPH oxidases and oxidative stress in brain degeneration. The review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. These enzymes make reactive oxygen species on purpose. Too much of those species creates oxidative stress. That stress runs through many brain disorders. The family now counts seven enzyme members.

The enzymes appear in neurons, glia, and vessel cells. Their activity can damage brain blood vessels. Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases both feature this stress. Huntington's disease, ALS, and multiple sclerosis do too. The authors link enzyme activity to each condition. They stress the neurovascular side of the damage. Blocking these enzymes may open new treatments, they argue.
europmc-pmc6396144:
Anderson and co-authors report a research article in The EMBO Journal on heart cell aging. Aging is the top risk factor for heart disease. Cell senescence was thought to need cell division and worn telomeres, the caps on DNA ends.

Heart muscle cells rarely divide, yet they still show a senescent state with age. Damage sat at telomeres even when telomere length stayed normal. Faulty mitochondria could drive that damage. Clearing senescent cells eased age-linked heart problems in tests. The work separates telomere damage from telomere length in heart aging.
europmc-pmc6402144:
Perperoglou and co-authors review spline methods in the R language, in BMC Medical Research Methodology. Splines let a regression curve bend smoothly with the data. They have become a standard tool in health studies.

Good software matters as much as good theory, the authors argue. They survey the R packages that fit splines inside regression models. Simulated and real data show how each package behaves. The review is part of a series guiding observational research methods. It helps analysts pick a spline tool and use it with care. Worked examples make each package's strengths plain.
europmc-pmc6431044:
Lun and co-authors present EmptyDrops, a statistical method for telling real cells from empty droplets in droplet-based single-cell RNA sequencing. These protocols profile tens of thousands of cells at once, but many droplets capture only stray RNA floating in the solution. Simple count cutoffs wrongly discard small or quiet cell types.

EmptyDrops tests each droplet's profile against the ambient RNA profile and flags significant departures as genuine cells. Simulations showed more power than existing callers while holding the false discovery rate down. On real datasets it rescued distinct cell types that other methods threw away. Analysts working on large cell atlases gain a safer first filter for their data.
europmc-pmc6437844:
Oliver and co-authors question the one-sided praise for coproduction in health research, the model where stakeholders help design and run studies. Advocates promise better uptake and impact, yet the field lacks agreement on what coproduction is or which techniques achieve which outcomes. Costs and risks, the authors argue, are rarely mentioned at all.

Five cost types are catalogued: harm to the research itself, to the process, professional and personal risks for researchers and stakeholders, and risks to scholarship at large. Tensions between partners' interests run through all of them. The advice is caution: name the exact motivation, pick strategies built for the wanted outcome, and evaluate honestly.
europmc-pmc6441044:
Patel and co-authors test four store-bought kits against the classic spin method for pulling exosomes out of cell culture fluid, judging each on yield, purity, and fitness for later work. Exosome research has boomed, but each lab prepares its samples its own way, and results are hard to compare.

The Invitrogen kit gave the most vesicles, yet their sizes spread wide and they held up worst. Mass checks found plastic-like chemical leftovers in the mix. Its exosomes also slowed cell growth, a hint of toxic residue. The other methods kept vesicles under 150 nanometers, stable and with RNA of like quality. The iZON column did let some non-vesicle clumps through. The head-to-head guides labs to pick by what they plan to do next.
europmc-pmc6468544:
Vidak and co-authors review cysteine cathepsins outside their old home in the lysosome, where they were long cast as bulk demolition enzymes. Eleven family members exist in humans, and in cancer and inflammation they are overproduced and secreted into the extracellular space, where they do precise editing as well as degradation of matrix proteins.

That precision changes how the enzymes should be treated as drug and diagnostic targets. Cutting specific extracellular proteins can release signals, reshape tissue, and feed tumor growth or joint destruction. Balance against their natural inhibitors appears decisive, since removing an inhibitor enlarged tumors in mouse models. Translational prospects and new measurement tools close the review.
europmc-pmc6476344:
Merino and co-authors map the biospace of life on Earth through its extremophiles, microbes thriving where temperature, acidity, pressure, radiation, or salt would kill ordinary cells. Prokaryotes have owned most of evolutionary history and occupy nearly every niche, including the subsurface, and they even survive spells in space with its vacuum and radiation.

Organisms stacking several extremes at once, polyextremophiles, may be the planet's most abundant life. Calling their homes extreme is a human-centered habit, since the conditions are their normal. The survey weighs what these limits imply for life's origin and for the search on other worlds, and marks the knowledge gaps plainly.
europmc-pmc6505044:
Tsuchiya and co-authors trace a backup death pathway in immune cells, writing in Nature Communications. The enzyme caspase-1 normally kills cells by pyroptosis, a bursting death driven by the protein gasdermin D. Yet cells that lack gasdermin D still die when caspase-1 fires. The team asked what kills them instead.

In macrophages without gasdermin D, inflammasome triggers set off apoptosis, the tidier form of cell suicide, driven largely by caspase-1 itself. The route ran through Bid, caspase-9 and caspase-3, and could end in a second bursting stage. Brain neurons and mast cells hold little gasdermin D, and both died by this same caspase-1 route under stress. The work maps how cell type decides which death caspase-1 delivers.
europmc-pmc6514244:
Mantere, Kersten and Hoischen review long-read sequencing in medical genetics. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Genetics. Standard sequencing reads short fragments of DNA. Short reads struggle with structural variants and repeat regions. They also fail at phasing alleles and telling apart near-identical genes.

Long reads average more than 10 kilobases from single molecules. They need no PCR step, so native DNA marks stay visible. The authors survey work on human genetic disorders. Long reads have found disease variants that short reads missed. They can span repeat expansions and resolve haplotypes. Pseudogenes become easier to separate from true genes. The piece ends with prospects for routine whole-genome use.
europmc-pmc6710244:
Bull and co-authors measured real menstrual cycles using data from a phone app. Their study drew on records from the Natural Cycles app. Users logged bleeding, body temperature, and hormone tests. The team wanted to know what normal cycles actually look like outside clinics.

They studied 612,613 ovulatory cycles from 124,648 users. The mean cycle lasted 29.3 days, with a mean first phase of 16.9 days. Cycles got slightly shorter as women aged from 25 to 45. Women with a body mass index over 35 had more varied cycle lengths. The findings matter for women timing pregnancy.
europmc-pmc6723444:
Berrazaga and co-authors compare plant and animal proteins for keeping muscle mass. Plant proteins offer health and environmental gains. They build muscle less well, though, because they digest less fully and run low in key amino acids such as leucine. That matters most for older people fighting muscle loss.

Plant amino acids are burned for energy more often than used for muscle building. The review tests four fixes. Eating more protein per meal helps, with amounts above 30 grams showing gains. Adding missing amino acids, breeding better crops, and blending plant sources can also close the gap. With these steps, plant protein can support muscle nearly as well.
europmc-pmc6739444:
Ho and co-authors studied how bone marrow niches change during aging. Blood stem cells live in niches, snug pockets in the marrow that control them. With age, these stem cells pile up yet work worse. Neighboring megakaryocyte cells normally keep them quiet. The team asked how these partnerships shift in normal and premature aging.

In aging mice, support niches shrank near bone but grew farther away. Nerve signals in the marrow rose and pushed production of myeloid cells. A drug that activates one receptor reversed the early myeloid and stem cell expansion in progeroid mice. It also restored stem cells' closeness to megakaryocytes. Fixing the niche may thus ease age-linked blood changes.
europmc-pmc6790244:
Yue and co-authors showed that the RNA-marking enzyme METTL3 drives spread of gastric cancer. The m6A mark is one of the most common chemical edits on messenger RNA. It shapes RNA stability, splicing, and translation. METTL3 installs much of this mark. The team measured it in gastric cancer tissue and tested its effects in cells and mice.

METTL3 levels were raised in gastric cancer. High levels predicted poor patient survival. The enzyme proved necessary for the transition process that lets tumor cells move, and for metastasis in animals. In one tissue set, a third of samples stained strongly for METTL3. Its rise tied to deeper nodal and distant spread. Blocking this pathway may slow gastric cancer's advance.
europmc-pmc6818444:
Von Haehling and co-authors set out updated ethical guidelines for the Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle. The journal covers wasting, muscle loss, and related fields. Its rules also cover two sister journals. Every author who submits a paper must certify that the work meets these standards.

The guidelines state that all listed authors must have approved the paper and made a real, independent contribution. No one who earned authorship may be left off. The update restates duties on honest reporting and fair credit. Editors ask the corresponding author to confirm all of this, for the whole team, at the time of submission.
europmc-pmc6857444:
Strongman and co-authors report a study in The Lancet on heart risks after cancer. Cancer survival has improved greatly in recent decades. Survivors may, though, face raised risks of cardiovascular disease years later, from the illness or its treatment. Evidence across many cancer types was scarce. The team used linked United Kingdom health records to fill that gap.

They built cohorts of survivors of the 20 most common adult cancers from primary care, hospital, and registry data. Each survivor's later rates of specific heart and vessel diseases were compared with people without cancer. Risks differed widely by cancer type and by the heart condition in question. Some survivors carried clearly raised long-term risk. The authors say follow-up care should reflect that pattern.
europmc-pmc6859644:
Chen and co-authors benchmark tools for a new kind of single-cell data, in Genome Biology. Single-cell ATAC sequencing reads which parts of the genome lie open in each cell. It profiles thousands of cells at once. The data are sparse by nature, since each cell holds only two copies of its DNA. Only 1 to 10 percent of open sites show up per cell.

The team built a framework to judge 10 analysis methods on 13 real and synthetic datasets. They scored how well each method grouped cells and recovered known types. Some approaches performed solidly nearly everywhere, with one public blood dataset tripping most of them. The results give labs a guide for choosing tools.
europmc-pmc6875144:
Rolls offers a new account of the cingulate cortex in Brain Structure and Function. This belt of cortex sits deep along the brain's midline. It has been tied to emotion, action, and memory, three roles that seem unrelated. Rolls argues they follow from the region's wiring. Its front part receives reward and non-reward news from the orbitofrontal cortex.

Its rear part instead receives spatial and action information from parietal areas. Joining reward to action lets the front support emotion and action-outcome learning. Outputs from the rear reach the hippocampal memory system, grounding its memory role. Rolls also links patterns of connection in depression to excess non-reward signalling.
europmc-pmc6888544:
Laganà and co-authors review the origins of endometriosis, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. In this disease, tissue like the womb lining grows outside the womb, causing pain and infertility. Its causes form a many-sided puzzle that is still unsolved. The authors gathered the English-language evidence from database inception to June 2019.

Candidate sources for the stray tissue include stem cells of the womb lining, leftover embryonic tissue, bone marrow cells, and the abdominal lining itself. Genes, epigenetic marks, and immune factors all seem to contribute. Enzymes that chew through tissue, the MMP family, run high in affected women. The review weighs each proposed route against the molecular evidence.
europmc-pmc6894344:
Li and co-authors review ways to turn tumour macrophages into allies, in Molecular Cancer. Immunotherapy has become a powerful weapon, yet most solid tumours barely respond. Their local environment suppresses attack. Tumour-associated macrophages flood that environment. Left alone, they help the tumour grow, spread, and grow new vessels, while shielding it from immunity.

The review sorts strategies for flipping these cells: killing them off, blocking their recruitment, or reprogramming them to fight. Early attempts have shown effects across tumour types in lab and clinical studies. One older drug, trabectedin, turns out to kill such macrophages selectively through a death-receptor route. The authors argue macrophages should be treated as partners in immunotherapy design.
europmc-pmc6907144:
Alquicira-Hernandez and co-authors present scPred, in Genome Biology. Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals the distinct cell types inside a tissue. To use that knowledge, a new cell must be matched to a known type from its gene activity alone. Trial and error classification wastes the atlases already built. A supervised method can learn from them.

ScPred first reduces the data's dimensions and selects informative features without bias toward any type. A machine learning model then assigns each cell a type, with a probability attached. The authors tested it on pancreas tissue, blood cells, colorectal tumour biopsies, and circulating dendritic cells. Accuracy stayed high across all four, including types the model had rarely seen.
europmc-pmc6912544:
Kuhn and co-authors review oligodendrocytes, in the journal Cells. These cells wrap nerve fibres in myelin, the insulation that lets signals travel fast in the brain and spinal cord. They grow from progenitor cells that persist in the adult nervous system, ready to migrate and multiply. Making myelin is energy-hungry work, which leaves the cells exposed to toxic insults.

Their damage shows up in multiple sclerosis, schizophrenia, and Alzheimer's disease, among others. When oligodendrocytes die, progenitors can replace them and rewrap fibres, a repair called remyelination. The review follows the cells from development through that repair, and into roles beyond insulation that recent work has uncovered.
europmc-pmc6927944:
Pelaia and co-authors review interleukin-5 in severe asthma. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Physiology. Interleukin-5, or IL-5, drives eosinophil biology. It shapes their growth, recruitment, survival, and degranulation. Those cells fuel eosinophilic airway inflammation.

Recent work has clarified how IL-5 acts. It builds, sustains, and amplifies the inflammatory response. That central role makes it a prime drug target. Some therapies block IL-5 itself. Mepolizumab and reslizumab work that way. Benralizumab instead blocks its receptor. These biologics can help patients with severe T2-high asthma. Such asthma often resists inhaled and systemic steroids. The review weighs the gains for that group.
europmc-pmc6937944:
Madissoon and co-authors test how long human tissue stays usable for single-cell studies. Their study appeared in Genome Biology. The Human Cell Atlas aims to map every cell type in the body. Fresh samples often travel far before processing, and delays can ruin data quality.

The team stored healthy lung, spleen, and oesophagus tissue cold, then profiled cells over 72 hours. They gathered 240,000 high-quality single-cell profiles from at least five donors. Within the first 24 hours, cold time barely affected cell yield or data quality in any tissue. By 72 hours, warning signs appeared, including fewer lung T cells and more background RNA in spleen. The protocols, they conclude, safely buy a day for sample transport.
europmc-pmc7015244:
Wang and co-authors present a systematic review and meta-analysis in the Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle. They ask a practical question about ageing. Do muscle mass, strength, and physical performance predict later dependence in daily tasks? The tasks cover basic self-care and the wider tasks of living independently at home.

The team searched four databases through 7 June 2018. They kept longitudinal studies of adults aged 65 and over. Eighty-three articles covering 108,428 people entered the review, and 45 entered the pooled analyses. The authors report that low muscle mass, weak grip, slow gait, and poor balance or chair-stand scores all raised the odds of worsening dependence. They conclude that simple muscle measures can flag older adults at risk.
europmc-pmc7018944:
Kingra and co-authors present a computing design in Scientific Reports. Standard computers keep memory and processing apart, so data shuttles back and forth and slows everything down. Logic-in-memory designs compute inside the memory array itself. The catch is that arrays used for logic often lose their stored data in the process.

The team proposes SLIM, a scheme built on bilayer analog OxRAM devices. Their bitcell performs logic operations, such as a two-input NOR gate, while keeping the stored state intact. That makes the approach suited to the storage side of digital systems, including solid-state drives, rather than only to processors. Experiments and array-level analysis support the design, including a refresh method for larger arrays.
europmc-pmc7048044:
Dunstan and Scott present a methods study in BMC Psychiatry. They examine Zung's Self-rating Anxiety Scale, a widely used screening tool for anxiety disorders. The scale has a cut-off score that flags a likely disorder. Recent work had questioned whether the current cut-off of 36 is set too low.

The authors compared scale scores with diagnoses from the Patient Health Questionnaire. Their samples held 210 community adults and 141 adults in treatment for anxiety. Standard formulas put the ideal cut-off between the current point and Zung's original point of 40. Weighing missed cases against false alarms, they advise keeping 36 for clinical screening. For research use, they favour the original cut-off of 40.
europmc-pmc7056644:
Virtanen and co-authors present SciPy 1.0 in Nature Methods. SciPy is an open-source library of scientific algorithms for the Python language. First released in 2001, it has become a standard tool, with over 600 code contributors, thousands of dependent packages, and millions of downloads each year. Higher-level libraries such as scikit-learn build directly on it.

SciPy supplies core routines for optimisation, integration, interpolation, eigenvalue problems, and algebraic and differential equations, plus structures such as sparse matrices and k-dimensional trees, all layered on NumPy's arrays. The paper surveys the library's powers and its open development practices, and picks out recent work, such as a faster nearest-neighbour search rewritten in C++. Analyses of gravitational waves are among the landmark results that ran on SciPy. The 1.0 milestone marks a community tool reaching full maturity.
europmc-pmc7082344:
Xie, Chen, and Fang review targeted therapy for colorectal cancer, in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. Colorectal cancer caused nearly 881,000 deaths in 2018, and surgery plus chemotherapy long formed the standard care. Outcomes stayed poor, above all once the cancer had spread.

Targeted drugs attack specific pathways instead of all fast-growing cells. Early successes included cetuximab, which blocks the EGFR receptor, and bevacizumab, which blocks new blood vessel growth. Newer agents target other pathways and immune checkpoints. The review explains how each drug class works, where each falls short, and how treatment guidelines are changing as trials accumulate.
europmc-pmc7119644:
Maenner and co-authors report autism spectrum disorder rates among 8-year-old children in the United States for 2016, in MMWR Surveillance Summaries. The Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring Network reviewed medical and education records at 11 sites, and trained clinicians judged each case against standard diagnostic criteria.

Across the sites, autism prevalence was 18.5 per 1,000 children, about one in 54. Boys were affected 4.3 times as often as girls. Rates ranged from 13.1 per 1,000 in Colorado to 31.4 in New Jersey. White, black, and Asian or Pacific Islander children had similar rates, while Hispanic children were lower at 15.4. Among children with IQ data, 33% had intellectual disability.
europmc-pmc7142144:
Liu and co-authors report a nanoparticle system that both supplies and conserves reactive oxygen for cancer therapy, in Nature Communications. Light-based and chemical treatments that kill tumors with reactive oxygen stall because tumors lack oxygen and hydrogen peroxide. Their agent carries calcium peroxide and a light-sensitive dye inside a coated particle.

Under laser light, the dye makes singlet oxygen and heat, which melts the coating. The exposed calcium peroxide then reacts with water to release oxygen and hydrogen peroxide, feeding both therapies at once. The carrier also drains glutathione, the molecule tumors use to mop up reactive oxygen. The combined strategy strongly inhibited tumor growth in cells and animals.
europmc-pmc7214244:
Shah and co-authors explain why a protein called BCMA is a prime target in multiple myeloma. Their review appeared in Leukemia. Myeloma treatment advanced greatly in a decade, yet no cure exists. Many patients stop responding or tolerate drugs poorly. Fresh mechanisms of action are badly needed.

BCMA sits mainly on mature B cells, the lineage that turns malignant in myeloma. Its activity is tied to tumor growth in lab models. Therapies aimed at it include engineered CAR T cells. These constructs redirect a patient's own T cells onto the cancer. Newer versions carry extra stimulating domains to boost attack. Other BCMA approaches are also in development. The review weighs the promise and the open questions.
europmc-pmc7244544:
Li and co-authors show that an RNA mark called m6A boosts sugar burning in cancer cells through a gene named PDK4. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Cancer cells favor glycolysis, a fast but wasteful way to make energy. Sequencing of marked RNA pointed to PDK4 as a key player. The mark sits on the gene's message and raises its output.

Two reader proteins carry the effect, one speeding protein production and one stabilizing the message. Erasing the mark on PDK4 with a targeted CRISPR tool cut both the protein and glycolysis. A further loop emerged: a factor called TBP raises the enzyme that writes the mark in cervical cancer cells. The chain links RNA editing to tumor metabolism. Each link is a possible point of intervention.
europmc-pmc7301644:
Aleström and co-authors give joint advice on how to house and care for zebrafish in the lab. Their guidance aims to put European rules for test animals into daily practice. Zebrafish are a key model in biology and medicine. Care varies a lot from lab to lab, and that spread can quietly hurt how well results repeat.

The advice comes from a joint group of European fish-model and lab-animal bodies. In place of fixed values, it gives ranges for things like water heat and quality, inside which fish stay well and results stay sound. That choice respects the routines that already work in many labs. It also fits the wide range of waters zebrafish live in in the wild.
europmc-pmc7343844:
Couturier and co-authors map the cell family tree inside glioblastoma, a deadly brain cancer, in Nature Communications. They read gene activity in 53,586 single cancer cells and compared it with 22,637 cells from normal fetal brain. The aim was to see how the tumor's mixed cell types relate to each other.

The cancer copies a normal development pattern. Its cells form a three-branch hierarchy centered on glial progenitor-like cells, which resemble young brain support cells. Those progenitors hold most of the dividing cells and, by a motion-tracking method, appear to spawn the other types. Because the hierarchy is now mapped, the authors can point to targets specific to the cancer stem cells at its root.
europmc-pmc7457244:
Zeng and co-authors review METTL3, an enzyme that marks RNA, and its roles in cancer. The mark, called m6A, is the most common change on messenger RNA. METTL3 is the sole active maker in its complex.

Evidence shows METTL3 drives many cancer types. Some effects need its marking work, others do not. It can push tumors on or hold them back, by tissue and context. The review sums up these dual roles and the paths beneath them. The known shape of the METTL3 and METTL14 pair aids drug design. Blocking or tuning METTL3 could form a new cancer treatment route. The authors set out where tests of such drugs stand and what blocks progress.
europmc-pmc7556044:
Sidhom, Obi and Saleem review methods for isolating exosomes from fluids and media. Exosomes are small vesicles that cells use to signal. Clean isolation is needed for sound study of them.

Common methods include ultracentrifugation and ultrafiltration. Other options use capture agents, microfluidics or precipitation. Each method carries its own trade-offs in purity and yield. The review focuses on size exclusion chromatography as an option. Exosomes from that method were fairly pure and functional. The method is reproducible and scalable in practice. It is also low cost and needs no special expertise. Direct comparison studies are still needed, the authors note.
europmc-pmc7567644:
Pashayan and co-authors present the ENVISION consensus statement on personalized breast cancer detection and prevention. The network gathers research groups working on risk-based care. A consensus conference was held in 2019 to set priorities.

Four priority areas were named by the network. First, risk tools should work for women of all ancestries. Second, markers are needed to track response to prevention. Third, new non-surgical prevention should target poor-prognosis cancers. Fourth, trials should pair outcome tests with modeling studies. The statement reviews risk prediction and stratified screening. It also covers legal and ethical issues for rollout. Health systems must be ready to learn and adapt.
europmc-pmc7598944:
Cruz Rivera and co-authors present SPIRIT-AI, a guideline for protocols of AI intervention trials. Trial protocols set out plans before a study runs. Clear protocols help readers judge design and bias.

The guideline extends the SPIRIT 2013 statement for AI work. It was built with its companion CONSORT-AI guideline. A Delphi survey involved 103 stakeholders in two stages. A consensus meeting drew 31 stakeholders together. Checklist piloting involved 34 participants in testing. The extension adds 15 new protocol items. Protocols should describe the AI tool and required skills. Input and output handling must be spelled out. Human-AI interaction and error plans are also required.
europmc-pmc7734744:
Zhou and co-authors review circular RNAs and how they work with proteins. Circular RNAs are single strands closed into loops. They occur across life, from viruses to mammals. They can sponge small RNAs, guide gene activity, and serve as templates for proteins. A newer theme is their direct play with proteins.

Circles can act as decoys, scaffolds, or recruiters for proteins. They can alter how proteins meet, hold proteins aside, or move them to new cell sites. Distinct patterns of these RNAs mark many diseases. The authors say this makes them strong candidates as diagnostic markers and drug targets for future care.
europmc-pmc7805044:
Tao and co-authors review the low-oxygen world inside pancreatic cancer and how to target it. Pancreatic cancer is often found late. It spreads early and has a poor outlook. Its tumors pack in stroma and matrix but few blood vessels. The result is severe, lasting oxygen shortage.

Low oxygen reshapes tumor behavior. It reprograms fuel use and boosts stem-like traits. Invasion, spread, and abnormal vessel growth follow. Stromal cells change under the same stress. These shifts also blunt treatment. The authors explain the machinery behind each effect. They then survey oxygen-based treatment ideas, including trial work. Combination therapy is a main theme.
europmc-pmc7826844:
Sallam and colleagues surveyed adults in Jordan, Kuwait, and other Arab countries about COVID-19 vaccines. At the time, new vaccines raised hope for slowing the spread of the virus. Yet false claims about the virus and the shots spread fast. The team asked how many people would take a vaccine. They also asked whether belief in secret plots shaped that choice.

The online survey ran in December 2020 and drew 3414 replies. The authors reported that just 29.4% of respondents said they would take a COVID-19 vaccine. They reported that 27.7% believed vaccines would inject microchips. They also reported that 23.4% linked vaccines to infertility. The authors reported higher belief scores were tied to more hesitancy. People who relied on social media showed more doubt, they reported. Readers get clear tables by age, sex, schooling, and source of news.
europmc-pmc7890144:
Kitamura and co-authors report a cohort study of sarcopenia in older adults in Japan. Sarcopenia is the loss of muscle mass and strength that comes with age. Evidence on it in Asian populations has been limited. The team measured its frequency and its link to death and disability.

They followed 1851 community-dwelling residents aged 65 years or older for 5.8 years. Sarcopenia was found in 11.5% of men and 16.7% of women. Low blood albumin, weak cognition, low activity, and recent hospital stays were tied to the condition in men. People with sarcopenia faced higher risks of both death and new disability. Muscle loss paired with weakness carried the clearest risk. The study gives Asian health services firm local numbers for planning care.
europmc-pmc7891044:
Supasa and co-authors report a laboratory study of antibodies against the SARS-CoV-2 variant B.1.1.7 early in its spread. The variant spread fast in the UK and carries changes in its spike protein. One change, N501Y, sits where the spike meets human cells. The team tested whether blood from infected or vaccinated people could still block it.

The variant carries 9 amino acid changes in the spike. The authors found it was harder to neutralise than the parent virus. Some common public antibodies lost strength because of the N501Y change. But broad escape was not seen. Blood from people who had recovered or been vaccinated still worked overall. The study offers a careful check on how far one variant can dodge immunity, and where the weak points lie.
europmc-pmc7900244:
Kyriakidis and co-authors present a review of vaccine strategies against SARS-CoV-2. The virus had caused more than 1,866,000 deaths by early January 2021. Labs across the world raced to build a vaccine. Most designs aim to raise antibodies against the spike protein, which the virus uses to enter human cells.

More than 64 vaccine candidates were in development at the time of writing. They rest on several platforms, each with its own strengths and limits. The review compares those platforms side by side. Thirteen candidates had reached phase 3 trials, the last step before approval for wide use. The authors explain how each approach tries to block the virus at the ACE-2 receptor. Readers get a clear snapshot of the vaccine race at a key moment.
europmc-pmc7925544:
Yin and co-authors report a mouse study on how an RNA mark shapes tumour growth through immune cells. The mark, called m6A, is placed on RNA by an enzyme named METTL3. Its role inside macrophages was unknown. The team removed the Mettl3 gene from myeloid cells and watched how tumours behaved.

Tumours grew faster and spread more in the altered mice. More regulatory T cells and mixed-type macrophages entered the tumours. Without the mark, a gene called SPRED2 was read less well. That loss fired up two growth pathways and fed the tumour. A standard immune therapy, PD-1 blockade, also worked less well in these mice. The authors name METTL3 as a possible drug target. The work ties a small RNA edit to the whole tumour immune setting.
europmc-pmc7946244:
Cumston presents a history of herpes from the earliest times to the nineteenth century. The paper opens with the Hippocratic Collection, which says little on skin pathology. Herpes is named there, but only in passing. Ancient doctors may have treated skin lesions as deformities rather than diseases, Cumston suggests. That attitude shaped what they bothered to record.

The term herpes was used in early Greek medicine for chronic skin affections. Galen used it with care as well. Cumston follows the thread through the school of Alexandria, whose masters survive only in fragments. Celsus and later compilers carry the story onward. Side remarks on skin lesions in general fill out the account. The paper is a guide to how one word's meaning shifted across two thousand years.
europmc-pmc8043944:
Ashton and co-authors develop a blood test for the earliest stages of Alzheimer's disease. The test measures tau phosphorylated at threonine 231, called p-tau231. The marker was established in spinal fluid, not blood. The team built an ultrasensitive Simoa assay for plasma. They validated it in four independent cohorts totaling 588 people.

Plasma p-tau231 identified Alzheimer's patients with high accuracy, at AUC 0.92–0.94. It separated them from amyloid-negative healthy adults and from other dementias. In a brain-donor cohort, it flagged Alzheimer's pathology years before death. The marker rose earlier than plasma p-tau181 did. It climbed before amyloid scans crossed their standard positive threshold. That early rise could help trials recruit people sooner. Treatment may work best at exactly that stage.
europmc-pmc8069344:
Thi and co-authors review lipid-based nanoparticles, from cancer drugs to the COVID-19 vaccines. The speed of those vaccines rested on decades of delivery research. Lipid particles carried the mRNA safely into cells. Approved products such as Doxil and Onpattro proved the route earlier. More than 50 nanopharmaceuticals have reached the market in total.

The review sorts the carriers into five families. Liposomes, niosomes, and transfersomes come first. Solid lipid nanoparticles and nanostructured lipid carriers follow. For each family, the authors give the traits a given cargo demands. Small drugs, genes, and vaccine antigens each load differently. The survey sticks close to products with approval or in trials. Open problems close the review. The authors frame it as a design guide for the next particle.
europmc-pmc8230044:
Pham and co-authors review heart rate variability measures and teach their analysis. Heart rate variability has spread fast through psychology research. Cheap sensors and clear clinical links drove that growth.

Yet the steps from heartbeat signal to index are easy to get wrong. Users without a maths background can misread the measures. The authors sort the main indices and what each one means. Their tutorial walks through a sound analysis path. Standard steps should lift reproducibility across studies. The piece serves newcomers and seasoned users alike. The tutorial uses plain steps that new labs can copy at once.
europmc-pmc8293344:
Esteves, Rueff, and Kranendonk give a brief review of cytochrome P450 enzymes in foreign compound handling. These membrane proteins form a large superfamily in humans. They process many drugs, toxins, and body compounds.

The enzymes run phase I metabolism, the first step in clearing xenobiotics. Their chemistry rests on a heme group that activates oxygen. The review covers eight main topics across the field. Early sections trace absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. Later ones weigh genetics, regulation, and toxicology. The piece offers a compact entry into a vast enzyme family.
europmc-pmc8308544:
Braun and co-authors set up a method to detect microplastics in placenta and first stool. Plastic pollution exposes everyone through food and air. Health effects in humans stay under debate.

Animal work shows particles crossing cell barriers with harm. First reports hint that exposure may start before birth. Readouts risk contamination, so method rigour is key. The pilot screened tissue from two caesarean births. It hunted particles larger than 50 micrometres after chemical digestion. Fourier methods confirmed the material. The protocol readies larger clinical studies of early exposure. Contamination control sits at the heart of the protocol.
europmc-pmc8437544:
Li and co-authors study butyrate, a gut microbe product, and its grip on neutrophils in bowel disease. Talk between host and microbes keeps the gut in balance. How metabolites steer neutrophils in inflammatory bowel disease was still unclear.

The team took neutrophils from patients and healthy donors and tested their signals. Butyrate sharply cut the cells' output of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines. It also curbed their movement and their release of web-like traps. A drug that mimics one of butyrate's actions copied the effect. In mice with colitis, butyrate eased gut lining inflammation. The work marks butyrate as a brake on harmful neutrophil action.
europmc-pmc8543044:
Palombo and co-authors introduce SANDI, a model for imaging cell bodies and neurites by diffusion MRI. Older models treat brain water signal as flow in thin fibers plus a hindered pool. That view works at low settings but fails in gray matter at high ones. The missing cell body part may be the cause.

SANDI adds the soma, the body of any brain cell, as its own compartment. Simulations show how soma size and density shape the signal. Tests against real scan data mark where the model holds. The method aims at non-invasive maps of soma and neurite density. Such maps could sharpen brain microstructure research.
europmc-pmc8656144:
Zhang and co-authors announce a new extracellular nanoparticle they name the supermere. Cells release many tiny particles that carry proteins and RNA. Supermeres differ in shape from known particles called exomeres. They are also taken up by tissues far more in the body.

Their cargo differs from that of other particles. Supermeres are rich in proteins linked to cancer, Alzheimer disease, and heart disease. Most extracellular RNA travels with supermeres, not with other particles. Cancer supermeres changed cell behavior in tests. They raised lactate output and passed drug resistance to other cells. The authors see supermeres as a source of disease markers and drug targets.
europmc-pmc8664944:
Leger and co-authors present Nanocompore, a method to find chemical changes on RNA with nanopore sequencing. RNA carries many small chemical marks that alter its shape and behavior. Nanopore direct RNA reading can sense these marks. The team built a framework that spots them by comparison.

The method weighs a sample against an unmodified control. It needs no training set and can use repeat samples. Tests found distinct marks at the right positions in lab-made RNA. The team then mapped the m6A mark in yeast and human RNA. Checks with other methods backed the results. The data also showed marks that share single RNA strands.
europmc-pmc8674144:
COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative reports a global study of human genes that shape COVID-19 risk and severity. Genes may help explain why illness hits some people harder. The network pooled genome-wide studies from 46 studies in 19 countries. Up to 49,562 patients with COVID-19 took part.

The work found 13 gene regions tied to infection or severe disease. Some regions match known links to lung and immune disease. Gene-based tests backed a causal role for smoking and body mass in severe illness. They did not back such a role for type 2 diabetes. The authors say these regions point to body pathways that drugs could target.
europmc-pmc8688144:
Xu and co-authors show that a grape seed compound, procyanidin C1, acts on aged cells and extends life in mice. Aged cells build up with age and release harmful factors. The team screened natural products for effects on these cells. Grape seed extract and this compound stood out.

At low doses, the compound curbed the harmful secretions. At higher doses, it killed aged cells by raising oxidative stress. In mice, it cleared aged cells after tumor treatment and boosted chemotherapy. Given at intervals, it eased physical decline in old mice. Survival also rose. The authors see it as a lead for age-related care.
europmc-pmc8709944:
Marei and co-authors review p53 signaling in cancer growth and therapy. The p53 protein guards the genome by halting the cell cycle when DNA is damaged. Its gene is mutated in about half of all human cancers. When p53 fails, damaged DNA gets copied and tumors can grow unchecked.

Mutant p53 does more than lose its guard role. Many mutant forms gain new cancer-driving traits. They help cancer cells grow, spread, and escape death. The review traces the pathways behind these acts. It then covers treatment ideas that aim to restore p53's tumor-blocking work. The protein's reach makes it a prime therapy target.
europmc-pmc8743544:
Schwengers and co-authors introduce Bakta, a command-line tool for fast, standard annotation of bacterial genomes. Genome counts keep rising, and local tools beat central services for many teams. Older tools lean on taxon-specific databases or close reference genomes. Bakta was built to work across taxa without that crutch.

The tool runs a full annotation workflow in one pass. It detects small proteins and uses genome metadata. An alignment-free step speeds gene labeling and adds database links. Results come in standard formats plus a rich JSON file. Broad tests, on isolates and mixed genomes, showed Bakta beat rival tools on function labels and cross-references.
europmc-pmc8763644:
Lotfollahi and co-authors introduce scArches, a deep learning method that maps new single-cell data onto reference atlases. Big atlases now serve as references for smaller studies. Batch effects and data sharing limits block easy use of them. Their method uses transfer learning to fit new data to a reference without sharing raw data.

Tests spanned mouse brain, pancreas, immune, and whole-organism atlases. The method kept biological signal while it removed batch effects. It used far fewer parameters than building a merge from scratch. It could also fill in missing data types. COVID-19 samples mapped to a healthy reference kept their disease traits. That let the team spot disease-linked cell states.
europmc-pmc8883344:
Kumar, Mills, and Lapierre review p62, a protein that links cell cleanup with stress and aging. Cells must clear damaged proteins to stay healthy. That housekeeping, called proteostasis, fails with age. p62 is a receptor for selective autophagy. It ferries chosen cargo to destruction. It is best known for clearing protein clumps. Newer work ties it to clearing mitochondria and fat droplets too.

The authors show how p62 coordinates two cleanup systems. It bridges autophagy and the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Its effects on aging run both ways. Too little or too much can harm proteostasis. Defective p62 shows up in diseases of aging. Neurodegeneration gets close attention. The authors ask whether tuning p62 could restore balance. They treat it as a promising but tricky target.
europmc-pmc9134144:
Montazersaheb and co-authors overview cytokine storm in COVID-19 and the treatments aimed at it. Severe COVID-19 can drive an uncontrolled release of pro-inflammatory signals. That storm damages the lungs and can lead to acute respiratory distress syndrome. It is a leading cause of death in these patients.

The review focuses on four key signals: interleukin-6, interleukin-1, interleukin-17, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha. Each plays a part in lung harm through damage to the airway lining. The authors weigh drugs that block each signal in turn. No specific cure exists for the sickest patients, they note. Calming the inflammatory response may still raise survival. Readers get a concise guide to a central danger of severe infection.
europmc-pmc9485144:
Wang, Wu, and Sun review targets and biomarkers for tumor immunotherapy, split by response and non-response. Cancer bends the immune system to escape attack. Immunotherapy aims to wake anti-tumor immune cells back up. Checkpoint blockade and adoptive cell transfer lead the field.

Some tumors that resist all else shrink for years on these drugs. Yet the overall response rate still needs work, the authors stress. The review walks through checkpoint targets on T cells. PD-1, CTLA-4, LAG-3, and TIGIT each get a section. Stimulatory molecules and NK cell checkpoints follow. Cellular therapies from TILs to CAR designs are also covered. The authors stress biomarkers that can guide who gets which drug. Learning from past wins and failures should shape future trial design.
europmc-pmc9964744:
Singh and co-authors review polycystic ovary syndrome, its causes, care, and future treatments. The syndrome mixes hormone and metabolic faults. Typical traits include missed ovulation, infertility, obesity, insulin resistance, and polycystic ovaries. Many risk factors may push a person toward the condition.

Listed factors span lifestyle, diet, pollutants, genetics, and gut imbalance. Nerve and hormone changes plus obesity also play roles. These forces can raise insulin, oxidative stress, and androgen levels. Faulty follicle growth and irregular cycles follow. The review weighs gut repair through probiotics, prebiotics, or fecal transplant. MicroRNA therapy appears as another future route. Readers get causes and care options in one survey.
faraday-experimental-researches-vol2-184:
Volume 2 of Faraday's Experimental Researches in Electricity appeared in 1844, holding Series 15 through 19. Michael Faraday's researches had by then moved from the first shock of induction toward the deep laws of electric action in matter. The papers here continue his electrochemical work.

Faraday tested how currents pass through gases and liquids and how electricity relates to chemical change. He also probed the nature of induction through different materials, work that fed his growing picture of lines of force. That picture later became the field concept in the hands of Maxwell. Volume 2 shows the middle stage of the research program that Volume 1 began and Volume 3 completed.
frus-1861-d144:
On 17 August 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote a further letter to William Dayton. It is document 144 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The second Paris letter of that day takes up its own point in the file. Seward's desk rhythm, seen across the volume, was to clear each topic in turn. The pair gives readers a full day of the French agenda in miniature. A full day of French business in miniature still reads as a tidy piece of craft. Tidy craft in a crisis is rarer than bold words, and worth far more.
frus-1861-d244:
Writing from Washington on 8 July 1861, William H. Seward addressed James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. The printed record keeps it as Document 244 in the President's message volume for 1861. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d44:
George Dallas wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 May 1861. The dispatch is document 44 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

May was the month of change in London, as Dallas wound down and Adams arrived. Dallas kept reporting until the end of his term. His letters from those weeks give readers the view of a departing envoy, watching a crisis grow past his watch. The handover between Dallas and Adams was smooth, a credit to both men's care. Smooth handovers abroad spared Washington one whole class of needless worry.
frus-1862-d144:
15 September 1862 brought Charles Francis Adams a fresh letter from Secretary Seward in Washington. The printed record keeps it as Document 144 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d244:
Document 244 opens the French file of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume: a report dated 6 December 1861 from William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

France under Napoleon III watched the American war with close, self-interested eyes, and Dayton's post was second in weight only to London. His reports tracked French talk of backing the South or pressing a truce. This early letter came as the Trent crisis with Britain still filled the news, and Paris waited to see how it ended. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d344:
Two Seward dispatches to Paris are dated 10 November 1862, and the first is Document 344 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France.

By 10 November, word was spreading that Britain would not join France in acting on the war. Seward's letters that day wrote from a position slowly strengthening. The Paris brief now turned toward what France might do alone, in Mexico or toward the South. This dispatch opens the file's late-autumn phase, after the crisis peak. Southern agents were active in Paris too, seeking loans, ships, and friends at court.
frus-1862-d44:
Writing from Washington on 4 April 1862, William H. Seward addressed Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The printed record keeps it as Document 44 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. By then, in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d444:
Hermann Kreismann, the American consul in Berlin, received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 6 September 1862. It is Document 444 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Consuls handled the practical edge of foreign policy: shipping, seamen, trade papers, and the protection of citizens abroad. Kreismann, a German-born Chicago editor, served the Union in the Prussian capital alongside Minister Judd. An instruction addressed to a consul rather than a minister points to business of that practical kind. Letters like this widen the picture of wartime diplomacy beyond courts and cabinets, down to the offices where Americans abroad actually got help.
frus-1862-d544:
On 4 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Roest van Limburg. It is Document 544 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

Seward wrote as Lee's army crossed into Maryland and the government braced for the autumn crisis. His note to the Dutch minister kept the Washington end of the Netherlands file in order at a moment when larger matters pressed. The correspondence's subjects remained the standing ones of neutral trade and maritime right. There is a kind of reassurance in the file's regularity. Through the worst weeks of 1862, the letters between Seward and Van Limburg went back and forth like clockwork. The relationship they served never cracked.
frus-1862-d644:
On 27 November 1861 Townsend Harris wrote his last letter in this run of the Japanese file, addressed to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 644 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Four days after his previous dispatch, Harris wrote again from Edo, in the closing weeks of his mission. He would leave Japan the following spring. His health was broken by the post he had created. His final letters report the treaty system standing and the legation's affairs in order for his successor. The volume's Japanese strand thus ends where it began, with the first minister's own hand. It is a quiet, fitting close to the farthest-flung correspondence in the record of 1862.
frus-1863p1-d144:
Charles Francis Adams closed a three-letter day with this dispatch of 3 April 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 144 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The last sheet of the day wound up a set sent at the height of the ship question. Adams's April mail is among the most tense in the volume, as Britain weighed whether to let Southern warships sail. This letter ends the 3 April three. It is a working piece of the watch that, in the end, helped keep the British fleet out of the South's hands.
frus-1863p1-d244:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 23 July 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 244 of the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Adams was told to deal chiefly with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary. Seward's letters armed him with facts and wording for those meetings. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d344:
On 29 December 1862, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It appears as document 344 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

British ships stopped by the Union blockade, and British subjects held as prisoners, supplied much of London's complaint list. Lyons delivered those protests in formal notes like this one. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d44:
On 13 December 1862, Judah P. Benjamin wrote to Edwin De Leon. Benjamin ran the Confederate state office in Richmond; De Leon was a Southern agent working in Europe. The letter is document 44 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

De Leon served the South as a roving hand in Europe, where the work mixed talks, print, and quiet deals. Benjamin's letters to such men carried orders and cash-side news from home. This one came in mid-December, as the year of the South's best hopes closed. It is part of the group of Confederate papers printed in the Union's record, a rare chance to read the foe's mail.
frus-1863p1-d444:
A dispatch dated 4 April 1863 went from Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d544:
From Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward: a letter dated 30 May 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d644:
The 23 October 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d144: Secretary of War Henry Stimson wrote to General Marshall, the Army Chief of Staff, on November 20, 1943. The letter is Document 144 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Stimson-to-Marshall letters carried the War Department's mind on the great choices of the war, and this one was written two days before Cairo opened. The record gives the two men and the date. Its subject is in the printed text.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d244:
The President's Log, the official booklet recording Roosevelt's trip to Africa and the Middle East in November and December 1943, is introduced by an editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume. The note exists to explain what the log is before its text is printed in the pages that follow.

The booklet runs to sixty-six numbered pages, with front and back matter and some fifty pages of pictures and appendices. Lieutenant William Rigdon prepared it, and Rear Admiral Wilson Brown approved it. Inside are the President's party list, an itinerary, sea and air travel charts, a foreword, and the log itself. Eleven appendices follow, from a citation for General Eisenhower to the Cairo and Tehran communiqués.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d344:
Alexander Kirk, the American minister in Egypt, wrote a short secret memorandum at Cairo on 26 November 1943 about his custody of the Cairo communiqué. It records a small errand at the center of the conference's secrecy.

That afternoon Harry Hopkins handed Kirk a copy of the communiqué on the Anglo-American-Chinese talks and asked him to hold it until instructions came from Tehran about its release. The timing was undecided, but Kirk would get twenty-four hours' notice so the three countries could publish at the same moment. Kirk was also to notify the Chinese legation when the word came. His own task, as he summed it up, was simply to see that American correspondents in Cairo received the text through the Office of War Information.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d44: Roosevelt also wrote to Churchill on October 14, 1943, making at least three summit letters in a single day. This one is Document 44 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The date fell in the final week of preparation for the Moscow Conference of foreign ministers. The record gives the parties and the date and leaves the contents to the text. It rests in the Foreign Relations volume with its companions of that busy day.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d444:
Marked with a footnote in the printed volume, this second set of Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes from December 5, 1943 covers another session of the joint American-British command at Cairo. The Second Cairo Conference was then deciding the next phase of the war against Germany and Japan. The State Department later published the record in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Session minutes preserve the order of business, the officers' exchanges, and the conclusions reached before the chiefs reported upward to Roosevelt and Churchill. Having two records from one day shows how much was pressed into these meetings. For a reader tracing how Allied plans took final shape, that density is the point.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d544:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on January 11, 1944, keeping up the steady channel between the department and the White House. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume, among the follow-up papers of the new year.

Hull's January traffic with Roosevelt mixed the conferences' unfinished business with the planning of the postwar order, a subject Hull cared about deeply. The Secretary had built his reputation on patient, formal diplomacy, the opposite of summit improvisation. For readers, the message shows the permanent government digesting the leaders' December decisions and fitting them into policy that could last.
frus-1944-quebec-d144:
Roosevelt replied to Churchill's Italian report the next day, August 30, 1944, in telegram 611. He was glad to hear how General Wilson had concentrated his forces and renewed the offensive. His own chiefs believed a vigorous attack, pressed with everything available, should force the enemy into the Po Valley.

The president stressed destroying German forces while they were within grasp, lest divisions escape to other fronts. He was confident Eisenhower would be satisfied that the Mediterranean effort was mauling troops that might otherwise face him. On the future use of Wilson's armies, Roosevelt suspended decision until the campaign's results were known. Trieste and Istria, he said, they would renew at Octagon, the Quebec meeting.
frus-1944-quebec-d244:
Hull asked Roosevelt for instructions on the French lend-lease agreement on September 11, 1944. The sticking point was Jean Monnet's request for industrial items to restart French production for the civil population. Under the July 15 memorandum Roosevelt had approved, such long-life industrial goods could go on credit only if necessary to the war in Europe or to forces just after an armistice.

Applied now, Hull wrote, that rule flatly rejected Monnet's program of over a billion dollars in industrial items. He recommended neither rejection nor approval. Instead, a list mechanism would leave the president complete discretion, item by item, as French behavior warranted. The Foreign Economic Administration would submit proposed French programs to Roosevelt before they joined the list.
frus-1944-quebec-d44:
September 1, 1944 opened with a Churchill message to Roosevelt. It was the first day of the conference month. The State Department placed the letter in the Quebec 1944 volume.

September opened with Allied armies at the German frontier. The Quebec meeting stood eleven days away. Churchill's letters ran ahead of him across the Atlantic. They stated what Britain needed from the conference. For readers, the message marks a final approach. The Prime Minister was at sea or about to sail. The agenda for the meeting was effectively set. Only the arguments in person remained.
frus-1945-50-intel-d144:
Formal minutes cover the Second Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board, held on 26 March 1946. It survives in print as document 144 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. Washington was still building a peace-time spy service, run for the moment by the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group.

As minutes, the text sticks to the business of the meeting: items raised, views stated in brief, and the choices the group reached. The brevity is the point: what the group did not settle, the minutes do not claim it did. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d244:
A memorandum from Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter reached the State–Army–Navy–Air Force Coordinating Committee on 22 October 1947. The State Department prints it as document 244 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The National Security Act had just taken effect. The CIA had replaced the old group, and the Council had just begun to meet.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d344:
A memorandum dated 12 April 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Executive Secretary of the Intelligence Survey Group (Blum). The reader was Allen W. Dulles, Mathias F. Correa, and William H. Jackson. It survives in print as document 344 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. Across Washington, the new security bodies were moving from setup work to the real business of the Cold War.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d44: A White House memorandum dated 7 November 1945 sits among the department papers of the intelligence volume. Papers from the president's house carry special weight in such a run. Since every department knew the final choice on a central intelligence system would be made there. The title gives no author, so the paper stands on its origin and date. Written while the Budget Bureau's plan was gaining ground in the autumn contest of 1945.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d144:
Premier Mikolajczyk appealed straight to the President, and Ambassador Ciechanowski delivered the plea in Washington. The Polish ambassador's covering note, sent on 27 October 1944, passes on Mikolajczyk's telegram of the day before. Both texts are printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Mikolajczyk protests the pressure on his government to accept the Curzon Line at once, without any reservations. All his work, he writes, has aimed at Polish-Soviet understanding, for Poland's sake and for the common cause. Yet his nation would feel terribly deceived, he warns, if this were the answer to its sacrifices and its unbroken part in the war. He asks the President for a reply and decisions at the earliest possible moment.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d244:
One China policy for three allies is the aim of this briefing book paper of 13 January 1945. “Unity of Anglo-American-Soviet Policy Toward China” is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It names the discords that could wreck the aim before they grow.

Some British elements, the paper warns, seem for imperial reasons to want a weak and possibly divided China after the war. A second fear runs the other way. Russia may use the Chinese Communists to carve out a separate area in the north or in Manchuria. The recommendation follows plainly. The United States should take the lead in helping China build a strong, stable, and unified government. Such a China could be the chief steadying force in the Far East. British and Russian help should be sought to that end.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d344:
Bremen and Bremerhaven would stay under full American control, under an agreement the Combined Chiefs of Staff approved at Yalta in February 1945. The enclave, drawn on an attached map, covered the ports and their ground. American military government would run it, including disarmament and the breaking up of German war power there.

At the same time, the American commander was to follow the broad policies used in the British zone around it. He kept the right to depart from them on military grounds when he judged it needful. Transit rights each way — American stores southward, British movement toward Austria — complete the bargain.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d44: Roosevelt answered Churchill on 6 January 1945, the same day the prime minister's latest message arrived. His reply is document 44 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering Malta and Yalta. Same-day exchanges show the machinery at full stretch, with the president's staff turning cables around quickly because the Mediterranean journey was now only weeks away.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d444:
A whole frontier might fall to Britain alone, and London disliked the prospect in this statement of February 10, 1945. If British proposals for occupation zones in Austria were approved, the entire Austro-Yugoslav frontier would be a British responsibility. Yugoslavia had not asked to alter the Styrian stretch. But it had advanced claims to Klagenfurt and parts of Carinthia, lost in the plebiscite of 1919.

Action might be needed to resist Yugoslav efforts to press those claims. Yugoslav partisans might also advance into Carinthia during operations and hold ground there. For Britain to stand alone in such a quarrel, the paper argues, would be invidious. The warning proved exact within months.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d144:
British Minister John Balfour delivered London's draft agenda for the summit in a letter dated May 29, 1945. The letter is document 144 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Churchill had told Truman that his government was drawing up, at the President's wish, a list of subjects for the next meeting of heads of government.

Foreign Secretary Eden now asks Balfour to forward the enclosed list to Acting Secretary Grew, so the President can be informed. The list itself is printed with the next document. Balfour's short covering letter marks the moment the conference stopped being only about dates and houses. The British put their proposed business in writing. And the long argument over Poland, Germany, and the Balkans took paper form.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d244:
Ambassador Winant reported the Foreign Office's protest in full in a second telegram dated July 15, 1945. The message is document 244 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, and it tells the same story as the extract printed earlier in the volume.

An official named Harvey was considerably disturbed, Winant writes. And the British Embassy in Washington was told to ask for a postponement. The postponement would last until Italy's future status could be discussed at the Big Three meeting. London held that Italy's admission was tied to the peace treaty, and its Berlin delegation was fully briefed to discuss it there. With Churchill and Eden both away, the Foreign Office could not decide in the time given. The question would go to Eden, to raise with Byrnes, while London strongly urged delay.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d344:
Elmer Davis, who ran the Office of War Information, wrote to President Truman on July 4, 1945, with an idea to hold in mind at Berlin. His suggestion concerned action after the conference, not during it. The central problem of Germany, Davis argued, was the reeducation of the German people.

Without that change, he warned, every other measure would be a brief patch at best. The aim was a Germany no longer dangerous to its neighbors. Davis noted that the news service his office ran with the Army, through papers, radio, and newsreels, was already the real start of that teaching, whether planned or not.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d44:
Prime Minister Churchill sent President Truman a personal and top secret telegram from London on May 31, 1945. It is document 44 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference, sent as the Allied leaders arranged their first meeting since Germany's surrender. Churchill's own plans, he says, depend on the date Truman picks.

Churchill also raises a point of pride and fairness. He reports good talks with Truman's envoy Joseph Davies, but warns he will not attend a meeting that simply continues a private conference between Truman and Stalin. The three leaders, he insists, should meet at the same time and on equal terms. He closes by saying he looks forward to meeting Truman in person for the first time.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d444:
American supervision of Greek elections is put to President Truman in a memorandum from the Secretary of State dated July 4, 1945. The question, it opens, raises an issue of the first importance. America has repeatedly affirmed President Roosevelt's purpose. He stated it in his State of the Union message of January 6, 1945. Peoples, Roosevelt said, have the right to choose the form of government under which they will live.

The memorandum adds a further obligation. The right of liberated peoples to choose their government must not be defeated by interim authorities holding power in the meantime. At the end of the paper stands the President's own manuscript endorsement: I agree, Harry S Truman. The decision was thus taken at the top.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d544:
Secretary of State James Byrnes answered Secretary of War Stimson in a brief wire sent July 12, 1945. Byrnes was aboard the cruiser Augusta, sailing with President Truman to the Potsdam Conference. His reply is document 544 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the conference.

Byrnes says he has Stimson's wire and has talked it over with the President. The lend-lease question, he adds, is a complex one. He suggests the two men talk it over in person at Terminal, the code name for Potsdam. Editors note that a second reply went out the same day, and no one can now tell which was sent first.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d644:
Ambassador Winant passed on British Foreign Office views on the Levant from London on July 9, 1945. His secret wire is document 644 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The remarks came from a Foreign Office official that day.

The official said France's offer to hand over the Troupes Speciales had come too late to help France. Made earlier, it might have bought a return favor. Syrians instead see it as only partial payment for the damage done to Damascus. The 45 days set to work out the transfer were called useful, since delay could cool tempers. As French elections neared, de Gaulle might grow more willing to compromise. On troop withdrawal, the official doubted any early move and preferred that a conference be put off.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1044:
British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden wrote to Secretary Byrnes from Berlin on July 23, 1945, about the coal directive for zone commanders in Germany. Both foreign offices had debated changes to the draft. Eden reports that London now agrees with the revised text handed over in Washington on July 11. A matching directive will go out at once to the British zone commander as an interim order.

Eden asks how Truman means to raise the directive with Stalin, at a plenary session or in private. He stresses that coal is among the most dangerous world shortages. Winning Russian support for the European Coal Organisation matters, he argues, since Polish support would likely follow.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1144:
Staff of the British team at Potsdam drafted this memorandum on 18 July 1945, early in the talks. Each side used such papers to set out its case in full. A memorandum could be handed across, read aloud, or kept as the team's own record of its stand.

British papers of this kind put London's argument in London's words. The other teams then knew what to answer, and later readers know what was claimed. This one dates from the first week, when stands were still being staked out. It keeps the British view in its own phrasing, inside the American record of the summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1244:
The United States team tabled this proposal on 24 July 1945. Formal proposals were the bargaining chips of the summit. Each one claimed ground in writing and forced the other teams to answer in kind, amend, or refuse.

A paper from the second week came after the opening stands were known. The trades had begun, and drafts now aimed at terms the others might accept. This proposal is one such move. Kept in the official record, it shows what Washington put on the table at that point, in the exact words its team chose.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1344:
