President Truman wrote to Prime Minister Winston Churchill on 24 July 1945, while both men led their delegations at Potsdam. The two had met in person only days before, at the start of the conference. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Letters between heads of government sit at the top of the diplomatic pile, above cables and staff papers. Even at a summit where the men could talk face to face, some things were still put in writing to make them firm. This exchange belongs to the last week of Churchill's wartime premiership. It ended while the conference was still sitting, giving the letter a place in two stories at once.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-144: Standing in the run of unnumbered pieces after document 710, this short note speaks for the editors of the Potsdam volume. Editorial notes in the Foreign Relations series exist to keep the archive legible. One might cite the file a paper came from. Another might point ahead to a later text. This note does that quiet work for its neighbors.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-44:
Benjamin Cohen's notes on the plenary session of July 20, 1945, catch the debate over liberated Europe in shorthand. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Cohen records the foreign ministers' report being received, then the argument that followed.

A change in the Council of Foreign Ministers text was adopted, providing for a permanent secretariat. Discussion then turned to what the foreign secretaries favored for Bulgaria, Rumania, and Greece. Molotov indicated that present restrictions should be relaxed now that the war had ended. Churchill intervened on elections with a point of language and duty. Supervision of elections, he insisted, does not mean control, and Byrnes offered the softer word observation instead. Byrnes then proposed Italy's admission to the United Nations, paired with a declaration against admitting Spain.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d744:
Document 744 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 25, 1945. It comes from the heart of the conference's second week. Staff drafted it to move a question forward inside the team. The paper was preserved and printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official series.

Mid-conference drafts show ideas under pressure. Writers knew the other sides' lines by now. Readers can watch American drafting adjust to that knowledge. The document's value is its timing: late enough to be informed, early enough to still shape events. Such papers are the negotiation's true workshop floor.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d844:
The Acting Secretary wrote to Melbourne in Rumania on July 28, 1945, in document 844. Washington sent further guidance to its acting representative in Bucharest. The letter dates from the conference's last days. It was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

A second guidance letter in the same run shows a channel in heavy use. Melbourne's reports had built a file that demanded answers. Readers see the home office responding at matching pace. The document pairs with the July 28 letter to the same post in this volume. Together they show Washington steering Bucharest through the summit's closing turns.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d944: William Clayton sent this short memorandum to Edwin Pauley on July 28, 1945. It passes along a paper from the United States Group Control Council staff. That paper raises questions about the return of art objects looted during the war. Clayton says America might accept the first two recommendations in it. He asks Pauley's views on the third, which turns on replacement of art versus simple return. He hopes the two of them can send General Clay a joint memorandum on the subject.
frus-1961-63v10-d44: Adolf Berle, chair of the Latin America task force, wrote to Secretary Rusk as a White House talk on Cuba broke up. Camp leadership was set, and the operation kept standing. He asks for a fresh meeting late in the week. A CIA paper, he notes, warns that scrapping the operation could set off blasts in three or four Central American states. Nicaragua and Guatemala are named. Berle thinks the risk drawn too large, Guatemala aside, but urges that all offices settle one line before the choice is made.
frus-1961-63v11-d44:
President Kennedy's letter to Chairman Khrushchev of October 22, 1962, went with his speech on the Cuba build-up. He states his core fear at the start: that Moscow might misread American will. No sane man, he writes, would plunge the world into a war none could win.

Vienna's pledges are recalled, and Berlin named as the line that must hold. Missile bases in Cuba cross that line. The reply, Kennedy insists, is the minimum needed. He asks Moscow not to widen the crisis. The letter is the crisis's formal opening, calm in form and absolute in content.
frus-1977-80v06-d144:
A letter from President Carter to Soviet General Secretary Brezhnev, dated September 17, 1978, reports the Camp David accords. It is document 144 in Volume VI of the 1977-1980 Foreign Relations series. Carter tells Brezhnev that Sadat and Begin have signed two framework documents after thirteen days of talks. One frames peace in the Middle East as a whole. The other frames a peace treaty between Egypt and Israel. Carter calls the result a historic step.

The letter sets out the terms: a five-year transition in the West Bank and Gaza, self-rule for their people, and phased Israeli withdrawal from Sinai. It notes one open issue, the Israeli settlements in Sinai. The Knesset, Carter writes, will decide on them within two weeks.
gao-gaoreports-b-295444:
GAO ruled in files B-295444 and B-295444.2 on February 18, 2005, in the protest brought by TekStar, Inc. The Air Force had cut the firm's offer from the competitive range in a purchase of base operations support for Eareckson Air Station in Alaska. The buy was a total set-aside under section 8(a). TekStar said its offer had been scored unfairly. GAO denied the protest. The record showed that the scoring was sound and that it tracked the criteria stated in the solicitation.

Exclusion from the range is among the harshest steps in a negotiated purchase. It stands where the written record backs the scores given.
gao-gaoreports-b-295744:
Dated April 21, 2005, GAO files B-295744 and B-295744.2 record Metro Machine Corporation as the protester. The Navy had awarded Norfolk Shipbuilding and Drydock Corporation a contract to repair and modernize amphibious assault ships based at Norfolk, Virginia. Metro attacked the cost realism work and the talks held with it. The ruling backs the agency on each digest point. Its realism method was sound and rested on the offers as filed. This copy is a redacted version cleared for release.

The agency need not chase an audit report's findings where it sought the facts from the offeror itself. Talks on labor rates were full enough to put Metro on notice.
gao-gaoreports-b-296244:
Southern California Engineering protested an Interior Department award to swap pumps at Hoover Dam in GAO decision B-296244, dated July 11, 2005. The winner was Moltz Constructors. The buyer was the Bureau of Reclamation. The firm's bid was ruled not fit on tech grounds. It said that call was unfair.

GAO denied the protest. The bid lacked clear detail on how the work would be done. It also lacked detail on the new pumps to be set in place. That thin plan left the agency unsure the job could be done well. A bid must show its plan, not just name the task. Thin detail can sink a bid.
gao-gaoreports-b-298444:
Bausch & Lomb, Inc. protested sole-source orders by the Department of Veterans Affairs. The orders went to Alcon Laboratories, Inc. for eye surgery equipment. The gear serves cataract care at VA centers in Albany and Syracuse, New York. GAO decided B-298444 on September 21, 2006.

VA claimed an urgent need made Alcon the only fit source. GAO found that claim flawed. Other firms had shown interest in the buy. Yet the agency never weighed what their equipment could do. Urgency alone does not excuse a skipped market check. The sole-source path was improper here. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299044:
Global Communications Solutions, Inc. protested a Navy delivery order to Globecomm Systems, Inc. The Naval Air Systems Command ran the buy. The order covered satellite communications systems with a set operating mode. GAO decided B-299044 and B-299044.2 on January 29, 2007.

The flaw lay in the buying method. The agency used small purchase steps for a commercial item. Rules cap that path at purchases of $5 million or less. The expected value here topped $5 million. The agency thus had no power to use that path. A buy run past a clear cap cannot stand. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299144:
B&S Transport, Inc. protested its removal from a Defense Logistics Agency competition. The buy sought one firm to run a tire privatization effort. That work spans tire supply for vehicles worldwide. GAO ruled in B-299144 on January 22, 2007.

The agency scored the firm's proposal as unfit. It also found the bid could not be made fit without major rewrites. GAO read the record behind those calls. The flaws marked were deep, not minor gaps. A bid in that state can be cut from the range. The firm is a small business, but size does not cure deep flaws. The removal was fair. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299344:
J. Womack Enterprises, Inc. protested Air Force awards for mechanical and electrical construction work. The projects sit at Robins Air Force Base in Georgia. The contracts went to RCA Contracting, Inc. and MAPCO, Inc. The buy was a HUBZone set-aside. GAO decided B-299344 on April 4, 2007.

The firm said bad past work facts were used in a flawed way. GAO found the agency's view of its past work fair. That view rested on a sound sense of weak prior jobs. Claims of bias by race and gender lacked proof. The score was a past-record call, not a fitness bar. It needed no referral path. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299744:
Computer Literacy World protested a General Services Administration task order to Electronic Data Systems. The order covered a contractor-run fix for federal identification card needs. The plan had to span the full card process end to end. GAO ruled in B-299744 and B-299744.4 on August 6, 2007.

The case turned on one list. The firm read the terms to need each item on the Approved Products List at bid time. The agency had told firms a distinct date in a Q&A round. Items had to be listed by Milestone 1, in performance. GAO found the firm's read strained. The agency's own answer set the true date. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-308044:
Home internet costs for telework staff may be paid back in this GAO decision, B-308044, dated January 10, 2007. The Patent and Trademark Office runs a telework plan. Staff do office work from home. Fast internet at home helps them do that work. The office asked if it could pay staff back for the home service.

GAO held that it may. The cost ties to the telework plan and to office work done at home. GAO urged care in return. The office should check the payments from time to time. Checks should show the service serves work ends. They should also guard against private misuse of the paid service.
gao-gaoreports-b-308944:
Stale funds parked at a sister agency are condemned in this GAO decision, B-308944, dated July 17, 2007. GovWorks, an Interior fund shop, bought goods for the Defense Department. Defense sent buy orders to fund four deals. Most orders failed to name the goods or work sought. GovWorks still spent past-year funds on three of the deals in fiscal year 2005.

GAO held most of the orders never bound Defense funds at all. One order for laser printers did bind them. But GovWorks acted 17 months later, past the funds' life. That buy met no need of the funds' year. Defense must charge fiscal year 2005 funds and report any shortfall. GovWorks must add checks to stop vague orders.
gao-gaoreports-b-311244:
IBV, Ltd. lost its protest in GAO decision B-311244, dated February 21, 2008. The Air Force sought trash haul work at Andrews Air Force Base. The call ran as a set-aside for small firms at large. IBV is a firm owned by a hurt veteran. It said the call should have been set for its class. It said it should have won a sole-source deal in the class path.

GAO denied the protest. The deal chief found the class path would not draw a fair price. Bids that came in bore that find out. Each class bid ran well past the cost gauge. Price facts can back a wider set-aside class.
gao-gaoreports-b-311344:
The Boeing Company won its protest. GAO ruled in B-311344 on June 18, 2008. The Air Force sought a new fleet of air tankers in the KC-X race. The award went to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation. Boeing bid its KC-767 tanker for the work. It fought the scores, the talks, and the pick. The fight is one of the largest in GAO's protest files.

GAO sustained the protest on a string of grounds. The pick did not weigh bids by the call's own rank of points. It gave the winner marks for past a cap the call said would earn none. Talks with Boeing were skewed and led it wrong. The file did not back a key claim on the winner's jet.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-244:
Financial Audit, GAO-05-244 of May 26, 2005, holds GAO's own audit of the Securities and Exchange Commission's books. The commission, set up in 1934, guards the honesty of U.S. stock markets. A 2002 law tells it to file audited books with Congress and the budget office each year. GAO took the first audit on, under its own audit power.

GAO tests three things for fiscal year 2004. It tests if the books are sound in all big respects. It tests if the checks on money reports and law hold firm. It tests if the commission kept the laws that bind it. The full audit trail fills the text.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-344:
District of Columbia's Drinking Water, GAO-05-344 of March 31, 2005, follows a lead scare in the capital's taps. News tales of high lead in the water shook trust in those who guard it. A federal rule tells water works to curb lead at the tap. The Army Corps' Washington Aqueduct treats the water. The city water arm sends it to homes. A regional arm of the Environmental Protection Agency watches both.

Teamwork has grown firm, the title grants. GAO asks what each arm does to cut lead. It asks how well they find and shield those at most risk. It checks how peer works teach the public.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-544:
Help for troops leaving service, above all reservists, is assessed in GAO report GAO-05-544, released on May 20, 2005. The Transition Assistance Program is run jointly by the Defense, Labor, and Veterans Affairs departments. It serves those with at least 180 days of active duty who separate or retire. Reservists and Guard members have been called up in the largest numbers since the Korean War.

The program's four parts are meant to ease the move to civilian life. Take-up is highest for required counseling before separation. Reservists, though, demobilize within days of coming home. They may get counseling in a group with no personal attention. Their benefits briefing can last 45 minutes instead of half a day. Job preparation may be skipped entirely. Use of the disability part is unknown, since it is not tracked. Agencies have updated materials and taken workshops overseas. GAO said reservists still get a thinner service.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-644:
Data quality at the farm statistics service is checked in GAO-05-644, a report dated September 23, 2005. The Information Quality Act told agencies to guard the accuracy of what they publish. The service met the budget office's process rules: it wrote guidance and set up a way to seek corrections. During the review it also sharpened how it logs public input on the farm census.

Gaps sit in the fine print. Nine key products of the 2002 Census of Agriculture skipped any talk of data limits, against the service's own openness rules. Correction pleas sent outside the act's channel are handled informally, with no log kept.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-744:
Dated August 8, 2005, GAO-05-744 surveys what the federal government does about corporate social responsibility abroad. Big U.S. firms employ millions of workers in other lands. Their work raises issues of labor, the environment, and human rights. There is sharp debate over the right federal role. GAO mapped agency programs and gathered views on that role.

GAO found no broad federal mandate in this area. Still, it counted over 50 programs at 12 agencies. They fall into four roles: backing, aiding, joining, or requiring such efforts. Many are small and serve wider agency aims. Most people GAO spoke with who work in the field wanted the government to back firms' own voluntary steps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-144:
Buying reform at the Department of Veterans Affairs stalls in GAO-06-144, a report dated October 19, 2005. VA spent $7.3 billion on goods and services in 2004. A review by the Naval Supply Systems Command made 24 recommendations to fix VA's buying work. VA accepted all of them. GAO picked 7 as key and tracked the agency's progress a year later.

Progress was thin. VA had finished none of the seven key steps. Three had seen no action at all: a long-term improvement plan, sound management metrics, and a strategic plan supplement. Four others, such as a contract review board, had seen only partial work. Key leadership posts sat empty for 15 and 25 months. VA also set no deadlines or progress measures. GAO urged set time frames and a way to track results. VA agreed with the findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-544:
Doctors and nurses who treat veterans must be screened before they start. Issued May 25, 2006, report GAO-06-544 reviews practitioner screening at the Department of Veterans Affairs. In March 2004, GAO found gaps in the department's screening rules. The department agreed with four GAO recommendations to improve screening. This study follows up on that work. It sampled about 60 practitioner files at each of seven facilities.

GAO judged how far the department has put the advice in place. It tested whether facilities follow screening requirements. Steps have been taken to improve screening, GAO found. Facility compliance with the rules is poor, it added. Readers see policy gains beside field failures.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-644:
Guarding United States farms from foreign pests and disease is the topic of GAO-06-644, a GAO report dated May 19, 2006. Agriculture generates over $1 trillion in yearly economic activity. A foreign pest or disease, brought in by accident or on purpose, could do vast harm. Inspectors check passengers and cargo at ports of entry under the Agricultural Quarantine Inspection program. That duty had moved from one agency to the border protection agency.

GAO found that the two agencies had taken steps to strengthen inspections and train officers. Still, management and coordination problems left gaps between them. Those gaps, GAO said, raised the risk that harmful pests or disease would slip through. The report shows how a handoff between agencies can weaken a front-line defense.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-944:
Plans to keep foster children safe when disaster strikes are surveyed in GAO report GAO-06-944, dated July 28, 2006. There were 48 federally declared disasters in 2005. Hurricanes Katrina and Rita scattered thousands of Louisiana foster children to 19 states, and broke up care for a long stretch.

GAO counted states with statewide child welfare disaster plans, and listed what those plans hold. It checked if states hit by 2005 disasters had plans in place. It also set out how the Department of Health and Human Services aids state planning. Federal action, the title states, is needed so every state has such a plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-144:
The Army keeps tanks and supplies parked overseas and on ships, ready for war. In GAO-07-144, dated February 15, 2007, GAO judged the Army's report on that prepositioning program. Congress had ordered the Army to assess the program in a 2006 law. GAO checked whether the report covered the required ground. It also named the big problems the program still faces. GAO visited sites in South Carolina, Europe, South Korea, and Kuwait.

The Army's April 2006 report met the law's terms, GAO found. It said over $4 billion was needed for new gear and spare parts. But the report was outdated when GAO reviewed it. The Army had dropped its 2012 strategy as no longer viable. It was writing a new one with less gear afloat. GAO flagged weak upkeep of gear held by contractors in Kuwait. Over one-quarter of that gear failed quality checks in a one-year span.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-344:
In 2005, 37 million people lived below the poverty line, roughly 13 percent of all Americans. GAO reviewed what that costs the nation in GAO-07-344, issued January 24, 2007. GAO read the economic research on poverty's effects. It looked for links to health, crime, and jobholding. It also looked for links to economic growth. Outside experts checked the draft report.

The research links poverty with adverse outcomes, GAO found. Poor health, criminal activity, and weak work attachment all rise with poverty. Several channels drive the health gap. They include less access to care and more exposure to hazards. Studies also suggest a drag on growth. Areas with higher poverty rates show slower income growth per person. Poverty thus costs more than the aid programs themselves. Lost output and lost earnings compound the toll.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-44:
People without cars were left behind when New Orleans emptied, and GAO-07-44, dated December 22, 2006, asks how to stop a repeat. More than 1,300 people died in Hurricane Katrina. Many who died had no vehicle and no way out. State and local governments hold the main duty for disaster plans. GAO asked how well they fold carless residents into those plans.

GAO read plans and studies and spoke with officials in five big cities and four states. It found that most places were not well prepared. Federal help had gaps, and no rule required practice drills for this group. Roles among levels of government were fuzzy. GAO urged clear duties and real rehearsal. The stakes are plain: the next storm will test the same weak spots.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-444:
Looted Iraqi ammo depots fed the bomb campaign against U.S. troops, and GAO-07-444, dated March 22, 2007, traces that failure. After the March 2003 invasion, U.S. forces could not guard Iraq's many munitions storage sites. Looters emptied them on a wide scale. Bombs built from the stolen shells caused about half of all U.S. combat deaths and wounds in Iraq.

GAO read war plans, doctrine, and spy reports and spoke with senior officials. It found a gap between plan assumptions and ground truth. Too few troops stood guard, and no theater-wide risk survey was done. For future wars, GAO said, site security must enter planning early. The report presses the Pentagon to carry the lesson into its next operations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-844:
Computer systems at the Department of Veterans Affairs are covered in GAO-07-844, dated June 15, 2007. The department spends nearly $1 billion a year on information technology. Its projects have long faced management troubles. In October 2005, it began centralizing IT control under its chief information officer. The shift moves about 6,000 staff and should end by July 2008. GAO checked the plan against six success factors. It also checked how the chief will answer for the full IT budget.

The plan covers parts of most success factors, GAO found. A governance plan won approval, but its boards are not yet set up. Duties for staff in the new structure are named. A skills inventory to place staff well is missing, though. No team owns the change effort day to day. Performance metrics to track progress lag as well. GAO urged a dedicated team, faster metrics, and a firm schedule. The department generally agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1044:
Exports of harmful electronic waste are targeted in GAO report GAO-08-1044, issued August 28, 2008. More U.S. consumers now recycle old electronics. Some firms instead ship the items to developing countries. There, unsafe recycling can harm health and the environment. Tubes from old screens are a special risk, since each can hold 4 pounds of lead.

Since January 2007, the Environmental Protection Agency has required notice before such tubes are exported. GAO tracked where exported devices end up. It also tested the strength of federal controls. GAO staff even posed as foreign buyers of broken tubes. The report urges stronger enforcement and wider regulation.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-344:
Freedom of Information Act backlogs are tracked in GAO report GAO-08-344, issued March 14, 2008. Agencies must answer most FOIA requests within 20 or, in some cases, 30 working days. Executive Order 13392 pushed agencies to cut overdue requests, and GAO studied data from 21 agencies.

Requests received and processed kept rising from fiscal years 2002 to 2006, though the pace flattened. Pending requests grew too, driven mainly by the Department of Homeland Security, above all its Citizenship and Immigration Services arm. Of 16 agencies reporting fresh figures, 9 cut their backlogs and 5 grew theirs. DHS cut its overdue backlog by 29,972 requests, about 29 percent. GAO recommended that the Department of Justice give agencies clearer guidance on tracking and reporting overdue cases.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-44:
Report GAO-08-44 from GAO, dated February 8, 2008, deals with highway public-private partnerships. States are turning to private partners to build and run highways as demand strains public budgets. GAO studied deals in the United States and the experience of Australia, Canada, and Spain.

Partnerships can deliver new roads without public funds up front and can share risk with firms. But there is no free money. Tolls on a private road are likely to rise faster than on a public one. Deals can also cost more than standard procurement while cutting public control. U.S. deals guard the public mainly through contract terms, while other nations use set public-interest tests. GAO suggested Congress order shared criteria for spotting national interests at stake. The Transportation Department disputed several findings.
gi-bill-1944:
Congress passed the Servicemen's Readjustment Act in 1944, as war still raged. The GI Bill thanks returning veterans with concrete, lasting help. College fees, home loans, and business aid stand at its core.

Millions went to school on the bill who could never have paid. Millions more bought homes and filled the growing suburbs fast. The act built the broad American middle class of the postwar years. Critics note that Black veterans often faced blocks at the local level. A grateful nation's check still ranks among its best investments ever made. Its name, the GI Bill, became shorthand for earned opportunity in America.
gregory-great-morals-on-job-vol-1-1844:
Pope Gregory the Great wrote his Morals on the Book of Job, the Moralia in Job, in the late 500s, near the start of his time as pope. Volume one of the Rev. James Bliss English translation came out in 1844 in the Library of the Fathers series. It holds Parts One and Two of Gregory's huge work.

Gregory reads Job line by line and draws three layers from the text: the plain story, a picture of Christ and the church, and a lesson for the reader's own conduct. Job's patience under loss becomes a guide for prayer, humility, and trust. Medieval readers treated the Moralia as a handbook of the inner life.
heine-wintermaerchen-1844:
Heinrich Heine wrote Deutschland: Ein Wintermaerchen, Germany: A Winter's Tale, in Paris in early 1844, and the hosted text is the German original. Heine had lived in exile in France for years. The long poem tells of a trip home in winter, crossing the border and passing through Aachen, Cologne, and Hagen on the way to Hamburg, where his publisher waited.

Each stop sparks satire. Heine mocks Prussian soldiers, censors, church power, national pride, and the dream of a restored empire, and he dreams in one famous passage of a freer, fairer Germany. The poem's mix of jokes, songs, and anger made it a classic of German political verse. Prussian authorities seized copies, and a warrant awaited Heine if he stayed.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
The Earl of Leicester enters John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands in the first part of chapter seven. Leicester, Elizabeth's favourite, lands in Holland to a triumphal entrance. Motley sketches his pedigree with relish: a grandfather executed, a father beheaded after near-regal power. Rapacity, ambition, and the genius to succeed were his inheritance.

Elizabeth, it seems, mounted the throne largely to shower gifts on this favourite. Now he comes as governor over a republic that did not elect him. English troops and Dutch pride must somehow share a war. The chapter sets up the quarrels that dominate the next years of the history. Motley's portrait is unsparing but vivid, an American republican judging a courtier sent to rule freemen. Ceremony, banquets, and suspicion fill the opening scenes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-isaac: Aaron ben Isaac of Rechnitz, in modern Rohoncz, Hungary, is named in this very brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. He was the author of a midrashic commentary on the Bible. The first portion, on Genesis, was published in 1786 at Sulzbach. It appeared under the title Bet Aharon, or House of Aaron. The entry gives no dates for his life and no further works. Its whole evidence is two bibliographies, Benjacob's Ozar ha-Sefarim and Wiener's Bibliotheca Friedlandiana, which it cites by page and number.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aboab-also-writ:
Aboab was an old Spanish family name, spelled in several forms. The family can be traced to the thirteenth century. Its members spread to Holland, Italy, Turkey, Africa, and America, and many were noted scholars.

Long lists follow individual Aboabs across the centuries. Abraham Aboab got a tower at Altea from King Don Jaime in 1263. Isaac Aboab wrote Menorat ha-Maor, a popular book of rabbinic ethics. Isaac da Fonseca Aboab led the Amsterdam community and served in Brazil. Samuel Aboab, a strict and learned rabbi, led Verona and Venice in the seventeenth century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-hay:
Spanish scholar Abraham ben Hayyim ben Remok was born at Barcelona about the middle of the fourteenth century. He wrote a commentary on the Psalms that still rests in manuscript at Oxford. His preface tells part of his own life story.

Persecution that began in late June 1348 forced him out of Barcelona. He moved to Barbastro in Aragon and stayed over thirty years, until 1391. Then persecution struck again: his house was looted and he was jailed. He later took part in the public debate at Tortosa in 1413 and 1414. Jews then were even barred from keeping Torah scrolls and prayer books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-nahmias: Under the heading Abraham Nahmias of Venice, the text gives a sole credit and then points elsewhere. The credit is a rendering of Thomas Aquinas on Aristotle's Metaphysics. For the rest, readers are referred to Nahmias, Abraham, entry one. Venice enters the record only through that heading form, not through any story told here. Nothing is said about when he lived or what else he wrote.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abstinence-644:
Abstinence means giving up joys that are lawful in themselves. The entry says it counts as a good trait only when it serves a higher aim. Jewish teaching starts from the call to be holy in Leviticus xix. 2. That call asks for the whole person to grow, not for the flesh to be crushed. The rabbis taught that the world was made for human life, not for waste.

Talmudic voices warn against vows that deny the self for no cause. The Nazarite, who gave up wine, still had to bring a sin gift. Maimonides faults a monk-like path in food, drink, or marriage. Yet the entry also grants self-denial a place as training. Simon the Just tells of a youth who vowed to cut his hair to fight pride. The close praises the middle way of Maimonides: moderation, not excess.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adoni-bezek-844: Adoni-bezek was a Canaanite king in the town of Bezek. Judges i. 5 to 7 tells his tale. Judah beat him, and he fled but was caught. His thumbs and great toes were cut off. He owned the act as just pay. He had done the same to seventy kings. Such wounds left a man unfit for war. He could not run and could not draw a bow. Midrash asks why so great a king is left off the king list in Joshua xii.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-b-joseph-94: Aha, son of Joseph, was a Babylonian amora. He flourished in the fourth and fifth centuries. His life was unusually long. In youth he heard Hisda lecture, in 306. In old age he debated with Ashi II. Ashi died in 427. The entry also notes his asthma. Mar Ukba set a cure of asafetida for him. The dose was three ounces over three days. Kahana treated him in a later attack.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alkalai-abraham: Abraham ben Samuel Alkalai was a legal scholar in Turkey. He lived in the late 1700s and the early 1800s. His main work sorts the laws of the four Turim by letter. Notes by him run through the whole set. The work came out at Salonica in 1798. It filled two volumes. A new edition came out in 1840. He also printed two volumes of responsa in 1813-14.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alyashar-jacob-:
Jacob Saul Alyashar was chief rabbi of Jerusalem. He was born at Safed on June 1, 1817. He was taken to Jerusalem in 1823. In 1855 he became a fellow judge there. In 1869 he rose to chief judge. In 1893 all sides picked him as chief rabbi. The sultan backed the pick by a firman.

He spoke five tongues, among them Arabic and Greek. His books all bear the word Ish in their titles. That word holds the first letters of his name. Ten works are listed in the entry. They hold sermons, responsa, and rulings. One set was still in course of printing in 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amu-or-aamu-144: Amu is an old Egyptian word for the Semites. Books for lay readers cite it quite often. Its first sense may rest on a tool of war. The word seems to mean bearers of the throwing-stick. That stick was the mark of the desert folk. A Semitic root for the word is less likely. The word shows in a text of the sixth line of kings. At times it names men past the Semites as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ardit-or-ardot-:
Ardit, or Ardot, is the name of a family that moved from Aragon to Turkey, where its descendants still live. The entry lists its known members one by one. Abraham Ardit lived at Barcelona in 1483. Ephraim Ardit, at Smyrna, wrote a commentary on Maimonides' Mishnah Torah, printed at Salonica in 1791 with his responsa and sermons.

A nephew added notes to that work and sermons of his own. Hayyim Moses Ardit held a manuscript of Joseph Caro's responsa that reached print in 1791. Isaac ben Solomon Ardit wrote a huge commentary on the treatise Arakin, printed at Salonica in 1823. Raphael Ardit followed with a commentary on Shebu'ot in 1826. One member of the family, Isaac Abraham Ardit, took Christianity yet kept the family name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aryeh-lion-1844:
Aryeh, meaning lion, is a name found often among Jews, this entry explains. The first known bearer lived in the middle of the second century and is cited in tractate Pesahim. His real name was Judah. Aryeh, in its fuller form Gur Aryeh, Lion's Whelp, taken from Genesis chapter 49, was an added name of praise, not his given name.

No other early case of the word used so is known. Later, Italian and German-Polish Jews used Aryeh often as a religious name beside secular names such as Leo, Leopold, and Lowe. The full form Gur Aryeh stayed rare and mostly Italian, as with Finzi Gur Aryeh in the seventeenth century. Judah and Aryeh often pair as the religious names of men called Leon in daily life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashes-1944:
Ashes, in Hebrew efer, carry a set of fixed meanings in the Bible, and this entry sorts them. Ashes stand for worthlessness in persons and words, as in Genesis, Isaiah, Malachi, and Job. In the Red Heifer rite of Numbers chapter 19, the ashes of the offering go into water. That water is sprinkled on a person defiled by contact with a corpse, and its power comes from the sacred offering itself.

Grief gives the word its widest use. Mourners cast ashes on the head, or sat, lay, and rolled in them, as in Samuel, Job, Jonah, Esther, and Jeremiah. The entry warns that in many such passages dust would translate the Hebrew as well or better. Humiliation, more than burning, is the sense that binds the uses together.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asson-michelang:
Michelangelo Asson was an Italian physician and medical author. He was born at Verona on June 21, 1802, and died at Venice on Dec. 2, 1877. An uncle raised him after his father died. He studied at Padua and Pavia and took his medical degree in 1825. He practiced at Verona, then moved to Venice in 1831.

At Venice Asson built a large practice and became a leading surgeon of northern Italy. During the cholera outbreak of 1835 he opened an extra hospital. In 1840 he became chief surgeon of the city hospital. He did medical duty in the fighting of 1849 and again in 1859-60. He later taught anatomy and surgery. The entry lists about 120 essays and books by him, on subjects from cholera to the spleen. It judges his work useful for its picture of Italian medicine, though not lasting in importance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aus-of-kuraiza-:
Aus was a poet of the Jewish tribe of Ḳuraiẓa in Medina. When Mohammed besieged the tribe, the wife of Aus saved her life by embracing Islam. She urged her husband to do the same. He refused, and made his answer in verse on the spot.

The verses, as the entry gives them in English, pledge him to live by Moses and his code. They call Mohammed's faith empty talk. The entry notes a catch in the text. One line now praises Mohammed's religion, but such changes are common, it says, in hostile poems passed down by Muslim writers. A second poem of like temper is also credited to Aus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azazel-scapegoa:
Azazel is a mysterious being named in the rite of the Day of Atonement, in Leviticus. On that day the high priest set two goats before God and cast lots over them. One lot fell for the Lord, and that goat was killed as a sin offering. The other lot fell for Azazel.

Over the Azazel goat the priest laid both hands and confessed the people's sins. A man then led it out to a lonely place and let it go in the wilderness. The entry asks what Azazel is. Rabbis read the word as the rugged cliff the goat was thrown from. Most modern scholars, after Ibn Ezra and Naḥmanides, take Azazel for a goat-like desert demon. The entry argues that sending the goat did not own Azazel as a god. It was a picture of sin carried away from the camp.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baal-kore-liter: Baal-kore means, word for word, the master of reading. The term names the person who reads the weekly portion aloud from the scroll of the Law in the synagogue. That reader is usually the ḥazan, the cantor. But the entry is careful to add that it need not be the cantor. Any fit person who takes the reading holds the title for that service.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baermann-of-lim: Baermann of Limburg was a German writer who lived at Frankfort-on-the-Main at the end of the seventeenth century and into the next. He published there in 1712 a Judæo-German play with the Hebrew title "Mekirat Yosef" (The Sale of Joseph), made for Purim. Played at Frankfort at Purim in 1713, it won much success. Many Christians were in the crowd, and Jewish students from Prague and Hamburg acted in it. The same play was staged at Metz and became a favorite Purim piece among Polish Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-banking-2444:
Banking, strictly, means taking money on deposit and lending it out on interest. In that sense it is fairly new. A few deposit banks stood in medieval Italy, and the first great issue banks were those of Amsterdam and Hamburg in the early seventeenth century. The entry warns that calling medieval Jewish finance "banking" is an error. Those men took no deposits. They ran loan operations under special terms with the state.

Great Jewish financiers of the Middle Ages worked with royal treasuries, and their property fell to the crown in the end. Later, Marano merchants spread through the Spanish and Portuguese world empire. In the nineteenth century, houses such as the Rothschilds held a near monopoly of state loans until about 1848. Credit banks founded by smaller Jewish bankers then broke that grip. The firms, the entry insists, fought each other as hard as any rivals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baron-henry-254:
Henry Baron, a French painter, was born at Besançon in 1816 and died at Geneva in 1885. He was one of the foremost representatives of the historic genre in France. He depicted chiefly the lighter side of social life in the Renaissance and the rococo period. His paintings show the facile, skilful touch of the French school of the eighteenth century, with brilliancy of color and great variety of detail.

Well-known works include "Andrea del Sarto Painting His Wife as Madonna del Sacco" and "Palestrina in the Midst of an Assemblage of Musical Ladies." Two others, with the water-color "Feast in the Tuileries During the Paris Exposition of 1867," are in the Luxembourg Gallery. His water-colors were deservedly popular, and his illustrations to Rousseau, Boccaccio, Fénelon, and Perrault are equally known. He took medals in 1847, 1848, 1855, and 1867, a decoration in 1859, and several commissions from Napoleon III.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bassevi-von-tre:
Jacob Bassevi von Treuenberg was a court Jew and financier born in 1580. He grew rich and won favor with three emperors, lending funds in particular to Ferdinand the Second for the Thirty Years' War. He died at Jung-Buntzlau on May 2, 1634.

Ferdinand raised Bassevi to the nobility and gave him broad rights to trade, hold property, and live where he pleased, free of taxes. Bassevi used his standing to guard Jews in the empire and Italy. He helped protect the Prague quarter in 1621 and paid part of a fine laid on Rabbi Lippman Heller. He moved to Gitschin in 1631 after some trouble the entry does not explain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beer-jules-2744:
Jules Beer was a composer born in Paris in 1833, a son of Michael Beer and a nephew of the composer Meyerbeer. He still lived in Paris in 1902. Two short comic operas, heard by private audiences in 1859 and 1861, were his first tries.

An opera of 1862 and a grand opera staged at Brussels in 1871 followed, with more stage works after. None won marked success. The entry judges his output above the usual amateur level. A vast setting of a psalm for soloists, chorus, and orchestra, heard in 1868, stands out in the list. His piano works include salon pieces whose titles the entry lists in its closing lines.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belorado-the-ol:
Belorado is a city in the Spanish province of Burgos with Jews as early as the end of the eleventh century. Its charter of 1116 orders that no difference be made between Jew and Christian when injuries between them are judged.

Tax figures from 1291 show a community as large as its neighbors. Jews had to live apart near a tower and could trade with Christians only on market day, a right later taken away. A dispute of 1408 over street work and pasture rights fills the middle. After 1492 their houses were sold off cheap. The old Jewish quarter kept a new name after the expulsion, Barrio Nuevo, which it still bears today.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beni-israel-294:
Beni-Israel names the native Jews of India, living mainly in the Bombay presidency. They were once called Saturday Oil-Pressers, from their chief trade and their Sabbath rest. Their own tradition tells of Jews fleeing persecution who were wrecked near islands in the Indian Ocean, with seven men and seven women saved.

The entry traces two revivals of their practice, one linked to David Rahabi and a later one in 1796. It then covers their feasts, names, and customs in detail, from betrothal to marriage rites. Contact with other Jews later brought their rites closer to Sephardic use, with prayer-books in their own tongue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berek-joselovic: Berek Joselovich, also called Berko, was a Polish colonel under Kosciusko and Napoleon. Born at Kretingen in the second half of the eighteenth century, he was killed in battle near Kotzk in 1809. In 1794 Kosciusko charged him with raising a light-horse regiment from the Jews of Warsaw. He led 500 men with bravery in the defense of Warsaw, then lost nearly all of them at Praga. He later served in the Polish Legion and died fighting Austrian hussars. A mound marks his memory at the spot.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernstein-josep: Joseph Bernstein, called Joe, was an American prize fighter born in New York city in November 1877. He first stepped into the ring in 1894 and won five fights that year. In 1895 he won four bouts and drew two, marking himself a featherweight of proven skill. Few boxers of his age fought so often. In seven years he fought nearly 80 battles, winning 44, drawing 26, and losing 7. The entry names four men he defeated in that run.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bertinoro-obadi:
Obadiah Bertinoro, called Bartinoro, was a celebrated rabbi and commentator on the Mishnah who lived in Italy in the second half of the fifteenth century and died in Jerusalem about 1500. He reached Jerusalem on March 25, 1488, after a journey begun in October 1486.

The entry describes how he became spiritual head of Jerusalem's Jewish community, won abolition of the oppressive annual tax of 400 ducats, and founded a yeshibah after Spanish exiles arrived in 1492. It then explains his Mishnah commentary, drawn mainly from Rashi and Maimonides and printed with nearly every edition since 1549, and his travel letters, valued as a reliable medieval record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bezalel-ben-sol: Bezalel ben Solomon came from Kobryn. He preached at Slutzk in the government of Minsk. Later he preached at Boskowitz in Moravia. He died some time before 1659. The entry lists six works by him. The first gathers homilies on the Bible. It has seven parts, each named for a patriarch or king. Two councils ordered its printing at Lublin in 1666. Another work treats Sabbath laws in thirty-nine chapters. A third explains a hard Midrashic passage. Two works survive only in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bittern-kippod-: Bittern treats the Hebrew word ḳippod. The entry asks what creature the word names. Isaiah pairs it with cormorant and raven. Zephaniah sets it singing in upper lintels. Another Isaiah verse makes it a wading bird. Those clues point to a bird, the entry argues. The bittern fits that picture well. It is nocturnal, solitary, and a wader. Ancient versions instead read "porcupine." Later Hebrew and Arabic usage support that reading. The entry finds the porcupine reading hard to sustain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boaz-3444:
Boaz was a wealthy man of Bethlehem in Judah and a kinsman of Naomi and Ruth. The entry follows the book of Ruth. When Ruth appealed to his kinship, he bought back the family land sold by Naomi.

Boaz then married Ruth, in the entry's words, to raise up the name of the dead. Their son Obed was, by tradition, the grandfather of David. Rabbinic sources call Boaz a just and pious judge. They credit him with the custom of greeting others in God's name. Some rabbis also linked him with Ibzan of Bethlehem, a judge named in the book of Judges. Josephus placed his life in the time of Eli.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brann-solomon-3: Solomon Brann was a German rabbi born in Rawitsch on Nov. 3, 1814. He studied at the yeshibah in Lissa and at the Berlin University. In 1839 he joined the rabbinical board of his native city. There he pioneered preaching in German among its Jews. Since 1853 he has been rabbi at Schneidemühl, the entry says. He wrote often for German scientific periodicals of his day. His notes on the Jerusalem Talmud appear in the Krotoschin edition of 1866.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brotherly-love-:
Brotherly love means love for one's fellow man as a brother. The entry takes the phrase from a Greek word for love of brothers. It traces the trait to the Essene brotherhoods, who made it a special virtue. Its Jewish root is the command in Leviticus to love thy neighbor as thyself.

A long debate follows over how wide neighbor reaches. Akiba called the Leviticus verse the great principle of the Law. Ben Azzai pointed to Adam, made in God's image, to include all men. Hillel gave the rule in negative form to a heathen questioner. The entry also treats the Good Samaritan story and later teachers, ending with synod declarations from 1869 and 1885.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-burmania-bartho:
Barthold Dowe Burmania was a Dutch statesman and ambassador at the court of Vienna in the eighteenth century. The entry calls him a man of broad sympathies and a firm friend of the Jews. When Maria Theresa ordered the Jews expelled from Prague on Dec. 18, 1744, Dutch Jewish communities asked him to act.

Burmania pressed the Austrian court again and again, with English help. He won delays, first to the end of February and then another month. Prague's Jews were still exiled on March 31, 1745. He then fought the wider expulsion from Bohemia and Moravia, and the edicts softened in May. Full return to Prague came only in 1748, after pressure from foreign ambassadors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-calvo-emanuel-3: Emanuel Calvo was an Italian physician and Neo Hebraic poet born at Salonica late in the seventeenth century. In youth he moved to Leghorn with his learned father, Raphael Calvo. On Oct. 23, 1724, he took his medical degree at Padua. He practiced medicine at Leghorn with real success and leaned toward the Cabala late in life. Poems of his appear in a Leghorn collection printed in 1846. He was a close friend of the poet Castello and of Luzzatto, who praised him in verse and kept up a correspondence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-canada-14644:
Canada, a federation of provinces in British North America, first shows Jews in firm records during the last French and English fight for the continent. Commissary Aaron Hart, a London born Jew of 1724, served on Amherst's staff as Montreal fell. He later settled at Three Rivers and became seignior of Bécancour. Other Jewish officers and traders joined him in the new British colony.

Montreal's community grew strong enough to form a congregation, Shearith Israel, in 1768. The long entry then follows families, synagogues, and civic rights across the provinces. Its sources include assembly journals, statutes, and family records of the Harts and Davids. A closing theme is the political standing of Jews in Canada, argued from Lower Canada papers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carmanians-r-v-: Carmanians are a people named in II Esdras xv. 30. In that passage they join battle with the nations of the dragons of Arabia. The dragons win at first, then suffer defeat themselves, as verse 33 reports. The entry links the passage to the age of the Sassanids. It recalls Sapor I, dated 240-273, who invaded Syria and took Antioch. Odenathus and Zenobia drove him back. Aurelian later defeated Zenobia and took her captive. The name survives in Kirman, a district of southeast Persia on the Persian Gulf.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-catalan-moses-h: Moses Ḥayyim Catalan, an Italian poet born in Padua, was the son of the physician Abraham Catalan. He served as rabbi in his home town and died there at an advanced age in 1661. His rhetorical pamphlet on man, Meẓaref ha-Sekel, was never published. He wrote a wedding poem for his sister Perla that can be read as Hebrew or as Italian. In 1645 he wrote a like poem for Shabbethai Astruc. An elegy on Lamentations in ottava rima was also printed by him at Padua.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coen-giuseppe-4:
Giuseppe Coen, an Italian painter, was born in Ferrara in 1811 and died in Venice on Jan. 26, 1856. Orphaned young, he had to pick a trade and chose art. He followed Canaletto's manner of landscape and building views. His facade of Ferrara Cathedral, shown at Venice in 1840, won wide praise and a silver medal from his home city in 1841.

Study at Rome from 1843 brought him the friendship of Massimo d'Azeglio. Commissions followed back home, one from the Duke of Brunswick. In 1850 he settled in Venice and became one of the first to practice artistic photography there. His Venice views took a medal at the Paris Exposition of 1855. In 1849 he was among the first Jews elected to Ferrara's town council.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-colenso-john-wi:
John William Colenso, bishop of Natal and English Bible critic, was born at St. Austell, Cornwall, on Jan. 24, 1814, and died on Jan. 20, 1883. Cambridge trained, he taught at Harrow and wrote popular schoolbooks on arithmetic and algebra. Made bishop in 1853, he mastered Zulu for his mission and translated Genesis, Exodus, and Samuel into that tongue.

Sharp questions from his Zulu interpreters about clashes inside those books pushed him to test them. His Pentateuch and Book of Joshua Critically Examined began in 1862 and stirred the theological world. He attacked the count of 600,000 fighting men at the Exodus as beyond belief. Deposed for heresy in 1863, he was upheld by the Privy Council and kept his see for life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cremieux-gaston:
Gaston Crémieux was a French socialist and writer. He was born at Nîmes on June 22, 1836. He died at Marseilles on Dec. 1, 1871. He began as a lawyer at Aix in 1856. Poor clients in Nîmes won him the name Avocat des Pauvres, lawyer of the poor. At Marseilles from 1862 he campaigned in speech and print against Napoleon III.

His audiences were mostly working men. He preached the advanced theories of international socialism to them. For an uprising on Aug. 8, 1870, he drew six months in prison. The September revolution freed him and made him procurator at Marseilles. In 1871 he stood with the Marseilles Commune, though he opposed needless bloodshed, before the rising fell.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cyprus-4344:
Cyprus is the large island in the easternmost basin of the Mediterranean. Its Hebrew name, Kittim, could mean all the western islands and coasts. Josephus says the island took its name from the city Kition. Its people were first perhaps Carians, then Phenicians, then Greeks. Jews were numerous there in the days of the emperor Caius. They stood in close ties with the islanders, and a Roman decree for Jewish subjects was sent to Cyprus too.

War brought losses. In the fight over Ptolemais, Cyprian forces fell to Hebrew commanders sent by Cleopatra. By 610 the Jews were numerous enough to join a rising against the Greeks under Heraclius. Benjamin of Tudela later found several Jewish communities there. One group, he reports, kept the Sabbath from Saturday morning to Sunday, a practice the entry calls a heresy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dagesh-4844:
Dagesh is the dot placed in the center of a Hebrew letter. It marks either a doubled pronunciation or, for six letters, a hard sound in place of a soft one. The name may come from a Syriac root meaning to prick. In the old Masoretic texts, though, the word named the strong pronunciation itself. Its weak partner was called rafe. The term turns up first in a Talmud note on one letter of the word eḥad in Deuteronomy.

From the Masorah the word passed to the grammarians. Saadia named part of his grammar for dagesh and rafe. The entry argues that the dagesh is older than the vowel points. It once did some of their work, marking state and vowel type. Its set use by a dot belongs to the Tiberian system, while the Babylonian system at first used no dot at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-ben-hayyi:
Known by the abbreviation RadaK, Ḥayyim ha-Kohen's son David served as rabbi at Corfu and later at Patros, Greece, at the start of the sixteenth century. He had studied under Judah Minz. He was a contemporary of Elijah Mizraḥi and of Moses Alashkar, with whom he corresponded and later argued.

David became prominent through his attacks on Benjamin Ze'eb, who had allowed an 'agunah, a woman whose husband was missing, to marry on a Gentile's testimony. Nearly all of David's works burned in a fire at Adrianople. Only thirty-three responsa survived, arranged by his son-in-law David Vital and published at Constantinople in 1537.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deep-5044:
Deep, as used in the Bible, is studied here in its figurative senses. Set against rock, a picture of refuge, the deep stands for misfortune and sorrow. A deep pit means great danger, and the depths of Sheol mean utter affliction. The Psalms speak from the depths in prayer.

The word also marks what cannot be measured or understood. Sinners are said to deepen their sins. God's thoughts are called deep, and so are a man's words and plans. To make deep can even mean to hide or deceive. The entry closes with a note that cuneiform texts call wisdom itself the deep, something hard to reach and seldom found.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deutsch-israel-: Israel Deutsch was a German rabbi born in Zülz, Prussian Silesia, on April 2, 1800. From 1829 until his death he served as rabbi in Beuthen. He won distinction as a preacher, Talmudist, and Hebraist. With his brother David he wrote a vigorous defense of rabbinical Judaism in 1843, and a second tract against the Brunswick rabbinical conference in 1845. After his death on June 7, 1853, his brothers Abraham and David printed pieces from his literary remains at Gleiwitz in 1855.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dobritz-5244: Dobritz is a town in Bulgaria, twenty-six miles north of Varna. The entry counts about 200 Jews there in a total population of 14,000. The community was founded in 1870 and is run by three of its leading Jews. It built a synagogue in 1897 and keeps a small mixed school. Its Jews work as ironmongers, tinsmiths, watchmakers, and small traders. Four or five Jewish families also live at nearby Baltchik.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-lasi-be: Eleazar Lasi ben Joseph was a German Talmudist. He was born in Berlin on Sept. 24, 1740. He died at Hamburg on Jan. 22, 1814. He studied at Bamberg and at the school in Schwersenz. After his marriage he settled at Posen as a judge. In 1781 he followed his chief to Altona. There he rose to head of the court for three towns. Altona, Wandsbeck, and Hamburg all came under his court. His chief book glosses a code of Jewish law. It was printed by his son Moses in 1815.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-en-kelohenu-574: En Kelohenu is an old hymn of the Jewish rite. Its name means there is none like our God. It follows the Additional Service at feasts in the order. Many rites sing it on Sabbaths as well. Four titles for God march through its first verse. Our God, our Lord, our King, and our Savior they run. Their lead words spell out the word Amen. Two more verses open with Blessed and with Thou. Sephardim and Ashkenazim add unlike verses to round the count.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fayyumi-nathana: Nathanael al-Fayyumi was a Talmudic scholar and philosopher who worked in Yemen about the middle of the twelfth century. He wrote Bustan al-Ukul, a work of thought in Judeo-Arabic, in seven parts. They cover God's unity, man as a small world, obedience, repentance, trust, the Messiah, and the future life. He quotes Saadia, Bahya, and Judah ha-Levi. Gottheil took him for the father of Jacob al-Fayyumi, to whom Maimonides wrote the Letter to Yemen. Steinschneider called that link doubtful.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-forti-hortensiu: Hortensius Johanan Ḥazaḳ Forti was a Jewish convert to Christianity who lived in the sixteenth century. The short entry says he was born at Gorima. He settled at Prague under Maximilian II. He wrote a Hebrew grammar, printed at Prague in 1564-1566. He also wrote a work on the mystic meaning of letters. In it he dwells on the different ways of writing the Holy Name. That work was printed by Kircher in a large work on Egypt. Two short source lines close the notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frenkel-israel-:
Israel Frenkel was a Russian Hebraist and teacher born at Radom, Russian Poland, on September 18, 1853. He studied Talmud under Samuel Mohilever, chief rabbi of Radom. At the same time he learned Hebrew, German, and French. Since its founding in 1882 he has taught at the Talmud Torah of Radom. His work in Hebrew is chiefly translation. He turned Lessing's play about Sarah Sampson into Hebrew, printed at Warsaw in 1887.

He also turned the songs of a German play about William Tell. A Polish play of his became a Hebrew drama in six acts. Its heroine is Esther, the Jewish mistress of a Polish king. He writes for a Hebrew paper as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ge-ullah-redemp:
Geullah is the blessing that follows the Shema in prayer. Its name means redemption. It recalls God freeing of Israel from bondage in Egypt. It closes with words that bless the one who redeemed Israel. The morning form runs much longer than the evening form. Both tell of the leaving of Egypt and the crossing of the Red Sea.

Both forms quote the Song on the Sea, with its line asking who is like God among the gods. A German rite adds a plea for the Rock of Israel to rise and help. Sephardim reject that plea as foreign to the blessing. Talmud teaching urges that Geullah be joined to the prayer that follows, with no break between them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gebini-from-lat: Gebini was an officer of the Second Temple whose task was to call out the rite of the hour. His cry ran: Priests, attend to the sacrifice; Levites, tune the hymn; Israelites, take your places. His voice is said to have reached Agrippa at eight miles off. The king then rewarded him richly. Other tales say his calls were heard at Jericho, ten miles away. The name Gebini may have become a title for all who later held the crier post.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gracian-hebr-he:
Gracian, in Hebrew Ḥen, is a Spanish Jewish family. It descends from Judah ben Barzilai. Its members lived mostly at Barcelona from the thirteenth to the sixteenth century. Most used the name Ḥen. One member signed himself both Solomon Ḥen and Solomon Gracian. Several family members joined Solomon Adret in 1305. They signed a protest against teaching philosophy.

The entry then lists the family's chief members one by one. Astruc Vidal Gracian and Bonseñor Gracian wrote responsa on taxes. Other members flourished at Candia in the sixteenth century. Several names appear only as signers of the 1305 protest. Three members get their own linked entries. They are Shealtiel, Solomon ben Moses, and Zerahiah ben Isaac.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hagiz-samuel-be: Samuel ben Jacob Ḥagiz of Fez was the father of Jacob Ḥagiz and grandfather of Moses Ḥagiz. An epitaph dates his death to 1634. He edited Solomon Duran's "Tif'eret Yisrael" about 1596. He also wrote two works printed at Venice that year. "Debar Shemu'el" is a haggadic commentary, above all on Deuteronomy Rabbah. "Mebaḳḳesh ha-Shem" is a set of sermons on the Pentateuch. The short entry gives no other facts about him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-harari-judah-ar: Judah Aryeh Harari was a liturgical poet who lived at Montpellier in the second half of the thirteenth century. Abraham Bedersi praised him highly in the poem "Hereb ha-Mithappeket." Several of his piyyutim survive in the ritual of Carpentras and in Mahzor manuscripts. The surname means "of the mountain" and was borne by other scholars of Montpellier and Marseilles as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hebraists-chris:
Christian Hebraists were Christian scholars who studied Hebrew and Jewish writings. Early church fathers learned Hebrew lore from Jewish teachers. Jerome's teachers are even named. As church and synagogue drew apart, that learning faded. What reached medieval scholars came mostly through translations.

The Renaissance and Reformation revived the study. Patrons paid for Hebrew chairs at Louvain and Paris. Pico collected Hebrew manuscripts, and Reuchlin wrote a modern Hebrew grammar. Through the sixteenth century, Christian scholars sat openly at the feet of Jewish teachers. The long article names grammarians, dictionary makers, printers, and editors of the Masorah. It frames the field as a measure of ties between the two faiths.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-helmet-or-7544:
Helmet looks at head armor in the ancient world of the Bible. At first, it seems, only kings, officers, and great men wore helmets. Goliath and Saul are the two men named with bronze helmets. Later the helmet became part of a common soldier's full kit. Chronicles says Uzziah equipped the whole army with helmets and armor.

Most helmets were not metal at all. They were leather caps, round and close-fitting, with a flap to guard the neck. Syrian and Hittite fighters wore such caps, as Egyptian carvings show. Metal bands or rings stiffened the leather. Cheek pieces guarded the ears on finer pieces.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirsch-siegfrie:
Siegfried Hirsch, born at Berlin on Nov. 5, 1816, was a German historian and cousin of Theodor Hirsch. He studied history at Berlin and Königsberg from 1833 to 1836. A prize essay on King Henry I appeared in 1834, while he was still a student.

Hirsch became a lecturer at Berlin in 1842 and assistant professor two years later. Like Stahl, he worked for purifying the Church and wrote for a church paper. His main work, a history of Henry II, was left unfinished at his death. Others printed it in three volumes from 1862 to 1875. He died at Paris on Sept. 11, 1860.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ithamar-8344: Ithamar was the youngest son of Aaron by Elisheba and was consecrated to the priesthood with his father and brothers. When Nadab and Abihu died, he and Eleazar were told not to mourn them and were named Aaron's successors. In the wilderness he oversaw the Gershonite and Merarite Levites who carried the Tabernacle and its gear. The high-priesthood later passed into his line through Eli. It stayed there until Solomon took it from Abiathar and gave it back to Eleazar's house.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-asher:
Jacob ben Asher, known as the Ba'al ha-Turim, was a German codifier and Bible commentator who died at Toledo, in Spain, before 1340. The few glimpses of his life contradict each other, the entry warns. He was a son of Asher, his chief teacher, and he emigrated with his father to Spain. In 1317 he and his brother Judah were made treasurers of the family's alms money.

Jacob was poor all his life and knew great want; his living seems to have come from lending money. He did not follow his father as rabbi of Toledo; his brother Judah took that office. He wandered through many lands and noted their differing customs, which his Turim quote. His pupil David Abudarham, writing in 1340, already speaks of him as dead. The entry calls him one of the pillars of rabbinic learning, known across the Jewish world through the Turim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-napht: Jacob ben Naphtali ha-Kohen was an Italian printer born in Gazolo who worked in the sixteenth century. Before 1556 he managed Tobiah Foa's printing house at Sabbionetta, which issued Abravanel's "Merkebet ha-Mishneh" in 1551. In 1556 he moved to Mantua and ran the press at Rufellini's house, first alone, then with Meir b. Ephraim Sofer, then alone again from 1560 to 1563. His first Mantua book was Elijah Levita's "Sefer ha-Bahur"; his last was the "Midrash Yelammedenu."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-wolf-:
Jacob ben Wolf Kranz, the Dubner Maggid, was a Russian preacher born at Zietil about 1740 who died at Zamosc on Dec. 18, 1804. At eighteen he took a preacher's post at Meseritz. He moved on through Zolkiev, Dubno, Wlodawa, and Kalisch to Zamosc. At Dubno he stayed eighteen years. He left it for Wilna at the call of Elijah, the Gaon, who, recovering from sickness and unable to study, wanted Jacob's talk for diversion.

The entry calls him an unrivaled preacher. His gift was the parable: stories from human life that made hard passages plain and settled tangled points of law. He was also a strong scholar, often consulted. All his books came out after his death, through his son Isaac and his pupil Plahm. They include the "Ohel Ya'akob" on the Pentateuch and an ethics book built in eight gates.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jewish-messenge: Jewish Messenger was a weekly paper printed in New York. Samuel M. Isaacs founded and edited it from January 1857. On his death his son Abram S. Isaacs took the chair in May 1878. The paper held a conservative line in religion. Under its first editor it took a clear stand against slavery before and during the Civil War. For one year it issued a learned supplement with work by noted scholars. In 1903 it was merged into The American Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jubilees-book-o:
The Book of Jubilees, also called Little Genesis, is a retelling of Genesis and part of Exodus in the form of a revelation. The entry places its writing between 135 and 105 before the common era, in the reign of John Hyrcanus. It carries the views and customs of a strict Pharisaic or Hasidean school, though one scholar cited argues for an Essene source.

Written first in Hebrew, the book passed into Greek, then into Latin and Ethiopic. The Latin form is incomplete, while the Ethiopic text survives whole and was printed by Dillmann in 1859. Its tales add detail to the Bible story, such as set days for Adam and Eve entering Eden. Its calendar scheme hints at a time when Jewish timekeeping was not yet fixed by rabbinic rule.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kansas-14444:
Kansas is one of the northern central states of the United States. It joined the Union in 1861. Jews are thought to have settled early at Kansas City. Leavenworth was the first city in the state with a Jewish congregation. Its town lots were first sold on Oct. 9, 1854. Within a year enough Jews lived there for a minyan.

In 1859 the Leavenworth Jews formed the congregation B'nai Jeshurun. A synagogue rose in 1864 at Sixth and Osage streets. An Orthodox group split off in 1881 as House of Jacob. The entry also notes small groups at Topeka and other towns. Most held services only on holy days. It puts the Jewish population of the state in 1904 at about 3,000.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kaufmann-david-:
David Kaufmann was an Austrian scholar born at Kojetein, in Moravia, on June 7, 1852. He died at Karlsbad on July 6, 1899. He studied at Breslau for ten years, at the seminary and the university alike. He took his doctorate at Leipsic in 1874. He was ordained rabbi on Jan. 29, 1877.

That year Kaufmann took chairs at the new rabbinical school at Budapest. He taught history, the philosophy of religion, and preaching. He held those posts until his death. As the school's librarian he bought a great Padua library for it. His own output ran to 546 items by one count. His chief work surveys how Jewish and Arabic thinkers treated the traits of God. Other books cover Jewish families, synagogue art, and Heine's forebears.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kirkisani-abu-y:
Abu Yusuf Ya'ḳub al-Ḳirḳisani was a Karaite dogmatist and exegete. He flourished in the first half of the tenth century. A native of Circassia, he traveled throughout the Orient. In 937 he wrote the "Kitab al-Anwar," an Arabic work on the precepts. He also wrote a commentary on the parts of the Pentateuch that do not deal with laws.

The "Kitab al-Anwar" comprises thirteen treatises. Its first gives a survey of the Jewish sects in time order. Ḳirḳisani counts the Rabbinites among those sects. He admires Anan, yet often disagrees with him. He also blames the Karaites for neglecting rabbinical literature. Later treatises defend reason as the foundation of faith. Most of the work is still extant in manuscript at St. Petersburg.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-koletkar-moses-: Moses Koletkar held the rank of sirdar bahadur in the Anglo-Indian army, and the entry traces his service step by step. He enlisted in the Eighth Regiment Native Infantry on April 1, 1842, and later moved to the Twenty-seventh Regiment. He became jemidar and native adjutant on Jan. 1, 1853. Promotion to subahdar came on Nov. 6, 1858, and to subahdar-major on Jan. 24, 1876. He fought at Hyderabad and at Kolhapur, winning medals for both. He is also said to have given the first warning of the mutiny to officers of his regiment.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kuhn-moriz-9544: Moriz Kuhn, an Austrian physicist born at Brünn in Moravia on Jan. 11, 1843, studied at the polytechnic there and at Vienna. He entered state service in 1865. Posts in weather and earth magnetism work followed in 1867 and 1868. In 1870 he became professor of mathematics and physics at a Vienna state school. He edited school journals from 1872 to 1889. His papers treat Lichtenberg figures and links among pressure, volume, and heat in gases, dated 1873 and 1875. A paper on conic lines dates to 1868.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levin-israel-so: Israel Solomon Levin, a Danish grammarian and linguist, was born in Randers in 1810. He died in Copenhagen in 1883. He graduated from the Randers high school. He then worked as editor of a critical journal and as a translator of novels. He wrote several works on Danish grammar. The chief one named is "Dansk Lyd og Kjönslære," from 1844. He also wrote two novels, both printed in 1848. One tells war tales for common readers. The other draws scenes from life in Hamburg.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowenberg-juliu:
Julius Löwenberg, a German geographer, is the subject of an entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Strzelno, Prussia, in 1800, he was educated in Berlin. There he came to know Alexander von Humboldt, who helped him in various ways. He died at Berlin on December 12, 1893.

The article is mainly a record of his books on geography and exploration. They include an Africa volume in 1835, a historical-geographical atlas, and a history of geography. He also wrote a biography of Humboldt and an account of Humboldt's travels in America and Asia. Late works covered the history of discovery and voyages in the polar zones. The entry closes with his last years in Berlin's Jewish home for aged people. It is a quiet end for a scholar backed by Humboldt himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-machir-ben-abba:
Machir ben Abba Mari, compiler of the Yalkut ha-Makiri, is treated in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Almost nothing is known about the man himself. Neither his country nor his century can be fixed. Steinschneider guessed that he lived in Provence, and scholars still debate his date.

The article therefore studies the book instead of the life. Like the Yalkut Shimoni, it gathers Talmudic and midrashic sayings, but only for the later Bible books. It covers Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, the twelve Minor Prophets, Psalms, Proverbs, and Job. Machir said he wanted to gather the scattered sayings into one group. His sources ranged across both Talmuds, the Tosefta, and many midrashim. Only parts survive in print, including Isaiah in 1894 and Psalms in 1899. The entry maps a lost scholar through the remains of his anthology.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manasseh-prayer:
Prayer of Manasseh, a short Greek poem of repentance, is examined in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. It is ascribed to Manasseh, son of King Hezekiah, held captive in Babylon. Chronicles says the king prayed there but does not give his words. The prayer fills that gap. It survives among canticles attached to the Psalms in some Greek manuscripts.

The article tells the legend the prayer carries. Manasseh, starved on bran bread and vinegar water in prison, repented and humbled himself. Fire then melted his iron chains, and he was restored to Jerusalem. The Church never declared the prayer canonical, the entry notes. Luther kept it, and it stands in the English Apocrypha. The text itself praises God's mercy and His promise of repentance to sinners. The piece shows how a missing prayer in the Bible invited a later writer to compose it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-martinique-1044:
Martinique is an island in the West Indies and a French colony. Its Jewish history fills a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Gotthard Deutsch and S. Kahn. Dutch Jews settled there early in the seventeenth century and did well in trade. Trouble began after France took the island in 1635. Jesuit pressure kept pushing the authorities against them.

The article goes through the decrees one by one. Jewish commerce was banned in 1658 and then restored. New limits came in 1664 and 1669. In 1671 Colbert spoke for the Jews, and Louis XIV granted them religious liberty and equal privileges. That protection died with Colbert, an edict of 1683 ordered the Jews banished, and the Code Noir that followed drove them off the island.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-medicine-10544:
Medicine among the ancient Hebrews opens a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Solomon Schechter, C. D. Spivak, Joseph Jacobs, and Frederick T. Haneman. Health and sickness alike came from God, so the healer worked as the messenger of God. The Law itself sanctioned practice. A man injured in a fight must be “thoroughly healed” at the cost of his attacker. Joseph kept house physicians, and Isaiah names the surgeon, the dresser of wounds.

One point is stressed early: unlike other early peoples, the priests of Israel never monopolized healing. Moses gave them only the policing of contagious disease, and no biblical priest is shown practicing medicine. Prophets heal instead: Elijah and Elisha raise children, and Isaiah cures Hezekiah with a fig plaster. It quotes the praise of the physician by Ben Sira. It also notes the court expert, the rofe, whose testimony decided criminal cases.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-ben-sim:
Menahem ben Simeon was a French Bible commentator. He worked at the end of the twelfth century. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn give him a short notice in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A native of Posquières in Provence, he was a pupil of Joseph Kimhi and worked on the Prophets. The Bibliothèque Nationale in Paris holds his commentaries on Jeremiah and Ezekiel in a single manuscript.

The entry dates what it can. The Jeremiah commentary was completed in 1191. The Ezekiel commentary breaks off mid-chapter. It stops in the middle of the fortieth chapter. It is unfinished, or imperfectly preserved. Nothing else of his life is recorded. The bibliography is a single line. It points to Gross's "Gallia Judaica." The notice preserves the bare outline of a Provençal exegete whose work survives, where so many contemporaries' does not, in a Paris codex.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-metz-isaac-1074:
Isaac Metz was a German scholar who lived at Hamburg in the first half of the nineteenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He is remembered for careful work on two classics of Hebrew literature rather than for any public office.

His main work was Ḳehillat Dawid, a catalogue of David Oppenheimer's famous library, which Lazar Embden translated into Latin at Hamburg in 1826; Jacob Goldenthal later added an index. Metz also published an edition of Judah ha-Levi's Cuzari at Hanover in 1836, based on the Venice editions of 1547 and 1594. The bibliography cites Steinschneider's Bodleian catalogue and Zeitlin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-milwaukee-10844:
