Shanza Zaib and seven colleagues ask how forest soil fungi weather a drought-and-downpour cycle. Their 2026 study sits in managed beech forests of central Slovakia. An eighteen-day dry spell ended with heavy rain. Soil was sampled just before the rain and seven days after. Both the litter layer and the mineral soil below were tested. DNA barcoding identified the fungi, and an enzyme assay gauged decomposition potential.

Depth, not rain, ran the show. Litter and mineral soil held clearly different fungal communities. Root-linked fungi and soil decomposers ruled the mineral layer. Pathogens and litter specialists crowded the surface. The rewetting changed nothing detectable within a week. Community mix, diversity, and enzyme activity all held steady. Forest fungi may simply shrug off single short drought cycles. Longer or repeated extremes remain the open question this baseline helps frame.
plos-pone-0352644:
Jason Maikos and seven co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One trial of prosthetic ankle-foot devices. The users had below-knee limb loss. Ninety-one people took part, a mix of veterans, service members, and civilians. Each person tried three device types in random order. One was a springy energy-returning foot. One was an articulating foot. One was a powered foot. Each got a week of adjustment time. Thirteen people without limb loss gave reference values.

Lab gait measures were by far the most sensitive to device type. Nineteen measures differed, mostly at the ankle. Timed walking and mobility tests showed no clear device effect. Survey scores split in a telling way. Measured gait looked most natural on the powered foot. Yet users said they preferred the simpler non-powered devices. The authors say prescriptions should weigh both kinds of proof for each person.
plos-pone-0352744:
Fei Hao and co-authors build a drone-based system for naming desert grassland plants from the air when only a handful of labeled examples exist. Desert rangelands need watching for ecological security, and hyperspectral cameras see species-level detail, but training data are scarce. Their method learns how to learn. One branch reads fine local texture. A second, sequence-based branch reads wide spatial patterns. A meta-learning routine then teaches the pair to adapt from few examples.

Across test scenes the system classified species with accuracy above ninety percent on headline measures and stayed steady as sample sizes shrank. Hao and colleagues present it as a practical route for agencies that must map fragile rangelands without funding huge labeling campaigns first.
plos-pone-0352944:
This entry is a formal retraction notice issued by the PLOS One editors in 2026, withdrawing an earlier article that claimed a receptor called GPR91 helps drive heart enlargement under pressure overload. Readers should not rely on the original article's conclusions. The editors acted after concerns were raised about the paper's overlap with a previously published article by a partly shared author group, which the paper never cited.

Both articles studied the same signaling pathway in the same animal model and reported similar methods, results, and conclusions. The notice also lists figure problems, including unexplained symbols and unlabeled panels, a missing ethics approval number, and anesthesia practices that may not have met accepted standards. The first author maintained the two papers differed in scope, but the editors retracted the article.
plos-pone-0353244:
Zhou and colleagues, in a 2026 engineering study, test a new connector that ties steel facade panels to a building's frame. Prefabricated steel walls need joints that are strong, cheap, and easy to fit on site. Their design grouts a stud inside a small steel tube, borrowing from sleeve grouting used elsewhere in construction. Eighteen test pieces were pulled until they failed, and computer models replayed the tests.

Strain grew from the stud's ends outward, and the models matched the real failures closely. The connector held up well even with weak grout and a shallow stud embedment, which cuts cost and eases site work. A formula the team derived for the load at which the connector yields predicted test results with small error. The authors offer the detail and its design math as a ready option for prefabricated steel facades, filling a gap in standards.
plos-pone-0353344:
Li and colleagues compared nurse-led sedation care for patients on breathing machines in a 2026 study. Keeping patients calm but not too deeply asleep helps them leave the ventilator sooner. Records from one intensive care unit over two years split patients into usual doctor-led care and a nurse-led plan with daily targets and frequent checks.

Patients under nurse-led care spent less time on the ventilator and fewer days in intensive care. Signs of too-deep or too-light sedation also fell. Confusion rates were lower but not clearly so, and death rates did not differ. Structured nurse control of sedation looks like a safe way to free patients from machines sooner.
plos-pone-0353744:
Fang Chen and seven colleagues characterise a long non-coding RNA that runs high in lung adenocarcinoma, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. These RNAs do not build proteins but steer other genes. Found through public cancer datasets and confirmed in tumour cell lines, the RNA — known by the code RP3-340N1.2 — was dialled down in laboratory experiments to see what the cancer cells would do.

Silencing it slowed the cells' growth, movement, invasion, and colony formation, and shrank tumours grown in mice. The RNA appears to work by soaking up a small regulatory RNA, freeing a signalling protein that feeds a growth pathway. Restoring that protein's activity reversed the silencing effect. The chain is a candidate target for future lung cancer drugs.
plos-pone-0353844:
Yolacan, in a 2026 mathematics paper, introduces a new kind of mapping for cleaning up blurred signals and images. The work sits in fixed point theory, the study of processes that settle by repeating a step. The new mapping blends a known family with a directed graph, and the paper proves that a two-step repeating method built on it converges.

Proof alone is not the whole story: the method was tried on standard blurred images spoiled by motion blur and random noise. It restored them with quality scores that beat three classical methods and matched a leading edge-preserving approach. On one-dimensional signals it did even better, with high scores on both sharpness and structural likeness to the original. Yolacan presents the framework as a mathematically grounded addition to the deblurring toolbox, with its strength proven rather than merely observed.
plos-pone-0353944:
Farzaneh Ramezani, Farzaneh Saki, and Mohammad Reza Zoghi Paydar present a protocol, published in 2026, for a trial of brain-and-body training. The training aims to protect female volleyball players' knees. Players whose knees collapse inward on landing face high risk of tearing the anterior cruciate ligament. A spike or quick cut must often be decided in a split second, under divided attention.

The planned eight-week trial will randomize players aged eighteen to twenty-three with confirmed inward knee collapse. One group gets standard neuromuscular training. The other gets the same training fused with cognitive challenges that mimic game pressure. Landing mechanics will be filmed under calm and distracted conditions. Brain activity, muscle firing, balance, and strength will be tracked too. The design targets the game-real moment when injuries actually happen.
plos-pone-0354144:
Md Riyadh Arefin and six colleagues flood tea plants to find which varieties survive waterlogged soil, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study from Bangladesh. Tea earnings matter greatly to the country, and erratic rains increasingly drown the bushes. Eight candidate genotypes plus two standard clones endured two weeks under water, then two weeks of recovery, while twenty-three growth and chemistry traits were measured.

Flooding cut photosynthesis, leaf numbers, and root weight, while protective chemicals rose in leaves and roots. Comparing stress-tolerance scores separated the hardy lines from the fragile ones. The authors argue that breeding from the tolerant genotypes is the practical route to tea harvests that survive a wetter climate.
plos-pone-0354244:
Aneesa Rasheed Anwar and three co-authors turn fruit peel waste into a water-holding gel for dry farms, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The work responds to the United Arab Emirates' harsh conditions: scarce water, poor soil, and heavy reliance on chemical fertiliser. They extracted pectin from orange peel and starch from banana peel, then linked them into soft gels using calcium and a common synthetic polymer.

Laboratory checks confirmed the raw materials were pure and stable, and microscope images showed a well-connected, porous structure suited to soaking up water. Such gels could store rain or irrigation water in soil and release it slowly, cutting waste in arid farming.
plos-pone-0354344:
Seline Verbaan led a team of eight authors on this 2026 protocol for a randomized trial preparing older patients for leg artery surgery. People over sixty-five with severely blocked leg arteries face long hospital stays and poor recovery. The planned Dutch trial will enroll three hundred patients across centers for a combined program of exercise, nutrition, and support before their operation, or usual care.

Outcomes span hospital stay, complications, patient reports, and costs. As a protocol it reports a plan, not findings. Verbaan's team designed it to settle whether prehabilitation belongs in routine vascular care.
plos-pone-0354744:
Shalinder Sabherwal and colleagues present in 2026 a full picture of eye care need and service capacity in one catchment area. They paired a population survey of avoidable blindness in older adults with a new module that checks what local providers actually offer. People aged fifty and above were examined in large numbers.

Blindness was more common in women, and unoperated cataract caused most blindness and severe loss. Glasses coverage was low, especially for women, and records on surgery and diabetes eye care were patchy across providers. Linking need to capacity this way, the authors argue, gives planners a firmer base than either source alone.
plos-pone-0355044:
Carolina Messer-Soubelet, Bernardo Riffo, and Omar Barriga build a questionnaire to measure how well school professionals read minds, their own and others', when teaching children with autism. This mind-reading capacity shapes classroom inclusion, yet it is usually studied in clinics, not staff rooms. Nearly three hundred professionals in Chilean schools with inclusion policies completed the new self-report tool, whose structure the team probed with factor analysis.

The answers settled into a multi-part scale grouped under two broad domains: spotting others' mental states and spotting one's own. Early reliability checks supported the tool. Messer-Soubelet and colleagues offer it as a first step toward training that treats perspective skills as something schools can measure and grow, rather than assume.
plos-pone-0355244:
RETRACTED: The PLOS One Editors issued this 2026 retraction notice, withdrawing a global review that had pooled trials of integrated palliative care against standard care for cancer patients. Readers should not rely on that review's pooled findings. The main problem was a basic statistical error in how effects were calculated and combined.

Effects figured as simple mean differences were reported as standardised differences, though studies used different scales, so one unit did not mean the same thing across studies. Data extraction for several included studies was also in doubt, and some study labels could not be traced at first. An independent statistical adviser judged the error likely changed the findings greatly.
plos-pone-0355544:
Emre Karaduman and co-authors studied how fear of COVID-19 related to coping among one thousand female university students after the emergency phase. Fear was the pandemic's central emotion, yet its link with coping in this group was unclear. Their 2026 survey measured fear levels and outbreak coping strategies with standard scales.

Greater fear came with more active coping, not less. Two experiences changed that relationship's strength. Being physically active moderated the link, and so did having personally tested positive or negative for the virus. Karaduman and colleagues suggest habits like regular exercise, and firsthand infection experience, keep shaping fear and coping long after the crisis headlines fade.
plos-pone-0355744:
Hao Liu and seven colleagues examine a hard call in HIV care in this 2026 study from seven Chinese medical centers. Some patients on treatment keep a small but persistent amount of virus in their blood, too low to count as failure yet too high to ignore. Doctors disagree on whether switching their drug regimen helps, so the team looked back at real-world records for just over one hundred sixty such patients.

About two thirds of patients who switched regimens had fully suppressed virus a year later, nearly the same share as those who stayed on their original drugs. Virus levels drifted down and immune cell counts rose modestly in both groups, with no clear advantage for switching. The authors say the results argue against switching automatically, though they note the study's modest size and retrospective design.
plos-pone-0355844:
Hamis Daniel Wambura, Gration Mutashoberwa Rwegasira, and Martin John Martin survey what drives infestation by the African sugarcane stalk borer in Tanzania. The moth larva tunnels cane stalks and can cut yields steeply while draining sugar content. Teams sampled hundreds of field blocks across low, middle, and high elevations in both seasons, counting larvae and damage in random stalk bundles from each block.

Infestation ran highest at high elevation in both seasons, and the interplay of season, elevation, and crop age shaped levels significantly. Wet season damage at altitude stood out, boring was worst low in the stalk, and mixed-variety blocks plus two named cultivars suffered most. Wambura and colleagues give growers a risk map for targeting scouting and control.
plos-pone-0355944:
Hanno Schmidt and co-authors checked if plain, one-step genome tools sort Legionella germs as well as a heavy multi-step pipeline. Legionella can cause a grave lung ill, and hospitals must trace water strains fast, often with no computing whiz on staff. Their 2026 study sequenced nineteen water isolates.

Each tool split the germs into the same two big family groups. Kinship thumbed its nose at distance: one group turned up in towns far apart, while both groups shared one hospital floor. Plain tools matched the big pipeline's sharpness across the set. Schmidt and colleagues say low-fuss genome work can back routine water safety hunts in plain labs.
plos-pone-0356144:
Harsimran Kaur Brar and seven colleagues investigate how a parasite that causes leishmaniasis rewires the human immune cells it inhabits, in this 2026 laboratory study. Leishmania parasites ship tiny RNA fragments, clipped from their transfer RNAs, into host macrophages inside bubble-like exosomes. The team synthesized two such fragments and used precision protein measurement to watch what changed inside a human macrophage cell line exposed to them.

Each fragment altered the levels of roughly twenty macrophage proteins, and about a third of those changes appeared to favor the parasite's survival. In infected macrophages, both fragments were found physically lodged in the host's Argonaute protein complexes, the machinery that uses small RNAs to silence genes, with one fragment preferring a specific Argonaute partner. The authors present this as the first demonstration that these smuggled RNAs tilt the host proteome toward the parasite.
plos-pone-0356244:
Yaw Adusi-Poku and colleagues asked whether software that reads chest X-rays for tuberculosis could save Ghana money as well as lives. Their 2026 study tested symptomatic patients at twenty-three facilities. It compared the usual route, symptom screening and human-read films, against computer-aided detection. The software was set at three different strictness levels. The team then modeled total costs and health gains.

The middle setting won outright. It was tuned to Ghanaian data rather than the vendor's default. It proved both cheaper and healthier than standard care. It saved the system roughly ten thousand dollars across about seven hundred patients. It also gained healthy life years. The main saving came from sparing costly molecular tests for people the software cleared. Local calibration, the authors show, is where the economic case is made.
plos-pone-0356544:
Minjin Kim and Eunha Shim build a disease-spread model to test a worry about imperfect vaccines: could they push a virus to evolve escape from immunity? Vaccines protect in three ways, by blocking infection, easing symptoms, and cutting spread, and each way may be partial. Their model tracks sick and silent infections in vaccinated and unvaccinated groups and totals the pressure favoring escape strains.

Each kind of protection lowered escape pressure, but none alone tamed it under most settings, while combined protection worked far better. When several protections were weak at once, pushing coverage higher could paradoxically raise escape pressure above the level with no vaccine at all. Kim and Shim say vaccine design should chase balanced strength across all three effects, not one headline number.
plos-pone-0356644:
Jiaxing Li and colleagues charted pancreatic cancer that strikes before age fifty among women of childbearing age worldwide. This group's metabolic profile overlaps the disease's prime years. Their 2026 two-stage study mined global burden data from 1990 to 2023. It counted deaths and lost healthy years. It then checked the leading risk signals against a hospital case-control dataset.

Deaths and disability in this group more than doubled over the period. Population growth and aging drove most of the rise, rather than rising rates. Rates did climb in poorer regions, though. High blood sugar accounted for the largest share of attributable burden by far. It held up as an independent risk factor clinically. Body weight's role blurred into the same metabolic pathway. The authors urge metabolic prevention aimed at younger women.
plos-pone-0357044:
Junqiang Xu and colleagues tracked how green Henan Province, China, became between 2000 and 2023, using satellite measures of plant cover across four river basins. Their 2026 study mapped where vegetation thickened or thinned, then separated the fingerprints of climate from those of human action, weighing rainfall, temperature, terrain, and soil.

The province greened overall, with scattered pockets of decline. Terrain and soil, especially in combination, explained much of the patchiness, and each basin's vegetation answered weather differently. After climate effects were removed, human activity still showed a mostly positive push, from restoration and farming practices, with harm concentrated in smaller areas. Basin-by-basin evidence like this helps officials target land care where it actually works.
plos-pone-0358044:
Yoritaka Akimoto and coauthors published a 2026 brain-imaging study in PLOS ONE on how Japanese babies hear speech sounds. Listeners sometimes tell two sounds apart more easily in one order than the reverse, a quirk called directional asymmetry, but its brain basis in infancy was unclear. Using light-based brain imaging safe for babies, the team played five- and nine-month-olds two sound contrasts: lateral versus rhotic, and labial versus back-of-mouth.

A clear asymmetry appeared only in the younger group, and only for the lateral–rhotic contrast, in a patch of right temporal cortex known for tracking sound detail. The brain response dipped for the harder direction of change, which the authors link to the heavier processing load of the trickier sound. By nine months it had faded. They read the result as evidence that young infants lean on raw acoustic detail before firm sound categories form.
plos-pone-0358244:
Dan Liu, Zhen Zeng, and Ting Li work on locating connected vehicles precisely at city intersections, in a 2026 PLOS ONE article. Satellite positioning signals get blocked by buildings exactly where traffic is densest and most dangerous. Their answer is cooperation: cars and roadside sensors share what they sense so the group can pin down positions that no single vehicle could manage alone.

Their model blends a robust statistical filter, built on belief propagation, with a spatial attention mechanism that weighs which signals matter most. In hardware tests with roadside units, test vehicles, and 5G vehicle links, the combined model beat single methods, with position error around fifteen centimeters and near total coverage. Performance slipped under ring shaped networks, heavy congestion, and communication failures, which the authors flag as open problems.
plos-pone-0358344: Schröder and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on the spongy bone inside the human spine. Using CT scans, they measured how the density of cancellous bone changes with age and sex. This inner bone gives vertebrae much of their strength. Knowing how it thins over life helps doctors judge fracture risk and plan implants that must grip aging bone.
plos-pone-0358444:
Melissa Kennedy led a team of seven archaeologists reporting early findings in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their subject was a group of large stone structures called mustatils, built by Neolithic herders in the lava fields of northwest Saudi Arabia. The site lies in the Harrat Khaybar, a vast old volcanic field.

Kennedy and her co-authors share the first results from digging and survey work at these sites. The remains point to ritual use, which adds new detail to what is known about early cult practice in Arabia. Stone monuments this old change how scholars picture belief and gathering in the region's deep past.
plos-pone-0358644:
Denise Fuchten and three co-workers check whether surveys for ringing ears and for low mood are secretly measuring the same thing, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Ringing distress and depression correlate strongly in patient studies, but the surveys might manufacture part of that link by asking overlapping questions. The team took six tinnitus and seven low mood surveys and mapped every item onto the World Health Organization's functioning classification.

The low mood surveys covered a narrower band of life, fourteen groups against the tinnitus surveys' twenty-three. Seven groups were shared, including sleep, attention, emotion, and energy. Overlap varied wildly by instrument: one tinnitus questionnaire shared as little as a tenth of its content with low mood surveys, another nearly three quarters. One low mood scale overlapped the tinnitus set almost completely. Choosing which pair to use, the authors conclude, can predetermine how entangled the two conditions appear.
plos-pone-0358744:
Tianchen Zheng and Zhidong Dai published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies retired elite athletes in China who are moving into work as school coaches. The focus is occupational adaptation, how these former stars adjust to a very different job after their competing careers end.

Elite athletes retire young, often with fame but narrow training for other work. Teaching sport in schools is a natural next step, yet the classroom demands new skills and identity. Sports authorities planning second careers for athletes, and the schools receiving them, are the readers for an account of this transition.
plos-pone-0359944:
Abiy Shenkut Abebe, Belete Yazie, and Melaku Menale wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about cattle breeding in northwest Ethiopia. Smallholder farmers keep most of the cattle, and breeding programs often fail by ignoring what those farmers want. The authors combine what farmers say they value with what their choices reveal, to set breeding objectives.

Joining both kinds of evidence gives a truer picture of valued traits, from milk yield to hardiness. The authors present the results as evidence for breeding program design, aimed at officials who set goals for Ethiopia's smallholder herds.
pmc-10655444:
Yong Tang and co-authors compare, in a 2023 eye surgery study, two ways to clear the gel inside the eye during a lens fixation operation. The operation fixes a replacement lens for patients whose own lens has slipped out of place. Surgeons can clear the gel from the front or through the back wall of the eye.

The study covered fifty-three patients and fifty-six eyes, split between the two routes. Hidden retinal holes or weak spots appeared in about one in ten eyes. Vision results and complication rates after six months were much the same for both routes. Age and the state of the gel and retina should guide the choice, the authors say.
pmc-10659644:
Yan-Hong Ma, Yin Yang, Jing-Hui Li, Bo-Chen Yao, Qing-Liang Chen, Lian-Qun Wang, Zhi-Gang Guo, and Su-Zhi Guo wrote this study, put out in two thousand twenty-three. It asks how two genes, NDUFB11 and NDUFS3, link to atherosclerosis and to venous thrombosis.

The team merged data sets on artery disease and chronic stress, then ran gene contrast and network analyses to find core genes. Eight stood out, most tied to the cell's energy plant, the mitochondrion, and its inner membrane. Enrichment checks pointed to energy and protein pathways. A database cross-check tied the core genes to key diseases, and cell-level blot tests backed the findings. The pair may serve as markers for both ills.
pmc-10660444:
Roman and co-authors describe a UK cohort built to track the long-term health of childhood cancer survivors. The cohort grew out of a national case-control study run in the early 1990s. It includes 3,125 people who had cancer before age 15 and survived at least five years. A comparison group holds 7,156 people of the same age and sex from the general public.

Follow-up now runs through links to national health records. The linked data cover deaths, new cancers, and hospital care. That setup lets the team compare survivors' later health care with typical patterns. Findings can show which late effects need more follow-up care. The profile paper lays out the cohort's design and data sources.
pmc-10693444:
Michael Peters and co-authors watch how heart cells organize themselves on synthetic fiber mats in two thousand twenty-three. In real organs, a fiber web called the extracellular matrix holds cells in patterns that keep tissue working. Lab-grown tissues copy that web with spun fibers, but cell types may answer its cues in unlike ways.

Three heart cell types, muscle, valve, and vessel lining, were seeded onto mats spun by a rotary jet method at varied alignment levels. The cells crept into the web and reshaped their inner skeletons to match the fibers. Valve cells aligned most eagerly on mid-aligned mats. The results guide scaffold design for each heart tissue.
pmc-10693644:
Shailab Shrestha, Najwa Taib, Simonetta Gribaldo, and Aimee Shen studied how a gut pathogen divides its cells, in a paper from twenty twenty-three. Two enzymes were thought to be vital for building the wall segment that splits a bacterium in two, in all species. The pathogen in view causes severe gut infection and forms hardy spores.

To their surprise, this species lacks the usual enzyme pair. Its wall enzymes have shifted to serve spore making instead, and normal division runs on a different enzyme of a broad class. That enzyme had never been cast as the core divider before. The authors suggest the odd division machinery could be a unique drug target in this group of bacteria.
pmc-10694144:
Soheila Sharafinia and others built a magnetic light catalyst in two thousand twenty-three. Toxic waste needs fast, visible-light cleanup. Their hybrid layers carbon nitride sheets with two partners. One partner is a nitrogen-doped perovskite mineral. The other is a zinc ferrite that acts as a magnet. A simple reflux method built the stack.

Many tests proved what the mix could do. Breakdown topped ninety percent for several poisons. Rhodamine dye was among the test targets. Short light times were enough for cleanup. Partner synergy boosted reactive oxygen output. Its magnet pull allows easy pickup after use. One mix did best in the series. Real water treatment could use such tools again and again.
pmc-10694944:
Yesica López and colleagues give the first genetic proof that opossums in Colombia host the bacterium Borrelia puertoricensis. Borrelia species are disease-causing spirochetes with complex spread cycles, and many use rodents as reservoir hosts. Spirochetes that look like Borrelia had been seen in opossums more than once. But genetic proof that these marsupials host them was missing.

The team tested fifty-three stored serum samples from common opossums near Colosó, in Colombia's Sucre department. A real-time PCR test for the genus, aimed at a ribosomal gene, screened the samples. About one in five tested positive. Positive samples went through more PCR and Sanger sequencing of two genes. One went to next-generation sequencing. Reads matched Borrelia genomes, and typing sequences gave the species.
pmc-10697044:
Li Xia Yu and six colleagues pool prior studies on Klotho, a protein tied to aging. They ask whether low blood levels of it warn of worse days ahead for people with diabetic kidney disease. Single studies had disagreed. The team gathered 17 studies with 5,682 patients in all.

Low Klotho showed no firm link with the amount of protein in the urine. But it did track with worse outcomes: faster kidney decline, more eye and heart harm, and higher death risk. Age, study design, and kidney function at the start may explain some of the spread between studies. The authors say Klotho may serve as a warning marker, but more work must prove its worth.
pmc-10704744:
Meier and co-authors ask Rwandan stakeholders what shapes the labor market for health supply chain workers. Good supply chains for medicines need skilled managers at every level. Rwanda faces gaps in that workforce's size and training. The team interviewed 39 stakeholders in group and solo sessions in 2019. Interviewees spanned those who run the system and those who train or supply workers. Views covered both demand for and supply of such staff.

Themes point to training limits and unclear career paths among the drags. Demand signals from health programs also shape hiring. The study gives planners a map of where the market fails. Fixes can then target the true bottlenecks.
pmc-10712244:
Ofhani Prudance Musekwa and Lufuno Makhado explore, in a 2023 case study, what families face when they care for a person living with epilepsy. Caregivers do much of the daily work of seizure care, yet their own grasp of the condition and the help they get from professionals are rarely examined. The study's title signals that the strain runs deeper than anxiety alone.

Fifteen family members took part in face-to-face interviews: eleven parents and four siblings, most of them the main caregiver. Two themes emerged from the accounts. One covered hands-on practice, how families handle seizures and treatment. The other covered knowledge, counseling, and support, where families felt thin backing from health workers. The authors conclude that caregivers need care themselves, and that stronger support would lift standards for the whole family.
pmc-10713244:
Mei-Feng Chen and six colleagues investigated a protein called EDIL3 as a possible protector of joint cartilage. Damaged human cartilage contains much more EDIL3 than undamaged cartilage, but its effect was unknown. Agents that prevent cartilage cell loss and matrix breakdown are needed against osteoarthritis. The twenty twenty-three study used human cartilage plugs in the lab and mice that develop osteoarthritis spontaneously.

Giving EDIL3 protein kept cartilage cells evenly distributed and preserved their numbers in the plugs. In mice, it slowed disease progression and maintained matrix-producing cells. Breakdown of aggrecan, a key matrix component, was reduced. Damage scores fell and the bone plate under the cartilage became more porous. The results suggest EDIL3 actively defends cartilage rather than merely marking damage, making it a candidate therapy.
pmc-10717444:
Xiao Li and ten co-authors built a lab model of COVID-19 in heart cells, in a study published in two thousand twenty-three. They grew heart muscle cells from human stem cells and infected them with the virus that causes COVID-19. Then they tracked the cells' protein mix hour by hour as the infection ran its course.

The protein pattern changed in clear stages. Early on, the virus hit the cells' fat and energy systems. Later, it weakened their power to repair damaged DNA. Each stage carried its own set of changed proteins, which the team read against maps of how the virus interacts with human proteins. That work pointed to drug targets matched to each stage. The authors argue for care that fits the stage of illness, found early.
pmc-10719544:
Anthony Kweki and co-authors review trial proof in a 2023 paper on training heart specialists with simulation. Heart and vessel care has grown more complex, and most procedures now thread tools through the skin to cut patient risk. Trainees need much hands-on exposure to gain skill, yet practice on real patients carries the risk of errors and harm before that skill is won.

Simulation offers a way to build skill away from the bedside. The review gathers randomized controlled trials in cardiology and vessel medicine from 2010 onward, from any country, that test whether simulator training moves skills to real work. The authors weigh how the trials were run and what they found. Their summary can help training programs decide where simulators earn their cost.
pmc-10727544:
Ayse Erbakan and co-authors report a 2023 study of close, intensive care for people with type 2 diabetes whose blood sugar was far above target. All patients had a key long-term sugar measure at or above a high threshold, but their past paths differed. Some were newly diagnosed, some had slipped from good control, and others had run high for a long time.

The team split patients into four groups by that past pattern and gave all of them three months of intensive treatment with close follow-up. They then judged how well the care worked in each group. The design tests a fair question: does a patient's sugar history change how much tight, short-term care can help? The answer can guide how clinics spend effort on the hardest cases.
pmc-10735544:
Nancy Kusmaul reflects on aging policy advocacy in social work in this 2023 paper. She writes as an alumna of the Health and Aging Policy Fellows Program. That program has trained aging experts for over ten years through placements in Congress, federal agencies, and advocacy groups. Its alumni network exceeds 150 fellows from many professions.

Kusmaul is a mid career social work faculty member in the non residential track. She recounts lessons from her fellowship year and how they shaped later policy work. Alumni keep shaping aging policy as officials, academics, and advocates. Her account shows social workers concrete paths into policy roles. The motto she cites is that networks get things done.
pmc-10736244:
McMullen and Fisher discuss how to measure the goals, priorities, and preferences of people in nursing homes in twenty twenty-three. Evidence shows that the goals of those who live there are often missed during care. If care matched those goals, outcomes could improve and gaps between groups could shrink. A twenty twenty-two National Academies report urged better measures of the care experience.

The talk covers a subcommittee plan to add such measures to federal quality programs. It sets out how candidate measures of resident experience would be found and tested. One proposed measure checks whether the care a person gets matches the goals that person stated. Reporting results in public would support shared decision making and open debate. The speakers frame the work as reform that empowers residents and families.
pmc-10736944:
Alfons Ramel tests whether nutrition therapy after hospital discharge helps older adults in Iceland, in work published in 2023. The therapy followed a standard care process and lasted six months. It included home visits, phone calls, and free delivery of energy- and protein-rich foods and supplements.

The trial split 106 patients over age 65 between therapy and usual care before they left a geriatric unit. The therapy group gained weight and ate more than controls. Fewer of them were readmitted to hospital at one, six, and twelve months, and their stays were shorter at every check. Emergency visits, deaths, and moves to long-term care did not differ. Ramel argues the therapy is of real clinical value for discharged older adults.
pmc-10737244:
Lydia Li, Rita Hu, Jay Kayser, and Joonyoung Cho track well-being across the move into widowhood. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, uses nine waves of yearly data from Medicare members. At the start, more than three thousand seven hundred people were married. Five hundred ten lost a spouse during the study years.

Right after a death, low mood rose and good feelings fell. Then, over the next years, low mood eased and good feelings rose again. Near four years out, both trends bent back a bit. The authors use each person as their own base, so the shifts shown are real within-person change.
pmc-10737744:
Felicia Gabrielsson-Järhult and Ingemar Kåreholt chart telemedicine use across ages in two Swedish regions from 2020 to 2022. Cheap, subsidized care raised fears that video visits would inflate costs and widen gaps. All private remote consults in the area were counted. About 106,000 people held 343,000 consults over the three years.

Visit counts per person barely differed by age group. The share of people using the service differed hugely, though. Use among those over sixty-five stayed low and swung with the pandemic months. Peaks hit just over twenty percent for the younger-old group, then slid back down. The authors conclude the age gap in digital care remains wide.
pmc-10738644:
Qu and Burr studied COVID-19 worries and depression in older Americans in twenty twenty-three. Worries covered personal health, family health, money, getting help, and the future. The team asked whether race, ethnicity, and education changed how strongly worry linked to depression.

They used a national sample of adults over fifty from the twenty twenty Health and Retirement Study. Depression meant three or more symptoms on a standard scale. Higher worry, overall and in each domain, meant higher depression risk. One link differed by race: worry about the future tied less strongly to depression among Black older adults than White older adults. Education did not change the links. The authors urge providers to reach vulnerable older adults in future emergencies.
pmc-10739144:
Laura Klepacz, Jeremy Hamm, and Eric Cerino study uneven thinking skills in a 2023 paper drawn from a national US sample. A person's scores can vary across mental tasks, a spread called cognitive dispersion. Past work hints that a wide spread may warn of later decline. Yet the field is young, and the traits that go with spread in the general public were not well mapped.

The team used the Midlife in the United States study, with more than four thousand adults. They built the spread from six tasks that span several mental domains and compared it with each person's average score and background traits. In a twist on past findings, wider spread here lined up with protective traits, both mental and social. The result urges care before spread is read as a simple danger sign.
pmc-10739444:
Wadkin and five co-authors review how computers help study human stem cells for eye medicine in this two thousand twenty-three paper. Stem cells hold promise for eye repair and for modeling eye disease in the lab. Grown in dishes or as small organoids, they let researchers test drugs without patients. But their behavior is complex and spans many scales. Reading that behavior calls for new tools.

The review covers image analysis and computational modeling of these cells. Models blend smooth and discrete methods to track cell fate and shape. Such tools can clarify how cells sort themselves and respond to cues. They may also speed diagnosis and therapy design. The authors map where the field stands and what it needs next. The audience is eye researchers and modelers alike.
pmc-10740944:
Ye Zhao and co-authors read the gene response of sea cucumber larvae to the twin stresses of a changing ocean in a 2023 study. The animal builds a light skeleton, so acid water and warm water both threaten its early life. The team raised larvae under two temperatures and two carbon dioxide levels, pairing today's ocean with end-of-century projections.

They tracked development and measured gene activity at four early stages, from blastula to the final larval form, using RNA sequencing. Acid conditions clearly harmed growth and development. The gene patterns show which pathways the larvae switch on to cope, and where coping fails. Sea cucumbers support fisheries and ecosystems across Asia's coasts. Knowing the molecular stress points helps predict which stocks will bend or break as oceans change.
pmc-10741944:
Andrea Jimenez-Vergara and co-authors grow human neural stem cells on a coating borrowed from the brain's own support cells, in a 2023 study. Stem cells could repair damaged nerves, but expanding them in the dish usually costs them their versatility. Astrocytes, the brain's helper cells, naturally keep stem cells thriving nearby.

The team harvested material secreted by astrocytes and used it as a dish coating. Spectroscopy and electron microscopy characterized the layer. Stem cells on it multiplied faster than on standard coatings, including one derived from reprogrammed human cells. Markers of stemness stayed expressed while early neuron markers behaved as hoped, suggesting growth without premature specialization. A coating that expands stem cells while keeping their options open is a practical step toward cell therapies for nerve repair.
pmc-10742244:
Lukas Scheipner and a large team published a urology study in twenty twenty-three asking whether a patient's other illnesses predict bladder cancer coming back. Non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer recurs often after resection. The Charlson-Deyo index, a standard tally of comorbid diseases, had never been tested as a recurrence predictor.

Records covered one thousand seventy-two patients treated between twenty ten and twenty eighteen. About sixty-one percent carried a high comorbidity burden. Their recurrence rates ran higher at both one and six years of follow-up. After adjustment, a high score independently raised recurrence risk by about forty-two percent. The finding suggests general health status belongs in bladder cancer follow-up planning, not just tumor features.
pmc-10742644:
Tian Li and co-authors present a 2023 protein census of a vinegar bacterium facing its own acid. Acetobacter pasteurianus both makes and endures strong acetic acid, the heart of vinegar brewing. The team grew it with none, mid, and high starting acid and read its proteins at two growth phases with a label-free method. Over two thousand proteins were counted. Under acid, the early phase leaned on fat burning while muting core cycles and energy paths.

The growth phase flipped the play, feeding acid into the main cycle and sugar paths. Phase-timed retooling, it seems, is the tolerance trick. Brewers gain named proteins to breed or tune for bolder vinegar runs.
pmc-10743044:
Ting Ding and eleven colleagues published a 2023 study on a gene that shapes flowering in rapeseed, also called Brassica napus. The gene, BnPLP1, is a match for a known gene in the model plant Arabidopsis. That gene adds fatty tags to proteins, a step that steers growth and stress response.

Plant tests show BnPLP1 speeds flowering time. It also makes plants taller and lengthens the main flower stalk. The team found two such genes in the rapeseed genome and cloned the first for study. Traits like flowering time decide when a crop can be sown and picked. A gene that moves all three traits is a useful handle for breeders.
pmc-10748144:
Soufyane Hba and co-authors review chalcones, a family of plant compounds, as candidate drugs for colon cancer, in work published in 2023. Colon cancer is a major global health burden and needs new treatment approaches. Chalcones can interfere with several signalling pathways that drive the cancer's growth and spread.

The review covers how natural chalcones and their derivatives act on cancer cells. It stresses that most evidence is still pre-clinical, so safety and efficacy in patients remain unproven. Open problems include how to order treatments, how resistance arises, and how chalcones pair with other therapies. Loading chalcones into nanoparticles may deliver them to tumours more effectively. The authors map both the promise and the work still needed before clinical use.
pmc-10750044:
Ya-Xi Luo, Ying-Hai Zhu, and Xiu-Qing Yao map a decade of research on exercise for older adults, charting where the field concentrated and where it is heading. Healthy aging research has boomed as populations gray. Their bibliometric study pulled nearly twenty-eight thousand publications from the Web of Science covering twenty thirteen to twenty twenty-two.

Annual output more than doubled across the decade. Keyword co-occurrence sorted the literature into five major clusters, and co-citation analysis traced the knowledge base's bursts and evolution. A bibliometric toolkit tracked how themes shifted year by year. The authors also mapped which countries, institutions, and researchers collaborate most. The result is a visual atlas meant to guide newcomers and funders to hotspots and gaps.
pmc-10769544:
Ha-Eun Lee and Jang-Seu Ki report the complete mitochondrial genome of the mauve stinger jellyfish, in two thousand twenty-three. The jellyfish is a well-known stinging species, yet its full small genome had not been read before. Mitochondrial genomes are widely used to trace how species relate to each other.

The genome proved to be a straight molecule, unusual among animals, with a familiar set of protein and RNA genes. Two extra reading frames sat at one end, as in its relatives. Its gene layout matched other jellyfish of the same class. A family tree built from thirteen protein genes placed it closest to the Chrysaora group of jellyfish.
pmc-10776044:
Jingzhuang Zhao and six colleagues sequence the complete mitochondrial genome of a Chinese loach fish, Triplophysa nanpanjiangensis, for the first time. The genus is a favorite for studying how geology shapes evolution in Asian highlands. Using nanopore sequencing, they assembled the circular genome of 16,558 base pairs.

It holds the standard set: twenty-two transfer RNA genes, thirteen protein-coding genes, two ribosomal RNA genes, and one control region. A phylogenetic tree places the species as sister to Triplophysa zhenfengensis within the genus. The authors present the genome as a new resource for molecular phylogeny of this diverse fish group. Such references support both evolutionary studies and species identification in the field.
pmc-10811144:
Hannah Alsdurf and co-authors measure the staff time needed to grow care for latent tuberculosis. Latent infection means the germ rests in the body with no illness yet. World health leaders urge more treatment of this stage to end the disease by 2035. The study, published in 2023, watched health workers through full workdays at twenty-four sites in five lands.

Watches ran before and after a push to strengthen latent care. At sites with the push, time on latent care rose by nine percent. Time on active disease care fell by eleven percent in the same sites. Control sites showed no such shift. The authors warn that growth in latent care needs new staff, or active care will lose time.
pmc-10822944:
Mao Li and colleagues measure maize roots with the mathematics of shape itself, in this study from twenty twenty-three. Linking genes to plant form is biology's grand mapping problem, and roots are its hard case: branched three-dimensional systems flattened by usual phenotyping into a few hand-picked numbers. The team digitized whole root systems of young maize from a mapping population bred for nitrogen research.

Three lenses were compared: eighty-four conventional traits, a topological method, persistent homology, that reads branching shape without pre-deciding what matters, and the combined trait space. Each lens found mostly different gene loci, meaning each sees variation the others miss. Root form, in other words, is not close to exhausted by standard measures. The authors argue that data-driven shape traits belong in the genotype-to-phenotype map, especially for organs too complex for a ruler.
pmc-10869544:
Kihyoun Park and nine colleagues published a study of a new drug candidate against gout. Gout is caused by monosodium urate crystals that trigger the NLRP3 inflammasome, an immune complex that drives painful inflammation. A protein called NEK7 is essential for switching that complex on, making it a drug target.

The team designed NEK7 inhibitors from a family of thienopyrimidine compounds, screening them by kinome profiling. In macrophages from mouse bone marrow, the compounds were tested for their ability to block the release of interleukin-1 beta, the inflammasome's main output, after crystal stimulation. They also checked the binding between NLRP3 and NEK7 directly. A selective NEK7 blocker could calm gout flares at their source.
pmc-10885344:
Mohammed Behairy and seven co-authors test whether a single letter change in an immune gene tilts the odds of two skin diseases, in a study published in 2023. The gene makes mannose-binding lectin, a patrol protein of the innate immune system. One common variant weakens it, and variants of this kind often track with autoimmune illness.

The diseases are psoriasis and vitiligo, one causing scaly inflamed plaques, the other destroying skin pigment. The team combined computer predictions of the variant's effect on the protein with genotyping of 489 people, patients and controls. Real-time PCR read each person's version of the gene. Pairing computation with case data lets the authors argue both mechanism and association, a template for variant studies in other immune conditions.
pmc-10985744:
Estera Banasik and three co-authors review COVID-19 in bowel disease patients in a 2023 paper. Data from East-Central Europe were scarce, so they gathered cases from a Polish specialty center in the pre-vaccine period. Among several hundred patients, about one in eleven caught the virus. Most cases were mild; about one in five needed hospital care. No deaths or short-term complications occurred.

Severe cases had more active bowel disease and more steroid use, and none were on biologic drugs. Longer illness tracked with more other conditions. A quarter of infected patients developed new gut symptoms. The authors say the bowel disease itself did not raise infection risk.
pmc-11003644:
Alex le May and Lucie Hazelgrove-Planel ask whether advocacy groups can escape grant dependence in this 2023 paper. The survey covers grantees of AmplifyChange, a fund for sexual and reproductive health and rights. Civil society groups drive campaigns, policy debate, and inclusion of excluded voices. Nearly all of them run mostly on grants.

Tracking global funding for this field is itself difficult. Available trend data uses broad population and reproductive health categories. The authors map what other income the surveyed groups actually have. Membership fees, services, and donations play small roles for most. Grant cycles leave advocacy exposed to donor shifts. Diversifying income is easy to urge and hard to do, the survey suggests.
pmc-11225444:
Bruno Basil and five co-authors measured how common diabetes in pregnancy has become in Makurdi, Nigeria. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, deals with gestational diabetes. Its load climbs across sub-Saharan Africa. A true current rate can steer policy and care. The team ran a forward watch at many hospitals. Two hundred eighty-one pregnant women were read for traits and risk marks in the early weeks.

A standard sugar drink test came at the set mid span of pregnancy. Rates and the top risk traits were then weighed. Readers who run mother care in the region get a fresh count of a rising ill. That count can shape screen plans for clinics with thin means.
pmc-11538544:
Abebe Fola and co-authors track malaria drug resistance markers in southern Zambia across six years, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Samples from eight health centers were genotyped with a targeted probe method, covering most of over four hundred fifty infections. Validated artemisinin resistance mutations stayed rare.

One mutation tied to slow drug clearance in Africa reached about thirteen percent and rose over time, with signs of selection. A partner-drug tolerance pattern also grew. Five new mutations in the same gene appeared at low rates in later years. Resistance to an older drug pair sat near total. Policy watch is the clear message.
pmc-11571844:
Ludo Masole, Chikwendu Ede, and Adelin Muganza published a burn care study in two thousand twenty-three on a blood marker after surgery. Procalcitonin rises with bacterial infection and can signal sepsis. Burn patients are at high risk, but surgery itself may move the marker.

Thirty-four patients were recruited around burn wound cleaning surgery. Blood was drawn on the day of surgery and the three days after, with cultures on the first and last days. Marker levels rose over the days and sat above the normal cut-off in most patients either way. By day three, levels differed clearly between patients with positive and negative cultures. The authors suggest burn units need a higher cut-off, though the group was too small to set one.
pmc-11576944:
Julie McGeoch and Malcolm McGeoch wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It reports finding hemoglycin, a polymer first identified in meteorites, in ordinary sea foam collected from two Rhode Island beaches.

Cosmic dust rains onto Earth constantly, and the same polymer has turned up in living and fossil stromatolites. The team concentrated the foam's surface-loving molecules with a solvent extraction. Mass spectrometry identified the polymer directly, or through its breakdown pattern. Leftover isotope enrichment pointed to an origin beyond Earth. The authors suggest the polymer's tough lattices may help sea foam hold its bubble structure. Its lightness, they add, could come from sunlight splitting bonds and releasing hydrogen. The claim, if it holds, means space-borne material lands in the surf today, not only in ancient rocks.
pmc-11580244:
Lydia Kaduka and co-authors published a study in 2024 on heart disease prevention in Kenya. Heart and vessel disease is rising fast in the country and straining clinics. Markets are busy social hubs that health services have barely used. The team tested whether clinics and markets could run prevention stalls together.

They worked in one county in western Kenya with about 590 thousand people. Thirty-five stakeholders from health and other fields mapped what such stalls would need. Surveys then checked clinics and markets for readiness. Both had basic buildings and clear leadership. Most clinics lacked key heart drugs, and no clinic-market link existed yet. Still, both sides were willing to partner. The authors list the gaps that must close before stalls can open.
pmc-11580344:
Wasnyo and a large team report a study from twenty twenty-four on how teen diet and activity habits group together. Teens in poorer countries face rising long-term disease risk, yet habit data are sparse. The team surveyed over five hundred teens in Cameroon, Jamaica, and South Africa. They sorted teens by wealth level around home and school. Surveys scored food habits, food knowledge, active time, and screen time. A grouping method then sorted teens into three habit clusters.

Food knowledge and healthy food intake scored poorly at all sites. High screen time grouped with weaker food scores in a steady pattern. That pattern held across wealth levels in at least two cities. The authors say cutting screen time could ripple into better food habits. They back joint programs over single-habit ones.
pmc-11585244:
Jun Chun and co-authors show that a protein powder borrowed from a crop fungus makes potatoes grow better and shrug off cold, in a 2024 paper. The protein, VDAL, is a weapon the fungus Verticillium dahliae secretes, yet at the right dose it boosts growth and yield in rice, wheat, and cotton. Potatoes, grown from tubers rather than seed, had barely been tested. The team treated pre-basic seed tubers and watched both shoots and roots.

Treated tubers sprouted better and grew sturdier plants above and below ground. Yields rose by up to about nineteen percent in greenhouse and field trials. Gene activity tracking and hormone measures pointed at cytokinin, a growth hormone, as the middleman. Cold resistance told the same story: treated tubers withstood late-spring cold, but a drug that blocks cytokinin erased the advantage. The authors frame VDAL as a cytokinin-driven growth aid.
pmc-11585544:
Gronberg and five co-authors study a speech linked gene in songbirds, in work from twenty twenty-four. Loss of function in the SETBP1 gene causes a human disorder with speech deficits. How the gene acts in brain areas for learned vocal sounds was poorly known.

Male zebra finches are a classic model for vocal learning. The team mapped where SETBP1 appears in the song system of the brain. The finch gene had more parts and forms than the human one. The protein sat alongside other known speech linked proteins in key song nuclei. Levels in one nucleus were higher in birds that sang, hinting at a direct role.
pmc-11586444:
Melissa Lenert, Emily Debner, and Michael Burton used mice in two thousand twenty-four to test whether feeling nerves help control the ovaries. Hormone treatments for fertility problems can cause unwanted side effects, so new pathways matter. They removed a metabolism gene called LKB1 only from sensory neurons in female mice.

Females without the gene had fewer nerves reaching the ovary and faster egg follicle turnover, yet they produced larger litters. Male partners carrying the same change had no effect on fertility, pointing to a female-specific pathway. Fertility researchers gain a fresh lead: the energy use of sensory nerves shapes reproduction itself.
pmc-11590344:
Jennifer Pillay and co-authors published this review set in 2024 on stopping falls among older adults who live at home. A fifth to a third of seniors fall each year, and falls bring fractures, lost function, and heavy costs. The set was built to guide a Canadian task force. One review weighed gains and harms of many non-drug programs. Two more asked how patients value outcomes and which programs they prefer.

The team swept four data banks and leaned on an earlier review for older trials. Programs ranged from exercise to home checks, and a network method let unlike programs be compared through shared rivals. Outcomes ran from falls and hip fractures to quality of life and long-term care entry. The authors frame the work as the evidence base for national advice on fall prevention in primary care.
pmc-11600644:
Li and a large team present a trial from twenty twenty-four on chest epidural anesthesia and lung pressure in belly surgery. Sixty adults having major upper abdominal surgery split into two groups. One group gets epidural plus general anesthesia; the other gets general alone. The epidural group reaches a lower minimum driving pressure during ventilation. Collapsed lung areas after surgery also occur less often there. Overall lung complication rates do not differ significantly, though. Driving pressure itself is the lone factor tied to complications in their models.

The authors credit the epidural with easing lung strain during surgery. Adding pressure-guided ventilation erases the edge for complications. Intensive care stays and death rates are tracked as safety checks.
pmc-11600944:
Xiaofang Fu and five co-authors ask whether moving more protects the lungs in a specific early pattern of harm, in a study published in twenty twenty-four. The pattern keeps a normal ratio between two breathing measures while one of them runs low. It is seen as an early stage on the road to chronic lung disease.

The team used survey data from United States adults gathered between twenty and twenty twelve. People with the pattern reported the least activity of three groups, below even those with full lung disease. After adjusting for other factors, high activity levels linked to lower odds of the pattern. The link bent rather than running straight, and it ran strongest in adults carrying extra weight. The authors back activity as a prevention step.
pmc-11605644:
Muragaki and six co-authors report a study from twenty twenty-four on how low-grade brain tumors come back after surgery. The team looked back at eighty-one adults whose tumors had returned. The group had fifty-one cases of one tumor type and thirty of a second type. Follow-up after the first surgery lasted a median of just under seven years, as the study reports it.

Most tumors came back at the same spot, and most came back more than two years later. Early return, fast growth, and return at a new spot all linked to shorter survival. Taking out more than ninety percent of the tumor at first surgery softened those gaps. The work helps doctors plan care after surgery.
pmc-11605944:
Dorina Esendağlı and a large team study long hospital stays for COPD flare-ups in a 2024 paper. Flare-ups of chronic obstructive lung disease raise the risk of harm and death. Some patients stay far longer than others, and the team sought the factors behind long stays.

The DiMECO study followed 434 patients admitted with flare-ups at many centers. A stay of nine days or more counted as prolonged. Candidate factors were grouped into four pillars: the patient, the disease, the treatment, and hospital use. Early analyses flagged which factors tracked with long stays. The goal is to spot hard-to-manage flare-ups sooner.
pmc-11606444:
Young-Cheul Shin and a large team solve the shapes of a signaling enzyme that keeps itself switched off, in a twenty twenty-four study. The enzyme, PLC-gamma-2, relays signals from cell surface receptors. A multi-part brake region holds it quiet, but how the parts work together was unclear. The team froze the enzyme in three off-state shapes using crystal and electron microscopy.

The brake parts grip the core loosely and flexibly, with one part touching a tail helix never seen in contact before. A fourth shape showed the enzyme bound to a growth receptor's active part. The maps explain how the brake loosens for activation and guide future work on this switch.
pmc-11612044:
Axel Bartoli and eight co-authors build a half-auto scan tool that sizes the kidney ground each artery feeds, to plan aorta repair in folks with a joined horseshoe kidney. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Such kidneys bear extra arteries in odd counts and paths, so cuts risk wide harm. The tool tags artery mouths and ends on scans and gives each patch of kidney to its nearest end.

Mean artery count was four, and mean whole kidney size near three hundred sixty units. Loss guessed from pre-surgery scans tracked true loss post-surgery with a tight link. Two readers matched well. The team says the tool can show which arteries can be cut with care.
pmc-11615344:
Eilers and co-authors map genes for making orange plant pigments across a family of lactic acid bacteria. The pigments, carotenoids, guard cells and find wide use in food and cosmetics. Some bacteria that do not use sunlight still make a C30 form of them. The team screened over 4,200 bacterial genomes for pigment gene clusters. Genes named crtMN, key to the C30 pigment, showed in about 7.7% of species.

These genes turned up in 14 of 34 genera in the family. They seem to have been gained more than once, and moved sideways in some groups. The pattern hints the pigment helps bacteria fit insect-linked and wandering lifestyles. The study ties gene spread to habitat.
pmc-11615644:
Johanna Stedt and four co-authors use drone video to watch harbour porpoises hunt in Danish coastal waters, in a two thousand twenty-four marine biology paper. Porpoises burn energy fast and eat varied prey, but wild foraging is notoriously hard to observe.

Foraging appeared in almost sixty percent of the daylight drone recordings. Porpoises chased single fish and whole schools, hunted alone and in groups of varying size, and switched tactics with context. The authors argue some strategies spread through information transfer and social learning. The footage gives rare direct insight into a flexible predator, and underlines how much porpoises depend on coastal feeding areas threatened by fisheries bycatch.
pmc-11616644:
Jorgelina Marino and co-authors report twin disease outbreaks in endangered Ethiopian wolves in this 2024 paper. Rabies and canine distemper struck the same wolf population in 2019. One wolf was infected with both viruses at once. Close monitoring of the packs let the team detect both outbreaks as they unfolded.

Both diseases can arrive from domestic dogs that live near the wolves. Partial vaccination cover did not prevent the double outbreak. The authors warn that models built for one disease may understate extinction risk. Two diseases at once can hit harder than either alone. Conservation teams working near dog populations should plan for simultaneous outbreaks, not just single ones.
pmc-11621844:
Robert Boyd and Peter Richerson published a reflective essay in twenty twenty-four on the field they helped found: cultural evolution. About fifty years ago, work by Cavalli-Sforza, Feldman, and the two authors began applying population biology's ideas to how culture changes. The seed became a vital field with many publications and its own scientific society.

Writing as insiders, they recount the origins from their own vantage and take stock of what the approach has explained. They close by naming the questions still open, including where the field might head next, hedged with a parenthetical maybe. The essay doubles as memoir and agenda: a founding generation handing the unsolved problems to its successors.
pmc-11629644:
Hang Yu, Yuan Tian, Long Rong, Yunlong Cai, Guanyi Liu, Yan He, and Xinyue Guo test a camera capsule steered by magnet and cable in two thousand twenty-four. Swallowed camera capsules let doctors view the upper gut with no sedation. Guiding the capsule well, and seeing enough of the stomach wall, are the main challenges.

Thirty volunteers at a Beijing hospital swallowed the capsule between September and November of two thousand twenty-two. A robot arm with a magnet, plus a thin cable, steered it through the food pipe and stomach. No harms were reported, and the stomach exam took about half an hour on average. Steering worked in all cases, and most of the stomach lining was seen in most volunteers.
pmc-11630844:
Taro Kono and co-authors report a case in two thousand twenty-four of emergency heart surgery on a newborn. The baby was born with a missing heart valve, called tricuspid atresia, and a badly narrowed path out of the right side of the heart. Blood flow to his lungs depended on a fetal vessel that should stay open after birth.

That vessel had closed early, and after birth no trace of it could be found. The baby's blood oxygen sat near sixty percent. Surgeons placed a shunt at once to route blood to the lungs. Flow through the narrowed path then proved unstable, so that route was blocked off, and recovery went smoothly.
pmc-11636544:
Qiu and Xu published in twenty twenty-four a study building a gene test for Alzheimer's disease from a cell process called phase separation. In this process, cell contents sort into droplet-like zones. The process is linked to several brain diseases, but good diagnostic markers are scarce. The pair gathered one hundred forty-nine related genes from databases. Network and regression tools narrowed that list to six key genes.

A risk model built on those six genes sorted patients well in several data sets. Accuracy stayed high in training, internal checks, and two outside sets. The genes tie to oxidative stress, cell death, and cancer pathways. Their levels also tracked immune cell presence in tissue. The authors offer the signature as an aid to earlier detection.
pmc-11640044:
Eva Meixner and a large team review in 2024 the blood side effects of strong treatment for cervical cancer. The standard care mixes radiation with a weekly chemo drug, and newer trials add more drugs at the cost of more blood harm. The team asked what drives that harm and whether it changes outcomes.

They reviewed one hundred forty-seven patients treated over two decades. Severe low white cell counts were rare, and no case reached the most dangerous grade. Hemoglobin, the red cell measure, fell most after the fourth week. Patients whose hemoglobin sank lowest had worse local control of the cancer. Those who needed transfusions also fared worse overall. The authors urge close blood care through the full course.
pmc-11641744:
Nicole Nourie and seven co-authors review BK virus infection in kidney transplant care. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. The virus can wake in a grafted kidney and harm it, a top worry after transplant. Blood levels of the virus now sit at the heart of how doctors spot and track active disease.

Gaps stay in flags that can warn of the virus before it blooms, or call how a case will end. Urine tests, antigen hunts, and immune reads are in study. Care today leans on lower immune suppression, with add-on drugs still in doubt. Cell-based immune care is in trials. Watchful testing plus fast action can cut the load.
pmc-11642144:
Marco Di Mauro leads a large team in a pilot study of a lung artery stiffness mark in heart pump patients. The paper is from two thousand twenty-four. A left-sided pump, an LVAD, can leave the right heart to fail soon after the fit. The mark, arterial elastance, gauges the load the right heart pumps against.

They review a small set of past fits at their centres. A third of patients hit right heart failure, split between mid and severe. The newer form of the mark alone does not split severe from the rest. Paired with the pressure in the central vein, both forms split the groups well. The pair can tier risk before the fit.
pmc-11642344:
Adam Cwudziński, Jan Falkus, and Angelika Podolska-Loska braid, in a 2024 study, computer models, water models, and plant data to understand how sulfur is scrubbed from hot metal before steelmaking. The pretreatment's efficiency decides both steel quality and cost. Mixing in the ladle, where reagents meet metal, is where the process lives or dies, and it is hard to watch inside a three-hundred-ton vessel of melt.

A turbulence model, checked against a water mock-up of the ladle, predicted mixing times and power for the full vessel. Feeding those into reaction models gave the transfer-limited rate, with stated limits. Industrial trials then supplied the reality check: the process rate constant swings widely, and sulfur removal lands anywhere from sixty to ninety-eight percent. The authors' point is methodical: only the three views together show which lever governs the rate.
pmc-11642544:
Mirek, Piekło, and Garbacz-Klempka studied how heat cycles slowly damage the grey cast iron moulds used to cast steel ingots, in work published in twenty twenty-four. Each pour heats the mould sharply and each cooling strains it, so cracks grow over time in a process called thermal fatigue.

The team measured temperatures and wall movement on a real foundry mould built for ingots of up to six tons. They used those readings to check a computer model of the heat, stress, and bending in the walls. In the lab, iron samples went through up to sixty heating and cooling rounds that matched real use. Strength and stiffness fell fast in the first ten rounds, and microscope images showed how cracks start and spread. The results point to design changes that could make the moulds last longer.
pmc-11643244:
Qi Jia and co-authors synthesized two lanthanide coordination polymers, two-dimensional networks built from a flexible ring-shaped ligand with six acid arms. The two versions use dysprosium and terbium, and they share the same structure. The team grew the crystals with heat in solvent and mapped their arrangement. The ligand binds while partly stripped of its hydrogen ions, a semi-deprotonated form never before seen for this kind of ligand in polymers.

Measurements on the dysprosium version showed slow magnetic relaxation when a magnetic field was applied, a behavior prized for future memory and quantum devices. The terbium version glowed in the solid state at room temperature, and the team studied that luminescence. The work adds design knowledge for lanthanide materials, a family valued for magnetism and light emission. It shows that flexible multi-arm ligands can yield orderly, predictable networks.
pmc-11644044:
Hugo Duarte and ten colleagues published a materials study in two thousand twenty-four on rigid foams made from plant residues. Tannin foams already serve as fire-safe insulation. Replacing tannin with lignin, a paper industry byproduct, might add water-cleaning power.

Two lignins differing in size and acidity fully replaced tannin in the foam recipe. The alkali lignin foam soaked up methylene blue dye at two hundred twenty milligrams per gram, through a multilayer process. Foams survived at least five use-and-clean cycles. They also resisted flame effectively. The authors pitch the material as a double-duty product: building insulation that can also scrub dye from wastewater. Water scarcity and energy costs motivate the work.
pmc-11649144:
Lilin Zhao, Jinpeng Wang, and Shang Zhang put out a building study in 2024 on highway project budgets in the United Kingdom. Builders add contingency money to bids for surprise costs. Estimators assign very unlike amounts for the same risk. Outside forces on those choices were well studied, but personal ones were not.

The authors talked with a dozen seasoned cost estimators. A follow-up group session checked the talk findings. Thirteen factors shaping those judgments emerged from the talks. Several were personal skills or habits rather than project facts. They included talking with those affected and looking back on past work. Being open to project shocks also mattered. The study argues how estimators judge merits a look beside formal risk models.
pmc-11650244:
Jia-Yi Li and six co-authors test a multi-color glow scan to guide gallbladder keyhole surgery with more ease. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. A green dye glow is now used to spot bile tubes in this surgery and cut harm risk. But the plain one-color glow can wash out weak tube signs and tire the eyes.

Past cases from one Beijing hospital held one hundred fifty-five patients in three groups. One group had no dye, one had one-color glow, and one had multi-color glow. Harm after surgery was low and like in all groups. Surgeons rated the multi-color view as more clear and more kind to the eyes. The team backs its plain use.
pmc-11650444:
Guido and a large team set out a study plan in twenty twenty-four to test better ways to find tuberculosis in Ethiopia. Tuberculosis, a lung disease caused by slow-growing germs, still kills very large numbers of people each year. Most cases occur where money and health care are scarce, so cheap and safe tests matter.

The plan compares chest ultrasound, chest X-ray, and computer-aided reading of X-rays. It covers a broad group of patients, not just people with HIV, and adds deep screening of household contacts. Index cases are confirmed with fast gene tests. The team will weigh how well each method finds disease, and note that ultrasound skill varies by user.
pmc-11650644:
Lukas Kirchner and co-authors published a 2024 study of how a bacterium breaks down daptomycin, a powerful antibiotic. Daptomycin is a last-line treatment for difficult skin and lung infections. A newly found strain resists it at a high level. Two genes in that strain, called drcAB, do the work, and the team asked what they do to the drug.

They placed the gene pair in a laboratory bacterium and switched it on. They then compared drug samples exposed to that strain with plain control samples, using high-resolution mass spectrometry. The gene pair works in two steps. First it attaches a new piece to one part of the drug. Then it cuts the core ring of the drug with water, which destroys its power. Computer-generated breakdown patterns matched the measured ones, which supports the structures the team proposed.
pmc-11651444:
Huaigang Chen, Liu Yang, and three co-authors test if a spine disease causes heart disease. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, looks at ankylosing spondylitis, a long-term swelling of the spine. People with this disease get heart problems more often, but cause and effect are unclear. The team uses genes as a natural test in European data.

Gene traits tied to the spine disease link to higher risk of heart failure. Links also show up for high blood pressure and stroke from a blocked vessel. The effects are small but consistent across checks. The authors ran repeat and stress tests to firm up the claims. The work suggests the spine disease itself adds heart risk.
pmc-11651744:
Qu, Cheng, Liu, and Zhang studied in twenty twenty-four a gene that is high in skin cancer of the melanoma kind. The gene, CTNND2, had been tied to other cancers but not well checked in this one. They read its level in tumor tissue and in cell lines in the lab.

Its level was much higher in tumors than in near skin, and higher in cancer cells than in plain skin cells. When the gene was cut down, cells grew, moved, and spread less in their tests. Grip on key skin glues fell too. A grip path in the cells lost drive when the gene was cut.
pmc-11652644:
Lorenzo Lotti, Costanza Carbonari, Giulio Calvani, and Enio Paris craft a new tube law for soft pipes squeezed unevenly from outside, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Classic laws link pipe area to the in-out pressure gap under even squeeze only. Body tubes, though, face mixed squeeze in real life.

Lab flow through a soft tube mimicked a male urethra at work. The new law matched the lab runs better than classic forms. The authors say the model can extend to many vessel types. Better laws sharpen flow models for care and design alike. Readers get a law that owns up to lopsided loads.
pmc-11653644:
Mohamed Badran and his team build a sticky mixed send kit that joins tiny drug sacs with a gel that feels acid grade, to treat eye ills from fungus. Their 2024 study loads the fungus drug itraconazole for good send to the eye front.

Itraconazole by mouth brings harm through the whole body. Plain use on the eye works in a poor way. Sacs were coated with hyaluronic acid, with chitosan, or with both.
