They were then put into gels that grow thick on the eye. Coats made sacs more large and changed their face charge. Drug load stayed high all through. Plain sacs let the drug out fast. Coated sacs let it out in a slow, firm way. The joined gels showed top thick and flow traits. The chitosan-coated form did in a marked way in more tests told of here.
pmc-11655544:
Arian Zarriz, Baptiste Journaux, and Matthew Powell-Palm measure the lowest point at which salty water can stay liquid under pressure, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. At normal pressure that limit is the eutectic point, but pressure shifts it in heat and mix. They name the absolute limit the cenotectic, meaning universal melt.

Constant-volume freezing and melting tests found the point for several brines. The results bound how thick ice crusts can grow on ocean worlds in our solar system. They also bound the depth of the final ocean left as such a world freezes. A general definition of the point closes the paper.
pmc-11656544:
Xiaohui Luo and Fei Xiang compare oxygen delivery methods during bronchoscopy in a retrospective study from two thousand twenty-four. Patients with low blood oxygen risk dangerous drops during the scope procedure. High-flow nasal oxygen is a stronger support than a standard nasal cannula.

Records covered two hundred thirty-two patients treated over five years. Deep oxygen dips below ninety percent hit under four percent of the high-flow group, against seventeen and a half percent with standard oxygen. Overall adverse events were also far fewer with high-flow support. Better baseline oxygen status protected against dips in both groups. No serious complications occurred either way. The authors conclude high-flow oxygen steadied patients through the procedure.
pmc-11656644:
Sijing Wu and twelve co-authors published a cardiology imaging study in twenty twenty-four linking a simple blood fat ratio to dangerous plaque features. The atherogenic index of plasma combines triglycerides and protective cholesterol into one number. Whether it tracks the fragile plaques that actually rupture was the question.

Optical coherence tomography, a light-based scan inside the artery, was performed in patients with acute coronary syndrome, and three hundred thirty-two were analyzed. Moving from the lowest to highest index quarter, thin-capped plaques rose from nine to fifty-three percent. Macrophage buildup, rupture, and erosion all climbed too. Adjusted analysis kept the index strongly tied to fragile plaque and rupture, supporting it as a cheap risk flag.
pmc-11656944:
Haohui Liu and co-authors built a competency model in 2024 for an overlooked workforce in China's public health system: school actual education teachers. Beyond coaching sport, these teachers deliver health education and raise student health. Yet the country's health services remain unevenly supplied, and nobody had specified what a PE teacher must be able to do in that service role. The authors used grounded theory, a word-based method that builds a model upward from interviews rather than testing a preset scheme.

Forty-eight people, PE teachers and research staff who study them, were chosen purposively from diverse regions of China for semi-ordered interviews, and the transcripts were coded with word-based study software. The resulting model organizes teacher health service competence into three sizes, the first of them health service beliefs, giving education authorities a concrete yardstick for training and testing.
pmc-11657844:
Andrew Kwiringira and co-authors published this study in 2024. It measures what seasonal malaria prevention did for young children in two Ugandan districts. Starting in 2021, children under five got monthly full courses of malaria medicine through the high-transmission season. The team used national health records in a time-series design. They compared the eight rollout months with the fifty-two months before.

In Kotido, malaria cases ran forty-three percent below the level expected without the program. In Moroto, the drop was about twenty-one percent. Both changes cleared statistical checks. Before the rollout, Uganda had not used this approach, though it works across the Sahel. The authors recommend extending it to other high-burden districts. Their numbers suggest a large national gain is within reach.
pmc-11658444:
Shuyin Duan and co-authors test how a blood inflammation index relates to liver fat and liver scarring, in a study from 2024. The index, called SII, blends counts of platelets and two white cell types. Past work tied it to fatty liver, but its link to scarring was less clear.

The team used a national United States survey from 1999 to 2018, with 21,833 adults. Three scores each stood in for scarring and for fat buildup. Higher SII went with more liver fat on all three fat scores, yet with less scarring on all three scarring scores. The links bent rather than running straight, per a flexible curve check. The authors present the split pattern as a fact care teams should weigh.
pmc-11663544:
Jacqueline Itambo, Brenda Owusu, Danielle McCamey, and Diana-Lyn Baptiste published a 2024 discursive review arguing for advanced practice nurse education in sub-Saharan Africa. Advanced practice nurses are trained beyond basic nursing to diagnose, prescribe, and lead care. The region has very few such programs.

The authors searched PubMed, CINAHL, and Google Scholar for evidence on COVID-19's impact in sub-Saharan Africa and on the advanced practice role. The pandemic disrupted routine immunization and facility-based care, raised disease burden, and exposed the fragility of the workforce. They argue the crisis proved the strategic value of advanced nurses, who can keep essential services running when doctors are scarce. The review draws concrete lessons for education policy.
pmc-11667144:
AI tools for reading medical scans work well in the lab, yet almost none reach daily hospital use. Vikash Gupta led a large team of clinicians, researchers, and industry experts who spent years meeting weekly to map why. Their report lays out how radiology work actually flows, where AI stalls on the way in, and what hospitals truly need before a model can join the team.

They offer a sorting scheme for AI uses, backed by real cases of models already running in hospitals. They also point to MONAI, a free open toolkit built by a wide consortium, as a shared base for building models that other sites can copy. Standards, they argue, are the bridge between a good model and a used one.
pmc-11673544:
Belkacem El Amrani and co-authors review the living factors that shape ectomycorrhizal partnerships in two thousand twenty-four. These partnerships join tree roots with fungi that trade nutrients, and they keep forests healthy. The review asks which biological players decide whether such a partnership forms and thrives.

Three themes organize the survey. First comes diversity: richer mixes of host plants and fungi change how the partnerships form and succeed. Second comes host specificity, the close matching between certain fungi and certain trees. Third come microbial interactions, where bacteria and other fungi can help or hinder the main partnership. The authors draw out lessons for managing forests and restoring damaged land.
pmc-11674044:
Zhang and a large team study children born with a faulty back passage who also have a tethered spinal cord in twenty twenty-four. A tethered cord is pinned low in the spine and can harm bowel control. The team reviewed one hundred fourteen children treated at one hospital. They asked which traits raise the odds of the pairing, and whether cord freeing surgery helps bowel function.

Children with mid or high forms of the passage flaw had far higher odds of a tethered cord. Other birth flaws also raised the odds. After cord surgery, constipation eased clearly in children with the low form. For mid and high forms, bowel function tied with peers. The team backs active surgery for such children.
pmc-11674344:
Javier Ros and a large team of co-authors published this cancer study in 2024. It gathers real-world records for patients with metastatic colorectal cancer carrying the BRAF V600E mutation, a group with few options once standard drugs fail. The patients, treated in Spain and Italy, received trifluridine/tipiracil, a chemotherapy pill known to extend survival in hard-to-treat disease. Data on this mutated subgroup had been missing.

Twenty-six patients were included, with a median age of 61. Their cancer stayed quiet for a median of 2.3 months, and median survival was 6.6 months. Patients with favorable traits, fewer spread sites and a slower course, lived longer than those without, though the gap was not statistically firm. General fitness was the clearest survival marker. Side effects were mostly mild drops in blood counts. The authors call the benefit modest and ask for prospective studies.
pmc-11674744:
Yuji Ishino and co-authors look for a simple scan sign that warns of heavy blood loss during spine tumor surgery, in a study from 2024. The surgery removes cancer that has spread to the spine, and heavy bleeding is one of its main risks. The team studied a dark flow signal seen inside tumors on standard MRI scans.

The review covered 88 surgeries at one hospital between 2010 and 2024. The flow signal appeared in 71 patients, and its width averaged 1.8 millimeters. Wider signals linked strongly to greater blood loss during surgery. In the final analysis, the signal width was the strongest single predictor among the factors checked. The authors say surgeons should weigh this easy scan measure when planning how to control bleeding.
pmc-11675244:
Iluta, Nistor, Buruiana, and Dima review the Wnt signaling pathway in tumor biology and cancer stem cells, in a review from twenty twenty-four. Relapse and spread drive most cancer deaths and trace to stem-like cells. Those cells self-renew and resist therapy through pathways like Wnt. Wnt normally guides embryonic development and adult tissue upkeep.

Dysregulated Wnt signaling correlates directly with tumor growth, spread, and drug resistance. Crosstalk with Hedgehog and Notch networks complicates targeted therapy design. Side effects on normal tissues further limit blunt Wnt blockade. Emerging inhibitors promise dynamic approaches to impair stem cells. Reversing resistance mechanisms is the central therapeutic prize.
pmc-11675544:
San and colleagues published in twenty twenty-four a systematic review of germ hazards in animal foods in Cambodia. Meat, fish, and other animal products can carry microbes that sicken people. Cambodia lacks broad data on such foodborne risks. The team gathered studies from two thousand to twenty twenty-two that met set quality rules. Forty-six studies passed for full review in the end.

Most studies were led by or with outside researchers, showing weak local surveillance. Fish parasites were the most studied hazard by far. Market fish carried parasites far more often than wild-caught fish. Bat meat viruses posed a possible spillover risk to people. Many likely hazards had never been studied there. The authors urge better hygiene, import checks, and tracking systems.
pmc-11676344:
The authors test whether common variants in the LAG3 and CD4 genes affect the risk of essential tremor in a Spanish population. Many lines of evidence link essential tremor with Parkinson's disease. Two CD4 variants showed a marginal link to Parkinson's risk in Chinese and Spanish studies. Both genes help modulate inflammation, and inflammatory markers have also been tied to tremor. The team genotypes 267 patients with familial tremor and 270 matched controls.

Three variants are tested with targeted assays. One LAG3 variant shows a decreased tremor risk, but only in men carrying two copies of its C form. Age at onset links to none of the variants. The male-only signal loses significance after correction for multiple testing. The authors conclude the variants show no overall association with tremor risk, apart from that weak hint in men.
pmc-11676544:
Jixiang Wang and a team of co-authors build a glowing sensor for an antibiotic in food, reported in two thousand twenty-four. Tetracycline residues in milk and eggs need fast, safe detection. Their sensor pairs two light-emitting dots inside a molecularly imprinted shell.

Blue carbon dots react on contact with the drug, while red quantum dots sealed in silica give a steady reference glow. The sensor answered within one minute and detected the drug at low levels across a wide range. Results matched the standard chromatography method. Tests in milk and egg samples gave satisfactory recoveries. The design avoids direct contact with the toxic dots, keeping the test low in toxicity.
pmc-11677144:
Ahmet Alperen Canbolat and co-authors checked bovine colostrum in children's nutrition in 2024. Colostrum, the first milk a cow makes after calving, is dense with proteins, antibodies, the iron-binding protein lactoferrin. And complex sugars, and it is marketed more and more as a supplement for infants and children. The stakes are highest for preterm babies. Whose gut and immune systems are unfinished and who face a distinctive list of dangerous complications.

The review lays out the composition first. Then it turns to the evidence for growth and development in term and preterm infants. Then it works through the diseases where colostrum has been tried. These include necrotizing enterocolitis, infectious diarrhea, inflammatory bowel disease, short-bowel syndrome, newborn sepsis, and gut and respiratory infections. Medical trials for each condition are discussed, giving clinicians a single map of where the supplement's promise is tested and where it is only hoped.
pmc-11678344:
Anna Husted and co-authors published a set of laboratory protocols in 2024 for work on the hemoglobin of a marine worm, Amphitrite ornata. Hemoglobin normally carries oxygen in the blood. In this worm it also acts as a catalyst, with four observed activities that oxidize other substances. A protein with so many jobs is rare. Finding more examples is hard because the worms that carry such proteins are difficult to identify by eye alone.

The protocols pair visual inspection with DNA barcoding to identify the worm accurately. A gene sequence serves as the barcode for the species. Whole worms are then used to extract the hemoglobin, purify it, and study its properties. One catalytic activity is tested with a standard assay. A twin form of the protein is also produced in Escherichia coli bacteria.
pmc-11678744:
Shirley Shapiro Ben David leads a team on a parasite infection in pregnancy. Their study from twenty twenty-four is set in Israel. Cryptosporidium usually causes a short gut illness.

Little was known about its course in pregnancy. Pregnant women with positive stool tests were the cases. Matched women with negative tests formed the controls. Records gave symptoms, treatments, and birth outcomes. Birth weight, scores, and head size were logged. Most positive cases clustered in one year. Diarrhea was by far the top symptom.  Most cases came from higher income areas.
pmc-11679244:
Chagit Peles and four colleagues study expectant fathers' role in shaping the home food setting, in a twenty twenty-four paper. Fifteen partners of first-time pregnant women answered surveys and took part in talks during and after pregnancy. The team asked about their knowledge, attitudes, and habits around food kept and served at home.

Partners made food choices jointly with the mothers and felt driven to do better than their own parents had. Many saw their wives as the food experts in the house. Healthy food access at home was a common snag. Fathers-to-be treated the first pregnancy as a key chance to set a healthy pattern. The authors call for programs that include partners.
pmc-11680244:
Francesco Branda led a large team reviewing bacteria-based mosquito control in a 2024 paper. A natural bacterium living inside mosquitoes can block them from passing on viruses like dengue and Zika. The review weighs this approach against chemical spraying as climate change expands mosquito range and breeding sites. Warmer, wetter conditions make adaptable control more urgent, the authors argue.

They survey recent innovations, including pairing the bacterium with other biological tools. Artificial intelligence enters through modeling mosquito dynamics, timing releases, and monitoring spread in real time. The authors call for joined-up, data-driven programs, especially in regions most exposed to climate-driven disease.
pmc-11681944:
Mao Otake and five co-authors report, in a 2024 case study, a woman in her 40s whose epilepsy began late in life after a mild COVID-19 infection. She had a tonic-clonic seizure ten days after the infection. Electroencephalography, or EEG, showed persistent spike-wave complexes across the brain at 3 to 5.5 Hz, consistent with absence status epilepticus.

She was first treated with levetiracetam at 1,000 mg per day, but she had three further seizures of the same kind. Long-term video EEG monitoring then led to a diagnosis of late-onset idiopathic generalized epilepsy. A combination of valproic acid and lamotrigine kept her free of seizures for over a year. Her EEG still showed persistent spike-wave activity, which the authors link to lasting inflammation in the brain. They stress that EEG remains essential for recording this activity in outpatient care.
pmc-11688244:
Ana Ibanez-Pegenaute, Maria Ortega-Moneo, Robinson Ramirez-Velez, and Anton test if work on the breath-in flesh makes wind and brass band men and women more strong. The work came out in 2024. Band folks are sports stars of the breath sheet in the chest. Yet in their ranks, some gain from the work and some do not.

48 well band folks split into two groups. 33 took the train plan. 15 did not train at all. Train work meant hard, low-count breath-in sets with a gate tool. It ran two short rounds a day, five days a week, for 12 weeks. The team gauged top breath-in and breath-out push, first and last. They counted no-gain folks too. Those are band folks whose strength did not rise.
pmc-11690044:
Ryan Mace and co-authors ask health professionals what blocks early detection of subjective cognitive decline. Their study appeared in 2024. The condition means a person feels their memory slipping while tests stay normal. Catching it early opens the door to risk reduction for dementia. Yet fewer than half of such patients raise the topic with clinicians. The team ran video focus groups with 26 professionals from five clinics.

Four barrier themes emerged, starting with how varied the condition looks. The team mapped practical fixes using an established implementation playbook. Problems spanned clinic routines, patient reluctance, and unclear next steps after a flag. The authors offer concrete strategies for weaving screening into everyday care, so concerns are caught while change is still possible.
pmc-11691144:
Hitoshi Suda, Tadashi Wada, Kana Satoh, and Tamiko Uehara published a study in 2024 on the realities and challenges of elder abuse reported to the police in one Japanese city. Reports to the police have increased nationwide. The researchers asked whether more reports mean more cases legally substantiated as elder abuse.

The study used data from fiscal year 2019 in Matsudo City, covering 171 cases in total. The police reported seventy-three of them. In most of those cases, the perpetrator lived with the victim. Adult children were the most common perpetrators, followed by spouses. Of the police-reported cases, more than four in five were not substantiated as elder abuse under the law. The gap lies in the law's narrow definition: violence by a cohabiting person who is not a caregiver falls outside it. The authors urge a broader definition, in line with World Health Organization guidance.
pmc-11693044:
Benjamin Rosenstein, in a solo study from 2024, asks what medical students take away from a workshop on delirium, the acute confusion common in older hospital patients. Students reflected in writing after the session.

Eight themes emerged. Students had often seen delirium on their rotations without knowing how poor its outcomes are. Most had received little teaching on it. They judged the topic overlooked but important, and the workshop's skills directly useful. Unprompted, many reflected on ageist practices they had witnessed in care. Rosenstein argues delirium belongs in the standard curriculum: teaching it builds skill and may counter ageism at the same time.
pmc-11693144:
Laura McDaniel and six co-authors present a 2024 study that adapts a walking-analysis model to detect frailty. Frailty is a state of greater weakness and risk that comes with aging, raising the chances of falls and hospital care. The team fine-tuned GaitBase, a model first built to recognize people by their walk, using medical data instead.

Their data came from motion-capture video of 64 people classed as non-frail, pre-frail, or frail. Image tools produced body silhouettes and boxes from each frame, and the model used both silhouette and color video. Small datasets are a known problem, so the team used data augmentation and cross-validation to strengthen the results. A fast video-based check could help clinicians spot frailty earlier.
pmc-11694044:
Ye-Eun Park and co-authors study how cancer survivors use commercial health apps in a 2024 mixed-methods study. Care is shifting toward prediction and prevention, and apps can help with long-term follow-up after cancer. Yet older users may struggle with apps, and many users stop opening them, so the team asked what shapes steady use.

The study enrolled two hundred sixty-four survivors and paired survey answers with app use records. The survey was run in mid-2022. The authors use an extended model of technology acceptance, which links use to how useful and easy a tool feels, plus user skill and health state. Their results show which factors keep survivors engaged with an app. App makers and clinics can use that map to design tools patients stay with.
pmc-11698544:
Arumugam Balraj and Harini Ravikumar report the eye outcome of a child whose skull fused too early, in a case report from 2024. The girl, aged five, rubbed her right eye often and had held her head raised since birth. Her skull shape, tall and pointed, pointed to a condition called craniosynostosis.

Eye tests showed very weak vision in the right eye and normal vision in the left, with both eyes pushed forward and pale optic discs. Scans found early closure of several skull seams that narrowed the orbit tips and squeezed both optic nerves. Surgeons advanced the forehead bone to free the nerves. After surgery, the right eye's vision rose from 1/60 to 6/24. The authors credit modern surgery and team care.
pmc-11700544:
Four authors present a dental study from two thousand twenty-four on the inner canals of lower first premolar teeth in a Bengali population. Root canal shape varies between populations, and dentists need local data to treat teeth well. The study was done on extracted teeth outside the body.

The team used cone-beam CT scans on one hundred teeth from adults in West Bengal. They sorted the canals by a standard classification and noted details such as side canals and the shape of the canal opening. Three quarters of the teeth had the simplest single-canal form. Most of the rest had a canal that split into two near the tip.
pmc-11703644:
Mai-Linh Nguyen and five co-authors review how women's skin changes across the menstrual cycle in a 2024 paper. Hormone swings between cycle phases reach the skin, but the combined picture was scattered. Their scoping review searched major databases and, after screening hundreds of papers, kept a small set measuring elasticity, hydration, temperature, blood flow, and sweating in healthy women.

Elasticity rose at ovulation compared with the early phase. Hydration showed no clear change across phases. Skin temperature, blood flow, and sweating all ran higher in the later phase than the early one. The authors map where evidence is firm and where it is thin for future studies.
pmc-11708944:
Miriana d'Alessandro and colleagues map Europe's patient registries and biobanks for a rare lung disease, in this survey from twenty twenty-four. The disease is sarcoidosis, in which clusters of immune cells form in organs, most often the lungs. Progress on causes and care needs shared patient data and stored samples, which is why a European rare-disease network ran the survey.

The poll went to network members in two rounds and asked what each center collects, how samples are taken, and how they are stored. The picture that came back was patchy: many small collections, run in varied ways, with no shared frame. The authors say building disease-specific registries and biobanks is not optional but required. They call for merging efforts, steady funding, and coordination, so scattered samples can power strong research across borders.
pmc-11710844:
Klara Gawor and ten colleagues examine donated brains, published in 2025, to see how a second disease protein changes Alzheimer damage. In many patients, a protein called alpha-synuclein also builds up in the wrong shape. It spreads in two main patterns: one rising from low brain areas, and one centered on the amygdala. The team asked whether the amygdala pattern speeds the loss of nerve cells in the hippocampus, a key memory area.

They studied two hundred ninety-one brains from older people, with and without dementia. Brains with the amygdala pattern had fewer nerve cells in a hippocampus zone called CA1. Those patients also showed more of the late-stage changes tied to TDP-43, another clumping protein. A statistical model linked the pattern to cell loss only through tau and TDP-43 buildup. The authors say mixed disease needs more attention in diagnosis and trials.
pmc-11715044:
Michael Rafii, a researcher with a national trial network, wrote this overview, published in two thousand twenty-five, on how to run drug trials for Alzheimer's disease in people with Down syndrome. People with Down syndrome face a high risk of Alzheimer's disease as they age.

The paper sums up a decade of gains: brain scans and fluid tests now track the disease in this group, and thinking tests that catch its decline have been built and checked. A United States trial platform launched in twenty eighteen has enrolled more than two hundred adults with Down syndrome. Its first drug trial tests a treatment called ACI-24.060 for safety and effect, with two more trials planned. The paper shows how past cohort work now shapes real trials.
pmc-11724444:
McGuire, Naitore, and Ramu present a case report from twenty twenty-four on pacemaker pocket erosion with infection. A seventy-seven-year-old man arrives with infection signs and exposed device skin breakdown. Cultures from blood and wound grow the same staph germ. The full device and leads are removed successfully. Antibiotics follow, and he leaves hospital two days later. Device infections are rising as populations age, the authors note. Frailty and shallow placement raise the risk.

Early removal, within a day here, drives the good outcome. His earlier blood infection might have been cured by removal then. Timing-based removal rules are proposed for future guidelines. Close follow-up spans infection, heart, and wound teams.
pmc-11727144:
Ilias Theodorakos, Michael Skipper Andersen, and Dimitrios Kouroupis show that where an optimizer starts decides where it lands when fitting knee ligament properties. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Ligament stiffness values are usually borrowed from old papers as starting guesses, and nobody had checked the damage.

A synthetic knee with known true values generated fake laxity tests. Four starting guesses, from exact to far off, fed the same fitting routine. Small misses stayed harmless; far starts tripled the error in stiffness and strain. Worse, wrong parameters still reproduced the knee's motion almost perfectly. The authors warn that a good motion match does not prove the ligaments were truly found.
pmc-11728544:
Gao and colleagues show one loop strand blocks lung shift from a rare-earth dust in this twenty twenty-four study. The dust can scar lungs when breathed, and cell form shift drives that scar. How the shift starts at the strand scale was still dim.

Inside, cell and rat lung tests showed the dust push that form shift. Shift marks rose as coat marks fell in both test tracks. The loop strand's count fell in dust-hit cells and rat lungs. Raised strand counts then curbed the shift in both tracks as well. The strand works by soaking up one small kin strand in the cell soup.
pmc-11733544:
Munir Al-Zeer and Mohammad Abu Lubad study what a bacterial infection does to stem cells, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The pathogen, Chlamydia trachomatis, lives inside host cells and reshapes their gene activity to survive. The team used human mesenchymal stem cells as a clean, primary cell model.

After acute infection, three key transcription factors tied to pluripotency fell, suggesting the cells lost stem-like traits. Other markers rose, including ones linked to early cartilage formation and an enzyme tied to bone development. A stem cell marker fell at the same time. Medium from infected cells, by contrast, kept pluripotency markers up. The authors read the pattern as a push toward cartilage-like differentiation.
pmc-11740744:
Ijod and co-authors test how scald dips shift guard parts in mangosteen skin. Skin hues in that fruit could serve as born dyes in foods. Yet a brown tool, PPO, breaks those hues down in the skin. Hot wet and steam dips ran at 100 marks for set spans. Spans ran from zero to 120 ticks in the dip tests. Left PPO work, whole guard counts, and hue marks got read.

Dye parts and rust-fight scores join the read set per dip. Brown marks and hue traits round out the skin checks. A stream-mass tool named the guard parts in the skin bits. Left PPO fell in both dip types by firm counts. Hot wet killed it fast, with a half-life of 59 ticks. Steam took 121 ticks for the same half fall.
pmc-11740844:
Li and nine co-authors reviewed bio-nanopore technology for detecting biomolecules in twenty twenty-four. A bio-nanopore is a tiny hole, often a protein channel, in a membrane. When a molecule passes through, the electric current shifts, turning single-molecule events into readable signals.

The review covers recent progress across several uses. These include sequencing DNA and RNA, detecting proteins, and identifying small molecules. The method offers high throughput, low cost, and sharp sensitivity in real time, the authors note. They also look ahead to coming trends in the field. Their survey presents bio-nanopores as a versatile detection tool whose role in biomolecule analysis keeps growing.
pmc-11773644:
Sanna Nybacka, Anneli Peolsson, Per Leanderson, and Mireille Ryden run a pilot study in Sweden. Their work from twenty twenty-four links food, mind, and heart risk. It deals with adults in mid life.

The team used data from a diet sub study of two hundred folks. A short food form scored how well each diet fit guide rules. Forms also asked about stress, sleep, and life traits. Stats tests sought links to a blood fat risk mark. Food change is hard, and mind traits may play a part. The pilot maps those links.
pmc-11800144:
Helen Buse and eight co-authors report a 2024 study of drinking water inside a full-scale test plumbing system. The system mimics a home, with gas and electric heaters in both tank and instant forms. The team wanted to know how heater type and standing water affect water quality over time.

For 26 weeks the team tracked water use and took more than 400 samples at sinks and a shower. They sampled fresh water and water that had sat still for eight hours. Counts of common bacteria were lower in hot and shower water than in the incoming supply. The study shows how daily habits inside a building can change the water people actually drink and breathe.
pmc-11852344:
Sulayman el Mathari leads a team that tests four dimensional flow scans in heart disease. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy surgery. The standard surgery cuts a segment of the heart septum.

Some folks also get their mitral valve leaflet extended. Both routes give good clinic outcomes in the short term. Post surgery flow effects of each route were unexplored. Nine folks had flow scans after their heart surgery. Three had septum surgery alone, three had valve work too. Three healthy controls joined for a clean compare. Flow marks form the endpoints.
pmc-11920644:
Yu-Rim Lee and Jong-Sun Lee present a study protocol from two thousand twenty-four on predicting depressive symptoms from real-time phone and wearable data. Standard clinic visits and questionnaires spot depression late, missing chances for early help. Digital phenotyping promises continuous clues from daily life.

The study will recruit one hundred fifty Korean adults in their twenties who had felt depressed in the past two weeks. For two weeks, wearables and phones will passively record activity, heart rate, sleep, and steps. Participants will also answer mood check-ins four times a day through an app. Two measurement rounds span three months. Machine learning and multilevel models will hunt for the digital pattern that best forecasts symptoms. The authors aim to sharpen early detection and care.
pmc-11931344:
Ananta Aryal and co-authors assess daily function and other diseases in older clinic patients in Kathmandu, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Over four hundred adults aged sixty and up took part over a few months in two thousand twenty-four. Two standard scales graded basic self-care and wider daily tasks.

Near nine in ten were independent in basic self-care, such as feeding and dressing. Only about four in ten were fully independent on wider tasks like shopping and money handling. Near forty-four percent carried added diseases. The authors say the wider-task gap shows where support for older adults should focus.
pmc-11970144:
Xiangru Chen and Hongbo Gao report a randomized trial of a reinforced repair done during keyhole removal of the uterus, in a 2024 paper. The worry is pelvic organ prolapse after the operation, when pelvic organs drop because their supports are cut. The team tested whether rebuilding the top support level at the time of surgery prevents that drop.

The trial enrolled 360 women having the operation between 2018 and 2021. Women with no prolapse and women with mild prolapse were each split at random among three arms: simple closure, a standard suspension stitch, and the modified reinforced repair. At six and twelve months, the modified group scored better on the standard prolapse measure than both other groups. Other checks covered bladder symptoms, sexual quality of life, and pelvic ultrasound.
pmc-11983144:
Zijian Liu, Ruiyang Yin, and Jiaxing Tian review how tiny parcels shed by cells help drive type 2 diabetes and its complications, in a paper whose journal record is dated 2024. The parcels, extracellular vesicles, ferry proteins and small RNA pieces between cells and steer much of the body's signaling. As diabetes spreads worldwide, the vesicles' part in it draws growing attention.

The review follows the parcels through the disease's core troubles: weight gain, inflammation, insulin resistance, and the failure of insulin-making cells in the pancreas. It then traces how vesicles feed the complications that follow, from vessel damage to organ injury. The authors assemble these threads into one framework, aiming to give researchers a fuller map of how cell-to-cell parcels shape diabetes, and to point at spots where therapy might intercept the messages.
pmc-12083244:
Woerner, Eger, Kasaj, and Ehmke follow dental implants in soldiers with severe gum disease over decades, in work from twenty twenty-four. Peri-implantitis is inflammation around an implant that can destroy its bone support. Long term success of its treatment is poorly documented.

The retrospective study covered soldiers with treated stage three or four periodontitis in supportive therapy for at least twenty years. Frequency of peri-implantitis, patient risk factors for it, and ten year implant survival under treatment were measured. Few datasets run this long. The results show what disciplined maintenance can and cannot prevent in high risk mouths.
pmc-12107244:
Svetlana Raita and co-authors breed a protein-rich yeast by mutating it and selecting survivors on herbicide-laced plates. Their study appeared in 2024, though the catalog lists 2025. The yeast, already used for pigment, is a candidate single-cell protein for fish feed, where the amino acids lysine and methionine are prized. Two herbicide actives that block amino acid making were dosed to just stop the wild yeast, then used as the sieve after chemical mutagenesis.

Survivors overproduced the very acids the herbicides target: top mutants made up to thirty-seven percent more methionine and more lysine than the parent. The authors say the cheap selection trick can strengthen single-cell protein economics, easing pressure on farmed feed crops.
pmc-12659044:
Bingshu Wu and co-authors test a blended teaching plan for heart exams in medical training in two thousand twenty-five. Physical diagnosis links basic science to clinic work, and heart checks plus heart tracings are core skills. Their plan joins a staged teaching model with case work and acted-out scenes.

Two groups of thirty-eight students from the same class year were compared. One group learned by the standard route, while the other used the blended plan. The blended group scored higher on the final exam and on the total score, with clear gaps. Grades mixed ongoing checks with a final test, and a survey gauged how students rated the teaching. The authors present the plan as a way to deepen both knowledge and hands-on skill.
pmc-12661044:
Semih Alpsoy and Osman Ugur Sezerman, publishing in 2025, use deep learning to predict when cancer drugs will fail, and why. Drug resistance is one of the main reasons cancer treatment falls short. The team trained neural networks on cell-line data that combines gene activity, mutations, and copy number changes with measured drug responses. They then borrowed strength across related drugs through transfer learning.

The models beat rival methods at predicting responses in two independent test sets, one from patient-derived tumors and one from a large cancer atlas. Digging into four drugs, the team flagged specific pathways behind resistance. A metabolism route and a cell-grip route stood out for one drug, and a cleanup process for another. Some resistance links also sat in the copy number data. The authors note their findings match earlier lab studies, which supports the approach.
pmc-12692344:
Richard Morrow and co-authors study a 2025 question: how did the COVID-19 pandemic change testing for hepatitis B in British Columbia, Canada? Early work showed testing fell in the first months of the crisis. What happened over the longer term, and what happened for people who inject drugs, was less clear.

Using province-wide data, the team tracked three kinds of hepatitis B tests month by month. They compared a pre-pandemic span, from 2017 to early 2020, with a brief shift period and then the pandemic years through 2022. Their method looks for sharp breaks in the trend when policies changed. The study gives health planners a fuller picture of missed testing and of where catch-up efforts should focus.
pmc-12692544:
Lanjie Xu and ten co-authors surveyed the smell and taste genes of the safflower aphid, in a study published in 2025. The pest drains crops and spreads viruses, and its sensory genes also shield it from sprays. Fresh gene readings from the transcriptome of the pest found forty sensory genes in four families. Family trees showed species-specific twists, with two taste subfamilies gone.

Growth stage readings split nearly 2,000 genes by step. Two sensory genes fired just in the legs, one just in the antennae, and each had its stage. Shape marks held firm in two families and ran varied in the other two. The team presents the stage and tissue genes as targets for species-fitted pest control.
pmc-12693444:
Victoria Brinker and co-authors review breathing machine use before hospital arrival in brain injury care in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Ventilation can save patients with traumatic brain injury by steadying gases in the blood. Too much or too little oxygen or carbon dioxide can deepen brain harm.

Settings must respect brain pressure, blood flow, and lung safety at once. Gentle settings that guard lungs may strain the injured brain, and the best balance is unsettled. Harm begins soon after impact, so field care matters much. Yet out-of-hospital data are scarce. The authors sum what is known and flag the prehospital gap.
pmc-12699844:
Xuan Qiao and four co-authors build a risk chart for oral frailty in older patients with chronic lung disease. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Dry mouth, tooth loss, and gum ills make chew and swallow hard in this group, and oral frailty feeds swallow risk. Three hundred twenty patients at one large hospital in Shandong were screened with a frailty scale.

More than nine in ten patients met the frailty mark, a very high share. Food state, breath strain grade, and chronic ill type drove the risk most. A chart built on those marks split high and low risk with high truth in both build and check groups. Fit checks were sound, and the team sees clinic worth in the chart.
pmc-12707244:
Yanpeng Jin and four co-authors charted two decades of work on how health staff are taught. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, used a mapping tool called CiteSpace. They pulled papers on the health professions education model from a large index, from two thousand five to two thousand twenty-four. Close to three thousand papers fit. They mapped words, fields, lands, schools, authors, and cited works to see the shape of the field.

The maps show which themes rose, where the hot fronts sit, and which gaps press now. Such a view is built to feel fresh and full for teachers and scholars alike. Readers who run health training get a guide to where the field moves next.
pmc-12707444:
Ursa Potocnik Rebersak, Erik Brecelj, and Rok Schara test in 2025 whether gum disease care affects colon cancer patients. Gum disease has been linked to colon cancer, and two gum germs often turn up in cancer studies. The team asked whether treating the gums changes a blood marker of inflammation during cancer care.

They tracked the marker before surgery, just after, and at the first follow-up, in patients with and without gum treatment. The groups did not differ at any point. The team also tried to grow the two suspect germs from cancer tissue, and neither germ appeared. The authors report no link in their data, while noting the study's narrow scope.
pmc-12712544:
Charilaos Pylidis led a large team studying brown bears on the Balkan Peninsula in a 2025 paper. The region holds some of Europe's largest cross-border bear groups. Most past work stopped at country lines, which hides how bears actually move. The team used gene markers from four mountain ranges to trace links between eastern and western groups.

They found a main east-west gradient in gene patterns, with extra north-south structure and high overall diversity. Signs of past bottlenecks and isolation sat alongside ongoing movement across borders, mostly by males. Mountain data also echoed swings after the last ice age. The authors urge joint cross-border plans to keep the population connected.
pmc-12712844:
Abdulmajeed Albarrak, writing alone, reviewed why bleeding keeps returning in gastric antral vascular ectasia, nicknamed watermelon stomach. The condition dilates small vessels in the stomach's lower chamber, causing chronic blood loss and transfusion-dependent anemia, especially in older women. Cirrhosis, kidney disease, and autoimmune disorders raise the risk. Drugs help little and serve mainly as a bridge to procedures. Endoscopic treatment is first-line.

Argon plasma coagulation and band ligation are the workhorse techniques, effective and safe. Recurrence stays high, particularly in diffuse or severe disease. Radiofrequency ablation is a promising option for repeat bleeders, though long-term data are thin. Surgery removing the antrum is the last resort, with higher risks. The twenty twenty-five review orders the escalating options for clinicians facing a patient who keeps coming back anemic.
pmc-12715344:
Rashidan and colleagues review in twenty twenty-five lab-grown mini-organs that include immune cells, a step toward truer disease models. Mini-organs mimic real organs in shape and function and serve drug testing and disease study well. Yet most lack immune cells, even though those cells drive cancer, infection, swelling, and self-attack diseases.

The review covers what immune-ready mini-organs could do across those fields, plus healing and modelling of immune organs themselves. It surveys ways to add immune cells, where those cells come from, and why they often fade or fail in culture. It closes with how engineering, biobanks, and AI might fix those limits. The authors see these systems as strong platforms for tailored medicine.
pmc-12716244:
Dandan Bai and six co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on the burden of long term diseases in Asia-Pacific youth. The data span from nineteen ninety to twenty twenty-one in the Global Burden of Disease study. Deaths, years lost, and years lived with disability are the gauges. Rates are split by age, sex, place, and a development index.

Death rates from these diseases fell by near half over the span. Years lost to early death fell in step. Mental disorders bucked the trend: their deaths and burden rose. Boys died at higher rates, while girls carried more total burden. Poorer lands bore the heaviest load. The team flags youth mental health as the key worry ahead.
pmc-12727944:
Masahiro Kohzuki, a solo author, proposes a new umbrella term, physical inactivity syndrome, for the wide harm that flows from moving too little, in a 2025 narrative review. Ageing societies face a cluster of related problems: the wasting of bed rest, frailty, muscle loss, and disability picked up in hospital stays. Inactivity sits at the root of each, yet the older labels are either local, negative in tone, or too narrow.

The new term gathers these conditions under one roof and stresses that the damage spans body, mind, and social life. The review then sets out the rehabilitation and exercise approaches used to prevent and treat the syndrome. Kohzuki urges clinicians to grasp the full risk, build real skill in raising patients' activity, and act with confidence in daily practice.
pmc-12728144:
Riyad Alzhrani and three co-authors poll drug chain hands and care staff on shot drug shorts in Saudi Arabia. Their survey appeared in twenty twenty-five. Sterile shot drugs oft run short and harm care. Three hundred fifty forms came back from the two packs. Most chain hands held that chain breaks drive the shorts, with poor guess of need and thin source paths at the head.

Past two thirds of care staff said shorts hurt care through late cures, long stays, and high costs. Staff time was lost to hunts for swaps. Both packs backed AI and learn tools to fix guess and stock work by wide spans.
pmc-12729244:
Xiaochang Chen and colleagues test a gene that may guard arteries against plaque, in this study from twenty twenty-five. The gene makes Bambi, a decoy receptor that blunts a family of growth signals. Plaque grows when artery walls inflame and when scavenger cells called macrophages gorge on cholesterol and turn into foam cells.

The team gave extra Bambi to mice bred to form plaque, then fed them a fatty diet for fourteen weeks. Their artery plaques shrank, and their macrophages shifted from an angry state to a calm one, with key inflammation signals falling. In lab dishes, Bambi helped macrophages export cholesterol and resist turning into foam cells. Gene scans traced the effect to a chain: Bambi wakes a signal called Akt, which lowers a germ sensor, TLR4. The authors propose Bambi as a fresh target for drugs against clogged arteries.
pmc-12729444:
Chen, Loiselle, and Theurer test a seaweed feed that may cut cow methane. Cows burp methane, a strong warming gas, as they digest grass. Seaweed adds a compound that can curb that gas. The team fed the additive to grazing young female cows.

Two groups of eleven cows grazed the same pasture type. One group got the additive once a day by mouth. Dose rose over two weeks to a fixed full dose. That full dose ran for seven more weeks. A feed station tracked gas output nonstop for all cows. Full-dose weeks showed lower methane in the additive group.
pmc-12729844:
Ana Javor and co-authors survey, in a 2025 paper, the imaging tools used to examine bones in both human and animal medicine. Clear pictures of the skeleton guide diagnosis, follow-up, and research in the clinic and the lab. The review walks through the whole shelf: plain X-rays, density scans, CT, MRI, two kinds of ultrasound, and hybrid PET-CT.

Each method is weighed for what it shows best, its dose, cost, and reach. Fine-scale CT used in research can measure the tiny struts inside bone in three dimensions, which serves studies of bone biology and healing drugs. The authors note that artificial intelligence is starting to sharpen reading and tracking of bone disease. They stress that the choice of tool must fit the patient, the species, and the question.
pmc-12731244:
Xiang Hu and eight co-authors wrote a review in 2025 on the use of Chinese and Western care side by side for polycystic ovary syndrome. The ill health blends too much male-type hormone, poor egg release, and weak response to insulin. Each school treats it in its own way, and sick people quite often use both.

The review first sets out the new view of the cause: genes, hormones, sore tissue, and weak response to insulin. It then goes through Chinese ideas and tools, from herb mixes to skin needles. Trials hint that these add-ons can lift egg release, how the body uses fuel, and hormone signs when used with standard drugs. Weak points are mixed herb grades and shifts in how the pattern is read. The team backs joint care done with care, plus more work on how it acts.
pmc-12733044:
Jaewoong Lee and four colleagues systematically review every published case of disorders caused by variants in PPP2R1A, a gene encoding a scaffold piece of a master regulatory enzyme. Sixty patients across sixteen studies carried twenty-six distinct variants, mostly new missense changes clustered in one structural region.

Developmental delay and intellectual disability were universal. Half had epilepsy, and over eighty percent had brain malformations, especially of the corpus callosum. Two hotspot variants caused severe disease with high mortality, while another produced milder courses. Head size went both ways, small and large. The authors map the spectrum from lethal newborn presentations to survivable milder forms, noting that prenatal brain findings can trigger early genetic diagnosis.
pmc-12733344:
Kim-Anh Tran, Mai-Trang Le, Yung-Fu Huang, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It measures how money a household spends on tobacco affects children's health in Vietnam, using methods designed to show cause rather than mere correlation.

Tobacco spending can crowd out food and care, and smoke harms children directly. Drawing on a national living standards survey, the team ran several statistical models, including one that uses an outside lever to isolate cause. Every approach agreed: heavier tobacco spending raised the chance that a child would be hospitalized. The effect was strongest for children under six. It also varied by the child's sex, the mother's age at birth, and the region. The authors say the pattern exposes deep health inequalities and gives policy makers causal evidence against household tobacco use.
pmc-12735644:
Fitrah Ernawati and co-authors use national survey data in a 2025 study of nutrition in Indonesian children under five. Lack of key vitamins and minerals, along with poor growth, remains a heavy burden in this age group. The study looks at how growth measures line up with the levels of key micronutrients in the blood.

The team drew on the 2018 national basic health survey, with data on family traits, body measures, and nutrition status. Blood and other samples from five hundred fifty children aged up to fifty-nine months were tested for iron, zinc, calcium, and two key vitamins. By joining the survey records with the lab results, the authors give a national picture of hidden hunger. Such a picture can guide food and supplement programs for young children.
pmc-12735844:
Graziella Tocco, Francesca Esposito, and five co-authors report a new class of compounds against HIV. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, targets integrase, a viral enzyme that slips viral DNA into human DNA. The compounds block the enzyme at a side site, not the main one. All of them beat a known control compound in lab tests.

Four lead compounds also disturbed how the enzyme's parts swap and bind a human partner protein. Unlike older drugs of this kind, they did not clump the enzyme. Computer models point to two pockets near a sugar-binding site as the likely grip points. Mutant enzyme tests with and without sugar back that view.
pmc-12736844:
Tamara Erceg and four co-authors make a water-loving gel to carry farm microbes, in this twenty twenty-five study. The gel starts from pullulan, a natural sugar polymer. It is formed at room heat, which saves energy and keeps live microbes alive while they are mixed in.

Tests confirmed the chemical tweaks that let the polymer set into a gel. The gel swelled hugely, soaking up more than ten times its weight in water within hours, a good trait for a carrier. Under the microscope its inner structure suited slow release. Such gels could drip-feed helpful microbes to crops instead of dumping them at once.
pmc-12737644:
Mayla Sgrulletti and co-authors review the fight against pneumococcal disease and the vaccines chasing a moving target, in a 2025 paper. The bacterium kills and hospitalizes worldwide, above all in small children and the fragile. Conjugate vaccines cut vaccine-type disease steeply and shielded the unvaccinated too. Then replacement struck: types the shots miss rose to fill the gap.

Wider vaccines covering fifteen, twenty, and twenty-one types followed. The review also shows vaccination doubling as a diagnostic probe for hidden immune defects, a use hampered by messy assays. High-risk patients need tailored schedules. The authors pin the field's hopes on universal protein-based vaccines that no type can dodge.
pmc-12747844:
Zaid Muhanna and co-authors review a light-based blood treatment for a severe transplant complication in a 2025 analysis. Graft-versus-host disease arises when donor immune cells attack the patient after a stem cell transplant. When steroids fail, one second-line option treats the patient's blood cells with light outside the body and returns them.

The review pooled thirty-eight studies with more than twelve hundred patients. Response rates were highest in skin and gut disease and lower in the liver. Two thirds of patients could reduce their steroid dose. Patients with milder disease survived better than those with severe grades. Survival gains over other treatments were positive but not firm. The authors judge the treatment effective while calling for controlled trials of combined regimens.
pmc-12752144:
Nutbeam and a large team present a protocol from twenty twenty-five for setting research priorities in post-collision road care in the United Kingdom. Road injuries kill over a million people yearly worldwide. Care after a crash has drawn less research than prevention has. The project follows a known alliance method for priority setting. A national survey will gather open research questions from the public. A scan of guidelines and past recommendations will add candidates. Only questions the evidence leaves open will advance.

Patients, carers, clinicians, and policy makers all take part. A consensus workshop will pick a top ten list by group technique. Priorities will also map onto a five-stage survival chain. The authors aim to guide funders and services nationally.
pmc-12752844:
Poliana Guarçoni and colleagues pool the trials on counting carbohydrates for children and teenagers with type 1 diabetes, in this meta-analysis from twenty twenty-five. Seven studies, five hundred ninety-nine young patients, compared counters against non-counters on glycated hemoglobin, the three-month blood sugar average.

Counting worked: every variant of the method lowered HbA1c relative to control, with reductions between zero point seven and one point four percentage points, pooling at about zero point nine four. The best results came from experienced counters armed with an automated bolus calculator, technology plus skill. The authors stress that even the basic form of counting helped, which matters where devices are unaffordable. Their message to clinics: teach the method properly rather than assuming families will improvise it.
pmc-12755344:
Alexander Shayesteh and co-authors survey, in a 2025 study, how people who blame steroid creams for their skin troubles use health care. Topical steroid withdrawal is a disputed condition: many clinicians doubt it, yet online communities devoted to it are large and growing. The team posted a questionnaire in a Swedish Facebook group for the condition and left it open for four weeks.

Eighty-two adults with eczema answered. Half had seen a dermatologist and half a general practitioner about the withdrawal symptoms, and over a third had tried alternative practitioners. Yet among those still suffering, only a fifth or fewer kept any of those contacts going. Facebook and websites were the main information sources, far ahead of doctors. What patients asked for most was to be believed and understood. The authors map a gap between this community and routine care.
pmc-12755744:
Seung-Ah Choe, Eunjung Kim, and Mina Ha look at whether contact with heavy metals and two kinds of man-made chemicals is linked to puberty that starts too early or too late. Their study of Korean youth was published in twenty twenty-five.

The team used health survey data from one thousand four hundred and twenty-four young people. Blood tests measured lead, mercury, and cadmium, and urine tests measured bisphenol A and parts of phthalates. Youth also rated their own stage of growth. About three to four in each hundred had early puberty, and a like share had late puberty. The paper weighs single chemicals and mixes of them, and it adjusts for age, body size, and family income.
pmc-12758344:
Polycystic ovary syndrome upsets hormone balance in many women, and its inner workings are still unclear. Qi Zhang, Shujuan Zhu, and Bin Jiang look for clues in how genes are spliced, the editing step that lets one gene yield several proteins. Scanning gene data from patients, they found forty-two control genes, called transcription factors, whose splicing differed from normal.

A mouse model of the syndrome backed up the lead finding. Two related control genes, Nfkb1 and Nfkb2, were turned up, and one of them skipped a specific building block in its message. Both genes feed a signaling system tied to swelling and metabolism. The team suggests this splicing fault may help drive the syndrome and could seed new markers or treatments.
pmc-12785844:
Maria Fourikou and John Dotis review how gene faults lead to birth defects of the kidney and urinary tract in a 2025 article. These defects are among the most common birth malformations and are the leading cause of chronic kidney disease in children. They arise when key steps in kidney growth before birth go wrong, such as the first branching of the urinary bud.

New gene sequencing tools have widened the list of single-gene causes, including genes that control cell programs and hair-like cell parts. Faults in signaling paths and in the material around cells also play a part. Family background, gene regulation, and factors such as mother's diabetes shape how defects appear. New lab models, such as mini kidneys grown from cells, help test these pathways.
pmc-12786944:
Marta Cebolla-Verdugo and co-authors compare, in twenty twenty-five, melanoma diagnosis under face-to-face care and teledermatology referral in a tertiary hospital. Remote skin care has changed access a lot, but its effect on melanoma pathways was not fully known. The team reviewed two cohorts: eighty-nine patients diagnosed in person in twenty nineteen, and sixty-two via teleconsultation in twenty twenty-two. Those years bracket the pandemic shift to remote care. They collected data on the patients, their clinical traits, and their tissue test results.

A regression model weighed which factors tied a case to the teledermatology era. One hundred fifty-one patients were included in total. Three factors stood out as linked on their own, as the head text notes. The study informs how referral mode shapes when cases are found and what tumor features are seen.
pmc-12788444:
Gaurav Gupta and co-authors show that teaching teenagers about gum health in school actually changes their mouths. Adolescents are prone to gum disease through lax brushing and puberty's hormonal shifts. The trial split eight government schools, four hundred eighty students aged thirteen to fifteen, into a group with a six-month interactive program and a group given pamphlets only.

The program mixed videos, brushing demonstrations, and peer-led activities every two months. At six months, the taught group's gum inflammation score fell from one point eight nine to zero point nine one. Its plaque score fell from two point zero four to one point zero three. The pamphlet group barely moved on either measure. Assessors who scored the mouths did not know which group each student was in. The authors conclude that active school-based teaching, not paper alone, improves gingival health.
pmc-12798944:
Jasmine R Hilliard offers a two thousand twenty-five literature review on Black maternal health and its historical roots. Mistrust of medicine among Black women stretches across many eras. Generational mistreatment of their reproductive health still harms mental wellbeing and family health today.

The review surveys writing on the history of reproduction for Black women. It also covers studies of culturally sensitive care meant to improve provider interactions. Findings tie today's clinical habits to old racial stereotypes about strength, sexuality, and motherhood. Understanding that history, the author argues, can frame fairer care and cut deaths.
pmc-12801344:
Ruiyu Huang and her team dig into what drives, what blocks, and what pays off for med school youth who give their time to teach first aid to the folk at large. Their 2025 study hears from twenty-seven such youth at a med school in Sichuan, China.

A frame that weighs hope of gain next to cost gave the shape for the work, and it led to three main themes with eleven sub-themes. What drove youth took in a will to serve, self gain, prize plans, and peer pull. Blocks took in skill gaps, mind strain, hard facts of time and place, and time strain. Gains ran from mind gains to gains of use in real life, set out in full in the theme count. First aid work builds youth skill, yet how those youth fare had drawn scant past work.
pmc-12807944:
Dagmara Bogdanowska-Charkiewicz, Urszula Malinowska, and Jarosław Daniluk published an umbrella review in twenty twenty-six of meta-analyses testing the low-FODMAP diet for irritable bowel syndrome. An umbrella review sits atop the evidence pyramid, pooling the poolers. Sixteen meta-analyses covering one hundred forty-one studies and nearly ten thousand patients qualified.

The diet significantly lowered overall symptom severity scores and improved quality of life. No clear effect appeared for abdominal pain alone, stool consistency, stool frequency, or gut microbes. Bloating could not be pooled because studies measured it differently. Quality appraisal and a warning about ignored placebo effects temper the verdict. The authors conclude the diet helps, while urging readers to approach the numbers with caution.
pmc-12809944:
Williams and six co-authors link Mediterranean diet parts with gut microbes in fatty liver disease, in work from twenty twenty-five. Metabolic associated steatotic liver disease is fat buildup in the liver tied to metabolism. Diet shapes both the disease and the gut microbiota.

The case control study compared people with the disease and controls. Mediterranean diet constituents were inversely associated with certain gut microbes in the patients, the title reports. Which foods track with which microbes helps design dietary trials. A diet already proven heart healthy may also be tuned, food by food, to support liver health.
pmc-12812544:
Rogier de Best and co-authors reviewed animal studies on whether neck manipulation strains the arteries of the neck. The therapy is widely used and generally seen as safe, yet rare artery tears have been linked to it, and diseased arteries may be more at risk. Since such harm cannot be tested in people, the team gathered controlled animal experiments, published in 2025, on healthy and already-diseased animals. Six studies qualified. Most had unclear risk of bias.

In healthy animals, manipulation showed no clear effect on vessel stress, strain, or blood flow. In diseased animals, it raised the number of immune cells in the artery wall, a sign of inflammation, but did not change narrowing or vessel size. Diseased arteries also stretched less under load than healthy ones. No study reported deaths. The authors urge caution in reading animal results into human care, but say the inflammation signal deserves attention.
pmc-12816344:
Mazuz and Yamazaki build a care plan that arms staff to run mate robots in this twenty twenty-five study. Such robots aid old folks with dim minds, yet wards use them but rare. Staff skill, not the gear, is the gap the pair set out to close.

Inside, watch rounds and deep talks at one day ward fed the plan's build. Two themes rose: spark-and-play acts, and shared tales that bind the group. Those themes pack into a three-step run of spark, dream, and reply. Each round's feed then trues the next round's acts in the loop. The plan turns shelf robots into a plain staff tool for wards.
pmc-12819244:
Sophia Rotter and fifteen co-authors draw lessons from a German funding program that ran confirmatory animal and laboratory studies across many laboratories at once. Their report came out in 2026. Promising early findings often fail when treatments reach patients, so funders wanted to know which results hold up under strict repetition.

Seventeen studies set out to confirm earlier findings under rigorous, pre-planned designs. A companion project supported their methods and gathered shared experience. After four years, a workshop compared notes across the studies. Common pitfalls emerged in experimental setup and in coordinating many sites. The authors propose dedicated research coordinators, clearer rules for confirmatory work, and better integration of such studies into the research system. Their aim is evidence solid enough to guide real clinical decisions.
pmc-12820044:
Shuo Li and Chong Chen present a 2025 model for spotting small objects in drone photos. Drone shots pack tiny targets into cluttered scenes, which strains standard detectors. Their network, MFA-YOLO, adds three parts to a known fast base. One part mines fine local detail, the second merges features across scales with shared sparse filters, and the third splits the call between what and where so each can adapt.

On a standard drone test set, scores rose by several points over the base model. The new net also shed 17 percent of its parts, which aids live use. A second drone set backed its range. Lean, sharp spotting suits safety watch and rescue drones that run on small chips.
pmc-12821244:
Usama El-Awad, Arnold Lohaus, and Tilman Reinelt present a study from twenty twenty-five on social support and mental health in young male migrants in Germany. Their group holds refugees and immigrant origin peers from the Middle East. Support from kin, friends, and close others is thought to shield the mind. The team asks if it also blunts the harm of stress after migration.

More support went with fewer signs of anxiety and low mood in both groups. The blunting effect, though, showed only in the immigrant peers, not in the refugees. Refugees felt more post migration stress and less support from friends. The team says felt support alone may not shield refugees. Built support systems must grow.
pmc-12821644:
Natalya Semenova and a large team study, in twenty twenty-five, links among sleep problems, an antioxidant system, and gut microbes in menopausal women. Menopause disturbs oxidative balance and body rhythms. The gut microbiome may take part in both. Ninety-six women in this stage were checked with three sleep questionnaires. They covered insomnia severity, sleep quality, and daytime sleepiness. Blood levels of glutathione, a key antioxidant, and of GSTP1, an enzyme that uses it, were checked by immunoassay. The make-up of gut microbes was read by gene-based methods.

Several gut bacteria tracked with glutathione levels across sleep groups. A partly changed set tracked with the enzyme's level. The authors map a three-way link among sleep, these defenses, and gut microbes in this life stage.
pmc-12821844:
Marwa El-Mahdy, Eman Abulfadl, and Mona Dawood studied metal oxide nanoparticles in key lime plants in 2025. Tiny metal particles are now common in modern products, raising worries about environmental safety and crops. Key lime is rich in useful plant compounds, so shifts in its chemistry make it a good early warning model for particle toxicity.

Aluminium and copper oxide particles were compared for their effects on growth, protective compounds, and biochemical markers in laboratory-grown plants. The two particles acted differently, and the work traces how particles build up inside plant tissue. Careful use of aluminium oxide might help farming, the authors say, but careless use risks poisoning valuable plants.
pmc-12822044:
Raphaëlle Jacob and co-authors build a short questionnaire to measure how Canadian teens eat, judged against the 2019 Canada Food Guide. The guide speaks not just to food choice but to habits: cooking, eating with others, enjoying food. A brief screener for these practices existed for adults, but not for adolescents. The team set out to make and content-check a teen version for English and French speakers aged 10 to 17.

A first draft held 26 items, drawn from a literature review and set principles. Expert panels in nutrition, eating behavior, public health, and questionnaire craft reviewed it: 13 in English, 7 in French. Their cuts brought the list to 12. Two rounds of think-aloud interviews with teens, 18 in English and 13 in French, trimmed it to 11 items and fixed unclear wording. A short, plain tool is what surveys need to track teen eating habits at scale.
pmc-12822244:
Minseo Hwangbo and colleagues teach ultrasound software to find the cervix's canal region the same way every time, in this study from twenty twenty-five. Tracking cervical change in pregnancy helps predict preterm birth, but human readers draw the analysis box differently each time, and the cervix appears at any angle. Their framework first aligns the canal's inner and outer openings, then defines a standard region around it.

Five oriented object-detection models were benchmarked on over fourteen hundred transvaginal images, with a second hospital's images held back for external testing. The best, Oriented RepPoints, located the region with near-perfect precision and the smallest angle error. The authors offer the framework as the standardized front end that quantitative cervical tissue analysis has been missing, a step toward automated preterm risk assessment.
pmc-12822344:
Elhusseini and six co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on gene activity tied to lung function decline. Chronic lung disease worsens as breathing capacity falls year by year. Blood gene data come from a large study at five- and ten-year visits. Three angles are tested: same-time links, prediction of change, and joint drift. Hundreds of genes appear in each angle's lists. Only two genes overlap across all three angles. A twenty-gene signature is built from the data.

Stress and immune pathways dominate the joint-drift genes. The signature validates in a second study cohort. The authors offer molecular markers for decline. Drug targets may hide in those pathways.
pmc-12824344:
Sutichot Nimkulrat and seven colleagues study a protein that marks healthy insulin-making cells in mice, in a twenty twenty-five paper. The protein, CPEB1, is rich in mature beta cells and drops sharply in diabetes. Its job in these cells was unknown. The team deleted its gene in beta cells only, and in the whole body, in two mouse lines.

To their surprise, the cells kept their identity and worked normally without it. Gene reads showed the protein steers very different gene sets in male and female islets. The authors conclude CPEB1 is a sign of healthy beta cells but not a part they need, at least in mice.
pmc-12825244:
Hatem Tallima and Rashika El Ridi published this review update in 2025 on arachidonic acid, a fatty nutrient found in cell membranes. The authors argue it could one day serve against both schistosome worms and cancer. Both targets protect themselves with an outer membrane rich in a fat called sphingomyelin. That fat forms a tight barrier that keeps immune attack out, while letting nutrients in through pores the cell controls.

An enzyme on the membrane can break that fat down into a signal that pushes cells toward death. Arachidonic acid strongly activates the enzyme. On this reasoning, the authors present the nutrient as a safe candidate for stopping worm and tumor growth before it starts. They add a condition: it must become cheap and easy for people to obtain. The piece is a follow-up to their earlier work making the same case.
pmc-12829044:
Annabelle Weigert and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five modelling study of forces around the kneecap during bending. Kneecap instability stems from anatomy and muscle balance interacting. Sideways joint loading is hard to measure in living people.

Magnetic resonance scans from four donated limbs were turned into personalized bone and joint models. A computer-driven squat simulation flexed each knee under standard conditions. The models computed quadriceps force and the side-to-side component of joint reaction force. Such individualized estimates can guide surgery and rehabilitation planning for unstable kneecaps without invasive testing.
pmc-12830944:
Jung-In Kim led a large team building DNA markers to tell perilla varieties apart in a 2025 paper. The herb is grown across Korea for seed oil and leaves, and seed purity matters. Resequencing a set of cultivars yielded millions of variants, filtered down to thousands of high-confidence ones. From those they built a rapid test panel and validated the working markers across dozens of cultivars.

The markers mostly separated seed types from leaf types on their own. Tiny final sets, just a handful of markers each, could identify the widely grown cultivars, coded as simple barcodes. Tests also measured seed lot contamination, aiding breeders and the seed industry.
pmc-12831444:
Mingci Huang and co-authors add, in a 2025 study, a pathology-based idea to a self-supervised image method for lung cancer slides. Whole slide images are huge, and marking them by hand is slow, so models that learn without labels are valued. Their idea uses a simple fact: tissue near a spot tends to be of the same kind as the spot itself.

The method picks such neighboring spots as positive pairs for the learning step, using spatial adjacency as prior information. It was tested on 65 cases of lung squamous cell carcinoma, across four tissue categories: necrosis, tumor, stroma, and epithelium. Versions with the idea beat the plain self-supervised versions on most scores, in both full tuning and light probe tests. Side tests showed that overlap in sampling helped a little. Patches with a single tissue kind trained better than mixed ones.
pmc-12835444:
JaeEun Yang and Ah Rim Kim published a long-term cohort study in 2025. They followed mothers in South Korea after childbirth. Depression was tracked for seven years after delivery. More than one thousand mothers joined the panel study. Symptoms were checked at four points in time. The team modeled how symptoms changed overall. They also searched for predictors across three domains. Child, mother, and family factors were all considered.

More than half of mothers had at least one depressive episode. Among at-risk mothers, symptoms rose slightly over time. Individual paths varied a great deal between mothers. Early birth and low birth weight raised later risk. Depression before birth was another strong predictor. Postpartum depression also predicted later symptoms clearly. The study argues for support well beyond infancy.
pmc-12843944:
Li and six co-authors designed a button-sized antenna for wearable health networks in twenty twenty-five. Body area networks link sensors on or near the body for monitoring, and their antennas must be small, efficient, and safe against the skin. The proposed button antenna works in two industrial-scientific-medical bands, at two point four five and five point eight gigahertz.

In the lower band it behaves as a linearly polarized monopole radiating in all directions, suited to on-body links. In the upper band it acts as a cross-dipole with circular polarization aimed away from the body, for off-body links, with a very wide bandwidth. Prototype tests in free space and on the body confirmed both modes. Simulated absorption rates in a human model sat well below safety limits. The authors present the design as practical for wearable applications.
pmc-12845644:
Shuangyun Guo and co-authors published this air study in 2025 from Botou, a county-level city in China's Jing-Jin-Ji region. Fine dust in the air, PM2.5, carries water-soluble ions that sour the air and harm lungs. Most past work looked at big cities. The team sampled the dust for a full year, from March 2018 to February 2019, and split the ions by season and source.

Yearly dust levels ran more than twice the national limit. Nitrate was the top ion, then ammonium and sulfate, and the trio of formed-in-air ions made up about a third of the dust mass. Winter was the worst season for most ions. A source model blamed formed-in-air paths first, then crop-waste burning. The authors call for cuts to the gases that seed these ions and to open burning.
pmc-12848044:
Yuan Yao and six co-authors build a deep learning tool to find skin cancer in images. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Melanoma is among the most deadly skin cancers, and early finds are hard. Past image models struggle with the wide range of lesion looks and fail to focus on the key zones.
