Their model adds a scaled dot attention step to a UNet design. That step lets the model stress lesion zones and cut noise as it codes and decodes the image. On a large public set and two small check sets, scores for overlap and accuracy beat a set of rival models by a clear margin. The tool may aid early care in the clinic.
pmc-12849344:
Ya-Ling Yan and co-authors run a trial of all-around rehabilitation for frail older patients facing gut surgery, in a 2025 paper. Care for such patients usually mixes food support, exercise, and psychological help, but most studies stop at the operation itself. Their program spans the whole stay around surgery. Ninety-six frail patients with gut tumors at a Shanghai hospital were split evenly between the program and routine care.

Most patients had colon surgery, the rest stomach surgery, and the groups started alike. Frailty was scored at admission, the day after surgery, at discharge, and one week later. The design lets the team see whether support after surgery, not just before, bends the frailty path. The authors frame the trial as a test of full-journey rehabilitation for this vulnerable group.
pmc-12852844:
Yangyang Xia and co-authors study what makes motorcycle crashes deadly, and whether those factors shift over time, in a 2025 paper. They used United Kingdom crash records from 2016 to 2020, sorting injuries as minor, severe, or fatal. Single-vehicle and multi-vehicle crashes were modeled apart, with a flexible statistical model that allows hidden variation between riders. Likelihood tests checked whether the same factors held across years and crash types.

The models did transfer partly between crash types, but the drivers of severity moved across the five years. Riders aged 25 to 55 in single-vehicle crashes faced a higher chance of fatal injury. In multi-vehicle crashes, an older other driver sharply raised fatal risk. Forecast tests confirmed that severity odds differ by crash type and year. The authors argue safety policy should treat the two crash types separately.
pmc-12854244:
John Salib, Mark Salib, and Frederick Tiesenga report a bowel obstruction caused by a primary ventral hernia. Their case report from twenty twenty-five concerns a woman with no prior surgery. Bowel obstruction usually follows adhesions from earlier operations. Hernias are a rarer cause when the abdomen was never opened.

The patient arrived with growing belly pain and vomiting. A firm, stuck-out mass showed on her abdominal wall. Surgery found a trapped hernia holding damaged fatty tissue. Quick operation prevented bowel death and led to smooth recovery. The authors stress checking for hernia in obstruction cases without surgical history.
pmc-12859844:
Huayang Zhang and co-authors published this genetics study in 2025. It follows a family with repeated deep vein blood clots and a strong history of clotting trouble. Two siblings carried two different faulty copies of the gene for protein C, a natural brake on blood clotting. Inheriting faults in this gene is known to raise clot risk, but how each fault does its damage was unclear.

The team made both variant proteins in lab cells and tested them piece by piece. One fault mainly blocked the step that switches the protein on, leaving its working form intact. The other let activation proceed but weakened the active protein's cutting power, and it also trapped more protein inside cells. Together the two faults cut the clotting brake far more than either alone. The authors say mapping each fault's exact defect can guide personal treatment choices.
pmc-12875544:
Priya Jagia, Vineeta Ojha, and Gautam Sharma published an imaging case report in twenty twenty-five on a woman whose rare disease had wrapped itself around her heart. The forty-year-old arrived with chest pain and fluid repeatedly collecting around the heart. Cardiac MRI showed a sheath-like mass covering mainly the right side of the heart.

Imaging also found disease in her bones and around her kidneys, plus a pineal gland tumor. Biopsy of that tumor showed foamy immune cells with a marker pattern diagnostic of Erdheim Chester disease, a rare non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis. The authors stress that scanning the whole body, not just the painful organ, is what unmasks such diseases.
pmc-13087244:
Anwesha Bhattacharyya and Vineet Choudhary review how fat balance in the retina shapes eye disease, both inherited and acquired. Photoreceptor cells burn through membrane material fast and need a steady supply of lipids to rebuild. When that supply chain slips, stray fat deposits build up.

The misplaced lipids spark oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial trouble, and faulty signaling, all feeding retinal degeneration. The review walks through how lipid control works in a healthy retina, how genes or outside factors break it, and how the breakdown shows up across several retinal diseases. It closes by summarizing strategies that might blunt the damage.
pmc-13128544:
Xinyi Qi, Yuchen Gao, and Peiqing Sun frame how AI stirs mind strain in natural science work past fear of swap-out. Their view piece appeared in twenty twenty-six. AI tools now help read lots, code, read shots, tune tests, draft text, and even judge works. Yet the mind toll on science folks is thinly told. Past work on self-run labs, AI help in text and judge roles, and job strain feeds their frame.

Four parts make the frame: work sight, self stance, blame when thought is lent out, and shop air. Good AI use, they hold, must keep folk hand, learn growth, and a life-fit job, not just speed.
pmc-13142144:
Pablo Knoblovits and five co-authors present a man whose infertility was the sole sign of a rare syndrome. Their case report, from twenty twenty-six, covers Carney complex, an inherited condition that causes many tumors. The man, aged thirty-nine, made no sperm and had tiny calcium spots in his testes. He showed none of the usual outward signs.

His mother and brother had related traits, and a gene test found a fault in a known gene. A tissue sample showed sperm making had stalled and cells died early. Using retrieved sperm gave poor embryo growth, so the couple chose donor sperm. The authors urge doctors to count infertility as a possible clue.
pmc-13146044:
Mohamed Diab and seven colleagues pooled trial results on cell-based therapy for ischemic stroke. Stroke is a top cause of lasting disability, and recovery options stay limited. Cells given after a stroke might help the brain repair itself. Two decades of trials have not settled whether the idea works.

The team searched four databases and gathered nineteen randomized trials. Cell therapy showed no clear effect on deaths at three months. Harm events at twelve months also looked no worse than control care. Scores for nerve function improved a bit more with cell therapy at several time points, though pooled effects stayed weak. The authors call the safety picture reassuring but the benefit unproven. Bigger, better trials are still needed.
pmc-13149444:
Yaakov Greenwald and a team of co-authors describe a huge ongoing study of mental function during war, in a paper on the twenty twenty-three to twenty twenty-five Hamas-Israel war. Long-lasting traumatic stress can shape many parts of life. Few studies track it at this scale while it is still unfolding. The team gathered survey and interview data from three groups, more than sixteen thousand people in all.

The project tracks exposure, trust in institutions, and well-being at several levels, from the person to society. Early findings from the first waves are shown as examples. The authors document the design and future path of the work. They invite joint work across fields and borders to learn about risk and resilience in conflict zones.
pmc-13157144:
Mingyue Wang and six co-authors use three-dimensional dental scans to find what makes an impacted wisdom tooth eat into its neighbor's root, in a two thousand twenty-six dentistry study. External root resorption of the second molar is a hidden injury that can cost the tooth.

Five hundred thirteen impacted third molars were measured for angle, depth, and surrounding bone space. Resorption severity tracked impaction depth and cramped anatomy more than angle alone. The deepest class of impaction, especially where it touched the root's apical third, carried the highest risk, and women showed significantly more severe maxillary damage. The authors recommend proactive removal in high-risk anatomical profiles rather than watchful waiting.
pmc-13159244:
Topcu, Karip, Demir, and Kac present a study from twenty twenty-six on how chat models view dead bodies used in teaching. Bodies given for study remain key to anatomy classes, offering real form that models cannot match. The team asked four large language models about the meaning and duties tied to such bodies. They then grouped the answers by theme. All four models took a shared stance on the core points. They all favored the word donor for the person who gave the body.

The models stressed respect, lawful care, and good conduct toward donors. They stopped short of full personhood but granted clear moral worth. The authors say such models may reinforce ethical habits in students. That could help shape how young doctors see their role.
pmc-13159944:
Joining two ends of a blood vessel usually takes fine stitching, slow work in tight spaces. Marieke Hoogewerf and co-authors test a sutureless alternative, the ELANA end-to-end device, in a pilot study on pigs. Six animals received the device in a divided mammary artery, reached through a partial opening of the breastbone, and were followed for thirty-five or ninety days.

The join succeeded in four of the six animals. Three of those four sealed without any extra help; one needed a single stitch. Building the join took a median of eighteen minutes. The two failures came from trouble holding the vessel aligned while the device deployed. Every successful join stayed open to the end of follow-up, with no narrowing on angiography or under the microscope. The authors call the results promising but the technique demanding, and they ask for design changes that steady the vessel.
pmc-13164444:
Charles Riviere and Loic Villet check how exact bone cuts are in a style of knee replacement that follows each patient's own joint shape, in a 2026 study. In this method the surgeon cuts the thigh and shin bones by hand with manual tools. The team measured the cut pieces after surgery with a digital caliper.

They studied 73 patients and took 408 measurements at set points on both bones. On average the cuts came out slightly thin, missing the target by less than a third of a millimeter. The spread of errors stayed under one millimeter as well. The authors read this as good accuracy and precision for hand-guided cuts, without robots or custom guides.
pmc-13165444:
Drożdż and five co-authors treated plastic surfaces with plasma in this study from twenty twenty-six. Polyurethane is common in medical gear, but germs and cells react to its surface. A low-pressure fluorine-rich plasma added fluorine groups to medical-grade films. The treatment made the surface more water-repellent and roughly doubled its nanoscale roughness.

Bacterial sticking depended on the species. Three strains showed no steady change, but Escherichia coli clung far more to the treated films at every time point. Microscopy confirmed denser coverage by that bacterium. Human lung cells stayed alive and spread normally on the treated surface. Their shape shifted slightly, with shorter axes and smaller grip points. The authors weigh the trade-off for device design.
pmc-13168844:
Chun Wei and colleagues ask if zapping liver tumors with heat helps immune drugs work better, in this study from twenty twenty-six. The drugs, immune checkpoint inhibitors, are a mainstay for advanced liver cancer. Heat ablation, which kills tumor tissue with microwaves, may also wake the immune system, so the pair could do more than either alone.

The team reviewed fifty-two patients whose advanced disease had spread only a little. Twenty-one got the heat treatment plus drugs, and thirty-one got drugs alone. The paired group kept its disease in check far more often, and its members lived longer and went longer before the cancer grew again. The authors are careful: the groups were small, records lacked some tumor details, and hidden bias may remain. They frame the pairing as promising for select patients, to be proven in larger, planned trials.
pmc-13175144:
Ernster leads a large team reporting a second look at a drug trial, in work from twenty twenty-five. The trial tested donepezil, a memory drug, in breast cancer survivors who report thinking problems after chemotherapy. The main trial found no gain on formal thinking tests after twenty-four weeks.

This report covers what patients themselves said about their thinking, an outcome that matters in daily life. Women in the study had finished at least four chemo cycles one to five years before joining. The team also explored what traits link to reported thinking problems. Pairing test scores with self reports gives a fuller view of this common late effect.
pmc-13179444:
Shou-Wu Lee and six co-authors report real-world results for a liver cancer drug in Taiwan in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Lenvatinib is a first-line option when liver tumors cannot be cut out, but trial results may not match everyday practice. The team looked for traits that predict who does well.

One hundred eleven patients treated over three years were reviewed. About a third responded, and four in five gained disease control. Median survival was seventeen months. Patients with the best liver grade, and those also given local therapy, lived clearly longer. A tumor marker below a set cutoff predicted slower progression. The authors back tailored treatment plans and call for prospective confirmation.
pmc-13183144:
Pu Xu and colleagues published a prediction study in 2026. They modeled early pain after cesarean birth surgery. Records covered two years at one hospital. Pain was rated within the first day after surgery. The highest rest or movement score counted most. Moderate to severe pain defined the outcome group. Statistical screening searched for independent risk factors. A visual nomogram turned factors into risk estimates. Accuracy, calibration, and clinical usefulness were all tested. Internal validation checked the model further carefully.

Such models can flag high-risk mothers before surgery. Pain plans can then be tailored in advance. Extra monitoring and stronger relief can be prepared. The nomogram format suits bedside use by clinicians. Single-hospital data limit how widely it applies. Other hospitals should validate it before adoption.
pmc-13183344:
Beatrix Kunas and co-authors pilot an app for mobile health that is built for each user. It sends help for stress at the right time, for staff at work. Their 2026 pilot study tests the RELAX app, for care of stress from work.

Forty-six staff took part in a randomised trial with two arms. It ran over two spans of three weeks each. Sensors worn on the body gauged heart rate variability as a sign of stress. Questionnaires and checks at set moments were used too. The app set when to send help, from stress data in real time. It set what to send from what each user liked. The study looked for early signs that stress had fallen. It also looked at how the level of personalisation shaped that fall. And it looked at how users found the app as a whole.
pmc-13188844:
Zhen Wang leads a team on how rice fights disease sans losing yield. Their study from twenty twenty-six looks at two rice genes, IPA1 and OsNPR1. Disease strength often comes with a growth cost in crops.

The two gene products meet and boost each other in the cell core. When germs attack, one moves in and helps the other bind gene sites. That turns on good defense genes and turns off bad ones. In calm times, a third part keeps the guard low. The finds may help breed strong, high yield rice.
pmc-13191344:
Mogensen and colleagues test a synthetic host molecule, an acyclic cucurbituril called H4, as a sponge for drug pollutants. In solid form, H4 pulled acetaminophen out of water almost completely, and within minutes. Drug residues in water are a growing concern, and fast removal is hard to achieve with simple materials.

In a head-to-head test, H4 matched activated charcoal, the standard emergency adsorbent, at capturing the drug from simulated stomach fluid. That double showing matters: the same material could clean polluted water and serve in overdose care. The study presents H4 as a practical sequestrant, meaning a binder that locks a target away.
pmc-13191844:
Ying Zhang, Jing Yan, Meng Li, and Chaoyan Yue chart three decades of hepatitis C among Chinese women of reproductive age, in a two thousand twenty-six epidemiological study. The group, fifteen to forty-nine, matters for both women's health and transmission to children.

Global Burden of Disease data from nineteen ninety to two thousand twenty-one show every standardized rate falling faster than global averages, driven by genuine epidemiological improvement rather than demography. Yet China remained high-burden, with a large chronic reservoir and a chronic incidence rebound after two thousand ten, concentrated in the oldest band. Projections continue declining through two thousand thirty-five, more slowly. The authors urge sustained, age-tailored interventions.
pmc-13194244:
Svihla and Lladser worked in twenty twenty-six on a math way to tell why two germ groups differ, using their family tree. A wave-like basis can thin out the tree's link table for plain random trees. Real trees of life have a unlike shape, so it was not clear the trick still works.

They test a class of random trees that fits real trees of life more well. With sharp counts of path lengths they show the wave basis still near-thins the link table for most large trees. They also build a test for which tree splits count as real signs. A test on a germ mat gave splits that look like true signs.
pmc-13195744:
Amir Alsharabasy, Godspower Isaac, and Abhay Pandit review hemin nanozymes for use in cancer care, in a 2026 piece. Hemin is the iron part drawn from hemoglobin. It is shown as a core that staff can build into tiny systems that drive chemical change.

The review sets out how tumours can block standard care. Low oxygen, high acid, and high glutathione all play a part. Designs based on hemin join pathways that raise reactive oxygen species and weaken the guards that soak them up. The pathways span chemodynamic, photodynamic, ferroptotic, and metabolic routes. The team sorts past work into a design toolbox. It covers scaffold choice, how parts are tuned to work as a set, and how they are laid out in space. It gives rules for redox materials that adapt to a tumour and may move to real use.
pmc-13195944:
Yawei Hu, Yuanyuan Zhang, Fengxian Yao, and Guidong Liu show that phosphorus fertilizer can be a double-edged sword for orange trees short of magnesium, in a paper dated 2026. Magnesium deficiency yellows citrus leaves and cuts yield. Growers often add phosphorus freely, assuming nutrients only help.

Young navel orange trees grew in sand under two magnesium levels and three phosphorus levels. Without magnesium, leaves yellowed and veins corked, and high phosphorus sped the symptoms dramatically. The same high dose shrank old leaves yet pushed new shoots to grow, a split response. Measurements tied the damage to faster pigment loss, weaker photosynthesis, and more oxidative stress. Nutrient partitioning shifted between old and new growth. The practical lesson: fix the magnesium first, because phosphorus poured on a deficient tree feeds the wrong leaves.
pmc-13196344:
Yutong Hou, Shuna Yang, Yue Li, Wenli Hu, and Lei Yang study fresh stroke spots after bleeding in the brain. A bleed can be followed by small areas of new damage nearby, seen on special scans. The team looked back at 541 patients who had brain scans within two weeks of a bleed. About one in four showed these fresh spots.

Heavy wear of the brain's small vessels was strongly tied to the spots, and a six-point score for that wear sharpened the forecast. Narrowing of the large vessels in the skull also raised the odds, most when both problems came together. The paper helps doctors spot who faces added risk after a bleed.
pmc-13196844:
Nail Barama and a large team study carbon monoxide on a single-atom catalyst surface. Their surface science paper from twenty twenty-six examines rhodium on an iron oxide crystal. Infrared spectroscopy and scanning tunnelling microscopy supply the evidence. The work aims to bridge gaps between lab surface studies and real powder catalysts.

Three kinds of bound carbon monoxide appear in the spectra. Single molecules sit on isolated rhodium atoms in two settings. Paired molecules form mainly when rhodium pairs split apart. That pairing path stays blocked under vacuum conditions. At higher gas pressure, microscopy shows the paired form becomes reachable. The findings clarify how active sites change with pressure.
pmc-13197244:
Mariana Saiz Briceno and four co-authors map the evidence on technology-assisted therapies that help people with impaired vision use their remaining sight better. Their scoping review came out in 2026. More than two billion people live with vision impairment, yet only a minority can access rehabilitation services.

Twenty-five studies from a decade of literature met their rules, mostly from wealthy countries. Interventions included video-based remote therapy, portable electronic aids, virtual reality systems, artificial vision devices, and smart sensors. Reported gains covered visual function, independence, and quality of life, with high satisfaction and adherence. Remote delivery looked viable and cost-effective. The authors note that most studies are small, so larger and more geographically diverse trials are still needed.
pmc-13198544:
Younes Adam Tabi and colleagues probe how visual memory mixes up object features in a 2026 study. When people recall the wrong feature for an object, scientists call it misbinding. The usual story is a clean swap between two objects, but a one-way takeover could also occur, and standard tests cannot tell them apart.

Their new task asks people to report all features of all objects shown, in any order. A math model then splits errors into types. Both clean swaps and one-way replacements appeared in the data. In one-way errors, a forgotten feature is filled by another object's feature with nothing given back. The mix showed even when objects appeared one by one. Memory loss is messier than swaps alone.
pmc-13198844:
Yousef Marzouk and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a bone vessel tumor inside the nose. Hemangiomas are vessel growths; those inside bone make up about one percent of bone tumors and favor skull and spine. Nasal cases are very rare, and this spot had only a few reports.

Their patient was a 51-year-old man with blockage in both nostrils. A scope exam showed a greatly enlarged lower nasal turbinate, a bony fold inside the nose, with normal surface tissue. Scans showed a honeycombed mass arising from that bone. Surgeons removed mass and turbinate in one piece through the nose. Lab study confirmed a cavernous vessel tumor in bone. Recovery was smooth, with no return.
pmc-13201344:
Comics around the world are built from panels, yet basic facts about those panels are scarce, a gap addressed by a 2026 study authored by Neil Cohn. The research article measures panel counts and panel sizes across a large international corpus of comics.

The corpus holds 1,030 comics from 144 countries, with more than 14,000 pages and over 76,000 annotated panels. Panel patterns varied with drawing style, world region, language type, and publication year, the authors report. One relationship held everywhere: pages with larger panels had fewer of them. The study frames comics layout as a balance between local variety and shared structural rules.
pmc-13201944:
A traditional Chinese herbal formula used against sepsis is dissected with modern tools in a 2026 study headed by Muzi Peng. The research article investigates Liujun Jiaoxian Tang, combining chemical analysis of treated rat blood with network pharmacology to map how the mixture might act.

Mass spectrometry identified ninety active ingredients that reached the bloodstream from the formula. Matching those compounds against disease databases produced seventy-six shared targets, including AKT1, TNF, and PTGS2, which are tied to inflammation and immune response. Docking tests showed strong binding for compounds such as kaempferol. The authors present the map as a theoretical basis for clinical use and further experiments.
pmc-13202544:
Qianzi Liu, Minjia Tan, and Yehong Kuang test whether a joint score in psoriatic arthritis also reflects skin disease in a 2026 study. The score, DAPSA, was built to grade joint activity, while skin severity is graded by a separate index. Whether the joint score quietly carries skin information was unknown.

The team studied 646 patients at one Chinese hospital. Joint scores rose step by step from patients with clear skin to those with severe skin disease, and pain and swelling markers rose with them. After matching patients on muscle and joint activity, those with heavy skin disease still scored higher. The link was weak but steady. The authors suggest the joint score can serve as a rough whole-body gauge when skin grading is missing.
pmc-13202844:
Natalia Bezdieniezhnykh, Oleksandra Lykhova, and eight colleagues build a testing pipeline for wound-healing gels and sprays and run a new product through it, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-six. Good regenerative agents are scarce, and judging them needs more than one kind of evidence.

Their algorithm combines cell culture tests with animal experiments. In the lab, three cell lines, including skin-like and connective tissue cells, are exposed to the product. In animals, Wistar rats receive a simulated cut wound, are treated with the gel or spray, and are scored on a panel of healing indicators. The test product's main ingredient showed regenerative activity across the combined assessment. A staged pipeline like this filters out weak candidates before human use. It also gives developers a repeatable yardstick. The paper is as much about the evaluation method as about the particular gel.
pmc-13206844:
Yi Guan and co-authors published this eye study in 2026. Scarring of the cornea is a leading cause of vision loss worldwide, and treatments are few. The team focused on a protein called NREP and on a chemical tag system that controls how proteins get made. A reader protein named YTHDF1 spots these tags on RNA messages. The researchers asked whether that pathway drives corneal scarring after injury.

In mice, scarring after a chemical burn peaked at day fourteen, just as NREP levels rose. In cultured corneal cells, silencing NREP slowed growth and movement. It also blocked the scar-forming state that a growth signal normally triggers. Silencing the reader protein had the same effect and lowered NREP output. A drug blocking the reader did likewise. The findings point to this tag-reading pathway as a possible drug target for corneal scarring.
pmc-13209144:
Adding a second artery-directed treatment may extend survival in inoperable liver cancer, and a 2026 study led by Zhipeng Feng tests that four-part strategy. The research article contrasts 274 patients with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma who received chemoembolization plus arterial infusion chemotherapy, targeted drugs, and immune checkpoint inhibitors against a triple regimen without the infusion.

After matching the groups on baseline traits, the four-part regimen kept cancer controlled months longer and extended median survival by roughly half a year in the authors' analysis. Tumor shrinkage and disease control rates were also higher with the added infusion step. Side effects stayed manageable in both groups, supporting the combination for wider testing.
pmc-13212644:
Mia St Angelo and co-authors interview cancer patients in 2026 about how they choose care teams inside a rural hub-and-spoke health system. Specialist cancer care is scattered across a central hospital and smaller sites, so coordination shapes the patient experience.

Thirty-four patients treated for breast, lung, or colorectal cancer shared their views in semi-structured interviews. Past experience, personal rapport, and practical matters such as travel drove their choices of team and site. Experiences with individual clinicians then coloured how joined-up the whole team felt. No clear difference emerged between patients treated only at the hub and those split across sites, a result planners can use when designing rural services.
pmc-13213144:
George Bcharah and a large team ask in 2026 whether hormone replacement therapy around menopause raises the risk of tendon injuries. Estrogen influences tendon remodelling, and tendon problems are common in middle-aged women, yet the therapy link stayed unclear.

Using a national health records network, the team matched more than sixty-three thousand hormone users with an equal number of similar non-users. Users showed higher diagnosis rates for rotator cuff tears, biceps tendon inflammation, and both forms of tennis or golfer's elbow, while Achilles problems matched. Several repair operations also occurred more often among users. The association cannot prove cause, but it gives clinicians a factor worth weighing with patients.
pmc-13216144:
Lisa Weissmann and co-authors present a 2026 review of gender disparities in radiation oncology, spanning the field's history, its present workforce, and who gets to decide. About half of cancer patients receive radiotherapy, yet sex differences in radiation response remain poorly mapped.

The authors recount how women helped build early radiology while facing closed universities and little recognition, sometimes at the cost of radiation-induced illness. In Germany today, women form 45.1 percent of the specialty society's members and most trainees, yet hold only 27 percent of leadership posts and 18.9 percent of full professorships. Guideline panels show the same thinning at the top. Survey evidence ties part of the gap to unpaid care work and temporary contracts.
pmc-13216444:
Isabelle C. Santos and co-authors present a 2026 letter describing a prognosis score for acute myeloid leukaemia built from mitochondrial genes. Standard risk classes leave much of this blood cancer's behaviour unexplained, and the machinery that runs the cell's energy organelles is one place the missing signal might live.

Twelve genes involved in mitochondrial genome expression were selected from a training cohort of 121 patients and combined into a weighted score. Patients above the cut-off had far worse survival, with three-year overall survival of 19 percent against 55 percent below it. The split held across three independent validation cohorts totalling over 800 patients. The score outperformed the current European classification on discrimination tests. The authors propose it as an add-on for risk stratification.
pmc-13216744:
Wang and colleagues published in twenty twenty-six a structural study of drug-like molecules that wedge into unusual DNA junctions. Most DNA is a double helix, but three-stranded junctions also form. The team studied two compounds that combine a weak and a strong flat ring system. Crystal structures show how they grip a three-stranded junction. The grip distorts the DNA and breaks the junction's integrity in a local way.

One compound, with a four-carbon linker, fit the junction best. Its strong ring mainly blocked an enzyme that cancer cells need. Its weak ring mainly suppressed several cancer-linked genes. In mouse tumors of colon and lung origin, it worked potently with little liver harm. The work marks triplex junctions as real drug targets.
pmc-13217444:
Yung-Fong Tsai and co-authors ask whether diabetes drugs called GLP-1 receptor agonists protect a weakened aorta, in a 2026 study. An aortic aneurysm can tear or burst, and more than half of such events kill the patient. Few drug options exist for people living with an aneurysm. The team used records from 152 health organizations in the United States, covering 2016 to 2023.

They compared new users of these drugs with users of another diabetes drug class known to be neutral for the heart. After matching, each group held 3,857 patients with diabetes and an aneurysm. The GLP-1 group had lower risks of aortic tearing needing surgery, of blood pressure crises, and of death from any cause. The authors suggest these drugs deserve preference in this high-risk group.
pmc-13217944:
Stephanie Meciar and co-authors published a 2026 scoping review on the commercial practices of the arms industry and their effects on public health. Industries such as tobacco and alcohol have long been studied as commercial determinants of health, meaning ways business conduct shapes population health. The arms trade, the authors argue, has escaped similar scrutiny.

Searching four academic databases plus Google Scholar, the team gathered 41 studies published between 2004 and 2024 and coded them against a typology of commercial practices. Marketing and political practices appeared most often, while financial, labor, and supply chain practices were less documented. The review also surfaced tactics beyond existing frameworks, including bribery, surveillance of workers, and contesting workers' illness claims. Most studies covered firearms in the United States, leaving conventional and nuclear weapons and poorer countries understudied, which the authors flag as a gap.
pmc-13218144:
Nauzer Forbes and colleagues present the STRIPE study in a 2026 protocol, a five-arm randomized trial of intravenous fluid regimens to prevent pancreatitis after ERCP. ERCP is a scope procedure on the bile and pancreatic ducts, and inflammation of the pancreas afterward strikes 5 to 15 percent of patients, causing harm. Aggressive fluid infusions reduce that risk but run for up to a day, which does not fit outpatient care.

STRIPE tests whether brief hydration around the procedure can do the job. Five hundred five participants will be assigned one of 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, or 2500 milliliters of Ringer's lactate around the procedure. Patients, endoscopists, and assessors will stay blind to the dose. The main outcome is the blood amylase level 24 hours after the procedure, a marker for pancreatitis. Secondary outcomes include pancreatitis cases, unplanned healthcare visits, fluid overload, hospital stay length, and deaths within thirty days. The trial is registered and ethics-approved.
pmc-13220844:
Jun-Bo Ding, Mei-Xi Lin, Dan Zang, and Jun Chen review how microbes and their products choreograph immune cells in a 2026 paper. The microbiota, the bulk of the microbiome, influences how cancers start and grow, and the microenvironment is where immune cells attack cancer or stand down. Immunotherapy has transformed care, yet a share never responds, for reasons rooted in the gut.

It follows how microbial metabolites switch immune cells on, move them through tissue, and remodel behavior. It connects dynamics to treatment response, including the variability of anti-PD-1 and PD-L1. Two research platforms are proposed to move the field from correlation to mechanism. One is a monitoring model that tracks the microbe-immune conversation as it unfolds; the other is a co-culture pairing organoids with microbes. The authors frame the work as groundwork for therapies treating the microbiome as part of the prescription.
pmc-13222144:
Riccardo Mazzoli and colleagues monitor air quality in two Italian university classrooms from March 2022 to May 2023, in a 2026 feasibility study called MIRAI. Low-cost sensors tracked carbon dioxide and airborne particles in rooms differing in size and ventilation. The goal was judging infection risk from airborne spread using air measures as proxies.

The naturally ventilated room showed higher, more variable carbon dioxide and particle levels. The mechanically ventilated room stayed steadier, with occasional spikes. Full occupancy and cold months, when windows stayed shut, worsened readings in both rooms. The authors recommend such sensors as practical tools for spotting poor ventilation and prompting fixes that protect students and staff.
pmc-13223944:
Valerie Matarredona Pérez, Mercedes Guilabert, and Cristina Navarro Maciá lead a team mapping programs that teach family caregivers to give safe care at home. Their scoping review appeared in two thousand twenty-six. Aging populations and chronic disease are shifting care from institutions into homes. Family members now perform tasks once left to professionals, sometimes with costly mistakes.

Following scoping review standards, the team searched three major databases. Thirty-one studies of home safety education programs qualified. The review charts who was taught, what skills were covered, and which safety outcomes were measured. Programs spanned conditions from cancer care onward. Benefits are reported, but training to prevent and handle errors is understudied. The authors call out that gap for program designers. Their map shows where evidence exists and where it thins.
pmc-13224344:
Regina Maria Marquezini Chammes and Reginaldo Raimundo Fujita examine a 2026 review of ethics cases against ear, nose, and throat specialists in São Paulo state, Brazil. Medical error is sorted into three kinds: negligence through inaction, recklessness through hasty action, and malpractice through lack of technical skill. The authors ask which pattern dominates among otorhinolaryngologists who faced ethics proceedings.

Negligence emerged as the most frequent failing in the cases reviewed. Most sanctions imposed on these specialists stayed confidential rather than public. Rhinology and pharyngology produced the highest numbers of convictions, while otology attracted the most complaints. Placed against national figures on patient harm, the findings give the specialty a clearer map of where risk at work concentrates.
pmc-13226544:
Huang and colleagues compare four surgical strategies for infected knee replacements at a single centre. When infection takes hold around a knee implant, surgeons have four routes. They can clean and keep it. They can swap it in one operation. They can use an in-between staged swap. Or they can remove and replace it in two stages. Reports of failure under each route vary wildly.

The team looks back at their own cases and counts two hard outcomes: infection returning, and needing another revision operation. Counting both matters, since a strategy can clear infection yet still cost further surgery. Their numbers give patients and surgeons centre-specific grounds for a hard choice, where the best option depends on trading cure against burden.
pmc-13227744:
Omar Abdelaziz and colleagues pool a 2026 meta-analysis of steroid drugs given around first-time hip replacement surgery, restricted to randomised trials and graded for evidence quality. Earlier syntheses mixed hip and knee replacements together, blurring the answer. Twelve trials covering 1,128 patients measured pain, nausea and vomiting, opioid use, blood sugar, and hospital stay.

Steroids reduced pain modestly both at rest and while walking, with the largest walking-pain gain on the first day after surgery. Every average reduction, though, fell short of the improvement threshold patients themselves would count as meaningful for hip replacement. The authors' careful grading shows how a statistically real effect can still be clinically small, a distinction that matters for recovery-protocol decisions.
pmc-13228844:
Joseph Kirabira, Letizia Maria Atim, and Angela Spencer systematically review a 2026 evidence base on helping children and teenagers in lower-income countries learn their HIV status. Telling a child this diagnosis remains a public-health challenge, and programmes vary widely. Four databases plus Google Scholar were searched for intervention studies, then screened against strict eligibility rules.

From 260 retrieved studies, only six qualified, three of them randomised trials. Most interventions were delivered by health workers and mixed ingredients such as training, videos, books, and counselling. Outcomes measured ranged from safety and acceptability to how many children were actually told. Just two studies showed significant gains in disclosure rates, and inconsistent measurement across studies limited firm conclusions for policy.
pmc-13231544:
Sandra A Binning and Allison K Shaw offer in 2026 a reporting checklist for studies where animal infection meets animal migration. Reviews that combine many studies can go wrong when basic facts about each study system stay unstated. Experts often skip details they assume everyone knows, while readers from other fields guess wrongly.

Their fifteen-item list covers migration, parasites, and sampling choices that every paper should state plainly. Two worked examples show what each item reveals, plus a mock study that exposes how hard missing details are to recover later. Nearly every paper in a thirty-six-study test set missed at least one item, and many missed more than half. Clearer reporting would make cross-species lessons safer to draw.
pmc-13233544:
Augustin Tchassem Dimdie and colleagues published a 2026 case report on removing a broken guidewire fragment from a heart artery. A 58-year-old man had received stents in two coronary arteries at another hospital, where the guidewire snapped at a branch point and part stayed behind. A week later he returned with chest pain, since a retained fragment can trigger clots or block blood flow.

The team used intravascular ultrasound, a tiny camera inside the vessel, to watch the fragment in real time rather than relying on X-ray shadows alone. Guided by those images, they caught the fragment with a gooseneck snare and pulled it out without disturbing the stents. Recovery was uneventful, and the authors argue the technique can spare patients open surgery.
pmc-13234044:
Carolina Guidolin and Manuel Spitschan published a 2026 article making the case for podcasts as a tool in circadian and sleep science. The field stretches from molecular biology to public health advice, and its findings often fail to travel between specialists or reach the public. The authors argue that podcasting can carry new research, explain settled evidence together with its uncertainties, support university teaching, and nudge healthier sleep behavior.

They situate the format among modern science communication practices and discuss its weak points honestly: quality control without gatekeepers, limited reach, and the money and labor needed to sustain a series. The piece is a practical brief for researchers weighing whether the microphone is worth their time, drawn from experience engaging stakeholders through audio.
pmc-13234144:
Guido K W Frank and colleagues published a 2026 feasibility trial of ketogenic therapy for adults with anorexia nervosa. The eating disorder's core fears and body preoccupations often survive weight recovery and drive relapse. Fourteen weeks of a weight-maintaining ketogenic diet, very low in carbohydrate, were offered to twenty-two adults who were mildly underweight or weight-restored, and eighteen finished.

Symptom scores fell across restraint, eating concern, shape concern, and weight concern, and depression scores improved too. By the end, about seventy-two percent of participants scored within the normal range on both measures. Nobody's symptoms worsened and no clinically important weight loss occurred. Three months later, those who stayed on the diet relapsed less often by questionnaire than those who stopped. The authors call for a larger controlled trial.
pmc-13234344:
Peng Zhou and co-authors built in 2026 a portable device for detecting DNA and RNA away from central laboratories. Many people worldwide lack ready access to basic diagnostic testing, especially in rural and low-income settings. Their platform runs on smartphone power and uses a small chip with a laser-made graphene heater. The heater drives a copying method that works at one steady temperature.

The system detected targets present at only a few copies in a small sample volume. Steady power use for the heater was very low, around one hundred thirty milliwatts. pmc-13242944:

pmc-13243144:

pmc-13243744:

pmc-13244344:

pmc-13247644:

pmc-13269844:

The report warns that blast cells in such settings need urgent, careful work-up.
pmc-13283644:
Ziying Guan and co-authors created a wound gel in 2026 that pairs collagen with brown sugar for burn care. Brown sugar, the first extract from sugarcane, has a long history in Chinese traditional medicine. The gel also carried epicatechin, a plant compound, and the team checked whether the parts worked better together than apart.

It lowered an inflammatory signal, raised a calming one, and sped skin cell movement and growth. In mouse and rat burn models, treated wounds closed far faster, with about six percent of the wound left at day fourteen. pmc-13283744:

The authors offer the combined approach as a candidate for wider testing.
pmc-13284244:
Youth canoe results predict senior success only partly, test Christian Saal and colleagues in a 2026 machine learning study of German athletes. Body measures, fitness tests, and on-water times were gathered yearly. The question is who reaches national versus international level as adults.

Data spanned 1992 to 2019 for 729 young sprint canoeists in total. A boosted-tree model sorted senior level with acceptable overall accuracy. Precision for the international class stayed low, with many false alarms. The two-kilometer on-water test mattered most among all inputs. Newer validation cohorts from 2021 to 2023 showed weaker accuracy. Early promise needs careful reading.
pmc-13285444:
Huang and coauthors review how cell self-cleaning guards eye health. Cells break down worn parts and reuse the bits for fuel. That flow keeps cells in balance under stress and strain. When flow fails, eye illness can follow and harm sight.

Faulty cleaning links to macular wear, glaucoma, and cataracts. The review joins lab, gene model, and clinic proof on those links. It maps how cleaning works in each eye tissue type. It also sums up drug routes that tune the flow. Their aim is care that saves sight by fixing cell cleaning.
pmc-13285544:
Too much thrombin in the gut may turn friendly microbes hostile in Crohn disease, Guillaume Le Cosquer and co-authors report in a 2026 study. Thrombin, a clotting enzyme made by the gut wall, normally keeps microbes at bay. Stool from some Crohn patients held far more of it than stool from healthy people.

Lab biofilms grown from human colon samples broke apart under thrombin, shed bacteria that stuck hard to gut cells, and stirred immune alarms. Passing thrombin-touched microbes into germ-free mice sparked gut swelling and germ spread. In rats with colitis, blocking thrombin healed the biofilm coat and eased tissue harm. The authors name thrombin as a host lever on gut germ behavior.
pmc-13285744:

In their place, blood-born macrophages grew in number and split into groups that drive inflammation, scarring, and fat handling. One group also pulled in more blood cells, feeding a self-sustaining cycle. Blocking that pull, or shielding resident cells, may offer early treatment paths.
pmc-13286144:
Lu Han and colleagues test how soft soils behave once frozen for subway digging in a 2026 engineering study. Crews can freeze wet ground into a solid wall, then tunnel through it beneath a working station above. Four soils from the site, from silty clay to weathered volcanic rock, went through lab tests across a span of freezing temperatures.

Heat flowed through the soils faster as they grew colder, with the weathered rock gaining the most ground. Frozen strength rose as temperature fell, jumping hardest in one mid-range band of cold. Under steady load the soils crept in three stages, and long-term strength sat well below the quick-test value. Weathered rock proved strongest and mucky soil weakest, so the authors urge freezing plans tuned soil by soil, with close watch on weak layers.
pmc-13286544:
Patricia Genovese and colleagues ask whether underfeeding a mother rat during pregnancy and nursing leaves lasting marks on her sons' reproductive organs. The 2026 study mated thirty female rats, then fed half of them only half rations through pregnancy and lactation. Their sons were examined at one year of age, long after normal feeding resumed.

Grown sons of restricted mothers weighed less, were shorter, and had lighter testes with fewer Sertoli cells, the support cells that set sperm-making capacity. Cell division and death rates inside the testis looked unchanged. Surprisingly, their blood testosterone ran higher, and hormone receptors increased in the muscle-like cells around the tubules. Early hunger, the authors conclude, programs adult testis function in lasting ways.
pmc-13286744:
Qin Sun and colleagues build an artificial intelligence system that reads breast ultrasound images together with the written features radiologists record, such as lesion shape and margin. Their 2026 study tackles a known weakness: ultrasound reading varies with the operator, while earlier computer models ignored the structured descriptions experts rely on.

The network lets the clinical descriptors steer attention toward suspicious regions of the image. Testing used records from 252 patients, carefully split so training and evaluation never leaked into each other. The combined model scored higher than image-only or descriptor-only versions and kept a good balance between catching cancers and avoiding false alarms. Attention maps matched where experts look, around tumor edges. The authors pitch it as a second opinion tool.
pmc-13286844:
Erhayat Özgür Bayazıtlı and colleagues model how social media use connects with eating behavior among sports science students in Türkiye. The 2026 survey covered 1,576 students at 38 public universities. These students swim in health content online and may later model healthy habits for others, which makes their own eating attitudes worth understanding.

The proposed chain ran from social media factors through nutrition literacy, attitudes toward functional foods, acceptance of cravings, and emotional eating, ending at eating attitudes. Every link tested as statistically meaningful, and together the middle steps carried a substantial share of the total association. The full chain's own effect was tiny, however. Literacy about healthy eating online and acceptance-based coping stood out as key middle steps.
pmc-13286944:
Zhiguang Ren and a large team build vaccine proteins from the parts of the coronavirus spike that change most. Their study came out in 2026. The goal is breadth, since the virus keeps mutating to dodge immunity. The team fused repeat copies of the spike's binding part into single proteins. Insect cells made the proteins.

Tests in animals gauged immune response and shield from live virus. The three designs stirred cross-strain immunity to mixed degrees. Each gave strong shield in the challenge tests, the team reports. The authors pitch the method as a path to a vaccine that covers many strains at once. The same plan may speed design for the next pandemic virus.
pmc-13287044:
Yuqiao Zhang and colleagues find a counterintuitive pattern in allergy test data from 635 patients in northwestern China who were sensitized to mugwort pollen. The 2026 study asks what predicts a very strong antibody reaction to mugwort among people already positive for it. Mugwort is a heavy local allergy burden, yet the drivers of reaction strength were poorly understood.

A feature-selection method picked sensitization levels to ragweed, trees, and dust mites as the top predictors, all pointing downward: stronger reactions to those allergens meant weaker mugwort reactions. A machine learning model using them discriminated well on fresh data. The authors read the pattern as immunodominance, where dominant allergens mask others, and built a scoring chart for flagging high-risk patients.
pmc-13287144:
Kubra Ayse Dasdemir and Nihan Karatas wrote a 2026 narrative review asking what elastic therapeutic tape can and cannot do for worn, painful knees. They weighed proposed skin and muscle effects against trial evidence on pain, daily function, strength, joint position sense, and movement.

Five databases were searched to May 2026, and stronger designs were given more weight. Pain relief was brief and usually smaller than what patients would notice, while strength did not rise. Some gains appeared for position sense at certain angles and for bending the knee. The authors advise against tape alone, suggesting short use alongside exercise and education instead.
pmc-13287344:
Young-Han Lee and co-authors built a silicon battery anode in 2026 wrapped in several stretchy, conductive support layers made from tin, a cobalt silicide, graphite, and carbon. The design was made by a simple route the authors say can scale. Silicon stores much charge but swells and cracks as it works.

The layered supports keep electrical contact, let lithium ions move, and absorb swelling stress at several levels. Full cells reached energy density figures the authors report as 434.4 watt-hours per kilogram with liquid electrolyte. Values above 300 were reported for solid versions. Cycling held up well in both systems, the authors say.
pmc-13287444:
Ebrahim A Mattar and colleagues predicted dissolved oxygen in water in 2026 from other measured water properties, using a small public set of 200 samples. Their deep learning model was tuned by a search method named after ninja strategies, under a fixed split of training, checking, and test data.

Tuned settings clearly beat the untuned model on the same test budget, though exact error figures are missing from the summary text. The authors are careful about scope: the data are small, taken at single time points, and lack place and time structure. Wider testing on larger, varied monitoring sets is required before the model can support real water management decisions.
pmc-13287544:
Yunzhu Ruan and colleagues present in 2026 three relatives with drug-resistant focal epilepsy from an inherited condition tied to the GATOR1 gene group. All carried the same change in NPRL3. Early brain scans were read as normal or unclear, which often blocks referral for surgery.

One relative's scan showed a faint suspect patch, prompting fresh review for all three. Advanced imaging then found a seizure source in each person. Targeted removal followed. Every patient stayed seizure free for more than five years at last check. The authors argue that a gene linked to cortical malformation should trigger deep re-examination, even when first scans look clean.
pmc-13287844:
Bekzhan A Permenov and co-authors counted the research literature in 2025 on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, a machine that takes over heart and lung work for the sickest patients. Their database sweep covered English work from 1958 to 2025 and also tracked the small set of withdrawn papers.

A total of 26,786 papers were found, peaking in 2022. The United States led output, and one specialty journal and one medical school topped the lists. Pandemic papers drew the most citations and online attention. Only nine papers were retracted between 2012 and 2024. The authors present the map as a guide for future teams and partnerships.
pmc-13288044:
Alaa Mohammed Snobar, Chaza Nader Kouchaji, and Mohammed N Al-Shiekh ran a blinded trial in 2026 with 100 children aged four to six who needed a numbing injection in the lower jaw. Groups used a standard talk-show-do routine alone, a thumb sleeve visual trick, a popping fidget toy, or both distractions together.

Pulse, face-scale anxiety, and pain scores were tracked at set points. The combined distraction group tended to show the lowest pain and later anxiety. Solo routine tended to score worst. Yet no gap between groups passed statistical checks. The authors still offer the cheap tricks as gentle support tools for young children during dental injections.
pmc-13288544:
Mengyao Liu and colleagues review malnutrition risk models for dialysis patients in China. Their 2026 review searched nine databases. The cut date was January 26, 2026. Two reviewers screened work on their own. Each model was graded with the PROBAST tool.

Twelve studies made the cut. Pooled malnutrition hit 41 percent. Eight traits predicted risk in pooled tests. Age and blood calcium were on that list. Dialysis dose, sex, and vitamin D also counted. Diabetes and a heart marker counted too. Nine checked models split cases well on average. Yet all models had high bias risk. Weak data and poor reports drove that risk.
pmc-13288744:
Chao Fang and colleagues compare a deep brain hub across mammals in 2026. The hub is the claustrum. It links widely across the cortex. It figures in thought, mood, and brain states. Its borders and subparts stay disputed. Primate maps clash with each other too.

Marker genes were tracked in rat tissue. They were Nurr1, Oprk1, Lxn, and Cdh8. The pattern was matched in shrews and marmosets. Macaques were also checked. Cell layout and position joined the reads. Shared order appeared despite size and shape gaps. Set subdivisions can anchor fair cross-species reads, they argue.
pmc-13288944:
Marta Ruiz-Algueró and colleagues study doctor visits before MS starts. Their 2026 study uses health data from British Columbia. It tracks 2,038 people who later got MS. It also tracks 10,182 matched peers. Visits were counted for 15 years before onset.

Women with MS showed raised visits for most years. Men showed raised visits in just a few years. Vague symptoms drove much of the gap in women. Mental health and muscle issues also ran high. Eye and GP visits stayed high for years. Ages 30 to 49 showed the clearest pattern. Care use may warn of MS long before onset.
pmc-13289144:
Kristina Zeljic and colleagues write a 2026 perspective on climate change and youth mental health. The piece deals with poorer nations. Such nations face the worst climate harm. Yet their mental toll is likely undercounted. Most past work comes from rich nations.

A stark pattern drives the blind spot. Places most at risk have the least internet access. Surveys run online miss those places. Young people there live the crisis daily. Worry and strain can harm sleep and school work. The authors call for offline, local methods. Policies should rest on lived experience. Frontline voices must shape the response, they argue.
pmc-13289344:
Novatus Apolinary Tesha headed a 2026 systematic review on costs of HPV self-sampling for cervical cancer screening. Self-sampling lets women collect their own sample for HPV DNA testing, which may reach people who skip clinic exams. The authors gathered economic studies worldwide and asked whether cost results depend on how programs invite women.

Searches covered 2015 to 2025 and yielded 33 studies, spanning 11 low- and middle-income countries and nine high-income countries. Community campaigns dominated in lower-income settings, while mail opt-in and opt-out designs led in richer settings. Cost per woman screened varied by setting, as reported in the review. Most studies judging value found self-sampling cost-effective or cost-saving overall.
pmc-13289844:
Cameron J Harvey led a 2026 prospective pilot of an ambient artificial intelligence scribe in Hawaii Pacific Health clinics. Doctors spend hours in record systems, often after clinic, fueling burnout. The Abridge tool listens and drafts notes inside the Epic record system, and the pilot ran from December 2024 to February 2025 with a goal of 75 providers.

A total of 80 providers joined and 79 finished, producing more than 25,000 notes during the pilot window. Surveys before and during use were paired with system logs on time and note quality. High use meant the scribe helped in at least 60 percent of visits for that provider. Main focus was documentation time per visit, plus burnout and patient views.
pmc-13290444:
Pairing the diabetes drug metformin with the plant compound parthenolide hit breast cancer harder than either alone, Raghad Alomari and colleagues report in 2026. Both agents had shown anticancer hints separately; this study tested them together in cells and in mice.

Against three breast cancer cell lines, the combination interacted synergistically to slow growth. In mice carrying EMT6/P tumors, combined treatment shrank tumors significantly, cured half the animals, and caused no treatment-related deaths. Tumor tissue showed more caspase-3-driven apoptosis and less VEGF, pointing to cell suicide plus choked blood supply as the mechanisms, and blood markers of liver and kidney damage stayed normal. pmc-13290544:
Dystonia and chronic pain look unrelated, yet both grow from a cortex that rewires itself badly, Abteen Mostofi and Keyoumars Ashkan argue in a 2026 review article. Plasticity normally serves learning and recovery, but in these conditions it turns excessive or misdirected within the sensorimotor cortex.

pmc-13291044:
Spiritual care for dying children, and how to keep it steady across hospital and home, is examined in a 2026 qualitative study led by Loes Berkhout. Two themes emerged: referrals and coordination often fragment care, and good care depends on knowing the family story, matching language and culture, and working across professions. Parents valued carers who already knew their story without being told again.
pmc-13291544: A correction notice from 2026 fixes a figure in a Neandertal genome study by Diyendo Massilani and colleagues. All that is present here is the correction notice. Figure 2 and its legend appeared in the wrong form. Both are reprinted correctly in the notice. The study itself compares an Altai Neandertal genome with other ancient humans. Its findings lie outside what this notice can show.
pmc-13291744:

pmc-13292244:

pmc-13292444:

pmc-13292944:

pmc-13293444:

Their shortcut method aims to give builders a reliable design aid.
pmc-13293744:

Healing and looks trended better too, without firm gaps.
pmc-13293844:

Disease control looked good after nine months, but the authors stress that long-term outlook stays unclear because so few cases exist.
pmc-13293944:

The two sources held 2,040 and 1,855 articles. Yearly output sped up from 2015 and jumped after 2020. China led on volume with 535 papers, followed by the United States at 451 and Japan at 106, while the United States led on citations. Hot topics cluster around agents, techniques, and combined treatments.
pmc-13294244:
Janine Bowring and coauthors evolve phage-resistant Staphylococcus aureus in a 2026 lab study and measure the costs. Bacteria dodge virus therapy mainly by altering wall sugars that phages grip. pmc-13294344:

pmc-13294444:

The authors offer the agent as a way to find gut sores without a scope and to judge whether care is working.
pmc-13294844:
Yang Zhou and co-authors evaluate electrical muscle stimulation after hip replacement in a 2026 study. Poor sleep is common after hip arthroplasty and interacts closely with pain during recovery. Stimulating the gluteus medius muscle was tested as a way to improve both hip function and rest.

One hundred patients treated between January 2022 and August 2025 were divided into a stimulation group of 55 and a control group of 45. Sleep scores also favoured the stimulated group, and pain and sleep ratings moved closely together.
pmc-13294944:
Ya Chen and colleagues study metal dust inside collectors at a wheel factory in a 2026 article. Aluminium-magnesium dust from casting work can damage lungs and can explode when it builds up. Lab tests measured density, surface area, makeup, and particle size for each dust type. Heat treatment dust had the largest surface area, while shot blasting dust carried notable chromium and the greatest density. Computer flow models then showed how shape and size steer settling, trapping in swirls, and hot zones, informing safer collector design and worker protection.
pmc-13295344:
Charinya So-In and a large team map mouth microbes of dogs and cats by home setting in a 2026 pilot study. Oral germ communities shape pet health, yet how living alone or with other animals changes them was little known. Gene sequencing compared pets in single and shared homes.

Diversity and makeup differed between groups, though with some overlap in shared core members. Certain species rose or fell with housing style, and predicted functions varied for food handling and adapting to surroundings. Because those functions come from computer inference, the authors treat results as a baseline map for later direct studies of shared-home microbe movement.
pmc-13295544:
John Williams and colleagues review hearing harm linked to a thyroid eye drug in a 2026 article. Teprotumumab was the first targeted approval for thyroid eye disease and eases bulging and inflammation well. Reports since launch tie it to hearing loss, ringing, and ear fullness in some patients.

Ten studies with hearing test results met the entry rules for the review. Problems were usually both-sided high-frequency loss appearing after three to six infusions, and many deficits persisted after stopping the drug. Testing routines varied wildly and often skipped baseline measures. The authors urge agreed monitoring plans backed by prospective studies before harm becomes permanent.
pmc-13295844:
Wenxiao Xia and colleagues review, in 2026, heart inflammation linked to cancer drugs known as immune checkpoint inhibitors. Though uncommon, this side effect is often fatal, and its causes are still being mapped.

Current and possible treatments get attention, including cytokine blockers and JAK/STAT drugs. Tests for spotting and tracking the condition, from troponin blood tests to scans and biopsy, are weighed with their limits.
pmc-13295944:
Tobias Brandl and colleagues set out a 2026 trial protocol for postural tachycardia syndrome, where standing triggers a racing heart plus fatigue and brain fog. Drug options often help little, so the Vienna team test ear-based vagus nerve stimulation paired with slow breathing.

One hundred patients will be split into four groups mixing real or sham stimulation with paced or normal breathing for twelve weeks. The main measure is heart rate change during a tilt test, backed by symptom and quality-of-life scores. Daily hour-long sessions form the treatment, and results should show whether the pairing helps.
pmc-13296044:
Pedro Henrico Grazziotin Portal and colleagues set out a 2026 trial protocol in southern Brazil testing tocilizumab, an antibody that blocks interleukin-6 signalling, for stubborn depression. Inflammation may drive some resistant cases, yet few trials have targeted this pathway in psychiatry.

Twenty-two outpatients with resistant depression and raised inflammation markers will receive one infusion of the drug or saline on top of usual care, with neither side knowing which. Mood, thinking and blood markers will be checked over four weeks, and ten healthy volunteers provide comparison samples. The small study is framed as proof of concept.
pmc-13296144:
Sun A Ock and co-authors build, in 2026, a renewable pig liver-like cell line for laboratory research. Real liver cells barely grow outside the body, so the team convert pig fibroblasts into liver-like progenitors using a gene delivery method that leaves no permanent change.

The new cells show liver features and keep growing over long culture. Their chromosomes stay stable and their telomeres, the caps that limit cell division, keep their length, supporting lasting growth. The cells fall short of fully mature liver cells, the authors note. Still, they offer a repeatable system for studying liver biology and drug safety.
pmc-13296844:
Junhong Wu, Baijun Zhang, and Hengrui Liu build a gene signature for lung adenocarcinoma that spreads to the brain, in a 2026 study. Spreading cells must resist anoikis, the death program that normally kills detached cells. Single-cell and bulk gene data were combined to find anoikis-related features of brain metastasis.

An eight-gene signature tracked patient prognosis and showed early promise in separating primary tumours from brain metastases. Macrophage signalling in the tumour surroundings also appeared involved in adaptation. The team used a language-model-assisted search plus docking to nominate candidate compounds, with early laboratory checks on one gene and one compound. Much more validation is needed before clinical use, the authors caution.
pmc-13296944:
John Dotis reviews, in 2026, food-based options for children who keep getting urinary infections, where repeated antibiotics breed resistance. Cranberry compounds, probiotics, certain vitamins and the sugar D-mannose are weighed for how they might block germs through the gut-bladder connection.

Standardised cranberry doses near a stated daily level may cut recurrence, while probiotics and vitamins A, C and D could add support by tuning microbes and immunity. Studies vary widely in design and dose, and strong child-specific trials are few. Dotis proposes a layered prevention plan matched to each child's risk, with better trials to follow.
pmc-13297544:
One nuclear protein may sit at the crossroads of gene splicing and DNA repair in glioma, proposes a 2026 review led by Xi Wu. The protein, ARGLU1, is presented as a possible hub linking RNA polymerase II pausing, spliceosome activity, and homologous recombination in the most common malignant brain tumor.

The authors are candid that direct glioma evidence remains limited and validation in glioma cohorts is still missing. Because the protein is intrinsically disordered, they suggest degrader strategies such as PROTACs as a route to drug it.
pmc-13297644:
Routine practice backs consolidation immunotherapy after chemoradiation for advanced lung cancer, at least when tumors express PD-L1. PD-L1-positive patients who never got the drug fared worst of all. The authors read the pattern as support for the treatment's value outside trials, and as a reminder that PD-L1 testing and actual access to consolidation therapy shape survival.
pmc-13297844:
Yuxin Han and colleagues work out the capacity of fading radio channels when meaning, not raw bits, is what counts, in a 2026 theory paper. Semantic communication groups signals that mean the same as interchangeable, which changes the maths of channel limits. The team applied that grouping to the channel's fading strength, and later to its noise as well.

Formulas and firm bounds for the semantic capacity were derived for both cases. A neural network search found the best grouping of channel states under set limits. At a strong signal level, the worked example reached a high semantic rate per unit of spectrum. The frame fits inside both classical and semantic theory, the authors note.
pmc-13297944:
Judging burn depth from photographs is error-prone, so Yamile Montecinos-Rodríguez and co-authors trained a small neural network to do it in a 2026 study. Using clinical images from a private wound clinic, they built a compact model to separate second-degree from third-degree burns.

pmc-13298744:

Young adults got deformed wing virus by injection, mimicking mite transmission, plus sacbrood virus by feeding, then returned to colonies. Immune responses depended on virus type, relative amounts, and infections the bees already carried. The authors confirm harmful interaction between the two viruses, with consequences for bee health and colony dynamics worth colony-level focus.
pmc-13299144:

pmc-13300144:
Elena Violeta Iborra-Palau and others explore patient experience inside a nursing-led psoriasis phototherapy unit in Spain, in a 2026 qualitative study. Interviews with 72 patients at a tertiary hospital were analysed thematically. Stress was named the main trigger. Patients as a group asked for a permanent specialist nurse guide. The authors argue clearance alone is insufficient without integrated, patient-centred support.
pmc-13300644:
Life after spinal cord injury is shaped by mood, work, and social connection, and Hyun-Ju Ju and two colleagues map how researchers treat those forces in two countries. Employment mattered everywhere, framed as economic strain in Korea and vocational outcomes in the United States. Participation themes split too, between community transition in Korea and accessibility in America.
pmc-13301044:

pmc-13303044:

pmc-13303844:
Mustafa Altintaş and colleagues describe fall injuries during a harsh snowfall and icing spell in Diyarbakır, Türkiye, in a 2026 emergency study. Cities unused to long winter weather can face sudden surges of weather-linked trauma.

A single hospital reviewed 943 patients who arrived with arm or leg injuries during the episode. About half had a fracture, most injuries hit the upper limbs, and most visits fell on days at or below freezing. Roughly four patients in five were treated without surgery. Age and outdoor temperature were checked for how well they flagged who would need an operation.
pmc-13304444:

MicroRNAs circulate stably in plasma and help drive the scarring, electrical rewiring, and inflammation that sustain the arrhythmia.

Mechanistic plausibility, it concludes, has not yet become routine clinical utility. Detection of the atrial substrate before a stroke and prediction of recurrence after ablation remain unmet needs. The paper closes by mapping what the field must standardize before blood tests enter practice.
pmc-13305144:

Between the 2015 to 2017 wave and the 2021 to 2023 wave, daily energy intake fell by 250 kcal per day, alongside drops in carbohydrate, protein, and fat intake. Models weighed gender, residence, schooling, wealth, smoking, activity, body size, chronic diseases, and study center.
pmc-13306144:
Shlomit Shalitin, Moshe Phillip, and Michal Yackobovitch-Gavan analyse real-world records in 2026 for 1,035 Israeli adolescents who had weight-loss surgery between 2010 and 2024. Sleeve gastrectomy was the main operation, and follow-up lasted a median of nearly six years. Outcomes covered body mass, blood pressure, and laboratory measures.

Blood pressure and several metabolic measures also improved durably. Teenagers who started heaviest remained heaviest throughout follow-up, despite clear gains. The authors read the data as support for surgery as a long-term option in severe adolescent obesity.
pmc-13306744:

Droplets sized 130 to 210 nm carried a charge of −30.89 mV and trapped 98.61% of oil in the given figures. Free oil stayed under 7.5% in early storage, with strong bacteria control. The mix kept its form well in store tests, a key need for food use.
pmc-13307044:
Mohamed-Amine Ouacha and Sandrine De Temmerman report in 2026 a thirteen-year-old girl whose holiday laser pointer damaged the centre of her right retina. The uncertified green device, bought in Spain, was rated at a dangerous power level. She already had a lazy left eye and a small squint, which raised the stakes.

Examination found a blind spot near fixation and a pigment lesion at the macula, with imaging showing disruption of the light-sensing layer. Care was conservative: observation plus strict avoidance of further exposure. Three months later, right-eye acuity had returned to full marks, though the authors call recovery partial yet incomplete in structural terms. Their warning targets parents and regulators. High-power pointers sold as toys, they argue, need stronger controls and public awareness.
pmc-13307644:

Blocking routes attack fungal growth, toxin-making pathways, or the toxins directly with enzymes and germs. Each route carries trade-offs in exactness, lasting power, safety, and conduct inside real foods. Breakdown product safety gets special focus throughout. Pairing trapping with blocking, the authors argue, could deliver stronger and more lasting defence.
pmc-13307844:
Solon Alberto Orlando and colleagues test pet dogs in Guayaquil, Ecuador, in 2026 for leptospirosis, a bacterial disease people can catch from animal urine. No single symptom predicted a positive result, which underlines how easily the illness is misread. Bulk food buying emerged as a risk factor only after statistical adjustment. Owners also reported frequent close contact with their dogs. The authors argue for vaccination drives and better diagnosis under a One Health policy.
pmc-13309544:

Advanced colon cancer links closely to gut microbe and immune imbalance, so a gut-based route drew interest.

The authors propose a gut-to-immune chain behind the effect.
pmc-13309744: Computational Intelligence and Neuroscience is the journal named on a 2026 retraction notice for a 2023 article by S. Krishnamoorthy and co-authors on an automatic system using connected medical devices to detect multiple sclerosis. The publisher, John Wiley & Sons Ltd, withdrew the article after an inquiry found signs of systematic manipulation of the publication process, including scope problems, citation misuse, and compromised peer review. The notice gives no new findings; it serves only to strike the article from the record and warn readers against relying on it.
pmc-13310544:

pmc-13310644:

pmc-13310744:

pmc-13310844:

pmc-13311144:

pmc-13312444:

pmc-13312544:

pmc-13312844:

pmc-13314744:

pmc-13314844:

pmc-13315044:

pmc-13315844:

pmc-13316244:

pmc-13316444:

pmc-13317144:

pmc-13317244:

pmc-13317544:

pmc-13318244:

pmc-13318544:

pmc-13318644:

pmc-13319044:

pmc-13319844:

pmc-13320344:
