pmc-13320444:
Koosha kamali and co-authors report a 2026 case of repeat vein clots in a transplant kidney caused by a squeezed pelvis vein. A 62 year old man got a left side kidney transplant and then clotted again and again in leg and graft veins. Two urgent clot removals saved the graft each time, yet no surgical cause could be found for the returns.

Deeper checks found May-Thurner syndrome, where a pelvis artery presses the main leg vein against the spine and chokes its flow. A stent was placed in the squeezed vein and long term blood thinning was set. Hidden vein squeezes should be hunted when graft clots return without a clear cause, the team urges.
pmc-13320644:
Caroline E. Owens and colleagues study, in 2026, barriers to healthy eating among adults in the United States. Poor nutrition drives much heart disease and diabetes, and policy has long used food insecurity, mainly a money and quantity measure, as a stand-in for access. Nutrition security is a broader idea covering steady access to foods that support health.

A short validated screener asks not only whether people struggle to eat healthily but also which specific barriers they face. Those barriers extend beyond price to taste and family preferences, knowledge, time, cooking equipment and local shop availability. This cross-sectional study extends earlier validation work by examining how barrier patterns relate to personal characteristics and diet-related health conditions, aiming to guide more precise interventions than income support alone.
pmc-13322344:
María Florencia Fernandez and colleagues issue a 2026 correction to their study of faecal microbiota transplantation in children who had stem cell transplants. The original article reported that transplanting gut microbes helped the gut microbiome recover in these young recipients. The correction updates only the funding statement for the article.

Support came in part from Fundación Bunge y Born, from Fundación Garrahan, and from an Argentine science ministry fund, grant PICTO-2021-UCTH number 0004 as printed in the notice. Fundación Garrahan also helped cover the article processing charges. The original version has been updated to carry the full statement, and no findings are altered by the change.
pmc-13322644:
Nancy Hodgson and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, whether online training for a dementia care program works as well as in-person training. The program coaches caregivers of people with dementia in all-inclusive elder care sites. Eleven sites were split at random, with staff trained online at four and in person at seven.

Therapists and nurses in both groups gained like amounts of knowledge and skill, with like satisfaction. Caregiver pairs who got the program after each training type were also compared at four months. Early results found no clear gaps between the routes. If the tie holds, online training could spread the program at lower cost and wider reach.
pmc-13322844:
Xianglin Wan and co-authors run a randomised trial in 2026 on dual-task gait training for people after stroke who must cross obstacles. They enrolled 35 patients, split between motor dual-task training and cognitive dual-task training, for three sessions a week over four weeks.

Both forms of training improved stride and step measures, walking speed, clearance over the obstacle and balance control, based on body motion and joint measures taken before and after. Brain oxygen signals in both frontal areas fell during crossing, which the authors read as more efficient use of brain resources. No measure differed clearly between the two training types, so either approach helped in this small trial.
pmc-13323244:
Zhi-Yong Xiao and co-authors pool studies of reproductive tract microbes in female infertility, in a 2026 meta-analysis of pooled studies. Searching four databases to the end of 2025, they kept observational studies of women aged 18 to 45 years that used high-throughput sequencing and compared infertile patients with fertile controls.

Across 27 studies with 2,174 participants, infertile women showed higher microbial diversity on several indices and lower Lactobacillus abundance, while Prevotella and Burkholderia ran higher in the pooled results. Patterns differed by sampling site within the tract. Quality and certainty were graded with standard tools. The authors treat the microbial signature as a lead for diagnosis research, not yet a clinical test.
pmc-13324144:
Giulia Fois and a team of co-authors trace a brain path that sharpens attention in mice, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. A chemical messenger, acetylcholine, feeds the front brain region that balances focus and restraint. The team recorded and steered the circuit during a cued number task.

One sub-region quieted after a brief start burst, and that quiet seemed needed to finish response chains well. Its chemical supply came almost solely from one basal forebrain zone. Switching that supply on calmed the region and raised optimal responses. The map refines how attention circuits are wired.
pmc-13324544:
Gitima Deka and Pil-Hoon Park review leptin at the meeting point of obesity, immunity, and cancer in a 2026 article. Leptin is a hormone from fat tissue that controls appetite and energy use, and blood levels run high in obesity.

Fresh evidence shows leptin acts on immune cells inside tumors and can wear them down, blunting the attack on cancer. It also rewires how both immune and cancer cells burn fuel, which may fuel growth. The picture is not one-sided, since leptin can boost immunity in some settings. The authors weigh pairing leptin-targeted drugs with immunotherapy. Their account frames leptin as one link between extra body fat and weaker cancer control.
pmc-13324744:
Hazim Sheet Jasem and colleagues combine a vision transformer with classic machine learning to grade artery plaque in ultrasound images in a 2026 study. Sorting plaque inside vessels guides heart disease diagnosis and treatment choices.

Their three-stage system first pulls global features with a vision transformer trained with Mixup blending. A second stage reads local texture through Gabor filters with support vector machine and random forest classifiers. A weighted vote then merges both views. On 3,867 intravascular ultrasound images across three plaque classes, the hybrid reached 89.39 percent accuracy and an F1 score of 88.45 percent. Each part alone scored lower, which supports the blended design.
pmc-13324844:
Steven M Taddei and colleagues show how three bacteria together build tougher biofilms on urinary catheters in a 2026 study. Long-term catheter users often carry mixed, symptom-free colonies that shrug off catheter changes and antibiotics.

Proteus mirabilis, Enterococcus faecalis, and Escherichia coli are the most common co-tenants. Grown together, they formed far more biofilm than alone or in pairs, even under flow on silicone catheters. The three-species film also resisted ciprofloxacin and nitrofurantoin in species-dependent ways. Protein analysis flagged an L-fucose use pathway in E. coli as a key helper, and E. coli settling first drove the boost. Mixed colonies from real patients behaved the same way.
pmc-13325144:
Dagoberto Cabrera-German and co-authors blend MXene flakes into lead iodide films at the precursor stage in a 2026 materials study. Lead iodide is usually treated as a passing step toward perovskite solar films, but its early structure may steer the final material.

Films were spun from a water and ethanol mix that lets the MXene enter during growth. Film thickness stayed nearly flat across loadings, while roughness and surface texture shifted. Diffraction confirmed the basic 2H lead iodide frame survived, though stacking signals changed. Light tests showed a kept absorption edge with dimmer glow, hinting at charge redistribution. The work treats the precursor itself as a tunable material.
pmc-13325444:
Maria Huidobro and co-authors present a two-scale light method for watching chemistry at electrodes in a 2026 paper. Spectroelectrochemistry joins voltage control with light readings, but weak starting light can warp the spectra.

Their multiscale setup measures through two path lengths at once inside one cell. Strong absorbers that would swamp a long path stay readable on the short path, while faint species still show on the long one. That pairing keeps absorbance math honest across a whole reaction run. Early and late species in an electrode process can thus be tracked with one setup. The approach targets mechanism studies, electrochromic materials, and exact concentration work.
pmc-13327444:
Dania Al-Sharify, Jiangming Sun, and Andreas Edsfeldt review how artery disease linked to type 2 diabetes is changing in a 2026 article. Heart and vessel events have fallen over the past decade, yet people with diabetes still carry about double the risk of those without it. The authors ask which plaque traits now set diabetic disease apart.

Recent human plaque studies find little difference in fat or inflammation markers, possibly because modern treatment already handles those routes well. Other traits stand out instead, such as thin fibrous caps and large dead cores, plus processes like oxidative stress and faulty clearing of dead cells. Targeting those less-treated routes may cut the remaining vessel risk in diabetes.
pmc-13327544:
Julie Warin and co-authors review the notochord, the rod that defines backboned animals, in a 2026 article. The structure supports the early embryo and sends signals to nearby tissues, and in mammals its cells persist inside spinal discs as the soft nucleus pulposus. The authors gather what is known from development through disc formation.

They trace the signals that set aside axial tissue and commit cells to the notochord line. That knowledge then guides stem cell models, including flat patterns and 3D organoids in mouse and human work. Such models open ways to study disorders from faulty notochord function and the disc wear of later life. Open questions close the review.
pmc-13327744:
Kalevi Kairemo and Akram Al-Ibraheem write a 2026 commentary on the uneven world spread of theranostics. These paired scan-and-treat methods use radioactive drugs, such as lutetium-177 agents aimed at prostate or hormone receptor targets, to find and hit cancer. Rich regions hold most of the capacity.

North America, Western Europe, and Australia offer wide networks of scanners, isotope supply, and trained staff, while large parts of Africa, Latin America, and Asia have little or no service. Surveys find almost no use of the newest targeted treatments in low-income countries. Cost, rules, supply chains, and workforce gaps all feed the divide, and the authors press for fairer build-out of these services.
pmc-13328044:
Sahar Jaffal and Sawsan Oran test, published in 2026, whether vitamin E eases pain in mice and rats, and through which signals. The fat-soluble vitamin is an antioxidant with nerve-protecting effects, but its pain record was patchy. The team ran three pain tests in mice: a writhing test, a tail-flick test, and a hot-plate test. Rats got a paw-swelling test for inflammation. Vitamin E was given and with blockers of one heat-sensing channel or of two kinase pathways. Tissue was stained for the channel.

Vitamin E cut writhing and lengthened heat tolerance. Blockers showed the heat channel drove the heat effects, and the kinases helped carry the brain relief. Against swelling, the vitamin did nothing. Skin staining for the channel ran high where vitamin E met the swelling agent. The authors propose vitamin E as a helper drug in pain plans, not a cure.
pmc-13328344:
Fengchao Wan and co-authors build a forecast for forceps delivery in first-time mothers in a 2026 study. Spotting high-risk labors early in the second stage could sharpen care and cut harm to mother and baby. Records from one Yibin hospital, 2017 to 2024, matched 346 forceps deliveries with 346 spontaneous vaginal deliveries.

Five signs at the start of the second stage independently raised forceps odds. They were body mass index at or above 28, fetal belly circumference at or above 340 mm, and grade II or III meconium-stained fluid. A head facing away from the front position and a long active phase completed the set. The model built from them was checked for accuracy, calibration, and clinical usefulness.
pmc-13328644:
Zhang, Ma, Huang, Zhu, Zhao, and Yang study in twenty twenty-six the strength and slope safety of a copper mine waste dump in China. Mines pile soil-rock mixes into huge dumps that can slide, so their stability matters. The team sampled the mix at several rock shares, ran lab pressure tests, and simulated the dump slope under varied groundwater, rain, and plant root depth.

Stickiness and friction shifted strongly with rock content, and one curve model fit the lab data best. Shallower groundwater weakened the slope, and longer, harder rain cut safety in a steepening curve. Roots helped stability, though extreme rain could still trap water and undo the gain. The findings guide dump management.
pmc-13329344:
Ningxin Zhang and colleagues examined the double-edged link between fatty liver disease and outcomes in chronic hepatitis B. Their 2026 study recruited hepatitis B patients from 2012 to 2022 through electronic medical records, dividing them into groups with and without metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, with follow-up through January 2024. Among 8,052 patients followed for a median 3.9 years, the team compared cumulative incidence of severe liver disease and cardiovascular disease.

Fatty liver disease was tied to a 39% lower risk of severe liver disease, with similar protection against cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, stronger in hepatitis B surface antigen-positive patients. Conversely, fatty liver disease tracked with higher cardiovascular risk, driven by coronary artery disease and arrhythmia, though the overall association did not reach significance. Findings held after propensity score matching. The authors conclude that fatty liver disease may protect the liver while still raising cardiovascular risk.
pmc-13329544:
Kawtar Iraqi Houssaini and team told of Foley catheter cervix softening across all three trimesters. Their 2026 descriptive study at Mohammed VI University Hospital in Marrakesh ran from October 2024 to February 2025. It took in 104 patients: 37 first-trimester, 14 second-trimester, and 53 third-trimester, when prostaglandins were out of stock. Foley catheter softening has won fresh interest for safety, low cost, ease of use, and lower over-stimulation risk than drugs.

Across all trimesters, 72.1% started labor within twelve hours of catheter insertion. Mean start-to-birth spans were 17.5 hours in the first trimester, 16.8 in the second, and 12.2 in the third. Induction worked in 100% of first- and second-trimester cases and 94.3% of third-trimester cases, with no mother deaths. Among third-trimester live births, 77.1% scored 8 or higher on five-minute Apgar. The team calls Foley catheter induction workable and safe across trimesters in low-resource settings.
pmc-13330544:
Krystian Mirowski and team studied how environmental exposures shape tolerance failure in autoimmune liver disease. Their 2026 review treats primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, and autoimmune hepatitis as three distinct organ-specific forms sharing loss of tolerance centrally, yet target tissue, onset age, and genetics vary. The paper asks how exposures shape tolerance failure and tissue injury across the three.

The signal is clearest in PBC, where evidence on smoking and recurrent urinary infections lines up with work on xenobiotic PDC-E2 modification, cholangiocyte apotope biology, and exposomic data. PSC is better explained through gut-liver-microbiome links, while AIH shows a weaker, more mixed signature, muddied by drug-induced liver injury that mimics it. The team lists limits of current exposomic methods and proposes phenotype-resolved goals, arguing that environmental shaping does not replace central tolerance loss but explains how failure becomes durable and tissue-selective.
pmc-13331344:
Rossella Gioco and colleagues report saving an exposed breast implant with a chest wall flap in a 2026 case. A 54-year-old woman developed local infection and implant exposure after nipple-sparing mastectomy and reconstruction above the muscle with a silicone implant. Cancer return was ruled out, and standard conservative care failed.

Standard care for exposure is often implant removal and delayed rebuilding. Here the team used an anterior intercostal artery perforator flap to cover the defect and keep the implant. The authors call the method workable and less invasive for chosen patients without wide tissue loss. Clear rules for when salvage fits are still lacking, they note.
pmc-13331444:
Jinfeng Miao and colleagues published a retrospective cohort study in 2026 asking whether adding a balloon guide catheter improves clot-removal results in one narrow stroke group. Their patients had sudden blockage of the intracranial internal carotid artery caused by an embolus, a group poorly covered by recent trials.

Records came from a two-center stroke registry covering 397 patients, of whom 90 had the balloon device used during their procedure. The team balanced the groups with propensity matching and overlap weighting, then compared independence at 90 days and first-pass blood flow return. Balloon use was linked to higher odds of independence, more complete first-pass reopening, and fewer stray clots, though the overall disability shift was not significant. The authors argue the device may help in this group while calling for larger prospective trials to confirm it.
pmc-13332144:
Vinuta Shetty, Raju Patel, and Tanmoy Majumder present a 2026 materials study on a glucose sensor that needs no enzyme. Steady, sharp sensors matter for diabetes care. The team grew tiny rods of copper oxide laced with silver on an electrode. A hot water method made the rods, and a battery of scans confirmed their shape and makeup.

The silver-laced rods beat plain rods at sparking the reaction that reveals glucose. The sensor read glucose across a wide range, down to a very low limit. Repeat tests gave steady results, and common other substances did not fool it. Results of this grade point to cheap, enzyme-free test strips. Such strips could last longer in hot or remote clinics.
pmc-13332844:
Hajar Menay and colleagues report a 2026 case of tibialis anterior muscle herniation managed without surgery at first. Muscle herniation means muscle tissue bulges through a defect in its fascia covering, most often in the tibialis anterior muscle of the shin. The patient was a 55-year-old man with painful intermittent swelling on the front-outer right leg that grew more prominent on standing and activity, after a distant history of trauma. Examination found a soft, tender mass over the middle leg without nerve deficits.

Dynamic ultrasound showed a fascial defect with tibialis anterior protrusion, confirming the diagnosis. Care was conservative: rest plus compression bandaging. After three months, pain had eased markedly and hernia size had partly shrunk. The case reminds clinicians to include muscle herniation when weighing chronic leg pain with intermittent swelling. It also shows that conservative care can succeed before surgery is considered.
pmc-13333344:
Zhaoyang Liu and colleagues surveyed Chinese knowledge workers in 2026 on a puzzle of the AI age. Using generative AI seems to make staff both share more knowledge and hide more of it. Their model, built on the automation-augmentation paradox and appraisal theory, proposes two opposing paths.

Surveys from 428 knowledge workers supported every hypothesis. AI use raised self-confidence, which fed sharing, and raised job insecurity, which fed hiding. The sharing effect was the stronger of the two, so the paths partly cancelled out in a competitive mediation pattern. The authors combined both behaviors into one score, the difference between sharing and hiding, to capture the net tilt. A competitive workplace climate turned up the volume on both paths at once. They advise firms to pair AI rollout with knowledge rules that reward openness and calm fears of replacement.
pmc-13333444:
Rune Johan Krumsvik and colleagues argue in a 2026 paper that artificial intelligence, woven into human judgment as symbiotic intelligence, could help Norway understand and prevent suicide. Suicide is the leading cause of death worldwide at ages 10 to 24, and Norwegian rates hit a 25-year high in 2024 despite decades of prevention work.

The authors stress that no single factor explains suicide. They flag three risk fields. First come young people's digital lives, where social media carries both copycat harm and protective effects. Second come shock-like events, whose media echo may raise risk, even shifting birth outcomes. Third is alcohol, found in the blood of four in ten Norwegians who die by suicide, which sharpens impulsivity. They propose AI language analysis of social media to detect risk windows. They add access to anonymized data for monitoring, and wearables with check-ins feeding early-warning systems, as a supplement to clinical care.
pmc-13335544:
Xiaolu Wei and co-authors designed a recyclable high-strength steel with physics-informed machine learning in a 2026 materials study. Quenching and partitioning steels usually need a separate chemistry per grade, which complicates welding and recycling.

Their framework bridges from abundant hardness data to scarce tensile data using metallurgical descriptors. It lifts tensile prediction accuracy to an R-squared of 84 percent against 74 percent for a purely data-driven baseline, with steadier behavior on small datasets. A multi-objective genetic algorithm then searched composition and processing space for one alloy that could hit three grade targets, Q&P980, Q&P1180, and Q&P1380, by heat treatment alone. A single unified composition promises simpler production and a scrap stream that stays valuable instead of mixed and downgraded.
pmc-13336044:
Lifu Sun and colleagues study 2026 brown fat cell sheets easing heart muscle I/R injury through NRG4-ErbB4 iron death blocking. Heart muscle I/R injury causes heart cell death and heart failure in part through iron death.

The authors made fat cell sheets and placed them onto the starved heart muscle in a rat I/R model to test treatment effect. Fat cell sheet placement greatly improved cardiac function, reduced infarct size and scarring, and eased adverse reshaping while boosting new vessel growth. In vitro, medium from fat cell sheets promoted heart cell survival, preserved pumping performance, and blocked cell death and iron death under low-oxygen stress. In detail, these effects were run by switching on the NRG4-ErbB4 axis and later PI3K/AKT and NRF2/HO-1 antioxidant signal paths.
pmc-13336444:
Ehsan Rashidniyaghi and colleagues study 2026 how protein-frame mixing works through soap-like-driven surface design. Protein-frame mixing offers a good plan for protein steadying across matter and medical uses. However, the small-scale workings of protein-frame links remain little known, blocking planned control over their chem and physical traits.

The authors develop a soap-like-guided plan to tune building of protein-frame composites through surface design. They found that the surface setting between proteins and frames is the main factor for packing power, shape hold, and working results. Soap-like agents such as GMO increase the protein's solvent-open surface area, hinting at some reshaping of the protein surface and water shell. Surface GMO enhances protein packing by 20 percent and speeds frame growth by 30 percent.
pmc-13336544:
Vaibhav Venkatesh and colleagues report a 2026 case-control study on vitiligo, a skin condition where pigment cells are lost. Their focus is the T helper 17 pathway, a branch of the immune system tied to long-term inflammation. They ask whether this pathway runs too hot in people with the disease.

Blood tests compared 30 patients with 30 healthy volunteers. Patients had higher IL6, higher STAT3 and RORC gene activity, and higher IL17A, while IL10 was much lower at 2.5 times below control levels in the patient group. IL23 differed little. The pattern points to an overactive pathway and suggests new drug targets for calming it.
pmc-13337344:
Nakai Kazuaki studied in 2026 whether finerenone improves blood and plasma volume markers in real world people with type 2 diabetes plus long term kidney disease. Large trials show finerenone cuts heart and kidney events, but its effect on anaemia and markers such as serum albumin had not been reported. The study followed 20 patients who started finerenone with no other drug changes for a year either side.

Trend analysis showed haemoglobin and haematocrit rose after starting finerenone, with patterns examined by SGLT2 inhibitor use and baseline anaemia. The findings suggest finerenone may ease anaemia alongside its known organ protection. Small numbers and the observational design mean larger studies must confirm the effect before it changes practice.
pmc-13337444:
Shun Hu and Yue Xu pool trials of combined endurance and resistance training in heart failure in a 2026 meta-analysis. Nine studies met their criteria after searching domestic and international databases through November 2025, with quality checked by the Cochrane risk tool. The question was whether mixing aerobic work with strength training beats usual care.

Patients on combined training improved peak oxygen use and quality of life clearly more than controls. Their six-minute walk distance also rose by a pooled margin that favored training strongly in the forest plot results. Sleep and depression scores, however, did not differ significantly between groups. Sensitivity checks kept the findings stable, supporting combined exercise as a core part of heart failure rehabilitation.
pmc-13337644:
Changhui Deng and colleagues report a randomized trial from 2026 on sedation for a bile duct procedure done with an endoscope. Sixty patients at Shifang People's Hospital were split evenly between two drug plans. One group received propofol alone, and the other received remimazolam besylate added to propofol.

Heart rate and blood pressure stayed steadier in the combined group, and those patients needed less propofol overall. Their sedation scores were higher and pain scores were lower, while doctors rated satisfaction higher. Patient satisfaction and procedure success were similar in both groups. Fewer problems around the procedure occurred with the combined plan, which the authors present as an effective and safer option.
pmc-13339044:
Jérémie Tachet and a large team track ruxolitinib drug levels in routine Swiss care in a 2026 observational study. Trial data describe this blood cancer and immune disease drug well, but real-world handling varies more. Blood levels, body factors, and harm links were examined.

A total of 221 steady measurements came from 77 adults across several centers as reported. Clearance varied widely between people, by 45 percent in the reported spread. Strong blockers of liver enzymes CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 cut clearance by 39 percent as modeled. Simulations predicted trough and daily exposure for standard doses, testing whether level-guided dosing could help routine care.
pmc-13339644:
Emma Audi and a large team find a safer route to blue azulene acid derivatives in a 2026 study. Guaiazulene is cheap and keeps azulene's unusual electronics, yet making its carboxylic acids usually needs toxic reagents such as phosgene. Their route starts with oxalyl chloride instead.

Heating or bromide then removes carbon monoxide, and a chosen nucleophile finishes the product. Both oxalic and carboxylic acid families become reachable by steering that loss as reported. Experiments and calculations together support a concerted halide shift during carbon monoxide loss. The method widens access to deep-blue building blocks for materials and dye work.
pmc-13340044:
Wanqiu Lin and colleagues isolated a virus that kills drug resistant Vibrio parahaemolyticus in 2026, a germ that threatens shrimp farms and food safety. Multidrug resistance is rising under antibiotic pressure, and phage therapy offers a possible alternative. The team pulled the phage, named Phi170, from sewage at a shrimp farm.

Phi170 showed a short latent period of 10 minutes, an eclipse near 60 minutes, and a burst size of 426 particles per cell. It tolerated a broad range of acidity and temperature and rapidly suppressed its host in lab tests. The phage is a promising candidate for aquaculture biocontrol, pending safety and field trials.
pmc-13341444:
Mental distress among Shanghai STD clinic patients is surveyed by Yanting Wang and colleagues in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Questionnaires reached 3,360 patients at 10 randomly chosen public institutions between September 2020 and December 2021, using the GAD-7 and PHQ-9 scales.

Anxiety symptoms appeared in 10.8% of participants and depression symptoms in 13.9%, with higher rates among women, younger patients, singles, and those with weak disease knowledge or no local residency. Regression tied anxiety to age, marital status, and residence factors, and depression additionally to gender and education. The authors argue psychological care belongs inside routine STD management.
pmc-13341844:
Solo spotlight raises anxiety for orchestral wind players, in a 2026 study by Shuai Yang's team. The cross-sectional survey classified 152 wind instrumentalists into solo-exposed principals (74) and regular section players (78), measuring performance anxiety, social anxiety, and trait anxiety with standard inventories.

Solo-exposed players reported more performance anxiety, with an effect size of 0.44, and more social anxiety, at 0.38. Social anxiety statistically carried 44.98% of the exposure-to-anxiety link. Experience softened the gap: group gaps showed mainly among less seasoned players. Because the design is cross-sectional, the authors treat direction cautiously, but section leaders clearly warrant targeted support.
pmc-13342244:
Guomei Gong and co-authors surveyed Chinese university students in 2026 about pneumoconiosis, the lung disease caused by breathing dust over time. Using the knowledge-attitude-practice model, the team measured what students know about prevention, how they view it, and what they actually do.

An online survey in late 2025 drew 1,795 students from 84 universities across 33 provinces. Overall scores were middling, with knowledge the weakest part and attitudes the strongest. Students outside Han ethnicity, non-medical fields, and several northern and western regions scored lower, while good health and self-rated knowledge scored higher. The authors call for targeted teaching to close the gaps before graduates enter dusty workplaces.
pmc-13342744:
Priyanka Gupta and three co-authors wrote a case note in 2026 on a pus sac under the jaw caused by germs that shun air. Deep neck sores, which quite often start from teeth, tend to mix more than one kind of germ. Air-shun germs are missed a lot, since they are hard to move and hard to grow.

Pus from the patient grew two such germs, Prevotella buccae and Dialister pneumosintes, named in the sample. Both proved sensitive to metronidazole, a penicillin mix, meropenem, and clindamycin. The team warns that if staff skip tests for air-shun germs, a grave sore may get too weak a cure. They also urge set drug tests for these germs as drug proof grows. The case adds two named germs to the books.
pmc-13343144:
Ana Claudia Amaral and a large team report 2026 safety and delivery tests of a gene therapy virus carrying GBA1 into the brain. Faulty GBA1 causes Gaucher disease and raises risk of Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia, so delivering a working copy to the central nervous system is an active trial goal.

In newborn mice, delivery into brain fluid gave good gene activity and enzyme gains with no harm seen. Adult primates told a split story. Fluid delivery reached the spinal cord and nerve roots but hurt tissue and barely reached the brain. Direct injection into deep brain sites worked locally with fewer distant effects. Safer brain-wide delivery still needs better tools.
pmc-13343844:
Chaofan Ai and co-authors map active prophages, viral DNA woven into soil bacteria, across the globe in 2026. Dormant viral passengers can aid their hosts, yet switchable ones were long viewed as time bombs. The team fused over 123,000 bacterial genomes with soil virus and metagenome data to judge their real role.

Their new database holds 21,397 high-confidence active prophages, about a third of the soil viral population in the analysis. Active forms carried larger, richer genomes than dormant kin and packed extra genes for carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur cycling plus heavy metal defense. Far from pure threat, these prophages act as mobile toolkits that help bacteria adapt and spread into new niches.
pmc-13343944:
Samuel D. Burgos and co-authors screen chromatin-targeting drugs for ways to wake sleeping HIV in 2026. Antiretroviral therapy cannot clear the silent viral reservoir, the core barrier to a cure, so the team tested 84 small molecules aimed at the packaging machinery that keeps viral genes shut.

One compound, BAY-299, reawakened viral expression and boosted known waking agents in cell models. Gene knockout tests showed its true target: removing the host protein TAF1, not its partner BRD1, freed viral transcription while barely touching host genes. TAF1 loss also raised acetylation marks along the viral genome. TAF1 now stands out as a fresh drug target against the latent reservoir.
pmc-13345644:
Tokuni and Tamura examined in 2026 how hidden bias may shape care for people with prolonged disorders of consciousness, conditions where awareness is absent or minimal for long periods. Families often report faint signs of response that clinicians may read differently, since judgment leans on observed behavior and caregiver reports. The team interviewed seven family caregivers in Japan who support such patients at home.

Caregivers said their readings of responses were often brushed aside or recast as wishful thinking, which limited their role in assessment and decisions. The authors propose a model in which diagnostic sensitivity depends on context: awareness of bias and better dialogue with families should sharpen how faint signs are weighed. Drawing on disability studies, they argue that small slights in everyday exchanges can close off chances to spot recovery, and that fixing communication is a clinical task, not a courtesy.
pmc-13345744:
Ibrahim Güler and co-authors map what cosmetic surgery costs across the United States in a 2026 state-level analysis. Advertised prices for six common procedures were gathered from 100 metropolitan areas, giving 600 price points, then set against state income, output, and cost-of-living adjustments to find the real burden.

Average prices ran from 6,234 dollars for liposuction to 14,639 dollars for facelifts, which also scattered widest. State prices rose with personal income, and New York stayed priciest even after adjustment, yet Michigan and Kentucky jumped to second and third in real cost, passing California. One average procedure eats nearly 20 percent of yearly per-person income in Kentucky, against about a tenth in richer states.
pmc-13346844:
Elif Yılmaz Biçer, Beyza Güney, and Merve Bankoğlu Güngör test how well dentists can predict final tooth colour for thin zirconia crowns, in a lab study from 2026. Specimens of a shade-gradient zirconia were made at 0.4 mm, 0.6 mm, and 0.8 mm thickness over an A1 shade base. Colour was read with try-in paste and with resin cement before and after hardening.

Colour gaps were largest for the thinnest pieces, where the mean gap reached 1.45 in the reported units, and thicker pieces matched more closely in the same tests. The paste-to-cement comparison showed the largest shift, so the authors warn that shade checks in thin work can mislead the final result.
pmc-13348244:
Qiliang Sun and colleagues traced in 2026 how distant tectonic and climate shifts can trigger repeated submarine landslides in the South China Sea, with tsunami potential. Tectonics and climate were long suspected to unsettle slopes, yet how they drive failures again and again over geological time was unclear.

More than ninety percent of a roughly 1,900-metre-thick Plio-Quaternary sequence consists of landslide deposits that began abruptly about five and a half million years ago. Uplift of the Red River basin strengthened the Indian summer monsoon, boosting sediment supply, steepening the margin, and raising pore pressure until slopes failed widely. The study links continental change far inland to hazards offshore, improving long-term risk reading for coastal margins.
pmc-13348844:
Sarah C House and co-authors looked back in 2026 at pregnancy and birth in patients with inflammatory bowel disease who have an ileal pouch-anal anastomosis. This is a surgically made reservoir after colon removal. Advice on birth mode often conflicts. Caesarean is often picked from fear that vaginal birth might harm the sphincter and worsen long-term pouch function.

A single-centre chart review covered patients with bowel disease, a pouch, and a full pregnancy from 2002 to 2021. Birth mode, complications, and pouch function pre- and post-birth were charted. The descriptive data aim to swap conflicting views for observed outcomes. They help patients and clinicians pick a birth plan that guards both mother and pouch.
pmc-13349944:
Yuhan Zhang and Yupin Liu told in 2026 of imaging of a rare, fierce NUT carcinoma in the maxillary sinus with raised alpha-fetoprotein, a mix that can mislead diagnosis. NUT tumours carry a NUTM1 gene rearrangement and most often arise in midline head, neck, chest, or mediastinal sites. They hit teens and young adults and progress fast with early spread.

Scan traits are often vague and overlap with other fierce sinonasal cancers. Alpha-fetoprotein rise is classically linked to liver and germ cell tumours, not to non-hepatic epithelial cancers. The case spells out scan patterns, pathology with abrupt keratinisation, and the unsure meaning of the marker rise. Charting this case helps radiologists and pathologists weigh NUT tumours sooner in like sinus masses.
pmc-13350044:
Zhijin Chai and co-authors built an anatomy-aware deep learning system in 2026 for grading lower back degeneration on MRI. Ageing discs and joints cause much back pain. But automatic grading struggles with unclear anatomy. It also misses links between neighbouring spine levels.

Their framework first maps vertebrae, discs, and the spinal canal. This anchors each level. It then reads image patches together with body measurements. A small transformer follows how damage at one level relates to the next. The system grades each segment and sums a patient-level burden score. On public data it beat comparison systems. Anatomy-first designs may read spinal scans more like clinicians do.
pmc-13350344:
Ding Nan and colleagues presented two contrasting eye findings after radioactive iodine treatment for thyroid cancer in a 2026 case report. Scans after therapy sometimes show the tracer collecting around the eye, and the cause can be harmless or dangerous.

One patient's uptake came from an artificial eyeball; the other's was cancer that had spread to the eye socket. By comparing symptoms and scan features side by side, the authors draw out the clues separating a false alarm from true metastasis. Getting this rare call right changes treatment completely, from simple reassurance to urgent cancer care, so a practical checklist has real value.
pmc-13350544:
Hua-Jie Niu and colleagues described two cases in 2026 of Libman-Sacks endocarditis, sterile growths on heart valves seen in lupus. The condition affects roughly a tenth to a sixth of lupus patients, favouring the mitral and aortic valves, and risk climbs with antiphospholipid antibodies.

Unlike infected valve disease, these growths are clumps of fibrin, platelets, and immune material from autoimmune attack, and they can wreck valves or break off into the circulation. Ultrasound of the heart is the main detection tool. The two cases show how the growths appear on echocardiography, helping clinicians separate this quiet threat from infection, which demands very different treatment.
pmc-13350644:
Connor P Craig and co-authors told in 2026 of a first-ever catheter valve swap, placed in its normal spot, for a man with a heart pump. Marked tricuspid leakage is common after assist device placement. It raises death risk. Yet surgical tricuspid work has not consistently shown gain.

A 46-year-old man with medically refractory severe leakage and right ventricular failure after assist device placement got the Evoque transcatheter valve system. The procedure proved technically feasible. It eased symptoms and cut need for chronic inotropic backing. As the first report of this valve system in an assist device patient, the case opens a less invasive option for a group with few good alternatives.
pmc-13351644:
Binbin Yang and co-authors charted in 2026 magnetic foreign body ingestion in children. Many magnets can pull across bowel walls and cause severe gut injury. Best care remains debated. Large studies and world consensus are lacking.

Looking back at 160 hospitalised children from mid-2016 to mid-2025, the team weighed two groups. One group got conservative care. One group got surgery. Life traits, symptoms, scans, treatments, and outcomes were weighed. Multivariable models forecast surgery, perforation, and long stays. About 39 percent needed surgery. The experience helps clinicians spot high-risk ingestions early. It also guides when watchful waiting is safe.
pmc-13352644:
Wu and co-authors show that a macrophage surface protein helps stomach cancer grow in this 2026 study. The protein, SLAMF8, sits on macrophages, the immune cells that infiltrate tumors. Its role in the stomach cancer immune environment was unclear.

Database analysis tied high SLAMF8 levels to worse patient outcomes. The protein appeared mainly on macrophages inside tumors. In lab-grown tumor macrophages, reducing SLAMF8 curbed the M2 state, a mode that shields tumors. Raising it pushed macrophages toward that state by damping one pathway and activating another. Macrophages with extra SLAMF8 sped cancer cell growth in dishes and in mice, and weakened killer T cells. The protein looks like a treatment target.
pmc-13352744:
Fei Jia led a 2026 real-world study of pharmacogenomic testing in clinic psychiatry, asking whether gene-guided giving helps results. The idea is that a patient's genes shape how mental drugs are processed, so test results might steer drug and dose choices. Evidence from ordinary inpatient care, rather than guided trials, has been scarce.

Inpatients with schizophrenia, major depressive illness, or bipolar illness admitted from January 2022 to March 2024 were split into a tested group and a match group. Results were matched between the groups after accounting for setting gaps. The study gives hospitals a grounded view of whether genetic testing adds seen benefit in everyday mental care.
pmc-13352944:
Sofia Patri leads a 2026 nanogel study that tunes the temperature at which tiny drug carriers shrink and release their load. Heat-responsive gels can flip structure on cue, enabling timed release under body or applied heat. Gels were built from three ethylene glycol based monomers, singly and in blends, while keeping the material body-friendly and breakable.

Particles measured 200 to 350 nm across and shrank below 100 nm at their switch point, tuned within 1 degree of target. One blend hit switch points of 37, 47, and 52 degrees at set mix ratios. A docetaxel-linked gel loaded drug at 93 percent efficiency and released about 90 percent on heating, far above steady controls.
pmc-13354444:
Ghodratollah Maddah and colleagues report a sacrococcygeal teratoma with severe buttock deformity in a young woman in 2026. Such germ cell tumours are common in infants yet very rare in adults. A 24-year-old Afghan woman had heavy gluteal distortion with pelvic pain plus trouble sitting and walking.

Teratoma belongs on the list for any mass in front of the sacrum, and MRI plus CT scans together pin down the lesion. When growth pushes backward past the coccyx, full removal with coccyx excision through a trans-sacral route gives good surgical and cosmetic results. Adult cases usually trace to quiet tumours left untreated since childhood, so awareness aids timely care.
pmc-13354844:
Mossaab El Mousadik and others told of acute appendicitis striking during stem cell infusion for HIV-linked lymphoma, in 2026. Appendicitis is exceptionally rare during autologous stem cell transplantation, and its symptoms overlap with conditioning-related gut harm and neutropenic bowel swelling. No prior report had told of it during transplantation for HIV-linked lymphoma.

The patient was a thirty-nine-year-old man with stage IV HIV-linked diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of non-germ centre type, with gastric involvement. The report details how the team seen appendicitis amid the expected harm of transplantation and managed it. Transplant teams gain a rare but instructive warning that belly pain during infusion demands a broad differential, not only the usual suspects.
pmc-13355244:
Zhi-Yuan Gao and co-authors built a 2026 model to predict when low-grade prostate cancer found on biopsy turns out worse after surgery. Such cancers often suit watchful waiting, yet surgery sometimes shows a higher grade, which clouds the choice. The team studied 312 men at one Chinese hospital who had biopsy then surgery.

Nearly 46 percent had their grade raised after surgery. Age, share of positive biopsy cores, and a high scan score each raised that risk on their own. A chart built from these factors sorted patients fairly well in both test groups. The authors call the tool exploratory and say it needs checks at other centers before clinic use.
pmc-13356744:
Yosef A. Abitew and others studied chromatin accessibility in the jejunum of two high-yielding laying hen strains under other P supply, in 2026. Optimising dietary P matters for lasting egg making, hen welfare, productivity, and reducing excess excretion. P shapes gene levels and epigenetic regulation in the gut, but those effects during the shift to laying were unclear.

Chromatin accessibility was profiled in jejunal tissue as hens of two strains moved into egg making under divergent mineral P levels. Age, strain, and P jointly shaped the epigenetic and transcriptional landscape. Poultry scientists gain insight into how food and genetics jointly programme gut function at a critical making stage.
pmc-13358544:
Lifen Cai and co-authors present a 2026 study on predicting breast cancer spread without surgery. The key question is whether cancer has reached the armpit lymph nodes, which guides treatment. Checking those nodes now needs an operation. The team built a scan-based model to answer the question before any cut.

They studied 327 women with early breast cancer and mined their ultrasound images for fine patterns inside the tumor and in a thin rim of tissue around it. Machine learning models joined these patterns with standard patient facts. A tool that reads both zones could spare some women an operation and still sort risk well.
pmc-13358744:
Doyir Bagra and co-authors survey skin problems in pregnancy in a 2026 study from eastern India. Pregnancy brings many harmless skin changes from shifts in hormones and blood flow, but some itchy rashes can threaten mother or baby. The team examined women at a routine pregnancy clinic to record what they found.

They studied 138 women at Burdwan Medical College and Hospital between 2023 and 2025, with lab tests where infection was suspected. They also checked how the problems linked to the stage of pregnancy and number of past pregnancies. A clear local picture helps clinic staff tell normal changes from rashes that need fast care.
pmc-13358844:
Tingting Xie and co-authors study heart drugs in a dangerous mix of conditions in a 2026 paper. Patients with sepsis, a severe infection response, often develop a new irregular heartbeat called atrial fibrillation, and their outlook worsens. The team asked whether giving a beta-blocker drug within the first day in intensive care changes survival.

Using a large intensive care database covering 2008 to 2022, they balanced treated and untreated patients on key traits. They then measured deaths at 30 and 90 days and tested whether organ failure scores explained part of any link. The results can guide a common bedside choice that proof has so far left murky.
pmc-13358944:
Riccardo Di Leo and others built a dual-action gold(I) prodrug for ovarian cancer, in 2026. Ovarian cancer spreads early, relapses frequently, and offers limited options once platinum pushback develops. A drug that attacks two vulnerabilities at once might beat pushback that single-target drugs cannot.

The prodrug RDL-15 joins a gold(I) pharmacophore derived from auranofin with a scaffold inhibiting the gelatinases MMP-2 and MMP-9, thereby disrupting both redox regulation and outside matrix shifts. It retained micromolar killer action in lab tests. Cancer teams gain a rationally built choice that pairs redox disruption with matrix blockade against a hard-to-treat cancer.
pmc-13359544:
Changzeng Liu and co-authors present a new way to read brain signals during listening in a 2026 study. Decoding which sounds a person hears from brain waves is hard because the responses unfold over time and mix with background noise. Their method first models how sound features drive brain responses, then compares those patterns across sound types.

Tested with two kinds of brain recording, the approach proved far more sensitive than older ones. It showed the brain favors biological sounds, like voices, and uses a wider network than expected, reaching into emotion and deep brain areas. A sharper decoding tool could one day support fair tests of hearing and perception.
pmc-13360944:
Sergio Juárez-Méndez led a 2026 study to sort a childhood brain tumor by its gene patterns. Medulloblastoma falls into four molecular groups, and the group a child is in shapes the outlook strongly. Two of the groups look so alike at the gene level that sorting them is very hard. The team used unsupervised machine learning on gene activity data to find a simpler marker set.

They profiled 25 fresh tumors on gene chips and compared them with already sorted cases from public stores. Data mining across these sets pinned down a small gene profile tied to the four groups. A cheap, clear sorting test matters because treatment intensity hinges on the group. The work points toward a marker panel that more hospitals could run.
pmc-13361944:
Yi Liu and co-authors studied why re-steamed bread loses quality in storage in a 2026 food paper. Many breads are chilled, then steamed again before eating. The team tracked how cold storage time and matcha, powdered green tea, changed the bread's gluten and starch. Both shape texture: gluten gives the springy network, starch firms as it ages.

Long cold storage broke the bonds holding gluten together and let water escape, while starch aged faster. The result was harder bread with less volume. A small matcha dose, up to about one percent, steadied the gluten bonds and slowed starch aging. Past that level, tea compounds attacked the gluten and sped water loss, shrinking the loaf. The study finds the matcha sweet spot for bakers.
pmc-13363144:
Víctor Dante Ayaviri-Nina and a large team report a 2026 survey of household food insecurity in Guamote Canton, Ecuador, a poor rural area. Using a standard Latin American food security scale, they visited 368 households and sorted each into secure or mildly, moderately, or severely insecure. A statistical model then weighed which social factors tracked with worse food access.

Higher income and more schooling both cut the odds of food insecurity. Households in rural zones and those led by women faced higher odds of the moderate and severe levels. Access to nutrition information also mattered. The authors argue that jobs, schooling, and basic living conditions are the levers most likely to ease hunger in the canton.
pmc-13363244:
Gwang-Jun Choi and colleagues present a 2026 study on sedation run by the procedure team, rather than an anesthesia team, for heart catheter tests in young children. They reviewed 342 procedures in 307 children under six at one major center from 2020 to 2022, logging safety events and what predicted them, including a standard risk score for the procedure.

About seven percent of procedures had a safety event, and every child recovered fully with on-the-spot care. Newborn age and genetic conditions raised the risk most. Events grew as the risk score rose, and no sedation events occurred at the lowest scores. The authors say trained teams can run such sedation safely across a wide risk range, judging each child as a whole.
pmc-13365444:
Harikumar K Chandrasekharan and Ross Donaldson present a two thousand twenty-six photonics study mapping light behaviour inside multimode fibres. Such fibres carry many light patterns at once, and their polarization shifts under stress. Most tools probe only one polarization, hiding the rest.

Their platform uses single-photon detector arrays with picosecond timing. It watches two polarization channels at the same time across about a thousand spatial points. Tests revealed linked motion between fibre modes under stress. Full polarization vectors were rebuilt per point. The scalable setup opens fast, detailed fibre studies for communications and quantum work.
pmc-13366344:
Exner and colleagues review radiotheranostics for disseminated and rare melanoma, in 2026 nuclear medicine research. Theranostics pairs a radioactive imaging agent that finds a tumor target with a matching radioactive therapy against the same target. Melanoma that has spread widely resists most treatments, and rare forms such as mucosal and uveal melanoma fare worst. The review surveys preclinical and clinical radiopharmaceuticals built for melanoma targets, judging their promise for diagnosis and therapy alike.

Context numbers frame the need: five-year survival falls from over 90 percent for early skin melanoma to about 35 percent once distant spread is present at diagnosis. Uveal melanoma, arising in the eye, makes up roughly 4 to 5 percent of cases, and about half of those patients eventually develop metastases, overwhelmingly to the liver. Median survival for metastatic disease had reached only 21.1 months by 2018 despite modern drugs. Exner argues targeted radioactive agents could reach disease that systemic drugs cannot.
pmc-13366744:
Baosheng Zhao and co-workers ask in 2026 what blocks nurse trainees in China from use of class and skill lessons on the ward. Ward time should turn book facts into real care skill, yet blocks cut faith and raise quit risk. The team sorts talks by a three part frame.

Blocks fall in three groups. One is trainee traits like low drive and self trust. Next come plan flaws like book to ward gaps and thin feed back. Last come ward states like weak watch and rank bound air. Fixes must hit all three tiers, they hold, from drive boosts to ward lead change.
pmc-13367044:
Roxanna Barnaby and others showed that outer membrane sacs from Bacteroides fragilis inhibit CFTR chloride secretion in human colon organoids, in 2026. Bacteroides species reside in mucus, and their sacs likely mediate talk with the host, but effects on intestinal ion transport were unclear. A human organoid model could test host-pathogen link straight.

Two strains were studied: enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis producing toxin BFT-2, and a non-toxigenic strain, with vesicle effects on mucosal defence and CFTR chloride secretion checked in primary colon organoids. Toxin-containing sacs suppressed chloride secretion. The study links gut germ sacs to intestinal fluid balance, with meanings for diarrhoeal disease and cystic fibrosis-related gut failure.
pmc-13368844:
Ryhlander, Ringström, Lindkvist, and Hedenström study patient experience of gut endoscopic ultrasound in Sweden, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Technical quality of the procedure is well studied, patient experience less so. Three hundred six outpatients complete experience questionnaires after conscious sedation. Anxiety, pain, and discomfort are scored on visual scales.

Care is rated dignified and respectful overall by patients. Median pain and discomfort scores stay low during the procedure. A prior bad endoscopy experience best predicts higher anxiety. Female sex also predicts more anxiety, pain, and discomfort. Tailored information and support should target those at-risk patients.
pmc-13370144:
Dempsey and colleagues tested in 2026 whether the Parenting Occupations and Purposes Framework, a scheme that sorts what parents do into activities and their aims, fits real family life in Ireland. The framework had been built from theory but never checked in daily practice. Forty-four parents used a phone app to log their parenting moments in real time over seven days, yielding 1,150 reports.

Every category in the framework appeared in the logs. Attending to children's basic needs was the most common activity, while asking for help appeared only once, and meeting children's basic needs dominated the aims, with parent growth aims rarest. Parents also reported activities the framework lacks, such as faith practices, buying treats, and checking on children by text. The authors judge the framework sound for Ireland but ripe for added cultural and digital categories.
pmc-13371544:
Songphon Buddhasiri and colleagues published a veterinary study in 2026 on air pollution and cattle health in northern Thailand. Chiang Mai faces heavy seasonal smoke from biomass burning, and outdoor dairy animals breathe that air for weeks. The team asked whether fine particles in the air change the mix of microbes living in the upper airways of young dairy cattle, a mix that may affect lung disease risk.

Swabs from the noses of healthy heifers were compared between a clean-air period and a smoky period. During heavy pollution, the airway microbe mix became more varied overall, and its makeup shifted in clear ways. Some common groups fell, while several groups linked to bovine respiratory disease rose on average, though not by a proven margin. The authors say longer studies should test whether these shifts raise disease risk.
pmc-13371744:
Mansueto and three co-authors built a nine-stage model of recovery from gambling disorder in twenty twenty-six, based on the words of people who have lived it. Recovery here means more than stopping gambling; it includes rebuilding identity and meaning, and researchers had no shared map of the journey.

The team interviewed ten people who call themselves recovered and ten who are still recovering. Comparing the two groups, they traced nine stages, from first admitting the problem to a final stage of growth after trauma. Each stage carries its own helpers and hurdles, which differed somewhat between the groups. Both groups named all nine stages, though their experiences inside them varied. The authors argue care should fit the stage a person is in. A shared model could also help services and patients speak the same language.
pmc-13374744:
Bernsen and co-authors offer a practical guide to gene-based drug screening before treatment in child cancer care. Children respond to drugs in varied ways, and cancer therapy leaves little room for error. Gene tests can link variants to how a drug is handled or how toxic it proves. Guides exist for over 100 gene-drug pairs. Yet routine screening before treatment is still rare in pediatric oncology.

An earlier study found 16% of 1,151 patients could gain dose or drug changes from screening. The team then built screening into routine care in the Netherlands. The guide shares steps, pitfalls, and lessons from that rollout. It aims to help other centers adopt the same practice.
pmc-13375344:
Madakaripura Rangaswamy and colleagues review how helpful bacteria native to Brassica crops, the cabbage family, can defend crops against disease, in 2026 plant microbiome research. Spray controls face tightening rules while infections still cut yield and quality. The review gathers what is known about the communities on and inside Brassicas and the mechanisms those microbes use against pathogens. It asks how growers might deploy local strains as living crop guards in place of sprays.

Native bacteria, already adapted to local soils and weather, emerge as the most reliable options in the authors' judgment. Their biocontrol mechanisms include competing with pathogens, producing germ-killing compounds, and priming the plant's defenses. The review details how to isolate and screen such strains for useful traits, then assemble regional consortia, mixtures that work together. Practical hurdles remain, from formulation stability to regulation. Madakaripura Rangaswamy argues field fit, not lab performance, decides success in the field.
pmc-13375944:
Ding and colleagues build a virtual group of malaria patients for drug models. Real malaria changes the body in ways that shift drug levels. Healthy test subjects do not show those shifts. The team set key body traits from past studies. One blood protein more than doubled. Albumin fell. Liver enzyme levels fell too. Blood flow rose, and the stomach emptied more slowly.

They tested the virtual group on four known malaria drugs. Blood protein levels moved drug exposure the most. Enzyme levels and blood flow came next. Kidney function had little effect. The group gives drug makers a safer way to pick doses for sick patients.
pmc-13376144:
Hao Dong and co-authors built a deep learning tool to sharpen maps of chromatin contacts in two thousand twenty-six. Proteins that bind DNA mediate long-range contacts that control genes. Direct lab methods for such contacts are costly and scarce, and earlier models had limited resolution.

Their framework, GraphChIAr, starts from Hi-C contact maps and adds many protein binding profiles plus sequence data. It can estimate contact strength down to near-nucleosome resolution, far finer than the input. A shift-distance feature lets it predict contacts between distant genome sites across the whole genome. Checks against known mediators like CTCF showed high accuracy. Code is publicly available.
pmc-13377044:
Bohuan Fang and co-authors watch collagen assemble in real time and find the process runs on unstable building blocks, in work published in 2026. Collagen is the main structural protein in the tissue that supports cells. It builds up in layers of organisation, and faults in that build-up drive disease and ageing.

Using a fast-frozen microscopy method that captures steps over time, the team resolved two key intermediate forms in the assembly path. The basic unit is a triple helix that is metastable, meaning it easily changes shape. That fragility carries through the whole cascade, making assembly sensitive to local conditions. Later stages gain stability, and the final collagen holds its form in the body. Defective intermediates lead to faulty assembly. The authors propose simple rules that govern the cascade.
pmc-13377644:
Jonathan D Bolland and colleagues explain environmental DNA detection with a pizza analogy in a 2026 paper. Environmental DNA from water samples offers cheap, broad freshwater biodiversity data, yet false positives, false negatives, and technical jargon confuse decision makers. The authors propose a memorable analogy to clarify detection probability in typical metabarcoding workflows.

In the analogy, the pizza is the site, slices are water samples, bites are PCR replicates, toppings are species, and olives are a rare species. Eating more slices and taking more bites raises the chance of finding a rare topping, just as more samples and replicates raise detection odds. The piece aims to help scientists, practitioners, and policymakers grasp why absence of evidence is not evidence of absence in eDNA surveys.
pmc-13377844:
Yoshiaki Kinoshita and others show that upper lung asymmetry marks distinct phenotypes in idiopathic pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis in a 2026 study. This progressive lung disease favours the upper lobes with elastofibrosis, yet the meaning of asymmetry was unclear. Lung volumes from CT scans were measured in 102 patients with the disease, 56 with idiopathic pulmonary scarring, and 50 healthy controls.

Asymmetry appeared in about 40 percent of disease patients, with right-main asymmetry in about 31 percent and left-main in about 9 percent. Right-main cases tended to occur in male smokers, while left-main cases tended to occur in non-smokers with higher pneumothorax risk. Lower lung capacity and higher asymmetry independently predicted risk. The ratio offers a simple CT marker for phenotyping this rare disease.
pmc-13378244:
Nidhi Anand and colleagues present a fatal case of vascular air embolism in a ventilated preterm infant in a 2026 report. A male twin born at 29 weeks and 4 days with hydrops of unknown cause had bilateral pleural effusions drained before birth, with drains later dislodged. At birth he needed intubation and chest drains on both sides for persistent effusion.

At eighteen hours, he deteriorated suddenly with slow heart rate and low blood pressure. Chest X-ray first showed left pneumothorax and intracardiac air, prompting a second left drain, and air was aspirated from the arterial line. Despite resuscitation, he died, and post-mortem was declined. Repeat imaging showed extensive air embolism in heart, subclavian, neck, and abdominal vessels. The case warns that ventilated preterm infants with air leaks face high fatal embolism risk.
pmc-13380144:
Ana Pérez-del-Olmo and Aneta Kostadinova review a 2026 account of DNA barcoding in a group of parasitic flatworms that infect fish and the birds that eat them. Barcoding uses a short stretch of DNA to identify species. For the genus Diplostomum, the most species-rich in its family, sixteen years of barcoding have changed the picture of diversity.

The review updates names and records for 49 species and species-level lines identified so far. It assesses progress on species counts, where each form lives, life cycles, and which hosts each uses. It also flags problems in how the new data are used. The authors argue that global coverage is still far from complete.
pmc-13381544:
Le Coz, Boustila, and Imbach build a new way to rate soccer attacks that takes time into account, in a paper from twenty twenty-six. Old tools rate each play by where the ball is, but they treat plays as if time does not matter. In real games, a fast break and a slow build-up are not the same. The new tool tracks what players do, where they do it, and how long each step lasts.

The team fits the tool to game data from France and from a Europe-wide cup. Their score gives the chance of a goal in a set time span. It beats the old time-blind tool on two tests. The score is most useful late in a game, when the clock shapes each choice.
pmc-13383144:
Xin Feng's team compared sputum versus lung wash fluid for gene-based pneumonia diagnosis, in a 2026 study. Finding the germ in community-acquired pneumonia guides treatment, but some patients cannot undergo bronchoscopy or yield wash fluid promptly. Targeted gene sequencing of sputum, an easier sample, might fill the gap.

Between August 2023 and May 2025, 181 patients gave both sputum and wash fluid on the same day for the gene test. The team compared germ finding and pathogen naming between the two samples head to head. The comparison tells doctors when sputum testing can stand in for lavage and when the invasive sample remains needed.
pmc-13385444:
Jenna Myers and colleagues find that blood progenitor cells shrug off aging even as their stem cell parents decline in 2026 work. Stem cell aging is blamed for broad blood system decline in later life. The team tested whether the next tier down, multipotent progenitors, inherits that decline or resists it.

Young and old progenitors rebuilt blood equally well after transplant, a striking flat line across ages. Their gene programs, growth, and energy capacity also barely differed with age. The authors propose that one progenitor class acts as a buffer, shielding downstream blood production from stem cell aging.
pmc-13385844:
Yunning Chen's team reports a solar catalyst that strips fluorine from factory wastewater for over 500 hours, in a 2026 study. These compounds persist because aromatic stability blocks choosy carbon-fluorine cleavage, and OH radical making usually needs added helpers or Fenton chemistry. The team's carboxyl-bearing perylene diimide solid makes OH radicals through a carboxyl-peroxyacid cycle under visible light.

The solid reached 50.94 percent measured quantum yield for OH radicals at 600 nm and fully stripped fluorine from 100 mg per liter of the target, holding stable power beyond 500 hours. A peroxyacid intermediate with H-bond gating that weakens the oxygen-oxygen bond explains the low-barrier radical release. An outdoor flow reactor reached 95.85 percent breakdown.
pmc-13386244:
Maciej Rogala and colleagues compare life satisfaction in two bowel diseases, in a 2026 study from Poland. Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis both inflame the gut and disrupt daily life, work, and social ties. Quality of life in these diseases is often studied, but plain life satisfaction less so. The team asked whether the two groups differ and what satisfaction tracks with.

The study enrolled 109 patients with Crohn's disease and 101 with ulcerative colitis at a university hospital in Krakow. Average life satisfaction did not differ between the groups. Neither did the reported effects of disease on social and work activity. Within the Crohn's group, schooling level did link to satisfaction in a clear way. The authors suggest that support for patients should look beyond symptoms. Education, work, and social life shape how livable the illness feels.
pmc-13386844:
Xin Xu's team tested a spatial posture perception plus ball-tip workflow for pedicle screw placement in adult degenerative scoliosis, in a 2026 dual-center retrospective study. Freehand screw placement is hard when vertebrae rotate and pedicles deform. The team compared 44 adults having posterior thoracolumbar correction: 22 treated with the new workflow (320 screws) and 22 freehand (340 screws), judging accuracy on early postoperative CT.

Top-grade accuracy reached about 91 percent with the new workflow versus about 71 percent freehand, and clinically acceptable grades reached 96 percent versus 87 percent. Insertion ran faster, fluoroscopy exposures fell, and blood loss dropped, with no screw cut-outs versus five freehand. Deformity correction matched at one week and one year. Because the workflow was tested as a bundle, the separate contribution of spatial posture perception stays unproven.
pmc-13387144:
Kristen M. Rayfield and colleagues model which Caribbean bats survived and which vanished in a 2026 study.
