pmc-13412144:
Bryan Bertot and co-authors report in 2026 on 500 robot-assisted knee replacements aligned with a personalised technique called inverse kinematic alignment. Getting leg alignment right matters, since knees left far off target wear poorly and work badly. All operations at their centre between 2020 and 2022 used the Stryker MAKO robotic system, and patients were checked for a full year.

Of 487 knees with complete data, only 2.05 percent drifted more than three degrees from their immediate post-surgery target by twelve months. Average alignment shifted just 1.3 degrees over that year. Function scores and bending range, averaging 127 degrees of flexion, showed good recovery. Infection affected 1.2 percent of patients in this observational series.
pmc-13412544:
Phyllis Tawiah and colleagues ask in 2026 which simple body measurements flag high heart-disease risk among adults in Kumasi, Ghana. Clinics in poorer areas often cannot run lipid panels, so tape-measure indices could fill the gap. The cross-sectional study measured 480 adults aged 40 to 79 and scored each person's estimated ten-year risk with World Health Organization charts.

Elevated risk appeared in 56.9 percent of men and 38.8 percent of women in this urban group. Waist-to-hip ratio and a body shape index each tracked higher risk, while larger hip and mid-arm measurements tracked lower risk in adjusted models. Waist-to-hip ratio held up in women, and the shape index in men. The authors urge adding these measures to routine screening.
pmc-13415744:
A correction notice from 2026 fixes Figure 1 in an article on the pathobiology of anaplastic large cell lymphoma, a T cell cancer. During figure assembly, panel (a) picked up overlapping features from panel (b). The notice supplies the figure as it should appear, with a full revised legend.

The legend describes hallmark tumor cells and the typical marker pattern, including strong CD30 staining. It also explains how ALK staining patterns differ by the underlying gene fusion. Panels (a) and (b) show tissue from the same patient, meant for illustration. The authors apologize for the error and clarify how the two panels differ.
pmc-13416044:
Ahmed A. Elshamy and co-authors let a game rewrite its own levels to match each player's skill, in a 2026 framework study. Robot players trained at three skill levels plus human players supplied gameplay data for a classifier. The classifier sorts players as beginner, normal, or expert with about 98 percent accuracy.

Its verdict feeds a two stage language model pipeline that issues structured edits to the current level chunk. A physics checker based on shortest path search confirms the edited level can still be crossed. On Super Mario Bros. levels, about 74 percent of full levels stayed playable after edits, close to the original eighty percent baseline.
pmc-13416544:
A team at Peking University People's Hospital studied transplant outcomes for children with a rare leukemia gene change, in a paper from twenty twenty-six. The change involves a gene called NUP98 and marks a hard-to-treat form of acute myeloid leukemia. All children in the study received stem cell transplants from donors.

Thirty-one children were followed for about three years on median. The most common subtype paired the gene with one partner, and many children also carried other mutations. A handful relapsed, typically within months. Three-year survival came to roughly three quarters. Children whose gene change was already undetectable before transplant fared far better than those still positive. The authors stress clearing the marker before transplant where possible.
pmc-13417344:
Changyuan Yu and co-authors add a value regularisation term to learning based predictive control for mobile robots, in a 2026 control study. Predictive control plans moves over a short horizon, while reinforcement learning tunes the long term cost online. Disturbances and model mismatch can erode both. Their term penalises state deviation inside the learning target itself.

Simulations on straight line and steering vehicle models showed the learning settled about 25 percent faster than the unregularised version. Worst case performance loss across mismatch tests stayed near 3 percent, far below classic controllers. Gains grew as tasks hardened. The method adds no extra online optimisation burden.
pmc-13417644:
De-Xuan Hu and colleagues show that solvent choice steers one rhodium catalysed reaction toward two different products, in a 2026 study. Starting from the same halogen bearing benzamide, an alcohol solvent strips the halogen cleanly, while a non water like solvent builds a phenanthridinone ring system instead. Both routes run efficiently in one step.

Related ring compounds were then tested against two DNA repair enzymes and for cancer cell killing. One compound blocked the first enzyme strongly and boosted a known drug's effect in colon cancer cells. Another blocked the second enzyme and shrank tumours in mice. The chemistry doubles as a drug lead source.
pmc-13418744:
Yi Sun and colleagues unveil a light-based method that watches single molecules twist at a surface without any labels attached. How molecules rotate where liquid meets solid shapes binding, friction, and crossing of barriers, yet that twisting motion has been hard to see directly. Their tool uses magnetic plasmon effects tied to tiny rods resting near a metal film.

Twist of a rod changes the phase of the light signal, turning rotation into a readable, direction-aware trace. The setup gathers the reflected signal through one lens and reads it with a sensitive camera. A twist-aware channel can split true binding shape from messy surroundings, expose hidden energy steps, and sharpen how well single molecules are told apart. The method gives surface science a fresh way to follow motion that older tools mostly missed.
pmc-13420044:
Shuang Jin and colleagues study older patients in England whose final hospital care cost the most yet satisfied their families the least. A small share of patients accounts for most hospital spending at the end of life. The data come from surveys of bereaved next of kin tied to two large hospitals.

The study set held 404 patients, with a mean age of 80.4 years in the reported group figures. Statistical models sorted which traits lined up with care that looked costly yet low in value to families. Views of relatives carry weight here, since the patients themselves could not be asked. Findings like these help services steer spending toward care that families experience as good, not just care that is intensive.
pmc-13420344:
Alireza Nikzad-Jamnani and colleagues recount a hard airway case where a breathing tube had to be replaced through a fiber-optic scope after major reconstructive surgery. The patient had received a free flap rebuild, chosen for better looks and function than other repairs. Swollen tissue and landmarks distorted by surgery blocked the normal view for tube placement.

Failed tube placement remains a leading cause of harm in anesthesia practice, by the closed-claims record the authors cite. The team chose an awake fiber-optic approach, letting the patient keep breathing while the scope found the path. Postoperative care continued in the intensive care unit. The case lays out the decision steps in order, giving airway teams a rehearsed route for the surprise difficult airway after flap surgery.
pmc-13420844:
Xavier Laurent and colleagues present MERItest, a combined scoring model for judging recovery six months after knee ligament reconstruction. That six-month mark is a risky crossing point, where athletes leave structured rehab for sport-specific work with widely varying readiness. Standard strength and jump measures often miss hidden deficits and the workarounds athletes adopt.

The model joins three domains in one reading: single-joint strength testing, three-dimensional motion analysis of jumping, hopping, and running, and a psychological readiness questionnaire. Each domain alone has blind spots that the union is meant to cover. The design weighs rigor against what clinics can actually run. Teams clearing athletes to return gain a fuller picture than any single test gives, at the phase where reinjury risk peaks.
pmc-13421244:
Ali Ebrahimpoor Gorji and Ville Alopaeus compare machine-learning approaches in a 2026 study that predicts how much hydrogen dissolves in different chemicals. How much hydrogen dissolves matters for storage and plant design, since the amount shifts with heat and pressure. Testing each mix by hand is not practical.

Their dataset held 3,761 measurements covering 100 chemicals. Their model used the simplest form of machine learning, a multiple linear regression. It read molecular clues within a structure-property framework. The team also ran internal checks that earlier models had skipped. It predicted well on both training and test portions. They argue that a plain, open model can match far more complex rivals here.
pmc-13421344:
Xiang-Jing Kong leads a large collaboration reporting, in a 2026 paper, sponge-like crystal frameworks that store methane for natural gas vehicles. Storing gas by adsorption at moderate pressure would be safer and cheaper than liquefying or compressing it, yet materials must hold and release a large amount per fill.

Their metal-dipyrazolate frameworks flex between narrow-pore and large-pore forms as methane enters. One zinc framework delivered 173 cubic centimetres of gas per cubic centimetre of material across a common pressure range. It delivered more at higher pressure. It also resisted the water damage that ruins an earlier benchmark material. Tests in 250-millilitre tanks showed the performance survived repeated cycles. Structural studies and modelling explain the pore switching.
pmc-13421544:
Bhuiyan and colleagues report a 2026 trial of an artificial intelligence system that detects age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of blindness, from photos of the back of the eye. The team enrolled 845 adults over 50 with no prior diagnosis at clinics in New York City. Three eye specialists graded dilated-eye photos as the reference standard.

Judged per patient, the system separated referable disease, meaning more than early disease, from milder states with strong accuracy. It caught about nine in ten referable cases while clearing most healthy ones, scores the authors rate as strong for screening. The photos were taken without dilating drops, so the setup fits routine clinics. A tool like this could flag at-risk patients during ordinary visits and speed referrals, catching disease while steps can still slow its advance toward blindness.
pmc-13421744:
Addisu Legesse Chaka and colleagues tested salt iodine levels across Ethiopia in 2026, sampling 1862 household and market salts from nine regions and two city administrations. Iodized salt prevents deficiency disorders, yet coverage has swung over the years, possibly with what shoppers know and do.

Adequate iodine reached 88.1 percent of household salts and 89.1 percent of market salts, lowest in Tigray and Afar, while only about half of women had heard of iodized salt and many added salt after cooking. The paper links better coverage to asking for iodized salt, lidded storage, and late salting, giving nutrition teams concrete habits to promote.
pmc-13422244:
Ojo, Loh, and Seidel present in 2026 a case of Bouveret syndrome, in which a gallstone escapes into the stomach outlet and blocks it, in a man in his mid-eighties. The condition is rare and has no agreed treatment guideline.

The man arrived after four days of vomiting following meals, on top of months of worsening difficulty swallowing and weight loss. Doctors first treated him for gallbladder inflammation before identifying the blocked outlet. Attempts to remove the trapped stone through an endoscope, a flexible camera tube, failed. The team then broke the stone with lithotripsy, a shattering technique, and retrieved the pieces through a surgical opening in the stomach, choosing gastrotomy alone with no further operations. The authors add the case to the small literature on managing this gallstone complication.
pmc-13422344:
Lederer and colleagues tested in 2026 whether holograms help dental students judge root canal anatomy better than X-rays. Root canal shape decides how tooth-saving treatment is planned, and flat X-rays can hide its three-dimensional form. In a controlled trial, 79 students in years four to six each judged six tooth cases.

Holograms clearly improved students' counts of root canals in three teeth with several roots. For a standard shape classification, holograms helped clearly in only one tooth type. Judging treatment difficulty gave mixed results, favouring X-rays in two cases and holograms in one. The authors conclude that holograms aid some tasks, chiefly spotting extra canals in complex teeth. The team presents holography as a useful teaching add-on and calls for more study on where it helps most.
pmc-13422644:
Barnett, Lam, and Anastasopoulou compare in 2026 the heart safety of romosozumab, a bone-building antibody that blocks sclerostin, against two older bone-building drugs, teriparatide and abaloparatide. Warnings about heart risk followed romosozumab from an earlier trial.

Using the TriNetX real-world health records network, the team matched patients over 50 with osteoporosis by their baseline risk and followed them for one year. The romosozumab group showed lower rates of combined major heart events than the comparison group. It also showed lower rates of heart attack, heart failure, and death taken one by one, plus better overall survival. Stroke rates did not differ clearly. The authors stress the results show association, not proof of cause, and cannot by themselves change the drug's warnings.
pmc-13423144:
Ruth A Hackett leads a study of loneliness among middle-aged and older adults in England who live with breathlessness. The symptom limits social life as well as movement. Its link with loneliness had barely been measured, so the team turned to a national ageing survey from 2010–11 covering 8,195 people aged 50 and over.

The symptom affected 28.4% of participants, and 19.3% met the survey threshold for loneliness. That share climbed steadily with symptom grade. It reached 34.9% at the worst grade assessed, against 16.3% among those free of it. People with worse symptoms also more often lived alone, were unmarried, and reported depression, long-term illness, and mobility trouble. The authors argue breathlessness care should screen for loneliness too.
pmc-13423444:
Takashi Ueno and seven colleagues evaluate a modified laparoscopic Wells rectopexy for rectal prolapse, an operation that fixes the rectum to the sacrum with mesh. Recurrence and mesh problems trouble the standard version, especially in elderly patients with small pelvises. The team therefore trimmed the mesh during surgery. They fixed it with both tacks and a continuous barbed suture.

Reviewing 29 patients treated between 2014 and 2025, median age 78, they found every operation finished laparoscopically with almost no blood loss and a median stay of four days. One minor complication occurred. Over a median follow-up of 190 days, only one prolapse recurred, at thirty months, supporting the tailored approach.
pmc-13423944:
Manouchehri, Datta, and Levin review in 2026 whether arnica, a plant remedy, and bromelain, an enzyme from pineapple, reduce ecchymosis, the bruising that follows facial plastic surgery. Single studies had suggested a benefit, but results conflicted.

Their systematic search to August 2025 found ten studies with 696 patients, most covering nose surgery or eyelid surgery. Eight studies tested arnica, and about two thirds of those reported clearly less bruising at some point after surgery. The two arnica studies that measured swelling also found less of it. Only two studies tested bromelain, and just one found less bruising by day seven. Side effects were rare and mild, but wide differences in dose and measurement blocked a pooled analysis.
pmc-13424144:
Zhi Dong leads a fifteen-author team solving the structure of the smell receptors that let pea aphids detect their sex pheromones. Two receptor proteins, working with a shared partner, answer separately to the pheromone parts nepetalactol and nepetalactone, guiding mates to each other and keeping species distinct.

Cryo-electron microscopy captured one receptor pair in three states: empty and closed, loaded and closed, and loaded and open. The channel joins one specific receptor with three copies of the partner. When the pheromone docks, the receptor shifts shape and the pore widens unevenly, letting ions flow and signalling detection. The authors offer the mechanism as a base for designing kinder, pheromone-based pest control.
pmc-13424344:
Mueller and colleagues investigate in 2026 whether acid-suppressing proton pump inhibitors interfere with dasatinib, a leukemia drug whose absorption falls as stomach acidity drops. They ask whether patients taking both switch treatments sooner.

Using German health insurance claims from 2010 to 2024, the team followed adults with chronic myeloid leukemia starting dasatinib, in groups of 297 newly treated and 372 already-treated patients. About one in five also took a proton pump inhibitor. After matching patients on background risk, those with the acid suppressor switched to another therapy earlier in both groups. The link reached statistical firmness in the already-treated group, where the switching rate ran nearly double that of matched patients without the suppressor. The authors say the pattern fits the known interaction and supports avoiding the combination when possible.
pmc-13424444:
Le and a large team compare in 2026 two ways of taking kidney biopsies from children at a referral hospital in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. A biopsy means taking small tissue samples. One method guides the needle with live ultrasound images; the other works blind.

The retrospective study covered 221 children biopsied between May 2018 and April 2025, with 173 guided procedures and 48 blind ones. Guided biopsies collected more glomeruli, the kidney's tiny filters, per sample and more often reached the counts doctors consider adequate. Rates of inadequate samples, visible blood in urine, and major complications did not differ clearly between methods. Lower kidney function before the procedure predicted later bleeding, which was mostly blood visible in the urine rather than major bleeding.
pmc-13424644:
The Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency's Infectious Disease Countermeasure Task Force reports the system it built to guard the Korean delegation at the Milano Cortina 2026 Olympic and Paralympic Winter Games. Mass gatherings of that scale raise the risk of infections spreading among crowds and across borders. The agency wanted protection for its athletes. It also wanted evidence for future event planning.

Before the Games, the agency set up an interagency coordination network. The network reached the national sports and Paralympic committees. The agency also wrote a preparedness plan and staffed a task force with a central headquarters and field units. During the event the team held situation meetings, ran surveillance and risk assessment, and logged every suspected and confirmed case for later evaluation.
pmc-13424744:
Shahabuddin and colleagues examined in 2026 what makes embedded implementation research work in low- and middle-income countries. In this approach, research sits inside health programs to find delivery bottlenecks and raise the use of proven care. The team drew on surveys, documents, and case studies from 24 completed UNICEF-supported projects in 11 countries carried out between 2015 and 2022.

Shahabuddin found that two-thirds of projects fed findings into policy or program changes, most often through new immunisation plans, digital tools, and stronger community engagement. Half reported measurable gains in service delivery, such as higher vaccine coverage. Early involvement of decision makers, fit with program cycles, and shared reporting helped uptake. Weak political backing, rival priorities, and poor funding after the research ended were the main barriers the team recorded.
pmc-13425044:
Wang and colleagues published a 2026 study on a gentler way to remove soft cataracts. Cataract surgery breaks the clouded lens with ultrasound before drawing it out. Soft lenses need less force, but standard chopping can still tear the lens bag. The team compared their new flip method against the usual quick-chop method.

The study covered 176 eyes with soft-grade cataracts split between both methods. The flip method needed clearly less ultrasound time during surgery. Energy use, sight after surgery, and cornea measures matched between groups overall. Two lens-bag tears occurred in the quick-chop group and none with the flip. The authors offer the flip method as a safer route for soft lenses. Shorter ultrasound time also means less heat exposure for eye tissues.
pmc-13425544:
Safia Lakehal and Guleed Adan explored what neurology trainees value in grand rounds in a 2026 qualitative focus group study. The work took place at a tertiary neuroscience centre in North West England, where the weekly grand round is the main recurring organized teaching session for trainees. Its teaching value had never been formally studied from the trainee viewpoint before.

Semi-structured focus groups gathered views from eligible trainees across seniority levels. Discussion addressed didactic formats and whether public questioning feels safe for learning, helping educators see which features of a long-running teaching tradition still serve trainees well.
pmc-13427044:
Stynen and colleagues surveyed ticks in 2026 around Strasbourg in eastern France, a region where tick diseases are established. The tick Ixodes ricinus is well known in forests, but its presence in city parks is less studied. The team collected questing ticks, meaning ticks waiting on plants for a host, at eight sites: a botanical garden, four urban parks, and three peri-urban forests.

Well-kept urban parks showed low risk of tick bites and of the infections tested, including Lyme disease bacteria. Peri-urban alluvial forests, the wet woods along rivers, showed high risk, with dense young ticks and many infected ones. The authors warn that greener cities under climate change could raise tick risk if parks are not managed with it in mind. They recommend tailored park management and public awareness campaigns.
pmc-13427444:
Anh T. Tran and coauthors mined a neutral blood pressure trial for hidden responder subgroups in a 2026 post hoc machine learning analysis. The ATACH-2 trial found no overall benefit from intensive blood pressure lowering after brain hemorrhage, possibly masking gains in select patients. Their team trained an XGBoost model on two-thirds of the control arm, 326 patients, to predict poor three-month outcome defined by disability scores.

Applying the model to 499 treated patients and 163 held-out controls, with SHAP explanations ranking each factor's contribution, searched for people whose risk profile predicts benefit. Explainable analysis offers a cautious route to personalizing acute hemorrhage care without a new trial.
pmc-13427544:
Abdullah Al-Abcha and colleagues follow, in a 2026 Mayo Clinic study, what happens over time to people with a moderately leaking mitral valve. The records cover 8,687 patients who had heart ultrasound scans between 2010 and 2023. Most leaks were functional, meaning the valve itself was normal but the heart around it was diseased. Follow-up lasted a median of just over four years.

About two thirds of patients were alive four years later, and many had been hospitalized for heart failure. The leak grew severe in roughly one third of patients, while only about one in nine had a valve procedure. Survival looked better for the degenerative type before other health factors were taken into account. The figures argue for closer watch and for trials on when to intervene.
pmc-13427644:
Anja Ehrhardt comments, in 2026, on a strategy for lasting protection against HIV by reprogramming blood stem cells inside the body. Most gene therapy takes stem cells out, alters them in a lab, and returns them, which is slow and costly. The study under discussion instead sends a helper-dependent adenovirus straight to the stem cells. Those cells then seed the blood system with cells that release antiviral agents over the long term.

The commentary traces earlier in-body attempts since 2016, including fat-based particles and other viral shells. A newer shell built from a rarer adenovirus type may dodge existing immunity in many people. Its targeting knob also avoids red blood cells, a snag seen in primates. Readers get a guided tour of a field moving from lab benches toward simpler one-step treatment.
pmc-13428444:
Bao and colleagues tested in 2026 whether two blood markers of neutrophil extracellular traps can help diagnose sepsis and predict who will die. Traps are web-like strands that white blood cells cast out to catch germs, and they spill the marker proteins MPO and CitH3 into blood. The team studied 126 sepsis patients of rising severity and sixty healthy controls.

Both markers climbed step by step from plain sepsis to severe sepsis to septic shock, and both ran higher in patients who died within twenty-eight days. Used together, the pair identified sepsis with high accuracy and predicted death better than the standard infection markers. Each marker also independently predicted death in adjusted analysis, alongside organ failure scores and lactate, a sign of poor circulation. The authors propose the pair as an add-on test for sepsis care.
pmc-13429244:
Rita Landgraf wrote a 2026 commentary arguing that aging should be treated as a shared public health task, not a niche concern. She links Delaware's fast-aging population with the 2024 United States national framework for a plan on aging.

More than one in five Delaware residents is already 65 or older, and over 55 million Americans now fall in that age group. The federal framework, built by 16 agencies, joins health care with housing, transport, work, and social services under shared principles. Landgraf urges Delaware to align policy, buildings, and community systems so people can stay healthy, independent, and respected as they age. She frames preparation for longer lives as both a duty and a chance for the state.
pmc-13430444:
Xianyang Hu and co-authors used gene data in a 2026 study to ask whether proteins tied to swelling in the blood help cause vaginal thinning and soreness after menopause. The condition stems mostly from low estrogen and often goes untreated. The team tested 91 such proteins with gene tools drawn from large studies of people with European roots.

Six proteins stood out. Two went with higher risk, while four went with lower risk. Extra checks found no clear sign that other traits skewed the results. A separate look at vaginal tissue data backed one finding, since the protein with the strongest support showed lower levels in thinned tissue. The authors urge care, since many proteins were tested at once, and they call for checks in new groups.
pmc-13430844:
Joel T Minion and colleagues listen to care aides who look after long-term care residents whose behaviours may signal past trauma. Many residents may carry trauma or post-traumatic stress, often alongside dementia or complex mental health needs, and aides give most of their direct care in Canada.

In autumn 2024, open interviews with 24 aides from six urban Alberta homes explored that work, building on thirteen earlier interviews from 2023. Questions evolved as data grew, and themes were drawn by reflexive analysis. The study gives voice to aides who feel overlooked while handling distress behaviours, and it points managers toward support that matches the emotional load.
pmc-13431944:
Christoph Steup and colleagues show how alternative splicing of the P2RX4 receptor can block a promising drug pairing in bowel and pancreatic cancer. Combining chemotherapy with P2RX4 blockade was proposed to prevent resistance spread between cells, but patient selection needs a reliable marker.

P2RX4 levels were measured by gene sequencing and tissue staining in both cancers, with isoform locations traced in lab cells and patient-derived tumour organoids. Protein levels diverged from RNA levels because splicing reshuffled the receptor, and variation between patients ran larger in bowel cancer than in pancreatic cancer. The work warns that RNA alone cannot pick responders for this pairing.
pmc-13432844:
Zhengkai Gan and co-authors surveyed male college students in Hangzhou in 2026 on what shapes their plans to take a vaccine against a common virus that can drive cancers. Shots for males count as a key lever to cut world harm from this virus. Forms reached more than thirteen hundred students through a staged pick across school years.

Near two thirds said they would take the shot. A three-step math build told a clear tale. Plain traits explain a sliver of plans. Belief parts of a planned-act frame lifted the share to a quarter. Germ facts plus felt risk pushed it near a third. Felt power to act led the drivers, ahead of warm views, peer pull, and germ facts. Felt risk of catch also fed stronger plans. Easier access and lower cost join school drives as the authors' picks.
pmc-13433644:
Kathy Truong and co-authors revisit pneumatosis intestinalis, the finding of gas inside the bowel wall on scans, in work from twenty twenty-six. The sign can mean a harmless quirk or a life threatening gut problem. Like images can hide unlike causes, so care teams must weigh the whole picture.

The review walks through linked scan signs, from vein gas and clots to wall thickening or thinning. Less specific signs, such as free air and fluid, gain meaning only in context. The authors note where lab markers mislead and where patient groups need special care. Risk sorting plans now in progress close the piece. A team approach is stressed throughout.
pmc-13434644:
Leire Izagirre-Urizar and a large team link a fuel carrier to myelin upkeep in the spinal cord in 2026. Myelin wraps nerve fibers and frays in multiple sclerosis. The carrier, MCT2, moves small fuel molecules into the cells that make myelin. Its levels fall in the progressive form of the disease.

Deleting the carrier in mouse cord did not kill the maker cells. Fat making enzymes fell, swelling rose, and myelin upkeep failed instead. Nerve fibers showed strain, which a high fat, low sugar diet eased. Feeding plans might offset the carrier loss in patients. The study frames myelin care as an energy problem.
pmc-13435444:
Gokhan Sayer's team asked in 2026 whether showing patients photos before ingrown toenail surgery changes how they judge the result afterward. Photo previews have lifted satisfaction in other surgical fields, but no one had tested the idea for toenail surgery done by the Winograd method. The team looked back at 126 patients treated between early 2022 and mid-2024, split by whether standard pre-op photos were shown.

Both groups improved on pain, skin-related quality of life, foot function, and satisfaction over twelve months, yet the photo group ended with less pain and clearly higher satisfaction. Recurrence and other scores did not separate the groups in the reported results. Surgeons get a cheap, simple step worth testing: a photo preview may shape expectations and leave patients happier with the same operation.
pmc-13435544:
Aradhya and colleagues surveyed 130 emergency medical staff in Southern India in 2026 about safety, comfort, and design inside ambulance patient cabins. Poor cabin design can injure crews and slow care during transport, yet Indian evidence on these ergonomic problems has been scarce.

Limited cabin space was the top complaint, named by sixty percent of respondents, and half struggled to reach equipment during care. Half also worried about where the attendant seat sits while treating patients. Uneven roads and sudden vehicle breakdowns were the leading causes of transport injuries. Performing CPR was the task most often linked to injury, and back pain was the most common long-term health hazard, reported by well over half. Views differed significantly with work experience, and the authors urge design research.
pmc-13435844:
Xiaolu Ji and coauthors map other health issues in 52,098 children with ADHD at a Nanjing hospital in 2026. Records span 2015 to 2025, with boys at 78.9 percent of the group. One in five children carried at least one added chronic issue or health problem.

Tic disorder was the single most common added issue. Intellectual disability paired with autism was the most common pair where pairs occurred. Grouping math found a core pattern of tics, learning disability, epilepsy, sleep trouble, and obesity. Most children sat in the six to eleven age band. Screening at diagnosis should cover that core set, the team argues.
pmc-13436744:
Nathan A Roberge and coauthors show how a phage protein disarms hair like filaments across many bacteria in 2026. The protein Aqs1, from a Pseudomonas phage, blocks type four pilus motors. Those filaments drive surface crawling, DNA uptake, and protein export in many germs.

Aqs1 grips a shared patch on the motor protein that powers filament growth. The grip loosens the six part motor ring, so motors fail to gather at filament bases. A flexible linker near the patch tunes ring contact, a new control detail. Blocking rivals filaments also stops other phages that dock there. The patch offers a template for broad anti virulence drugs.
pmc-13437244:
Seonji Kim and colleagues compared bleeding risk between two blood pressure drugs taken alongside modern blood thinners. People with atrial fibrillation often receive both kinds of drug. Telmisartan blocks a body pump that clears thinners more strongly than olmesartan does, which could raise thinner levels. Their 2026 Korean study followed patients nationwide from 2016 to 2023, with 27,851 people on telmisartan and 20,010 on olmesartan.

Major bleeding, counted as bleeding in the brain or gut, occurred more often with telmisartan. Rates were about nine cases per thousand person-years against about seven, and the adjusted risk ran about a third higher. Gut bleeding alone drove the gap, with risk about half again as high. Brain bleeding and stroke rates did not differ clearly between the groups. The authors suggest that the pump-blocking strength of a companion drug deserves a place in prescribing choices for patients on thinners.
pmc-13437444:
Stephanie Legere and colleagues show how a danger signal called IL-33 helps the body clean up dead cells after inflammation. Clearing spent cells, called efferocytosis, falls to macrophages armed with a surface receptor named MerTK. Their 2026 mouse study injected IL-33 into the belly cavity and watched the local immune scene over two days.

Within forty-eight hours, MerTK-carrying macrophages grew more numerous and ate dead cells faster when tested. IL-13 appeared in cavity fluid soon after the injection, before lymphocyte groups showed any change. Mast cells proved a major early source: mice bred without them made far less IL-13 three hours after treatment, while mice lacking eosinophils matched normal levels. Lab cultures confirmed mast cells can answer IL-33 within hours. The authors link the chain to human care, settings with high levels of a decoy receptor for IL-33, or with few mast cells, tend to fare worse.
pmc-13437544:
Aisha AlMulla and co-authors scanned cancers for changes in the genes that govern how the body handles medicines. Such drug-handling genes are usually studied as inherited traits, yet tumors mutate them too, and that side is poorly mapped. Their 2026 study merged mutation, gene copy, and gene activity data for 765 tumors across seven cancer types, using forty drug-handling genes.

Single-gene changes were uncommon, averaging under nine percent of tumors per gene-cancer pair when all change kinds were counted. Still, the pattern was far from random: changes clustered in a few transporter genes, including ABCB1 and its relatives. In sixty-four gene-cancer pairs, extra gene copies matched higher gene activity after strict correction, a sign the changes may truly alter drug handling. Their call is for studies recording actual treatments, so this tumor-side pharmacology can be tested against real drug responses.
pmc-13438144:
Raja, Nehra, Dogra, and Rastogi built a simple two-terminal memristor, a resistor whose resistance remembers past voltage, from an amorphous calcium zirconate thin film sandwiched between gold and a conductive glass electrode. Such devices are candidates for dense memory and brain-like computing that conventional flash cannot scale to.

The device switched reliably and reproducibly at low operating voltages of about plus or minus 1 volt in their testing. It endured 1.2 times ten to the fifth switching cycles and held stored states for over 5.5 times ten to the third seconds without power. Uniformity held up both cycle to cycle and device to device across the fabricated samples examined. Spectroscopy supported a mechanism in which oxygen vacancies line up into conductive filaments that form and rupture with each switch, and the authors propose logic and data encryption uses.
pmc-13438844:
Ji Hoon Kim and colleagues built an anti-counterfeit fingerprint that can be wiped and redrawn on demand. Optical physical unclonable functions scatter light through random microstructures to make labels no factory can copy twice. Their flaw is permanence: once read by thieves, a fixed fingerprint cannot change. Earlier resettable versions answered to heat or light, risking accidental resets. Their 2026 design instead answers only to a splash of solvent.

Tiny polymer cubes sit loose inside square wells, free to shift and turn. Solvent swells them until they touch the walls; as it evaporates, they settle into a fresh random arrangement, minting a new fingerprint. A machine-learning reader learns each new pattern for authentication. Between resets, the tags shrugged off environmental and mechanical abuse in testing. A label that stays put through shipping and weather, then refreshes only when its owner chooses, fits supply chains needing repeated proof.
pmc-13438944:
Zehui Li and colleagues show the failing heart-control system in ALS carries news about how fast the disease will run. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is known for killing motor neurons, yet the autonomic nerves that pace the heart also falter. Their 2026 study recorded day-long heart rhythms in 95 newly diagnosed patients and 39 controls, then followed the patients for a median of about twenty-one months.

Patients at the most advanced stage already showed faster progression, more breathing and swallowing symptoms, and weaker heart-rate variability. One measure mattered most: patients whose variability fell below a threshold near 111 milliseconds survived significantly worse, even after statistical adjustment. The authors argue a cheap, painless heart recording at diagnosis could flag patients needing closer watching and earlier support. It also strengthens the case that ALS is a whole-body disease whose non-motor signs deserve a place in prognosis.
pmc-13439344:
Yan Wu's team mapped future climate risks in 2026 for the Northeast Tiger and Leopard National Park, a global biodiversity stronghold under climate threat. Managers lacked a full risk picture for adaptation planning. The team downscaled climate models to fine resolution and contrasted two extreme futures under a high-emissions path, a dry-hot future and a warm-wet future, choosing the better bias correction method first.

Both futures warm, but threats split: dry-hot brings drought, habitat decay, and wildfire, while warm-wet disrupts wildlife corridors and raises flood and geological hazards. The park thus faces a twin drought-and-flood threat, not a single disaster type. Park managers get a versatile adaptation brief that argues against one-hazard planning.
pmc-13439444:
Ye and nine co-authors report embryo selection for a woman who carries a BRCA1 fault. Their case report, from twenty twenty-six, comes from a fertility clinic in China. The patient's family carries a variant that raises breast cancer risk sharply. She had also faced three years of infertility.

The team built a breast cancer risk score from many small gene effects. Weights were tuned for Asian ancestry using a large British data bank plus local data. Embryos were tested for the family variant and for chromosome health. Risk scores and family history ranked the embryos together. The chosen embryo lacked the variant. The patient conceived and delivered a healthy baby.
pmc-13439844:
Mohamed Khalid's team reviewed nebivolol plus valsartan in 2026 for high blood pressure, a leading global killer where many patients need more than one drug. The beta-blocker plus angiotensin blocker pairing promised control with fewer side effects, but evidence was scattered. Following systematic review rules, the team searched three databases to February 2025, screened ninety-nine studies, and kept six, including two randomized trials.

The combination lowered systolic and diastolic pressure with adherence and quality of life data reported alongside safety, though the small, mixed study set limits firm ranking against other pairings. Clinicians get a consolidated, cautious case for this pairing in patients needing dual therapy. Larger head-to-head trials are still needed.
pmc-13441244:
Sarah Ajabnoor and Lara Tashkandi survey Saudi adults with irritable bowel syndrome to find which foods set off their symptoms. Diet strongly affects this common gut disorder, yet trigger patterns may differ by country and habit. The authors built a food trigger score combining how many foods provoke symptoms and how badly.

Ninety-eight adults answered a structured online questionnaire. Spicy foods led the list, followed by legumes, cabbage, milk, and fried foods. Older age and worse symptoms predicted higher overall scores. Chronic illness raised scores for some food groups in particular. The authors argue for dietary advice tailored to the individual rather than one standard list.
pmc-13442444:
Sarang Jeong and colleagues test whether night owls carry distinct fuel marks in their blood in a 2026 study of 272 adults. The adults came from a 2022 health cohort in Gangwon, and a short quiz sorted them into morning, middle, or evening types. Fasting blood levels of three fuel goods, pyruvate, lactate, and citrate, were checked for each group.

Most health marks looked alike across the three types. Pyruvate ran higher in evening types than in morning types in each adjusted model, with the gap holding at p below 0.048 in the main checks. Lactate and citrate showed no such gap. The gap stayed when people on fuel-illness drugs were left out. The team links the pyruvate rise to slower burn in cell power plants, a link past animal work hinted at, and calls for direct tests of that chain.
pmc-13442544:
Zhaorui Yang and colleagues survey what heart patients know and do about early extra beats in a 2026 study at Yichun People's Hospital. The beats, called premature ventricular contractions, fire from the lower heart chambers ahead of time. From March to June 2025, 544 valid surveys came back from people with a firm diagnosis.

Scores showed poor know-how, with a mean mark of 11.34 points out of 23 in that section. Outlook scores sat mid-range, and daily practice scores sat mid-range as well. More know-how tracked with a better outlook and better habits in the checks. Path models put outlook between know-how and habits, so facts may shape acts through views. The team urges plain teaching that lifts facts and views together, since more than half the group had no current care for the beats.
pmc-13442844:
Xin-Yu Xu and colleagues report a light-driven way to add boron to plain carbon chains in a 2026 chemistry paper. Such boron goods serve as prized building blocks for drugs and fine goods, yet picky placement on dull chains stays hard. Their method pairs a light-fed catalyst with a cobalt partner to steer the add.

The path runs through a metal-hydrogen step that hands a hydrogen atom to the chain, then a radical step that sets the boron. Chains with one, two, or three side groups all took boron at the Markovnikov spot, the more swapped carbon. Mild terms, fast rates, and wide scope mark the gain over past routes. Tests with goods drawn from natural products also worked. Math checks and control runs back the path they propose.
pmc-13443744:
Mazdak Ebadi and colleagues propose a 2026 battery-free solar desalination design that pairs maximum power point tracking with a sun tracker to run reverse osmosis modules off the grid. The controller estimates the best panel voltage from open-circuit voltage and temperature, then switches modules on in sequence before the peak is reached.

A calendar-driven tracker needs no light sensor, and pre-sized capacitors absorb the tracker motor's start-up surge in place of a battery, with a two-stage return routine parking the panels. Tests on a 1,100 watt array feeding ten modules totaling 860 watts lifted desalination output by 71 percent. The design suits remote water supply, though long-term wear and cloudy-day behavior remain to test.
pmc-13444244:
Jing Cai and colleagues report a 2026 study showing that tumor-infiltrating B cells help block spread in nasopharyngeal carcinoma, a cancer whose advanced cases fail mainly through distant metastasis. Combining single-cell sequencing with multiplex imaging, the team compared B cell patterns in metastatic and non-metastatic tumors, then tested function in cells and mice.

B cells crowded non-metastatic tumors and built complete tertiary lymphoid structures absent in metastatic disease. In lab and humanized mouse tests, these B cells and their secretions curbed growth, migration, and transition programs while triggering cell death, and removing B cells sped progression. Two signals, IL-12 and CXCL13, drove the defense, supporting B cell and lymphoid-structure immunotherapy designs.
pmc-13444644:
Junda Huang and colleagues describe an artificial intelligence aided blood test that hunts for hidden monoclonal proteins, early signs of a bone marrow disorder, in a 2026 report. The usual lab methods work slowly and miss the scale needed for wide screening, so many cases surface late, after harm is done. Their platform pairs mass spectrometry with machine learning to flag weak signals on its own.

After training on more than five thousand stored blood samples, the system screened over twelve thousand adult patients in real hospital use. It found the marker proteins in about seven in every hundred patients, rising past one in ten among those aged fifty or more. Many positive cases were new, which points to a large pool of unseen risk that routine checks could catch.
pmc-13445744:
Hao Dong and coauthors develop a 2026 multi-site model for calling lung-lining pleural spread before surgery in stage T1 spreading lung adenocarcinoma, a call that shapes removal and lymph node plans. The team pulled CT and medical data from 316 patients across three centers, splitting two centers into training and test sets and holding the third as an outside test.

The tumor-inner scan-pattern model beat tumor-edge, joint, and medical models, with sorting power near 0.82 to 0.84 across all three sets. Openness analysis ranked the model's key texture traits. Surgeons gain a proven pre-surgery aid, though future use must confirm the model guides better surgeries, not just better guesses.
pmc-13446344:
Hannah van Kolfschooten and colleagues caution that the European Union's Safe Hearts Plan leans too hard on artificial intelligence to fix heart care, in a 2026 viewpoint. The plan, launched in late 2025, is the bloc's first full strategy for its top killer, and it casts AI as a prime tool for prevention, diagnosis, and care. The authors test that bet against law and practice.

A gap yawns, they argue, between what models can predict and what clinics can deliver, held open by weak readiness in systems, staff, and rules. Murk around liability and patient rights adds drag. Their close is that AI must sit inside strong legal and working frames, aimed at better outcomes rather than at sharper forecasts alone.
pmc-13447144:
Zhipeng Sun and colleagues test a 2026 image model for spotting very early lung adenocarcinoma on CT scans. Two early forms, one still in place and one barely invasive, can look like tiny nodules and are hard to catch. The team improved a standard detection model with added attention and multi-scale features meant to help with small targets.

Scans came from two hundred twenty-five confirmed lesions treated at one hospital in Fujian. Most images trained the model, while a held-out set from separate lesions tested it fairly. The improved version kept strong overall accuracy and did better under the strictest test of exact location. Separate removal tests showed the gains came from combining the new parts, suggesting a useful aid for early detection work.
pmc-13447544:
Wang and co-authors weighed three ways of finding bone marrow spread in 122 mantle cell lymphoma patients. The ways were PET/CT scanning, flow cytometry of marrow samples, and the standard marrow biopsy. Knowing marrow status matters. Most patients present at late stage, and the result shapes prognosis talks.

Against biopsy, PET/CT managed sensitivity of only 57.4 percent and specificity of 55.9 percent in this retrospective series. That is barely better than chance. Flow cytometry performed far better once a lymphoma cell share above 5.925 percent counted as positive. It reached sensitivity of 90.7 percent and a negative predictive value of 91.4 percent in the same patients. Age and a prognostic score of six or more forecast both progression-free and overall survival. Certain cell shapes did too, in multivariable analysis. A lymphoma cell share of at least 30 percent predicted earlier progression on its own.
pmc-13447844:
Zhichen Xiong and colleagues show that tiny molecular tweaks program where protocell droplets float in 2026 origin-of-life work. Early Earth oceans may have hosted simple droplets that needed to sort into layers, meet and exchange molecules to grow complex. Scarcity of ingredients makes such organisation hard, so small structural differences must do heavy lifting in any plausible account.

Droplets formed from simple fat-like molecules rose or sank depending on isomer shape, chain length and partner ion. Concentration and temperature could move droplets after forming, driving collisions and fusions that mix contents and create new substances. Internal study showed a sponge-like build of hydrated flexible layers, with buoyancy set by layer thickness ratios. Layered positioning could grant access to light or chemistry at different depths, the authors suggest.
pmc-13448344:
Siobhan Darlington and colleagues test a 2026 ecology study of how neighboring cougars divide food in a multi-prey landscape in British Columbia's southern interior. Analyzing 875 kill sites from 27 females and 11 males plus prey data from 146 cameras, the team tested whether diet similarity tracks sex, season, prey availability, and home range overlap.

Males killed larger prey like moose and elk while females killed more deer, with deer species differing where large prey ran scarce. Female pairs supported resource partitioning while male-female pairs supported competition, and diets diverged most in summer when ranges expanded. The work shows how sex, season, and overlap jointly shape predator diets.
pmc-13448544:
Abdulrahman Alanazi and Basmah Alanazi report depression linked to oral semaglutide in a patient with type 2 diabetes in a 2026 case study. The daily diabetes pill belongs to a drug family whose brain effects remain under watch, with scattered reports of low mood despite reassuring trial averages. A dose-linked pattern with deliberate retesting had not been described for the oral form before this case.

A fifty-four-year-old man with no psychiatric history developed moderately severe depression within two weeks of stepping his dose up. A two-drug antidepressant combination brought remission within four weeks. When the diabetes dose was raised again under a structured rechallenge, depression returned at similar severity, then settled for good after permanent discontinuation. A standard causality score rated the link probable, and mood checks during dose escalation are advised.
pmc-13448644:
Wengang Kang and co-authors reconstruct a thousand years of change in a Tibetan lake ecosystem in 2026 work joining sediment records with Earth system models. Tibetan lakes are shifting fast under warming, yet telling outside forcing apart from natural internal swings over long spans is hard. Diatoms, tiny algae preserved in lake mud, record past water conditions in fine detail.

Two response pathways emerged across the millennium. In one, volcanic cooling and internal variability governed early conditions until recent forced warming shortened ice cover and raised meltwater inflow, triggering diatom shifts without precedent in the record. In the other, salt-tolerant diatoms tracked monsoon-driven freshening governed by tropical rain belt movement. Modern aerosol swings and meltwater now override older drivers, and continued divergence from the natural range is expected.
pmc-13449444:
Xiaomin Wen and colleagues publish in 2026 a step-by-step protocol for collecting tiny communication vesicles from mouse astrocytes primed with a growth factor. Astrocytes, the brain's support cells, release extracellular vesicles loaded with proteins and RNA that talk to neurons. Priming them with fibroblast growth factor-2 pushes the cells toward a protective state, and their vesicles shield dopamine neurons from mitochondrial damage in Parkinson disease models.

The protocol walks through culturing primary astrocytes, priming them, and spinning the vesicles down by stepped ultracentrifugation. Check steps follow in detail: electron microscopy for shape, nanoparticle tracking for size counts, western blotting for marker proteins, and mass spectrometry for full protein cargo. The authors note these sacs also support synapse formation in those models. They intend the method to standardize a possible cell-free therapy for Parkinson disease work.
pmc-13449844:
Molla Amsalu Tadesse and colleagues reviewed prior reviews of prehabilitation before bowel surgery in a 2026 umbrella review. Colorectal surgery carries risks of complications and death, and preparing patients beforehand with exercise, nutrition, or other support might improve recovery. Single reviews had varied in scope, so a review of reviews was needed.

The team searched major databases for systematic reviews comparing prehabilitation with usual care on complications, hospital stay, and functional capacity. Nineteen reviews covering 27,065 participants were included, most rated high quality, with only slight overlap of primary studies overall. Quality was graded with standard tools and bias checks were run. Surgical teams gain a consolidated verdict on whether prehabilitation earns its place in bowel surgery pathways.
pmc-13450544:
Sara Mubarak and co-authors describe a 2026 case where blisters and patchy skin color gave away a body-wide protein disease. The illness, AL amyloidosis, lays down clumps of faulty protein that can harm many organs. Their patient was a woman aged 68 with a year of painless blisters on both legs.

Her legs also showed mixed dark and pale patches, blood-flecked crusts, and scratch marks. The authors say color change of this kind has not been tied to the disease in print before. The case warns clinics that odd skin signs can be the first clue to a hidden protein disorder that needs a full body check.
pmc-13450944:
Nanti E. Adoukonou and others put out a 2026 fix to their work on patients who shift from belly dialysis to blood dialysis. The first paper, in Kidney360 in 2025, gave risks of shift by cause, but slips had crept into the notes for Figures 4 to 6. The fix swaps two cause tags that had been mixed up.

Figure 4, first tagged for mind and social causes, is now tagged for infections. Figure 5, first tagged for infections, is now tagged for mind and social causes. The model tweaks stay the same in each. The fix puts each risk score back with its true cause, so readers do not read the wrong cause from the charts. It is a tag fix only; the core models and their tweaks stand as first put out.
pmc-13451344:
Saxler and colleagues test how physical activity relates to the health of white matter, the brain wiring that links regions, in a large population study from Bonn, Germany. Their 2026 analysis covers 4,188 adults in the Rhineland Study. Participants wore a small motion sensor to record real activity, rather than recalling it. Brain scans gave several measures of white matter quality for the whole brain and for 27 tracts.

More energy spent on activity tied to one marker of fiber spread, with gains that leveled off at high activity. In motor tracts, activity linked to lower fiber density in younger adults. Yet with rising age, activity tied more strongly to higher density and freer water flow in upper brain fibers. Body weight, heart and metabolic health, and inflammation partly carried the effects. The authors say gains look largest for people who sit most and for older adults.
pmc-13451544:
Debora Iapadre and others took stock of flip-catalyst work in 2026, where one reaction can be steered to either mirror form of a product. Mirror forms can act quite unlike each other in the body, so a flip switch is prized in drug and chem making. The short review picks fresh, high-mark cases that use plain, non-chiral cues.

Four flip routes are weighed: a change of solvent, a plain reagent or add-in, and a tiny tweak to the catalyst, with how each flip works laid out case by case. Other flip routes get a brief note. Chemists gain a compact guide to make both mirror forms from one set-up, with no need to swap the catalyst's own chirality.
pmc-13451944:
Muhammad Bilal Jamshaid and co-authors describe in 2026 a thyroid cancer that announced itself through starving fingers and toes. Their patient, a woman aged 37, had four years of color swings in her middle fingers and outer toes, a Raynaud-like pattern. Her feet were cold, toe ulcers had formed, and foot pulses ran weak.

Drug after drug failed, and two right toes turned gangrenous. A full-body scan found no vessel swelling yet lit up a small lump in her right thyroid. A needle test pointed to papillary thyroid cancer, and removing the gland settled the vessel syndrome fully, a first for this cancer kind. The case links stubborn limb vessel trouble to hidden tumors.
pmc-13452144:
Jordi Tortosa-Carreres and co-authors sift in 2026 why two urine blood tests clash on the same sample in clinic analyzers. One test is a dipstick, the other a cell counter, and gaps between them can stall care. The team drew 3,399 urine samples from distinct primary care patients run on one analyzer family.

A ratio of small red cells to all red cells tied most strongly to the clash, with a second ratio for burst cells pulling the other way. Dirt in the sample and urine acidity also raised clash odds, while germ and white cell counts lowered them. The authors say the clash follows a set pattern that labs can flag in advance.
pmc-13452244:
Guang Zhu and co-authors trace in 2026 a three-part chain that lets cervical cancer burn sugar fast and spread. The chain starts with NQO1, a redox guard found high in these tumors. The team showed NQO1 calms a fuel sensor, cuts cell rust, and shields a low-oxygen switch from the cell's shredder.

That shielded switch then turns up a third player, SIX1, which boosts sugar-burning genes and a shape shift that helps cancer move. Cutting any of the three parts in turn slowed sugar flow, tumor growth, and spread in mice. The authors name the whole chain as a drug target for a cancer that still kills heavily.
pmc-13452844:
Asfour and team built the GRAFT score, a bedside tool predicting skin graft failure after skin cancer excision, from 162 patients treated at a single center. They screened candidate variables with regression, kept the independent predictors, and validated the model internally by bootstrapping before assigning risk groups.

Only two factors survived multivariable modeling: blood-thinning anticoagulation, with an odds ratio of 6.40 for graft failure, and grafts placed on the lower body, with an odds ratio of 3.19 in the cohort. The resulting score discriminated acceptably, with an area under the curve of 0.72, and calibration testing showed no lack of fit at a p-value of 0.87 overall. Observed failure rates separated cleanly across its tiers: 7.5 percent in the low-risk group, 26.0 percent at intermediate risk, and 60.0 percent in the high-risk group. The authors recommend external validation next.
pmc-13454044:
Richard E Brown traces how two Spanish pioneers shaped Donald O Hebb's theory of how the brain organizes behavior. Hebb, born in Nova Scotia in 1904, built his ideas across posts in Montreal, Chicago, Harvard, and Florida. His 1949 book put forward synaptic change, cell assemblies, and phase sequences as the machinery of thought. Brown's 2026 paper reads Hebb's unpublished notes and drafts from 1932 to 1947.

The key borrowed piece, Brown shows, is the reverberatory circuit: loops of neurons that keep firing after a stimulus ends. That notion came from Rafael Lorente de Nó, who built on Santiago Ramón y Cajal's idea of closed circuits. Hebb folded the loop into his theory of assemblies that fire in sequence. The paper follows how that lineage later fed psychology, neuroscience, and computer models of the brain.
pmc-13454444:
Xichang Lin and seven colleagues describe, in 2026, a bubble trick that keeps a chemical electrode clean during heavy use. Making green hydrogen wastes energy on oxygen release, so chemists seek partner reactions that yield useful products instead. Their test reaction turns benzylamine into benzonitrile, a valuable chemical, but the product coats the electrode and poisons it.

The team deliberately allowed some oxygen release at the surface. Rising bubbles swept the oily product away before it could stick. A prototype device ran at high current for over 40 hours, with about 55 percent of the charge going to the target reaction. Output stayed steady where a bubble-free setup would foul. The authors argue that pairing product-making reactions with self-cleaning bubbles could suit large-scale hydrogen plants that also want chemical co-products.
pmc-13454844:
Black and colleagues map how the parasite Leishmania responds to replication stress in this 2026 genome-wide study. When DNA copying stalls, exposed single-stranded DNA can destabilize the genome, and Leishmania's flexible genome generates such stress naturally. Almost nothing was known about its stress response, so the team tracked two marker proteins, gammaH2A and RPA1, across the genome with and without induced stress.

Stress hotspots coincided with places where DNA replication begins and where transcription ends, the reading of genes in long multi-gene stretches. When copying stalled, response factors gathered at early replication origins in patterns suggesting forks moving outward in both directions. Under chronic stress, factors also spread to wider gene-start regions, suggesting backup strategies. Removing the ATR kinase changed RPA behavior, revealing its role in juggling transcription and replication.
pmc-13455344:
Xiaoyan Zhang and colleagues decode the genome of a dry-land plant prized for surviving extreme drought in a 2026 study. Cynanchum thesioides grows where water is scarce, yet the genes behind that toughness and its exact place in plant family trees stayed unclear. The team built a chromosome-level genome of 242 million bases and compared it with relatives, pairing gene counts with gene activity data.

Family tree work placed the plant in the Apocynaceae family, close to two relatives, while gene families tied to protective plant chemicals were larger than in other Gentianales species. Genes for lignin, the stiffening material in plant walls, also shifted in activity, with key families clustered on chromosomes 3 and 9. Breeders and plant scientists gain candidate genes for drought tolerance and a firmer taxonomic home for a useful dry-land resource.
pmc-13455644:
Juan Jin and nine colleagues use, in a 2026 genetics study, a natural experiment method to ask whether an age-linked blood condition truly causes cancer. The condition, clonal hematopoiesis, arises when one mutated blood stem cell outgrows its peers, stirring inflammation. Using gene variants as stand-ins, the team tested links with 18 cancers covering 612,576 cases in large databases.

Genetic liability to the condition tracked with higher risk of thyroid, lung, kidney, and brain cancers, plus two skin cancers. The signal held under strict correction for many tests. A subtype driven by one gene, DNMT3A, showed the same pattern. Effects also varied by cancer subtype within organs. Sensitivity checks supported the readings. Because the method mimics a lifelong randomized exposure, the authors argue the link is likely causal, and they urge timely screening for the blood condition in cancer prevention plans.
pmc-13457644:
Mengdie Chen and seven colleagues published this 2026 case report and literature review on severe pneumonia caused by Chlamydia psittaci, a bacterium caught from birds that causes psittacosis. Their patient was one man, aged 50, whose severe lung infection was complicated by deep vein thrombosis, a dangerous blood clot. The infection is uncommon and hard to diagnose, so the authors also gathered published severe cases to draw lessons for clinicians.

Polymerase chain reaction testing confirmed the diagnosis in their patient, and he recovered on the antibiotic omadacycline. The review portion analysed 55 cases of severe disease, summarising causes, symptoms, diagnostic routes and treatments. Bird contact through inhaled dust from feathers or droppings is the usual exposure route, the authors note. Symptoms start non-specifically with high fever and cough, which delays recognition. Without standardised treatment, severe psittacosis can kill 10 to 20 percent of patients, a figure the authors cite to urge earlier testing.
pmc-13458244:
Merrill and colleagues read in 2026 the charts of 89 kids who got new kidneys at one US hub, to find what makes a graft wake late. A late wake, called DGF, means wash care in the first week, and it dims the graft's long odds. Adult rules blame warm and cold spans with no blood flow. The team weighed those spans, donor kind, and pump rides, where a machine feeds the graft on its trip. Four years of grafts fed the count.

One in ten grafts woke late. Warm span stood out: the late set ran twelve minutes more at the mid mark. Dead donor grafts ran near twice the risk of live ones. Cold span showed no clear split, a break from adult rules. No pump ride graft woke late at all. The team backs pump rides for kid grafts, and war on warm span.
pmc-13458844:
Ahmed Onayzan Alshammari and colleagues pool the head-to-head evidence between a surgeon's bone and factory-made substitutes. Autograft remains the gold standard for coaxing vertebrae to fuse, but harvesting it wounds a second site and supply is limited. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis follows PRISMA methods, grades certainty with GRADE, and screens the literature to nine studies comparing autograft with ceramics, i-Factor, demineralized bone matrix, and bioactive glass.

Fusion rates tied, with an odds ratio of 1.24 and a confidence interval crossing one. A clinical success measure favored synthetics, at an odds ratio of 1.78, while reoperation and complication rates matched. Blood loss leaned toward synthetics without significance, and the analysis detected publication bias. The verdict stays humble: synthetics look like a reliable alternative sparing donor-site pain, but certainty is low, the recommendation weak, and longer trials are needed before the gold standard steps aside.
pmc-13459344:
Yina Cao and co-authors tested a service learning program that sent dental students to teach oral health to children with autism spectrum disorder. Service learning blends community service with coursework, and children on the spectrum often miss out on dental guidance adapted to them. Their 2026 study enrolled 102 fourth year dental students in a six module program spanning theory, field investigation, data analysis, and delivering health education. It measured knowledge, confidence, and professional attitudes before and after.

Students improved across the board. Correct understanding of a standard gum probing index jumped from 65.7 percent to 92.9 percent after the program, a significant gain. Their self rated understanding of autistic children's oral hygiene rose sharply as well, from about 32 to about 44 on the scale used. Attitude and willingness scores also improved in the analysis. The authors present service learning as a practical route to dentists who are competent and comfortable treating vulnerable children.
pmc-13459444:
Poonam Vinayamohan and co-authors tested in 2026 whether plant-derived compounds can slow the spread of antibiotic resistance genes between poultry bacteria. Resistance genes pass from one bacterium to another through conjugation, a direct cell-to-cell transfer. The study followed one such gene moving from Salmonella Heidelberg, a poultry pathogen resistant to many drugs, into ordinary Escherichia coli, across broth, chicken manure, and water.

Four plant chemicals were tried. Carvacrol and beta-resorcylic acid cut gene transfer in broth and manure, while carvacrol and caprylic acid worked in water. Feed carrying one compound also reduced transfer inside chicken gut tissue tested outside the body. Treated Salmonella dialed down its transfer genes. Larger live-bird studies are still needed.
pmc-13461544:
Albertema and colleagues compared in 2026 two nurse-led bladder training plans for kidney transplant patients at a Dutch academic hospital. Good bladder function matters for graft success, but training guidance is thin. The older plan set hourly urination with regular checks of leftover urine. The newer plan, used from 2022, tailored timing to each patient's urine output before surgery. The study covered 211 patients across the two periods.

Albertema found no differences between the plans on the main outcomes: leftover urine above the threshold, urinary infection, or needing a catheter again within three months. One interaction stood out: older patients faced higher re-catheter risk under the new plan than under the old. The authors note the tailored plan may still aid patient comfort and ease nurse workload, even without outcome gains, but the age signal deserves care in practice.
pmc-13461644:
Tom Macleod and co-authors compare skin and blood markers between psoriasis patients with and without psoriatic arthritis, hunting for signs that predict joint disease. Their 2026 study focuses on neutrophil elastase, an enzyme that damages tissue, and elafin, the inhibitor that restrains it and a known skin marker in psoriasis.

Matched skin and serum samples were analysed from patients with skin-only psoriasis, patients with joint involvement, and healthy controls, with validation in independent arthritis groups. The balance between elastase and elafin differed significantly between the patient groups, with elafin expression reduced in psoriatic arthritis samples. The ratio of elastase to a second inhibitor was also raised in joint disease compared with skin-only disease, healthy controls, and other arthritides. The authors conclude that patients who develop joint disease have a reduced capacity to regulate neutrophil enzymes in both skin and blood.
pmc-13461844:
Ying Wang leads a 2026 comparison of two first treatments for chronic myeloid leukemia in China, a blood cancer driven by a gene fusion. No trial has tested the two drugs, asciminib and flumatinib, against each other. Asciminib blocks the protein at a novel pocket, while flumatinib is a second-generation blocker sold only in China. The team compared them indirectly through a rival, imatinib, used in both source trials.

Patient-level data from one trial were reweighted to match the other trial's patient mix, a method called matching-adjusted indirect comparison.
