pmc-13479344:
Catherine R. Drury and coauthors published a 2026 study of unfair gaps in eating disorder care across social groups. Shut-out groups face higher eating disorder risk and steeper barriers to care, yet clinic samples are rarely read across group lines at once. The sample held 3,016 adult women treated at partner United States sites for varied forms of the illness.

Patients filled in a standard eating disorder survey at intake and discharge. Race, ethnic group, and sexual orientation came from the patients themselves, while area poverty stood in for social and money status. Layered models tested how illness depth at entry and gains by discharge varied across combined groups. The authors look for stacked disadvantage that one-factor checks would hide, with the goal of showing treatment programs exactly where results lag.
pmc-13479444:
Simara Larissa Fanalli and coauthors published a 2026 pig feeding study using gene co-expression analysis to find the regulatory networks behind fat deposition in muscle. Fatty acid composition in pork matters for meat quality and human nutrition, yet the gene control layer is tangled. Pigs received diets with either 1.5 or 3.0 percent soybean oil across a 98-day growth and finishing period.

Muscle RNA was sequenced and grouped into co-expressed gene modules, which were then tied to measured fatty acid profiles. This network approach highlights hub genes and transcription pathways that may steer how dietary fat becomes tissue fat. The authors aim to give breeders and nutritionists molecular targets for producing pork with a healthier fatty acid balance.
pmc-13479544:
Edward Coote, Nitesh Patel, and Rajesh Vijayanarayanan present a 2026 cost-effectiveness model asking whether treating gum disease could pay for itself by preventing strokes and heart attacks in the United Kingdom. Gum disease is common and tied to higher cardiovascular risk. Their Markov model followed 65-year-olds with severe gum disease and no prior cardiovascular events.

Non-surgical gum treatment effects were taken from large international cohort studies, suggesting sizeable relative risk reductions. Over a 25-year horizon, treatment added about 9,755 euros in costs and about half a quality-adjusted life year per patient in the model. Sensitivity analyses varied the assumptions and calculated how large the protective effect must be to meet national value thresholds. The authors frame dental care as a candidate cardiovascular prevention investment for the health service.
pmc-13479944:
Paris and colleagues gave the eHealth Literacy Questionnaire to French patients with chronic kidney disease in 2026, the first test of the tool in this group. The questionnaire measures how confidently people find, judge, and use health information online, a skill that shapes access to transplant waiting lists. They recruited 371 patients between January and March 2023, who also completed three other questionnaires on literacy and daily independence.

The standard structure of the tool did not fit these patients, and a four-factor split described their answers most meaningfully in the analysis. Each of the four scales held together reliably, and scores peaked on the scale called feel safe and in control in the patient group. Scores bottomed out on using technology to process health information, leading the authors to recommend reshaping the questionnaire before using it to design digital services for kidney patients.
pmc-13480044:
Xiaopeng Sun and colleagues offer a 2026 pooled review of vitamin D and low thyroid function. The team searched four databases through February 2024 and kept five drug trials and eleven watch-style studies, with 4,152 people in all. They weighed hormone and antibody levels and judged how firm the proof was with a standard grading tool.

People given vitamin D showed clear drops in thyroid-stimulating hormone and in a key thyroid antibody tied to immune attack on the gland. Low vitamin D in blood also linked to higher odds of having low thyroid function in the first place. The authors advise routine checks of vitamin D in these patients. Gaps remain, since trial counts were small and results varied across studies, so larger trials would sharpen the picture.
pmc-13480244:
Jian Xu and colleagues describe a 2026 technique for reopening fully blocked lung arteries by coming at the clot from behind. Two women with chronic clot-based lung hypertension had segment branches sealed shut, a pattern that defeats standard balloon work from the front. One was aged thirty, the other sixty-three.

In the first case a wire slipped through tiny links between neighbouring branches and crossed the block from the far side, letting a balloon open the vessel. In the second case the backward wire could not re-enter the main trunk, so it stayed as a guide mark while a front wire crossed with its help. Both procedures succeeded with no complications. Side links inside the lung can serve as a back door when the front route fails, the team concludes.
pmc-13483444:
Kripa and Jeyalakshmi built a grading system for mangoes whose skin barely changes color as they ripen, defeating human sorters. Their 2026 study targeted a Thai variety that stays yellow from unripe to ripe. The system fuses camera images with internal chemistry readings, such as sugar content and acidity, inside one deep-learning model. A swarm-based tuner then adjusted the model's settings.

The fused system sorted mangoes into maturity stages with about 98 percent accuracy on its held-out test share. That beat the image-only and single-network baselines the authors evaluated alongside it. Three different image networks contributed visual features, while a small dedicated network encoded the chemistry values. Kripa notes the approach is non-destructive, since fruit is graded without being cut open, but the chemistry inputs still require sampling from each batch.
pmc-13483844:
Renu Chane reviews pinocembrin, a honey and propolis compound gaining attention as a multi-target cancer candidate. Published in 2026, the survey covers the chemistry of this dihydroxyflavanone and its actions across breast, prostate, colon, lung, ovarian, and skin cancer models. Several major growth and inflammation pathways are modulated at once by the compound.

Laboratory evidence shows halted cell division, triggered cell death through two routes, reduced blood vessel growth, and blocked tissue invasion programs. Chemical tweaks such as added hydroxyl groups or sugar attachments improved potency or availability in structure studies. Poor water solubility and fast clearance remain the main obstacles, now being tackled with micelles, liposomes, and nanoparticle carriers. Pairing with standard chemotherapy showed synergy alongside low harm to normal cells in early work.
pmc-13485144:
Emily M. Eshleman and others examine tuft cells, rare sensor cells in the gut lining, and their role in swelling bowel disease. In 2026, the study finds fewer tuft cells in the lower intestine of children with the disease and greater vulnerability to gut swelling in mice lacking them. A controller protein called HDAC3 proves vital for forming tuft cells from intestinal stem cells.

Removing HDAC3 only from mature tuft cells left their numbers unchanged yet still worsened colitis, because repair signals and characteristic tuft cell pathways weakened. Blocking HDAC3 in human colon organoids also lowered repair-related signals. The authors propose that strengthening tuft cell function could help prevent or treat bowel swelling, with HDAC3 as a key internal control.
pmc-13487144:
Feng and team subjected red mud, the caustic waste left from alumina refining, to repeated wetting and drying to see how stockpile material weathers. Red mud piles sit outdoors for years, and rain cycles can change their strength and slope safety. Their 2026 study ran two red mud types through up to twelve drying-wetting cycles, measured strength and microscopic change, then simulated pile stability under extreme rainfall.

The two muds moved in opposite directions: one type weakened steadily, while the mixed type grew markedly stronger with cycling. The mixed mud's compressive strength rose from about 116 to about 150 kilopascals, and its cohesion roughly doubled across the cycles tested. Simulated slope safety factors stayed above the critical threshold and rose slightly with cycling under extreme rain. Feng says mineral makeup explains the split, so each stockpile needs its own weathering assessment.
pmc-13487344:
Sreevidhya Palakkot and Arun Banik review hearing tests as early flags for brain decline. In their 2026 review, hearing loss tends to come before motion and thought signs in many brain diseases. The set spans Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, frontotemporal dementia, and ALS. Harm shows in both the ear and the brain's sound hubs, in shapes that vary by disease.

Hard tests include brainstem sound waves, focus-linked brain waves, and speech-in-noise checks. Such tests are cheap, safe, and close in sharpness to set blood or fluid marks. Self-rated hearing and test scores part ways in ways worth tracking over time. A set hearing test pack in brain clinics could flag disease years early. It could also help split look-alike dementias that baffle staff today.
pmc-13488044:
Mohamed Bouallou and co-authors report an unusual jaw tumor case in a 2026 paper. A 17-year-old girl had a painless swelling beside the nose that kept growing. Plasmacytoma in the upper jaw is very rare at her age.

Scans showed a large lesion with a mixed pattern of bone loss and hardening, plus mineral deposits inside. Lab tests confirmed a single-clone plasma cell tumor, and checks ruled out multiple myeloma. She received radiotherapy and reached complete remission. No return was seen at 21 months. The authors stress matching scan and lab findings to avoid misreading such cases as more aggressive tumors.
pmc-13488144:
Daiki Yamashige and colleagues, with the Japan Oncology Network in Hepatobiliary and Pancreas, set out a 2026 trial protocol called STARDOM. Patients with operable or borderline pancreatic cancer often need a stent to drain a blocked bile duct during chemotherapy before surgery. Standard wide metal stents last well yet can trigger gallbladder or pancreas inflammation, while plastic stents are gentler but clog sooner.

The trial will enroll 330 adults at eighty-nine Japanese centers and assign them at random to a wide metal stent, a narrow six-millimeter metal stent, or a plastic stent. The main measure is freedom from stent-related problems at twelve weeks. No results are reported, since enrollment and follow-up define the work ahead.
pmc-13488244:
Kui Zhao and colleagues review how a DNA-sensing immune pathway talks with energy metabolism inside tumors in a 2026 article. The pathway, called STING, detects stray DNA inside cells and switches on interferon and inflammatory signals that can attack cancer. Tumors also rewire how they burn sugar, oxygen, fats, and the amino acid glutamine, and the review traces traffic in both directions between those fuel systems and STING signaling.

Metabolic stress can wake or mute STING, while STING activity reshapes fuel use and the immune mix around a tumor in the patterns the authors assemble. That two-way link makes paired targets attractive, where a metabolism drug and an immune drug strike the same neighborhood. The authors lay out combination ideas for testing.
pmc-13490544:
Liping Wang and others ask whether entering entrepreneurship competitions improves Chinese college students' employability. In 2026, the study studies survey data from 3,595 students in Sichuan Province, using likelihood-score matching to compare people with similar non-participants. Employability is measured as students' own perception of their job prospects amid a crowded graduate market.

Participation clearly raised perceived employability, with larger effects for women and smaller effects at higher-ranked schools. The authors recommend that universities actively guide students into competitions, build quality platforms, and tailor support by student group. Policymakers and educators get quantitative evidence for a popular but earlier unproven extracurricular plan.
pmc-13491344:
Sean P. Lyden and colleagues report three-year results for a through-the-wall bypass system in long leg artery blockages in a 2026 final trial report. The DETOUR system routes a covered stent through the neighboring vein to bypass diseased femoral-popliteal segments longer than twenty centimeters, a percutaneous alternative to open bypass. The single-arm international trial enrolled 202 patients with severe leg artery disease at thirty-two sites, and 200 received the system.

Average treated length topped thirty-two centimeters. The bypass stayed open without assistance in about fifty-eight percent of patients at three years in the reported results, while freedom from repeat procedures and major limb events sat in the mid-sixties. Vein clots occurred in about four percent, with no lung clots reported.
pmc-13491744:
Corentin Fouéré leads a ten-author team investigating in 2026 how DNA methylation, a chemical mark on DNA, shapes where new mutations appear in cattle genomes. Brand-new mutations are rare, only a few dozen per generation, yet they seed all genetic variation. The researchers tracked mutations accumulating across generations in Holstein and Montbéliarde families and also mined rare variants in a large sequenced Holstein panel.

One change stood out: cytosine turning into thymine at CpG sites, the spots where methylation commonly sits. That enrichment was strongest where CpG sites are sparse, and it grew with local methylation levels in sperm, eggs, and body tissues alike. Mobile DNA elements called SINEs and LINEs, especially young ones, also mutated faster than the genome at large. The findings mirror patterns known from other mammals.
pmc-13491944:
Kaibo Hu and five colleagues ask in 2026 whether the ratio of fat to muscle predicts future coronary artery disease better than weight alone. Body scans from 398,435 UK Biobank volunteers free of heart disease, diabetes, and cholesterol treatment at entry supplied total and regional ratios. Over a median follow-up beyond twelve years, 10,740 participants developed coronary disease.

Higher ratios everywhere meant higher risk in both sexes, yet the leg ratio stood alone after mutual adjustment, remaining a strong predictor in women and men while trunk and arm ratios faded. Blood metabolite patterns explained over seventy percent of the statistical link, suggesting body composition works largely through metabolism. Adding leg ratio to standard risk factors measurably improved classification, especially for women.
pmc-13493044:
Stephanie J Lax leads a long author list counting in 2026 how many people in England live with Takayasu arteritis, a rare inflammation that scars the aorta and its great branches. Drawing on national hospital records from 2006 to 2023, the RECORDER team produced the largest European estimates yet for this disease. Case-finding methods were checked against specialist cohorts.

About 1,285 people were living with the condition in mid-2022, a prevalence near twenty-three per million, with more than seventy new diagnoses in a typical year. Incidence held steady across the period except for a thirty percent dip during the first pandemic years, likely reflecting missed or delayed care. Women and people of Asian or other minority ethnic backgrounds were affected disproportionately, and the median age at diagnosis was fifty-three.
pmc-13493744:
Pablo Balado-Simó and four colleagues survey in 2026 the shifting treatment landscape for melanoma in children. The cancer makes up only one to four percent of melanoma cases, yet it behaves unlike its adult counterpart. Three subtypes dominate childhood: spitzoid tumors, melanomas growing inside large birthmarks, and conventional melanoma. Surgery remains the backbone, and most drug treatment is borrowed off-label from adult practice.

Immune checkpoint drugs and targeted BRAF and MEK combinations are being adapted, with scattered prospective and retrospective outcome data. Trials in progress test engineered CAR T cells, natural killer cell infusions, blockers of the Wnt signaling pathway, and cancer vaccines. Rarity starves the field of pediatric-specific dosing and long-term safety evidence, and the authors call for molecular profiling, dedicated trials, and attention to children's developmental and emotional needs.
pmc-13494044:
Yuhan Wang and co-authors report a 2026 study of Jingling Granules, a herbal formula used in Chinese medicine, and its effect on atherosclerosis, the build-up of fatty plaques in artery walls. The team asked whether the granules slow plaque growth by raising autophagy, the cell process that clears worn parts, and by cutting cell death in the vessel lining. Their focus was the mTOR pathway, a switch that controls both processes.

In mice fed a high-fat diet, the granules improved blood lipids, shrank plaque, and lowered inflammation. Treated vessel cells also cleared waste better and died less often. When a drug that turns mTOR back on was added in cell tests, those gains vanished, which supports the idea that the formula works by blocking that switch. The authors see promise for early disease, though the work stays at the animal and cell stage.
pmc-13494544:
Hu and colleagues present NexusGene, a computational framework for picking out the genes that drive cancer from messy biological networks. Gene networks are noisy and differ wildly between patients, so prediction tools miss real drivers and flag false ones. Their 2026 method first cleans the network itself, weighing each connection by how uncertain the underlying data are. It then runs several prediction models whose results are merged with help from clustering, grouping genes by their distribution patterns before combining votes.

Benchmarked against six current methods across seven combined cancer networks and thirty-one single-cancer networks, NexusGene came out best overall. Its advantage grew largest exactly where networks were most heterogeneous, the setting that defeats simpler tools. The authors frame the system as both stronger and more interpretable, since the uncertainty scores show which parts of a network the predictions rest on.
pmc-13495144:
Caner İşevi and colleagues report a 2026 study of thoracolithiasis, a rare, harmless condition in which a loose stone-like body sits in the chest cavity around the lung. Most known cases move freely and harden with calcium, yet data on fixed forms stayed scarce. The team reviewed twenty confirmed cases from a Turkish chest surgery center spanning 2010 to 2024, and set them beside a review of past reports.

None of the twenty stones moved, and most lacked calcium, which can make them look like cancer on scans. Two in five patients also had lung cancer, and three in ten had the stones alone. Hardened stones sat in older patients, while the lone form showed up more in women who did not smoke, and all lone cases led to exploratory surgery. The authors sort the condition into two patterns and warn that fixed, soft stones are easy to mistake for malignancy.
pmc-13495244:
Félix Alain leads a 2026 interview study of how health officials and community leaders in Madagascar view faith and cultural blocks to measles vaccination. Measles still kills many infants there, and outbreaks recur despite mass campaigns, most recently in late 2024. The study sat inside a national review of that campaign across all twenty-three regions.

Stakeholders blamed deep faith and custom most. Some evangelical and Pentecostal teaching rejects vaccines outright, holding that divine healing makes them needless meddling. Many caregivers also mistake vaccines for cures for the sick rather than shields for the healthy, and doubt that modern medicine lengthens life. Mistrust of institutions, fear of side effects, and low schooling add weight. A third of caregivers could not name one routine vaccine. The authors argue campaigns must answer beliefs, not just deliver doses.
pmc-13499744:
Jessica Baldwin and co-authors interview in 2026 caregivers of young children with mucopolysaccharidosis type II, also called Hunter syndrome, a rare inherited storage disorder that appears around ages two to four. Most children follow a severe course affecting the brain, with developmental decline across nearly all body systems. Sixteen caregivers in the United States and the United Kingdom described the symptoms and daily impacts that mattered most for children aged two to five.

Every caregiver reported cognitive decline and disruption to family life. Speech problems, trouble walking and climbing stairs, poor hand movement, hearing loss, and frequent infections were each reported by nearly all families, while frustration and stiff joints were also widespread. Communication, mobility, and joint and muscle problems ranked as most bothersome, and the authors note that enzyme therapy available since 2006 has not removed this heavy burden.
pmc-13499844:
Stephen J Freedland and colleagues survey in 2026 how United States physicians decide that returning prostate cancer counts as high risk when scans show no spread. The setting is biochemical recurrence, a rising PSA blood marker after curative treatment in cancer still sensitive to hormone therapy, where the high-risk label opens newer treatment options. Eighty-seven urologists and radiation oncologists shared their criteria and chart data for 460 patients diagnosed between April and November 2023.

Physicians weighed several factors together, led by how fast the PSA marker doubles, the size of its rise after treatment, and the tumour grade score. Doubling time was named most important by over half, with a typical threshold near six months in the reported medians. That cut-off is stricter than many guidelines suggest, which the authors flag as an education opportunity that could widen access to newer therapies.
pmc-13503744:
Lia Griaznova and three colleagues model how a Nipah virus protein may grip a human control protein, in a 2026 computer study. Nipah is a deadly virus that kills between 40 and 75 percent of those it infects. Its W protein is loose and shapeless, yet it latches onto 14-3-3 proteins that steer cell growth, death, and defense.

The team used a fold-prediction tool to build a thousand models of the paired complex, then kept nine that met two shape tests. Long motion simulations in a physics engine refined the set to three steady forms. One form stood out for shape and energy. The work shows the grip is plausible and gives a base for screening small drugs that might block it.
pmc-13505044:
Zijun Yan leads a team studying how mental load changes the way people with obsessive-compulsive disorder look at contamination images, in a 2026 study. Attention bias, a pull toward feared cues, helps keep OCD symptoms going. Working memory load may loosen the brain's grip on that pull.

Fifty-eight patients and 59 healthy peers did a memory task while their eyes were tracked over free viewing. Patients locked onto contamination images early and had trouble looking away midway through viewing. Load level changed the pattern: under heavier load, patients' trouble letting go began sooner and ran stronger. First-gaze direction differed by group alone. The authors read the results as a sign that limited mental control sustains threat focus in OCD.
pmc-13505144:
Masami Kashimura, Mirai So, and Yoichi Sekizawa examined how well the Japanese version of a self-report depression inventory performs in a large group. The questionnaire covers the nine symptom areas used to diagnose major depression. Their data came from an earlier Japanese trial of internet-based therapy, with 1,187 participants whose average age was about forty-three.

Factor analyses pointed to a single overall dimension behind the answers, and scores proved steady over a short retest gap. Agreement with other measures was partly confirmed, supporting the scale's meaning. The authors conclude that the Japanese inventory measures depressive symptoms soundly across all nine areas. Readers gain a checked tool for screening and follow-up in Japanese settings, where earlier checks had used far smaller groups.
pmc-13506544:
A team led by Mahendar Thudi reviews why crossing crops with their wild kin so often fails, and how breeders can get past those blocks. Wild kin hold gene variety that helps crops face pests, drought, and heat. Yet crosses between species often yield weak or sterile offspring.

Blocks arise before mating, when pollen fails on the flower, and after, when seeds or embryos die. The review maps the gene factors behind these blocks. It covers lab methods such as embryo rescue and cell fusion that bypass them. New gene tools may even let breeders switch the blocks on or off, making cross failure a trait they can control.
pmc-13506644:
Pedro Goes Nogueira-de-Sá, José Eduardo Pereira Wilken Bicudo, and José Guilherme Chaui-Berlinck build a 2026 model that compares energy waste in insect and mammal urine systems. Insects use Malpighian tubules, which make urine by secreting ions, while mammals filter blood in the kidney and then reabsorb most fluid. The model treats ion flow as electric current to estimate entropy, or wasted energy, per unit of urine.

Cases cover mosquito, stick insect, fruit fly, and locust systems, set against human, mouse, and cattle kidneys across a huge size range. Insect systems proved more economical, yet the gap stayed surprisingly small. Shared physical limits may shape how all such transport tissues can perform.
pmc-13507144:
Yue Wang, Kelvin Shum, Yuyang Song, and Tian Chen show, in 2026 work, that flat wafer methods can make free-standing curved 3D structures with set shapes. Standard chip making works flat, yet curved devices serve medicine, antennas, and curved electronics. Their trick uses tiny auxetic cells, patterns that widen when stretched, with two stable shapes.

Designers flatten the target curved mesh on paper, then tune each cell so its second stable state gives the local stretch that the curve needs. A spherical cap popped from a flat disk by indentation matched plans in tests and models. Paraboloid reflectors with tunable focus followed light rules well. Stable deployment needs no support frame.
pmc-13507744:
Jie Wan and five co-authors ask whether blood levels of vitamin B12 link to death risk in American adults with obesity, in 2026 work. They drew on a national health survey covering years from 1999 to 2014. The group included 8,301 adults with obesity, followed for a median of just over nine years. During that time 1,347 of them died. Models adjusted for age, sex, health factors, and other illnesses.

Risk did not fall in a straight line as B12 rose. People in the lowest groups and the highest group both faced higher death risk than those in the middle. A threshold near the middle of the range marked where the pattern flipped. The authors suggest keeping levels in a middle band and watching them over time, while noting that a survey study cannot prove cause.
pmc-13508244:
Zhenyu Tian and four co-authors follow people with fatty liver disease to see whether a combined blood index predicts later clusters of metabolic disease, in 2026 work. The index mixes inflammation, blood fats, and blood sugar into one number meant to capture insulin resistance. Variants add body size measures like weight, waist, or waist-to-height to that core. The study drew 109,181 UK Biobank participants who had fatty liver but no metabolic disease cluster at the start. They were followed for a median of 16 years.

In that time, 4,219 people developed a cluster of at least two conditions among diabetes, heart disease, and stroke. All four versions of the index pointed the same way: higher scores meant higher risk. Versions using waist size showed the strongest links. Adding the indices also sharpened prediction beyond standard factors. Extra analyses probed which body systems carry part of this link.
pmc-13508344:
Hanqiang Li and Xiangwen Ji study how feeling truly oneself shapes the pull of peer pressure and of fear of missing out in students online, in 2026 work. The survey covered 397 Chinese university students. It measured peer pressure, self-authenticity, online social comparison, social media addiction, and fear of missing out, often called FoMO. Statistical modeling then mapped how these traits connect, and whether authenticity changes the strength of those links.

Social media addiction and online comparison carried part of the path from peer pressure to FoMO. Students with higher self-authenticity scored lower on every risk measure in the model. Authenticity also weakened the direct link between peer pressure and FoMO until that link faded from significance. Because the survey captured one moment, the authors treat the patterns as associations, not proof of cause. The work points to self-knowledge as a buffer worth building.
pmc-13508444:
Roghaye Khodaei and three co-authors compare the mental aftermath and social support of spontaneous versus induced abortion among women in Iran, in 2026 work. The study recruited 611 women in two cities of East Azerbaijan Province, through clinics and informal settings like parks and mosques. Of the group, 321 had lost a pregnancy naturally and 290 had chosen an induced abortion. Time since the event ranged from three months to five years. Standard questionnaires scored depression, anxiety, stress, and felt support.

Stress scores ran significantly higher in the induced abortion group. Felt support was low in both groups overall, though its shape differed. Women after induced abortion leaned more on friends, while women after spontaneous loss felt more support from a significant other. The authors call for family education, stronger support systems, and timely mental health screening after either kind of loss.
pmc-13508544:
Sarah Brennenstuhl and four co-authors ask which students know where campus mental health help sits, in 2026 work. Data came from a 2022 wellbeing survey at one large multi-campus institution with full mental health services. Models weighed structural traits, attitudes toward help seeking, and need signals like distress and suicidal thoughts as predictors of knowing campus and off-campus options.

A third of students did not know where to find campus help. Ignorance of off-campus help ran higher, at forty-five percent. Older students, Asian students, and international students were less likely to be in the dark about campus services. Living off campus and having a disability without formal accommodations raised the odds of not knowing. Higher distress also slightly raised those odds, a worrying pattern. The authors target orientation and outreach at the groups most likely to be lost.
pmc-13508644:
Kauer and co-authors examine the bleakest corner of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia care. Their 2026 paper studies patients whose disease no longer responds to targeted drugs. One group resists both main inhibitor classes. The other resists one class and also carries high-risk genetic changes such as TP53 damage. The authors assessed their outlook and whether a donor stem cell transplant, called alloHCT, could help.

In this retrospective single-centre analysis, both high-risk groups had a poor prognosis regardless of earlier chemoimmunotherapy. The transplant proved feasible in this population and, the authors report, may overcome drug resistance in some patients. They caution that its exact benefit and best timing remain undetermined. The paper frames transplantation as a realistic option where drug options have run out, pending stronger comparative evidence.
pmc-13509944:
Carlos Fernandez-Pereira and Alfredo E. Rodriguez review trials of pills given after a bare-metal heart stent to keep the vessel from narrowing again, in 2026 work. Drug-coated stents narrow less often, yet they cost more and demand long courses of blood-thinning drugs, which limits their use in many places. Three randomized trials compared bare-metal stents plus oral drugs against drug-coated stents.

The pills studied were rapamycin, prednisone, and colchicine, each calming growth or inflammation in vessel walls. In carefully chosen patients, results with the pill strategy matched those of coated stents. The authors present the pairing as a possible low-cost route where coated stents are out of reach or unsafe. They also say larger and longer trials must confirm safety, settle doses, and find which patients suit the approach best.
pmc-13511744:
Jiaqian Zhu, Yuxin Li, Yuxuan Liang, Jie Yu, Kaiyu Chen, and Chenghua Li identify a receptor that lets sea cucumber immune cells cast DNA traps against an invading bacterium, in 2026 work. The traps are web-like strands thrown out to pin and kill germs, and their release depends on surface receptors spotting the invader. The team studied a Toll-like receptor in Apostichopus japonicus and its response to a Vibrio strain from diseased animals.

The receptor rose after infection and its outer part bound several germ wall pieces plus the invader's tail protein, flagellin C, which other related receptors did not recognize. Silencing the receptor cut trap formation and lowered trap-linked defense proteins, and it also blocked traps triggered by the pure tail protein. A partner signaling protein sits downstream of the receptor. The authors map a full recognition-to-trap route in this farmed species.
pmc-13512344:
Xiangjun Cui and nine co-authors mine multi-layer data for proteins that read chemical marks on histones, the spools that package DNA, and test their value in colorectal cancer, in 2026 work. These reader proteins help govern anti-tumor immunity, yet their joint roles in outlook and immune subtypes were murky. The team fused several omics layers through a graph attention network, then ran immune profiling and checked leads in outside cohorts.

Four core genes cleared every screen, showing steady outlook value and strong ties to anti-tumor immune activity. Core and helper genes sat in key metabolic and immune pathways. Single-cell readings, docking simulations, and other computer assays filled out their profiles, and one drug, sapitinib, was singled out for its fit against the encoded proteins. The authors offer the four-gene signature as a candidate marker set and drug target list for precision immune therapy.
pmc-13514844:
Snoussi and colleagues studied a 2026 investigation of Allium atroviolaceum, a wild onion relative eaten as a functional food. Different parts of the plant may carry different protective chemicals, yet their contributions were poorly mapped. The team combined chemical profiling, computer target modelling, and bench antioxidant tests across flowers, leaves, bulbs, and stalks.

Flowers held the richest anthocyanins and flavonoids, the pigment and plant compounds tied to antioxidant action, and they scavenged free radicals most strongly in two standard assays. Flower stalks best slowed fat oxidation in a third assay, protecting a pigment from bleaching. Network analysis flagged stress and inflammation proteins including PTGS2, and one compound, caffeoyl pinoresinol, bound that target most strongly in modelling. Snoussi stresses these target links are predictions needing cell tests.
pmc-13514944:
Peña-Fernández and colleagues measured three little-studied elements, zirconium, hafnium, and tellurium, in wild mushrooms from Leicester and Leicestershire, England, in 2026. Wild fungi absorb elements from their surroundings and can serve as living monitors of environmental contamination. The team analyzed 121 mushroom samples and twenty-six topsoil samples from urban and peri-urban spaces using mass spectrometry.

Zirconium and hafnium appeared in every mushroom and soil sample, while tellurium showed up in 118 of the 121 mushrooms yet stayed below detection in all soils. Median mushroom levels were 170 nanograms per gram of dry weight for zirconium, 270 for hafnium, and 110 for tellurium, with some species and parks higher. Levels of the three elements rose and fell together strongly across parks. Because soil and mushroom sampling sites overlapped poorly, the authors could not pin down sources or soil-to-fungus transfer, and they present the work as an exploratory baseline.
pmc-13515644:
Liudmila Leppik and seven colleagues hunt blood signatures of traumatic brain injury in badly hurt patients, in a 2026 proteomics study. Outcome after brain injury is hard to forecast, especially when the rest of the body is also injured. The team profiled proteins in plain blood plasma and in a fraction rich in tiny cell-made vesicles. Groups covered seventy-five patients: brain injury alone, brain injury with other trauma, and trauma without brain injury, plus twenty-four healthy volunteers.

The vesicle fraction yielded far more changed proteins than plain plasma. Most changes reflected body-wide injury rather than the brain wound itself, with plasma proteins pointing to metabolism and vesicle proteins to protein turnover. The vesicle pair also tracked consciousness scores and the need for brain surgery. Leppik's team names them as candidate markers for further study.
pmc-13517244:
Huaming Xi and co-authors present a review, published in 2026. It covers how viruses injure the intestinal barrier. This layered gut lining absorbs nutrients. It also keeps microbes and toxins out of the body. The authors cover viruses such as rotavirus. The pig coronavirus PEDV is also covered. Shared ways of breaking the barrier down are the focus.

Viruses loosen the tight junctions sealing gut cells. They trigger several forms of cell death. They thin the protective mucus layer. They also unbalance the gut microbe community. These harms reinforce one another. They drive inflammation. Barrier repair is a promising therapy direction. Diet and microbe-based treatments also look promising.
pmc-13517744:
Xuelian Li and four colleagues test the herbicide diquat on pregnant rats and their fetuses in a 2026 preliminary study. Diquat is restricted in many countries for its wider toxicity, but its effects during pregnancy are thinly mapped. Dams received repeated below-lethal doses at two levels, and the team read maternal hormones, stress chemistry, blood metabolites, and fetal skeletons.

The high dose cut estradiol while two pituitary hormones held steady. Stress markers shifted clearly, signalling oxidative strain in the mothers. Fetuses paid the heavier price: skull, breastbone, tail, and pelvis bones hardened late or not at all, with some litters affected completely. Metabolite profiles split cleanly from controls, pointing at hormone-making, amino-acid, and salt-balance pathways. Li's team presents the pattern as early evidence that diquat unsettles pregnancy chemistry and delays the fetal skeleton's build-out.
pmc-13518044:
Ismail and colleagues reported a 2026 case of cerebral Kounis syndrome, in which a severe allergic reaction triggered spasm of a brain artery and produced a stroke mimic. The patient was a previously healthy 45-year-old man working outdoors who developed full-body itching and rash, near-fainting, breathlessness, palpitations. Abdominal pain, together with sudden weakness of his right side and slurred speech.

Ismail describes how prompt intramuscular epinephrine and other anti-inflammatory treatment brought rapid, complete recovery in the emergency department, and brain imaging and other studies showed no lasting damage. Kounis syndrome is named for allergy-driven spasm of the heart's arteries, which is often mistaken for a heart attack; this case extends it to the cerebral circulation. The authors stress that recognizing allergy as a stroke cause matters, because epinephrine given early is the crucial treatment and delay risks misdirected care.
pmc-13519444:
Manikanda Prabu V and colleagues measured jaw muscle activity before and after braces treatment across different bite problems. Published in 2026, the observational study recorded surface muscle signals from the temporalis, masseter, and digastric muscles at rest, while clenching, and while swallowing. Patients carried Class I, II, or III bite patterns, and signals were compared before treatment and after.

No clear change appeared for Class I or Class III patients across the three muscles. Class II patients, especially women, showed marked gains in muscle activity after treatment, pointing to neuromuscular adjustment as the bite improved. Early discomfort during treatment can first dampen muscle use, so the later gains read as recovery plus adaptation. Readers get a measured view of how braces reshape muscle function, not just tooth position.
pmc-13520144:
Silvia Armiraglio, Simona Perniciaro, Angela Bossi, and Massimo Agostino Agosti simulate a new newborn sepsis protocol in 2026 called Neosafe, designed to cut needless blood tests and antibiotics. Under Neosafe, 2.4 percent of infants would have had blood investigations versus 4.1 percent under the calculator, and 2.2 percent would have received antibiotics versus 4.0 percent. pmc-13520244:
E E Schippers and four colleagues build in 2026 an artificial intelligence model that warns a Dutch emergency department of crowding an hour before it hits. Trained on electronic records and staffing data, their memory-based neural network used ambulance diversion status as the truth signal for real crowding.

Pre-notified arrivals, mid-acuity patient counts, and supervisor numbers carried the most predictive weight. Calibration stayed reasonable. pmc-13521244:
Claire E Shudde and colleagues engineer in 2026 a switch that turns on a key survival signal inside regulatory T cells. The switch needs no IL-2, the usual growth signal for these cells. Regulatory cells calm self-attack in the body. IL-2 care also fires up attack cells, and cell therapies fade fast.

Treated cells also blocked colon inflammation at onset. Suppression of harmful cells grew stronger, and cell identity held firm for longer.
pmc-13521944:
Mingliang Chu and Musen Liu model in 2026 what keeps tourists loyal to old village sites. Visitor income funds heritage upkeep and rural life. The survey held 330 valid replies. Three stat methods checked the model from distinct angles.

Real feel, guest co-creation, online word of mouth and service quality each lifted image, joy or felt value. One link failed, from service quality to joy. Image, joy and value then drove loyalty with force. Joy and value also acted as must-pass gates for loyalty. Site managers gain a ranked lever list that goes past plain service upgrades.
pmc-13522344:
Martin Stumpf and Giulio Antonini build in 2026 a step-by-step maths method for short pulses in media that jump in time. Time-jump media can bend waves in ways fixed media cannot. Study of such media stays hard, so fresh tools help.

State-variable theory for steady-piece systems frames the method. A worked case tracks waves on a line whose traits switch at a set time. The line acts as a time-layered slab. Bounce and bend at time walls fall out of the maths with ease. Designers of fast-switch antennas and cloaks gain a hand route. Brute-force simulation is not the only path here.
pmc-13522444:
Yezhang Ding and collaborators investigate whether dopamine shapes the tiny germs living around plant roots in a 2026 study of a model grass. Dopamine was among the most common compounds released in root fluids, and its level varied across plant lines. Ten plant lines were grown with a defined community of sixteen bacterial members so that links could be tested directly.

Higher dopamine in root fluid tracked the abundance of six bacterial members, and lab growth tests showed dopamine affected those same isolates. Treating soil with dopamine also enriched a broad bacterial group, matching the other results. The work suggests one root chemical can steer the root community, a point of interest for managing crop microbe communities with more care.
pmc-13523144:
Katherine Longardner leads a team studying blood pressure drops and thinking problems in Parkinson disease in a 2026 study. Twenty-nine patients without dementia, ten of whom had orthostatic hypotension, meaning blood pressure falls on standing, completed a word fluency test lying down and upright on a tilt table. A light-based head scanner tracked oxygen levels in the front of the brain throughout.

The interaction between group and position was significant for letter fluency: patients with the blood pressure problem performed worse and made more errors while upright. Their brain oxygen signals also shifted in a pattern suggesting harder mental effort. No one reported symptoms during testing. The authors propose light-based brain monitoring as a clinically useful way to detect posture-related brain dysfunction in autonomic failure.
pmc-13524144:
Jindal and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the combined use of two drugs, montelukast and bilastine, for allergic rhinitis, the allergy-driven inflammation of the nose lining. The condition is triggered by antibody responses to allergens, and the released histamine and leukotrienes cause itching, sneezing, and a runny nose in children and adults alike. The team gathered studies from 2003 to 2023 that tested each drug alone and together.

Jindal found that several trials show the pair eases daytime and total nasal symptoms more than either drug alone, with the clearest gains in moderate to severe lasting disease. The two drugs complement each other: bilastine, a newer antihistamine, gives fast relief with little drowsiness, while montelukast blocks leukotrienes to cut inflammation. Data comparing the pair against other paired products on the market remain thin, so best use and long-term safety need more study.
pmc-13524944:
Park presented in 2026 a game theory study of decisions made in sequence across scale-free networks, where a few hub members hold most links. Real choices unfold step by step, and each agent reacts to those who moved earlier. Park extended bounded rationality, the idea that people choose near-best rather than best options, from one-shot games to sequential ones, using a form of backward reasoning adjusted for limited rationality.

Park ordered agents by network centrality, how connected each member is, and let later movers weigh earlier actions. As the rationality setting rose, the near-best outcomes converged on subgame perfect equilibria, the textbook solution for sequential games. In all four scenarios tested, sequential play protected more than the one-shot baseline, and centrality ordering beat random and reverse orders. Tests on banking, disease, and sports data showed the same pattern, hinting at a shared mechanism.
pmc-13526644:
Gautam Jalori and co-authors build, in twenty twenty-six, patient-specific computer models of airway collapse in infants with Robin Sequence. In this birth condition, an underdeveloped jaw and a backward tongue cause the upper airway to obstruct or collapse in cycles. Clinical checks give no hard numbers and miss the dynamic behavior. Their method extracts airway motion from four-dimensional CT scans. It then runs a moving-mesh fluid dynamics analysis for patients with complete collapse. Airflow is graded by instant measures, velocity, pressure, and energy loss, plus cycle-averaged breathing work.

The collapsing airway was compared with a synthetic non-collapsing twin. To reach the same air volume, the collapsing case needed about double the computed breathing effort. A real non-collapsing patient validated the synthetic control.
pmc-13526844:
Yang and co-authors build an AI pipeline in this 2026 materials paper. It designs fibrous network materials. These are the woven or printed fiber architectures behind soft robotics and tissue scaffolds. The pipeline respects whether the design can actually be made. Their Regular Fibrous Network Framework links topology generation, mechanical simulation, and reinforcement-learning optimization in one loop.

A construction algorithm enforces single-fiber continuity, the Eulerian path condition that lets one unbroken strand form the whole network for knitting or printing. A graph neural network then predicts the nonlinear, J-shaped and C-shaped force curves these networks show. The learning module rediscovers better shapes within minutes. It reaches roughly 50 percent higher strength at 20 percent lower mass. Optimized flat networks were projected onto curved surfaces and physically printed by two 3D methods, validating the digital-to-physical chain the authors propose as a general design paradigm.
pmc-13527044:
Kang-Ping Xiong, Hong Weng, and colleagues identify a detox enzyme moonlighting as a brake on prostate cancer's fat supply. Sequencing patient tumors showed GSTM4 sharply reduced, with low levels tracking higher fat content. Restoring it slowed cancer cell growth and migration and suppressed tumors and bone spread in mouse models.

Starved of new lipids, tumors stalled. A clinically approved ACLY-blocking drug, bempedoic acid, also showed anti-tumor potential. The authors nominate this three-protein axis as a therapeutic target in advanced prostate cancer.
pmc-13527144:
Haiyan Gu, Jie Bai, Jun Xie, and Cui Zhang build, in a 2026 study, an AI generation model for presenting China's Grand Canal culture to the world. The canal is the world's largest and longest ancient waterway, yet its global reach suffers from mixed terms, missing cultural context, and slow manual text production. A backpropagation neural network was trained for the task.

The team built a Chinese-English corpus, cleaning about 150,000 candidate sentence pairs down to 120,000 verified pairs. A three layer feedforward network with momentum tuning and adaptive learning rates was built in PyTorch and tested on a high-end graphics chip. Scores beat a translation baseline and a paid service on key measures, and human judges gave cultural fidelity a score of 4.1 out of five.
pmc-13527944:
Ganesh Dey and five colleagues publish a 2026 protocol for a randomized trial in Bangladesh. The trial tests two added exercises for adults with lumbar spondylolisthesis. In that condition one back bone slips over another and causes lasting pain. Seventy-two patients with low-grade slips will be recruited at a rehabilitation center in Savar.

Everyone receives standard physiotherapy three times a week for six weeks. Half also practice abdominal hollowing, which trains deep trunk muscles. They also stretch the piriformis muscle in the hip. Pain on a ten-point scale is the main outcome. Disability and fear of movement are also measured, with a check four weeks later. Assessors will not know group assignments.
pmc-13528044:
Shauna L. Mangum and four colleagues survey treated adults with Gaucher disease type 1 in a 2026 study. The disease is a rare inherited storage disorder. Standard therapies improve many lab measures, yet patients often keep hurting. Ninety-seven adults on enzyme or substrate therapy answered an online survey. Pain and fatigue each predicted worse physical and mental quality of life. Age also predicted the physical side. Scores sat below United States norms in seven of eight areas. The authors say standard markers miss much of the daily burden. They urge clinics to track patient-reported outcomes routinely. New add-on treatments aimed at symptoms are needed, they argue.
pmc-13528144:
Wanmai Woonkaew and four colleagues survey harmful childhood experiences and low mood among Thai medical students in a 2026 study. The survey ran from April to July 2025 at one faculty and two linked centers in the south. Five hundred forty students answered anonymously online. The median age was twenty-one. Standard Thai questionnaires scored early adversity and depressive symptoms.

About fifty-five percent reported at least one adverse experience. Physical neglect was the most common, then parents splitting, then mental illness at home. About eighteen percent met the symptom cutoff for depression. Moderate childhood adversity more than doubled the odds of symptoms. Current life stress raised odds nearly sixfold. Physical illness also mattered. The authors call early hardship a lasting weak point. Support during training should ask about it, they argue.
pmc-13529844:
Arya Rahgozar and Pouria Mortezaagha built an auditable pipeline that speeds full-text screening for systematic reviews. Published in 2026, the method tackles the bottleneck where eligibility clues hide across long, varied papers, tested within a population-health modeling review network. A language-model judge then reviews highlighted passages with reasons and confidence, softening scores when evidence runs thin rather than rejecting outright. Readers get a traceable shortcut, with full mixed-label validation still ahead.
pmc-13530744:
Bussey-Sutton and colleagues present in 2026, as conference paper 45, a study of whether bow-legged alignment, called varus, endangers cartilage grafts placed in the inner compartment of the knee. Eight grafts, about fifteen percent, failed over an average follow-up just past three years. The femoral angle, joint line convergence, and joint line tilt showed no link. The authors flag even modest varus as a threat to graft survival.
pmc-13531744:

Sequencing confirmed Babesia, Bartonella, or both in five of the six subjects. Four carried Babesia, spanning three species, and two of them hosted more than one species at once. One Bartonella species was confirmed in two individuals. All six gave borderline results on sensitive Bartonella tests. The authors stress that such small numbers cannot prove cause, but they argue these hidden infections deserve study as possible cofactors in chronic illness and suicidality.
pmc-13531844:
Bauer and coauthors test if all-or-none words in speech mark depression. Twisted thought patterns help keep depression going over time. Words like always, never, and must show that pattern in writing. Past work tied such words to depression in texts.

The team recruited 144 adults in three matched groups. One group had clinical depression, one had mild signs. The third group had no depression history at all. Daily phone prompts caught speech and mood in real life. Word use was then weighed against diagnosis and mood. Spoken all-or-none words may give a live mood mark.
pmc-13533044:
Canpolat writes to the editor in 2026 about predicting sudden cardiac death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, where thickened heart muscle can trigger lethal rhythms without warning. The letter discusses a study by Balaban and colleagues on two ECG-derived indices, ICEB and its corrected variant, which summarise the balance between the heart's electrical activation and recovery. pmc-13533244:

pmc-13534144:

It showed no clear gain in the next five months either.

Two longer trials did show less grief at six months or more. Short-term drops in low mood also showed. The proof base was weak, so Fu urges larger, stronger trials. One-to-one online talk therapy looks most worth testing next.
pmc-13534444:

A causal surrogate learned from low and high detail simulations maps heat drive to interface motion with high accuracy. pmc-13534644:

pmc-13536244:

pmc-13536644:

The coating was perceived as feasible, with operational lessons drawn from each group's vantage point. Inductive thematic analysis sorted the experiences into themes. pmc-13536744:

That flexibility should ease recruitment for smoking research while keeping checks on smoking status dependable.
pmc-13537344:
Yuki Kikuchi and co-authors test whether early total clozapine dose predicts a severe drop in infection-fighting white cells in a 2026 nationwide Japanese study. pmc-13538144:

A threshold value marks where large cones are barred, and stress peaks mark the gaps between fissure segments.
pmc-13538344:

pmc-13538644:

pmc-13539544:

pmc-13540844:

pmc-13540944:

pmc-13542444:

pmc-13543344:

pmc-13543544:

pmc-13544744:

pmc-13544944:

One burn erased the fault in three seconds and spared normal conduction. No return appeared afterward.
pmc-13545144:

pmc-13545744:

Zhibo Tan and co-authors reviewed in 2026 whether giving chemotherapy and radiation before surgery for locally advanced rectal cancer makes the later operation harder or riskier. Worry about that question has kept some clinicians from following guidelines. The authors searched two major databases for studies from 2000 to early 2026, covering trials, real-world series, and earlier reviews.

Longer waits, stronger drug regimens, newer radiation methods, and added immunotherapy likewise showed no clear increase in surgical burden. The authors still want better long-term evidence for particular patient subgroups.

Ren, Zhou, Dong, and co-authors hunt for genes that drive esophageal cancer. Their 2026 paper screens squamous cell carcinoma, an aggressive throat cancer. Outcomes for this cancer remain poor worldwide. About half of all global cases occur in China. The team searched copy-number-altered genes for hidden drivers.

A CRISPR library targeted 406 candidate genes in their screen. One gene, GJB6, stood out as a tumor suppressor. Low GJB6 levels tracked with worse patient outcomes. GJB6 raises levels of a second gene, GRHL3, via calcium signals. GRHL3 in turn switches GJB6 back on transcriptionally. Together they form a self-reinforcing protective loop. Breaking the loop switches on AKT signaling instead. AKT activity then pushes the cancer forward. A drug called capivasertib blocks AKT in cells. It reversed the harm caused by losing GJB6. GJB6 may thus flag patients for AKT-targeted therapy.
pmc-13548544:
Lin Zhang and colleagues build a machine learning tool to tell chikungunya apart from dengue at a patient's first hospital assessment, in a 2026 modeling study. The two mosquito-borne fevers circulate together and start alike, while the molecular tests that separate them are scarce in many endemic clinics. The team trained eight models on routine symptoms and standard blood results from 1,058 confirmed infections.

A gradient boosting model performed best and most steadily, splitting cases into training and held-out test groups. Platelet count and rash repeatedly carried the most weight in its decisions, matching known clinical patterns. The finished model was placed on a simple web platform that returns a risk estimate from a handful of everyday measurements. The authors offer it as practical decision support where laboratory confirmation is out of reach.
pmc-13548644:
Clelia Suriano and colleagues give aging mice weekly doses of irisin, the hormone-like messenger released with exercise, in a 2026 study of bone and muscle decline. Irisin is known to build both tissues, raising hopes it could counter the paired wasting of old age. Twelve-month-old mice received the treatment for eight months, after which their thigh bones and muscles were scanned, bent, sliced, and read for gene activity.

Treated mice kept denser, better-structured cortical bone with more fine struts and fewer bone-eating cells. Their muscles kept orderly fibers and lower levels of two atrophy genes. A shared thread was sclerostin, a protein that blocks bone building: irisin lowered its gene in bone and, newly shown here, its presence in muscle. Dish experiments confirmed irisin switches the gene down in muscle precursor cells, while sclerostin itself hampers their maturation.
pmc-13549144:
Lennart Bohrmann and colleagues turn a known gut hormone blocker into radioactive tracers for tumors carrying its receptor, in a 2026 radiopharmaceutical study. Tumors such as medullary thyroid cancer display the cholecystokinin-2 receptor, and earlier tracers based on hormone mimics had drawbacks. The team built four new ligands on the antagonist drug nastorazepide, varying the linker and the metal-gripping chelator, and labeled them with two radioactive metals.

The new tracers latched onto receptor sites three to four times better than a reference tracer, with strong binding strength. One lead compound entered receptor-bearing cells at twice the rate of its siblings and, in mice, piled into tumors quickly with favorable tumor-to-organ ratios and high stability in the body. A first therapy test showed no significant tumor kill, so the authors frame the lead as a promising scaffold needing optimization.
pmc-13550644:
Xianglu Jia, leading twelve colleagues, published a 2026 comparison of eight rose cultivars grown at Nanning Botanical Garden in China, asking why their petals differ in color. The team measured color values, pigment content, petal structure, antioxidant capacity, and nutrient and mineral levels. Their aim was to name the main drivers of color and pick the strongest cultivar for planting.

Pigments such as anthocyanins and carotenoids mainly set color, splitting the roses into deep-toned and light-toned groups. Deep tones tied to petal thickness, certain enzymes, and phosphorus, boron, and calcium, while light tones tied to sugar, another enzyme, nitrogen, and zinc. One blue-hued rose stood apart through higher pH and calcium, and a combined score ranked the golden cultivar R4 highest.
pmc-13551344:
Lord, Harding, Crowther, and Lin summed up in twenty twenty-six what reviews say on easing pain when blood is drawn from new-born babies. They searched four data banks for reviews of trials on this task. Care acts ranged from drugs and skin creams to sweet drinks and skin-to-skin holds.

Twenty-two reviews met their bar for sound search and bias checks. Sweet drink, with or without a suck aid, cut pain scores for heel pricks in a clear way. Skin-to-skin holds cut scores too, with mid-grade proof. Breast feeds and kin acts looked good but need more proof. For many drugs proof was too thin to judge.
pmc-13551844:
Ting You, with seven colleagues, published a 2026 study of a voice-based test for a throat cancer. The cancer grows in the nasopharynx, behind the nose. Most patients are found late. A blood test tied to a virus misses many cases. The team recorded voice from 359 patients with advanced disease and 304 healthy controls. Recordings came from one hospital between 2022 and 2025.

A learning system sorted the voices by their sound traits. On a fresh test set of 133 people, it reached accuracy in the mid-eighties. It caught close to nine in ten patients. It was less sharp on healthy controls. The team calls the result an early promise only, and they demand wider tests before screening use.
pmc-13551944:
Koki Yokawa, with eight colleagues, published a 2026 case report of a pinched heart outflow tract after redo surgery. A 69-year-old woman had a valve replaced earlier for infection. Months later the valve loosened and leaked, and a false bulge formed at the aortic root. The valve ring was destroyed. Surgeons redid the root replacement with a graft insertion method. Part of the graft sits inverted inside the ventricle.

Scans after surgery showed the outflow tract narrowed to a small width. The width was less than the size of the implanted valve. Flow MRI showed blood speeding up at the pinch. That pattern confirmed a working blockage, not just a narrow look. The team warns that the graft's inner part can crowd the outflow path. They advise shape plus flow imaging after such repairs.
pmc-13553044:
Zhang and colleagues published in twenty twenty-six a review of lysine acetylation, a reversible chemical tag on proteins. Cells add and remove this tag to control many processes. It shapes gene expression, cell division, DNA repair, and signal relay. The enzymes that add and remove the tag are themselves tightly regulated. When acetylation goes wrong, disease can follow. Links are documented to cancer, heart disease, chronic inflammation, and neurological disorders.

The review covers the adding and removing enzymes in detail. It explains their roles in how diseases develop and progress. Cross-talk with other protein modifications gets special attention. Targeting acetylation pathways may yield new treatments, the authors argue. They gather recent findings into a guide for drug developers. The aim is fresh strategies for clinical use of this biology.
pmc-13554444:
Bella Rhea Lavifa Sanjaya and two colleagues review ginseng's power to switch on the cell's master antioxidant guard in a 2026 paper. That guard, called Nrf2, controls genes that keep chemical balance inside cells. The team searched recent studies from 2018 to 2025 on ginseng forms, from raw extracts to clinic injections. Effects were checked in dishes, animals, and patients.

Ginseng activates the guard and tunes the proteins that hold or release it. Protection showed against oxidative stress, inflammation, and several forms of cell death. Removing the guard in test models erased much of the benefit, proving the link. Clinic studies on red ginseng products reported gains with good safety. The authors see wide promise for chronic disease care.
pmc-13555944:
Devrim Dumludag and Ozge Gokdemir ask what shapes life contentment and belonging for Turkish migrants in the Netherlands in a 2026 survey. Their data cover 1,006 people who rated identity, whom they compare themselves with, and unfair treatment they feel. Two outcomes were tracked: contentment with life, and strength of belonging in the host country.

Calling oneself Dutch, or a citizen of the world, tied to higher scores on both outcomes. Comparing oneself with Dutch natives also helped. Leaning on comparisons with the home community, and feeling more unfair treatment, pulled both scores down. Joining local groups and more years in the country strengthened belonging. The authors stress the yardsticks in people's heads, not just jobs and income.
pmc-13558444:
Satoshi Makita, Hiroo Uchida, Akinari Hinoki, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It proposes two simple ratios from chest scans to warn surgeons when keyhole surgery on a child's chest mass is likely to turn difficult.

A tumor's raw size misleads in children, whose chests offer little working room. The team reviewed sixty-five children operated on between 2007 and 2025, most by minimally invasive surgery. They measured the tumor against the chest's own height and width. Five of the fifty-six keyhole cases hit complications during surgery. Both ratios ran far higher in those children, roughly double the calm cases. Other imaging risk signs added context. The authors offer the ratios as cheap adjunct markers for choosing between keyhole and open surgery before the first incision.
pmc-13558644:
Behrad Eftekhari and four colleagues tested in 2026 which admission blood markers best forecast death in patients with multiple injuries. Five candidates were compared in a prospective study at an Iranian trauma centre between May and August 2023, covering 114 patients with moderate to severe injury scores. Outcomes were death in hospital and length of stay, and accuracy was ranked with standard receiver operating analysis.

About one patient in nine died. Non-survivors arrived with worse injury and consciousness scores plus higher levels of the inflammatory marker IL-6 and of lactate, a sign of poor tissue perfusion. IL-6 proved the sharpest single predictor, ahead of base deficit and lactate, while two older inflammation markers, CRP and sedimentation rate, performed weakly. The authors suggest pairing inflammatory and perfusion markers for early triage, noting that lactate remains vital where IL-6 testing is unavailable.
pmc-13558744:
Junjie Wang and six colleagues built in 2026 an explainable scoring chart that sorts low platelet counts by cause. Platelets can fall because the marrow makes too few or because the body destroys them too fast, and telling the two apart early guides very different care. Their retrospective study covered 185 patients admitted to a Suzhou haematology department between 2020 and 2025, most in the underproduction group, and three feature selection methods plus regression narrowed the candidate markers.

Four routine measures survived: age, mean platelet volume, and two ratios built from standard blood counts. Six competing models were compared, and a generalised linear model turned the four markers into a paper nomogram with discrimination above ninety percent and clean calibration. Decision analysis showed more net benefit than any single marker. Explanation plots show which way each value pushes a patient's score, keeping the tool readable at the bedside.
pmc-13559244:
Guiyu Zhou and colleagues investigate whether dipeptidase 1, an enzyme known as DPEP1, helps drive idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a scarring lung disease with no clear cause. Their 2026 study combines public gene-expression data, blood samples from patients, and a mouse model of lung fibrosis. DPEP1 levels were tracked against lung function and against arachidonic acid, a fatty acid involved in inflammation.

DPEP1 ran high in fibrotic lung tissue, mainly in the cells lining pulmonary blood vessels, and higher levels matched worse breathing measures. Blood arachidonic acid fell in patients and dropped further as DPEP1 rose. In mice given bleomycin to scar the lungs, blocking DPEP1 with cilastatin sodium eased fibrosis and calmed inflammatory signals. Treated mice also recovered healthier levels of the fatty acid and related molecules. The authors propose DPEP1 as a treatment target worth pursuing.
pmc-13560844:
Tereza Manousaki and colleagues deliver a full genome for the Mediterranean monk seal, one of the world's rarest marine mammals and the Mediterranean's only pinniped. Their 2026 genome report builds the full sequence of a female seal as part of a European genome effort. Centuries of hunting shrank the species to a remnant; it now counts as at risk.

Fewer than one thousand seals remain worldwide in current counts. The assembly covers 2.4 billion bases arranged into sixteen chromosome-scale pieces plus the X chromosome and a mitochondrial genome, built from 316 contigs with strong continuity stats. The seals shelter and pup in marine caves and hunt as chance-taking top hunters. Present threats center on coastal building, tourism pressure, pollution, and thinned prey from overfishing. The authors frame the genome as a tool for protection and management of an emblematic species.
pmc-13561244:
Mussie Gezahegn Teklewold and three colleagues published this 2026 cohort study on preventing shivering after a spinal block for caesarean delivery, at a large Ethiopian hospital. Shivering after a spinal block is common and hard on the body, and paracetamol has been suggested as a preventive. Evidence from poor settings was thin, so the team compared mothers given the drug in advance with those who were not, from January to April 2025.

One hundred mothers scheduled for caesarean section under a spinal block were enrolled and split into exposed and unexposed groups. Shivering struck 30 percent of the paracetamol group against 54 percent of the comparison group, a clear gap. Shivering severity also differed between groups. Temperature, blood pressure and side effects were tracked through surgery. The authors conclude that preventive paracetamol cuts both how often shivering strikes and how bad it is, and they encourage direct comparisons with other preventive drugs.
pmc-13562344:
Jie Zhang and two colleagues ask whether bowel inflammation and mental illness share part of their genetic roots. Their 2026 study uses summary data from large genome-wide studies, including a combined analysis of 486,601 people for inflammatory bowel disease. The team compared that data with results for eight psychiatric disorders. They measured overall overlap, overlap within small genome regions, and single genes that might drive both kinds of illness.

Clear overall links appeared with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, anxiety, autism, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Local analysis flagged 274 genome regions, and combined methods pointed to 21 shared genes, among them NOD2 and IL10. Immune signalling and nerve-cell pathways stood out in the shared biology. The findings support a gut-brain connection written partly into DNA, and they suggest targets for treating both conditions together.
pmc-13562544:
Azadeh Alavi and co-authors brought quantum-flavored math to a conservative test in 2026: predicting muscle loss in mice with lung disease. Skeletal muscle dysfunction accompanies chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, but preclinical cohorts are small, so fancy models must be tested carefully. The team studied over two hundred mice exposed to cigarette smoke, using blood and lung-wash biomarkers to predict thigh muscle weight, quality, and force.

Their method maps synthetic shape-based reference objects through a kernel space, compresses them with random projections fitted only on training data, and feeds low-dimensional modeled quantum regression circuits. It was benchmarked against classic ridge and kernel models under equal cross-checking folds. The study's value lies as much in its discipline as its winner: equal folds and conservative testing keep small-sample machine learning honest. A standard quantum methods must meet to be believed.
pmc-13564244:
Xuesong Xu and Shichong Qiao study a gene circuit that may protect the jaw joint's cartilage from wearing away, in a 2026 paper. Jaw joint osteoarthritis starts when cartilage cells die off and the joint surface breaks down. A gene called FoxO3 helps keep those cells healthy, but its levels drop in diseased joints, and the team asked what controls it.

Working with rat jaw joints and cells in dishes, they found that raising FoxO3 eased cartilage damage and lifted levels of two healthy cartilage proteins. It also lowered two enzymes that chew cartilage up. A small RNA, miR-223-3p, normally binds FoxO3's message and holds it down. A long non-coding RNA named OIP5-AS1 can soak up that small RNA like a sponge, freeing FoxO3. The authors present this three-part circuit as a possible drug target.
pmc-13564344:
Enzo Freire Santana do Amaral and co-authors published a 2026 review on stomach disorders in dairy cows around calving. The weeks before and after a cow gives birth are a risky window for illness. Two problems of the abomasum, the cow's true stomach, stand out: it can slip out of place, or develop ulcers. Both cut milk output, harm welfare, and lead to early removal from the herd.

The review gathers the risk factors and explains how they connect. Low energy balance, low blood calcium, and body-wide inflammation sit at the center. Inflammation stirs up signaling proteins, disturbs calcium, and slows the gut's natural movement. A sluggish stomach then fills with gas and shifts, while its lining weakens toward ulcers. Other illnesses of the period, such as ketosis and womb infection, add to the risk. The authors also sum up recent gains in spotting and treating these disorders.
pmc-13569044:
Ian Kim and co-authors measure, in a 2026 experiment, the hidden mechanical shock of a single water droplet hitting a surface, using a fast piezoelectric sensor and high-speed filming. Droplet erosion is usually blamed on splashing or pressure spikes, yet the first instant of impact had never been captured directly.

A strong strain pulse arrived within two milliseconds of contact, followed by rapid vibrations at the water-solid boundary during the first twenty milliseconds, before any rebound. Vibration speed depended on surface stiffness, while pulse size grew with droplet size and fall speed. The signals give engineers a firmer basis for predicting how repeated droplets fatigue and erode materials.
pmc-13569344:
Assel Muratovna Shigayeva Ferreira and colleagues measured quality of life in adults living with Long COVID two years or more after infection, publishing the cross-sectional study in 2026. Long COVID can linger after even mild illness, yet its lasting toll on daily life in primary care was unclear. The team surveyed 226 adults in João Pessoa, Brazil, who had mild-to-moderate COVID-19 in 2021, using a standard five-dimension health questionnaire.

Those with Long COVID scored markedly lower on overall health utility than those without persistent symptoms, with the worst effects in anxiety and depression, pain and discomfort, and usual activities. Women, older adults, non-White participants, people with chronic disease, and those with less schooling fared worst. The authors call for targeted rehabilitation and multidisciplinary primary-care support for long-term survivors.
pmc-13569544:
Toshinobu Hayashi leads a 2026 multicentre retrospective study of whether continuous pharmacist support keeps gastric cancer patients on full-dose S-1 chemotherapy after surgery. Records for 225 patients at twelve institutions compared ongoing pharmacist monitoring for at least half the treatment against less regular contact, with statistics adjusted for starting differences.

Completion of all eight cycles was nearly identical between groups, near fifty-four percent, and dose changes were equally common. Patients with continuous support, though, maintained a higher share of their planned dose over time. The benefit is about dose intensity rather than finishing, a distinction that matters when judging pharmacy services in cancer care.
pmc-13571344:
Raid Faraj and colleagues report, in a 2026 case, a 50-year-old woman whose heart artery was blocked mid-procedure by a torn piece of her own wrist artery wall. She had come for a stent procedure through the wrist after exertional symptoms and a positive stress test showed a tight narrowing in a major heart artery.

Pushing the catheter through a resistant, spasming wrist artery proved difficult and required a longer sheath. New images then showed a hazy blockage at a branch point, with chest pain and heart attack changes. Suction restored flow and retrieved a three-centimeter fragment, confirmed under the microscope as artery wall with all three layers. Wrist flow stayed intact, yet the lesson on gentle catheter handling is sharp.
pmc-13572044:
Na'ama Epstein-Rigbi and colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, how two receptors on innate immune cells shift during oral immunotherapy for food allergy. This treatment feeds patients slowly rising doses of the food they react to. Such therapy can desensitize patients and sometimes leave lasting tolerance, driven mainly by regulatory T cells and calming signals, while the role of front-line cells such as eosinophils and monocytes stayed unclear.

The receptors under study belong to the CD300 family, one activating and one inhibitory, both sensing fatty molecules on cell surfaces. Tracking their levels during therapy tests whether these cells merely follow the calmer environment or actively help build tolerance. The answer could reveal new markers for judging whether treatment is working.
pmc-13572344:
Ya Liu and colleagues study, in a 2026 mouse and tissue study, a circular RNA called circ_0001313 that runs high in colorectal cancer and may help tumors hide from the immune system.
