pmc-13573344:
Sarah M Griffiths, with six colleagues, reports a 2026 gene study of an endangered fish found only in the Galápagos Islands. The white-spotted sand bass, called camotillo, feeds local small-scale fishing and has declined hard in recent decades. It sits on the endangered list, yet nothing was known about how its populations connect across the reserve.

The team sampled the fish across the Galápagos Marine Reserve and read its genes for variety and mixing. Their headline results point to high connection between sites and rich genetic variety within the stock. That pattern suggests larvae or adults move widely enough to link local groups into one broad population. For managers, wide links mean local losses can be refilled from elsewhere, but also that harm can spread. The gene map gives a first base for guarding this endemic fish.
pmc-13573444:
Florian Reizine, with a large multicentre team, reports a 2026 study that sorts intensive care patients with a fungal blood infection into three types. Records covered 492 patients from 16 French intensive care units, treated from 2015 to 2023. A blind clustering method grouped patients by their starting traits. One group held mostly blood cancer patients with deep immune suppression. A second held older patients, many with liver cirrhosis and gut-source infection. A third held younger patients with catheter-source infection and lower severity. Death at 90 days ran near 63 percent overall and split by group, from about half to near three quarters. pmc-13575644:
Gauri Kalra, Apurva Mishra, Kusum Bharti, and Vijay Prakash Mathur review how parenting style shapes a child's dental visit. Their review, from twenty twenty-six, links home style to two outcomes. One is how the child behaves in the dental chair. The other is how much tooth decay the child has had.

Decay results were too mixed to pool, so they are told as a story. Parents who had bad dental visits themselves may pass fear on, the authors note.
pmc-13576844:

Four materials went into the soak: a 3D-printed composite, lithium disilicate, a ceramic network filled with polymer, and a nanoceramic resin block. Specimens sat in hydrochloric acid and cola, with distilled water as the control, and color, clarity, roughness, and hardness were checked before soaking and again after.

Lithium disilicate resisted acid best on both optical and mechanical measures, while the 3D-printed resin proved least stable. Stomach acid damaged the materials more than cola did, and water changed almost nothing. Dentists choosing materials for patients with reflux or heavy soft-drink intake should weigh this ranking, the authors conclude.
pmc-13577244:
Durrheim and co-authors argue that measles can act as both a tracer and a tugboat for vaccine systems. Measles spreads so fast that outbreaks expose weak spots in coverage and care access. Its return worldwide also reflects conflict, displacement, doubt, and low funding.

Bill Foege, a leader in wiping out smallpox, held that measles eradication could cut health gaps. Chasing it demands high coverage, sharp disease tracking, good labs, and fast outbreak response. Those same strengths build sturdy health systems overall. The authors tie this case to the Immunization Agenda 2030 and its equity goals.
pmc-13578244:
Júlia Gisbert-Pérez and co-authors survey problem gaming among Mexican university students in a 2026 study of 712 young adults. About two in a hundred met the study bar for likely gaming disorder, rising to about five in a hundred among those who play. Long weekly hours and play driven by escape or by violent thrills went with higher risk.

Impulsive traits, above all giving up too soon on hard tasks, also raised the odds. Playing for fun, feeling backed by friends, and skill at reading one's own feelings all linked to lower risk. Support from peers stood out in the final model, so the authors call for campus programs shaped to local culture that build peer ties and steady habits.
pmc-13578344:
Alain Miffre and colleagues offer a 2026 lab method for a key trait of dust and other particles floating in air. Laser radar systems, called lidar, read the sky by how particles block light and bounce it back. The ratio of those two measures helps name the particle type, yet it is hard to pin down for odd shaped grains.

Their method pairs a straight back scatter test with a ring down test that times how fast light fades in a mirrored tube. No guess about grain size, shape, or makeup is needed. Water drops checked the setup against known theory first. Desert dust then gave a set ratio at green light, plus a companion measure of how the grains twist light, both offered for checking sky models.
pmc-13578844:
Ruyu Yan and colleagues used linked health records from British Columbia to compare when tapering off opioid agonist treatment is safest. Guidelines recommend this treatment as long-term care, yet many patients wish to stop eventually, and guidance on timing is thin. The study followed people who completed induction with methadone or buprenorphine/naloxone between 2010 and 2020.

Starting a taper within three months raised the odds of finishing it sharply, for both drugs, but also raised the risk of death compared with tapering after twelve to forty-eight months. The same trade-off appeared at three to six months and six to twelve months. Early tapering therefore offers a better chance of completion at a real cost in safety.
pmc-13579844:
Shatong Zhao and a team of co-authors probe why prenatal valproic acid exposure tilts male offspring harder toward autism-like behavior. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. The epilepsy drug is a known developmental risk, and iron-driven cell death, ferroptosis, is a suspect mechanism.

Adolescent mice of both sexes, exposed before birth or at two weeks old, faced social and anxiety tests. Both sexes showed social deficits and anxiety, males clearly worse. Brain sections from the prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and striatum were stained and counted. Biochemical assays, microscopy, and protein blots tracked the ferroptosis machinery. The prefrontal cortex emerged as a sex-sensitive hotspot. Comparing exposure windows in males tested whether timing softens the blow.
pmc-13580044:
Xue-Er Cheng and colleagues analyzed global syphilis trends in two thousand twenty-six. Syphilis is rising again among women of reproductive age. It threatens both reproductive and maternal health. The team used global burden estimates across many countries. Data covered three decades of incidence and prevalence. Models projected the burden forward to two thousand forty-six.

Cases concentrated in poorer regions worldwide. Women in their twenties carried the highest burden. Population growth drove much of the case increase. Inequality measures compared rich and poor settings. Both absolute and relative gaps were tracked. Health planners gain a forecast for prevention programs. Pregnant women need screening most urgently.
pmc-13580344:
Shuaiwei Guo and a large team of co-authors hunt blood proteins that flag neck artery plaque, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. They enrolled 128 people: forty-one with stable plaque, forty-nine with unstable plaque, and thirty-eight healthy controls. Ultrasound judged each plaque's state.

Seven set proteins were measured in blood, led by agrin and ADAMTS8. Agrin ran clearly higher in plaque patients than in controls. The team scored how well each protein, and the set combined, split plaque from no plaque and stable from unstable. Blood markers, they argue, could widen screening beyond scans.
pmc-13581444:
Caleb Wilson, Zoë York, and Flavius Balacenoiu test newer insecticides against the emerald ash borer in central Kentucky, in a study dated twenty twenty-six. This invasive beetle kills ash trees across the United States. The common sprays used against it harm helpful insects and face growing limits. The team drenched forty-one young white ash trees with two diamide insecticides at three rates each.

Six months later, only the highest rate of one spray cut beetle larva counts well below untreated trees. Three treatments lowered attacks by one helpful wasp, while woodpecker feeding was unchanged. Oddly, a wasp species never released in Kentucky was already present, the farthest south it has been found established. The authors see one spray as a workable swap for older chemicals.
pmc-13581744:
Ziran Lei and four co-authors report a rare airway case in a 2026 paper. A woman in her mid thirties had worsening breathlessness and wheezing for a month. Scans and a camera exam found a single polyp growing inside her windpipe, narrowing it by over half at the tightest point. Such growths are usually cancerous, so the team moved fast.

An emergency procedure froze and removed the growth, bringing quick relief. Lab work showed reactive tissue, not cancer, with signs of a common virus in some immune cells. Gene testing confirmed abundant virus in the tissue. The authors stress that full lab workup avoids misdiagnosis in rare airway lesions, and that follow-up should watch for regrowth.
pmc-13582544:
Wenting Yu and Chenggang Wu published this study in 2026 on students training to be interpreters. The work is hard on mind and feelings, and the authors ask what keeps students engaged in learning it. They surveyed 306 students at five universities in China. The study links three things: resilience, the ways students manage feelings, and engagement in their studies.

Two such ways were compared. Reframing a situation in a better light, called cognitive reappraisal, went with resilience and with stronger engagement on every measure. Hiding feelings showed no such links. In the authors' model, reframing carried part of resilience's effect on engagement, between a quarter and a half depending on the measure. Because everything was measured at once, they caution that the arrows may not run in the direction drawn.
pmc-13582644:
Elyette Lugo and colleagues survey spine surgeons worldwide on judging neck fusion healing. Their survey study from twenty twenty-six exposes wide practice variation. After neck disc surgery, doctors must confirm bones have fused. No single accepted rule defines a successful fusion check.

Thirty survey questions went to leading cervical spine experts. Four in ten invited experts completed the survey. Plate fixation dominated preferences at all surgery levels. Metal cages were the most chosen spacer devices. Imaging choices and fusion criteria varied substantially between surgeons. Follow-up length hinged on fusion status and patient satisfaction. Standard criteria would make research and care more comparable.
pmc-13582744:
Valerio Foschi and colleagues review thermospermine, a plant growth chemical with two jobs, in a 2026 paper. The compound, a twin of the common spermine, is made mostly in stem plumbing tissue by one named gene. Plants missing that gene grow dwarfed with too much woody plumbing, a clue found in the model plant Arabidopsis decades ago.

Later work showed the compound reins in wood growth by steering how certain messages get read into protein, with a marked spot on the protein building machine as its grip point. The authors ask for studies in simple plants and algae to find its first job.

pmc-13589944:
