Xingyun Shi and colleagues published a 2026 chromosome-level genome assembly for the fungus that causes tea anthracnose, a leaf disease that cuts tea yield and quality in China. The fungus, Sinodiscula theae-sinensis, had no good reference genome, which blocked work on how it infects and how it relates to close cousins on tea. The team combined three sequencing technologies to close that gap.

Long-read and short-read sequencing, plus a chromosome-shaping method, produced an assembly of about forty-one million DNA letters. Nearly the whole genome landed on nine chromosomes, and a completeness check against standard fungal genes scored above ninety-eight percent. The team predicted just under ten thousand protein-coding genes, with repeat sequences making up a small slice of the genome. They present the assembly as a reference for studying how this pathogen attacks tea and how its family evolved.
pmc-13624044:
Ashlyn Austin and three co-authors review the tools for profiling animal odours and putting them to work in managing animals. Smell runs much of animal communication, from mating signals to predator warnings, and the chemistry behind it lies in volatile organic compounds, light molecules that evaporate easily. Capturing those molecules faithfully is the craft this review teaches.

Profiling runs in three steps: collecting the scent, moving it into an instrument, and identifying its parts. The gold standard detector is gas chromatography with mass spectrometry, usually fed by headspace sampling or tiny fibre collectors that trap scent from the air above a sample. Liquid extraction still matters for heavier, stickier compounds. Newer options sniff samples directly or use electronic noses, trading detail for speed. No single route wins everywhere, the authors stress: the method must match the target molecules, or the odour story gets distorted.
pmc-13624244:
Leslye F Conde leads a report of a swallowed fish bone that migrated into the body's largest vein, the inferior vena cava, and triggered a blood clot. The patient, a seventy-year-old woman treated for advanced bile duct cancer, arrived with a month of night sweats, chills, and abdominal pain. Scans showed the clot holding a foreign body reaching into a kidney vein, plus a clot fragment in the lung.

X-ray guidance could barely show the bone, so the team threaded an ultrasound probe inside the vein to locate it within the clot. A snare failed to grip it, and operators switched to rat-tooth forceps, pulling it out under X-ray and live ultrasound views. The patient went home without symptoms on blood thinners, and a later scan showed the clot and inflammation resolved. The authors recommend intravascular ultrasound when foreign bodies defeat ordinary imaging.
pmc-13624444:
Wajiha Zia and three colleagues test whether graphene strengthens the acrylic used for denture bases. Polymethyl methacrylate is the standard denture material but bends and breaks too easily. The team made seventy-six specimens, half with a quarter percent graphene mixed in, and subjected half of each group to thermocycling that simulates mouth aging.

Graphene-reinforced specimens showed higher flexural strength and stiffness in both aged and unaged conditions. After thermocycling the strength advantage reached statistical significance, while aging itself mainly affected stiffness rather than strength. The authors conclude a small graphene addition genuinely improves a workhorse dental material, a step toward dentures that survive longer in service.
pmc-13625944:
Noora Puusa, Eeva Harju, Maija-Liisa Kalliomäki, and Elina Haavisto gather what is known about opioids for children with cancer and how families feel about them. Their integrative review searched four databases in August 2023, updated the sweep through 2024, and kept sixteen studies. Morphine and fentanyl were the workhorse drugs, given mostly by vein or by mouth and gut routes, for pain that can be severe across treatment.

Family research proved thin. Parents voiced worry about opioids, sometimes wanting to refuse them, yet also reported satisfaction when pain eased, and they asked for fuller information and guidance. Studies of brothers and sisters were almost absent. The authors call for staff training and research that follows families through each phase of a child's cancer.
pmc-13626144:
Noor Abu Eid and four co-authors measure how common anemia is among pregnant women in central Jordan, and what raises the risk. They surveyed 297 women at three medical facilities between August and November 2023, asking about background, pregnancy history, food habits, and anemia knowledge, and they checked hemoglobin values. Two statistical models, a standard regression and a small neural network, agreed on the main patterns and sorted women with fair accuracy.

Just over half the women were anemic. Risk rose in later pregnancy and after several prior abortions, while women taking nutritional supplements were far less likely to be anemic. The authors press for tighter antenatal screening and focused food support, since anemia in pregnancy endangers both mother and child and remains stubbornly common in the region.
pmc-13626344:
Chee Luan Lim and colleagues survey adults at a public clinic in central Singapore about advance care planning, the talks that record wishes for future treatment. Uptake in Singapore lags despite wide agreement on its worth, so the team handed out questionnaires in three languages to patients aged twenty-one and over. Of 471 forms, 363 came back complete, from adults averaging fifty-six years old, and the survey rated how helpful and how burdensome planning felt.

Planning scored as clearly beneficial and barely burdensome. Fear of death was the top reason people dodged the talk, named by about a quarter, yet that fear faded with age, chronic illness, and family experience of serious sickness. A brush with cancer or a hospitalized relative warmed attitudes, which suggests timing conversations to life experience.
pmc-13627144:
Rebecca Aguiar and co-authors study, in twenty twenty-six, whether children's wrist fractures get fair follow-up care regardless of family means. After a first closed reduction and cast, some distal radius fractures slip and need repeat reduction or surgery. Disparities are known in adult bone care, less so in children. The cohort held two thousand seventy-two young patients across centers. Two hundred seventy lost reduction after the first fix. The team compared second procedure rates by race, insurance, neighborhood opportunity and deprivation scores, and distance to the center.

Thirty-five children, about thirteen percent, had a second procedure, at a median of twelve days. Those needing one had greater fracture angulation at baseline. Models clustered by site weighed how social factors shifted the odds of intervention.
pmc-13629244:
Ismael Fernández-Fernández and eight colleagues mined routine nursing records from seven public hospitals. They described how vein access devices are used, and how often they fail. These devices are the tubes placed in veins for treatment. Their 2026 study captured over 200,000 device episodes. All were in hospitalised adults over one year.

Short vein catheters dominated practice. Yet they stayed in place the shortest time and failed most often. Medium and long devices lasted longer with fewer failures. Their use varied unevenly across hospitals. Gaps in the records were widespread. Key details were missing from many files. The authors urge matching device choice to expected treatment length. They also urge standard records. Hospitals could then compare care and cut repeat insertions.
pmc-13629544:
Daniel Schumacher and colleagues introduced a paper collection on competency-based training in 2026. Health training is shifting toward proven competence. The shift is expanding fast worldwide. This foreword frames a series of papers. The papers give practical implementation guidance. Educators and programme leaders are the audience.

Good rollout needs adaptive change, they argue. Core parts must stay faithful, though. Learner and supervisor relationships matter greatly. Local context should shape each programme. Implementation itself needs systematic study. Outcomes need study as well. Together, the papers support careful global adoption. Local teams still must adapt the guidance.
pmc-13630844:
Rachel Blue and seven colleagues measured what three surgical routes to the foramen magnum let a surgeon reach and do. They worked in five cadaveric heads. This gateway at the skull base is crowded with arteries and lower cranial nerves. Choosing between a through-the-nose route, a side route behind the ear, or both has rested largely on judgement.

Guidance tools and 3D imaging measured working freedom, angles of attack, and exposed volume at key landmarks. The side route gave far more freedom and volume. Most of it sat behind and to the side. The nasal route offered a narrow direct path to the front and middle. Combining both maximised total access. The authors turn the numbers into guidance. Approach can now be matched to lesion position with more confidence.
pmc-13630944:
Donglai Li and three colleagues reviewed what vitamin D signalling does to the beta cells of the pancreas. These cells make insulin, and their loss drives diabetes. The team gathered 26 lab studies. They spanned cell cultures, isolated tissue, and animal models. The studies tested vitamin D itself, its analogues, or direct activation of its receptor.

Protection was the dominant pattern. Vitamin D blunted beta cell death from many triggers. They included inflammatory signals, oxidative stress, excess sugar or fat, and chemical toxins. It worked through quieter inflammatory paths and steadier cell powerhouses. It also eased stress responses while keeping insulin output and cell identity. One exception sat in insulinoma cell models. There the active hormone sometimes restrained growth instead. The authors read the effect as real but context-bound.
pmc-13632544:
G. R. Aizetullova and four colleagues published this 2026 registry study, written in Russian, on parathyroid gland disease in the Chuvash Republic. The parathyroid glands control blood calcium by releasing a hormone, and overproduction causes the common disorder called primary hyperparathyroidism. The team drew on a nationwide Russian registry of such patients. They reviewed cases followed from 2014 to 2025 at a regional veterans' hospital.

The regional rate came to roughly seventy-three cases per one hundred thousand people. Nearly nine in ten patients were women, mostly in older age groups. Cases clustered in the cities of Cheboksary and Novocheboksarsk rather than spreading evenly across the republic. Detection has risen sharply in recent years. The authors credit better access to specialist care, while also raising possible environmental factors such as trace element balance in local water. They judge the registry a proven tool for planning endocrine services.
pmc-13633344:
Fleischer and a team including Rasche survey myeloma patients on treatment free intervals in twenty twenty-six. Multiple myeloma care often involves continuous therapy and frequent hospital contact. Those contacts burden patients in body, mind, and logistics. The team asked how patients value breaks between treatments.

One hundred patients at a German centre answered a mixed methods survey over twelve months. About half rated breaks between inpatient treatments as maximally important. Separation from family was the top inpatient stressor reported. Regular check ups reassured most patients, though some found them burdensome. Only seven percent accepted higher relapse risk for longer breaks. Preferred break lengths varied widely. The authors support trials of preference sensitive scheduling.
pmc-13634744:
Patryk Sztandarski and seven colleagues reviewed how scientists measure injuries that broiler chickens suffer while being caught before slaughter. Catch damage serves as a welfare and meat quality indicator, yet studies define and measure it in wildly different ways. The team searched the literature for studies of injuries tied to catching and preslaughter handling. They compared injury definitions, scoring systems, sampling choices, and how each study decided where an injury came from.

Assessment ranged from farm checks and holding-area inspections to slaughter line scoring, company records, camera systems, and blood markers. Many studies leaned on bruising, fractures, or dead-on-arrival counts, which blend damage from every preslaughter stage rather than catching alone. Few studies separated fresh injuries from old ones, and reporting of observer training was spotty. The authors argue these gaps bias results and block comparison between studies. They call for shared definitions and standard scoring.
pmc-13639644:
Funa and Gabay wrote a letter in 2026 extending a study of switching diabetes patients from oral semaglutide to weekly tirzepatide. The original study found quality of life improved after the switch, even though blood sugar and weight barely changed at three months. The letter argues that GLP-1/GIP therapy, which mimics two gut hormones, should be judged by burden, expectations, and daily routine as well as by metabolism.

They suggest smaller rice portions, healthier main dishes, fewer sugary drinks, and planning for celebration meals without stigma. They warn that patients priced out of supervised care may buy unverified products online, with quality and dosing risks. Future studies, they argue, should track quality of life, motives, affordability, sourcing, and side effects together.
pmc-13642044:
Thomas Sahlström Månsson and two colleagues present a Swedish cohort study on timing of effective antibiotics in bloodstream infections caused by drug-resistant bacteria. Patients often start on a drug the bacteria resist, and whether that early mismatch harms them was uncertain.

The multicenter review covered 644 patients in southern Sweden from 2013 to 2022, and nearly half received ineffective first therapy for over a day. That delay showed no significant link with thirty-day death, intensive care admission after adjustment, or longer hospital stay. The authors say the finding could support holding back the strongest antibiotics in low-resistance settings.
pmc-13642344:
Li and a large team identify a guardian of germ cell identity in this 2026 developmental biology study. Primordial germ cells are the embryonic precursors of sperm and eggs. They must silence the ordinary body-cell program while they migrate to the future gonads. The study shows an enzyme called TRIM37 enforces that silence.

Mouse embryos lacking TRIM37 began losing germ cells at embryonic day 9.5 and had none left by day 12.5 of development in the team's counts, with survivors drifting toward body-cell states. TRIM37 physically binds a partner protein, TRIM28, tags it with ubiquitin, and the pair enters the nucleus to keep body-cell genes locked down, working alongside a factor called AP2 gamma. Forcing TRIM37 out of the nucleus, crippling its tagging activity, or mutating the tag sites on TRIM28 all broke germ cell maintenance. The complex emerges as a fate safeguard during migration.
pmc-13642544:
Ali Panahpour and two colleagues present a 2026 light study that brings a trick called photonic doping into near-infrared light. In this trick, tiny specks inside a near-zero material make it act in odd ways, like a perfect magnetic mirror. Losses had kept the trick in the microwave range until now.

The team set a neat array of tiny glass-like beads inside a low-loss layered cavity that acts as near-zero material near its cutoff. The build gave sharp, lone tones across several wave orders, with a strong boost to magnetic light effects. The authors say this opens fine spectroscopy, lasers, and tuned light emission at these wavelengths.
pmc-13642944:
Yi-Shian Peng and Sen-Yung Hsieh present a 2026 analysis of whether two kinds of brain support cells age in step with each other. Microglia guard the brain, while oligodendrocytes insulate nerve fibers, and each had been studied mostly on its own.

Using mouse single-cell data from embryo to twenty-four months, the team found both cell types were the most changeable glial groups across life. Late in life their inflammatory and senescence programs rose together with near-perfect timing agreement, while astrocyte activity centered on development. The authors propose shared timing programs that may feed age-related brain vulnerability.
pmc-13644444:
Peixin Wang and co-authors test whether two gene methylation marks spot dangerous cervical cell changes equally well before and after menopause. Their study appeared in 2026. The marks, on the PAX1 and JAM3 genes, promise to triage women after abnormal screening. The team reviewed 705 women who had colposcopy at a Chinese center, 192 of them postmenopausal, and graded each against tissue results.

In postmenopausal women the tests shone: sensitivity near ninety and eighty-two percent for the two marks. In younger women both hovered near sixty percent. Combined use also favored the older group. The authors say menopause changes the test's worth, and triage rules should be set separately for the two groups rather than pooled.
pmc-13645544:
Muhammet Talha Han and eight colleagues surveyed university students in Türkiye about sport attitudes, life satisfaction, and mental toughness under pressure, which they call psychological resilience. Their sample held 481 undergraduates at two universities. Students completed three short scales covering views on sport, satisfaction with life, and resilience. The team then tested whether resilience sits between the other two measures.

Students who viewed sport more warmly also reported higher resilience, and resilience in turn tracked with higher life satisfaction. A direct link between sport attitudes and satisfaction remained even after resilience was counted. The authors stress that these are links, not proof of cause, since the survey ran once and never measured real sport participation. Even so, the results hint that campus sport culture may support student well-being.
pmc-13645744:
Laia Monserrat and twenty-six colleagues test a new treatment idea for metastatic breast cancer that responds to estrogen, in a 2026 study. Most such cancers also carry the androgen receptor, a target usually linked with male hormones. The team gave a drug called EP0062, which activates that receptor, to tumor models grown from patient tissue in mice. They compared its effect with drugs that block estrogen signaling.

The new drug shrank tumors about as well as the estrogen-blocking drugs, even in tumors carrying mutations linked with drug resistance. Tumors with changes in a gene called GATA3 seemed especially sensitive. Gene activity patterns tied to sensitivity were found, and adding a second drug helped some resistant tumors respond. The authors propose receptor activation as a fresh option for patients whose cancers no longer answer standard hormone therapy.
pmc-13646044:
Hua Ren and eight colleagues pool randomized trials on magnetic brain stimulation as a treatment for mild cognitive impairment, an early stage of memory and thinking decline. The method, called rTMS, pulses magnetic fields through the skull to nudge brain activity without surgery. Fourteen studies with fifteen datasets compared real stimulation against sham treatment. Thinking was scored with standard tests of memory and mental state.

Scores after treatment favored real stimulation on all three test types used. Results varied a great deal between studies, which weakens confidence in any single number. The effect shifted with stimulation speed and with the brain spot targeted. Side effects did not rise clearly compared with sham treatment. The authors say the method may help, while calling for larger, tighter trials with uniform methods before clinics adopt it widely.
pmc-13649444:
Norazlina Zamberi and Zalmizy Hussin argue that stress training for police investigators must fix the workplace, not just the officer. Detectives face heavy case loads, grim digital proof, and tight scrutiny, and burnout harms both their health and the quality of their work. Their piece draws on studies from 2022 to 2026.

Research they cite shows that how a force is run shapes stress more than trauma exposure alone. Control over workload, debriefs, and feedback on case outcomes all eased harm. They propose two pillars of training: one that builds each officer's coping skills, and one that reshapes leadership, climate, and work systems. Resilience, they say, is built by the structure around the officer.
pmc-13649644:
Anuj Punnoose and four colleagues designed a pre-surgery exercise plan for people set to have keyhole hip surgery for a hip socket clash, in a study published in 2026. Whether such prehabilitation helps in this group was unknown. They built the plan step by step under a national framework for complex health programmes.

Patient input shaped the plan, past trials set dose and format, world experts agreed on core targets, and muscle tests graded each move by effort and pain risk. The result is an eight-week, two-phase plan of strength, motion, balance, heart fitness, and teaching, done partly at home with digital checks. Moves that jam the hip were cut out. A small trial will now test if the plan is workable and safe.
pmc-13649944:
Xingqi Wang and a team of co-authors set out a whole-system view of pelvic floor stress disorders in women, in two thousand twenty-six. These disorders stem from injury to the support structures of the pelvic floor and from stress imbalance across them. Pregnancy, vaginal birth, and age are among the main linked factors, and such disorders form most pelvic floor problems.

The authors argue that care should treat the pelvic floor as one biomechanical system, not a set of separate symptoms. Their perspective reviews advances, current challenges, and future directions in the field. They call for a shift from symptom-oriented care to mechanism-based management. That shift rests on cause, function, and the whole floor's mechanics.
pmc-13650044:
Nouhaila Ben Khizzou, Mourad Aarabe, Lhoussaine Alla, and Ahmed Benjelloun review AI-managed patient pathways in this two thousand twenty-six review and meta-analysis. Hospitals hope AI can smooth care pathways, cut stays, and prevent readmissions. Under PRISMA twenty twenty, the authors searched Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed. Eligible studies covered hospital patients whose care followed the clinical pathway method with AI help. Designs included trials, before-and-after studies, and quasi-experimental ones. Thirty-one studies qualified.

Most studies reported good money outcomes: shorter hospital stays and fewer readmissions under AI-assisted pathways. The reviewers note report quality limits firm conclusions, since random sequence generation was well described in only twenty-four studies, partial in five, and poor in two, hampering bias checks. Data were pulled with structured methods on the Covidence platform. The authors present a cautiously good verdict on AI pathway tuning pending stronger trials.
pmc-13651044:
Jordana Salma and twelve co-authors, in 2026, assess an exercise program built with immigrant South Asian older women in Edmonton, Canada. The eight-week STRONG program mixed online health education with in-person exercise, and the review used an implementation framework sharpened by a lens on gender, migration, and age.

Thirty-four women took part. Trusted ties, community champions, and family backing drew women in, and attendance stayed high, with women reporting better physical function and social ties. Families formed an unspoken contract, supplying digital help and rides, while South Asian facilitators merged medical skill with holistic, strength-based care. Staying power was threatened by structural inequities such as transport and digital access, though ties with local groups helped it last. The authors argue that programs succeed when built on relational safety, and that lasting change means fixing the barriers around them, not only motivating individuals.
pmc-13651744:
M Yunus Pamukoglu and two co-authors clean a priority herbicide out of water with a nanocomposite grown the green way. Atrazine, a weed killer that lingers, flagged under European water rules, was the target. Their adsorbent blends amine-decorated silica with iron nanoparticles made using licorice root extract as the reducing and stabilizing agent.

Benchmarks from the group's earlier work confirmed a porous structure with ample surface area. A statistical response-surface design varied acidity, starting herbicide strength, and adsorbent dose together, and a checked quadratic model located the sweet spot near neutral acidity with a low dose. Equilibrium behavior matched a model of layered, varied-energy binding, and the uptake speed followed chemistry-controlled kinetics. Outside confirmation runs matched the predicted removal, and capacity reached a respectable level for a lab material. The authors frame the result as proof of concept for green-made cleaners of pesticide contamination.
pmc-13669044:
Thorsten Meiser and colleagues teach researchers to correct for the habits people bring to rating scales, in this tutorial from twenty twenty-six. Some respondents hug the middle of a scale; others leap to the extremes. These response styles have nothing to do with the questions, yet they bend the scores and muddy what the scale claims to measure.

The tutorial walks through two model families, IRT and IRTree, that split each answer into the trait of interest and the style behind it. Worked in the R statistics language, the lesson covers building the models, fitting them, and reading the results. A dataset on self-rated metacognitive competence shows the fix in action: trait scores shift as style is stripped out, in the directions theory predicts. The authors end with new developments in this corner of psychometrics.
pmc-13676844:
Yuetong Guo and Libo Shi investigate a long non-coding RNA, LINC01537, that runs high in breast cancer and tracks with poor survival. Working in two aggressive cell lines, they measured what happens when the RNA is knocked down, and mapped the regulatory chain it sits in.

Knockdown slowed proliferation, migration, and invasion while promoting cell death. The RNA works as a sponge: it soaks up a tumor-suppressing microRNA, freeing the growth-promoting gene EZH2 from restraint. Blocking the microRNA rescued the cancer cells from the knockdown's effects, confirming the chain. The authors nominate the axis as a therapeutic candidate for triple-negative and HER2-positive breast cancers, pending animal validation.
pmc-13679144:
Rajendran Kishore Kumar, Suryaa Manoharan, Ekambaram Perumal, and Balasubramanian Murugesapandian build a glowing probe that senses two targets in work dated two thousand twenty-six. The probe is based on a coumarin dye and lights up more when its parts clump in water-rich mixes. One target is cobalt ions, which matter for both health and the environment.

The probe glows green, and cobalt turns that glow off at very low levels, well below one part per billion range in scale terms the authors report as a tight bound. When ATP, the cell energy carrier, is added, the glow comes back, which allows repeat sensing. The team also shows logic-gate use, on-site tests, and imaging in cells.
pmc-13680944:
Bassem Chamma and co-authors reviewed studies comparing two operations for craniosynostosis, a birth condition where skull bones fuse early and deform the head and face. Both operations move the midface forward: one moves forehead and midface as a single block, the other moves it alone. The team searched the literature and gathered 63 articles, extracting data on face changes, eye, airway, and brain effects, plus infections and appearance problems.

The single-block operation moved the midface further on average, and nearly all its patients had device-based lengthening, compared with about two-thirds for the other operation. Both helped breathing during sleep to a similar degree. The single-block operation carried higher rates of spinal fluid leaks, seizures, and meningitis. The authors conclude both operations work, with a trade-off between greater movement and greater risk, and call for research on appearance and sleep outcomes.
pmc-13682444:
Taylor J. Stevenson and colleagues studied waste clearance in Parkinson's disease in 2026. Parkinson's builds up clumps of a protein called alpha-synuclein. Clumps also gather in the fluid around the brain. Their harmful role there was poorly understood. The team found the protein in the brain's tough outer covering too. Mouse models then tested cause and effect. Protein placed at brain borders changed local immune behavior. It also disrupted waste clearance from the brain.

One inflammatory signal rose in the fluid. That signal was tumor necrosis factor. Both it and the protein clumps harmed drainage cells. Those cells line the lymph vessels that clear the brain. The authors position border immunity as a disease contributor. Border tissues become candidate treatment targets under this view. The work shifts attention from brain cells alone.
pmc-13683044:
Laurel Raffington leads a large team reporting a cash gift trial in this twenty twenty-six paper. Low-income mothers in the United States got a monthly gift, either a few hundred dollars or a small sum, during their child's first four years. The team asked whether the larger gift left marks on body aging and thinking, read from DNA patterns.

Saliva samples from hundreds of mothers and children gave two scores: one for pace of aging, one linked to thinking skills. As the team had predicted, children in the high-gift group aged more slowly by the DNA measure. The study tests whether income support can shape health from the earliest years.
pmc-2395244:
Haas, Salzberg, Zhu, and co-authors describe automated tools for annotating gene structure in organisms with nuclei. Their EVidenceModeler program predicts where protein-coding parts of genes lie. A companion program assembles aligned pieces of RNA evidence into full gene models.

Together, the tools weigh several kinds of evidence at once, including alternate spliced forms and untranslated regions at gene ends. Automation matters because hand annotation cannot keep pace with new genomes. Consistent computer annotation gives researchers a reliable first map of a genome's genes to test and refine.  Gene models from the pipeline feed directly into public genome databases.
pmc-2954944:
Levac, Colquhoun, and O'Brien advance the methodology of scoping studies, a way of mapping health research evidence. Scoping studies were growing in popularity when they wrote. A first framework for doing them had appeared in 2005, giving the approach an excellent foundation.

The authors argue that foundation now needs refinement as use spreads. They clarify steps and choices so scoping studies stay rigorous rather than loose summaries. Clearer methods help teams map what evidence exists on a topic before deciding whether a full systematic review is worthwhile.  The authors close by urging clearer reporting so future reviews can compare methods.
pmc-4053844:
Kim, Pertea, Trapnell, and their co-authors described TopHat two in 2013. TopHat is a widely used program that aligns RNA sequencing reads to a genome, handling the gaps where introns have been spliced out. The new version added many major upgrades to the first release.

TopHat two can align reads of varied lengths from the newest sequencing machines. It also allows for insertions, deletions, and gene fusions, which older handling could miss. Accurate alignment is the step that lets labs count gene activity and find new transcripts. This update kept a core RNA-seq tool fit for fast-changing data.
pmc-5563544:
Yoon, Ha, Kwon, and their team launched EzBioCloud in 2017, a database for naming bacteria and archaea. New sequencing tools let labs name microbes from their genome data with far more precision than before. The species rules in use, though, rest on gene comparisons that old databases handled in patchy ways.

EzBioCloud unites two data types in one taxonomically consistent system: the standard 16S marker gene and whole-genome assemblies. A user can look up an unknown strain and get a name backed by a curated reference. Sound, shared naming matters in clinics, in food safety checks, and in surveys of soil and water. Mixed names had long confused all three.
pmc-7056644:
Pauli Virtanen, Ralf Gommers, Travis Oliphant, and a large community presented SciPy 1.0 in 2020. SciPy is the open-source library of scientific algorithms for Python. Since its first release it became a de facto standard tool.

Hundreds of contributors built its optimization, statistics, signal processing, and numerical routines. Thousands of other packages depend on it, from physics to finance. The paper documents the library's structure and governance at its mature milestone. Nearly every Python data workflow touches SciPy somewhere, which makes the reference unusually far-reaching. The paper also serves as the citable record of the library's design and maintenance model.
pmc-7119644:
Matthew Maenner, Kelly Shaw, Jon Baio, and coauthors reported autism prevalence among eight-year-olds in this 2020 surveillance report. The ADDM Network tracks autism in children across sites in the United States. Consistent tracking shows whether rates are truly changing.

The report covers children who turned eight in the study year across the network's sites. About one in fifty-four children was identified with autism spectrum disorder. Boys were identified far more often than girls, and rates varied by site and record access. The figures guide planning for school and health services for autistic children.
pmc-7619544:
Ibrahim Knani leads a team that builds targeted fat bubbles for pancreas tumors. Their work from twenty twenty-six deals with liposomes that carry drugs. Old ways to add antibodies to bubbles are slow and bespoke.

Each old method needs chem change for each antibody used. That can twist the antibody and block its binding site. Their bubbles bear a catcher antibody on the surface. It grabs any cure antibody by its tail end fast. The binding face then points outward, ready to work. Cell tests showed sharp targeting with this set up.
podcast-dannyjones-SiBFtwbyv44:
Doctor Jack Kruse is a neurosurgeon who left conventional practice to preach a medicine of sunlight, circadian rhythm, and quantum biology. He joins Danny Jones to lay out his system. The episode's billing calls him exiled, and Kruse embraces the frame. He casts himself as a brain surgeon punished for telling truths about light and health. Those truths, he says, threaten profitable medicine. DARPA's mind control research is woven through his account.

Jones follows Kruse through the physics and the grievances alike. Parts of his advice, morning light, regular sleep, match mainstream guidance; his grander claims about quantum biology and agency plots are his own and are contested by his former profession. The episode preserves the full Kruse doctrine in his commanding style. Listeners can extract the practical core and judge the rest as they see fit.
podcast-joerogan-3qHkcs3kG44:
Investor and writer Naval Ravikant joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1309. Naval helped build AngelList and became known for short, sharp posts on wealth and happiness. Rogan gives him the show's full-length format to lay out his thinking without hurry.

Naval argues that wealth comes from owning assets and using leverage, not from trading hours for pay. He then turns to happiness, which he treats as a skill that can be trained like any other. The episode has become one of the show's most shared talks, prized for how much ground each short answer covers.
podcast-joerogan-Vt9K6kmpx44:
Joe Rogan turns to Jordan Peterson's new grasp of the Bible in a segment from his show. Peterson is the psychologist whose lectures on Bible tales drew a vast crowd. His turn to faith surprised fans and foes alike.

Rogan works through what Peterson says he found in the old tales: maps of how to live, not just rules from a god. He asks why a man of science was so moved by the book. The segment is short and warm. Listeners get a quick look at a famed shift. The library holds the file as an archive record of the talk.
podcast-joerogan-_bN4spt3744:
Biologist Richard Dawkins joins Joe Rogan for episode 1366 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Dawkins is one of the best known voices for evolution and against faith. His books shaped how a whole age talks about genes and God.

Dawkins and Rogan talk through the case for evolution and his hard line on religion. Rogan presses him on the pull of faith and on foes who call him cold. The talk is calm and sharp at once. Listeners get a famed mind at full length. The library keeps the episode as a record of a rare clash of world views.
poe-mesmeric-revelation-1844:
Edgar Allan Poe set Mesmeric Revelation in print in 1844. The form is a death bed talk held by art. A man in a mesmeric trance, close to death, speaks with the scribe. He tells what God, stuff, and the soul are past the veil of flesh.

Stuff is not dead, the voice holds, but one fine spread of force. Each grain of it can think, feel, and at last join the whole. Death is a shift, not an end, in this strange scheme. The tale is the most famed of Poe's works on the mesmeric creed.
quicherat-proces-jeanne-darc-vol2-1844:
Quicherat's second volume, printed in 1844, carries his Joan of Arc edition from sentence toward review. It completes the papers of the 1431 condemnation trial. It then opens the rehabilitation proceedings of 1455 and 1456, a full generation later.

The shift in the records is stark: the same deeds are read first as crimes, then as grounds for honor. Judges and clerks of the 1450s re-open each charge the first court had pressed. The volume bridges the fire at Rouen and the inquiry that undid its verdict. Readers watch a famous case reverse itself in its own papers.
religion-natural-and-revealed-1844: A garbled title page, stamped by a national library, is all that opens this work on religion, natural and revealed. Its full title joins natural theology to the moral bearings of phrenology and physiology. The doctrines taught by those studies, it says, are compared with those enjoined in the Scriptures. A further part is promised: a phrenological account of a future state, holiness, sin, rewards, punishments, depravity, a change of heart, will, foreordination, and fatalism. No author's name is legible, and no year is printed.
religion-natural-and-revealed-or-the-nat: Long pages of a scanner's notice about public domain books and proper use open this record, before any page of the work itself. Past that notice, a title page begins, misread by the scan in places: Religion; Natural and Revealed: or, The Natural Theology. There the matter shown ends. No author is named in what is printed here, no table of contents follows, and the further lines of the title page are cut off. The work's own argument cannot be reported from such a start.
sandby-mesmerism-opponents-1844:
George Sandby answered mesmerism's first British critics in Mesmerism and Its Opponents, from 1844. Sandby was a clergyman who had watched mesmeric cures at close range. His narrative of cases replies to doctors and editors who scorned the practice. Detailed case histories carry the weight of his argument.

Patients relieved of pain and fits tell their own part in his pages. The book records the first wave of English controversy over mesmerism. Charges of fraud and folly met charges of closed minds. Sandby writes as a witness more than a theorist. His cases fed the movement's early defense. The volume is a primary record of a public fight.
schiller-poems-first-period-1844:
The Poems of Schiller: First Period gathers the young Schiller's lyrics in the Bohn Standard Library translation. The poems date from his stormy first years as a writer, before Weimar classicism calmed his style. Some of them stand inside his early play The Robbers, sung or quoted by its outlaws.

Love, rage at tyrants, and wild joy in nature drive these early pieces. The verse is rough, bold, and full of youthful excess by design. Readers can hear the voice that shocked Germany in 1781 taking shape. The Bohn set sorted Schiller's poems by period so English readers could trace his growth. This first volume gives the raw material of the later master.
schiller-poems-second-period-1844:
Schiller's middle years produced the poems in this second-period volume of the Bohn translation. By then Schiller had settled into study, friendship with Goethe, and steady fame. The Song of the Bell, his most loved long poem, belongs to this era of his work.

In that poem the casting of a church bell frames the whole course of a human life. Birth, love, work, loss, and death pass in its stanzas like scenes at a foundry. Other pieces here treat art, gods, and the dignity of man. The voice is calmer than the young rebel's, but the moral fire remains. Lyric readers rank this period at the height of Schiller's power.
schiller-poems-suppressed-1844:
Schiller chose not to reprint some of his early poems, and the Bohn editors gathered those pieces as the Suppressed Poems. They complete the four-volume English set of his poetry. In them the young writer speaks without the guard he later kept on his work.

The suppressed pieces show sharper satire, bolder feeling, and rougher craft than he later allowed. Some attack named targets of his youth with open scorn. Others try forms and tones he soon outgrew and disowned. Scholars value the set because it shows growth honestly, false starts included. English readers in the Bohn volumes could meet the whole Schiller, not only the polished classic. The volume rewards those who like a poet unbuttoned.
schiller-poems-third-period-1844:
The late poems in this third-period Bohn volume include Schiller's great ballads of his Weimar years. The Diver sends a young page to the sea floor for a king's golden cup, twice. The Glove tests a lady's love with a cruel and famous gesture among wild beasts.

Other ballads treat hostages, cranes, and rings, each turning on fate and honor. Schiller wrote these pieces in friendly rivalry with Goethe in 1797, their ballad year. The tales move swiftly, with clear scenes and ringing morals that never preach. Generations of German schoolchildren learned them by heart. In English they remain the easiest gate into Schiller's poetry.
sir-perceval-of-galles-thornton-1844:
Sir Perceval of Galles is a Middle English romance preserved in the Thornton manuscript. J. O. Halliwell edited it for modern readers in 1844. It gives the Grail hero Perceval a rough, funny English shape, quite unlike the solemn French versions.

Perceval grows up wild in the woods, knowing nothing of courts or arms. His blunders are comic, but his strength is real, and he fights his way toward knighthood. The poem is kin to the Welsh tale of Peredur, retold in a northern voice. Readers meet the innocent fool of the Grail story at his most boisterous and earthy.
siris-a-chain-of-philosophical-reflexion:
A 1744 chain of philosophic reflections opens, in these worn pages, with verse in praise of tar. The poem hails the juice of the never-fading pine as cheap yet divine in virtue. Long-s type and rough scanning leave many lines hard to read, though the drift stays clear.

From lowly tar the verse climbs by gentle steps through air, fire, and aether to the highest skies. Sense, fancy, reason, and mind pursue truth's clue through nature's maze, the poem holds. A scorned mechanic who credits all to size and weight gets mocked for missing the spirit behind the scene.
slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of-slave: Slave Narratives gathers talks with former slaves into a folk history of slavery in the United States. The typed records were made by the Federal Writers' Project in 1936-1938 and put together by the Library of Congress project at Washington in 1941. One part is Volume II, the Arkansas Narratives, Part 5. Its list of those who spoke runs from Charlie McClendon and Lizzie McCloud through Avalena McConico, Ike McCoy, and Richard H. McDaniel.
snorri-heimskringla-laing-1844:
Samuel Laing published The Heimskringla; Or, Chronicle of the Kings of Norway in 1844, the first English translation of Snorri Sturluson's kings' sagas. Snorri, an Icelandic poet and chieftain, wrote the Heimskringla in the 1200s. It tells the story of Norway's kings from mythic times to his own age.

Sagas of kings such as Olaf Tryggvason, Saint Olaf, and Harald Hardrada fill the chronicle, drawn from poems and oral memory. Battles, voyages, and feuds move at saga pace, terse and vivid. Laing's version founded the study of Norse history in English. Readers who want the Vikings in their own tradition's telling still start with Snorri.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5044:
Gerald R. Ford gives three yearly addresses in one set. Their dates are January 15, 1975, January 19, 1976, and January 12, 1977. Three stars part each address from the next. The first looks back twenty-six years. A freshman member of Congress stood in the well of the House then. Sam Rayburn faced him as he swore the oath. That young fellow was full of high hopes.

Two days later that freshman stood at the chamber's back. President Truman reported on the state of the Union there. He told the 81st Congress that the state of the Union is good. Today that same man from Michigan stands in Truman's place. He must report the reverse to the house. The state of the Union is not good, Ford says. Millions of Americans lack work at this hour. Slump and rising prices press the land at once.
synopsis-of-phrenology-presenting-genera:
A Synopsis of Phrenology was printed at Boston by A. J. Wright in 1844. It is a fourth edition, revised. It presents the general principles of the science. It describes the mental organs and their location. It tells how the organs assist or counteract each other.

A fuller title page promises also the general principles of phrenology with a description of the peculiarities of the male and female head. No author's name is printed on the pages at hand; library marks give the year and a call number only. The little book belongs to the wave of cheap phrenology manuals that taught American readers to read character, talent, and temperament from the bumps and shape of the skull.
thackeray-barry-lyndon-1844:
William Makepeace Thackeray published Barry Lyndon in 1844, a novel in the form of a rogue's memoir. Redmond Barry is an Irish adventurer who tells his own story with great pride. He serves as a soldier, deserts, and becomes a gambler and cheat across Europe. He marries a rich widow to gain rank and wealth.

Barry boasts even as his schemes ruin others and himself. Thackeray lets the narrator expose his own vanity on every page. The book first appeared as The Luck of Barry Lyndon in a magazine. Its unreliable narrator was ahead of its time. Readers now prize its irony and pace.
the-brochure-series-of-architectural-ill:
The Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration, Volume I, Number 6, for June 1895, shows Renaissance Panels from Perugia. The plates give carved walnut panels from the choir stalls of the Church of San Pietro de' Casinense in Perugia. Stefano da Bergamo designed them in 1535. The piece calls them fine examples of the ornament of the later Italian Renaissance.

That form of ornament was first used in flat painted panels on pilasters, as in Raphael's work in the Vatican Loggia, drawn from Roman work found on the Palatine. The piece then quotes C. Howard Walker, from The Technology Architectural Review, on the two motives of such panels. One is a continuous scroll, rising from a strong base leaf in equal turns, left and right. The other, the usual one, grows from a central axis, the ornament spreading in symmetry on either side.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: No. 44 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated September 9, 1897. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a premium offer. The premium is a bound volume of the paper itself, sent post-paid. They are bound in cloth, with the title stamped on side and back. Part I contains the numbers from November 11, 1896 to February 18, 1897. Part II runs from February 25 to June 3, 1897.
the-knickerbocker-or-new-york-monthly-ma:
The February 1844 number of the Knickerbocker leads with Thomas Cole. His subject is Sicilian scenery and antiquities. The magazine is volume twenty-three, number two. Cole was the landscape painter. Travel's pleasure comes chiefly after the journey, he reflects. One sits by one's own fireside, free of fatigue. Describing distant wonders to untraveled friends is a harmless vanity. His sense of Sicily's beauty outlasted his European stay.

He gives the island its ancient frame. Sicily is the Mediterranean's largest island. It was once called Trinacria for its triangular shape. Its girth runs about six hundred miles. Three capes face Africa, Greece, and Italy. Etna towers above all like an enthroned spirit. It is visible a hundred miles at sea. Sicily was the granary of Rome. Enna's plain was famous for honey. Its spring flowers were so fragrant that hounds lost the scent. A painter's eye governs the whole account.

Volume twenty-three of the Knickerbocker was published by John Allen of Nassau Street in 1844. This January record presents the volume's title page and index start. Only that index opening is present here. The articles themselves do not appear. The list for A alone maps the magazine's range. J. G. Saxe's Apostrophe to an Old Hat appears. A lady writes on the rights of women. Thomas Cole climbs Mount Ætna. A buffalo hunter spends a night on the prairie. A winter trip to Trenton Falls follows.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, March 14, 1829, No. 360, illustrates the grand entrance to Hyde Park. Lord Burleigh's maxim heads the article: a realm gains more by one year's peace than ten years' war. Decimus Burton designed the entrance, a screen of fluted Ionic columns with three carriage archways, two foot entrances, and a lodge. The whole frontage extends about 107 feet.

The central entrance projects boldly on four columns, its side gateway columns turned to show two faces. A beautiful frieze decorates the central blocking, representing a naval and military triumphal procession. Mr. Henning the younger designed it, son of the modeler famed for his Elgin marbles reproductions, and the model showed in the Suffolk Street Gallery. Bramah manufactured the iron gates, bronzed and hung on gun-metal rings. Readers get peace celebrated in columns and a copied Parthenon procession.
the-trial-or-more-links-of-the-daisy-cha:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Trial, the 1864 sequel to The Daisy Chain, opens under a French epigraph about not asking frogs to vote on draining a marsh. Richard May, nearly thirty and incumbent of Cocksmoor though still looking like a young deacon, comes in to find a tea-cup waiting. Ethel reports their father gone out with Dr. Spencer toward illness in the Lower Pond Buildings, where a knell rings for a child dead, she believes, of scarlatina. Aubrey mimics the doctor's consternation.

Then letters from Edinburgh burst upon the room: five notes in one cover, which their father calls 'The Infants' Honeymoon' and means to file in the family archives. His own share, signed 'Still his own White Flower' with real daisies enclosed, pleased him deeply. Yonge resumes her family chronicle in pure dialogue, affection and parish trouble mixed from page one. A sibling record gives only the chapter list.
tob-13144:
Swami Vivekananda taught Bhakti Yoga, the path of devotion, in lectures later gathered as a book. Bhakti is love of God as the heart's way to the Absolute. Vivekananda spoke of it with the fire that marked all his teaching.

He treats prayer, ritual, images, and the guru, arguing that forms help love grow until it needs no props. Real bhakti, for him, asks nothing back and loves God for God's own sake. The talks move from outer worship to a love so full it ends all sense of separation, and they show the devotional side of Vedanta clearly.
tob-4144:
Griffith's verse Ramayana opens with volume one in 1870, and India's beloved epic found its English singer. Prince Rama, exiled from his father's court through a queen's demand, withdraws to the forest with his wife Sita and brother Lakshmana. There the demon king Ravana steals Sita away to Lanka.

The search for Sita, the alliance with the monkey hosts, and the march toward the island war all begin in this volume. Griffith's flowing lines carried Valmiki's Sanskrit to Victorian drawing rooms. Verified from the 1919 edition, his first volume still reads as the warmest entry into the great story of Rama.
tob-4244:
T. W. Rolleston retold the myths of the Celtic peoples for general readers in Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race. Cuchulain's boyhood deeds and last stand, Finn and the Fianna, the Tuatha Dé Danann arriving in Ireland, and the great voyage tales fill the narrative. Rolleston aimed at story first, where Charles Squire, his contemporary, aimed at system.

Less scholarly than Squire and more narrative, the book gives the stories as stories, in readable English dress, with the Irish material especially full. Rolleston, an Irish writer involved in his country's cultural revival, wrote to make a heritage available. For many readers this remains the Celtic myths' friendliest single-volume telling.
turgot-oeuvres-daire-vol1-1844:
Eugène Daire edited the works of Turgot for a great series of French economists, and the first volume appeared in 1844. Turgot, who died in 1781, had been Louis the Sixteenth's finance minister and the Enlightenment's best hope in power. Daire's edition gathered writings that had been scattered or buried since the Revolution.

Volume 1 holds the young Turgot: his Sorbonne discourses on the progress of the human mind, his encyclopaedia articles, and early pieces on trade and money. Readers watch the statesman-philosopher in his formative years, forming the ideas he would later try to enact. His praise of free trade and his sketch of history as progress both appear here. The volume lets the mind that would reform France be studied before power came, and before power broke it.
turgot-oeuvres-daire-vol2-1844:
Daire's edition of Turgot's works closed with a second volume in 1844. The first volume had shown the young thinker; this one gives Turgot the minister. By the 1770s Turgot ran first a province, then the finances of France itself, the great test of Enlightenment ideas in office.

The volume prints his edicts, his official letters, and his plans to free the grain trade, end forced labor on roads, and cut court waste. Each reform met fierce resistance from the privileged orders it threatened. In 1776 the king dismissed him, and the attempt to save the monarchy by reform collapsed with his fall. Daire's edition preserves the record of that campaign in Turgot's own words. It reads as the Enlightenment in power, and its tragic defeat, documented by the man who led it.
un-ga-res-44:
India brought a complaint to the young United Nations in 1946: the treatment of people of Indian origin in the Union of South Africa. The General Assembly took up the charge in Resolution 44, adopted on 8 December 1946. It was one of the first times the Assembly judged how a member state treated people inside its own borders.

The Assembly states that the treatment has harmed friendly ties between India and South Africa, and that ties will worsen without a fair settlement. It holds that the treatment must match the deals struck between the two states and the pledges of the UN Charter. Both states must report back at the next session.
un-ga-res-a-69-44:
Missiles that can carry mass-kill warheads are the target of Resolution A/69/44, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The spread of such ballistic missiles, it says, feeds growing strains on safety at home and abroad. The text recalls Assembly votes on the point since 2004 and the UN's duty, under the Charter, to guard peace.

Praise goes to the Hague Code of Conduct against Ballistic Missile Proliferation, adopted at The Hague on 25 November 2002. The code asks states to show restraint and to share word of their missile plans in advance. Such open steps, the Assembly holds, build trust and help curb the spread of the missiles themselves.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 44 was adopted on 8 December 1946, at the fifty-second plenary meeting. It took up India's complaint about the treatment of Indians in the Union of South Africa. The Assembly stated that this treatment had harmed friendly ties between the two member states. It would harm them more without a fair settlement. The treatment should match the two governments' agreements and the Charter. Holding that, the Assembly asked both to report back at the next session on steps taken.

Resolution 69/44 of the General Assembly supports the Hague Code of Conduct against Ballistic Missile Proliferation, adopted at The Hague in 2002. The Assembly welcomes the fact that 137 states have subscribed to the voluntary code. The code builds transparency through pre-launch notifications and annual declarations on missile and space policies. It calls on states that have not subscribed to do so. This applies especially to those with ballistic missile or space launch capabilities. It urges subscribers to widen participation and improve how it is carried out.
un-sc-res-1244: Among the formal acts of the United Nations Security Council sits Resolution 1244, which the catalog dates to 1999. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later.
un-sc-res-1344:
UNMEE, the border mission for Ethiopia and Eritrea, was renewed in March 2001. On 15 March 2001 the Security Council extended it until 15 September 2001. Troop and observer levels stayed as set in 2000. The Council restated both states' sovereignty and borders. It also stressed their duties under humanitarian and refugee law. The December 2000 peace deal framed the whole text.

Both parties had to finish the steps left under their agreements. Rearranging forces to create the Temporary Security Zone mattered most. The Council stressed a hard link in the deal. The peacekeeping mission would end only when the border was fully drawn and marked. The parties also had to fund the boundary commission.
un-sc-res-144:
A quarrel between Cuba and the United States reached the Council in July 1960. Cuba's foreign minister addressed the members. On 19 July 1960 the Council decided to pause its own debate. It would wait for a report from the Organization of American States. Both countries belonged to that regional body. Its charter, like the United Nations Charter, favored peaceful settlement. The Council noted the deep concern the dispute had caused.

Regional states were invited to help find a peaceful solution. Meanwhile every other state had to avoid acts that raised tension. The step favored the regional route over a New York fight. Cuba objected, but the adjournment held. The dispute soon hardened into a lasting feature of the Cold War.
un-sc-res-1444: From the Council's official record comes the text numbered 1444, catalogued here at 2001. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1544: Resolution 1544 stands in the Council's numbered sequence as a formal act of the fifteen-member body. The version here is the official record as transcribed on English Wikisource. Readers get the complete decision text: the findings the members recorded first, then the operative paragraphs through which the Council exercises its power over peace and security questions.
un-sc-res-1644:
The Hariri murder inquiry was extended on 15 December 2005. The investigation commission's report, S/2005/775, laid out its findings on the 14 February 2005 Beirut bombing. It had killed former prime minister Rafiq Hariri and 22 others. Lebanon's prime minister wrote on 5 December asking for six more months. The Council praised the commission's professional work under hard conditions.

The Council welcomed the report. As the commission advised and Lebanon asked, it extended the commission's mandate for a further six months. Syria's duty to cooperate fully and without conditions was underlined once more. The commission would report on the inquiry's progress every three months, or sooner if events required. The Council noted Lebanon's wish that those finally charged be tried by a court of an international character. The commission could also give Lebanon technical help on its inquiries into the other attacks since October 2004.
un-sc-res-1744:
Resolution 1744 let the African Union send its own peace mission into Somalia, a country without a working central government since 1991. Somalia's weak interim government faced Islamist fighters and clan militias. The Council backed African troops as the force on the ground.

The text sets the mission's tasks: guard government sites and airports, protect aid convoys, and help train Somali security forces. It also calls on other states to fund and supply the effort. Readers get the founding terms of AMISOM, the African-led mission that became a central actor in Somalia's long war.
un-sc-res-1844:
On 20 November 2008, Resolution 1844 on Somalia was adopted. Violence and blocking of the peace process continued across the country. Piracy off the coast was rising fast. Piracy money could pay for weapons that broke the long-standing arms embargo.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council creates targeted sanctions for Somalia. People and groups named by the sanctions committee face travel bans and asset freezes. No one may supply them with weapons or military help. The targets are those who threaten the peace deal, attack the transitional bodies or the African Union mission, break the embargo, or block aid. Listed names get a public summary of the reasons, and a way to ask for removal.
un-sc-res-1944: Resolution 1944, adopted in 2010, is a Security Council act kept in this collection through a transcription of the record. The fifteen members' joint text is the whole content: what they found, what they decided, and what they set in motion. The entry preserves that joint text entire, in the order and wording of its adoption.
un-sc-res-244:
A sharp crisis shook Cyprus in the autumn of 1967, and the Secretary-General appealed directly to Greece, Turkey, and Cyprus. His appeals went out in November and December that year. He offered his good offices to all three governments, and each of them accepted. His report of 8 December said the peacekeeping force was still required. Resolution 244 was adopted unanimously on 22 December 1967.

The Council extended the force's stationing for three months, ending on 26 March 1968. The parties were invited to use the Secretary-General's good offices at once. Moderation was called for on all sides. Above all, the text asked for a fresh and determined effort toward a lasting settlement of the Cyprus problem. The crisis of that autumn had shown how fast the island could slide back toward war between Greece and Turkey.
un-sc-res-344: The formal record of the Security Council includes the text numbered 344, catalogued for 1973. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-44: Palestine's future went back to the General Assembly under Security Council Resolution 44, passed on 1 April 1948. The Council had the Palestine Commission's first two monthly reports and its special report on safety in the land. The five permanent members had met, as asked in March, and their talks had been reported. The Council now asks the Secretary-General to call a special session of the Assembly, under Article 20 of the Charter, to weigh the future rule of Palestine anew.
un-sc-res-444:
Lebanon's interim force faced obstruction in the south in early 1979. On 19 January 1979 the Security Council renewed UNIFIL for five months. The new term ran until 19 June 1979. The Secretary-General's report described grave problems on the ground. The Council deplored the lack of cooperation, above all from Israel. Israel, it said, was helping irregular armed groups in the south. Those groups blocked the force's deployment.

Lebanon's government earned praise for sending its army south. The Council urged it to do more, in step with UNIFIL. The aim was to restore Lebanese authority in the area. The Secretary-General and the force's soldiers also won warm thanks. The text mixes a routine renewal with open frustration.
un-sc-res-744:
Security Council Resolution 744, adopted on February 25, 1992, recommended San Marino for membership in the United Nations. The tiny republic, ringed by Italy, counts itself the oldest surviving republic in the world, with roots in the year 301. Size had long kept it outside the world body, but the end of the Cold War opened the door to Europe's small states.

The Assembly admitted San Marino on March 2, 1992. The council's text is brief and formal, like all admission votes of that season. For San Marino, the seat carried a point of pride: a state older than most kingdoms at last took the same formal place as the largest powers in the General Assembly hall.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1244, adopted in 1999 under Chapter VII, sets the terms for ending the Kosovo crisis. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had agreed to the peace principles put forward in Belgrade on 2 June 1999. The Council demands an immediate, checkable end to violence and repression in Kosovo, and a rapid, phased withdrawal of all Yugoslav and Serb military, police and paramilitary forces.

The resolution sets up an international security presence in Kosovo, able to use all necessary means. It is to deter renewed fighting, disarm the Kosovo Liberation Army, and protect returning refugees. It establishes a United Nations interim administration. It is to run basic government, build democratic institutions for the interim, and hold elections, pending a final settlement. Both presences start for an initial twelve months. The Council reaffirms Yugoslavia's sovereignty and territorial integrity. It promises Kosovo substantial autonomy and real self-administration.

A shaky peace in the Horn of Africa needed more time in 2001. Ethiopia and Eritrea had signed their peace in Algiers the past June and December. A UN force, UNMEE, kept the two foes apart. Its term was set to lapse. Resolution 1344 passed with no dissent on 15 March 2001.

The force won six more months, to 15 September 2001. Both states had tasks to finish. Troops had to shift so a buffer zone could form. UN staff needed free roads and a direct air link between the two capitals. Mine maps had to change hands. The text ties the force's end to a drawn and marked border. Both sides had to fund the team doing that work.

Cuba and the United States faced off at the Council in July 1960. Havana's foreign chief spoke of threats from the north. The split had grown since Castro's rise. A rule from the Charter's book framed the clash. So did the pact of the Americas group, the OAS. Resolution 144 passed on 19 July 1960 by nine votes to none. Poland and the Soviet team held back.

The Council chose to wait. Its own probe was put on hold. Word from the OAS would come first. That body had the case in hand. Its states were asked to help find a calm fix. All other states had to shun acts that would heat the clash. The move showed a young UN at ease with turf: some fights were left, for a time, to the region's own house.

Another year is granted to the International Security Assistance Force in Afghanistan on 27 November 2002. The force, authorized in December 2001, helped the Afghan authorities keep security in Kabul. Command had passed from the United Kingdom to Turkey in June 2002, with a joint German-Dutch lead planned next.

The authorization is lengthened for one year beyond 20 December 2002. States in the force may use all necessary measures to carry out its mandate. More contributions of troops, equipment, and money are called for, including to the force's trust fund. Its leadership is to report every three months through the Secretary-General on how the work is going.

Israel's military operation in Rafah, in the Gaza Strip, draws a response on 19 May 2004. Palestinian civilians had been killed in the area, and Israeli forces had demolished many homes in the Rafah refugee camp. Grave concern is voiced at the worsening situation in the territory occupied since 1967.

Israel is called on to respect its duties under international humanitarian law, and in particular not to demolish homes in breach of that law. An end to violence is demanded, and both sides are called on to carry out their duties under the Road Map peace plan at once. The vote was 14 in favour and none against, with the United States abstaining.

Resolution 1644, adopted on 15 December 2005, follows the inquiry into the Beirut bombing that killed former Lebanese prime minister Rafiq Hariri and 22 others on 14 February 2005. An International Independent Investigation Commission was helping Lebanon find who did it. Lebanon asked for six more months of that help, and the commission backed the request.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the commission's mandate until 15 June 2006 and demands that Syria cooperate fully and without delay. It notes with concern that Syria had not yet given full help. It also asks the Secretary-General to study what kind of international tribunal could try those charged, and lets the commission help Lebanon probe other attacks there since October 2004.

An African Union mission in Somalia, AMISOM, is authorized on 20 February 2007. Somalia's transitional federal institutions needed support to build national governance and hold an inclusive political process. The African Union, the Arab League, and the regional authority had all backed reconciliation, and the Union had offered to deploy.

African Union member states are authorized to establish the mission for six months. Its tasks include supporting dialogue and reconciliation, protecting the transitional institutions, and helping create conditions for aid delivery. The 1992 arms embargo is lifted for supplies and training meant solely for the mission and for building Somalia's security sector. Union members are urged to contribute troops and resources.

Somalia gains targeted sanctions in Resolution 1844, adopted on 20 November 2008. The 1992 arms embargo stood alone. The Council had warned it would act against those blocking a peaceful political process, threatening the Transitional Federal Institutions or AMISOM by force, or breaking the embargo. Piracy off the coast, it noted, might be financing embargo violations.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council imposes three measures on individuals and entities the Sanctions Committee designates: a travel ban, an asset freeze, and a targeted arms embargo. The embargo covers weapons and military assistance. Designation covers those threatening peace or the Djibouti Agreement, violating the arms embargo, or obstructing humanitarian aid. Basic-expense and other exemptions apply. The Committee must publish narrative summaries of reasons for each listing. It must notify states so listed persons are informed and handle delisting requests, including petitions through the Focal Point set up by Resolution 1730 (2006).

Haiti was preparing to vote nine months after the earthquake that struck in January 2010. Resolution 1944, adopted on 14 October 2010, concerns MINUSTAH, the United Nations mission in the country. Presidential and legislative elections were set for 28 November. Camps of displaced people still faced gang violence and health risks.

The Council extended MINUSTAH's mandate until 15 October 2011. Its strength stayed at up to 8,940 troops and 4,391 police. The mission had to support the elections and help rebuild the Haitian National Police. It also had to help the courts and speed up the resettlement of displaced families. Once a new government took power, a fresh review of security in Haiti would follow.

Weeks after a flare-up that nearly brought Greece and Turkey to war, the Council acted on Cyprus again. On 22 December 1967, it adopted Resolution 244 without dissent. The Secretary-General had appealed to all three governments that autumn. He had also offered his good offices, and each capital had replied.

His report said the island still needed the peace force. Cyprus agreed to the force staying on. The text restates the founding decision, Resolution 186. It then extends the posting for three months. The move kept troops in place while talks cooled tempers in Athens, Ankara, and Nicosia. It marks the Council mopping up after the November crisis.

A peace conference on the Middle East was about to open in Geneva in December 1973. It would meet under United Nations auspices. Resolution 338 had ordered talks on carrying out Resolution 242, the land-for-peace plan of 1967. Resolution 344 was adopted on 15 December 1973, just before the conference began.

The Council expressed the hope that the Geneva conference would move quickly. Its goal was a just and durable peace in the Middle East. The Council said it trusted the Secretary-General to play a full and effective part at the conference. He would chair its proceedings if the parties wished. He was asked to keep the Council informed of the talks. He also had to supply all the help and facilities the conference needed.

The Palestine partition plan had stalled amid growing violence by the spring of 1948. Under Resolution 42, the Council's permanent members had consulted and reported back. The Palestine Commission's progress reports were also before the Council. Resolution 44 was adopted on 1 April 1948. It passed the question upward. The Council asked the Secretary-General to call a special session of the General Assembly, under Article 20 of the Charter. The special session would consider the future government of Palestine further. That single step is the whole content of the resolution.

Some notes place this text in Cyprus. Its true home is south Lebanon. The force there, UNIFIL, was ten months old and blocked at every turn. Its second term had run out with tasks undone. The chief's report of 12 January 1979 laid out the mess. Resolution 444 passed on 19 January 1979 by twelve votes to none.

UNIFIL won five more months, to 19 June 1979. The Council blamed poor help from the sides, Israel most of all. Israel was charged with aiding armed bands in the south. Praise went to the force's troops and chiefs. Lebanon was cheered for sending its army south. It had to draw up a staged plan to retake full rule there. The Council vowed to meet in three months for a fresh look.

The world's oldest republic waited longest for its UN seat. On 25 February 1992, the Council adopted Resolution 744 without a vote. San Marino, a tiny enclave inside Italy, had applied to join the United Nations. Most states of its size had joined decades before.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit San Marino. The Assembly acted the next month. The microstate's late arrival fit a wider shift of the era. Even the smallest sovereign states were taking seats and votes. The UN edged closer to truly full membership. San Marino brought with it a claim to seventeen centuries of self-rule.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5344:
Section 5344 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers payments and repayments for some House staff costs. It sits in Chapter 53 of that title, on House Members, among the rules on costs and allowances. Part (a) states how such payments are to be made. Payments to staff under section 5343 are to be made as the rules of the Committee on House Oversight lay down for staff travel and other costs.

Repayments are to be paid on special voucher forms laid down by that committee. Part (b) of the section deals with added funds, as the text goes on to state. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5544:
Section 5544 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers the deposit of payments made to House Information Resources. It sits in Chapter 55 of that title, on House officers, in the part on the Chief Administrative Officer. The rule takes effect for fiscal year 2003 and each year after. It covers sums that office takes in from any office of the House as repayment for services given.

Such sums are to be deposited in the Treasury. They are to be credited to the account of the Office of the Chief Administrative Officer of the House, as the text goes on to state. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
ynglinga-saga-laing-1844:
Samuel Laing translated this saga in London in 1844, from the Heimskringla. It tells the story of the Yngling family from Odin to Halfdan the Black. The opening maps the world as its makers saw it. Seas cut the earth's circle into three parts, Asia, Europe, and Africa. North of the Black Sea lies Sweden the Great, home to giants, dwarfs, and dragons in the telling.

Odin rules Asgaard as priest, judge, and war leader. His people trust his blessing before battle. Tales follow of his brothers, hostage exchanges, and a severed head that still speaks. Readers get myth shading into early royal history.
zoist-vol-02-1844:
Volume two of The Zoist covers April 1844 to January 1845. Elliotson's journal presses on with its twin subjects, cerebral physiology and mesmerism. Case reports arrive from doctors across Britain who tried the mesmeric sleep. Operations without pain hold pride of place in the reports.

Somnambulists and their strange sight supply the journal's wonders. Critics in the medical press trade blows with Elliotson's circle in print. The journal binds those fights beside the clinical record. Across thirteen volumes the set forms the English movement's full archive. Volume two shows the fight at full heat. Surgeons, patients, and skeptics all speak here. The record stays primary and direct.
